status: 65 passages: the whole first chapter of the Stoic Constitution, the six sections behind Articles 1 to 6. Every passage was translated from the Greek alone by one model, checked against the Greek by a second, and each point was settled in writing by a third reading. The owner read the first six on 23 November 2026 and said “looks good”; the other 59 have not been read by the owner. None has been checked by a person who reads Greek.

method: A first translator was given the Greek of the passages and nothing else: no earlier translation, no article. It was asked for plain English of today that keeps the speaker, the person addressed, every “all” and “not”, and each image, and to translate one reading and note the other wherever the Greek is open.

A second reader was given only the Greek and that English, without the first translator’s notes, and asked to list every place where the English says more, less or other than the Greek. Across the 65 passages it raised 288 points and called no passage wrong.

Each point was then settled in writing: accepted, partly accepted or declined, with the reason. For the first six passages the editor of this project settled them; for the other 59 a third reader did, given the Greek, the draft and the points, and it also fixed faults neither earlier reader had caught (marked “Found while settling”). The result is the English shown here. Under each passage you can open both lists: what the Greek leaves open, and what the second reader questioned.

So that a Greek word does not become a different English word from one passage to the next, the settled renderings of the first six passages were given to the third reader as preferences (for example “the universe” for κόσμος, “the nature of the whole”, “the ruling part”); where a passage’s own argument needed another word, a note says so.

The 1634 translation numbers and cuts its sections differently from modern editions. Each of its passages was matched to the Greek by reading the openings and endings side by side. Where it joins two or more modern chapters, they are shown as one passage with the chapter breaks kept (6.9–10). Where it cuts inside a chapter, the passage carries a letter (11.8a is the first part, 3.11b a later part) and says which Greek it leaves out.
limits: All three readers are language models. A model’s Greek can be confidently wrong; the Greek is shown beside the English so that anyone who reads Greek can object.

The Greek is a digitised copy of Leopold’s edition and has slips of its own (an accent, a breathing, a misprinted letter). Where a slip was read through, a note says so. Where the text itself does not construe (8.35, 9.28a, 7.31b), the English marks the place and does not smooth it over.

Notes that rely on memory of the manuscripts or of an editor’s conjecture say “from memory, unchecked”. None was checked against a critical edition. In 5.8 the source prints ἐκεῖ σε (“you there”) where the text may be the one word ἐκεῖσε (“to that place”); the printed edition was not consulted.
The passage numbers are those of modern editions; the 1634 number is given beside each. The sections were grouped on the 1634 English, not on this translation.
A translated passage is never edited in place. A correction is a new revision with a new id; the old one is kept in the record.
footer: Greek: M. Antoninus Imperator ad se ipsum, ed. J. H. Leopold (1908), from the Perseus Digital Library, CC BY-SA. 1634 English: Meric Casaubon (Project Gutenberg 2680). The new English is this project’s own translation.

vectors.note: The sections were grouped on the 1634 English, and each centre is the mean of its own passages in that English, so a passage in 1634 English has a head start toward its own centre. Read the new numbers as: does the passage still belong here when said in today’s words?
