passages.greek: Παρὰ Διογνήτου τὸ ἀκενόσπουδον· καὶ τὸ ἀπιστητικὸν τοῖς ὑπὸ τῶν τερατευομένων καὶ γοήτων περὶ ἐπῳδῶν καὶ περὶ δαιμόνων ἀποπομπῆς καὶ τῶν τοιούτων λεγομένοις· καὶ τὸ μὴ ὀρτυγοτροφεῖν μηδὲ περὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐπτοῆσθαι· καὶ τὸ ἀνέχεσθαι παρρησίας· καὶ τὸ οἰκειωθῆναι φιλοσοφίᾳ καὶ τὸ ἀκοῦσαι πρῶτον μὲν Βακχείου, εἶτα Τανδάσιδος καὶ Μαρκιανοῦ· καὶ τὸ γράψαι διαλόγους ἐν παιδί· καὶ τὸ σκίμποδος καὶ δορᾶς ἐπιθυμῆσαι καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα τῆς Ἑλληνικῆς ἀγωγῆς ἐχόμενα.
passages.english: From Diognetus: not being busy over empty things; and disbelieving what is said by those who deal in marvels and by sorcerers about spells and about the driving out of spirits and things of that kind; and not keeping quails, nor getting excited over such things; and putting up with plain speaking; and becoming at home in philosophy, and hearing the lectures first of Baccheius, then of Tandasis and Marcianus; and writing dialogues as a boy; and wanting a pallet bed and an animal skin, and everything of that kind that belongs to the Greek training.

notes.note: Literally “the not-earnest-about-empty-things”.
notes.other_reading: no zeal for trifles

notes.note: The first are people who talk marvels and make wild claims, the second are sorcerers or plain cheats.
notes.other_reading: miracle-workers and charlatans

notes.note: δαίμονες are spirits, divine or lesser beings. “Demons” would bring in a later sense.
notes.other_reading: the casting out of demons

notes.note: Quails were kept for fighting and for a game of striking them, a fashionable pastime. The Greek says only “keep quails”.
notes.other_reading: not breeding fighting quails

notes.note: To be in a flutter over a thing, carried away by it.
notes.other_reading: nor being mad about such things

notes.note: Frank speech: being spoken to freely by others.
notes.other_reading: freedom of speech

notes.note: Literally “being made one of the household of philosophy”.
notes.other_reading: becoming familiar with philosophy

notes.note: To “hear” a teacher is to attend his lectures, to be his pupil.
notes.other_reading: and hearing first Baccheius

notes.note: A name not otherwise known and probably doubted (from memory, unchecked). It is given as it stands.
Literally “in a boy”: while still a boy.
notes.other_reading: in my boyhood

notes.note: A low pallet and an animal skin to lie under or on: the hard bedding of a philosopher’s life. The Greek has no articles and does not say how the skin was used.
notes.other_reading: a camp bed and a hide

notes.note: ἀγωγή is a course of training or a way of life: here the discipline of Greek philosophers.
notes.other_reading: the Greek way of life

check.note: “Wonder-mongers” is an archaic compound. A reader of today would say miracle-workers or people who peddle marvels.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “those who deal in marvels”. “Miracle-workers” is not used because the Greek word is about talking marvels, not working them.

check.note: With a teacher’s name the verb is to attend his lectures, to be his pupil. Bare “hearing Baccheius” is an archaism.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “hearing the lectures first of Baccheius, then of Tandasis and Marcianus”.

check.note: The Greek has no articles, and “the hide” is unclear: it is an animal skin used as a cover. “Camp bed” is a little modern for a low pallet.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “wanting a pallet bed and an animal skin”. “For a cover” is not added, since the Greek does not say how the skin was used.

passages.casaubon: Of Diognetus, not to busy myself about vain things, and not easily to believe those things, which are commonly spoken, by such as take upon them to work wonders, and by sorcerers, or prestidigitators, and impostors; concerning the power of charms, and their driving out of demons, or evil spirits; and the like. Not to keep quails for the game; nor to be mad after such things. Not to be offended with other men's liberty of speech, and to apply myself unto philosophy. Him also I must thank, that ever I heard first Bacchius, then Tandasis and Marcianus, and that I did write dialogues in my youth; and that I took liking to the philosophers' little couch and skins, and such other things, which by the Grecian discipline are proper to those who profess philosophy.

passages.greek:
ʽἘγὼ δὲ τούτῳ δίκαιον ἂν λόγον ἀντείποιμι, ὅτι οὐ καλῶς λέγεις, ὦ ἄνθρωπε, εἰ οἴει δεῖν κίνδυνον ὑπολογίζεσθαι τοῦ ζῆν ἢ τεθνάναι ἄνδρα, ὅτου τι καὶ σμικρὸν ὄφελος, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐκεῖνο μόνον σκοπεῖν, ὅταν πράττῃ, πότερον δίκαια ἢ ἄδικα πράττει καὶ ἀνδρὸς ἀγαθοῦ ἔργα ἢ κακοῦ.ʼ

Ὁὕτω γὰρ ἔχει, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, τῇ ἀληθείᾳ· οὗ ἄν τις αὑτὸν τάξῃ ἡγησάμενος βέλτιστον εἶναι ἢ ὑπʼ ἄρχοντος ταχθῇ, ἐνταῦθα δεῖ, ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, μένοντα κινδυνεύειν, μηδὲν ὑπολογιζόμενον μήτε θάνατον μήτε ἄλλο μηδὲν πρὸ τοῦ αἰσχροῦ.ʼ

ʽἈλλʼ, ὦ μακάριε, ὅρα μὴ ἄλλο τι τὸ γενναῖον καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ᾖ τοῦ σῴζειν τε καὶ σῴζεσθαι· μὴ γὰρ τοῦτο μέν, τὸ ζῆν ὁποσονδὴ χρόνον, τόν γε ὡς ἀληθῶς ἄνδρα ἐατέον ἐστὶ καὶ οὐ φιλοψυχητέον, ἀλλ’ ἐπιτρέψαντα περὶ τούτων τῷ θεῷ καὶ πιστεύσαντα ταῖς γυναιξίν, ὅτι τὴν εἱμαρμένην οὐδ’ ἂν εἶς ἐκφύγοι, τὸ ἐπὶ τούτῳ σκεπτέον τίνα ἂν τρόπον τοῦτον ὃν μέλλει χρόνον βιῶναι ὡς ἄριστα βιῴη.ʼ

Περισκοπεῖν ἄστρων δρόμους ὥσπερ συμπεριθέοντα καὶ τὰς τῶν στοιχείων εἰς ἄλληλα μεταβολὰς συνεχῶς ἐννοεῖν· ἀποκαθαίρουσι γὰρ αἱ τούτων φαντασίαι τὸν ῥύπον τοῦ χαμαὶ βίου.

Καλὸν τὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος. καὶ δὴ περὶ ἀνθρώπων τοὺς λόγους ποιούμενον ἐπισκοπεῖν δεῖ καὶ τὰ ἐπίγεια ὥσπερ ποθὲν ἄνωθεν κάτω· ἀγέλας, στρατεύματα, γεώργια, γάμους, διαλύσεις, γενέσεις, θανάτους, δικαστηρίων θόρυβον, ἐρήμους χώρας, βαρβάρων ἔθνη ποικίλα, ἑορτάς, θρήνους, ἀγοράς, τὸ παμμιγὲς καὶ τὸ ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων συγκοσμούμενον.
passages.english:
“But I would have a just answer to give this man: ‘What you say is not right, fellow, if you think that a man who is of even a little use must take into account the risk of living or dying, rather than look at this alone whenever he acts: whether he is doing what is just or unjust, and the deeds of a good man or of a bad one.’”

“For this is how it truly is, men of Athens. Wherever a person has taken up a post, judging it to be best, or has been posted by a commander, there, as it seems to me, they must stay and run the risk, taking nothing into account, neither death nor anything else, ahead of disgrace.”

“But, my dear man, see whether what is noble and what is good may not be something other than saving and being saved. For perhaps this, living for whatever length of time, is what one who is truly a man must let go, and he must not cling to life, but, leaving these matters to god and trusting the women who say that not even one person could escape what is fated, must consider what comes next: in what way he might live the time he is going to live as well as possible.”

Look round at the courses of the stars as if running round with them, and think continually of the changes of the elements into one another. For the impressions of these things wash away the dirt of life on the ground.

A fine saying of Plato’s. And indeed whoever is talking about human beings must also look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above: herds, armies, farms, marriages, divorces, births, deaths, the din of law courts, empty lands, the varied peoples of the barbarians, festivals, laments, markets, the mixture of every kind and the order put together out of opposites.

notes.greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ τούτῳ δίκαιον ἂν λόγον ἀντείποιμι
notes.note: The first three paragraphs are quotations copied without the author’s name: Socrates speaking in Plato (Apology 28b and 28d, Gorgias 512d to e: from memory, unchecked). Each is set in its own quotation marks.
notes.other_reading: But I would speak a just word against this man

notes.note: Literally “O human being”, a curt way of addressing someone, with no warmth in it. “Fellow” keeps it curt and keeps it apart from the “man” of the next clause, which is a different Greek word (ἄνδρα).
notes.other_reading: What you say is not right, man

notes.note: Literally “of whom there is some use, even a small one”. Kept close.
notes.other_reading: a man who is worth anything at all

notes.greek: κίνδυνον ὑπολογίζεσθαι τοῦ ζῆν ἢ τεθνάναι
notes.note: Two words tie the first quotation to the second. ὑπολογίζεσθαι comes back as ὑπολογιζόμενον, so both read “take into account”, and κίνδυνον comes back in κινδυνεύειν, so both read “risk”. “The risk of living or dying” is the chance of coming out alive or dead.
notes.other_reading: must weigh up his chances of life or death

notes.note: The Greek as given has a doubled breathing on the first word and no opening quotation mark for this second quotation, though it has a closing one; the stray breathing is probably what is left of the opening mark. The word is read as Οὕτω and the paragraph is marked as a quotation of its own.
notes.other_reading: For so it is, men of Athens, in truth

notes.note: The word covers anyone who rules or commands, an officer or a magistrate. The picture is of a soldier’s post, so “commander”.
notes.other_reading: or has been posted by someone in authority

notes.note: Literally “before the shameful”: nothing is to be counted as weighing more than disgrace. The English keeps the short “ahead of”.
notes.other_reading: taking nothing into account, neither death nor anything else, in comparison with what is shameful

notes.note: Literally “blessed one”, a polite and slightly teasing form of address in conversation.
notes.other_reading: But, my blessed friend

notes.greek: μὴ γὰρ τοῦτο μέν, τὸ ζῆν ὁποσονδὴ χρόνον, τόν γε ὡς ἀληθῶς ἄνδρα ἐατέον ἐστὶ
notes.note: μή with the indicative makes a guarded statement, “perhaps”, “it may be that”; it can also be heard as a question. The English takes the guarded statement. The forms in -τέον say what has to be done and are given as “must”, the word used for δεῖ in the other quotations.
notes.other_reading: For must not one who is truly a man let this go, living for however long a time?

notes.note: The Greek has the article, “the god”. The English follows the rendering settled for this translation, “god”, lower case.
notes.other_reading: leaving these matters to the god

notes.note: Literally “having trusted the women, that …”: a saying that women were known to repeat. The English keeps the women and adds only “who say”.
notes.other_reading: believing the old wives’ saying

notes.note: Literally “the thing upon this”: the question that comes next once that one is set aside.
notes.other_reading: consider what follows from this

notes.note: This paragraph is in infinitives used as instructions, with no person named; the participle is masculine singular, “as if one were running round with them”. The English uses commands without “you”.
notes.other_reading: as though you were running round with them

notes.note: φαντασία is “impression” throughout this translation: here the pictures of these things as they form in the mind.
notes.other_reading: For picturing these things washes away

notes.note: Literally “of the life on the ground”, set against the stars above. Kept as an image.
notes.other_reading: the dirt of earthbound life

notes.note: Literally “Fine, that of Plato’s”: “saying” is supplied for the bare article. The words may look back to the three quotations above or forward, making what follows a saying of Plato; the Greek as given puts a full stop after them, and the English is left equally open. From memory, unchecked: editors have doubted how these words join what follows.
notes.other_reading: Plato has a fine saying: whoever is talking about human beings must also look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above

notes.note: κάτω, “downward”, stands with no verb of its own; the English joins it to the one verb there is, as “look down at”. From memory, unchecked: some editors change κάτω to κατὰ, which would give “herd by herd”.
notes.other_reading: as if from somewhere above: by herds, armies, farms

notes.note: Herds of animals; the word is also used of crowds of people. Kept as “herds”.
notes.other_reading: crowds

notes.note: A “breaking up” or “loosing”. It stands next to “marriages” as “deaths” stands next to “births”, so it is read as divorces; the word is also used of settling quarrels and making peace.
notes.other_reading: peace treaties

notes.greek: τὸ παμμιγὲς καὶ τὸ ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων συγκοσμούμενον
notes.note: παμμιγές is “mixed of every kind”. The last word has κόσμος, “order”, inside it: “that which is being ordered together out of opposites”. “Order” is used here, as this translation allows where the sense of order is the point.
notes.other_reading: the medley of all things and the harmony arranged out of opposites

check.note: The Greek is about the speech, “you do not speak well”. “You are wrong” is blunter and drops the verb of saying.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “What you say is not right”, since the Greek verb is “say” and the fault it finds is in what is said.

check.note: The address is a plain, rather curt “man”. “Friend” adds a warmth that is not there.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “friend” is gone and the English reads “fellow”, which is curt and has no warmth. “Man” is not used because the next clause has “a man” for a different Greek word (ἄνδρα), and the two should not sound like one.

check.greek: καὶ ἀνδρὸς ἀγαθοῦ ἔργα ἢ κακοῦ
check.note: καὶ is dropped, so the second pair reads as a gloss on the first, where the Greek adds a second question. ἔργα is also plural, “deeds”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whether he is doing what is just or unjust, and the deeds of a good man or of a bad one”, with the “and” of the Greek and the plural “deeds”.

check.note: The Greek as given has a doubled breathing and no opening quotation mark for this second quotation, though it has a closing one. The English is right to treat it as a separate quotation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged, as suggested, and keeps this paragraph as a quotation of its own. A note now records the doubled breathing and the missing opening mark.

check.note: The Greek has a bare participle, “judging it to be best”. “Because” is added to resolve it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “has taken up a post, judging it to be best”, a participle as in the Greek, with no “because”.

check.note: κίνδυνον in the first quotation is “risk” and κινδυνεύειν here is “face the danger”, so a link between the two quotations is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “stay and run the risk”, so that “risk” answers “the risk of living or dying” in the first quotation, as κινδυνεύειν answers κίνδυνον.

check.note: γὰρ is dropped. The sentence gives the ground for the doubt just raised.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now begins “For perhaps this”, which gives γὰρ its word.

check.greek: ἐπιτρέψαντα περὶ τούτων τῷ θεῷ καὶ πιστεύσαντα ταῖς γυναιξίν
check.note: The two participles are subordinate to “must consider”, but the English makes three parallel duties. “Who say” is supplied, and τῷ θεῷ is “the god”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the two participles are now subordinate, “but, leaving these matters to god and trusting the women who say that not even one person could escape what is fated, must consider what comes next”, and “could” replaces “can” for the Greek “would escape”. “God” without “the” stays, as settled for this translation, and “who say” stays as the smallest link English needs; a note covers each.

check.note: ὥσπερ is “as if”. “As one running round” is stiff, and a reader may not see that it means imagining oneself running alongside.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “as if running round with them”, which gives ὥσπερ as “as if”. “You” is not added, because the Greek sentence names no person.

check.note: The Greek has only “that of Plato’s is fine”, and “saying” is supplied. It can point back to the quotations or forward to the view from above, and the third reader should decide which.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “A fine saying of Plato’s.” stays, with its full stop, because the Greek gives no sign whether it looks back or forward and the English should be as open as the Greek. The note now says that “saying” is supplied and sets out both ways of taking it.

check.note: δεῖ is “must” in the second quotation and “should” here and in the first quotation. δεῖ is the stronger word.
check.decided: Accepted: δεῖ is now “must” in all three places, “must take into account”, “must stay” and “must also look”. The forms in -τέον in the third quotation, which state the same necessity, read “must” as well.

check.note: After “marriages” this may be “divorces”; it can also mean settlements or peace-makings. “Separations” is vague and a reader cannot tell which is meant.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “divorces”. The list sets the word beside “marriages” as it sets “deaths” beside “births”, and the wider senses are kept in the note.

check.greek: τὸ παμμιγὲς καὶ τὸ ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων συγκοσμούμενον
check.note: παμμιγές is “mixed of every kind”, not “the whole of the mixture”, and “made up together” is not natural English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the mixture of every kind and the order put together out of opposites”. “Of every kind” gives παμμιγές, and “put together” is plain English that keeps the “together” of the Greek verb, which “composed” would lose.

check.note: Found while settling: “consider” stood both for ὅρα here and for σκεπτέον at the end of the same quotation, two different Greek words.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “see whether” for ὅρα, and “consider” is kept for σκεπτέον alone.

check.note: Found while settling: “looking down” supplied a second “looking” for κάτω, which has no verb of its own.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above”, so that κάτω goes with the one verb the Greek has and no verb is supplied.

passages.casaubon: Out of Plato. 'My answer, full of justice and equity, should be this: Thy speech is not right, O man! if thou supposest that he that is of any worth at all, should apprehend either life or death, as a matter of great hazard and danger; and should not make this rather his only care, to examine his own actions, whether just or unjust: whether actions of a good, or of a wicked man, &c. For thus in very truth stands the case, O ye men of Athens. What place or station soever a man either hath chosen to himself, judging it best for himself; or is by lawful authority put and settled in, therein do I think (all appearance of danger notwithstanding) that he should continue, as one who feareth neither death, nor anything else, so much as he feareth to commit anything that is vicious and shameful, &c. But, O noble sir, consider I pray, whether true generosity and true happiness, do not consist in somewhat else rather, than in the preservation either of our, or other men's lives. For it is not the part of a man that is a man indeed, to desire to live long or to make much of his life whilst he liveth: but rather (he that is such) will in these things wholly refer himself unto the Gods, and believing that which every woman can tell him, that no man can escape death; the only thing that he takes thought and care for is this, that what time he liveth, he may live as well and as virtuously as he can possibly, &c. To look about, and with the eyes to follow the course of the stars and planets as though thou wouldst run with them; and to mind perpetually the several changes of the elements one into another. For such fancies and imaginations, help much to purge away the dross and filth of this our earthly life,' &c. That also is a fine passage of Plato's, where he speaketh of worldly things in these words: 'Thou must also as from some higher place look down, as it were, upon the things of this world, as flocks, armies, husbandmen's labours, marriages, divorces, generations, deaths: the tumults of courts and places of judicatures; desert places; the several nations of barbarians, public festivals, mournings, fairs, markets.' How all things upon earth are pell-mell; and how miraculously things contrary one to another, concur to the beauty and perfection of this universe.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek:
Πόθεν ἴσμεν, εἰ μὴ Τηλαύγης Σωκράτους τὴν διάθεσιν κρείσσων ἦν; οὐ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ, εἰ Σωκράτης ἐνδοξότερον ἀπέθανε καὶ ἐντρεχέστερον τοῖς σοφισταῖς διελέγετο καὶ καρτερικώτερον ἐν τῷ πάγῳ διενυκτέρευε καὶ τὸν Σαλαμίνιον κελευσθεὶς ἄγειν γεννικώτερον ἔδοξεν ἀντιβῆναι καὶ ʽἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἐβρενθύετοʼ, περὶ οὗ καὶ μάλιστ’ ἄν τις ἐπιστήσειεν, εἴπερ ἀληθὲς ἦν· ἀλλ’ ἐκεῖνο δεῖ σκοπεῖν, ποίαν τινὰ τὴν ψυχὴν εἶχε Σωκράτης καὶ εἰ ἐδύνατο ἀρκεῖσθαι τῷ δίκαιος εἶναι τὰ πρὸς ἀνθρώπους καὶ ὅσιος τὰ πρὸς θεούς, μήτε εἰκῇ πρὸς τὴν κακίαν ἀγανακτῶν μηδὲ μὴν δουλεύων τινὸς ἀγνοίᾳ, μήτε τῶν ἀπονεμομένων ἐκ τοῦ ὅλου ὡς ξένον τι δεχόμενος ἢ ὡς ἀφόρητον ὑπομένων, μήτε τοῖς τοῦ σαρκιδίου πάθεσιν ἐμπαρέχων συμπαθῆ τὸν νοῦν·

Ἡ φύσις οὐχ οὕτως συνεκέρασε τῷ συγκρίματι, ὡς μὴ ἐφεῖσθαι περιορίζειν ἑαυτὸν καὶ τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ὑφ’ ἑαυτῷ ποιεῖσθαι·
passages.english:
How do we know that Telauges was not better than Socrates in his disposition? For it is not enough that Socrates died a more glorious death, and argued more nimbly with the sophists, and showed more endurance in spending the night out in the frost, and, when ordered to bring in the man from Salamis, was thought to have stood against it more nobly, and “swaggered in the streets”, a point one might well take note of most of all, if indeed it was true. But what has to be looked at is this: what kind of soul Socrates had, and whether he could find it enough to be just in his dealings with human beings and devout in his dealings with the gods, neither getting idly angry at vice nor yet being a slave to anyone’s ignorance, neither receiving anything allotted from the whole as something foreign or enduring it as something unbearable, nor handing his mind over to feel with the feelings of the poor flesh.

Nature did not blend the mind with the compound in such a way that it is not allowed to draw a boundary round itself and to bring what is its own under its own control.

notes.note: From memory, unchecked: Telauges was said to be a son of Pythagoras, and a lost dialogue by Aeschines, a follower of Socrates, was named after him. He stands here for a man of whom little is known.
Literally “From where do we know whether … not”. English says this more easily with “that … not”.
notes.other_reading: How do we know whether Telauges was not better than Socrates

notes.note: The settled inner state of a person, as against what they did or how they looked. “Disposition” is the nearest plain word.
notes.other_reading: in character

notes.note: ἔνδοξος is “held in honour”, “of high repute”: the word has both glory and fame in it. The English takes “glorious”.
notes.other_reading: died a more famous death

notes.note: An allusion to Socrates standing through a frosty night on campaign (Plato, Symposium 220: from memory, unchecked). The tense can also mean a habit.
notes.other_reading: used to spend his nights out in the frost with more endurance

notes.greek: τὸν Σαλαμίνιον κελευσθεὶς ἄγειν γεννικώτερον ἔδοξεν ἀντιβῆναι
notes.note: “The man from Salamis” is Leon, whom Socrates was ordered to arrest and did not (Plato, Apology 32c: from memory, unchecked). With Socrates as its subject ἔδοξεν is “seemed”, “was thought to”, or, less often, “resolved to”; γεννικώτερον is taken as the adverb “more nobly”, like the three adverbs before it. The English takes “was thought”, which keeps the list to what others could see of him.
notes.other_reading: and, when ordered to bring in the man from Salamis, more nobly resolved to refuse

notes.note: A quotation, marked as such in the Greek as given: the comic poet Aristophanes mocking Socrates in the Clouds (from memory, unchecked). The verb means to carry oneself proudly, to strut.
notes.other_reading: held his head high in the streets

notes.greek: περὶ οὗ καὶ μάλιστ’ ἄν τις ἐπιστήσειεν, εἴπερ ἀληθὲς ἦν
notes.note: ἐπιστήσειεν is “stop and give attention”, the verb given as “taken note” in 1.11; it can shade into “raise a doubt”. εἴπερ is “if indeed”, so the last clause is taken as a condition and not as the thing doubted.
notes.other_reading: about which one might well raise a doubt most of all, whether it was true

notes.note: The same verb as οὐ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ (“it is not enough”) above, now in the form “be content with”. “Enough” is kept in both so the echo can be heard.
notes.other_reading: whether he was able to be content with being just

notes.note: “At random”, “without thought”, and also “to no purpose”. “Idly” leaves room for both: anger at vice that has no aim and achieves nothing.
notes.other_reading: neither getting angry at vice without thought

notes.note: Literally “being a slave to someone’s ignorance”: giving way to what another person, not knowing better, wants or thinks. Kept as the image.
notes.other_reading: nor yet bowing to any person’s ignorance

notes.note: “The things dealt out from the whole”: each person’s share of what happens. τὸ ὅλον is “the whole” throughout this translation.
notes.other_reading: any of the things assigned to him by the universe

notes.greek: τοῖς τοῦ σαρκιδίου πάθεσιν ἐμπαρέχων συμπαθῆ τὸν νοῦν
notes.note: A play on πάθεσιν (what the flesh feels or undergoes) and συμπαθῆ (feeling along with it), kept with “feel with the feelings”. σαρκίδιον is a belittling form, “little flesh”, given as “the poor flesh”.
notes.other_reading: nor letting his mind share in what the bit of flesh undergoes

notes.greek: Ἡ φύσις οὐχ οὕτως συνεκέρασε τῷ συγκρίματι
notes.note: The verb “blended” has no object in the Greek as given: it is not said what nature blended with the compound. “The mind” is supplied from the last words of the chapter before (τὸν νοῦν), with which the “itself” that follows agrees in the Greek; the other candidate is “you”. “The compound” (σύγκριμα, “the thing put together”) is the body, or body and breath, as a thing made of parts.
notes.other_reading: Nature did not blend you with the compound in such a way

notes.greek: ὡς μὴ ἐφεῖσθαι περιορίζειν ἑαυτὸν καὶ τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ὑφ’ ἑαυτῷ ποιεῖσθαι
notes.note: The reflexive is the third-person form, which later Greek also uses for “yourself”; the English follows the supplied “mind” with “itself”. The passage is cut here in mid-chapter and the Greek ends at a colon; nothing was supplied at the end.
notes.other_reading: that you are not allowed to mark yourself off and to bring what is yours under your own control

check.note: ἔνδοξος is about honour and glory, not merely being well known.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “died a more glorious death”. The Greek word is about honour and high repute, which “famous” gave only in part; “famous” is kept in the note.

check.note: ἔδοξεν can be “seemed, was thought” or “resolved”. The English takes the first, which makes the refusal a matter of his reputation; the other reading fits the list of things he did.
check.decided: Declined: “was thought to have stood against it more nobly” stays. The participle “when ordered” is in the nominative, so Socrates is the subject of ἔδοξεν and “it seemed nobler to him” is not open; with a person as subject the verb most often means “seemed”, and the comparative is an adverb like the three before it. The other reading, “more nobly resolved to refuse”, is recorded in the note.

check.greek: περὶ οὗ καὶ μάλιστ’ ἄν τις ἐπιστήσειεν, εἴπερ ἀληθὲς ἦν
check.note: “Stop over” is unclear English, and the same verb is “taken note” in 1.11. The clause can mean “take note of most of all, if it was true” or “doubt most of all whether it was true”, and the English sits between them.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a point one might well take note of most of all, if indeed it was true”. “Take note” matches the same verb in 1.11, and εἴπερ is “if indeed”, a condition; the doubting sense is kept in the note.

check.note: ἀλλ’ is dropped. It answers “it is not enough that” and carries the turn of the argument.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now begins “But what has to be looked at is this”, which restores ἀλλ’ and the turn against “it is not enough”.

check.note: εἰκῇ can be “in vain” but is as often “at random, without thought, rashly”. The English has chosen the first.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “neither getting idly angry at vice”. “Idly” leaves both senses of εἰκῇ open, “without thought” and “to no purpose”, and the note gives them.

check.note: The verb has no object in the Greek as given. “Make the blend” hides the gap, so the reader cannot tell what is blended with what; “the compound” is also unexplained.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Nature did not blend the mind with the compound in such a way that …”, and the note says that “the mind” is supplied and that “you” is the other candidate. Square brackets are not used in the published English, and “compound” is kept and explained in the note.

check.note: The Greek names no subject, and ἑαυτὸν refers to whatever was blended, most naturally the mind, or “you”. “A person” turns it into a general statement about people.
check.decided: Accepted: “a person … themselves” is gone and the English reads “that it is not allowed to draw a boundary round itself”, the mind being what was blended.

check.note: ποιεῖσθαι is “make, bring”, not “keep”: the point is bringing what is one’s own under oneself, not holding on to it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to bring what is its own under its own control”, since the Greek verb is “make” or “bring” and not “keep”.

part.left_out: λίαν γὰρ ἐνδέχεται θεῖον ἄνδρα γενέσθαι καὶ ὑπὸ μηδενὸς γνωρισθῆναι. τούτου μέμνησο ἀεὶ καὶ ἔτι ἐκείνου, ὅτι ἐν ὀλιγίστοις κεῖται τὸ εὐδαιμόνως βιῶσαι καὶ μή, ὅτι ἀπήλπισας διαλεκτικὸς καὶ φυσικὸς ἔσεσθαι, διὰ τοῦτο ἀπογνῷς καὶ ἐλεύθερος καὶ αἰδήμων καὶ κοινωνικὸς καὶ εὐπειθὴς θεῷ.
part.why: The 1634 translation runs its section 7.37 on through the first sentence of chapter 67 (nature has not so mixed the mind with the body that it cannot mark itself off) and begins its 7.38 with the rest of the chapter.

passages.casaubon: How know we whether Socrates were so eminent indeed, and of so extraordinary a disposition? For that he died more gloriously, that he disputed with the Sophists more subtilty; that he watched in the frost more assiduously; that being commanded to fetch innocent Salaminius, he refused to do it more generously; all this will not serve. Nor that he walked in the streets, with much gravity and majesty, as was objected unto him by his adversaries: which nevertheless a man may well doubt of, whether it were so or no, or, which above all the rest, if so be that it were true, a man would well consider of, whether commendable, or dis-commendable. The thing therefore that we must inquire into, is this; what manner of soul Socrates had: whether his disposition was such; as that all that he stood upon, and sought after in this world, was barely this, that he might ever carry himself justly towards men, and holily towards the Gods. Neither vexing himself to no purpose at the wickedness of others, nor yet ever condescending to any man's evil fact, or evil intentions, through either fear, or engagement of friendship. Whether of those things that happened unto him by God's appointment, he neither did wonder at any when it did happen, or thought it intolerable in the trial of it. And lastly, whether he never did suffer his mind to sympathise with the senses, and affections of the body. For we must not think that Nature hath so mixed and tempered it with the body, as that she hath not power to circumscribe herself, and by herself to intend her own ends and occasions.

passages.greek: ʽἯι οὖν ὑπάρχει διανοίᾳ μεγαλοπρέπεια καὶ θεωρία παντὸς μὲν χρόνου, πάσης δὲ οὐσίας, ἆρα οἴει τούτῳ μέγα τι δοκεῖν εἶναι τὸν ἀνθρώπινον βίον; ἀδύνατον, ἦ δ’ ὅς. οὐκοῦν καὶ θάνατον οὐ δεινόν τι ἡγήσεται ὁ τοιοῦτος; ἥκιστά γε.ʼ
passages.english: “‘So, a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of all being: do you think human life seems anything great to the one who has it?’ ‘Impossible,’ he said. ‘Then such a person will count death, too, as nothing terrible?’ ‘Not in the least.’”

notes.note: The whole passage is a quotation, marked as one in the Greek as given: a piece of dialogue from Plato (Republic 486a: from memory, unchecked). The Greek starts “The mind, then, to which there belongs …” and goes on “to this one” (τούτῳ), a person; the sentence is broken at a colon to keep that turn. διάνοια is the faculty here, so “mind” and not “thought”.
notes.other_reading: So, to someone whose thought has greatness and a view of all time and all being

notes.note: Literally “what befits the great”: grandeur, largeness of mind. “Greatness” keeps the link with “anything great” (μέγα τι) in the question.
notes.other_reading: magnificence

notes.note: Looking at, viewing, contemplating. The English reads “a view of”.
notes.other_reading: the contemplation of all time and of all being

notes.note: οὐσία is “being” in Plato; a Stoic reader such as Marcus would also hear “substance”, the stuff of the world. Plato’s sense is kept since the words are his.
notes.other_reading: and of all substance

notes.note: “To this one”: masculine or neuter, so either the person who has such a mind or the mind. The answer speaks of ὁ τοιοῦτος, “such a person”, so it is taken as the person.
notes.other_reading: seems anything great to such a mind

notes.note: The set phrase “said he” of Plato’s narrated dialogues, which shows the passage is lifted from one.
notes.other_reading: said he

check.note: οὖν, “so, then”, is dropped. That is acceptable for an excerpt that begins in mid-argument, but the word is in the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now begins “So, a mind that has greatness”, which gives οὖν its word.

check.note: “The sight of all time” reads oddly. θεωρία is contemplation, a view taken.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a view of all time and of all being”, which is plainer than “the sight of” and is still a looking.

passages.casaubon: Out of Plato. 'He then whose mind is endowed with true magnanimity, who hath accustomed himself to the contemplation both of all times, and of all things in general; can this mortal life (thinkest thou) seem any great matter unto him? It is not possible, answered he. Then neither will such a one account death a grievous thing? By no means.'

passages.greek: Τῷ Περδίκκᾳ ὁ Σωκράτης περὶ τοῦ μὴ ἔρχεσθαι παρ’ αὐτόν· ʽἵνα, ἔφη, μὴ τῷ κακίστῳ ὀλέθρῳ ἀπόλωμαι,ʼ τουτέστι, μὴ εὖ παθῶν οὐ δυνηθῶ ἀντευποιῆσαι.
passages.english: Socrates to Perdiccas, on not going to him: “So that I may not die the worst of deaths,” he said, that is, so that I may not, after receiving a kindness, be unable to do one in return.

notes.note: There is no verb: “Socrates to Perdiccas”, as a heading for the saying. Perdiccas was a king of Macedon. From memory, unchecked: other ancient writers tell this of his son Archelaus.
notes.other_reading: Socrates said to Perdiccas

notes.greek: περὶ τοῦ μὴ ἔρχεσθαι παρ’ αὐτόν
notes.note: Literally “about the not coming to him”: his reason for refusing the king’s invitation.
notes.other_reading: on why he would not come to his court

notes.note: Literally “perish by the worst destruction”; noun and verb are close in sense, which “die the worst of deaths” keeps.
notes.other_reading: So that I may not come to the worst of ends

notes.note: “That is”: the explanation that follows keeps the speaker’s own voice, so it may be Socrates’ own words or Marcus’s gloss put in Socrates’ mouth. The Greek as given closes the quotation before it, and the English does the same.
notes.other_reading: “So that I may not die the worst of deaths, that is, receive a kindness and be unable to return it.”

notes.greek: μὴ εὖ παθῶν οὐ δυνηθῶ ἀντευποιῆσαι
notes.note: παθῶν is a slip in the copy for παθών. The Greek pairs “being done good” with “doing good in return”, kept as “receiving a kindness” and “do one in return”. The first is a participle, so what is feared is being unable to repay.
notes.other_reading: so that I may not be well treated and be unable to treat him well in return

check.greek: μὴ εὖ παθῶν οὐ δυνηθῶ ἀντευποιῆσαι
check.note: The participle is subordinate: the fear is of being unable to repay after being well treated. Joined with “and”, the “not” seems to cover being done a kindness as well, and “be done a kindness” is awkward.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “so that I may not, after receiving a kindness, be unable to do one in return”. The participle is subordinate again, so “not” falls only on being unable to repay.

passages.casaubon: What Socrates answered unto Perdiccas, why he did not come unto him, Lest of all deaths I should die the worst kind of death, said he: that is, not able to requite the good that hath been done unto me.

passages.greek: Ὁ Σωκράτης ἔλεγε· τί θέλετε; λογικῶν ψυχὰς ἔχειν ἢ ἀλόγων;—λογικῶν.—τίνων λογικῶν; ὑγιῶν ἢ φαύλων;—ὑγιῶν.—τί οὖν οὐ ζητεῖτε;—ὅτι ἔχομεν.—τί οὖν μάχεσθε καὶ διαφέρεσθε;
passages.english: Socrates used to say: “What do you want? To have the souls of rational beings or of irrational ones?” “Of rational beings.” “Of which rational beings? Sound ones or bad ones?” “Sound ones.” “Then why do you not look for them?” “Because we have them.” “Then why do you fight and fall out?”

notes.note: The tense is “used to say” or “was saying”. The exchange is not known from Plato or Xenophon (from memory, unchecked). The Greek as given marks each change of speaker with a dash; the English uses quotation marks.
notes.other_reading: Socrates said

notes.note: Literally “to have souls of rational ones or of irrational ones”. λογικός is “rational” throughout this translation; “beings” is added.
notes.other_reading: To have rational souls or irrational ones?

notes.note: ὑγιής is “healthy”, “sound”; φαῦλος is “bad”, “worthless”. The pair is not an exact opposite in Greek either.
notes.other_reading: Healthy ones or worthless ones?

notes.note: The verb has no object: “why do you not seek?” “Them” is supplied, the souls just named.
notes.other_reading: Then why do you not go looking?

notes.note: “Fight and differ”: the second verb is to be at odds, to quarrel.
notes.other_reading: Then why do you fight and disagree?

check.note: “Poor” reads as needy or pitiable. φαῦλος is “bad, worthless”, set against “healthy”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Sound ones or bad ones?”, since “poor” could be heard as needy or pitiable, which the Greek word is not. “Sound” stays for ὑγιῶν.

passages.casaubon: Socrates said, 'What will you have? the souls of reasonable, or unreasonable creatures? Of reasonable. But what? Of those whose reason is sound and perfect? or of those whose reason is vitiated and corrupted? Of those whose reason is sound and perfect. Why then labour ye not for such? Because we have them already. What then do ye so strive and contend between you?'

passages.greek: Ἀλέξανδρος δὲ καὶ Γάιος καὶ Πομπήιος τί πρὸς Διογένη καὶ Ἡράκλειτον καὶ Σωκράτην; οἱ μὲν γὰρ εἶδον τὰ πράγματα καὶ τὰς αἰτίας καὶ τὰς ὕλας καὶ τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ ἦν αὐτῶν ταὐτά, ἐκεῖ δὲ ὅσων πρόνοια καὶ δουλεία πόσων.
passages.english: And Alexander, Gaius and Pompey: what are they beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates? For the latter saw things and their causes and their matter, and their ruling parts were the same. But with the others, how many things to take thought for, and slavery to how many!

notes.note: Gaius is Gaius Julius Caesar, named by his first name beside Alexander the Great and Pompey. The name is left as the Greek has it.
notes.other_reading: Alexander, Caesar and Pompey

notes.note: Literally “what in relation to”: what do they amount to when set against the three philosophers. The chapter opens with δέ (“and”, “but”), as if continuing a thought.
notes.other_reading: what are they compared with Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates?

notes.note: “The ones”, set against ἐκεῖ δὲ, “but there”: the three philosophers, named last, as against the three rulers. The English makes this plain with “the latter” and “with the others”.
notes.other_reading: For these men saw things

notes.greek: τὰ πράγματα καὶ τὰς αἰτίας καὶ τὰς ὕλας
notes.note: “The things, and the causes, and the matters”: cause and matter are the two sides the Stoics found in each thing, so the last two are taken as the causes and the matter of the things.
notes.other_reading: saw things and causes and materials

notes.note: As given, “their ruling parts were the same”, and the Greek does not say the same as what: the same in all three men, or always the same and so not pulled about like those of the rulers. With one change of accent (ταῦτα) it would be “these were their ruling parts”. The text is probably doubted here (from memory, unchecked: readings meaning “were their own” have been proposed); the English translates what stands.
notes.other_reading: and their ruling parts were their own

notes.greek: ἐκεῖ δὲ ὅσων πρόνοια καὶ δουλεία πόσων
notes.note: Literally “but there, forethought for how many things and slavery to how many”, with no verb. “There” points back to the three rulers. The “how many” can be things or people.
notes.other_reading: But there, how much to plan for, and to how many masters they were slaves!

check.note: In the English of today “saw things” means imagined things that were not there, the opposite of what is meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the comma that set “saw things” off by itself is gone, and the English reads “saw things and their causes and their matter”, one run of three objects that cannot be heard as imagining. “Facts” is not taken, because the causes and the matter that follow belong to things and not to facts.

check.note: οἱ μὲν is the three philosophers, set against ἐκεῖ δὲ. “These men” can be read as all six or as the last three.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For the latter saw”, so that only the three philosophers can be meant.

check.note: The word as given is “the same” and the English follows it, but the reader cannot tell the same as what, and with another accent it would be “these”. The reading chosen should be stated and the doubt marked.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “were the same” stays, because the Greek as given says no more than that and does not say the same as what. The note now sets out the ways it can be taken, gives the reading with ταῦτα, and marks the doubt about the text.

passages.casaubon: Alexander, Caius, Pompeius; what are these to Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? These penetrated into the true nature of things; into all causes, and all subjects: and upon these did they exercise their power and authority. But as for those, as the extent of their error was, so far did their slavery extend.

passages.greek: Παρὰ Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Πλατωνικοῦ τὸ μὴ πολλάκις μηδὲ χωρὶς ἀνάγκης λέγειν πρός τινα ἢ ἐν ἐπιστολῇ γράφειν ὅτι ἄσχολός εἰμι, μηδὲ διὰ τούτου τοῦ τρόπου συνεχῶς παραιτεῖσθαι τὰ κατὰ τὰς πρὸς τοὺς συμβιοῦντας σχέσεις καθήκοντα, προβαλλόμενον τὰ περιεστῶτα πράγματα.
passages.english: From Alexander the Platonist: not often or without need to say to anyone, or write in a letter, “I am busy”; and not to keep excusing oneself in this way from the duties that relations with those one lives among call for, by pleading the business that surrounds one.

notes.note: “From Alexander the Platonist”, with no verb: what Marcus owes to him. From memory, unchecked: a Platonist philosopher who served Marcus as secretary for Greek letters.
notes.other_reading: What came from Alexander the Platonist

notes.note: ὅτι here introduces the words as spoken; it could also be reported speech. ἄσχολος is literally “without leisure”.
notes.other_reading: not to say or write that one has no time

notes.note: “To beg off”, “to ask to be excused from”. The infinitives name no person; “oneself” and “one” keep that.
notes.other_reading: and not to keep begging off in this way

notes.greek: τὰ κατὰ τὰς πρὸς τοὺς συμβιοῦντας σχέσεις καθήκοντα
notes.note: καθήκοντα is the Stoic term for the acts that are fitting for a person, here given as “duties”. They are those that go with one’s relations (σχέσεις) to “those who live with one”: household, friends, colleagues.
notes.other_reading: what is fitting in one’s ties to the people who share one’s life

notes.note: Literally “holding out in front the affairs standing round”: using the business one is in the middle of as a shield or pretext.
notes.other_reading: with the circumstances one is in as the pretext

check.note: περιεστῶτα is “standing round, surrounding”. “Pressing” adds urgency, and “pressing all round” is a little odd.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the business that surrounds one”. The Greek word is “standing round”, and “pressing” added an urgency it does not state.

check.note: Found while settling: “not to say to anyone often or without need, or write in a letter” tied the two limits to saying only, while in the Greek they stand before both verbs.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “not often or without need to say to anyone, or write in a letter”, so the limits cover writing as well as saying.

passages.casaubon: Of Alexander the Platonic, not often nor without great necessity to say, or to write to any man in a letter, 'I am not at leisure'; nor in this manner still to put off those duties, which we owe to our friends and acquaintances (to every one in his kind) under pretence of urgent affairs.

passages.greek: Οἷος ὁ Σωκράτης τὸ κῴδιον ὑπεζωσμένος, ὅτε ἡ Ξανθίππη λαβοῦσα τὸ ἱμάτιον ἔξω προῆλθε, καὶ ἃ εἶπεν ὁ Σωκράτης τοῖς ἑταίροις αἰδεσθεῖσι καὶ ἀναχωρήσασιν, ὅτε αὐτὸν εἶδον οὕτως ἐσταλμένον.
passages.english: What Socrates was like with the sheepskin tied round his waist, when Xanthippe had taken his cloak and gone out; and what Socrates said to his companions, who were embarrassed and drew back when they saw him dressed like that.

notes.note: No main verb: a note to himself, “what kind of man Socrates was”, pointing at a story Marcus knew. From memory, unchecked: the story does not survive elsewhere, so what Socrates said is not known.
notes.other_reading: Think what Socrates was like

notes.note: “Having girded on the fleece underneath”: wearing a sheepskin tied round the middle in place of clothes.
notes.other_reading: wearing only the sheepskin as an undergarment

notes.note: Xanthippe was Socrates’ wife. The cloak she took was his outer garment, perhaps the only one.
notes.other_reading: when Xanthippe took the cloak and went out

notes.note: “Having felt shame and having withdrawn”: they were ashamed, for him or at seeing him so, and stepped back or went away.
notes.other_reading: who were ashamed and went away

passages.casaubon: How Socrates looked, when he was fain to gird himself with a skin, Xanthippe his wife having taken away his clothes, and carried them abroad with her, and what he said to his fellows and friends, who were ashamed; and out of respect to him, did retire themselves when they saw him thus decked.

passages.greek: Σωκράτης καὶ τὰ τῶν πολλῶν δόγματα Λαμίας ἐκάλει, παιδίων δείματα.
passages.english: Socrates used to call the principles of the many, too, “Lamias”, things to frighten children.

notes.note: “Too” or “even”: it may add this saying to others, or mean that he gave the name even to what most people hold.
notes.other_reading: Socrates used to call even the principles of the many “Lamias”

notes.note: δόγμα is “principle” throughout this translation, the word Marcus uses for what a person holds and lives by; here it is what most people hold. “Principles” is kept so that the word can be recognised from passage to passage.
notes.other_reading: the beliefs of most people

notes.note: Lamia was a child-eating monster of Greek nursery tales, used to scare children into behaving. The name and the plural are kept.
notes.other_reading: bogeys

notes.note: Literally “terrors of little children”: things children are frightened of.
notes.other_reading: the terrors of small children

check.note: The δόγματα of the many are what most people believe. “Principles” suggests considered rules of conduct, which is not what is being called a bogey.
check.decided: Declined: “principles” stays. δόγμα is “principle” throughout this translation, and Marcus uses the one word both for what the many hold and for what a philosopher holds, so a second English word here would hide that. “Beliefs” is given in the note.

passages.casaubon: Socrates was wont to call the common conceits and opinions of men, the common bugbears of the world: the proper terror of silly children.

passages.greek: Παρὰ Φρόντωνος τὸ ἐπιστῆσαι οἵα ἡ τυραννικὴ βασκανία καὶ ποικιλία καὶ ὑπόκρισις, καὶ ὅτι ὡς ἐπίπαν οἱ καλούμενοι οὗτοι παρ’ ἡμῖν εὐπατρίδαι ἀστοργότεροί πως εἰσί.
passages.english: From Fronto: to have taken note of what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that on the whole these people we call patricians are somehow rather lacking in affection.

notes.note: Fronto was Marcus’s teacher of Latin rhetoric. “From Fronto”, with no verb, as in the other entries of this book.
notes.other_reading: What came from Fronto

notes.note: “To have stopped and given attention to”, “to have observed”. The same verb is “take note of” in 7.66.
notes.other_reading: to have come to see

notes.greek: ἡ τυραννικὴ βασκανία καὶ ποικιλία καὶ ὑπόκρισις
notes.note: The adjective “of a tyrant” can go with the first noun only or with all three; it is taken with all three. βασκανία is malicious envy and ὑπόκρισις is acting a part. ποικιλία is “many-colouredness”, so either changeableness or intricate cunning, and “shiftiness” has something of both.
notes.other_reading: what the envy that goes with tyranny is like, and its caprice and hypocrisy

notes.greek: οἱ καλούμενοι οὗτοι παρ’ ἡμῖν εὐπατρίδαι
notes.note: εὐπατρίδαι, “those of good fathers”, is the Greek word for the Roman patricians, the old noble families. “Among us”, which the English gives through the one who calls them so, means at Rome. The literal sense sits oddly beside the lack of affection that follows.
notes.other_reading: these people who are called the well-born among us

notes.note: στοργή is the love that is natural within a family, as between parents and children. The form is a comparative, “rather lacking” or “more lacking than others”, and πως, “somehow”, softens it.
notes.other_reading: are somehow more lacking in family affection than other people

check.note: ποικιλία is “variety”, so here either changeableness (caprice) or intricate cunning. “Shiftiness” sits near the second; the first is possible.
check.decided: Declined: “shiftiness” stays. The Greek word can be changeableness or cunning, and “shiftiness” has both in it, where “deviousness” or “caprice” would choose one; the note now gives both senses.

check.greek: οἱ καλούμενοι οὗτοι παρ’ ἡμῖν εὐπατρίδαι
check.note: οὗτοι, “these”, is dropped, and παρ’ ἡμῖν goes more naturally with “called”: “these people whom we call patricians”, not “those among us”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “these people we call patricians”, which restores οὗτοι and takes “among us” with “called”.

check.note: The comparative can be a real one, “rather less affectionate (than other people)”. “Natural” is supplied.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “are somehow rather lacking in affection”, with “somehow” for πως, “rather” for the comparative, and no “natural”. “Lacking in” is kept in place of “short of”, and the note gives the family sense of the word and the reading as a true comparative.

passages.casaubon: Of Fronto, to how much envy and fraud and hypocrisy the state of a tyrannous king is subject unto, and how they who are commonly called εὐπατρίδαι, _i.e._ nobly born, are in some sort incapable, or void of natural affection.

nearest.title: What I learned, and from whom

passages.greek: Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ Μακεδὼν καὶ ὁ ὀρεωκόμος αὐτοῦ ἀποθανόντες εἰς ταὐτὸ κατέστησαν· ἤτοι γὰρ ἀνελήφθησαν εἰς τοὺς αὐτοὺς τοῦ κόσμου σπερματικοὺς λόγους ἢ διεσκεδάσθησαν ὁμοίως εἰς τὰς ἀτόμους.
passages.english: Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver, once dead, came to the same state: for either they were taken back into the same seed-reasons of the universe, or they were scattered alike into atoms.

notes.note: A man who looks after and drives mules: the lowest of his servants, set beside the king.
notes.other_reading: his muleteer

notes.note: Literally “were brought to the same”: the same condition, or the same place.
notes.other_reading: ended up in the same place

notes.note: “Were taken up” or “taken back”. The English reads “taken back”, since on the Stoic view they return to what they came from.
notes.other_reading: they were taken up into

notes.note: A Stoic term: the reasons at work in the universe that act as seeds, from which each thing grows and into which it returns. λόγος is “reason” throughout this translation and “principle” is kept for δόγμα, so the English reads “seed-reasons” and not the more usual “seminal principles”.
notes.other_reading: the same generative principles of the universe

notes.note: The second alternative is the Epicurean one: a universe of atoms with no reason running it. ὁμοίως is “in the same way”, both alike.
notes.other_reading: or they were both alike dispersed among the atoms

check.note: “Seed-reasons” is a coined term that a reader of today will not understand.
check.decided: Declined: “seed-reasons” stays, with its note. The Greek term has λόγος in it, which is “reason” throughout this translation, and “principle” is kept for another Greek word (δόγμα), so “generative principles” or “seed-principles” would make two Greek words one in English.

passages.casaubon: Alexander of Macedon, and he that dressed his mules, when once dead both came to one. For either they were both resumed into those original rational essences from whence all things in the world are propagated; or both after one fashion were scattered into atoms.

passages.greek: Παρὰ Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ γραμματικοῦ τὸ ἀνεπίπληκτον καὶ τὸ μὴ ὀνειδιστικῶς ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι τῶν βάρβαρον ἢ σόλοικόν τι ἢ ἀπηχὲς προενεγκαμένων, ἀλλ’ ἐπιδεξίως αὐτὸ μόνον ἐκεῖνο ὃ ἔδει εἰρῆσθαι προφέρεσθαι ἐν τρόπῳ ἀποκρίσεως ἢ συνεπιμαρτυρήσεως ἢ συνδιαλήψεως περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ πράγματος, οὐχὶ περὶ τοῦ ῥήματος, ἢ δι’ ἑτέρας τινὸς τοιαύτης ἐμμελοῦς παρυπομνήσεως.
passages.english: From Alexander the grammarian: not to find fault, and not to pounce reproachfully on people who have come out with a wrong form of a word, a mistake in grammar or a jarring sound, but deftly to come out with just the very thing that should have been said, by way of an answer, or of backing them up, or of a joint discussion about the matter itself, not about the expression, or through some other such well-tuned reminder in passing.

notes.note: A γραμματικός taught language and the reading of the poets; “grammarian” is the usual word, wider than the modern sense of grammar.
notes.other_reading: From Alexander the teacher of literature

notes.note: The word can be active, “not rebuking”, or passive, “not open to rebuke”. What follows is about how to correct others, so the active sense is taken.
notes.other_reading: to be beyond reproach

notes.note: “To lay hold of”, “to seize on”: catching a speaker out. Given as “pounce on”.
notes.other_reading: not to take people up in a reproachful way

notes.greek: βάρβαρον ἢ σόλοικόν τι ἢ ἀπηχὲς
notes.note: Three school terms: a “barbarism” (a wrongly formed word; the Greek word is literally “foreign”, “not Greek”), a “solecism” (a wrong construction), and something “off in sound” (a wrong pronunciation or an ugly-sounding phrase). Each is given in plain words.
notes.other_reading: a barbarism, a solecism or something that sounds wrong

notes.note: “Dexterously”, with a light, tactful hand.
notes.other_reading: tactfully

notes.greek: αὐτὸ μόνον ἐκεῖνο ὃ ἔδει εἰρῆσθαι προφέρεσθαι
notes.note: “To bring forward that very thing alone that ought to have been said”: to use the right form oneself and nothing more. The verb is the one used of the speakers’ slip (προενεγκαμένων), so both read “come out with”; “just” is for μόνον.
notes.other_reading: to bring out only the expression that should have been used

notes.note: A rare word, “bearing witness along with”: confirming what the other person said, and using the right form while doing so.
notes.other_reading: or of adding one’s own testimony

notes.note: Another rare word, “taking up together” in talk or in thought: joining the other person in going over the point. It stands with two words for things said, so it is given as “a joint discussion”.
notes.other_reading: or of thinking the matter over together

notes.greek: περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ πράγματος, οὐχὶ περὶ τοῦ ῥήματος
notes.note: These words follow the third way and may belong to it alone or to all three; the English keeps the Greek order so that either can be heard. ῥῆμα is the particular word or phrase that was used.
notes.other_reading: all of them about the matter itself and not about the wording

notes.note: ἐμμελής is “in tune”, and so “graceful”, “tactful”; it answers ἀπηχές, “out of tune”, earlier in the sentence, and the image is kept with “jarring” and “well-tuned”. παρυπόμνησις is a reminder slipped in on the side.
notes.other_reading: some other such tactful hint

check.note: “Take people up” is unclear to many readers today. The Greek is “seize on, pounce on”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “not to pounce reproachfully on people who have come out with …”. The Greek verb is “lay hold of”, “seize on”, and “take people up” was unclear.

check.note: A “barbarism” is a wrong or foreign form of a word. “Outlandish” now means bizarre, which is a different thing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a wrong form of a word”, since “outlandish” today means bizarre. The literal sense of the Greek word, “foreign”, is given in the note.

check.note: This is the same verb as προενεγκαμένων, “come out with”: they utter the wrong expression, he utters the right one. “Bring in” loses the echo and the point that he simply uses the right form himself.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to come out with just the very thing that should have been said”, the same words as for the speakers’ slip, since the Greek verb is the same. “Himself” is not added, as the Greek has no word for it.

check.note: The word is more naturally a joint discussion than joint thinking.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a joint discussion”. The word stands with “answer” and “backing up”, both things said, and the sense “thinking over together” is kept in the note.

check.greek: περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ πράγματος, οὐχὶ περὶ τοῦ ῥήματος
check.note: The English ties this to the third way only, while in the Greek it may qualify all three. ῥήματος is also the particular expression, singular, not “wording” in general.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “the wording” becomes “the expression”, the particular phrase used. The words “about the matter itself, not about the expression” stay after the third way, where the Greek has them and where they can be heard with it alone or with all three; “all” is not added because the Greek does not decide, and a note records this.

check.note: “Well-tuned” is a literalism: ἐμμελής, “in tune”, means graceful, tactful.
check.decided: Declined: “well-tuned” stays. ἐμμελής, “in tune”, answers ἀπηχές, “out of tune”, earlier in the same sentence, and the English keeps that image with “jarring” and “well-tuned”; “tactful” is given in the note.

passages.casaubon: From Alexander the Grammarian, to be un-reprovable myself, and not reproachfully to reprehend any man for a barbarism, or a solecism, or any false pronunciation, but dextrously by way of answer, or testimony, or confirmation of the same matter (taking no notice of the word) to utter it as it should have been spoken; or by some other such close and indirect admonition, handsomely and civilly to tell him of it.

passages.greek: ὅρα γοῦν ὁ Κράτης τί περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ξενοκράτους λέγει.
passages.english: See, at any rate, what Crates says about Xenocrates himself.

notes.note: “At any rate”, “for instance”: it brings in a case that supports what came just before. This passage is one sentence from the end of a chapter, and what it supports is not in the Greek given; nothing was supplied.
notes.other_reading: See, for instance

notes.greek: ὁ Κράτης τί περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ξενοκράτους λέγει
notes.note: Marcus does not give the saying. From memory, unchecked: Crates is most likely the Cynic philosopher, Xenocrates was a head of Plato’s school known for his gravity, and the remark itself is lost. αὐτοῦ is “himself”, with the force of “even Xenocrates”.
notes.other_reading: what Crates says even about Xenocrates

part.left_out: Οἷον δὴ τὸ φαντασίαν λαμβάνειν ἐπὶ τῶν ὄψων καὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἐδωδίμων, ὅτι νεκρὸς οὗτος ἰχθύος, οὗτος δὲ νεκρὸς ὄρνιθος ἢ χοίρου· καὶ πάλιν, ὅτι ὁ Φάλερνος χυλάριόν ἐστι σταφυλίου καὶ ἡ περιπόρφυρος τριχία προβατίου αἱματίῳ κόγχης δεδευμένα· καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ τὴν συνουσίαν ἐντερίου παράτριψις καὶ μετά τινος σπασμοῦ μυξαρίου ἔκκρισις· οἷαι δὴ αὗταί εἰσιν αἱ φαντασίαι καθικνούμεναι αὐτῶν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ διεξιοῦσαι δι’ αὐτῶν, ὥστε ὁρᾶν οἷά τινά ποτέ ἐστιν· οὕτως δεῖ παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον ποιεῖν καὶ ὅπου λίαν ἀξιόπιστα τὰ πράγματα φαντάζεται, ἀπογυμνοῦν αὐτὰ καὶ τὴν εὐτέλειαν αὐτῶν καθορᾶν καὶ τὴν ἱστορίαν ἐφ’ ᾗ σεμνύνεται περιαιρεῖν. δεινὸς γὰρ ὁ τῦφος παραλογιστὴς καὶ ὅτε δοκεῖς μάλιστα περὶ τὰ σπουδαῖα καταγίνεσθαι, τότε μάλιστα καταγοητεύῃ.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts all of the chapter but its last sentence in its section 6.11 and makes that last sentence, on Crates and Xenocrates, a section of its own, 6.12.

passages.casaubon: See what Crates pronounceth concerning Xenocrates himself.

passages.greek: Λακεδαιμόνιοι τοῖς μὲν ξένοις ἐν ταῖς θεωρίαις ὑπὸ τῇ σκιᾷ τὰ βάθρα ἐτίθεσαν, αὐτοὶ δὲ οὗ ἔτυχεν, ἐκαθέζοντο.
passages.english: At their public shows the Spartans used to set the benches for foreign visitors in the shade, while they themselves sat wherever they happened to.

notes.note: “Lacedaemonians”, the formal name of the Spartans. The English uses the name a reader of today knows.
notes.other_reading: The Lacedaemonians

notes.note: ξένος is both “foreigner” and “guest”: visitors from other cities. μέν and δέ set them against the Spartans themselves, which the English gives with “while”.
notes.other_reading: for their guests

notes.note: “At the viewings”: public spectacles or festivals where people sat to watch.
notes.other_reading: at their festivals

notes.note: Literally “where it chanced”: anywhere, with no care for comfort.
notes.other_reading: and sat themselves anywhere

check.note: ξένοι here are visitors from other cities, guests. “Strangers” is weaker and can mean any unknown person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “foreign visitors”. The Greek word here means people from other cities who have come to watch, which “strangers” did not say.

check.note: μὲν and δὲ set the visitors against the Spartans themselves, and “and” flattens the contrast.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “while they themselves sat wherever they happened to”, so the contrast of μέν and δέ is heard.

passages.casaubon: The Lacedæmonians at their public spectacles were wont to appoint seats and forms for their strangers in the shadow, they themselves were content to sit anywhere.

passages.greek: εἰς τὸ πᾶν ἀεὶ ὁρᾶν, τί ἐστιν αὐτὸ ἐκεῖνο τὸ τὴν φαντασίαν σοι ποιοῦν, καὶ ἀναπτύσσειν διαιροῦντα εἰς τὸ αἴτιον, εἰς τὸ ὑλικόν, εἰς τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἰς τὸν χρόνον, ἐντὸς οὗ πεπαῦσθαι αὐτὸ δεήσει.
passages.english: Always see in full what that thing itself is which produces the impression in you, and open it out, dividing it into the cause, into the material, into the purpose, into the time within which it will have to be over.

notes.note: The words can be an adverb with “see” (“altogether, in full”, or “in every case”), or what is looked at, “look to the whole”, meaning the whole of the thing or the universe. The English takes “in full” because the question “what that thing is” follows at once as what is to be seen. The passage starts in mid-chapter, and the sentence before it, not translated here, breaks off at “for let your impulse be”, so these words may once have belonged to that sentence.
notes.other_reading: Always look to the whole: what that thing itself is which produces the impression in you

notes.note: The verbs here (“see”, “open out”) are infinitives, the notebook form for an instruction to oneself, and are written as commands. “See” is kept for this verb here and in 12.10; “look” is left for the different verb of 6.3.
notes.other_reading: Always to look in full at what that thing itself is … and to open it out

notes.note: Literally “the thing making the impression for you”; the dative “for you” can also be heard as “on you”. “Impression” is the Stoic term φαντασία: how a thing presents itself to the mind.
notes.other_reading: the thing that makes the impression on you

notes.note: An image: to unfold or unroll something folded up, as one opens a scroll or a folded cloth. It is kept as “open it out”.
notes.other_reading: and unfold it

notes.note: “The cause” here is the Stoic term for the active element that shapes a thing and makes it what it is, set against its material. It is not an earlier event that brought the thing about.
notes.other_reading: the causal element, the shaping principle

notes.greek: εἰς τὸ αἴτιον, εἰς τὸ ὑλικόν, εἰς τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἰς τὸν χρόνον
notes.note: The Greek says “into” four times and has no “and”: four separate heads, counted off one by one. The English keeps all four.
notes.other_reading: into the cause, the material, the purpose and the time

notes.note: Literally “the reference”, “the carrying back”: what the thing is referred to. The word has a range (relation, reference, the end something is directed to), and the English narrows it to “purpose”, as also in 12.10. The sister passage 8.11 asks at this point in the same list “What does it do in the universe?”, which supports the narrower sense.
notes.other_reading: into the reference, what it relates to

notes.note: The infinitive is a perfect: not “will have to stop” but “will have to have stopped”, to be over and done, which the English gives as “will have to be over”. “It” is neuter and so is the thing, not the impression (which is feminine in Greek).
notes.other_reading: the time within which it will have to have ceased

check.note: The English takes these words as an adverb with “see”, “in full”. They can as well mean “in every case” or “look to the whole”, and at a cut edge they may belong to the sentence before; the choice should not be silent.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English still reads “in full”, since “altogether” is a settled sense of the phrase and the question “what that thing is” follows at once as the thing to be seen. The note now sets out “in every case” and “look to the whole” as well, and says that the sentence before the cut breaks off at “for let your impulse be”, so the words may have belonged to it.

check.note: With an indirect question (“what it is”) the verb is an instruction to look and examine, and “see what it is” reads a little oddly as a command; “look at” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek verb is the plain word for seeing, the same one that opens 12.10, and Marcus has a different verb for “look” in 6.3, so “see” is kept for the one and “look” for the other. “See what it is” is ordinary English for an instruction to find out.

check.note: The Greek word means “reference”, that to which the thing is referred or related. “Purpose” is one way of taking it and is narrower than the Greek.
check.decided: Declined: “purpose” stays. The word means what a thing is carried back or referred to, and in this list that is the end it serves: the sister passage 8.11 has at the same place “What does it do in the universe?”. Bare “reference” would be heard today as a citation, and the note gives the wider sense.

check.note: “Will have to have ceased” is exact to the perfect infinitive but hard to read at first pass; “must come to its end” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the time within which it will have to be over”. “Be over” keeps the finished state that the Greek perfect expresses, which “come to its end” would turn into the act of stopping, and it reads at first pass.

check.greek: εἰς τὸ αἴτιον, εἰς τὸ ὑλικόν, εἰς τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἰς τὸν χρόνον
check.note: The Greek repeats “into” four times with no “and”, a deliberate count of four separate heads. The English runs them into one list and adds “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “into the cause, into the material, into the purpose, into the time”, with “into” four times and no “and”, as in the Greek. The Greek has “the”, not “its”, so “the” is kept.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “open it out by dividing it”, but the Greek has only the participle “dividing”, with no word for “by”, and the same participle is “dividing” in 12.10.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “open it out, dividing it into”, the same word in the same form as in 12.10.

part.left_out: Εἰ μὴ καθήκει, μὴ πράξῃς· εἰ μὴ ἀληθές ἐστι, μὴ εἴπῃς. ἡ γὰρ ὁρμή σου ἔστω ιη′
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 12.13 with 'Ever maintain thine own purpose' and begins its 12.14 here, where modern editions begin chapter 12.18; this Greek text prints both as chapter 12.17.

passages.casaubon: Of everything that presents itself unto thee, to consider what the true nature of it is, and to unfold it, as it were, by dividing it into that which is formal: that which is material: the true use or end of it, and the just time that it is appointed to last.

nearest.title: Taking a thing apart: matter, form and end

passages.greek: Τοιαῦτα τὰ πράγματα ὁρᾶν, διαιροῦντα εἰς ὕλην, αἴτιον, ἀναφοράν.
passages.english: See things as being of this kind, dividing them into matter, cause, purpose.

notes.note: Literally “such”, “of this kind”, said of the things. Nothing in the sentence answers “such”: it may point back to the chapter before, which is not part of this passage, or forward to the division that follows, and the English leaves it as open as the Greek. Some editions may print a fuller text in which words meaning “as they are” answer “such” (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: See things in this way, dividing them into matter, cause, purpose.

notes.note: An infinitive used as an instruction to oneself, written as a command.
notes.other_reading: To see things as being of this kind

notes.note: Three bare nouns with no “and”. “Matter” is the noun; the related adjective in 12.17b and 8.11 is given as “material”. “Cause” is the Stoic active element that shapes the matter, not an earlier event, and the third word is literally “reference”, what the thing is referred to, narrowed to “purpose” as in 12.17b.
notes.other_reading: into matter, cause, reference

check.note: The Greek as given says only “such”. “As they are” is not in these words, and adding it makes the claim that this division shows things as they really are.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “See things as being of this kind”, which says no more than “such”. It does not read “in this way” because the Greek word describes the things, not the manner of seeing, and may point back to the chapter before as easily as forward to the division.

check.note: From memory only: “such” with nothing answering it is abrupt, and the text may have lost a following “as they are”. If the English translates a restored text, that should be said openly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps to the words given and supplies nothing. The note says that “such” has nothing to answer it and that a fuller text with “as they are” may exist, marked as from memory, unchecked.

check.note: Here the Greek is the noun “matter”; in 12.17b and 8.11 it is the adjective “material”. Both were given as “material”, and “matter” is the plainer word for the noun.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “matter” for the noun here, and “material” is kept for the adjective in 12.17b and 8.11, so the two Greek forms can be told apart.

check.note: As in 12.17b, the word is “reference”, what the thing is referred to, and “purpose” narrows it.
check.decided: Declined: “purpose” stays, as in 12.17b, so that the word is the same in both passages. In this list what a thing is referred to is the end it serves, and bare “reference” would be heard today as a citation; the note gives the literal sense.

passages.casaubon: All worldly things thou must behold and consider, dividing them into matter, form, and reference, or their proper end.

nearest.title: Taking a thing apart: matter, form and end

passages.greek: Τοῦτο τί ἐστιν αὐτὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ, τί μὲν τὸ οὐσιῶδες αὐτοῦ καὶ ὑλικόν, τί δὲ τὸ αἰτιῶδες, τί δὲ ποιεῖ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, πόσον δὲ χρόνον ὑφίσταται;
passages.english: This thing, what is it in itself, in its own make-up? What in it is substance and material, and what is cause? What does it do in the universe? And how long does it last?

notes.note: A set philosophical phrase, “itself by itself”: the thing taken alone, apart from everything around it. The English reads “in itself”.
notes.other_reading: what is it, itself by itself

notes.note: The noun means how a thing is built or put together: construction, constitution. The dative is loose (“in”, “by”, “in respect of”), and the English reads “in its own make-up”.
notes.other_reading: by its own constitution

notes.note: One article covers both adjectives, so this is one element with two names, not two elements; literally “the substance-like and material of it”. In Stoic use “substance” (οὐσία) is the underlying stuff, close to “material”. The English says “what in it is”, without a word such as “part”, which the Greek does not have.
notes.other_reading: What is its substance, that is, its material

notes.note: Literally “the cause-like”: the Stoic active element that shapes the material and makes the thing what it is. The plain word “cause” is kept.
notes.other_reading: the causal element, the shaping principle

notes.note: “The universe” is the rendering settled for this word across the translation. “The world” is also possible; the Greek does not decide between the ordered whole and the world people live in.
notes.other_reading: What does it do in the world?

notes.note: The verb means “subsists”, “has existence”; with “how long a time” the English reads “last”. The tense is present, so the question is how long such a thing stands in being, not how long it has left.
notes.other_reading: and for how long a time does it exist?

check.note: One article covers both adjectives, a single element named twice. “Part” is supplied here and again with “cause”, and suggests a separable piece.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “What in it is substance and material, and what is cause?”, with no “part”. “Material” is kept rather than “matter” because the Greek here is the adjective, as in 12.17b, while “matter” is used for the noun in 12.10.

passages.casaubon: This, what is it in itself, and by itself, according to its proper constitution? What is the substance of it? What is the matter, or proper use? What is the form or efficient cause? What is it for in this world, and how long will it abide? Thus must thou examine all things, that present themselves unto thee.

nearest.title: The reason that governs the whole

passages.greek: Διηνεκῶς καὶ ἐπὶ πάσης, εἰ οἶόν τε, φαντασίας φυσιολογεῖν, παθολογεῖν, διαλεκτικεύεσθαι.
passages.english: Continually, and with every impression if possible, reason about nature, reason about the passions, practise dialectic.

notes.note: Three bare verbs with no “and”, infinitives used as an instruction to oneself, written as three commands. The first two are built on the word for reasoning or giving an account, hence “reason about”. The three seem to answer to the three parts of Stoic philosophy (physics, ethics, logic), each brought to bear on the impression; that is an inference, not something the Greek says.
notes.other_reading: apply the study of nature, the study of the passions, and dialectic

notes.note: A rare verb: “to give an account of the πάθη”. The noun’s range runs from “what one undergoes” and “feelings” to the Stoic sense of the passions, the feelings that disturb; the English takes the Stoic sense.
notes.other_reading: reason about feelings, about what one undergoes

notes.note: “To practise dialectic”, the Stoic name for the art of reasoning correctly: testing a statement by question and argument, and seeing what follows from what. “Logic” would be a wider and more modern label.
notes.other_reading: test it by argument

notes.greek: ἐπὶ πάσης, εἰ οἶόν τε, φαντασίας
notes.note: Literally “in the case of every impression, if it can be done”. “Impression” is the Stoic term φαντασία. “Every” is kept, with its own limit “if possible”.
notes.other_reading: in the case of every impression, if that can be done

check.note: The Greek has three verbs and no “apply”: three things to do with each impression. The English turns them into three school subjects brought to bear, and adds “apply” and an “and”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “reason about nature, reason about the passions, practise dialectic”, three verbs with no “apply” and no “and”, as in the Greek. It does not say “as a student of”, because the Greek names three things to do and no persons.

check.note: The word can be about the passions or more widely about what is undergone, affections of any kind. The English takes the first; the advice is to keep “passions” but be aware of the wider sense.
check.decided: Accepted: “the passions” is kept, as the point advises, now inside the verb phrase “reason about the passions”. The note sets out the wider sense, feelings or whatever one undergoes.

check.note: The verb is “to practise dialectic”, the testing of a statement by question and argument. “Logic” is a wider and more modern label.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “practise dialectic”, which is the verb the Greek has. The note explains dialectic as the testing of a statement by question and argument.

passages.casaubon: As every fancy and imagination presents itself unto thee, consider (if it be possible) the true nature, and the proper qualities of it, and reason with thyself about it.

passages.greek: Ἔσω βλέπε· μηδενὸς πράγματος μήτε ἡ ἰδία ποιότης μήτε ἡ ἀξία παρατρεχέτω σε.
passages.english: Look inside. With any thing, do not let either its own quality or its worth run past you.

notes.note: Open: “look inside” can mean inside things or inside yourself, and the Greek does not say which. Because the next clause is about the quality and worth of things, the English is left as bare as the Greek, “look inside”, which leans towards inside things.
notes.other_reading: Look within yourself.

notes.note: In Stoic use a thing’s quality is what makes it the kind of thing it is, and “its own” marks what is peculiar to this thing. The adjective is the one given as “its own” in 8.11 (“its own make-up”).
notes.other_reading: its particular quality, what it is in particular

notes.note: “Worth” or “value”, a Stoic term for how much a thing counts for. The English reads “worth”.
