notes.other_reading: its value

notes.note: An image: “let it not run past you”, as something that goes by before you notice; the image is kept. The Greek is negative throughout, “of no thing let neither … nor …”, which the English gives as “with any thing, do not let either … or …”.
notes.other_reading: Let neither the quality nor the worth of anything escape you.

check.note: The adjective means “its own, proper to it” and is given as “its own” in 8.11. “Particular” can be read as “some specific quality” and loses the link.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “With any thing, do not let either its own quality or its worth run past you”. “Of any thing” has moved to the front as “with any thing” so that “its own” has something to refer to.

passages.casaubon: Look in, let not either the proper quality, or the true worth of anything pass thee, before thou hast fully apprehended it.

nearest.title: Taking a thing apart: matter, form and end

passages.greek: Πρόσεχε τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ ἢ τῷ δόγματι ἢ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ ἢ τῷ σημαινομένῳ.
passages.english: Pay attention to the thing before you, or to the principle, or to the activity, or to what is meant.

notes.note: Literally “what lies under” or “what lies before one”: the thing itself that one is dealing with and that an impression is of. It can also be the matter in hand, the business being done, or in Stoic physics the underlying material. The English takes the first, and “you” is supplied, since the Greek says only “what lies before”.
notes.other_reading: to the matter in hand (or: to the underlying material)

notes.note: “Principle” is the rendering settled for this word across the translation: a settled view one holds and acts from. It could also be heard as the particular belief or judgment involved in the case.
notes.other_reading: or to the belief

notes.note: “Activity”: a thing’s being at work, or the act one is engaged in. “Action” is the narrower choice.
notes.other_reading: or to the action

notes.note: “What is signified”: a Stoic term from logic for the meaning that a word or statement carries, as against the sound of the words. The English reads “what is meant”.
notes.other_reading: or to the thing signified, the meaning

notes.greek: ἢ τῷ δόγματι ἢ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ ἢ τῷ σημαινομένῳ
notes.note: The Greek joins the four with “or”, not “and”, and “or” is kept. This is part of a chapter and the Greek ends here; nothing was supplied.
notes.other_reading: to the thing before you and the principle and the activity and what is meant

check.note: The Greek is “what underlies”, most naturally the object itself, the thing in front of you. “The matter in hand” reads as the task being dealt with, and “matter” collides with “material” and “matter” in the neighbouring passages.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the thing before you”. The Greek word is literally what lies under or before one, which in a list with principle, activity and meaning is most naturally the thing itself, and “matter” is now left for the different word in 12.10.

check.note: The word is a judgment or opinion held, as well as a principle or doctrine. “Principle” picks the second; the judgment being made about the object fits the list at least as well.
check.decided: Declined: “principle” stays. It is the rendering settled for this Greek word across the translation, and “judgment” is kept there for a different Greek word, so using it here would make two Greek words sound like one. The note records “belief” as the other reading.

check.note: Could be “the action” being done just as well as “activity” in general; the English is acceptable.
check.decided: Declined: “activity” stays. The Greek word names something’s being at work, which is wider than a single deed, and the point itself finds the English acceptable. The note records “action”.

part.left_out: Δικαίως ταῦτα πάσχεις· μᾶλλον δὲ θέλεις ἀγαθὸς αὔριον γενέσθαι ἢ σήμερον εἶναι.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 8.20 after the four things to attend to and begins its 8.21 with the rest of the chapter, 'Most justly have these things happened unto thee'.

passages.casaubon: That which must be the subject of thy consideration, is either the matter itself, or the dogma, or the operation, or the true sense and signification.

nearest.title: Taking a thing apart: matter, form and end

passages.greek:
Ἐξάλειψον τὴν φαντασίαν. στῆσον τὴν νευροσπαστίαν. περίγραψον τὸ ἐνεστὼς τοῦ χρόνου. γνώρισον τὸ συμβαῖνον ἢ σοὶ ἢ ἄλλῳ. δίελε καὶ μέρισον τὸ ὑποκείμενον εἰς τὸ αἰτιῶδες καὶ ὑλικόν. ἐννόησον τὴν ἐσχάτην ὥραν. τὸ ἐκείνῳ ἁμαρτηθὲν ἐκεῖ κατάλιπε ὅπου ἡ ἁμαρτία ὑπέστη.

Συμπαρεκτείνειν τὴν νόησιν τοῖς λεγομένοις. εἰσδύεσθαι τὸν νοῦν εἰς τὰ γινόμενα καὶ ποιοῦντα.

Φαίδρυνον σεαυτὸν ἁπλότητι καὶ αἰδοῖ καὶ τῇ πρὸς τὸ ἀνὰ μέσον ἀρετῆς καὶ κακίας ἀδιαφορίᾳ. φίλησον τὸ ἀνθρώπινον γένος. ἀκολούθησον θεῷ.
passages.english:
Wipe out the impression. Stop the pulling of the puppet strings. Draw a line around the present time. Recognise what is happening, whether to you or to another. Take the thing before you apart and divide it into what causes and what is matter. Think of the last hour. The wrong that person did, leave it there, where the wrong came to be.

To stretch thinking out alongside what is being said. To have the mind get inside the things that come about and the things that act.

Brighten yourself with simplicity and modesty and with indifference towards what lies between virtue and vice. Love the human race. Follow god.

notes.note: The word means the working of a puppet by its cords. The image is kept; what pulls the strings (impulses, passions) is not said here.
notes.other_reading: Stop being jerked about like a puppet.

notes.note: περιγράφω is to draw a line around, and so to mark off or to limit. The drawing of the line is kept; “the present of time” is given as “the present time”.
notes.other_reading: Limit yourself to the present moment.

notes.note: The verb covers both coming to know a thing and recognising it for what it is. The command is for a single act, so the English reads “recognise”.
notes.other_reading: Get to know what is happening

notes.greek: τὸ ὑποκείμενον εἰς τὸ αἰτιῶδες καὶ ὑλικόν
notes.note: τὸ ὑποκείμενον is literally “what lies under”, the object in front of one. The causal and the material are the two Stoic principles, the active cause and the matter it works on; one article covers both.
notes.other_reading: divide the underlying object into the causal and the material

notes.note: The dative is taken as the doer (“the wrong done by that one”), and the English reads “that person” since the form need not single out a man. The dative could just possibly be the one wronged.
notes.other_reading: The wrong done to that person

notes.note: Literally “took its stand” or “came into existence”. The point is that the wrong exists in the one who did it.
notes.other_reading: where the wrong has its footing

notes.note: The two sentences of this chapter are infinitives used as instructions, with no “you”; they are kept impersonal. νόησις is given as “thinking” to keep it apart from νοῦς, “mind”, in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: Keep your thinking in step with what is being said.

notes.note: The verb is to get into a thing, to slip or sink inside it. The English keeps the “in” and adds no “down”.
notes.other_reading: To have the mind sink into

notes.note: Literally “the things coming about and making”, under one article, and the second has no object. ποιεῖν is the Stoic verb for what acts as a cause; the English reads “the things that act” and supplies no object, so the Greek is not tied to the causes of just those events.
notes.other_reading: into the things that come about and the things that make them

notes.note: The verb is to make bright, and so also to wash clean or to cheer. The brightness is kept.
notes.other_reading: Cleanse yourself with simplicity

notes.note: αἰδώς is the sense of shame that holds a person back from what is unworthy. “Modesty” narrows it.
notes.other_reading: a sense of shame; self-respect

notes.note: No article: “god” or “a god”. Lower case as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: Follow a god.

check.note: The verb here is to recognise what is happening for what it is, in a single act, not a gradual getting acquainted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Recognise what is happening”. The Greek command is in the form used for one act, and “get to know” describes a slow process.

check.note: One article covers both participles and the second has no object. “Them” is supplied and fixes the makers as the causes of exactly those events.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “them” is removed, but “the things that bring about” is not English without an object. The English now reads “the things that come about and the things that act”, which leaves the second word as open as the Greek, and the note gives the reading with “them”.

check.note: The verb is to get inside, to slip or sink into. The “down” is not in the word, the “in” is.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To have the mind get inside”. The Greek prefix means “into”, and nothing in the word says “down”.

part.left_out: ἐκεῖνος μέν φησιν ὅτι ʽπάντα νομιστί, ἐτεῇ δὲ μόνα τὰ στοιχεῖαʼ, ἀρκεῖ δὲ μεμνῆσθαι ὅτι τὰ πάντα νομιστὶ ἔχει· ἤδη λίαν ὀλίγα.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 7.21 at 'love mankind; obey God' and begins its 7.22 with the rest of chapter 7.31, 'All things (saith he) are by certain order'.

passages.casaubon: Wipe off all opinion stay the force and violence of unreasonable lusts and affections: circumscribe the present time examine whatsoever it be that is happened, either to thyself or to another: divide all present objects, either in that which is formal or material think of the last hour. That which thy neighbour hath committed, where the guilt of it lieth, there let it rest. Examine in order whatsoever is spoken. Let thy mind penetrate both into the effects, and into the causes. Rejoice thyself with true simplicity, and modesty; and that all middle things between virtue and vice are indifferent unto thee. Finally, love mankind; obey God.

passages.greek: Τέσσαρας μάλιστα τροπὰς τοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ παραφυλακτέον διηνεκῶς καὶ ἐπειδὰν φωράσῃς ἀπαλειπτέον, ἐπιλέγοντα ἐφ’ ἑκάστου οὕτως· τοῦτο τὸ φάντασμα οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον· τοῦτο λυτικὸν κοινωνίας· τοῦτο οὐκ ἀπὸ σαυτοῦ μέλλεις λέγειν· τὸ γὰρ μὴ ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ λέγειν ἐν τοῖς ἀτοπωτάτοις νόμιζε. τέταρτον δέ ἐστι, καθὸ σεαυτῷ ὀνειδιεῖς, ὅτι τοῦτο ἡττωμένου ἐστὶ καὶ ὑποκατακλινομένου τοῦ ἐν σοὶ θειοτέρου μέρους τῇ ἀτιμοτέρᾳ καὶ θνητῇ μοίρᾳ, τῇ τοῦ σώματος καὶ ταῖς τούτου τραχείαις ἢ λείαις κινήσεσιν.
passages.english: Four turns that the ruling part takes must above all be guarded against without a break and, whenever you catch them, wiped away, saying over each one as follows: “This imagining is not necessary.” “This one dissolves community.” “This that you are about to say is not from yourself.” For count it among the most absurd things not to speak from yourself. The fourth is the one for which you will reproach yourself: that this is the mark of the more divine part in you being beaten and lying down under the less worthy and mortal portion, that of the body, and under its rough or smooth movements.

notes.note: Literally “turnings”: turns the ruling part (τὸ ἡγεμονικόν) takes away from its course. The English keeps “turns” and adds no “aside”, which the Greek leaves unsaid.
notes.other_reading: four lapses of the ruling part

notes.note: “Must be wiped off”, the same image of wiping a writing surface clean as ἐξαλείφω elsewhere. The form does not say by whom; the “you” comes only from the verb before it.
notes.other_reading: must be rubbed out

notes.note: Not φαντασία (“impression”) but φάντασμα, which in Stoic usage is a picture in the mind with nothing real behind it. “Imagining” keeps the two apart.
notes.other_reading: This impression is not necessary.

notes.note: Literally “apt to loosen fellowship”. κοινωνία is the noun behind κοινωνικός (“social”); the English reads “community”.
notes.other_reading: This one loosens the bond between people.

notes.greek: τοῦτο οὐκ ἀπὸ σαυτοῦ μέλλεις λέγειν
notes.note: Literally “this you are about to say not from yourself”. “Not from yourself” is taken as the point of the sentence, as the clause that follows shows: the words are not your own real thought.
notes.other_reading: You are not going to say this from yourself.

notes.note: ἄτοπος is literally “out of place”, and so strange or absurd. The English gives the sense, since nothing in the sentence turns on the literal one.
notes.other_reading: among the most out-of-place things

notes.note: The first three turns are each met by a sentence to say; the fourth is put differently, as the ground of a reproach you will make to yourself, and its content follows with ὅτι. The change of construction is kept.
notes.other_reading: The fourth is when you will reproach yourself that this is a case of

notes.note: Literally “this is of the more divine part being beaten”: the Greek genitive says whose sign or whose doing a thing is. The English reads “is the mark of”.
notes.other_reading: that this is the more divine part in you being beaten

notes.note: The verb is to lie down in the lower place, as on a dinner couch, and so to give way to someone. The image is kept as “lying down under”.
notes.other_reading: giving way to

notes.note: Literally “of less honour” or “of less value”, a comparative answering “more divine”.
notes.other_reading: the less honourable and mortal portion

notes.note: “Rough or smooth movements” is school language for pain and pleasure felt in the body; both this and “the portion of the body” are taken to depend on “lying down under”, so “under” is repeated. From memory, unchecked: the wording at this point has been doubted and some editions print something else (“gross pleasures”).
notes.other_reading: and its pains or pleasures

check.note: “Turnings of the ruling part” is not clear English. The Greek means turns away from the right course, lapses or deviations.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Four turns that the ruling part takes”, which is plain English and keeps the Greek image. “Aside” is not added, because the Greek word says only “turn”, and the note gives “lapses”.

check.note: The verb is to be on guard against. “Watched for” can be read as looked forward to.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “guarded against”. The Greek verb is the one for keeping guard, and it cannot mean waiting in hope.

check.note: The word here means absurd or strange. “Out-of-place” gives the make-up of the word, not its sense, and reads oddly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “among the most absurd things”. Nothing in the sentence turns on the literal “out of place”, which is recorded in the note.

check.greek: τοῦτο ἡττωμένου ἐστὶ καὶ ὑποκατακλινομένου τοῦ ἐν σοὶ θειοτέρου μέρους
check.note: The genitive says what a thing is the sign of. “Belongs to … being beaten” does not construe as English, and the second verb is to give way, to take the lower place.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that this is the mark of the more divine part in you being beaten and lying down under”. “The mark of” gives the genitive in plain English; “lying down under” is kept because the Greek verb is a picture of lying in the lower place, and the note gives “giving way to”.

check.note: Found while settling: “the one by which you will reproach yourself” makes the fourth turn the tool of the reproach, where the Greek makes it the ground of it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the one for which you will reproach yourself”. The Greek word means “in respect of which”.

passages.casaubon: Four several dispositions or inclinations there be of the mind and understanding, which to be aware of, thou must carefully observe: and whensoever thou doest discover them, thou must rectify them, saying to thyself concerning every one of them, This imagination is not necessary; this is uncharitable: this thou shalt speak as another man's slave, or instrument; than which nothing can be more senseless and absurd: for the fourth, thou shalt sharply check and upbraid thyself; for that thou doest suffer that more divine part in thee, to become subject and obnoxious to that more ignoble part of thy body, and the gross lusts and concupiscences thereof.

passages.greek: Ἐξάλειφε τὰς φαντασίας συνεχῶς σεαυτῷ λέγων· νῦν ἐπ’ ἐμοί ἐστιν ἵνα ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ψυχῇ μηδεμία πονηρία ᾖ μηδὲ ἐπιθυμία μηδὲ ὅλως ταραχή τις, ἀλλὰ βλέπων πάντα ὁποῖά ἐστι χρῶμαι ἑκάστῳ κατ’ ἀξίαν. μέμνησο ταύτης τῆς ἐξουσίας κατὰ φύσιν.
passages.english: Keep wiping out impressions, saying to yourself continually: “Now it is up to me that in this soul there be no wickedness, no craving and no disturbance at all, but that, seeing what kind of thing everything is, I use each according to its worth.” Remember this power in accordance with nature.

notes.note: “Continually” can go with “wipe out” or with “saying”. It is put with “saying”, which it stands next to; “keep wiping out” gives the form of the command, which is the one for an action that goes on.
notes.other_reading: Keep wiping out impressions continually, saying to yourself

notes.note: ἐπ’ ἐμοί is the Stoic phrase for what is in a person’s own power; the ἵνα clause gives what is in that power, a later Greek use.
notes.other_reading: Now it lies in my power that

notes.note: ἐπιθυμία is appetite or craving, one of the passions. “Desire” is kept for ὄρεξις, which is used in other passages of this section.
notes.other_reading: no desire

notes.note: ὁποῖα is “of what kind”: seeing the sort of thing each is comes before using each according to its worth.
notes.other_reading: seeing all things as they are

notes.note: The form is the same in the indicative and the subjunctive. It is taken as subjunctive, still hanging on the words before “that”, because the “but” answers the three things the soul is to be without; as indicative it would be a new statement of what is already done.
notes.other_reading: instead, seeing what kind of thing everything is, I use each according to its worth

notes.note: ἀξία is the worth or value a thing has. The phrase is “according to its worth”, not “as it deserves” in a moral sense.
notes.other_reading: I deal with each as it deserves

notes.note: “In accordance with nature” stands at the end with no article. It can describe the power (one you have by nature) or the remembering or using of it; the English leaves it as loose as the Greek.
notes.other_reading: Remember this power, as nature would have you.

check.note: The word stands between the command and “saying” and can go with either. The English puts it with “saying”, while the form of the command already means “keep wiping”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Keep wiping out impressions, saying to yourself continually”. “Keep” gives the form of the command, and “continually” stays with “saying”, the word it stands next to; the note gives the other reading. “Your” is not added, since the Greek has only “the impressions”.

check.note: The Greek is “of what kind”: seeing what sort of thing each is, which is what makes it possible to value each by its worth. “As they are” is weaker.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “seeing what kind of thing everything is”. “Everything” keeps the Greek “all”, which the suggested wording left out.

check.note: The form may continue “it is up to me that”, something still to be done, where the English states it as a fact.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but that, seeing what kind of thing everything is”, with the using still depending on what is up to the speaker. The Greek “but” answers the “no … no … no” of the clause before, so it most naturally carries that clause on; the note gives the other reading.

check.note: The phrase stands at the end with no article and may go with “power” or with the verb. The relative clause “which is” is not in the Greek and fixes one reading.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Remember this power in accordance with nature.” The added “which is” is gone, and the phrase hangs as loosely in the English as in the Greek; the note sets out the two ways of taking it.

passages.casaubon: Wipe off all idle fancies, and say unto thyself incessantly; Now if I will, it is in my power to keep out of this my soul all wickedness, all lust, and concupiscences, all trouble and confusion. But on the contrary to behold and consider all things according to their true nature, and to carry myself towards everything according to its true worth. Remember then this thy power that nature hath given thee.

passages.greek: Πειρῶ μὲν πείθειν αὐτούς, πρᾶττε δὲ καὶ ἀκόντων, ὅταν τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὁ λόγος οὕτως ἄγῃ. ἐὰν μέντοι βίᾳ τις προσχρώμενος ἐνίστηται, μετάβαινε ἐπὶ τὸ εὐάρεστον καὶ ἄλυπον καὶ συγχρῶ εἰς ἄλλην ἀρετὴν τῇ κωλύσει, καὶ μέμνησο ὅτι μεθ’ ὑπεξαιρέσεως ὥρμας καὶ ὅτι τῶν ἀδυνάτων οὐκ ὠρέγου. τίνος οὖν; τῆς τοιᾶσδέ τινος ὁρμῆς. τούτου δὲ τυγχάνεις· ἐφ’ οἷς προήχθημεν, ταῦτα γίνεται.
passages.english: Try to persuade them, but act even against their will whenever the reasoning of justice leads that way. If, however, someone uses force and stands in the way, change over to being content and free of distress, and use the hindrance for another virtue; and remember that your impulse was with a reservation, and that you were not desiring what is impossible. What were you desiring, then? An impulse of some such kind. And this you attain: the things we were led forward for, these come about.

notes.note: “Them” is not explained; the Greek does not say who they are.
notes.other_reading: Try to persuade people

notes.note: Literally “the reason of justice”: what justice, reasoned out, requires. “Reasoning” keeps λόγος close to “reason”, as in the glossary, and leaves “principle” for δόγμα.
notes.other_reading: whenever the principle of justice leads that way

notes.note: Two neuter adjectives used as states: being well pleased with what comes, and being without pain of mind.
notes.other_reading: pass over to contentment and calm

notes.greek: συγχρῶ εἰς ἄλλην ἀρετὴν τῇ κωλύσει
notes.note: Literally “make use of the hindrance towards another virtue”: the block on the just act becomes material for a different virtue. The Greek does not name it.
notes.other_reading: turn the hindrance to the exercise of another virtue

notes.note: ὑπεξαίρεσις is the Stoic “reservation”: an impulse (ὁρμή) made with the unspoken clause “if nothing prevents”. The one word is kept.
notes.other_reading: that you set out conditionally

notes.note: Literally “Of what, then?”, the case depending on “you were desiring” just before. The verb is repeated so that the question stands in English; “were you desiring” is added.
notes.other_reading: What, then?

notes.note: “An impulse of some such kind”, that is, an impulse with a reservation: what was wanted was the impulse itself, not the outcome.
notes.other_reading: Just such an effort as this.

notes.note: The hardest clause. προάγω is to lead forward, and the preposition with this case gives the purpose or the terms, not a place reached; the Greek does not say who did the leading, and it changes without warning from “you” to the first person plural. It can be read of what the impulse set out for, of what human beings were brought into being for, or of the terms on which the impulse was made.
notes.other_reading: what human beings were brought into being for, that is being done

check.note: “The reason of justice” is not English a reader will understand. The Greek is the reasoning or principle of justice, what justice requires on reflection.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the reasoning of justice”. That is clear and keeps the Greek word with “reason”, as the glossary has it; “principle” is not used because the glossary keeps it for another Greek word.

check.note: The Greek is two words, “Of what, then?”. With the verb supplied, the answer makes “desiring an impulse”, which the Greek is said to leave looser.
check.decided: Declined: the English still reads “What were you desiring, then?”. The Greek question word is in the case that the verb “desire” takes, and the answer is in the same case, so the Greek itself makes the impulse the thing desired. The note says which words are added.

check.note: The preposition with this case is “for the purposes for which” or “on the terms on which”, not a destination. The English takes it as a goal reached and is obscure, and the Greek does not explain the plural or who did the leading.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the things we were led forward for, these come about”. The Greek construction gives a purpose, not a place arrived at; “led forward” is kept for the verb, and the note sets out what the Greek leaves open.

passages.casaubon: Let us do our best endeavours to persuade them; but however, if reason and justice lead thee to it, do it, though they be never so much against it. But if any shall by force withstand thee, and hinder thee in it, convert thy virtuous inclination from one object unto another, from justice to contented equanimity, and cheerful patience: so that what in the one is thy hindrance, thou mayst make use of it for the exercise of another virtue: and remember that it was with due exception, and reservation, that thou didst at first incline and desire. For thou didst not set thy mind upon things impossible. Upon what then? that all thy desires might ever be moderated with this due kind of reservation. And this thou hast, and mayst always obtain, whether the thing desired be in thy power or no. And what do I care for more, if that for which I was born and brought forth into the world (to rule all my desires with reason and discretion) may be?

passages.greek: Μέμνησο ὅτι ἀκαταμάχητον γίνεται τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, ὅταν εἰς ἑαυτὸ συστραφὲν ἀρκεσθῇ ἑαυτῷ, μὴ ποιοῦν τι ὃ μὴ θέλει, κἂν ἀλόγως παρατάξηται. τί οὖν, ὅταν καὶ μετὰ λόγου καὶ περιεσκεμμένως κρίνῃ περί τινος; διὰ τοῦτο ἀκρόπολίς ἐστιν ἡ ἐλευθέρα παθῶν διάνοια· οὐδὲν γὰρ ὀχυρώτερον ἔχει ἄνθρωπος, ἐφ’ ὃ καταφυγὼν ἀνάλωτος λοιπὸν ἂν εἴη. ὁ μὲν οὖν μὴ ἑωρακὼς τοῦτο ἀμαθής, ὁ δὲ ἑωρακὼς καὶ μὴ καταφεύγων ἀτυχής.
passages.english: Remember that the ruling part becomes unconquerable when, gathered into itself, it is content with itself, not doing anything it does not want to do, even if it takes its stand without reason. What, then, when it judges about something with reason as well, and after looking all round it? This is why the mind free of passions is a citadel, for a human being has nothing better fortified to flee to, where they would from then on be beyond capture. So whoever has not seen this is ignorant, and whoever has seen it and does not flee to it is unfortunate.

notes.note: The participle is of something twisted or rolled together, as troops close up or an animal coils. The English reads “gathered into itself”.
notes.other_reading: when it has turned in on itself

notes.note: παρατάσσομαι is to draw up in line of battle, which goes with “unconquerable”. The sense is that it cannot be forced even when its resistance is mere stubbornness; “takes its stand” keeps something of the battle line.
notes.other_reading: even if it draws up its line without reason

notes.note: The first καί can be “also”, answering “without reason” just before, or the first half of “both … and”. The English takes it as “as well”, which marks the step from the weaker case to the stronger.
notes.other_reading: when it judges about something both with reason and after looking all round it

notes.note: Literally “having looked round”: with circumspection.
notes.other_reading: with reason and deliberately

notes.note: The glossary gives “thought” and allows “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here the faculty is meant, and νοῦς does not occur in the passage.
notes.other_reading: thought that is free of passions is a citadel

notes.note: πάθη in the Stoic sense: the disturbing emotions such as fear, craving, grief.
notes.other_reading: free of emotions

notes.note: ὀχυρός is said of a place that is fortified and hard to take, so the word carries on the citadel. The Greek has the adjective alone, with no noun for “stronghold”.
notes.other_reading: a human being has nothing stronger

notes.greek: ἐφ’ ὃ καταφυγὼν ἀνάλωτος λοιπὸν ἂν εἴη
notes.note: Literally “to which having fled for refuge he would thereafter be not to be taken”. The fleeing and the safety are split between two clauses, and “they” stands for the unmarked “human being”.
notes.other_reading: nothing better fortified in which to take refuge and be impregnable from then on

notes.note: Literally “without good fortune”. It may be said with some edge, of one who has the refuge and does not use it.
notes.other_reading: is wretched

check.note: The verb is to take one’s stand against, to resist. The literal battle line is obscure here, and the Greek tense is not “has drawn up”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “even if it takes its stand without reason”. The Greek verb form is not a past, and “takes its stand” is clear while still sounding of the battlefield; the note gives the literal line of battle.

check.note: The first “and” in the Greek means “also” and answers “without reason” just before. The English drops it, and with it the step from the weaker case to the stronger.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “when it judges about something with reason as well, and after looking all round it”. “As well” is placed after “with reason”, the words it belongs to; the note records that the Greek can also be read as “both … and”.

check.note: The word is said of a stronghold: secure, hard to take. It carries on the citadel, which “stronger” loses, and the Greek “for” is left to a colon.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “for a human being has nothing better fortified to flee to”. “For” is restored and “better fortified” carries on the citadel; “stronghold” is not added, because the Greek has only the adjective.

passages.casaubon: Remember that thy mind is of that nature as that it becometh altogether unconquerable, when once recollected in herself, she seeks no other content than this, that she cannot be forced: yea though it so fall out, that it be even against reason itself, that it cloth bandy. How much less when by the help of reason she is able to judge of things with discretion? And therefore let thy chief fort and place of defence be, a mind free from passions. A stronger place, (whereunto to make his refuge, and so to become impregnable) and better fortified than this, hath no man. He that seeth not this is unlearned. He that seeth it, and betaketh not himself to this place of refuge, is unhappy.

passages.greek: Μήτε ἐν ταῖς πράξεσιν ἐπισύρειν μήτε ἐν ταῖς ὁμιλίαις φύρειν μήτε ἐν ταῖς φαντασίαις ἀλᾶσθαι μήτε τῇ ψυχῇ καθάπαξ συνέλκεσθαι ἢ ἐκθόρνυσθαι μήτε ἐν τῷ βίῳ ἀσχολεῖσθαι.
passages.english: Not to be slovenly in actions, not to make a muddle in dealings with people, not to wander in impressions, not to shrink together or leap out in the soul at all, not to be without leisure in life.

notes.note: The whole passage is a string of infinitives used as instructions, with no “you”; it is kept impersonal. This verb is literally to drag or trail, and so to do a thing in a careless, trailing way.
notes.other_reading: Not to drag in actions

notes.note: φύρω is to mix up or knead together, and so to confuse. ὁμιλίαι can be conversations or dealings with people generally; the English takes the wider sense, which includes talk.
notes.other_reading: not to be confused in conversation

notes.note: To wander or rove. The Greek says “in impressions” (φαντασίαι), not “in thoughts”.
notes.other_reading: not to stray among impressions

notes.note: “Once for all”, and with a negative “not at all”. It is taken with both verbs that follow.
notes.other_reading: nor, in a word, to shrink together or leap out in the soul

notes.note: Literally “to be drawn together or to leap out”: the soul contracting (as in grief or fear) and bursting out (as in elation or anger). Both are kept as bodily images.
notes.other_reading: to be cast down or carried away

notes.note: ἀσχολία is the lack of leisure, being taken up with business.
notes.other_reading: not to be all business in life

check.note: The word can also be “conversations”: not to be confused in talk. The English takes the wider sense, which is defensible.
check.decided: Declined: the English still reads “in dealings with people”. The Greek word covers all keeping company with others, of which talk is one part, so the wider word shuts nothing out; the note gives “in conversation”.

part.left_out: Κτείνουσι, κρεανομοῦσι, κατάραις ἐλαύνουσι. τί οὖν ταῦτα πρὸς τὸ τὴν διάνοιαν μένειν καθαράν, φρενήρη, σώφρονα, δικαίαν; οἷον εἴ τις παραστὰς πηγῇ διαυγεῖ καὶ γλυκείᾳ βλασφημοίη αὐτήν, ἡ δὲ οὐ παύεται πότιμον ἀναβλύζουσα· κἂν πηλὸν ἐμβάλῃ, κἂν κοπρίαν, τάχιστα διασκεδάσει αὐτὰ καὶ ἐκκλύσει καὶ οὐδαμῶς βαφήσεται. πῶς οὖν πηγὴν ἀέναον ἕξεις καὶ μὴ φρέαρ; ἂν φυλάσσῃς σεαυτὸν πάσης ὥρας εἰς ἐλευθερίαν μετὰ τοῦ εὐμενῶς καὶ ἁπλῶς καὶ αἰδημόνως.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 8.49 at 'nor ever to want employment' and begins its 8.50 with the rest of the chapter, 'They kill me, they cut my flesh'.

passages.casaubon: Not to be slack and negligent; or loose, and wanton in thy actions; nor contentious, and troublesome in thy conversation; nor to rove and wander in thy fancies and imaginations. Not basely to contract thy soul; nor boisterously to sally out with it, or furiously to launch out as it were, nor ever to want employment.

passages.greek:
Λῃστὴς προαιρέσεως οὐ γίνεται· τὸ τοῦ Ἐπικτήτου.

Τέχνην, ἔφη, δεῖ περὶ τὸ συγκατατίθεσθαι εὑρεῖν καὶ ἐν τῷ περὶ τὰς ὁρμὰς τόπῳ τὸ προσεκτικὸν φυλάσσειν, ἵνα μεθ’ ὑπεξαιρέσεως, ἵνα κοινωνικαί, ἵνα κατ’ ἀξίαν, καὶ ὀρέξεως μὲν παντάπασιν ἀπέχεσθαι, ἐκκλίσει δὲ πρὸς μηδὲν τῶν οὐκ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν χρῆσθαι.

Οὐ περὶ τοῦ τυχόντος οὖν, ἔφη, ἐστὶν ὁ ἀγών, ἀλλὰ περὶ τοῦ μαίνεσθαι ἢ μή.
passages.english:
“There is no robber of the power to choose.” That is the saying of Epictetus.

“One must find an art,” he said, “for giving assent, and in the field of the impulses keep up attention, so that they are with a reservation, so that they are social, so that they are according to worth; and keep away from desire altogether, and use aversion towards none of the things that are not up to us.”

“So the contest,” he said, “is not about just anything, but about being mad or not.”

notes.note: Literally “a robber of choice does not come to be”: no one can rob a person of their choice. From memory, unchecked: the words are in the Discourses of Epictetus, the Stoic teacher (about AD 50 to 135).
notes.other_reading: No one can rob you of your choice.

notes.note: προαίρεσις is the word Epictetus uses for the faculty of choosing, the one thing that is fully one’s own. The English reads “the power to choose”, because “a robber of choice” would be heard today as “a favourite robber”.
notes.other_reading: a robber of the will

notes.note: τέχνη is an art or skill with rules. The sentence depends on δεῖ, “it is necessary”, with no person named; the English reads “one must” and lets the one phrase carry all four verbs, as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: We must find a method for assenting

notes.greek: ἐν τῷ περὶ τὰς ὁρμὰς τόπῳ
notes.note: τόπος (“place”) is the term Epictetus uses for one of the fields of training: assent, impulse, and desire and aversion. The English reads “field”.
notes.other_reading: in the topic concerning the impulses

notes.note: Literally “to guard the attentive [power]”: to keep attention awake.
notes.other_reading: to keep watch over the power of attention

notes.greek: ἵνα μεθ’ ὑπεξαιρέσεως, ἵνα κοινωνικαί, ἵνα κατ’ ἀξίαν
notes.note: The three clauses have no verb; “they are” is supplied, the impulses being the subject. ὑπεξαίρεσις is the “reservation” (“if nothing prevents”); κατ’ ἀξίαν is “according to the worth” of the thing aimed at.
notes.other_reading: so that they are conditional, for the common good, and in proportion to worth

notes.greek: ὀρέξεως μὲν παντάπασιν ἀπέχεσθαι, ἐκκλίσει δὲ
notes.note: ὄρεξις (“desire”, reaching for a thing) and ἔκκλισις (“aversion”, turning from a thing) are a fixed pair. “Altogether” is kept as the Greek has it.
notes.other_reading: to abstain entirely from desire, and to turn away from nothing that is not up to us

notes.note: Literally “about what happens along”: any ordinary matter. “Not about just anything” gives the idiom in the English that matches it.
notes.other_reading: is not about some trivial thing

notes.note: A contest, as in the games or in court, and so a struggle.
notes.other_reading: So the struggle

check.note: In today’s English “a robber of choice” can be misread as “a favourite robber”. The Greek means that nobody comes to be a robber of one’s power of choosing.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “There is no robber of the power to choose.”, which cannot be misread. The suggested “No one can rob you of your choice” adds “can”, “you” and “your”, none of which is in the Greek, and it loses the robber as a noun; it is given in the note.

check.note: The Greek phrase is the idiom for the ordinary or trivial: “no ordinary matter”. “Any chance thing” is word for word and not clear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “is not about just anything”. That is plain English for the Greek idiom, which is literally “whatever happens along”, and it stays closer to it than “trivial”; the note gives “some trivial thing”.

check.note: Found while settling: “desire must be kept away from altogether” is hard to read as English and can be heard as keeping desire away from something.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now runs on “One must find … keep up … keep away from … use”, so that the English reads “and keep away from desire altogether”. The Greek has one “it is necessary” governing all four verbs, with no person named.

passages.casaubon: 'Of the free will there is no thief or robber:' out of Epictetus; Whose is this also: that we should find a certain art and method of assenting; and that we should always observe with great care and heed the inclinations of our minds, that they may always be with their due restraint and reservation, always charitable, and according to the true worth of every present object. And as for earnest longing, that we should altogether avoid it: and to use averseness in those things only, that wholly depend of our own wills. It is not about ordinary petty matters, believe it, that all our strife and contention is, but whether, with the vulgar, we should be mad, or by the help of philosophy wise and sober, said he.

passages.greek: Μὴ ἀπορρέμβεσθαι, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ πάσης ὁρμῆς τὸ δίκαιον ἀποδιδόναι καὶ ἐπὶ πάσης φαντασίας σῴζειν τὸ καταληπτικόν.
passages.english: Not to roam away, but at every impulse to give what is just, and at every impression to keep the sure grasp.

notes.note: ῥέμβομαι is to roam or spin about; with ἀπο-, to roam off. The sentence is infinitives used as instructions, kept impersonal.
notes.other_reading: Not to be whirled off course

notes.greek: ἐπὶ πάσης ὁρμῆς τὸ δίκαιον ἀποδιδόναι
notes.note: ἀποδίδωμι is to give what is owed. ἐπί with the genitive is “in the case of” every impulse.
notes.other_reading: in every impulse to render what is just

notes.note: A Stoic term: the impression that is καταληπτική is the one that grasps its object so clearly that it cannot be false. Literally “to keep safe the grasping [quality]”: the sure grasp is a quality of the impression, not the thing grasped.
notes.other_reading: to preserve the power of sure apprehension

check.note: The word is the active form, what grasps or gives a sure grasp, the mark of the impression that can be trusted. The English turns the quality of the grasp into the object grasped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to keep the sure grasp”. The ending of the Greek word marks a power of grasping, not a thing that has been grasped.

passages.casaubon: Not to wander out of the way, but upon every motion and desire, to perform that which is just: and ever to be careful to attain to the true natural apprehension of every fancy, that presents itself.

passages.greek: Κτείνουσι, κρεανομοῦσι, κατάραις ἐλαύνουσι. τί οὖν ταῦτα πρὸς τὸ τὴν διάνοιαν μένειν καθαράν, φρενήρη, σώφρονα, δικαίαν; οἷον εἴ τις παραστὰς πηγῇ διαυγεῖ καὶ γλυκείᾳ βλασφημοίη αὐτήν, ἡ δὲ οὐ παύεται πότιμον ἀναβλύζουσα· κἂν πηλὸν ἐμβάλῃ, κἂν κοπρίαν, τάχιστα διασκεδάσει αὐτὰ καὶ ἐκκλύσει καὶ οὐδαμῶς βαφήσεται. πῶς οὖν πηγὴν ἀέναον ἕξεις καὶ μὴ φρέαρ; ἂν φυλάσσῃς σεαυτὸν πάσης ὥρας εἰς ἐλευθερίαν μετὰ τοῦ εὐμενῶς καὶ ἁπλῶς καὶ αἰδημόνως.
passages.english: They kill, they cut up like meat, they hound with curses. What, then, is that to the mind staying clean, sane, self-controlled, just? It is as if someone stood beside a clear, sweet spring and insulted it, yet it does not stop welling up with water fit to drink; even if they throw in mud, even if dung, it will very quickly scatter these and wash them out, and will in no way be stained. How, then, will you have an ever-flowing spring and not a well? If you guard yourself at every hour so as to be free, and with that to act kindly, simply and modestly.

notes.note: Three verbs with no subject and no object: “they” are unnamed, and the Greek does not say whom they kill. Nothing is added.
notes.other_reading: They kill you, cut you to pieces, drive you out with curses.

notes.note: Literally “they divide up as meat”, the word for portioning a carcass. The meat is kept.
notes.other_reading: they butcher

notes.note: Literally “what, then, are these things towards the mind’s remaining”: what bearing do they have on it.
notes.other_reading: How does that stop the mind from staying

notes.note: “Mind” rather than the glossary’s “thought”, because the faculty is meant and νοῦς does not occur here.
notes.other_reading: to your thought staying clean

notes.note: φρενήρης is “sound in mind”; σώφρων is the virtue of self-control or moderation.
notes.other_reading: sound, temperate

notes.note: The comparison has no main clause of its own (“as if someone …”), and the construction then passes to plain statements about the spring. “It is” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: As if someone standing by a clear, sweet spring were to abuse it

notes.note: βλασφημέω is abuse in words. “Insulted” makes that plain and keeps it apart from the “curses” of the first sentence, which are another Greek word.
notes.other_reading: and cursed it

notes.note: Literally “will be dyed”: take the colour of what is thrown in.
notes.other_reading: will in no way be dyed

notes.note: A dug well or cistern of standing water, as against a spring that flows of itself.
notes.other_reading: and not a cistern

notes.greek: ἂν φυλάσσῃς σεαυτὸν πάσης ὥρας εἰς ἐλευθερίαν
notes.note: As given: “if you guard yourself at every hour for freedom”, the εἰς being the end you are guarded for; the English reads “so as to be free”. From memory, unchecked: the verb has been doubted and another verb (“grow”) proposed.
notes.other_reading: If at every hour you grow into freedom

notes.greek: μετὰ τοῦ εὐμενῶς καὶ ἁπλῶς καὶ αἰδημόνως
notes.note: Literally “together with the kindly and simply and modestly”, three adverbs under one article, with no verb. “To act” is supplied to carry them, and “with that” gives “together with”: the three go along with the freedom.
notes.other_reading: for freedom, together with kindness, simplicity and modesty

check.note: The verb is abuse in words, to curse or revile, which matters because mud and dung come next as a further step. “Abused” can be read as physical.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “insulted it”, which can only be abuse in words. “Cursed” is not used because the first sentence already has “curses” for a different Greek word, and the echo would be false.

check.note: The Greek is “even if … even if”, where the English has a plain “and if … or” and loses the rising force. The “yet” before it is likewise flattened to “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “yet it does not stop welling up” and “even if they throw in mud, even if dung”. Both Greek words mark a contrast that the plain “and” left out; “they” is kept for the unnamed “someone”.

check.greek: ἂν φυλάσσῃς σεαυτὸν πάσης ὥρας εἰς ἐλευθερίαν
check.note: “Keep yourself for freedom” is hard to follow. The verb is to guard and the preposition gives the end, and the three adverbs that follow say how, not three things kept alongside freedom.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “If you guard yourself at every hour so as to be free, and with that to act kindly, simply and modestly.” “Guard” and “so as to be free” are taken, and the three stay adverbs; but the Greek joins them to freedom with “together with”, so they are not made the manner of the guarding.

part.left_out: Μήτε ἐν ταῖς πράξεσιν ἐπισύρειν μήτε ἐν ταῖς ὁμιλίαις φύρειν μήτε ἐν ταῖς φαντασίαις ἀλᾶσθαι μήτε τῇ ψυχῇ καθάπαξ συνέλκεσθαι ἢ ἐκθόρνυσθαι μήτε ἐν τῷ βίῳ ἀσχολεῖσθαι.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the chapter's opening list of things to avoid in its section 8.49 and begins its 8.50 here, at 'They kill me, they cut my flesh'.

passages.casaubon: 'They kill me, they cut my flesh; they persecute my person with curses.' What then? May not thy mind for all this continue pure, prudent, temperate, just? As a fountain of sweet and clear water, though she be cursed by some stander by, yet do her springs nevertheless still run as sweet and clear as before; yea though either dirt or dung be thrown in, yet is it no sooner thrown, than dispersed, and she cleared. She cannot be dyed or infected by it. What then must I do, that I may have within myself an overflowing fountain, and not a well? Beget thyself by continual pains and endeavours to true liberty with charity, and true simplicity and modesty.

passages.greek: Ἀναγινώσκειν οὐκ ἔξεστιν. ἀλλὰ ὕβριν ἀνείργειν ἔξεστιν· ἀλλὰ ἡδονῶν καὶ πόνων καθυπερτερεῖν ἔξεστιν· ἀλλὰ τοῦ δοξαρίου ὑπεράνω εἶναι ἔξεστιν· ἀλλὰ ἀναισθήτοις καὶ ἀχαρίστοις μὴ θυμοῦσθαι, προσέτι κήδεσθαι αὐτῶν ἔξεστιν.
passages.english: It is not possible to read. But it is possible to hold back insolence. But it is possible to get the better of pleasures and pains. But it is possible to be above petty reputation. But it is possible not to be angry with the insensitive and the ungrateful, and more than that, to care for them.

notes.note: ἔξεστιν is “it is allowed” or “it is possible”, with no person named. It is kept impersonal, with one phrase for all five occurrences.
notes.other_reading: You are not free to read.

notes.note: ὕβρις is insolence or overbearing behaviour; the Greek does not say whose. The verb is to keep back or shut out.
notes.other_reading: to keep arrogance out

notes.note: πόνος is toil and also pain. Paired with “pleasures”, it is taken as pains.
notes.other_reading: pleasures and hardships

notes.note: A diminutive of δόξα (“reputation”) used with contempt.
notes.other_reading: to be above your little bit of fame

notes.note: Literally “without perception”: people who are dull, or who do not feel what is done for them. “Insensitive” can be heard both ways.
notes.other_reading: the stupid and the ungrateful

check.note: The word is as often “without perception, dull, stupid” as “callous”. “Unfeeling” picks the second.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the insensitive”, which covers both failing to notice and failing to feel, as the Greek word does. “Insensible” is not used because today it means unconscious; the note gives “the stupid”.

passages.casaubon: Thou hast no time nor opportunity to read. What then? Hast thou not time and opportunity to exercise thyself, not to wrong thyself; to strive against all carnal pleasures and pains, and to get the upper hand of them; to contemn honour and vainglory; and not only, not to be angry with them, whom towards thee thou doest find unsensible and unthankful; but also to have a care of them still, and of their welfare?

passages.greek: Ἐξαλεῖψαι φαντασίαν· στῆσαι ὁρμήν· σβέσαι ὄρεξιν· ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ ἔχειν τὸ ἡγεμονικόν.
passages.english: To wipe out an impression. To stop an impulse. To quench desire. To keep the ruling part in one’s own power.

notes.note: The four phrases are infinitives used as instructions, with no “you”; they are kept impersonal. The Greek nouns have no article; English needs one for “impression” and “impulse”, and can do without for “desire”.
notes.other_reading: Wipe out the impression.

notes.note: The verb is to put out a fire. ὄρεξις is desire, the reaching for a thing.
notes.other_reading: To extinguish appetite.

notes.note: The reflexive can point to the unnamed person (“in one’s own power”) or to the ruling part (“in its own power”). It is taken of the person, the one who is to do the keeping, which is the regular use of the word.
notes.other_reading: To keep the ruling part in its own power.

check.note: The singular without an article is not English (“To wipe out impression”, “To stop impulse”). The Greek has no article, but English needs one or a plural.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To wipe out an impression. To stop an impulse.” “To quench desire” stays as it was, since English allows that noun to stand bare, as the Greek does.

check.note: The reflexive can refer to the unexpressed subject of the verb, the person: “in one’s own power”. The English makes it the ruling part’s own power.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To keep the ruling part in one’s own power.” A Greek reflexive regularly points back to the one who does the action, here the person who is to keep the ruling part; the note gives the other reading.

passages.casaubon: To wipe away fancy, to use deliberation, to quench concupiscence, to keep the mind free to herself.

passages.greek: Μηδὲν ἐνέργημα εἰκῇ μηδὲ ἄλλως ἢ κατὰ θεώρημα συμπληρωτικὸν τῆς τέχνης ἐνεργείσθω.
passages.english: Let no act be done at random, or otherwise than according to a rule that goes to make up the art.

notes.note: Noun and verb are from one root (ἐνέργημα … ἐνεργείσθω), literally “let no activity be acted”. English cannot keep the echo without stiffness.
notes.other_reading: Let no action be carried out

notes.note: “At random”, without plan or purpose.
notes.other_reading: without a purpose

notes.note: A θεώρημα is a rule or proposition belonging to an art. The English reads “rule” and leaves “principle” for δόγμα, as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: according to a principle

notes.note: Literally “that helps to fill up the art”: a rule that is one of the parts making the art complete. The art is not named; the art of living is presumably meant.
notes.other_reading: a rule that completes the art

passages.casaubon: Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according to the most exact and perfect rules of art.

passages.greek: Ὅ τι ἄν τις ποιῇ ἢ λέγῃ, ἐμὲ δεῖ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι, ὡς ἂν εἰ ὁ χρυσὸς ἢ ὁ σμάραγδος ἢ ἡ πορφύρα τοῦτο ἀεὶ ἔλεγεν· ὅ τι ἄν τις ποιῇ ἢ λέγῃ, ἐμὲ δεῖ σμάραγδον εἶναι καὶ τὸ ἐμαυτοῦ χρῶμα ἔχειν.
passages.english: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good; just as if gold or emerald or purple were always saying this: “Whatever anyone does or says, I must be emerald and have my own color.”

notes.note: The word covers the purple dye and cloth dyed with it. The English keeps the bare color word, since the point is a thing that has its own color.
notes.other_reading: the purple dye

notes.note: Three things are named, but in the speech only the emerald speaks, and the English does not even this out. The Greek word is a green stone and may not be exactly the emerald of today.
notes.other_reading: I must be an emerald

notes.note: An unreal comparison. The verb is in the past tense of an unreal case, so “were always saying”.
notes.other_reading: as though gold or emerald or purple kept saying

notes.note: The verb is the plain “have”. “Keep”, which the setting suggests, would add the idea of holding on under pressure.
notes.other_reading: and keep my own color

check.note: The Greek verb is the plain “have”; “keep” adds the idea of holding on against pressure, which the setting implies but the Greek does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “have my own color”. The Greek verb is the plain word for having, and the holding on under pressure is left to the setting.

passages.casaubon: Whatsoever any man either doth or saith, thou must be good; not for any man's sake, but for thine own nature's sake; as if either gold, or the emerald, or purple, should ever be saying to themselves, Whatsoever any man either doth or saith, I must still be an emerald, and I must keep my colour.

nearest.title: Being good for its own sake

passages.greek: Ἄξιον ἑαυτὸν κρῖνε παντὸς λόγου καὶ ἔργου τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν καὶ μή σε περισπάτω ἡ ἐπακολουθοῦσά τινων μέμψις ἢ λόγος, ἀλλά, εἰ καλὸν πεπρᾶχθαι ἢ εἰρῆσθαι, μὴ σεαυτὸν ἀπαξίου. ἐκεῖνοι μὲν γὰρ ἴδιον ἡγεμονικὸν ἔχουσι καὶ ἰδίᾳ ὁρμῇ χρῶνται· ἃ σὺ μὴ περιβλέπου, ἀλλ’ εὐθεῖαν πέραινε ἀκολουθῶν τῇ φύσει τῇ ἰδίᾳ καὶ τῇ κοινῇ, μία δὲ ἀμφοτέρων τούτων ἡ ὁδός.
passages.english: Judge yourself worthy of every word and deed that accords with nature, and do not let the blame or the talk that comes afterward from some people pull you away; but if it is a fine thing to have been done or said, do not judge yourself unworthy of it. For those people have a ruling part of their own and act on an impulse of their own. You, for your part, do not look round at those things, but go the straight road right through, following your own nature and the common nature; and the road of these two is one.

notes.note: The verb is built on the same word as “worthy” in the opening words, so the English has “judge yourself worthy” and “do not judge yourself unworthy”. The words “of it” are supplied.
notes.other_reading: do not think it beneath you

notes.note: The article is singular and stands next to “deed”. The English takes it with both “word” and “deed”.
notes.other_reading: of every word, and of every deed that accords with nature

notes.greek: ἡ ἐπακολουθοῦσά τινων μέμψις ἢ λόγος
notes.note: Here the word that elsewhere means “reason” is plainly what people say, so “talk”. The participle is “following upon”, that is, coming after the word or deed; it could also be heard as blame that dogs a person.
notes.other_reading: the blame or the talk of certain people that dogs you

notes.note: Literally to draw off to one side, so to distract. The English keeps the pull, since the passage goes on to a straight road.
notes.other_reading: distract you

notes.note: The word for “fine” covers right, honorable and beautiful. The two verbs are passive and look back on a finished act, “to have been done or said”, and the English keeps them so.
notes.other_reading: if it is right that it should have been done or said

notes.note: Literally “use an impulse of their own”. “Their own” here means private to them, set against “your own nature” below, where the same adjective returns.
notes.other_reading: use an impulse of their own

notes.note: The relative is neuter plural, so it points to their ruling part and their impulse, not to the people: “those things”. The Greek stresses “you” against “those people”, which the English gives as “You, for your part”. “Look round at” is the literal sense of the verb.
notes.other_reading: But you, do not gaze about at them

notes.note: “Straight” is feminine with “road” understood, the road named in the last words, so the English says “road” in both places. The verb is the glossary’s “carry through”, which English does not say of a road; “go right through” keeps its sense of going on to the finish.
notes.other_reading: carry your course straight through

check.greek: ἡ ἐπακολουθοῦσά τινων μέμψις ἢ λόγος
check.note: “Follows from” reads in English as logical consequence. The Greek is the blame or talk of certain people that comes after the word or deed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the blame or the talk that comes afterward from some people”. The participle means coming after the word or deed, and “afterward” says so without a supplied “it”.

check.note: Both verbs are passive, “to have been done or said”. The English made them active.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if it is a fine thing to have been done or said”, with the passive of the Greek.

check.note: The relative is neuter plural, those things (their ruling part and their impulse), but “these” reads as the people. The stressed “you”, which answers “those people”, is also dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “You, for your part, do not look round at those things”. “Those things” cannot be heard as the people, and “for your part” gives the stressed “you” that the Greek sets against “those people”.

check.note: “Straight” has “road” understood and is picked up by “the road” in the last clause. With “course” here and “road” there the link is lost.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “go the straight road right through”, so that “road” stands in both places. “To its end” is not used, because the glossary keeps “through” for this verb and avoids “end”, which can be heard as dying.

passages.casaubon: Think thyself fit and worthy to speak, or to do anything that is according to nature, and let not the reproach, or report of some that may ensue upon it, ever deter thee. If it be right and honest to be spoken or done, undervalue not thyself so much, as to be discouraged from it. As for them, they have their own rational over-ruling part, and their own proper inclination: which thou must not stand and look about to take notice of, but go on straight, whither both thine own particular, and the common nature do lead thee; and the way of both these, is but one.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Δύο ταύτας ἑτοιμότητας ἔχειν ἀεὶ δεῖ· τὴν μὲν πρὸς τὸ πρᾶξαι μόνον ὅπερ ἂν ὁ τῆς βασιλικῆς καὶ νομοθετικῆς λόγος ὑποβάλλῃ ἐπʼ ὠφελείᾳ ἀνθρώπων· τὴν δὲ πρὸς τὸ μεταθέσθαι, ἐὰν ἄρα τις παρῇ διορθῶν καὶ μετάγων ἀπό τινος οἰήσεως. τὴν μέντοι μεταγωγὴν ἀεὶ ἀπό τινος πιθανότητος, ὡς δικαίου ἢ κοινωφελοῦς, γίνεσθαι καὶ τὰ προηγμένα τοιαῦτα μόνον εἶναι δεῖ, οὐχ ὅτι ἡδὺ ἢ ἔνδοξον ἐφάνη.
passages.english: One must always have these two kinds of readiness. The first is to do only what the reason of the kingly and lawgiving art suggests, for the benefit of human beings. The second is to change one’s mind, if it turns out that someone is at hand who sets one right and leads one away from some mistaken notion. But the leading away must always come from something persuasive, as being just or of common benefit, and what is preferred must be of that kind only, not because it appeared pleasant or well thought of.

notes.greek: ὁ τῆς βασιλικῆς καὶ νομοθετικῆς λόγος
notes.note: The two adjectives are feminine with no noun. “Art” is the usual word to supply; “knowledge” is also possible. The phrase may mean the principle of ruling and lawgiving, or reason itself in its role as king and lawgiver.
notes.other_reading: the reason that is king and lawgiver

notes.note: The verb ranges from “suggest” and “prompt” to “dictate”. The English takes the mild end.
notes.other_reading: dictates

notes.note: Literally to shift one’s position. The English has “change one’s mind” here and in 8.16; in 6.21, where the verb answers both judging and acting, it is the bare “change”.
notes.other_reading: to shift one’s ground

notes.note: The small word after “if” marks the case as one that may or may not arise, given as “if it turns out that”.
notes.other_reading: if perhaps someone is at hand

notes.note: The noun is what one supposes to be so, and it usually has a bad sense: a notion held on one’s own say, often with conceit. “Mistaken” carries that bad sense and is not a separate Greek word.
notes.other_reading: from some conceit

notes.greek: ἀπό τινος πιθανότητος, ὡς δικαίου ἢ κοινωφελοῦς
notes.note: Literally “from some persuasiveness, as of a thing just or of common benefit”. The English makes the abstract noun “something persuasive”.
notes.other_reading: from some plausible ground, such as that it is just or serves the common good

notes.note: A passive participle, “things led forward” or “put first”, and as a Stoic term “the preferred things”; the English keeps that plain passive sense. It can also be taken as the things that led one on to the change, the inducements. From memory, unchecked: other editors print a word meaning “the like” here.
notes.other_reading: and what moves one to it must be of that kind only

notes.greek: οὐχ ὅτι ἡδὺ ἢ ἔνδοξον ἐφάνη
notes.note: The second adjective is either “held in repute” or “bringing repute”; set beside “pleasant” the English takes the first, “well thought of”. Both adjectives are singular with no stated subject, given as “it”: the view one changes to.
notes.other_reading: not because it appeared pleasant or glorious

notes.note: The Greek is impersonal throughout, with no “you”. The English keeps “one”, which is stiff but is what the Greek has.
notes.other_reading: You must always have these two kinds of readiness

check.greek: ὁ τῆς βασιλικῆς καὶ νομοθετικῆς λόγος
check.note: “Art” is supplied, since the Greek leaves the feminine noun unsaid; it is acceptable but a choice. The word given as “reason” here is “speech” in 8.30.
check.decided: Declined: “the kingly and lawgiving art” stands, since the two feminine adjectives need a noun in English and “art” is the plainest word for the one most likely understood; the note records the supply. The glossary allows “speech” for the same Greek noun where that is its sense, as in 8.30.

check.note: The small word that marks the case as one that may happen is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if it turns out that someone is at hand”. The Greek marks the case as one that may or may not arise.

check.note: The noun is not a neutral opinion but a fancy or conceit, a mistaken notion one is attached to. “Opinion” is too weak and too neutral.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “from some mistaken notion”. The Greek noun has a bad sense, a thing merely supposed and often held with conceit, and the person in the sentence is being set right about it.

check.note: The English takes the word as the Stoic term “preferred things”, which a reader of today may not follow. It can also be read as the things that led to the change, and the text itself may be in doubt.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “what is preferred”, which is the plain passive sense of the participle (things put first) and reads as ordinary English, not as a term of art. “What moves one to it” needs the participle to be active in sense, which is possible but less natural for a bare noun phrase, so it goes into the note as the other reading, with the doubt about the text.

check.note: One adjective, “well thought of” or “glorious”, is expanded into a phrase, and “likely” is not in the Greek.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “pleasant or well thought of”, one short phrase with no “likely”. “Glorious” is not used because in English of today it also means simply splendid; the note gives it as the other reading.

passages.casaubon: These two rules, thou must have always in a readiness. First, do nothing at all, but what reason proceeding from that regal and supreme part, shall for the good and benefit of men, suggest unto thee. And secondly, if any man that is present shall be able to rectify thee or to turn thee from some erroneous persuasion, that thou be always ready to change thy mind, and this change to proceed, not from any respect of any pleasure or credit thereon depending, but always from some probable apparent ground of justice, or of some public good thereby to be furthered; or from some other such inducement.

nearest.title: Being good for its own sake

passages.greek: Λαλεῖν καὶ ἐν συγκλήτῳ καὶ πρὸς πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν κοσμίως, μὴ περιτράνως· ὑγιεῖ λόγῳ χρῆσθαι.
passages.english: To speak, both in the senate and to anyone at all, with decorum, not over-distinctly; to use sound speech.

notes.note: An infinitive used as a note of what is to be done, with no person, kept as “To speak”. The verb is the everyday word for talking.
notes.other_reading: Speak

notes.note: The adverb covers orderly, decent and modest. Said of how a person behaves it is propriety of manner, so “with decorum”.
notes.other_reading: in an orderly way

notes.note: A very rare word: the simple adjective means clear, distinct, piercing, and the prefix adds “exceedingly” or “too much”. The English takes it of delivery that is too carefully distinct; it may instead be a voice that is too piercing. The sense is not certain.
notes.other_reading: not in a piercing voice

notes.note: Literally “healthy”, the word used of eye and stomach in 10.35; of speech or reasoning English says “sound”. The noun can be speech or reason, and after “to speak” the English takes speech.
notes.other_reading: to use healthy reason

check.note: Said of behavior the adverb is “decently, with decorum, modestly”. “In an orderly way” suggests a well-arranged speech, not a manner.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “with decorum”. The adverb describes the manner of the person speaking, not the arrangement of the speech.

check.note: A rare word for over-distinct, over-articulated or studied delivery; the English makes clarity itself sound like the fault and is hard to follow. The other reading is “not shrilly, not too loudly”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not over-distinctly”, which puts the fault in the delivery, as the simple adjective (clear, distinct, piercing) and its prefix (too much) suggest. “Studied” is not used because the Greek word says only “too distinct”; the note records the other reading, a voice that is too piercing.

check.note: The noun may be “speech” or “reason”, and the English chooses speech. The adjective is the “healthy” word of 10.35, given as “sound” here.
check.decided: Declined: “to use sound speech” stands. The Greek adjective is regularly said of words and arguments in the sense “sound”, “healthy speech” is not plain English, and nothing in this passage depends on the echo of 10.35. The note records “healthy” and the reading “reason”.

passages.casaubon: Whether thou speak in the Senate or whether thou speak to any particular, let thy speech In always grave and modest. But thou must not openly and vulgarly observe that sound and exact form of speaking, concerning that which is truly good and truly civil; the vanity of the world, and of worldly men: which otherwise truth and reason doth prescribe.

nearest.title: Being good for its own sake

passages.greek: Δριμύτητά σου οὐκ ἔχουσι θαυμάσαι· ἔστω, ἀλλὰ ἕτερα πολλά, ἐφ’ ὧν οὐκ ἔχεις εἰπεῖν· οὐ γὰρ πέφυκα. ἐκεῖνα οὖν παρέχου, ἅπερ ὅλα ἐστὶν ἐπὶ σοί, τὸ ἀκίβδηλον, τὸ σεμνόν, τὸ φερέπονον, τὸ ἀφιλήδονον, τὸ ἀμεμψίμοιρον, τὸ ὀλιγοδεές, τὸ εὐμενές, τὸ ἐλεύθερον, τὸ ἀπέρισσον, τὸ ἀφλύαρον, τὸ μεγαλεῖον. οὐκ αἰσθάνῃ πόσα ἤδη παρέχεσθαι δυνάμενος, ἐφ’ ὧν οὐδεμία ἀφυίας καὶ ἀνεπιτηδειότητος πρόφασις, ὅμως ἔτι κάτω μένεις ἑκών; ἢ καὶ γογγύζειν καὶ γλισχρεύεσθαι καὶ κολακεύειν καὶ τὸ σωμάτιον καταιτιᾶσθαι καὶ ἀρεσκεύεσθαι καὶ περπερεύεσθαι καὶ τοσαῦτα ῥιπτάζεσθαι τῇ ψυχῇ διὰ τὸ ἀφυῶς κατεσκευάσθαι ἀναγκάζῃ; οὐ μὰ τοὺς θεούς, ἀλλὰ τούτων μὲν πάλαι ἀπηλλάχθαι ἐδύνασο, μόνον δέ, εἰ ἄρα, ὡς βραδύτερος καὶ δυσπαρακολουθητότερος καταγινώσκεσθαι. καὶ τοῦτο δὲ ἀσκητέον μὴ παρενθυμουμένῳ μηδὲ ἐμφιληδονοῦντι τῇ νωθείᾳ.
passages.english: They cannot admire your sharpness of mind. So be it. But there are many other things of which you cannot say, “Because I am not made for it by nature.” Offer those, then, which are wholly in your power: being genuine, dignity, bearing hard work, not loving pleasure, not complaining of your lot, needing little, kindness, freedom, plainness, no idle talk, greatness. Do you not see how many things you are already able to offer, for which there is no excuse of want of natural gift or of unfitness, and yet you still stay down below of your own will? Or are you actually forced to grumble, to be stingy, to flatter, to blame your poor body, to try to please, to show off and to be tossed about so much in your soul, because you were built without natural gift? No, by the gods. Rather, you could have been rid of these long ago, and be faulted only, if at all, for being rather slow and finding things rather hard to follow. And this too you must work on, not disregarding it and not taking pleasure in your dullness.

notes.note: “They” has no noun: people in general. The noun is sharpness or pungency, here of wit, and “of mind” is added so that it is not heard as harshness. The verb phrase is “they are not able to admire”, which can also be heard as “they have nothing to admire in”.
notes.other_reading: They have no sharpness of yours to admire

notes.note: Literally “for I am not by nature so”: the excuse as it would be spoken, beginning with its “for”, which the English gives as “Because”. The same root returns twice below as “natural gift”.
notes.other_reading: “I cannot, for I was not born for it”

notes.note: A word from coinage and metal: not debased, not counterfeit. “Genuine” is said of coin and of people alike.
notes.other_reading: being unalloyed

notes.note: Literally “having nothing over”, nothing more than is needed. It may be plainness of living or of manner.
notes.other_reading: having nothing in excess

notes.note: Greatness or grandeur, with no noun to say of what, and the English leaves it bare. Greatness of mind is probably meant.
notes.other_reading: high-mindedness

notes.note: Literally “you stay below”, with nothing to say below what: below what you could be, or simply low down. The English keeps the bare image.
notes.other_reading: you still fall short

notes.note: From an adjective meaning sticky, hence close with money, mean, and also clinging or importunate. The English takes the money sense.
notes.other_reading: to be grasping

notes.note: A diminutive of “body”, which in Marcus is slighting. “Poor body” carries it.
notes.other_reading: your little body

notes.note: The verb is to judge against someone, from finding fault to condemning. Its form here speaks of what would go on being said, not of a verdict already given, so “be faulted”.
notes.other_reading: and have been found guilty only

notes.note: The adjective normally means “hard to follow”; here it must be said of the person who follows with difficulty, that is, is slow to understand. Both adjectives are comparatives, given as “rather”, and “things” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: rather slow to understand

notes.greek: καὶ τοῦτο δὲ ἀσκητέον μὴ παρενθυμουμένῳ μηδὲ ἐμφιληδονοῦντι τῇ νωθείᾳ
notes.note: “This” is the slowness: it too is to be worked on. The first participle can mean “disregarding” or “letting the mind wander off”, and the English takes the first. The Greek is impersonal; the English has “you”, since the whole passage addresses “you”.
notes.other_reading: And this too is to be trained, by one who does not let the mind wander and does not enjoy being sluggish

check.note: Bare “sharpness” can be read as harshness of temper. The Greek here is keenness or quickness of wit.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “your sharpness of mind”. “Of mind” removes the risk of hearing harshness, and “sharpness” is kept because the Greek noun is itself a word for what is sharp or pungent.

check.note: The “for” of the Greek is dropped. The excuse is elliptical: “(I cannot,) for I am not made for it”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Because I am not made for it by nature.” The Greek word gives a reason and is not “But”; “Because” lets the excuse begin as it does in the Greek, as the answer of someone asked why not.

check.note: “Being unalloyed” is odd English for a quality of a person. The image is of unadulterated coin: being genuine, without falseness.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “being genuine”. “Genuine” is still a word said of coin, so the image is not lost, and the note records the metal sense.

check.note: Bare “greatness” will not be taken as something wholly in one’s power. The word is greatness of spirit, high-mindedness.
check.decided: Declined: “greatness” stands. The Greek is a bare adjective, “the great” or “the grand”, with nothing to say of what, and it is not the usual Greek word for greatness of soul, so adding “of mind” would narrow it. The note records “high-mindedness” as the likely sense.

check.note: “Nevertheless” is dropped, and with it the force of “though able”: though able by now to show so many things, you still, all the same, stay below willingly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and yet you still stay down below of your own will”, which gives the “nevertheless” of the Greek.

check.note: The word “actually” or “even” after “or” is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Or are you actually forced to grumble”.

check.greek: ἀλλὰ τούτων μὲν πάλαι ἀπηλλάχθαι ἐδύνασο
check.note: The “rather” after the oath is dropped, and the contrast between being rid of these and being charged only with that is flattened to “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Rather, you could have been rid of these long ago, and be faulted only, if at all, for”. “Rather” gives the turn after the oath, and “these” against “only” carries the contrast of the two halves.

check.note: The form is present, beside a completed “to have been rid”: “to be charged”, not “to have been found guilty”. “Found guilty” is also stronger than “be faulted”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and be faulted only, if at all, for”. The Greek form is present and the verb covers any judging against a person, so no verdict is implied.

check.note: “Hard put to follow” is unclear idiom. The sense is rather slow to follow, slow to understand.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “finding things rather hard to follow”, which is plain and keeps the shape of the Greek adjective (“hard to follow”, here said of the person who follows with difficulty). “Slow to understand” would repeat “slow”, which the Greek has only once.

check.note: “This” is the thing to be worked on, the slowness itself. “Train at this” leaves the reader unsure what “this” is and turns the object into a field of practice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And this too you must work on”, so that “this”, the slowness, is the thing worked on. “You” is kept for the impersonal Greek because the two participles that follow need a subject in English, and the note says so.

passages.casaubon: No man can admire thee for thy sharp acute language, such is thy natural disability that way. Be it so: yet there be many other good things, for the want of which thou canst not plead the want or natural ability. Let them be seen in thee, which depend wholly from thee; sincerity, gravity, laboriousness, contempt of pleasures; be not querulous, be Content with little, be kind, be free; avoid all superfluity, all vain prattling; be magnanimous. Doest not thou perceive, how many things there be, which notwithstanding any pretence of natural indisposition and unfitness, thou mightest have performed and exhibited, and yet still thou doest voluntarily continue drooping downwards? Or wilt thou say that it is through defect of thy natural constitution, that thou art constrained to murmur, to be base and wretched to flatter; now to accuse, and now to please, and pacify thy body: to be vainglorious, to be so giddy-headed., and unsettled in thy thoughts? nay (witnesses be the Gods) of all these thou mightest have been rid long ago: only, this thou must have been contented with, to have borne the blame of one that is somewhat slow and dull, wherein thou must so exercise thyself, as one who neither doth much take to heart this his natural defect, nor yet pleaseth himself in it.

passages.greek: Ἔθισον σεαυτὸν πρὸς τῷ ὑφ’ ἑτέρου λεγομένῳ γίνεσθαι ἀπαρενθυμήτως καὶ ὡς οἷόν τε ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ λέγοντος γίνου.
passages.english: Accustom yourself to be with what another person is saying, without inattention, and, as far as possible, be in the soul of the one who speaks.

notes.greek: πρὸς τῷ ὑφ’ ἑτέρου λεγομένῳ γίνεσθαι
notes.note: Literally “to come to be at what is said by another”, an idiom for giving one’s attention to a thing. The same verb returns in “be in the soul”, so the English has “be” both times.
notes.other_reading: to give your whole attention to what is said by another

notes.note: A rare adverb: “without thinking of something beside it”, or “without disregarding it”, as the related verb means in 5.5. “Without inattention” leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: without neglecting any of it

notes.greek: ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ λέγοντος γίνου
notes.note: Literally “come to be in the soul of the speaker”, now as a command. The English keeps “soul” and does not turn it into “mind”.
notes.other_reading: get inside the speaker’s mind

check.greek: ὡς οἷόν τε ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ λέγοντος γίνου
check.note: The last verb is a command, “be”. Without commas the English reads “as far as you can be in the soul”, and the command is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and, as far as possible, be in the soul of the one who speaks”, so that the command is heard.

check.note: The same verb comes twice: be at what is said, be in the speaker’s soul. “Keep close to” and “be” hide the step from one to the other.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to be with what another person is saying” and then “be in the soul”, one verb for the one Greek verb.

check.note: The same word family is “disregarding” in 5.5. Here it is expanded into a clause about straying thought.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “without inattention”, one short phrase for the one adverb. It leaves open both senses the word can have, not thinking of something else and not disregarding what is said.

passages.casaubon: Use thyself when any man speaks unto thee, so to hearken unto him, as that in the interim thou give not way to any other thoughts; that so thou mayst (as far as is possible) seem fixed and fastened to his very soul, whosoever he be that speaks unto thee.

nearest.title: Being good for its own sake

passages.greek: Εἰ μὴ καθήκει, μὴ πράξῃς· εἰ μὴ ἀληθές ἐστι, μὴ εἴπῃς. ἡ γὰρ ὁρμή σου ἔστω
passages.english: If it is not fitting, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it. For let your impulse be …

notes.note: The verb behind the Stoic term for a fitting act, often given as “duty”. The English keeps the plain “fitting”.
notes.other_reading: If it is not your duty

notes.note: The Greek as given stops here in mid-sentence, with no word to say what the impulse is to be; the English adds nothing and marks the break with three dots. In the edition the chapter goes on with words that the section division leaves to the next passage, and whether they complete this sentence is not clear. Taking the words as complete, with “yours” as the thing said of the impulse, is possible but strained.
notes.other_reading: For let the impulse be yours

check.note: The Greek as given breaks off with no word to complete it, and the English mirrors that without marking it. Reading it as complete (“let the impulse be yours”) is strained.
