Of his, that thou mayest consider whether in the estate of ignorance, or of knowledge. And then also must thou call to mind, that he is thy kinsman.

passages.greek: Πόνει μὴ ὡς ἄθλιος μηδὲ ὡς ἐλεεῖσθαι ἢ θαυμάζεσθαι θέλων, ἀλλὰ μόνον ἓν θέλε· κινεῖσθαι καὶ ἴσχεσθαι, ὡς ὁ πολιτικὸς λόγος ἀξιοῖ.
passages.english: Toil, not as someone miserable, and not as someone who wants to be pitied or admired, but want one thing only: to move and to hold back as civic reason thinks right.

notes.note: The verb means to labour and also to bear hardship or pain. “Toil” is used because it carries both the work and its hardness.
notes.other_reading: Bear your hardship

notes.note: “As a miserable person”: someone suffering under the labour, to be pitied. The word comes from the word for a struggle or contest, which may be felt after “toil”.
notes.other_reading: not like someone wretched

notes.note: Both forms can be middle (“to move and to check oneself”) or passive (“to be set moving and to be held back”). The English takes the middle: what is wanted is the person’s own moving and stopping, with reason setting the measure.
notes.other_reading: to be set in motion and to be held in check

notes.note: Literally “the political reason”: reason as it belongs to a πόλις, a community of fellow citizens. “Civic” keeps the adjective wide. The Greek does not say which city, and the Stoics also call the universe a city.
notes.other_reading: as the reason of a citizen (or: the reason of the community) thinks right

notes.note: The verb is “thinks fit”, “claims as right”, “demands”. The English takes the milder “thinks right”.
notes.other_reading: requires

check.note: “Hard” is added, and the verb also means to bear toil or pain, which suits “as a wretch” and “wanting to be pitied”. The English decides for plain work.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Toil”. The verb covers both hard work and bearing hardship, and “toil” carries both in one word without an added “hard”.

check.note: “Wretch” is old-fashioned and today suggests someone contemptible; the Greek means someone miserable, to be pitied.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “not as someone miserable”. The Greek word means a person in misery, one to be pitied, and “wretch” today suggests someone contemptible.

check.note: The “but” that sets this against the two refusals is dropped by starting a new sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: the passage is now one sentence and reads “but want one thing only”, so that the “but” of the Greek sets the one wish against the two refusals.

check.note: Both forms can be passive: “to be set moving and to be checked”. The English takes them as the person’s own acts.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the forms are open, as the point says, and a note records the passive reading. The English keeps “to move and to hold back”, because κινεῖσθαι is the ordinary Greek for a living thing’s own moving and the sentence says what the person is to want to do.

check.note: πολιτικὸς is an adjective, “civic, of the community”, and “of a citizen” narrows it to one person’s standing. ἀξιοῖ is “thinks right, claims”, a shade milder than “requires”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as civic reason thinks right”. πολιτικός is an adjective for what belongs to a city or community, not to one citizen, and ἀξιοῖ is “thinks fit” before it is “demands”.

passages.casaubon: Labour not as one to whom it is appointed to be wretched, nor as one that either would be pitied, or admired; but let this be thine only care and desire; so always and in all things to prosecute or to forbear, as the law of charity, or mutual society doth require.

nearest.title: Being good for its own sake

passages.greek: Ἑνὶ τέρπου καὶ προσαναπαύου, τῷ ἀπὸ πράξεως κοινωνικῆς μεταβαίνειν ἐπὶ πρᾶξιν κοινωνικὴν σὺν μνήμῃ θεοῦ.
passages.english: Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: going from one social act to another social act, with god in mind.

notes.note: “In one thing”. The Greek does not add “only”, and neither does the English.
notes.other_reading: Let one thing be your pleasure and your rest

notes.note: To rest upon something, to find one’s rest in it. The same verb is used of philosophy in 6.12 and has the same English there.
notes.other_reading: and lean on it for rest

notes.greek: ἀπὸ πράξεως κοινωνικῆς μεταβαίνειν ἐπὶ πρᾶξιν κοινωνικὴν
notes.note: Literally “passing from a social act to a social act”. “Social” (κοινωνικός) is the glossary word: an act that serves the common life of people with one another.
notes.other_reading: passing from an act for the common good to an act for the common good

notes.note: Literally “with memory of god”. The noun has no article, so “a god” is also possible.
notes.other_reading: with remembrance of god

passages.casaubon: Let this be thy only joy, and thy only comfort, from one sociable kind action without intermission to pass unto another, God being ever in thy mind.

passages.greek: Εἰ μητρυιάν τε ἅμα εἶχες καὶ μητέρα, ἐκείνην τ̓ ἂν ἐθεράπευες καὶ ὅμως ἡ ἐπάνοδός σοι πρὸς τὴν μητέρα συνεχὴς ἐγίνετο. τοῦτό σοι νῦν ἐστιν ἡ αὐλὴ καὶ ἡ φιλοσοφία· ὧδε πολλάκις ἐπάνιθι καὶ προσαναπαύου ταύτῃ, δι’ ἣν καὶ τὰ ἐκεῖ σοι ἀνεκτὰ φαίνεται καὶ σὺ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀνεκτός.
passages.english: If you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time, you would wait on the stepmother, and still you would be continually going back to your mother. That is what the court and philosophy are to you now. Go back here often and rest in philosophy, because of which the things there seem bearable to you, and you seem bearable among them.

notes.note: The verb means to attend on, serve, look after, and also to pay court to someone, the sense that prepares “the court” in the next sentence. “Wait on” is meant to carry both. The Greek says “that one” for the stepmother; the English names her.
notes.other_reading: you would pay court to the stepmother

notes.greek: ἡ ἐπάνοδός σοι πρὸς τὴν μητέρα συνεχὴς ἐγίνετο
notes.note: Literally “your going back to your mother would be continual”. The noun is from the same root as ἐπάνιθι (“go back”) below, so the English keeps “going back” and “go back”.
notes.other_reading: your return to your mother would be constant

notes.note: αὐλή is the court, the emperor’s palace and the life around it. By the order of the words the court answers to the stepmother and philosophy to the mother; the Greek does not spell that out and neither does the English.
notes.other_reading: the palace and philosophy

notes.note: Either “to this place” or “in this way” (as you would go back to your mother). The English takes “here”, meaning to philosophy, because the next clause sets it against “the things there”.
notes.other_reading: Go back in this way often

notes.note: “In this one”, feminine. The court and philosophy are both feminine nouns in Greek, and “this one” is the nearer of the two, philosophy. The English writes the noun so that it is clear which is meant.
notes.other_reading: and rest in her

notes.note: The preposition with this case gives a cause (“on account of which”), not a means (“by means of which”).
notes.other_reading: thanks to which

notes.note: “The things there”, that is at court, as against “here”.
notes.other_reading: what you meet at court

notes.note: The verb is carried over from the clause before, so “seem” is repeated. “Among them” is most naturally the things there (neuter), but the form could also be heard as the people there.
notes.other_reading: and you are bearable among the people there

check.note: The verb means to wait on, attend to, pay court to. “Duty” is brought in, and the courtier’s sense of the word, which prepares the court in the next sentence, is lost.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “you would wait on the stepmother”. The verb is the one for attending on someone and for paying court, and “duty” is not in it. The noun is kept because “her” would point to the mother, while the Greek “that one” points to the stepmother.

check.note: The Greek says “rest in her” or “in this one”. Naming philosophy is a gloss, made necessary only because “here” before it is unclear.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “rest in philosophy”. The Greek ταύτῃ is “this one”, the nearer of two feminine nouns, the court and philosophy; “her” or “it” would not say which, and “her” would bring in the mother, whom the Greek does not name here. A note records the choice.

check.note: ὧδε can be “here” (to philosophy) or “in this way” (as you would to your mother). The English chooses the first without sign.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the word is open, as the point says, and a note records “in this way”. The English keeps “here”, because the next clause sets it against “the things there” (τὰ ἐκεῖ), which gives ὧδε the sense of place.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “through which”, which can be heard as “by means of which”. The Greek preposition with this case gives a cause.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “because of which”. With this case διά means “on account of”, so philosophy is the reason the things at court seem bearable, not a tool for bearing them.

passages.casaubon: If it were that thou hadst at one time both a stepmother, and a natural mother living, thou wouldst honour and respect her also; nevertheless to thine own natural mother would thy refuge, and recourse be continually. So let the court and thy philosophy be unto thee. Have recourse unto it often, and comfort thyself in her, by whom it is that those other things are made tolerable unto thee, and thou also in those things not intolerable unto others.

passages.greek: Μηκέτι σου μηδεὶς ἀκούσῃ καταμεμφομένου τὸν ἐν αὐλῇ βίον μηδὲ σὺ σεαυτοῦ.
passages.english: Let no one hear you finding fault with life at court any more, and do not hear yourself doing it either.

notes.note: To blame, find fault with, complain of.
notes.other_reading: complaining about life at court

notes.note: “The life at court”: αὐλή is the emperor’s court, as in 6.12.
notes.other_reading: life in the palace

notes.note: Literally “nor you yourself”, with “hear” understood: you are not to hear yourself doing it, that is, not to complain even inwardly. μηδέ can be “nor” or “not even”; the English takes “nor” and supplies “hear” and “doing it”.
notes.other_reading: not even you yourself

check.note: The Greek is “nor you [hear] yourself”. The English can be misread as “not even you finding fault”, and μηδὲ may be plain “nor” and not “not even”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and do not hear yourself doing it either”. The Greek is “nor you yourself”, with “hear” carried over, and “not even you yourself” could be taken as “not even you finding fault”.

passages.casaubon: Forbear henceforth to complain of the trouble of a courtly life, either in public before others, or in private by thyself.

passages.greek: Ὠιδῆς ἐπιτερποῦς καὶ ὀρχήσεως καὶ παγκρατίου καταφρονήσεις, ἐὰν τὴν μὲν ἐμμελῆ φωνὴν καταμερίσῃς εἰς ἕκαστον τῶν φθόγγων καὶ καθ’ ἕνα πύθῃ σεαυτοῦ, εἰ τούτου ἥττων εἶ· διατραπήσῃ γάρ· ἐπὶ δὲ ὀρχήσεως τὸ ἀνάλογον ποιήσας καθ’ ἑκάστην κίνησιν ἢ σχέσιν, τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ παγκρατίου. ὅλως οὖν, χωρὶς ἀρετῆς καὶ τῶν ἀπ’ ἀρετῆς, μέμνησο ἐπὶ τὰ κατὰ μέρος τρέχειν καὶ τῇ διαιρέσει αὐτῶν εἰς καταφρόνησιν ἰέναι, τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν βίον ὅλον μετάφερε.
passages.english: You will look down on delightful singing, on dancing and on the pankration, if you divide the tuneful voice into each of its notes and ask yourself at each one whether this gets the better of you, for you will be ashamed; and with dancing, if you do the corresponding thing at each movement or pose; and the same with the pankration too. In general, then, except for virtue and what comes from virtue, remember to run to the parts, and by dividing them to come to look down on them; and carry the same thing over to the whole of life as well.

notes.note: ᾠδή is a song or singing; it has no article, and the English takes the activity, “singing”, beside “dancing”. “Delightful” can by its form go with the singing alone or with the singing and the dancing; the English leaves it with the singing.
notes.other_reading: delightful singing and dancing (or: a delightful song)

notes.note: The pankration was an athletic contest, all-in fighting that joined boxing and wrestling. The English keeps the name, which English also uses for the contest.
notes.other_reading: all-in fighting

notes.note: To think little of, to despise. The noun from the same verb (καταφρόνησιν) closes the argument, so “look down on” is used in both places.
notes.other_reading: You will despise

notes.note: φωνή is voice or sound, and ἐμμελής is “in tune”, “melodious”. The English takes the singing voice.
notes.other_reading: the melodious sound

notes.note: Literally “whether you are less than this”, the regular idiom for being overcome by something, giving in to it. “This” is the single note.
notes.other_reading: whether you are too weak to resist this one

notes.note: The verb means to be turned aside, and so to be put out of countenance or ashamed. The English takes “ashamed”; what you will be ashamed of (saying yes) is left unsaid, as in the Greek. It could also mean that you will be put off the thing itself.
notes.other_reading: for you will be put off it (or: for you will shrink from saying so)

notes.note: A participle (“having done the corresponding thing”) with no finite verb of its own; it hangs loosely on “you will look down on”. The English gives it as “if you do”, parallel to the first “if” clause.
notes.other_reading: and in the case of dancing, having done the like

notes.note: A held position, as against a movement: a pose or attitude of the body.
notes.other_reading: at each movement or posture

notes.note: Literally “to run to the things part by part”, the particulars as against the whole. The English keeps “run” (the verb of 9.22) and “parts”, so that “the whole of life” at the end answers it.
notes.other_reading: to go straight to the details

notes.note: Literally “by the division of them”. “Them” may be the things divided or the parts; the English “them” is open in the same way. The noun is not from the verb used above for dividing the voice (καταμερίσῃς), though the English has “divide” for both.
notes.other_reading: by analysing them

notes.note: “Carry it over to the whole life”: either life as a whole or the whole of one’s life. The English takes the first, as the counterpart of “the parts”.
notes.other_reading: apply the same to your whole life as well

check.note: The verb is “be turned aside, put off, abashed”. “Ashamed” (to say yes) is one reading; the other is “you will be put off it”, which fits the aim of the exercise as well.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the verb is open, as the point says, and the note now gives “you will be put off it” as the other reading. The English keeps “for you will be ashamed”: the Greek has no “from saying so”, and its “for” makes the clause a reason for putting the question, which suits shame better than a result.

check.note: The article in “a delightful song” makes it one song; the Greek is general, like “dancing” beside it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “delightful singing”. The Greek has no article and is general, like “dancing” beside it.

check.note: A reader of today may not know the word “pankration”. It is the right name, but nothing in the English says it is a fighting contest.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the name is kept in the English, since it is the proper name of one contest and English uses it too. The note says what the pankration was, so the gloss stands outside the text.

check.greek: τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν βίον ὅλον μετάφερε
check.note: The καὶ (“also, as well”) is dropped in “carry the same thing over to the whole of life”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now ends “to the whole of life as well”, which gives the καί. The same καί in the clause on the pankration is now given as “too”.

passages.casaubon: A pleasant song or dance; the Pancratiast's exercise, sports that thou art wont to be much taken with, thou shalt easily contemn; if the harmonious voice thou shalt divide into so many particular sounds whereof it doth consist, and of every one in particular shall ask thyself; whether this or that sound is it, that doth so conquer thee. For thou wilt be ashamed of it. And so for shame, if accordingly thou shalt consider it, every particular motion and posture by itself: and so for the wrestler's exercise too. Generally then, whatsoever it be, besides virtue, and those things that proceed from virtue that thou art subject to be much affected with, remember presently thus to divide it, and by this kind of division, in each particular to attain unto the contempt of the whole. This thou must transfer and apply to thy whole life also.

passages.greek: Ἐὰν ἀφέλῃς τὴν σὴν ὑπόληψιν περὶ τοῦ λυπεῖν σε δοκοῦντος, αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ ἀσφαλεστάτῳ ἕστηκας.—τίς αὐτός;—ὁ λόγος.—ἀλλ’ οὐκ εἰμὶ λόγος.—ἔστω. οὐκοῦν ὁ μὲν λόγος αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν μὴ λυπείτω, εἰ δέ τι ἄλλο σοι κακῶς ἔχει, ὑπολαβέτω αὐτὸ περὶ αὑτοῦ.
passages.english: If you take away your judgment about what seems to distress you, you yourself stand in the safest place. “Who is ‘yourself’?” Reason. “But I am not reason.” Granted. Then let reason, for its part, not be the one to distress itself, and if anything else of yours is in a bad way, let that form its own judgment about itself.

notes.note: The glossary word “judgment”. The verb at the end of the passage (ὑπολαβέτω) is the same word, so “form its own judgment” is used there to let the link be seen.
notes.other_reading: your opinion, your assumption

notes.note: The form can be neuter, the thing that seems to distress you, or masculine, the person who seems to. The English takes it as the thing, which is the wider reading.
notes.other_reading: your judgment about the person who seems to distress you

notes.note: The verb covers bodily pain, grief and annoyance. “Distress” can be said of both body and mind, and it is kept for the second occurrence (λυπείτω).
notes.other_reading: what seems to be hurting you … let reason not be the one to hurt itself

notes.note: The verb is a perfect with present sense, “you stand”, and it is kept as a present, not made a future. The superlative can mean “the safest place” or simply “complete safety”.
notes.other_reading: you yourself stand in complete safety

notes.note: The dashes of the edition mark changes of speaker in a short exchange. The objector’s two lines are put in quotation marks and the answers are left without. The question picks up the emphatic “you yourself” (αὐτὸς) of the first sentence.
notes.other_reading: “Who is this ‘self’?”

notes.note: Said flatly, with no qualification. The objector probably means “not reason only”, but the Greek has no “only” and none is added.
notes.other_reading: “But I am not just reason.”

notes.greek: ὁ μὲν λόγος αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν μὴ λυπείτω
notes.note: The Greek doubles the pronoun, “itself … itself”, to say that the distress would be reason’s own doing; “not be the one to” carries that. “For its part” gives the contrast with “anything else” in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: let reason at least not distress itself

notes.greek: εἰ δέ τι ἄλλο σοι κακῶς ἔχει, ὑπολαβέτω αὐτὸ περὶ αὑτοῦ
notes.note: αὐτὸ is taken as the subject, “let it, itself, judge”. It can also be the object, “let it suppose that about itself”. The “anything else of yours” is not named; the body is the likely candidate.
notes.other_reading: and if anything else of yours is in a bad way, let it suppose so about itself

check.note: The form can be neuter (the thing that seems to distress you) or masculine (the person who seems to). The English has chosen the thing without saying so.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “what seems to distress you”, since the neuter is the wider and likelier reading, and a note now records that the Greek could also mean the person who seems to distress you.

check.greek: ὁ μὲν λόγος αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν μὴ λυπείτω
check.note: “For its part” gives one small Greek word, but the stress on reason itself as the source of its own distress (αὐτὸς) is not carried.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “let reason, for its part, not be the one to distress itself”. The Greek doubles the pronoun to say the distress would be reason’s own doing, and the plain “distress itself” did not bring that out.

check.greek: εἰ δέ τι ἄλλο σοι κακῶς ἔχει
check.note: The Greek says “anything else of yours”. “In you” places the thing inside the person, which the Greek does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if anything else of yours is in a bad way”. The Greek word is a plain “to you, of yours” and says nothing of “in”.

passages.casaubon: If thou canst but withdraw conceit and opinion concerning that which may seem hurtful and offensive, thou thyself art as safe, as safe may be. Thou thyself? and who is that? Thy reason. 'Yea, but I am not reason.' Well, be it so. However, let not thy reason or understanding admit of grief, and if there be anything in thee that is grieved, let that, (whatsoever it be,) conceive its own grief, if it can.

passages.greek: Τὰ δόγματα πῶς ἄλλως δύναται νεκρωθῆναι, ἐὰν μὴ αἱ κατάλληλοι αὐτοῖς φαντασίαι σβεσθῶσιν, ἃς διηνεκῶς ἀναζωπυρεῖν ἐπὶ σοί ἐστι. δύναμαι περὶ τούτου ὃ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν· εἰ δύναμαι, τί ταράσσομαι; τὰ ἔξω τῆς ἐμῆς διανοίας οὐδὲν ὅλως πρὸς τὴν ἐμὴν διάνοιαν. τοῦτο μάθε καὶ ὀρθὸς εἶ.
passages.english: How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out, the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame? I am able to form the judgment I ought about this. If I am able, why am I disturbed? The things outside my mind are nothing at all to my mind. Learn this and you are upright.

notes.note: The glossary word “principles”. The Greek has only the article, so the English reads “the principles” without “your”, though the principles he himself holds are meant.
notes.other_reading: How can your principles be killed

notes.note: The input prints a full stop at the end of this sentence, but πῶς makes it a question and it is punctuated so. The verb means to be made a corpse, to be deadened; “killed” keeps the death. The Greek says “how else … unless”, and the English lets “unless” carry the “else”.
notes.other_reading: The principles cannot be made dead in any other way than by the putting out of the impressions that answer to them.

notes.note: Literally to kindle back into life: the word joins the fire image (σβεσθῶσιν, “are put out”) to the life image (νεκρωθῆναι, “be killed”). English has no one word for both, so the “life” half is lost in “fan back into flame”. “The impressions” is repeated where the Greek has only “which”.
notes.other_reading: which it is up to you to keep rekindling to life

notes.note: “Without a break”. It stands next to the verb of rekindling and is taken with it, as “keep”; it can also go with “it is up to you”.
notes.other_reading: the impressions it is at every moment up to you to fan back into flame

notes.greek: δύναμαι περὶ τούτου ὃ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν
notes.note: Here he turns from “you” to the first person, and the change is kept. “This” is whatever is in front of him and is not named. The verb is the glossary’s “judgment” word.
notes.other_reading: I can think what I should about this.

notes.note: The glossary gives “thought” for διάνοια, and “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty, which has an inside and an outside, so “mind” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: The things outside my thought are nothing at all to my thought.

notes.greek: οὐδὲν ὅλως πρὸς τὴν ἐμὴν διάνοιαν
notes.note: An idiom, “nothing at all in relation to”: they have no bearing on it, are no concern of it. The short English idiom “are nothing to” is kept.
notes.other_reading: have no bearing whatever on my mind

notes.note: A present, “you are upright”, where English might expect a future. The adjective means standing straight, on one’s feet, and also right or correct; “upright” leaves both open and adds no verb of standing.
notes.other_reading: Learn this and you are in the right.

check.greek: πῶς ἄλλως δύναται νεκρωθῆναι, ἐὰν μὴ
check.note: “Be made dead” is not natural English for the verb, and “how else … unless” is awkward, though the sense is right.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out”. “Killed” replaces “made dead” and “else” is dropped because “unless” already says it; the passive “are put out” is kept, since the Greek does not say who puts them out.

check.greek: ἃς διηνεκῶς ἀναζωπυρεῖν ἐπὶ σοί ἐστι
check.note: The word for “without a break” can go with the rekindling or with “it is up to you”, and the English hung “continually” at the end without choosing openly. The relative clause was also made a new sentence beginning “And”, which the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause is joined back to its sentence and reads “the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame”, with “keep” for the adverb, which stands next to the verb of rekindling in the Greek. A note gives the other reading.

check.note: The Greek is only “you are upright”, or “you are right”. “Stand” was added and fixed the bodily picture.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Learn this and you are upright”, with no added “stand”. “Upright” leaves both senses of the Greek word open, and the note gives “you are in the right”.

part.left_out: Ἀναβιῶναί σοι ἔξεστιν· ἴδε πάλιν τὰ πράγματα, ὡς ἑώρας· ἐν τούτῳ γὰρ τὸ ἀναβιῶναι.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 7.2 at 'Be always in this mind, and thou wilt be right' and begins its 7.3 with the rest of the chapter, the lines on living again.

passages.casaubon: What fear is there that thy dogmata, or philosophical resolutions and conclusions, should become dead in thee, and lose their proper power and efficacy to make thee live happy, as long as those proper and correlative fancies, and representations of things on which they mutually depend (which continually to stir up and revive is in thy power,) are still kept fresh and alive? It is in my power concerning this thing that is happened, what soever it be, to conceit that which is right and true. If it be, why then am I troubled? Those things that are without my understanding, are nothing to it at all: and that is it only, which doth properly concern me. Be always in this mind, and thou wilt be right.

passages.greek: Ἔξεστι περὶ τούτου μηδὲν ὑπολαμβάνειν καὶ μὴ ὀχλεῖσθαι τῇ ψυχῇ· αὐτὰ γὰρ τὰ πράγματα οὐκ ἔχει φύσιν ποιητικὴν τῶν ἡμετέρων κρίσεων.
passages.english: One is free to form no judgment about this and not to be troubled in one’s soul; for things themselves do not have a nature that produces our verdicts.

notes.note: Impersonal: “it is allowed, it is open”, a matter of freedom more than of bare possibility. “One is free” keeps it impersonal, since the Greek names no “you”.
notes.other_reading: It is possible to form no judgment about this

notes.note: “About this” with nothing named: the matter in front of him. The form could also be masculine, “about this person”.
notes.other_reading: to form no judgment about this man

notes.note: The verb is from the word for a crowd: to be bothered, pestered. “Trouble” is used for this word and its compound (ἐνοχλεῖν) throughout the section, and “disturb” for ταράσσειν, to keep the two apart. The Greek has “the soul”, where the article stands for the owner; “one’s” follows the impersonal opening.
notes.other_reading: and not to be bothered in the soul

notes.note: κρίσις is close in sense to ὑπόληψις, which the glossary renders “judgment”. Since both stand in this one sentence, κρίσις is given as “verdicts”, so that the two Greek words can be told apart.
notes.other_reading: a nature that produces our judgments

notes.note: Literally “a nature productive of”: things are not of a kind to make our verdicts for us.
notes.other_reading: things themselves are not of a nature to create our verdicts

check.note: The Greek word means “it is allowed, it is open to you”, a matter of freedom more than of mere possibility.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “One is free to form no judgment about this”, which gives the freedom. “You are free” is not used, because the Greek verb is impersonal and names no “you”.

check.note: “Troubled in the soul” is stiff for a reader of today; the article here stands for the owner.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not to be troubled in one’s soul”. The article is given as a possessive, but as “one’s” and not “your”, to match the impersonal opening.

passages.casaubon: It is in thy power absolutely to exclude all manner of conceit and opinion, as concerning this matter; and by the same means, to exclude all grief and sorrow from thy soul. For as for the things and objects themselves, they of themselves have no such power, whereby to beget and force upon us any opinion at all.

passages.greek: Τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν αὐτὸ ἑαυτῷ οὐκ ἐνοχλεῖ, οἷον λέγω, οὐ φοβεῖ ἑαυτὸ εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν. εἰ δέ τις ἄλλος αὐτὸ φοβῆσαι ἢ λυπῆσαι δύναται, ποιείτω· αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑαυτὸ ὑποληπτικῶς οὐ τρέψει εἰς τοιαύτας τροπάς. τὸ σωμάτιον μὴ πάθῃ τι, αὐτὸ μεριμνάτω, εἰ δύναται, καὶ λεγέτω, εἴ τι πάσχει· τὸ δὲ ψυχάριον τὸ φοβούμενον, τὸ λυπούμενον, τὸ περὶ τούτων ὅλως ὑπολαμβάνον, οὐδὲν μὴ πάθῃ· οὐ γὰρ ἄξεις αὐτὸ εἰς κρίσιν τοιαύτην. ἀπροσδεές ἐστιν ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, ἐὰν μὴ ἑαυτῷ ἔνδειαν ποιῇ· κατὰ ταὐτὰ δὲ καὶ ἀτάραχον καὶ ἀνεμπόδιστον, ἐὰν μὴ ἑαυτὸ ταράσσῃ καὶ ἐμποδίζῃ.
passages.english: The ruling part does not make trouble for itself; I mean, for example, it does not frighten itself into desire. But if anyone else can frighten or distress it, let them do so; for it will not, by its own judging, turn itself in such directions. Let the little body itself take care that it suffers nothing, if it can, and let it say so if it suffers anything. But the little soul, the thing that fears, that is distressed, that in general forms judgments about these things, will suffer nothing at all; for you will not lead it to such a verdict. The ruling part, so far as depends on itself, is in need of nothing, unless it makes a need for itself; and in the same way it is undisturbed and unhindered, unless it disturbs and hinders itself.

notes.note: The glossary’s “the ruling part”: the part of the soul that judges and directs.
notes.other_reading: the governing part, the directing mind

notes.note: The Greek doubles the pronoun, “itself … to itself”: the trouble would be its own doing. English carries this in “for itself”. “Trouble” is the word used for this verb throughout the section.
notes.other_reading: The ruling part does not itself trouble itself

notes.note: “Frighten itself into desire” is what the words say, and it is hard sense: fear does not lead into desire, and the next sentence speaks of frightening and distressing, not of desire. From memory, unchecked, editors have doubted the text here and suspect that words have dropped out or been altered. The English follows the Greek as given and does not smooth it.
notes.other_reading: it does not frighten itself or lead itself into desire

notes.note: Masculine, “anyone else”, a person; “them” is used for it as the glossary allows. It could loosely cover anything outside the ruling part.
notes.other_reading: But if something else can frighten or distress it

notes.greek: ὑποληπτικῶς οὐ τρέψει εἰς τοιαύτας τροπάς
notes.note: The adverb is made from the glossary’s “judgment” word: “in the way of judging”. Verb and noun are the same word in Greek, “turn itself into such turns”, meaning the changes of fear and distress; the English keeps one “turn” and gives the noun as “directions”. “Its own” gives the force of the doubled αὐτὸ … ἑαυτὸ.
notes.other_reading: for it will not of itself, through its judgment, change into such states

notes.note: A diminutive, as is ψυχάριον below. It is belittling rather than fond; both are kept as “little”.
notes.other_reading: the poor body … the poor soul

notes.greek: μὴ πάθῃ τι, αὐτὸ μεριμνάτω, εἰ δύναται, καὶ λεγέτω, εἴ τι πάσχει
notes.note: The verb πάσχειν (to suffer, to have something done to one) comes three times in two sentences and “suffer” is kept for all three. “Say so” fills in an object the Greek leaves out.
notes.other_reading: Let the body itself see to it, if it can, that nothing happens to it, and let it speak if anything does.

notes.note: Either “in general, in a word”, summing up the list, or “at all”, or “wholly”. It is taken as summing up, which is the usual sense where the word has no “not” beside it.
notes.other_reading: that forms any judgment at all about these things

notes.note: The two negatives with this verb form are read as the strong denial, “will certainly suffer nothing”, given as “nothing at all”.
notes.other_reading: need suffer nothing

notes.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἄξεις αὐτὸ εἰς κρίσιν τοιαύτην
notes.note: The verb is second person, “you will not lead it”, a sudden turn to “you” in a chapter otherwise about “it”; the turn is kept as the Greek gives it. From memory, unchecked, the form has been questioned. κρίσιν is “verdict” as in 6.52, to keep it apart from “judgment”.
notes.other_reading: for it will not be brought to judge so

notes.note: This word and ἔνδειαν in the next clause share the root for need, so “need” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: is self-sufficient, unless it creates a want for itself

notes.note: Each adjective is answered by its own verb in the next clause (ταράσσῃ, ἐμποδίζῃ); the pairs are kept as “undisturbed … disturbs” and “unhindered … hinders”.
notes.other_reading: untroubled and unobstructed

check.note: The English follows the Greek word for word, but “frighten itself into desire” is hard sense, and the text is probably at fault here. The reader will stumble and should be told why.
check.decided: Accepted: the literal “it does not frighten itself into desire” is kept and not smoothed, and the note now says plainly that the sense is hard and that the Greek is doubted here (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: The doubled “itself” copies the Greek idiom and reads clumsily in English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The ruling part does not make trouble for itself”. The Greek doubled pronoun is an idiom for “by its own doing”, which “for itself” carries, and “trouble” is kept for the verb.

check.note: A small Greek word sets “anyone else” against the ruling part itself, and the English dropped it.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now begins “But if anyone else”, so that the contrast with the ruling part itself is heard.

check.note: “Turn itself into such turns” keeps the Greek word play at the cost of sense: it reads as if the ruling part became a turn.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “turn itself in such directions”. One “turn” keeps the image, and the note explains that verb and noun are the same word in Greek.

check.note: The word ὅλως can sum up the list (“in general”) or mean “at all”, and the English takes the first. “The judgments” also adds an article the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the article is dropped and the English reads “that in general forms judgments about these things”. “In general” stands, because the Greek word usually means “at all” only beside a “not”, and here it closes a list; the note gives the other reading.

check.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἄξεις αὐτὸ εἰς κρίσιν τοιαύτην
check.note: The sudden “you will lead” in a chapter otherwise in the third person is kept faithfully; the verb has been questioned, from memory. Nothing to change unless the Greek is judged at fault.
check.decided: Accepted: “for you will not lead it to such a verdict” stands, since that is what the Greek as given says, and the note now marks the change of person and that the form has been questioned (from memory, unchecked).

passages.casaubon: This may ever be my comfort and security: my understanding, that ruleth over all, will not of itself bring trouble and vexation upon itself. This I say; it will not put itself in any fear, it will not lead itself into any concupiscence. If it be in the power of any other to compel it to fear, or to grieve, it is free for him to use his power. But sure if itself do not of itself, through some false opinion or supposition incline itself to any such disposition; there is no fear. For as for the body, why should I make the grief of my body, to be the grief of my mind? If that itself can either fear or complain, let it. But as for the soul, which indeed, can only be truly sensible of either fear or grief; to which only it belongs according to its different imaginations and opinions, to admit of either of these, or of their contraries; thou mayst look to that thyself, that it suffer nothing. Induce her not to any such opinion or persuasion. The understanding is of itself sufficient unto itself, and needs not (if itself doth not bring itself to need) any other thing besides itself, and by consequent as it needs nothing, so neither can it be troubled or hindered by anything, if itself doth not trouble and hinder itself.

nearest.title: Nothing happens that a human being cannot bear

passages.greek: Πολλὰ περισσὰ περιελεῖν τῶν ἐνοχλούντων σοι δύνασαι ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα, καὶ πολλὴν εὐρυχωρίαν περιποιήσεις ἤδη σεαυτῷ
passages.english: You can strip away many needless things among those that trouble you, things that rest wholly on your judgment, and you will at once make plenty of open room for yourself.

notes.note: περισσὰ is “more than is needed”. Three words in the sentence begin with περι- (περισσὰ, περιελεῖν, περιποιήσεις), a sound play English cannot keep.
notes.other_reading: Many of the things that trouble you are superfluous and you can remove them

notes.greek: ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα
notes.note: Literally “lying wholly upon your judgment”, with the preposition that gives “up to you” elsewhere in the section. The participle may give the reason; it is left as a plain description, since the Greek has no “since”. ὅλα is taken as “wholly”, not “all of them”.
notes.other_reading: since all of them lie in your own judgment

notes.note: Literally “wide space”, room to move. The image of space is kept.
notes.other_reading: a great deal of freedom

notes.note: “Already” or “at once”: the room comes with the stripping away, not later.
notes.other_reading: and you will already have made plenty of room for yourself

notes.note: The Greek as given stops here without a full stop: the sentence runs on in the rest of the chapter, which says by what means the room is made. Only what is given is translated, and the full stop that closes it is an addition.
notes.other_reading: and you will at once make plenty of open room for yourself, …

check.greek: ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα
check.note: The participle may give the reason (“since they lie wholly in your judgment”) and not just a description. The preposition is also the one of the “up to you” idiom used elsewhere in the section, which “rest on” does not echo.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “things that rest wholly on your judgment”. The Greek has a bare participle and no word for “since”, so the reason is left for the reader to draw, as in the Greek; the note records the causal reading and the echo of “up to you”.

part.left_out: τῷ τὸν ὅλον κόσμον περιειληφέναι τῇ γνώμῃ καὶ τὸν ἀίδιον αἰῶνα περινοεῖν καὶ τὴν τῶν κατὰ μέρος ἑκάστου πράγματος ταχεῖαν μεταβολὴν ἐπινοεῖν, ὡς βραχὺ μὲν τὸ ἀπὸ γενέσεως μέχρι διαλύσεως, ἀχανὲς δὲ τὸ πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως, ὡς καὶ τὸ μετὰ τὴν διάλυσιν ὁμοίως ἄπειρον.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 9.30 at 'thou shalt have room enough' and begins its 9.31 with the rest of the chapter, from 'To comprehend the whole world together in thy mind'.

passages.casaubon: Many of those things that trouble and straiten thee, it is in thy power to cut off, as wholly depending from mere conceit and opinion; and then thou shalt have room enough.

passages.greek: Μηδὲν πλέον σαυτῷ λέγε ὧν αἱ προηγούμεναι φαντασίαι ἀναγγέλλουσιν. ἤγγελται ὅτι ὁ δεῖνά σε κακῶς λέγει. ἤγγελται τοῦτο· τὸ δέ, ὅτι βέβλαψαι, οὐκ ἤγγελται. βλέπω ὅτι νοσεῖ τὸ παιδίον. βλέπω· ὅτι δὲ κινδυνεύει, οὐ βλέπω. οὕτως οὖν μένε ἀεὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πρώτων φαντασιῶν καὶ μηδὲν αὐτὸς ἔνδοθεν ἐπίλεγε καὶ οὐδέν σοι γίνεται· μᾶλλον δὲ ἐπίλεγε ὡς γνωρίζων ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ συμβαινόντων.
passages.english: Say nothing more to yourself than what the impressions that lead the way report. It has been reported that so-and-so is speaking ill of you. That has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported. I see that the child is sick. I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see. So always stay like this with the first impressions and say nothing further yourself from within, and nothing happens to you. Or rather, do say something further, as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.

notes.note: The participle means “going before, leading the way”. It is most likely meant of time, the impressions that arrive first, which the later phrase “the first impressions” (τῶν πρώτων φαντασιῶν) supports; “lead the way” keeps it a different word from “first”, as it is in the Greek. It can also mean “leading, principal”.
notes.other_reading: than what the principal impressions report

notes.note: The image is of a messenger bringing news. The same verb returns three times (ἤγγελται) and “report” is kept for all of them.
notes.other_reading: than what the impressions that lead the way announce

notes.note: The Greek word for an unnamed person, “so-and-so”.
notes.other_reading: a certain person

notes.note: “The child”, a small child. The article may stand for “my”, which would make the example his own; the English leaves it as the Greek has it. “The child” is repeated in the next sentence, where the Greek leaves the subject unspoken.
notes.other_reading: I see that my child is sick.

notes.note: The verb is “say in addition”, to add a comment to what was reported. It is built on the “say” of the first sentence (λέγε) and returns in the last, so “say … further” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: and add nothing yourself from within

notes.note: A present, “nothing happens to you”, kept as a present. It could be heard as “nothing is the matter with you”.
notes.other_reading: and nothing comes of it for you

notes.note: The Greek has only “or rather, say further”. “Something” is supplied, and what is to be said is not spelled out.
notes.other_reading: Or rather, do add a comment

notes.greek: ὡς γνωρίζων ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ συμβαινόντων
notes.note: The participle is “recognising, being acquainted with”, a little more than knowing: he is to speak as someone to whom each thing that happens is familiar. κόσμῳ is the glossary’s “universe”; “the world” would also fit.
notes.other_reading: as one who knows each thing that comes about in the world

check.note: The passage opens with “say” and closes twice with a compound of the same verb, “say in addition”. “Add” drops the saying, so the link between the first sentence and the last two is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “say nothing further yourself from within” and “do say something further”, so that the “say” of the first sentence is heard again at the end.

check.note: Two Greek words, “leading the way” and “first”, are both given as “first”. Marcus probably means the same impressions, but the difference is not visible.
check.decided: Accepted: the opening now reads “the impressions that lead the way”, and “first impressions” is kept for the later phrase, so that the two Greek words stay two in English. The note says that the same impressions are probably meant.

check.note: The article may stand for the possessive, “my child”, which would make the example Marcus’s own. The English leaves it neutral.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “the child”. The Greek has only the article and no word for “my”, and English “the child” can be heard of one’s own child just as the Greek can; the note gives “my child”.

check.note: The Greek verb is to recognise or be acquainted with, a little more than to know.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe”.

passages.casaubon: Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things, as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them. It is reported unto thee, that such a one speaketh ill of thee. Well; that he speaketh ill of thee, so much is reported. But that thou art hurt thereby, is not reported: that is the addition of opinion, which thou must exclude. I see that my child is sick. That he is sick, I see, but that he is in danger of his life also, I see it not. Thus thou must use to keep thyself to the first motions and apprehensions of things, as they present themselves outwardly; and add not unto them from within thyself through mere conceit and opinion. Or rather add unto them: hut as one that understandeth the true nature of all things that happen in the world.

passages.greek: Ὅτι πάντα ὑπόληψις καὶ αὕτη ἐπὶ σοί. ἆρον οὖν ὅτε θέλεις τὴν ὑπόληψιν καὶ ὥσπερ κάμψαντι τὴν ἄκραν γαλήνη, σταθερὰ πάντα καὶ κόλπος ἀκύμων.
passages.english: That all things are judgment, and this judgment is up to you. So take the judgment away when you wish, and, just as for someone who has rounded the headland, there is calm: all things steady, and a bay without a wave.

notes.note: The sentence opens with a bare “That”, with no verb of saying or remembering; it reads as a heading for something to keep in mind. It is kept bare, here and in 2.15, and no “remember” is added. πάντα is plural, “all things”, and returns in “all things steady”.
notes.other_reading: Remember that everything is what you judge it to be

notes.note: “And this is up to you”: the pronoun is feminine and points to the judgment, so the English reads “this judgment” to keep it from being heard as “this fact”.
notes.other_reading: and it is in your power

notes.note: The verb is to lift, and so to lift away, remove. The form is a single act, “take it away”.
notes.other_reading: So remove the judgment when you choose

notes.note: A sailing image: literally “just as to one who has bent round the cape”. The Greek has no “you” and no verb here; it may be felt as “for you, as for a sailor who …”.
notes.other_reading: and, like someone who has doubled the cape, you find calm

notes.greek: γαλήνη, σταθερὰ πάντα καὶ κόλπος ἀκύμων
notes.note: Three items with no verb; “there is” and a colon are supplied. γαλήνη is the calm of the sea; σταθερὰ is steady, standing firm; ἀκύμων is literally “waveless”.
notes.other_reading: calm, everything still, and a waveless gulf

check.note: “As for someone” reads in English as “concerning someone”, so the comparison with a sailor who has rounded the headland can be missed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “just as for someone who has rounded the headland, there is calm”. “Just as” makes the comparison unmistakable; “you find” is not used, because the Greek has no verb and no “you” here.

check.note: The bare “That …” copies the Greek note form, but a reader of today may take it for a broken sentence; the same holds for 2.15. Any fix adds a word.
check.decided: Accepted: the bare “That” is kept, in the same form here and in 2.15, because the Greek has no verb of remembering and none may be added. The note explains that it reads as a heading.

check.note: The Greek has only “and this is up to you”; the English repeats the noun.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “and this judgment is up to you”. The Greek “this” is feminine and so can only point to the judgment, while a bare English “this” would be heard as “this fact”; the note says so.

check.note: Found while settling: the word for “all things” in the first sentence returns here, and the draft gave it as “everything”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “all things steady”, so that the “all things” of the opening is heard again in the calm.

passages.casaubon: Remember that all is but opinion, and all opinion depends of the mind. Take thine opinion away, and then as a ship that hath stricken in within the arms and mouth of the harbour, a present calm; all things safe and steady: a bay, not capable of any storms and tempests: as the poet hath it.

passages.greek: Μὴ τοιαῦτα ὑπολάμβανε, οἷα ὁ ὑβρίζων κρίνει ἢ οἷά σε κρίνειν βούλεται, ἀλλὰ ἴδε αὐτά, ὁποῖα κατʼ ἀλήθειάν ἐστιν.
passages.english: Do not judge things to be such as the person who abuses you decides they are, or wants you to decide they are, but see them as they are in truth.

notes.note: The verb of the glossary’s “judgment” word, so “judge”. The Greek has no noun for what is judged (“such things as …”); “things” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: Do not take things the way the one who abuses you takes them

notes.note: The verb covers insult, outrage and high-handed ill-treatment, in word or act; “abuses” covers both word and act. “You” as its object is supplied from the σε that follows.
notes.other_reading: the person who insults you, the person who treats you with contempt

notes.greek: κρίνει ἢ οἷά σε κρίνειν βούλεται
notes.note: κρίνειν is a different verb from ὑπολαμβάνειν, though close in sense. “Decide” is used for it so that the two can be told apart; its noun, κρίσις, is “verdict” in 6.52 and 7.16.
notes.other_reading: as the person who abuses you judges them, or wants you to judge them

notes.note: “See them”: the pronoun standing alone after its verb is the ordinary “them”. With more weight on it, it would be “look at the things themselves”.
notes.other_reading: but look at the things themselves, as they truly are

check.note: The Greek verb is wider and stronger than insulting: to treat with insolence, to abuse or wrong someone.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the person who abuses you”, which covers ill-treatment in act as well as in word. The note records that “you” is supplied.

check.note: The pronoun may carry stress, “look at the things themselves”, as against the other person’s view of them; “them” gives only the weak sense.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “see them”. The pronoun stands alone after its verb, where Greek uses it as the ordinary “them”; the stressed sense would more naturally have the noun with it, as in 6.52. The note gives the stronger reading.

check.note: The verb is “decide” here, while its noun is “verdict” in 6.52 and 7.16, so the link between verb and noun is not visible.
check.decided: Declined: “decides” stays. “Judge” is already given to the other verb in this sentence, and the two Greek verbs have to be told apart; English has no plain verb made from “verdict”. The note names the noun and where it comes.

passages.casaubon: Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth, or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see what it is in very truth.

passages.greek: Ὅτι πᾶν ὑπόληψις. δῆλα μὲν γὰρ τὰ πρὸς τὸν Κυνικὸν Μόνιμον λεγόμενα· δῆλον δὲ καὶ τὸ χρήσιμον τοῦ λεγομένου, ἐάν τις αὐτοῦ τὸ νόστιμον μέχρι τοῦ ἀληθοῦς δέχηται.
passages.english: That everything is judgment. For what is said in answer to Monimus the Cynic is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true.

notes.note: A bare “That …” again, as in 12.22, with no verb of remembering; none is added. From memory, unchecked: Monimus is credited with saying that everything supposed is smoke or vanity, in words built on this same root, and Marcus’s phrase echoes him.
notes.other_reading: Remember that all is opinion.

notes.greek: τὰ πρὸς τὸν Κυνικὸν Μόνιμον λεγόμενα
notes.note: The preposition can mean “to” or “in answer to, against”. It is taken as the replies made to Monimus, which gives the contrast with the next clause: the objections are plain, but so is the use. It can also be the words addressed to him, or more sharply the things said against him.
notes.other_reading: what was said to Monimus the Cynic is plain

notes.note: From memory, unchecked: Monimus of Syracuse, a Cynic philosopher of the fourth century BC, a follower of Diogenes. The Cynics were a school known for blunt speech and contempt for convention.

“What is said”, singular: it is taken as Monimus’s saying itself, that everything is judgment, set against the plural “things said” in answer to it. Both are the same Greek participle, which “said” and “saying” let the reader hear.
notes.other_reading: the usefulness of what is said

notes.note: A food word. From memory, unchecked, it is used both of what feeds well and of what tastes good, and so of the good part of a thing, the pith. “What is nourishing” keeps a food image and suits the talk of usefulness.
notes.other_reading: if one takes the savour of it

notes.note: Literally “up to the true”: the saying is to be taken so far as it is true and no further.
notes.other_reading: within the limits of what is true

check.greek: τὰ πρὸς τὸν Κυνικὸν Μόνιμον λεγόμενα
check.note: The preposition can mean “said to” or “said against, in reply to” Monimus. The English has chosen the reply, which decides what the whole remark is about.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “in answer to”, which covers replies and objections alike and gives the contrast with the next clause. The note now sets out the other readings, “said to” and “said against”.

check.note: “Enough” adds a shade of concession. The Greek balances two things and gives them the same plain word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying”, with nothing added to the first “plain”.

check.note: The Greek word is what is savoury or pleasant to taste, and so the good part of a thing. “Nourishing” moves the picture from flavour to food value.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “what is nourishing in it”. From memory, unchecked, the Greek word is used of food that feeds well as well as of food that tastes good, and “what is good in it” would drop the food image; the note gives the flavour reading.

check.note: The Greek sets a limit: take it up to the point where it is true and no further. “As far as the truth goes”, after a comma, reads as “as regards the truth”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true”, without the comma, so that the limit is heard.

check.note: The same participle is “what is said” in the plural and then “the saying” in the singular. A reader cannot tell that the two share a word or whose saying is meant.
check.decided: Declined: “the saying” stands. The Greek changes from plural to singular, one saying against the many replies, and “said” and “saying” let the shared word be heard; “what he said” would add a “he” the Greek does not have. The note says whose saying is meant.

passages.casaubon: Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is sweet and pleasing.

passages.greek: Σήμερον ἐξῆλθον πάσης περιστάσεως, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐξέβαλον πᾶσαν περίστασιν· ἔξω γὰρ οὐκ ἦν, ἀλλὰ ἔνδον ἐν ταῖς ὑπολήψεσιν.
passages.english: Today I got out of all that hemmed me in, or rather I threw out all that hemmed me in; for it was not outside but inside, in my judgments.

notes.note: Literally “what stands around”: one’s circumstances, and especially hard ones, a crisis. The picture matters, since he goes on to say it was not “outside” at all, so the English reads “all that hemmed me in”, where “me” is supplied. The Greek repeats the noun and the English repeats the phrase.
notes.other_reading: Today I got out of every difficulty, or rather I threw every difficulty out

notes.note: This verb and ἐξέβαλον both begin with ἐξ-, “out”: “went out of” against “threw out”. The pair is kept with “got out of” and “threw out”.
notes.other_reading: Today I escaped all that hemmed me in, or rather I cast it out

notes.note: No subject is expressed; “it” is supplied, meaning all that hemmed him in.
notes.other_reading: for they were not outside

notes.note: The Greek has only the article, “in the judgments”; the English reads “my”, as English does where Greek leaves the owner to be understood.
notes.other_reading: but within, in the judgments

check.note: The Greek word is literally what stands around one, the circumstances that hem one in. The play of going out, throwing out, outside and inside rests on that picture, which “difficulty” does not carry.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “I got out of all that hemmed me in, or rather I threw out all that hemmed me in”. The phrase is repeated and not shortened to “it all”, because the Greek repeats the noun.

passages.casaubon: This day I did come out of all my trouble. Nay I have cast out all my trouble; it should rather be for that which troubled thee, whatsoever it was, was not without anywhere that thou shouldest come out of it, but within in thine own opinions, from whence it must be cast out, before thou canst truly and constantly be at ease.

passages.greek: Πάσης ὥρας φρόντιζε στιβαρῶς ὡς Ῥωμαῖος καὶ ἄρρην τὸ ἐν χερσὶ μετὰ τῆς ἀκριβοῦς καὶ ἀπλάστου σεμνότητος καὶ φιλοστοργίας καὶ ἐλευθερίας καὶ δικαιότητος πράσσειν καὶ σχολὴν σαυτῷ ἀπὸ πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων φαντασιῶν πορίζειν. ποριεῖς δέ, ἂν ὡς ἐσχάτην τοῦ βίου ἑκάστην πρᾶξιν ἐνεργῇς, ἀπηλλαγμένος πάσης εἰκαιότητος καὶ ἐμπαθοῦς ἀποστροφῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ αἱροῦντος λόγου καὶ ὑποκρίσεως καὶ φιλαυτίας καὶ δυσαρεστήσεως πρὸς τὰ συμμεμοιραμένα. ὁρᾷς πῶς ὀλίγα ἐστίν, ὧν κρατήσας τις δύναται εὔρουν καὶ θεουδῆ βιῶσαι βίον· καὶ γὰρ οἱ θεοὶ πλέον οὐδὲν ἀπαιτήσουσι παρὰ τοῦ ταῦτα φυλάσσοντος.
passages.english: At every hour take firm care, as a Roman and a man, to do what is in hand with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice, and to win yourself respite from all other impressions. You will win it if you carry out each action as the last of your life, rid of all aimlessness, of turning away in passion from what reason decides, of pretence, of self-love and of discontent with what has been allotted to you. You see how few the things are which, once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing: for the gods will demand nothing more of whoever keeps to these.

notes.note: The adverb means “sturdily, stoutly”. The English takes it with “take care”; by position it could also colour “to do what is in hand”.
notes.other_reading: take care, as a Roman and a man, to do what is in hand sturdily

notes.note: The word is “male”, not the ordinary word for a man. The English reads “a man” because “a male” reads oddly here; the same word comes back in 3.5a, where it is “male”.
notes.other_reading: as a Roman and a male

notes.note: One article and one pair of adjectives stand before four nouns. The English keeps a single “with” for the whole list, so that “exact and unfeigned” can be heard with dignity alone or with all four, as in the Greek. “Affection” is the noun of the word given as “warmly affectionate” in 6.30a and 1.17a.
notes.other_reading: with exact and unfeigned dignity, with warm affection, with freedom and with justice

notes.note: The word is “leisure, free time”. Since it is leisure from other impressions (φαντασίαι), the English reads “respite”. The verb, “procure, win”, comes twice in the Greek and is “win” both times.
notes.other_reading: to procure yourself leisure from all the other impressions

notes.greek: ἐμπαθοῦς ἀποστροφῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ αἱροῦντος λόγου
notes.note: The phrase rests on the idiom “reason proves (or requires) it”, literally “the reason that takes”. The English reads “what reason decides”, and “in passion” for an adjective that means “in the grip of a passion”. “All” stands once in the Greek, before “aimlessness”, and stays there.
notes.other_reading: of emotion-driven turning away from the reasoning that carries the point

notes.note: Literally “the things that have been allotted along with (you)”, the share dealt out together with a person’s life. “To you” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: discontent with the things allotted together with you

notes.note: Literally “flowing well”. It is a Stoic word for the happy life, “a good flow of life” (from memory, unchecked). The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: a prosperous life

notes.note: In Homer the word means “god-fearing”; later writers also used it as if it meant “godlike”. The English reads “god-fearing” because the next clause speaks of what the gods will demand, though that clause fits “godlike” as well.
notes.other_reading: a life that flows smoothly and is like the gods’

notes.note: The two opening particles together can mean simply “for in fact”, or the first can mean “too” (“for the gods too”). The English takes the first, since the passage names no one else who makes demands.
notes.other_reading: for the gods too will demand nothing more

check.greek: μετὰ τῆς ἀκριβοῦς καὶ ἀπλάστου σεμνότητος καὶ φιλοστοργίας καὶ ἐλευθερίας καὶ δικαιότητος
check.note: One article and one pair of adjectives stand before four nouns, so “exact and unfeigned” may qualify all four; the repeated “with” confined them to dignity.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice”, with one “with” as the Greek has one article, so the adjectives can be heard with the first noun or with all four. “Warm” is dropped before “affection” because it would close the list off again; a note records both points.

check.greek: σχολὴν σαυτῷ ἀπὸ πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων φαντασιῶν πορίζειν
check.note: “Leisure from impressions” is not followed at once, and “give” is weaker than the Greek verb, which is “procure, win”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to win yourself respite from all other impressions” and then “You will win it”, one English verb for the repeated Greek verb. “Impressions” stays for φαντασίαι, the rendering settled in the glossary, in place of “every other thought that presents itself”.

check.greek: ἐμπαθοῦς ἀποστροφῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ αἱροῦντος λόγου
check.note: “Passionate” reads as praise today, and “the reason that decides” is unclear; the Greek is a turning away, driven by passion, from what reason concludes.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “of turning away in passion from what reason decides”. “Passion” is kept because it is this translation’s word for the Greek root, as in “the passions of love” in 1.17a, and “any” is not added because “all” stands once in the Greek, at the head of the list.

check.note: The word is “god-fearing” in its old sense but was also used as if “godlike”; the choice should be marked.
check.decided: Accepted: “god-fearing” stays, and a note marks the choice and gives “like the gods’” as the other reading.

check.greek: καὶ γὰρ οἱ θεοὶ πλέον οὐδὲν ἀπαιτήσουσι
check.note: The first particle may carry “too” (the gods as well), which is dropped, and the verb is to demand what is due, stronger than “ask”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “for the gods will demand nothing more”. The two particles together often mean no more than “for in fact”, and the passage names no one else who demands, so “for the gods too” is given in a note as the other reading.

check.note: Found while settling: “once a person has mastered them, let them live” used “them” first for the things and then for the person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “which, once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing”.

passages.casaubon: Let it be thy earnest and incessant care as a Roman and a man to perform whatsoever it is that thou art about, with true and unfeigned gravity, natural affection, freedom and justice: and as for all other cares, and imaginations, how thou mayest ease thy mind of them. Which thou shalt do; if thou shalt go about every action as thy last action, free from all vanity, all passionate and wilful aberration from reason, and from all hypocrisy, and self-love, and dislike of those things, which by the fates or appointment of God have happened unto thee. Thou seest that those things, which for a man to hold on in a prosperous course, and to live a divine life, are requisite and necessary, are not many, for the gods will require no more of any man, that shall but keep and observe these things.

nearest.title: Gravity, and keeping the names I have taken

passages.greek:
Αἰσχρόν ἐστιν, ἐν ᾧ βίῳ τὸ σῶμά σοι μὴ ἀπαυδᾷ, ἐν τούτῳ τὴν ψυχὴν προαπαυδᾶν.

Ὅρα μὴ ἀποκαισαρωθῇς, μὴ βαφῇς· γίνεται γάρ. τήρησον οὖν σεαυτὸν ἁπλοῦν, ἀγαθόν, ἀκέραιον, σεμνόν, ἄκομψον, τοῦ δικαίου φίλον, θεοσεβῆ, εὐμενῆ, φιλόστοργον, ἐρρωμένον πρὸς τὰ πρέποντα ἔργα. ἀγώνισαι, ἵνα τοιοῦτος συμμείνῃς, οἷόν σε ἠθέλησε ποιῆσαι φιλοσοφία. αἰδοῦ θεούς, σῷζε ἀνθρώπους. βραχὺς ὁ βίος· εἶς καρπὸς τῆς ἐπιγείου ζωῆς, διάθεσις ὁσία καὶ πράξεις κοινωνικαί.
passages.english:
It is shameful that, in a life in which your body does not give out, your soul should give out first.

Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed: for it happens. So keep yourself simple, good, unspoiled, dignified, unpretentious, a friend of what is just, reverent toward the gods, kindly, warmly affectionate, strong for the work that is fitting. Struggle to remain the kind of person philosophy wanted to make you. Stand in awe of the gods, keep people safe. Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.

notes.note: The verb is the one used of the body just before, with “first” added in front: to give up, to fail from exhaustion. One English verb serves for both.
notes.other_reading: that your soul should be the first to say no

notes.note: A word made from “Caesar”, apparently coined here: to be made into a Caesar through and through. The English spells it out.
notes.other_reading: that you are not Caesarified

notes.note: Literally “that you are not dipped, dyed”. The dye in mind is probably the imperial purple, but the Greek does not name it and the English does not add it.
notes.other_reading: that you are not stained with the purple

notes.note: The word means unmixed, undamaged, pure. The English reads “unspoiled”.
notes.other_reading: pure

notes.note: Literally “without elegance, without polish”: no fine airs. It is the opposite of the “elegance” warned against in 3.5a. The English reads “unpretentious”.
notes.other_reading: plain

notes.note: The verb is to feel awe or shame before someone. “Stand in awe of” is used so that it is not taken for the same word as “reverent toward the gods” earlier in the list, which is a different Greek word.
notes.other_reading: Revere the gods

notes.note: The verb is “save, keep safe, preserve”. The English reads “keep people safe”.
notes.other_reading: save people

notes.note: The first word as given is a slip of the digitised text for the word “one”, and is read so; the verb “is” is supplied. The Greek uses two words for life in these two sentences, a life as it is lived and the state of being alive, and the English reads “life” and “living”.
notes.other_reading: one fruit of earthly life

notes.note: “Social” follows the glossary. The sense is actions done as a member of the community and for it, not sociable ones.
notes.other_reading: acts that serve the common good

check.greek: βραχὺς ὁ βίος· εἶς καρπὸς τῆς ἐπιγείου ζωῆς
check.note: Two Greek words, a life as lived and being alive, are both “life” in consecutive sentences, though the Greek varies.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “There is one fruit of living on earth”, so that the two Greek words are “life” and “living”. “Our existence” is not used: the Greek has no “our”, and “living” is the plainer word.

check.note: “Social actions” suggests sociability today; the Greek word means serving the community, the common good.
check.decided: Declined: “social actions” stays. “Social” is the rendering settled for this Greek word across the translation, and its negative is “unsocially” in 3.5a, so one English word is kept for it; a note gives the sense, actions done for the community.

check.note: The verb is to stand in awe of, to revere; “respect” is weaker.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Stand in awe of the gods”, which is the force of the verb. “Revere” is not used because “reverent toward the gods” already stands for a different Greek word in the list just before.

check.note: The verb is “save, keep safe, preserve”; “protect” is one narrowing of it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “keep people safe”, the broad sense of the verb; “save people” is given in the note.

check.note: The word is “without refinement or affectation”; beside “simple”, “plain” adds almost nothing and loses the point about affectation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “unpretentious”. The Greek word denies elegance and fine airs, which “plain” beside “simple” did not bring out.

check.note: Literal and right, but a reader may not see that the dye is the imperial purple; the Greek leaves it equally bare.
check.decided: Declined: “that you are not dyed” stays. The Greek does not name the dye, and a note says that the imperial purple is probably meant.

part.left_out: πάντα ὡς Ἀντωνίνου μαθητής· τὸ ὑπὲρ τῶν κατὰ λόγον πρασσομένων εὔτονον ἐκείνου καὶ τὸ ὁμαλὲς πανταχοῦ καὶ τὸ ὅσιον καὶ τὸ εὔδιον τοῦ προσώπου καὶ τὸ μειλίχιον καὶ τὸ ἀκενόδοξον καὶ τὸ περὶ τὴν κατάληψιν τῶν πραγμάτων φιλότιμον· καὶ ὡς ἐκεῖνος οὐκ ἄν τι ὅλως παρῆκε μὴ πρότερον εὖ μάλα κατιδὼν καὶ σαφῶς νοήσας· καὶ ὡς ἔφερεν ἐκεῖνος τοὺς ἀδίκως αὐτὸν μεμφομένους μὴ ἀντιμεμφόμενος· καὶ ὡς ἐπ’ οὐδὲν ἔσπευδεν· καὶ ὠς διαβολὰς οὐκ ἐδέχετο· καὶ ὡς ἀκριβὴς ἦν ἐξεταστὴς ἠθῶν καὶ πράξεων καὶ οὐκ ὀνειδιστής, οὐ ψοφοδεής, οὐχ ὑπόπτης, οὐ σοφιστής· καὶ ὡς ὀλίγοις ἀρκούμενος, οἷον οἰκήσει, στρωμνῇ, ἐσθῆτι, τροφῇ, ὑπηρεσίᾳ· καὶ ὡς φιλόπονος καὶ μακρόθυμος· καὶ οἷος μένειν ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ μέχρι ἑσπέρας, διὰ τὴν λιτὴν δίαιταν μηδὲ τοῦ ἀποκρίνειν τὰ περιττώματα παρὰ τὴν συνήθη ὥραν χρῄζων· καὶ τὸ βέβαιον καὶ ὅμοιον ἐν ταῖς φιλίαις αὐτοῦ· καὶ τὸ ἀνέχεσθαι τῶν ἀντιβαινόντων παρρησιαστικῶς ταῖς γνώμαις αὐτοῦ καὶ χαίρειν εἴ τίς τι δεικνύοι κρεῖττον· καὶ ὡς θεοσεβὴς χωρὶς δεισιδαιμονίας· ἵν’ οὕτως εὐσυνειδήτῳ σοι ἐπιστῇ ἠ τελευταία ὥρα ὡς ἐκείνῳ.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 6.27 at 'the only fruit of this earthly life' and begins its 6.28 with the rest of the chapter, the portrait of Antoninus Pius.

passages.casaubon: If in this kind of life thy body be able to hold out, it is a shame that thy soul should faint first, and give over, take heed, lest of a philosopher thou become a mere Cæsar in time, and receive a new tincture from the court. For it may happen if thou dost not take heed. Keep thyself therefore, truly simple, good, sincere, grave, free from all ostentation, a lover of that which is just, religious, kind, tender-hearted, strong and vigorous to undergo anything that becomes thee. Endeavour to continue such, as philosophy (hadst thou wholly and constantly applied thyself unto it) would have made, and secured thee. Worship the Gods, procure the welfare of men, this life is short. Charitable actions, and a holy disposition, is the only fruit of this earthly life.

nearest.title: Gravity, and keeping the names I have taken

passages.greek: Ὀνόματα θέμενος σαυτῷ ταῦτα· ἀγαθός, αἰδήμων, ἀληθής, ἔμφρων, σύμφρων, ὑπέρφρων, πρόσεχε μήποτε μετονομάζῃ, κἂν ἀπολλύῃς ταῦτα τὰ ὀνόματα, καὶ ταχέως ἐπάνιθι ἐπ’ αὐτά. μέμνησο δὲ ὅτι τὸ μὲν ἔμφρων ἐβούλετό σοι σημαίνειν τὴν ἐφ’ ἕκαστα διαληπτικὴν ἐπίστασιν καὶ τὸ ἀπαρενθύμητον· τὸ δὲ σύμφρων τὴν ἑκούσιον ἀπόδεξιν τῶν ὑπὸ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως ἀπονεμομένων· τὸ δὲ ὑπέρφρων τὴν ὑπέρτασιν τοῦ φρονοῦντος μορίου ὑπὲρ λείαν ἣ τραχεῖαν κίνησιν τῆς σαρκὸς καὶ τὸ δοξάριον καὶ τὸν θάνατον καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα. ἐὰν οὖν διατηρῇς σεαυτὸν ὲν τούτοις τοῖς ὀνόμασι μὴ γλιχόμενος τοῦ ὑπ’ ἄλλων κατὰ ταῦτα ὀνομάζεσθαι, ἔσῃ ἕτερος καὶ εἰς βίον εἰσελεύσῃ ἕτερον. τὸ γὰρ ἔτι τοιοῦτον εἶναι οἷος μέχρι νῦν γέγονας, καὶ ἐν βίῳ τοιούτῳ σπαράσσεσθαι καὶ μολύνεσθαι, λίαν ἐστὶν ἀναισθήτου καὶ φιλοψύχου καὶ ὁμοίου τοῖς ἡμιβρώτοις θηριομάχοις, οἵτινες μεστοὶ τραυμάτων καὶ λύθρου παρακαλοῦσιν ὅμως εἰς τὴν αὔριον φυλαχθῆναι, παραβληθησόμενοι τοιοῦτοι τοῖς αὐτοῖς ὄνυξι καὶ δήγμασιν. ἐμβίβασον οὖν σαυτὸν εἰς τὰ ὀλίγα ταῦτα ὀνόματα, κἂν μὲν ἐπ’ αὐτῶν μένειν δύνῃ, μένε ὥσπερ εἰς μακάρων τινὰς νήσους μετῳκισμένος· ἐὰν δὲ αἴσθῃ ὅτι ἐκπίπτεις καὶ οὐ περικρατεῖς, ἄπιθι θαρρῶν εἰς γωνίαν τινά, ὅπου κρατήσεις, ἢ καὶ παντάπασιν ἔξιθι τοῦ βίου, μὴ ὀργιζόμενος, ἀλλὰ ἁπλῶς καὶ ἐλευθέρως καὶ αἰδημόνως, ἕν γε τοῦτο μόνον πράξας ἐν τῷ βίῳ τὸ οὕτως ἐξελθεῖν. πρὸς μέντοι τὸ μεμνῆσθαι τῶν ὀνομάτων μεγάλως συλλήψεταί σοι τὸ μεμνῆσθαι θεῶν καὶ ὅτιπερ οὐ κολακεύεσθαι οὗτοι θέλουσιν, ἀλλὰ ἐξομοιοῦσθαι ἑαυτοῖς τὰ λογικὰ πάντα καὶ εἶναι τὴν μὲν συκῆν τὰ συκῆς ποιοῦσαν, τὸν δὲ κύνα τὰ κυνός, τὴν δὲ μέλισσαν τὰ μελίσσης, τὸν δὲ ἄνθρωπον τὰ ἀνθρώπου.
passages.english: Having given yourself these names: good, modest, truthful, clear-minded, like-minded, high-minded, take care that you never come to bear other names; and if you do lose these names, go back to them quickly. Remember that “clear-minded” was to mean for you a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded; “like-minded”, the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns; and “high-minded”, the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind. So if you keep yourself in these names, without craving to have others call you by them, you will be a different person and will enter a different life. For to go on being such as you have been up to now, and to be torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life, someone like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites. So put yourself aboard these few names, and if you can stay on them, stay, like someone who has moved to some Islands of the Blessed. But if you sense that you are falling away and are not prevailing, go away with a good heart to some corner where you will prevail, or even leave life altogether, not in anger, but simply, freely and modestly, having at least done this one thing, and only this, in your life: to leave it in this way. Toward remembering the names, though, it will help you greatly to remember the gods, and that what they want is not to be flattered, but for all rational beings to become like them, and for the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being.

notes.note: Three words built on one root (phron, “mind, thinking”): emphron, “in one’s mind, sensible”; symphron, “of one mind with”; hyperphron, “with mind above”, usually a word of blame (“haughty”) that is here turned to a good sense. Three words ending in “minded” are used so that the play shows; the definitions that follow carry the meaning, and “high-minded” is not meant in its ordinary English sense.
notes.other_reading: sensible, in agreement, above it all

notes.note: The word covers a sense of shame, self-respect and respect for others. The English reads “modest”, and “modestly” for the adverb near the end.
notes.other_reading: self-respecting

notes.note: The form can be passive (“are renamed”) or middle (“rename yourself”). “Come to bear other names” leaves open who does the renaming, as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: take care that you never change your names

notes.greek: κἂν ἀπολλύῃς ταῦτα τὰ ὀνόματα, καὶ ταχέως ἐπάνιθι
notes.note: The second “and” in the Greek sits awkwardly before “go back quickly”. It is read as marking the main clause (“then too”) and left untranslated; it may be a fault in the text.
notes.other_reading: and if you lose these names, then also go back to them quickly

notes.note: The first phrase is “attention that distinguishes”, stopping over each thing and telling it apart. The last word is rare: the state of not letting something slip past unconsidered.
notes.other_reading: an attention that takes each thing apart, and freedom from carelessness

notes.note: Literally “the common nature”, the nature shared by all things, which is the nature of the whole. The literal phrase is kept.
notes.other_reading: what the nature of the whole assigns

notes.greek: τὴν ὑπέρτασιν τοῦ φρονοῦντος μορίου ὑπὲρ
notes.note: The Greek explains the name by its own parts: “high-minded” is the stretching high (hyper) of the part that has mind (phron) above (hyper again) the things listed. “Lifting high”, “has mind” and “above” are chosen so that the explanation can be heard in English. “Above” is repeated where the Greek has it once.
notes.other_reading: the raising of the part that thinks above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh

notes.greek: λείαν ἣ τραχεῖαν κίνησιν τῆς σαρκὸς
notes.note: “Smooth or rough movement of the flesh” is a way of saying pleasure and pain. The image is kept. The second word as given is a slip for “or”.
notes.other_reading: above pleasure or pain in the flesh

notes.note: The word is “without perception”: dull, not noticing what is happening to oneself. “Senseless” is used, and “sense” for the verb of the same root further on (“if you sense that you are falling away”).
notes.other_reading: someone thoroughly dull

notes.note: Literally “life-loving”, always said with blame: holding on to life at any price.
notes.other_reading: cowardly

notes.note: Men who fight wild animals in the arena. The English reads “beast-fighters”.
notes.other_reading: men who fight wild beasts in the arena

notes.note: A future participle: “going to be thrown, such as they are”. It may state simply what awaits them or, more bitterly, what they are being kept for; “to be thrown” leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: though they will be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites

notes.note: The verb is the regular word for putting someone on board a ship. With the islands that follow, the picture of a boat is kept.
notes.other_reading: so set yourself upon these few names

notes.note: The Islands of the Blessed: in Greek story, the far-off islands where favoured heroes live on after death without toil.
notes.other_reading: to certain islands of the blessed

notes.note: The first verb is “fall out, fall away”; it is also the usual word for being driven into exile or cast ashore, which fits the picture of a settler. The second verb and the later “you will prevail” share a root, so “prevail” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: that you are being cast out and are not keeping the mastery

notes.note: Literally “having done this one thing only, at least”. The Greek says both “at least” and “only”, and both are kept.
notes.other_reading: having done this one thing at any rate in your life

notes.greek: καὶ εἶναι τὴν μὲν συκῆν τὰ συκῆς ποιοῦσαν
notes.note: This is read as still depending on “they want”: the gods want the fig tree to be doing a fig tree’s work, and so on. It can also be read as depending on “remember”, a statement of what makes each thing what it is.
notes.other_reading: and that it is doing the work of a fig tree that makes a fig tree, of a dog a dog, of a bee a bee, of a human being a human being
