check.greek: καὶ εἶναι τὴν μὲν συκῆν τὰ συκῆς ποιοῦσαν
check.note: The clause can hang on “they want” (the gods want the fig tree to do a fig tree’s work) or on “remember that” (a fig tree is what does a fig tree’s work). The English mixed the two and was hard to follow.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause is taken with “they want” and now reads “and for the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog”, and so on. The Greek infinitive follows straight on from the two that depend on “want”; the other construction is given in a note.

check.note: The verb can be middle (take other names) or passive (are given other names). “Renamed” sounds like something others do, while the next clause points to the person’s own doing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “take care that you never come to bear other names”, which leaves open, as the Greek form does, whether the new names are taken or given.

check.greek: κἂν ἀπολλύῃς ταῦτα τὰ ὀνόματα, καὶ ταχέως ἐπάνιθι
check.note: As given, a second “and” stands after the if-clause and before the command, and the English drops it without a sign. It is either a slip in the text or means “then too”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stays, “and if you do lose these names, go back to them quickly”, and the note on the stray “and” is kept, now with “then too” as its sense.

check.greek: τὸ δὲ ὑπέρφρων τὴν ὑπέρτασιν τοῦ φρονοῦντος μορίου ὑπὲρ
check.note: The Greek explains each name by its own parts: “high-minded” is the raising high of the minded part above pleasure and pain. English had four words for two roots, so the explanation no longer sounded like one; “high-minded” also has a ready English sense that is not this.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh”, so that “high” and “mind” answer the two halves of the name. “High-minded” is kept beside “clear-minded” and “like-minded” so that the three names still show their common root; a note says its ordinary English sense is not meant.

check.note: “An attention that tells each thing apart” is unclear: apart from what? The Greek is a discriminating attention directed at each particular thing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a discerning attention to each thing”. “In turn” is left out because the Greek says only “to each thing”.

check.note: “Signify” is stiff for a reader of today.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “was to mean for you”. “Mean” is used where the suggestion has “tell you”, so that the sentence can run on into the three definitions.

check.note: The double “by” in “to be called by them by others” is clumsy and for a moment unclear.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “without craving to have others call you by them”.

check.note: The word here is “insensible, dull”, not noticing what is happening to oneself; “without feeling” reads as cold-hearted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “someone thoroughly senseless”. The Greek word is about not perceiving what is happening to oneself, not about a cold heart.

check.note: “Only” is added. The future participle just says they are going to be thrown, as they are, to the same claws and bites.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “only” is removed and the English now reads “to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites”. “Though” is not added either, since the Greek has a bare future participle; the note gives the suggested wording.

check.note: The verb is “fall out, fall away, be thrown off course” and continues the picture of going aboard; “driven out” brings in someone doing the driving.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “that you are falling away”, with no one doing the driving. The note records that the verb is also used of exiles and of ships cast ashore.

check.greek: ἕν γε τοῦτο μόνον πράξας ἐν τῷ βίῳ
check.note: “At least this one thing only” is awkward, though each word answers a Greek one.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “having at least done this one thing, and only this, in your life”. Both “at least” and “only” answer a Greek word and neither is dropped, but they no longer stand side by side.

check.note: Found while settling: the verb given as “notice” is of one root with the word now given as “senseless” a few lines earlier.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But if you sense that you are falling away”, so that the echo of “senseless” can be heard.

passages.casaubon: Now that thou hast taken these names upon thee of good, modest, true; of ἔμφρων, σύμφρων, ὑπέρφρων; take heed lest at any times by doing anything that is contrary, thou be but improperly so called, and lose thy right to these appellations. Or if thou do, return unto them again with all possible speed. And remember, that the word ἔμφρων notes unto thee an intent and intelligent consideration of every object that presents itself unto thee, without distraction. And the word σύμφρων, a ready and contented acceptation of whatsoever by the appointment of the common nature, happens unto thee. And the word ὑπέρφρων, a super-extension, or a transcendent, and outreaching disposition of thy mind, whereby it passeth by all bodily pains and pleasures, honour and credit, death and whatsoever is of the same nature, as matters of absolute indifferency, and in no wise to be stood upon by a wise man. These then if inviolably thou shalt observe, and shalt not be ambitious to be so called by others, both thou thyself shalt become a new man, and thou shalt begin a new life. For to continue such as hitherto thou hast been, to undergo those distractions and distempers as thou must needs for such a life as hitherto thou hast lived, is the part of one that is very foolish, and is overfond of his life. Whom a man might compare to one of those half-eaten wretches, matched in the amphitheatre with wild beasts; who as full as they are all the body over with wounds and blood, desire for a great favour, that they may be reserved till the next day, then also, and in the same estate to be exposed to the same nails and teeth as before. Away therefore, ship thyself; and from the troubles and distractions of thy former life convey thyself as it were unto these few names; and if thou canst abide in them, or be constant in the practice and possession of them, continue there as glad and joyful as one that were translated unto some such place of bliss and happiness as that which by Hesiod and Plato is called the Islands of the Blessed, by others called the Elysian Fields. And whensoever thou findest thyself; that thou art in danger of a relapse, and that thou art not able to master and overcome those difficulties and temptations that present themselves in thy present station: get thee into any private corner, where thou mayst be better able. Or if that will not serve forsake even thy life rather. But so that it be not in passion but in a plain voluntary modest way: this being the only commendable action of thy whole life that thus thou art departed, or this having been the main work and business of thy whole life, that thou mightest thus depart. Now for the better remembrance of those names that we have spoken of, thou shalt find it a very good help, to remember the Gods as often as may be: and that, the thing which they require at our hands of as many of us, as are by nature reasonable creation is not that with fair words, and outward show of piety and devotion we should flatter them, but that we should become like unto them: and that as all other natural creatures, the fig tree for example; the dog the bee: both do, all of them, and apply themselves unto that which by their natural constitution, is proper unto them; so man likewise should do that, which by his nature, as he is a man, belongs unto him.

nearest.title: Gravity, and keeping the names I have taken

passages.greek: Μήτε ἀκούσιος ἐνέργει μήτε ἀκοινώνητος μήτε ἀνεξέταστος μήτε ἀνθελκόμενος· μήτε κομψεία τὴν διάνοιάν σου καλλωπιζέτω· μήτε πολυρρήμων μήτε πολυπράγμων ἔσο. ἔτι δὲ ὁ ἐν σοὶ θεὸς ἔστω προστάτης ζῴου ἄρρενος καὶ πρεσβύτου καὶ πολιτικοῦ καὶ Ῥωμαίου καὶ ἄρχοντος, ἀνατεταχότος ἑαυτόν, οἷος ἂν εἴη τις περιμένων τὸ ἀνακλητικὸν ἐκ τοῦ βίου εὔλυτος, μήτε ὅρκου δεόμενος μήτε ἀνθρώπου τινὸς μάρτυρος.
passages.english: Do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. Do not let elegance dress up your thought. Do not be a person of many words or a busybody. Further, let the god in you be the guardian of a living being that is male, old, engaged in public affairs, a Roman and a ruler, who has set himself in order, as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released, needing neither an oath nor any human being as witness.

notes.note: The negative of the word the glossary gives as “social”: acting without regard for the community one belongs to. “Unsocially” keeps the tie with “social actions” in 6.30a.
notes.other_reading: or without regard for the common good

notes.note: Literally “unexamined”. Said of the one acting, it can mean without having examined the matter, or without having examined oneself. The object is left open.
notes.other_reading: or without having examined yourself

notes.note: Literally “dragged in the opposite direction”: acting while something in you pulls against the act.
notes.other_reading: or with reluctance pulling against you

notes.note: Elegance, cleverness, prettiness in general. Fine wording is probably meant, since it is said to dress up thought and the next clause is about many words, but the Greek does not say so and the English keeps the general word.
notes.other_reading: Do not let fine phrasing dress up your thought.

notes.note: Two matching words, “many-worded” and “many-doinged”. The second is the usual Greek word for a meddler, and “busybody” gives that sense; the match between the two words is lost in English.
notes.other_reading: Do not be a person of many words or of many doings.

notes.note: “The god in you” is literal. It means the divine part in a person, which Marcus elsewhere calls the guardian spirit or the ruling part; the Greek here says only “god”.
notes.other_reading: the god within you

notes.note: One who stands in front of or over another: a protector, patron or one in charge. The English reads “guardian”.
notes.other_reading: let the god in you be in charge of a living being

notes.note: The word is “old man”, a man well on in years. How old it claims the writer is cannot be fixed.
notes.other_reading: an elder

notes.note: The word is not the noun for a citizen but an adjective, “of the city, taking part in its affairs”: a statesman, or a being made for life in a community. The English reads “engaged in public affairs”.
notes.other_reading: made for civic life

notes.note: Literally “having ordered (or drawn up) himself”. It may be a military picture, in keeping with the signal that follows. The verb is unusual in this use, and the text has been doubted here (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: who has taken up his post

notes.note: The army’s trumpet signal that recalls troops from the field. “To withdraw from life” translates the Greek “out of life”.
notes.other_reading: waiting for the recall to be sounded from life

notes.note: Literally “easily loosed”, like something lightly tied: with nothing to hold him back.
notes.other_reading: unencumbered

check.note: The word is not the noun for a citizen but the adjective for one made for the life of a city and engaged in public affairs; “a citizen” is a different and smaller claim.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “engaged in public affairs”. The Greek word is the adjective “of the city’s affairs”, not the noun for a citizen.

check.note: The ordinary sense is “meddlesome, a busybody”. “Of many doings” keeps the word’s parts to match “many words”, and a reader will hear “busy”, not “meddling”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Do not be a person of many words or a busybody”. “Busybody” gives the ordinary sense of meddling and still has “busy” in it; the lost match with “many words” is explained in a note.

check.note: The Greek word is elegance, cleverness, prettiness in general; “phrasing” limits it to words, which the Greek does not say.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Do not let elegance dress up your thought”, which no longer limits the word to phrasing. “Elegance” is used where the suggestion has “cleverness”, since the verb is about making something pretty.

check.note: The word is an old man, a man of advanced years; “older” softens it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “old”. The softening is removed, and the plain word is used in place of “a man of ripe age”.

check.note: “Unsocially” is unclear today; the sense is “without regard for the community, for others”.
check.decided: Declined: “unsocially” stays. It is the negative of “social”, the rendering settled for this Greek root, so one English word is kept for it; a note now gives the sense, acting without regard for the community.

check.note: The word is one who stands at the head, a leader as well as a protector; “be in charge of” is as likely as “guard”.
check.decided: Declined: “guardian” stays. The Greek word covers both a protector and one in charge, and the note gives “be in charge of” as the other reading.

check.greek: ἀνατεταχότος ἑαυτόν, οἷος ἂν εἴη τις περιμένων
check.note: The participle is “who has drawn himself up, set himself in order”; “taken up his post” adds “post”. The Greek also sets the comparison off as a clause of its own (“such as someone would be who waits”), which the English ran together with the posting.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “who has set himself in order, as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life”. “Post” is no longer added, and the comparison is a clause of its own, as in the Greek.

check.note: The word is “easily loosed, unencumbered”; “ready to go” loses the picture of being untied.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “easily released”, which keeps the Greek picture of being untied; “unencumbered” is given in the note.

part.left_out: ἐνέστω δὲ τὸ φαιδρὸν καὶ τὸ ἀπροσδεὲς τῆς ἔξωθεν ὑπηρεσίας καὶ τὸ ἀπροσδεὲς ἡσυχίας, ἣν ἄλλοι παρέχουσιν. ὀρθὸν οὖν εἶναι χρή, οὐχὶ ὀρθούμενον.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 3.5 at 'nor any man to be a witness' and begins its 3.6 with the rest of the chapter, 'To be cheerful'.

passages.casaubon: Do nothing against thy will, nor contrary to the community, nor without due examination, nor with reluctancy. Affect not to set out thy thoughts with curious neat language. Be neither a great talker, nor a great undertaker. Moreover, let thy God that is in thee to rule over thee, find by thee, that he hath to do with a man; an aged man; a sociable man; a Roman; a prince; one that hath ordered his life, as one that expecteth, as it were, nothing but the sound of the trumpet, sounding a retreat to depart out of this life with all expedition. One who for his word or actions neither needs an oath, nor any man to be a witness.

nearest.title: Gravity, and keeping the names I have taken

passages.greek: Πῶς προσενήνεξαι μέχρι νῦν θεοῖς, γονεῦσιν, ἀδελφοῖς, γυναικί, τέκνοις, διδασκάλοις, τροφεῦσι, φίλοις, οἰκείοις, οἰκέταις· εἰ πρὸς πάντας σοι μέχρι νῦν ἐστι τό· μήτε τινὰ ῥέξαι ἐξαίσιον μήτε τι εἰπεῖν. ἀναμιμνῄσκου δὲ καὶ δι’ οἵων διελήλυθας καὶ οἷα ἤρκεσας ὑπομεῖναι καὶ ὅτι πλήρης ἤδη σοι ἡ ἱστορία τοῦ βίου καὶ τελεία ἡ λειτουργία καὶ πόσα ὦπται καλὰ καὶ πόσων μὲν ἡδονῶν καὶ πόνων ὑπερεῖδες, πόσα δὲ ἔνδοξα παρεῖδες, εἰς ὅσους δὲ ἀγνώμονας εὐγνώμων ἐγένου.
passages.english: How have you behaved up to now toward the gods, your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, those who brought you up, your friends, those close to you, your household slaves? Does this hold of you up to now, toward all of them: “to have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong”? Call to mind, too, what things you have passed through and what things you have been strong enough to endure; and that the story of your life is now full and your service complete; and how many fine things you have seen; and how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many honours you have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people you have been considerate.

notes.note: The Greek gives no question mark. The opening is read as a question put to oneself; it could depend on an unspoken “consider”.
notes.other_reading: Consider how you have behaved up to now toward the gods

notes.note: The plural is “brothers”, and can cover brothers and sisters together. “Brothers” is kept.
notes.other_reading: your brothers and sisters

notes.note: Those who rear a child: nurses, foster-carers, the tutor who has charge of a boy. The English reads “those who brought you up”.
notes.other_reading: your tutors

notes.note: People who belong to one’s house or circle: kin, household, intimates. The English reads “those close to you”, and the same in 1.17a, where the word stands beside a separate word for relatives.
notes.other_reading: your relatives

notes.greek: εἰ πρὸς πάντας σοι μέχρι νῦν ἐστι τό
notes.note: Literally “whether toward all of them there is for you up to now the (saying)”. The “whether” has no verb to depend on, so the English makes a direct question; it could hang on the first sentence or on an unspoken “consider”.
notes.other_reading: and whether up to now it holds of you toward all of them

notes.greek: μήτε τινὰ ῥέξαι ἐξαίσιον μήτε τι εἰπεῖν
notes.note: A line of Homer, from the Odyssey, said of Odysseus as king and adapted to fit the sentence (from memory, unchecked). The adjective means “beyond what is right or due” and stands once in the Greek; the English repeats “wrong” to make the second half clear.
notes.other_reading: neither to have done anything out of bounds to anyone, nor to have said it

notes.note: The noun can be a story or record, or an inquiry and what is learned by it. The English reads “the story of your life”.
notes.other_reading: that your acquaintance with life is now complete

notes.note: A public service or duty performed for the community. The English reads “service”.
notes.other_reading: your public duty is finished

notes.note: The verb is passive with no person named: “how many fine things have been seen”. The “you” is carried over from the clause before, where the Greek has “for you”.
notes.other_reading: how many fine things have been seen

notes.note: The second noun is toil or hardship as much as pain. “Pains” is used because it stands here as the partner of “pleasures”.
notes.other_reading: how many pleasures and hardships

notes.note: Two compounds of “see”: to look over the top of, so to look down on, and to look past, so to disregard. “Look” is kept in both.
notes.other_reading: how many pleasures and pains you have despised, how many honours you have disregarded

notes.note: A matched pair on one root: without right feeling (unkind, unfair, ungrateful) and with right feeling (kind, fair, generous). “Inconsiderate” and “considerate” keep the pair.
notes.other_reading: to how many ungrateful people you have been kind

check.note: The verb is “look down on, disdain”; “looked beyond” is vague and milder, and the pair is “looked down on, looked past”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on”, beside “looked past” for the second verb.

check.note: The Greek passive carries on the “by you” of the clause before; English with no agent reads as if seen by anyone.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how many fine things you have seen”. The “for you” of the clause before carries over to this passive verb, and the note gives the literal form.

check.note: The word is toil or hardship as much as pain; with “endure” just before, “hardships” is at least as likely.
check.decided: Declined: “pains” stays, because the word stands here as the partner of “pleasures”, the usual pair. A note now gives “hardships” as the other reading.

check.note: The masculine plural can cover brothers and sisters together.
check.decided: Declined: “your brothers” stays as the literal rendering of the Greek plural; the note says it can cover brothers and sisters together.

check.note: The word can mean kin, relatives, rather than intimates in general.
check.decided: Declined: “those close to you” stays. In 1.17a the same word stands in one list with a separate word for relatives, so “relatives” cannot serve for it in both places; the note gives that reading.

check.greek: εἰ πρὸς πάντας σοι μέχρι νῦν ἐστι τό
check.note: The Greek is an indirect question, “whether”, hanging on the first sentence or on an unspoken “consider”; the English makes a fresh direct question and the dependence is lost.
check.decided: Declined: the direct question stays, “Does this hold of you up to now, toward all of them”. The Greek “whether” has no verb to hang on, and the note records that it may depend on the first sentence or on an unspoken “consider”.

check.note: The ellipsis “nor spoken any” is hard to parse; the Greek is “nor said anything (of that kind)”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong”, so that the second half can be parsed. “Wrong” is kept in place of “unfair”, since the Greek word means beyond what is right or due in general.

passages.casaubon: How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy domestics? thy servants? Is it so with thee, that hitherto thou hast neither by word or deed wronged any of them? Remember withal through how many things thou hast already passed, and how many thou hast been able to endure; so that now the legend of thy life is full, and thy charge is accomplished. Again, how many truly good things have certainly by thee been discerned? how many pleasures, how many pains hast thou passed over with contempt? how many things eternally glorious hast thou despised? towards how many perverse unreasonable men hast thou carried thyself kindly, and discreetly?

nearest.title: Gravity, and keeping the names I have taken

passages.greek: πάντα ὡς Ἀντωνίνου μαθητής· τὸ ὑπὲρ τῶν κατὰ λόγον πρασσομένων εὔτονον ἐκείνου καὶ τὸ ὁμαλὲς πανταχοῦ καὶ τὸ ὅσιον καὶ τὸ εὔδιον τοῦ προσώπου καὶ τὸ μειλίχιον καὶ τὸ ἀκενόδοξον καὶ τὸ περὶ τὴν κατάληψιν τῶν πραγμάτων φιλότιμον· καὶ ὡς ἐκεῖνος οὐκ ἄν τι ὅλως παρῆκε μὴ πρότερον εὖ μάλα κατιδὼν καὶ σαφῶς νοήσας· καὶ ὡς ἔφερεν ἐκεῖνος τοὺς ἀδίκως αὐτὸν μεμφομένους μὴ ἀντιμεμφόμενος· καὶ ὡς ἐπ’ οὐδὲν ἔσπευδεν· καὶ ὠς διαβολὰς οὐκ ἐδέχετο· καὶ ὡς ἀκριβὴς ἦν ἐξεταστὴς ἠθῶν καὶ πράξεων καὶ οὐκ ὀνειδιστής, οὐ ψοφοδεής, οὐχ ὑπόπτης, οὐ σοφιστής· καὶ ὡς ὀλίγοις ἀρκούμενος, οἷον οἰκήσει, στρωμνῇ, ἐσθῆτι, τροφῇ, ὑπηρεσίᾳ· καὶ ὡς φιλόπονος καὶ μακρόθυμος· καὶ οἷος μένειν ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ μέχρι ἑσπέρας, διὰ τὴν λιτὴν δίαιταν μηδὲ τοῦ ἀποκρίνειν τὰ περιττώματα παρὰ τὴν συνήθη ὥραν χρῄζων· καὶ τὸ βέβαιον καὶ ὅμοιον ἐν ταῖς φιλίαις αὐτοῦ· καὶ τὸ ἀνέχεσθαι τῶν ἀντιβαινόντων παρρησιαστικῶς ταῖς γνώμαις αὐτοῦ καὶ χαίρειν εἴ τίς τι δεικνύοι κρεῖττον· καὶ ὡς θεοσεβὴς χωρὶς δεισιδαιμονίας· ἵν’ οὕτως εὐσυνειδήτῳ σοι ἐπιστῇ ἠ τελευταία ὥρα ὡς ἐκείνῳ.
passages.english: Everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity, and his ambition to grasp matters; and how he would not let anything at all go by without first looking into it very well and understanding it clearly; and how he bore with those who blamed him unjustly, without blaming them in return; and how he hurried toward nothing; and how he did not accept slanders; and how exact an examiner he was of characters and actions, and not one to reproach, not one to jump at a noise, not suspicious, not a sophist; and how he was content with little, for example in housing, bedding, clothing, food and service; and how hard-working he was and how patient; and that he was the kind of man who could stay at the same thing until evening, not even needing, because of his plain diet, to pass his waste except at the usual hour; and his being firm and always the same in his friendships; and his putting up with those who openly opposed his opinions, and being glad if anyone showed him something better; and how he was reverent toward the gods without superstition; so that your last hour may come upon you with a conscience as good as his.

notes.note: The passage begins partway through a chapter and these words have no verb: “do” is understood, and the English leaves it without one. Antoninus is Antoninus Pius, the emperor who adopted Marcus. The list that follows also has no verb (“remember” is understood) and is kept as a list.
notes.other_reading: Do everything as a pupil of Antoninus

notes.note: Literally “well-strung”, of a string at the right tension: energy that does not slacken.
notes.other_reading: his steady effort for what is done according to reason

notes.note: The participle is present and general, “things that are done according to reason”. It could also be heard of what was being done in his time.
notes.other_reading: what was done according to reason

notes.note: The adjective is a weather word, “fair, clear, calm”. The English reads “calm”.
notes.other_reading: the fair weather of his face

notes.note: Literally “the not being empty-gloried”: no appetite for empty reputation.
notes.other_reading: his freedom from empty glory

notes.greek: τὸ περὶ τὴν κατάληψιν τῶν πραγμάτων φιλότιμον
notes.note: “Love of honour” turned onto getting a firm grasp of things. The noun for “grasp” is also the Stoic term for sure knowledge of a fact; the plain word is kept.
notes.other_reading: his eagerness to get a sure understanding of the facts

notes.note: The verb is “let pass, let go by, dismiss”. It is taken of letting a matter go without examining it.
notes.other_reading: he would never dismiss anything at all

notes.note: Literally “did not receive”: he did not take slanders in, did not give them a hearing.
notes.other_reading: he would not listen to slanders

notes.note: Literally “afraid of a noise”: easily alarmed.
notes.other_reading: not timid

notes.note: A professional teacher of clever speaking, and so anyone who shows off cleverness. “Sophist” is kept, as in 1.17a.
notes.other_reading: not a clever talker

notes.note: The word is “service”, here the servants who wait on a person.
notes.other_reading: attendants

notes.note: Literally “in the same”. It can be the same task or the same place, and the remark about not needing to leave except at the usual hour suits either. The English takes the task.
notes.other_reading: who could stay in the same place until evening

notes.note: Literally “the firm and the alike” in his friendships: he was steady toward his friends and did not change toward them.
notes.other_reading: his constancy and evenness in his friendships

notes.note: “With a good conscience”, said of “you”, with “as him” at the end: the last hour is to find you as it found him.
notes.other_reading: so that the last hour may find you with as clear a conscience as it found him

check.note: Equally “in the same place” (he could stay put until evening), which suits the remark about not needing to leave except at the usual hour.
check.decided: Declined: “at the same thing” stays. The Greek says only “in the same”, which fits a task as well as a place, and the note gives “in the same place” as the other reading.

check.note: The participle is present and general, whatever is done in accordance with reason; the past tense narrows it to things that happened to be done.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason”, a general present as in the Greek.

check.note: “Sameness in his friendships” is odd English; the sense is that he was constant and always the same toward his friends.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “his being firm and always the same in his friendships”. “Evenness” is not used here because it already stands for another Greek word earlier in the list.

part.left_out: Ὅρα μὴ ἀποκαισαρωθῇς, μὴ βαφῇς· γίνεται γάρ. τήρησον οὖν σεαυτὸν ἁπλοῦν, ἀγαθόν, ἀκέραιον, σεμνόν, ἄκομψον, τοῦ δικαίου φίλον, θεοσεβῆ, εὐμενῆ, φιλόστοργον, ἐρρωμένον πρὸς τὰ πρέποντα ἔργα. ἀγώνισαι, ἵνα τοιοῦτος συμμείνῃς, οἷόν σε ἠθέλησε ποιῆσαι φιλοσοφία. αἰδοῦ θεούς, σῷζε ἀνθρώπους. βραχὺς ὁ βίος· εἶς καρπὸς τῆς ἐπιγείου ζωῆς, διάθεσις ὁσία καὶ πράξεις κοινωνικαί.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the first part of the chapter, down to 'the only fruit of this earthly life', in its section 6.27 and begins its 6.28 here, at 'Do all things as becometh the disciple of Antoninus Pius'.

passages.casaubon: Do all things as becometh the disciple of Antoninus Pius. Remember his resolute constancy in things that were done by him according to reason, his equability in all things, his sanctity; the cheerfulness of his countenance, his sweetness, and how free he was from all vainglory; how careful to come to the true and exact knowledge of matters in hand, and how he would by no means give over till he did fully, and plainly understand the whole state of the business; and how patiently, and without any contestation he would bear with them, that did unjustly condemn him: how he would never be over-hasty in anything, nor give ear to slanders and false accusations, but examine and observe with best diligence the several actions and dispositions of men. Again, how he was no backbiter, nor easily frightened, nor suspicious, and in his language free from all affectation and curiosity: and how easily he would content himself with few things, as lodging, bedding, clothing, and ordinary nourishment, and attendance. How able to endure labour, how patient; able through his spare diet to continue from morning to evening without any necessity of withdrawing before his accustomed hours to the necessities of nature: his uniformity and constancy in matter of friendship. How he would bear with them that with all boldness and liberty opposed his opinions; and even rejoice if any man could better advise him: and lastly, how religious he was without superstition. All these things of him remember, that whensoever thy last hour shall come upon thee, it may find thee, as it did him, ready for it in the possession of a good conscience.

nearest.title: What I learned, and from whom

passages.greek: Τὸ τεχνίον ὃ ἔμαθες φίλει, τούτῳ προσαναπαύου· τὸ δὲ ὑπόλοιπον τοῦ βίου διέξελθε ὡς θεοῖς μὲν ἐπιτετροφὼς τὰ σεαυτοῦ πάντα ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς, ἀνθρώπων δὲ μηδενὸς μήτε τύραννον μήτε δοῦλον σεαυτὸν καθιστάς.
passages.english: Love the little trade you have learned, and rest in it; and go through what is left of your life having entrusted everything that is yours to the gods with your whole soul, and making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for a craft or skill: “little craft”, said modestly. The Greek does not say which craft; it may be philosophy as the craft of living, or a person’s own trade. “Trade” is used because “small craft” in English is a boat.
notes.other_reading: the modest skill you have learned

notes.note: Literally “rest yourself upon”: lean on it, find your rest in it.
notes.other_reading: be content with it

notes.note: Literally “as one who has entrusted”: the Greek “as” presents the entrusting as the footing on which the rest of life is to be lived. The English leaves “as” out so that “you” can run through the whole sentence.
notes.other_reading: as someone who has entrusted everything of their own to the gods

notes.note: “With your whole soul” goes by position with “entrusted”. It could be heard with “go through”.
notes.other_reading: go through what is left of your life with your whole soul

notes.greek: ἀνθρώπων δὲ μηδενὸς μήτε τύραννον μήτε δοῦλον
notes.note: The Greek sets “the gods” against “no human being”. The order of the two halves is kept, but English loses the pointed contrast of the two particles.
notes.other_reading: to the gods, entrusting everything; of human beings, tyrant to none and slave to none

check.note: In English “small craft” means a boat. The Greek is the diminutive of the word for a craft: the little trade or skill.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Love the little trade you have learned”. “Small craft” would be heard as a boat.

check.greek: ὡς θεοῖς μὲν ἐπιτετροφὼς τὰ σεαυτοῦ πάντα
check.note: The English switched person in mid-clause (“someone who”, then “your own” and “yourself”), which is not grammatical.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “having entrusted everything that is yours to the gods with your whole soul, and making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being”, with “you” throughout. The Greek “as” before the participle is left out to allow this, and a note records it; “as one who” is not used because it would again stand beside “your”.

check.note: The Greek particle links the second command to the first (“and for the rest”); the full stop dropped the link.
check.decided: Accepted: the full stop is gone and the English now reads “and rest in it; and go through what is left of your life”, which keeps the Greek link.

passages.casaubon: What art and profession soever thou hast learned, endeavour to affect it, and comfort thyself in it; and pass the remainder of thy life as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatsoever belongs unto him, unto the gods: and as for men, carry not thyself either tyrannically or servilely towards any.

nearest.title: Gravity, and keeping the names I have taken

passages.greek: Παρὰ τῶν θεῶν τὸ ἀγαθοὺς πάππους, ἀγαθοὺς γονέας, ἀγαθὴν ἀδελφήν, ἀγαθοὺς διδασκάλους, ἀγαθοὺς οἰκείους, συγγενεῖς, φίλους σχεδὸν ἅπαντας ἔχειν· καὶ ὅτι περὶ οὐδένα αὐτῶν προέπεσον πλημμελῆσαί τι, καίτοι διάθεσιν ἔχων τοιαύτην, ἀφ’ ἧς, εἰ ἔτυχε, κἂν ἔπραξά τι τοιοῦτο· τῶν θεῶν δὲ εὐποιία τὸ μηδεμίαν συνδρομὴν πραγμάτων γενέσθαι, ἥτις ἔμελλέ με ἐλέγξειν. καὶ τὸ μὴ ἐπὶ πλέον τραφῆναι παρὰ τῇ παλλακῇ τοῦ πάππου καὶ τὸ τὴν ὥραν διασῶσαι καὶ τὸ μὴ πρὸ ὥρας ἀνδρωθῆναι, ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ ἐπιλαβεῖν τοῦ χρόνου. τὸ ἄρχοντι καὶ πατρὶ ὑποταχθῆναι, ὃς ἔμελλε πάντα τὸν τῦφον ἀφαιρήσειν μου καὶ εἰς ἔννοιαν ἄξειν τοῦ ὅτι δυνατόν ἐστιν ἐν αὐλῇ βιοῦντα μήτε δορυφορήσεων χρῄζειν μήτε ἐσθήτων σημειωδῶν μήτε λαμπάδων καὶ ἀνδριάντων τοιῶνδέ τινων καὶ τοῦ ὁμοίου κόμπου, ἀλλʼ ἔξεστιν ἐγγυτάτω ἰδιώτου συστέλλειν ἑαυτὸν καὶ μὴ διὰ τοῦτο ταπεινότερον ἢ ῥᾳθυμότερον ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ ὑπὲρ τῶν κοινῶν ἡγεμονικῶς πραχθῆναι δέοντα. τὸ ἀδελφοῦ τοιούτου τυχεῖν, δυναμένου μὲν διὰ ἤθους ἐπεγεῖραί με πρὸς ἐπιμέλειαν ἐμαυτοῦ, ἅμα δὲ καὶ τιμῇ καὶ στοργῇ εὐφραίνοντός με· τὸ παιδία μοι ἀφυῆ μὴ γενέσθαι μηδὲ κατὰ τὸ σωμάτιον διάστροφα. τὸ μὴ ἐπὶ πλέον με προκόψαι ἐν ῥητορικῇ καὶ ποιητικῇ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐπιτηδεύμασιν, ἐν οἷς ἴσως ἂν κατεσχέθην, εἰ ᾐσθόμην ἐμαυτὸν εὐόδως προιόντα. τὸ φθάσαι τοὺς τροφέας ἐν ἀξιώματι καταστῆσαι, οὗ δὴ ἐδόκουν μοι ἐπιθυμεῖν, καὶ μὴ ἀναβαλέσθαι ἐλπίδι τοῦ με, ἐπεὶ νέοι ἔτι ἦσαν, ὕστερον αὐτὸ πράξειν. τὸ γνῶναι Ἀπολλώνιον, Ῥούστικον, Μάξιμον. τὸ φαντασθῆναι περὶ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν βίου ἐναργῶς καὶ πολλάκις οἷός τίς ἐστιν, ὥστε, ὅσον ἐπὶ τοῖς θεοῖς καὶ ταῖς ἐκεῖθεν διαδόσεσι καὶ συλλήψεσι καὶ ἐπιπνοίαις, μηδὲν κωλύειν ἤδη κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν με, ἀπολείπεσθαι δὲ ἔτι τούτου παρὰ τὴν ἐμὴν αἰτίαν καὶ παρὰ τὸ μὴ διατηρεῖν τὰς ἐκ τῶν θεῶν ὑπομνήσεις καὶ μονονουχὶ διδασκαλίας· τὸ ἀντισχεῖν μοι τὸ σῶμα ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον ἐν τοιούτῳ βίῳ· τὸ μήτε Βενεδίκτης ἅψασθαι μήτε Θεοδότου, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὕστερον ἐν ἐρωτικοῖς πάθεσι γενόμενον ὑγιᾶναι· τὸ χαλεπήναντα πολλάκις Ῥουστίκῳ μηδὲν πλέον πρᾶξαι, ἐφ’ ᾧ ἂν μετέγνων· τὸ μέλλουσαν νέαν τελευτᾶν τὴν τεκοῦσαν ὅμως οἰκῆσαι μετ’ ἐμοῦ τὰ τελευταῖα ἔτη. τὸ ὁσάκις ἐβουλήθην ἐπικουρῆσαί τινι πενομένῳ ἢ εἰς ἄλλο τι χρῄζοντι, μηδέποτε ἀκοῦσαί με, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι μοι χρήματα, ὅθεν γένηται, καὶ τὸ αὐτῷ ἐμοὶ χρείαν ὁμοίαν, ὡς παρ’ ἑτέρου μεταλαβεῖν, μὴ συμπεσεῖν· τὸ τὴν γυναῖκα τοιαύτην εἶναι, οὑτωσὶ μὲν πειθήνιον, οὕτω δὲ φιλόστοργον, οὕτω δὲ ἀφελῆ· τὸ ἐπιτηδείων τροφέων εἰς τὰ παιδία εὐπορῆσαι. τὸ δι’ ὀνειράτων βοηθήματα δοθῆναι ἄλλα τε καὶ ὡς μὴ πτύειν αἷμα καὶ μὴ ἰλιγγιᾶν, καὶ τούτου ἐν Καιήτῃ ὥσπερ χρήσῃ· τὸ ὅπως ἐπεθύμησα φιλοσοφίας, μὴ ἐμπεσεῖν εἴς τινα σοφιστὴν μηδὲ ἀποκαθίσαι ἐπὶ τὸ συγγράφειν ἢ συλλογισμοὺς ἀναλύειν ἢ περὶ τὰ μετεωρολογικὰ καταγίνεσθαι. πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα ʽθεῶν βοηθῶν καὶ τύχης δεῖται.ʼ
passages.english: From the gods: that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good people close to me, relatives, friends, nearly all of them; and that I was not carried away into any offence against any of them, although I had a disposition from which, if it had so happened, I might well have done something of the kind; but it is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up. And that I was not brought up for longer with my grandfather’s concubine; and that I preserved the bloom of my youth; and that I was not made a man before the season, but even took some time more. That I was placed under a ruler and father who was to take all the conceit out of me and bring me to the thought that it is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches and statues of this sort and similar show; but that one may draw oneself in until one is very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good. That I happened to have such a brother, able by his character to rouse me to take care of myself, and at the same time gladdening me with his respect and affection. That my children were not born lacking in natural gifts, nor deformed in their little bodies. That I did not make more progress in rhetoric, in poetry and in the other pursuits, in which I might perhaps have been held fast, if I had felt myself getting on easily. That I was quick to set those who brought me up in the rank they seemed to me to desire, and did not put it off with the hope that, since they were still young, I would do it later. That I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, Maximus. That I had an impression, clearly and often, of the life according to nature, of what kind of life it is, so that, as far as it rests with the gods and with the gifts, help and inspirations that come from there, nothing prevents me from living according to nature already, and that I still fall short of this is by my own fault and by not keeping to the reminders from the gods, which are all but teachings. That my body has held out so long in a life like this. That I touched neither Benedicta nor Theodotus, but that later too, when I fell into the passions of love, I recovered. That, though I was often angry with Rusticus, I did nothing more that I would have regretted. That my mother, who was to die young, still lived with me in her last years. That whenever I wanted to help someone who was poor or in need of something else, I was never told that I had no money to do it with; and that no similar need befell me myself, so as to take from another. That my wife is as she is, so compliant, so warmly affectionate, so unaffected. That I had no lack of suitable people to bring up my children. That remedies were given me through dreams, among others against spitting blood and against dizziness; and of this, at Caieta, as you will use. That, when I set my heart on philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, nor sit down to writing, or to resolving syllogisms, or to busying myself with the things in the sky. For all these things “need the gods’ help and fortune.”

notes.note: “Nearly all” may limit the whole list or only the last items (relatives, friends). It is left at the end, where it can be heard either way.
notes.other_reading: that nearly all my grandfathers, parents, sister, teachers, people close to me, relatives and friends were good

notes.note: The verb is to fall or rush forward: to be carried headlong into something.
notes.other_reading: that I did not fall into any offence against any of them

notes.note: The participle takes its time from the past verb, so “had”. The Greek does not say whether the disposition was still there at the time of writing.
notes.other_reading: although I have a disposition

notes.note: Literally “which was going to convict (or expose) me”. The English reads “would have shown me up”; “put me to the test” is also possible.
notes.other_reading: that would have put me to the test

notes.greek: τὸ τὴν ὥραν διασῶσαι καὶ τὸ μὴ πρὸ ὥρας ἀνδρωθῆναι, ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ ἐπιλαβεῖν τοῦ χρόνου
notes.note: One Greek word is used twice in two senses: the bloom of youth, and the due season. “Bloom” and “season” are chosen so that the second can be heard picking up the first. “Made a man” is meant sexually, and “took some time more” means he put it off even past the due time.
notes.other_reading: that I kept my youth unspoiled, and did not prove my manhood before the time, but even went beyond it

notes.note: The ruler and father is Antoninus Pius, who adopted Marcus; the Greek does not name him.
notes.other_reading: under a ruler who was also my father

notes.note: Literally “smoke”: the puffed-up self-importance that clouds the head. The English reads “conceit”.
notes.other_reading: all the vanity

notes.note: Literally “torches and statues, some such as these”, pointing at things familiar at court. Which torches and statues are meant is not said.
notes.other_reading: nor torches, statues and things of that sort

notes.note: Literally “to contract oneself nearest to a private person”: to cut one’s state down almost to that of someone who holds no office. The picture of drawing in is kept.
notes.other_reading: bring oneself down very nearly to a private citizen’s way of living

notes.note: The word is “low”: of a person’s bearing, lowly, abject, without dignity.
notes.other_reading: and not on that account be any meaner or slacker

notes.note: “In the manner of a leader.” The word is kin to the Stoic term “the ruling part”, but here it has the ordinary sense of one who commands.
notes.other_reading: what has to be done with authority for the common good

notes.note: “By his character.” The brother is Lucius Verus, Marcus’s brother by adoption (from memory, unchecked). The Greek does not say whether the character roused him as an example or as a warning, and that is left open.
notes.other_reading: by his way of life

notes.note: The verb is “to get in first, to do in good time”. The English reads “was quick to”.
notes.other_reading: that I lost no time in setting

notes.note: Those who reared him, as in 5.31; the same word is used below of the people who rear his children. It is narrower than “teachers”.
notes.other_reading: my tutors

notes.note: The Greek verb has no object: “did not put off, with the hope of my doing it later”. The hope may be one held out to them or his own expectation, and the English leaves that open.
notes.other_reading: and did not put them off with the hope that I would do it later

notes.note: The verb belongs with the Stoic noun for an impression (φαντασία): something presented itself to his mind. “Impression” keeps the glossary word.
notes.other_reading: that I pictured to myself, clearly and often

notes.note: Three parallel nouns, all “from there”: things handed on, acts of helping, and breathings-upon.
notes.other_reading: what is passed on from there, their help and their promptings

notes.note: A woman’s name and a man’s name. Nothing more is known of them; they are usually thought to have been slaves of the household (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: that I laid no hand on Benedicta or on Theodotus

notes.note: Literally “to become healthy”: love’s passions are treated as an illness he got over.
notes.other_reading: I was cured

notes.note: The infinitive does not show tense, so the Greek does not settle whether his wife was alive at the time of writing. The English reads “is”.
notes.other_reading: that my wife was as she was

notes.note: Literally “obedient to the rein”: ready to be persuaded, compliant.
notes.other_reading: so obedient

notes.note: The word is “aids”, and in medicine “remedies”; with spitting blood and dizziness the medical sense is taken. It is kin to the word for the gods’ “help” in the closing quotation.
notes.other_reading: That help was given me through dreams

notes.greek: καὶ τούτου ἐν Καιήτῃ ὥσπερ χρήσῃ
notes.note: These words do not construe as they stand and are generally thought to be corrupt (from memory, unchecked). They are given word for word, “and of this, at Caieta, as you will use”, and not mended; the last word could also hide a word for an oracle. Caieta is a town on the coast south of Rome.
notes.other_reading: and for this, at Caieta, as if by an oracle

notes.note: The first word is normally “how” or “in order that”; here it must be “when” or “as soon as”, a rare use.
notes.other_reading: that, however much I longed for philosophy

notes.note: Literally “sit down apart to writing”, that is, to composing treatises. Some editors read “the writers” here instead of “writing” (from memory, unchecked); the text is translated as given.
notes.other_reading: nor sit down over the writers

notes.note: The study of things aloft: the heavens and the weather, as a branch of natural philosophy.
notes.other_reading: questions about the heavens

notes.note: Marked in the edition as a quotation; the source is not identified. Literally “need helping gods and fortune”. The word for “helping” is kin to the word for the “remedies” given through dreams just above.
notes.other_reading: need gods to help, and luck

check.greek: καὶ τούτου ἐν Καιήτῃ ὥσπερ χρήσῃ
check.note: The Greek as given does not construe and its last word is ambiguous. The English printed a literal guess inside quotation marks the Greek does not have, so that it looked like a quoted saying; the break should be marked, not smoothed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the quotation marks are removed and the English now reads “and of this, at Caieta, as you will use”, word for word and as broken as the Greek. “As by an oracle” is not put in the text because the last word as given is “you will use”; the note says the words do not construe and gives that reading.

check.greek: βοηθήματα δοθῆναι ἄλλα τε καὶ ὡς μὴ πτύειν αἷμα
check.note: The Greek noun is “remedies”, plural and medical, and the phrase is “others and in particular”; “other remedies” dropped out and “help” lost the cures.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “That remedies were given me through dreams, among others against spitting blood and against dizziness”, with the plural, the medical sense and “others” restored.

check.note: The participle is contemporary with the past main verb, “though I had a disposition”; the English present says the disposition is still there, which the Greek does not commit to.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “although I had a disposition”, the participle taking its time from the past verb; a note records that the Greek does not say whether it lasted.

check.note: The verb is to rush headlong, to be carried away into something; “fall into” loses the rashness.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “was not carried away into any offence against any of them”. “Never” is not used, because the Greek says only “not” and “against any”.

check.note: The particle is adversative here: the offence was possible, but by the gods’ favour the occasion never arose. Without “but” the turn is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but it is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about”, which keeps the turn.

check.note: The Greek is “with my grandfather’s concubine”; “house” is supplied.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “with my grandfather’s concubine”, and “house” is no longer supplied.

check.greek: τὸ τὴν ὥραν διασῶσαι καὶ τὸ μὴ πρὸ ὥρας ἀνδρωθῆναι
check.note: One Greek word comes twice (the bloom of youth, the due season) and was given as “youth” and “the time”, so the echo was lost. “Kept unspoiled” explains the verb “preserved”, and “become a man” can be read as merely growing up where the Greek means it sexually.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “preserved the bloom of my youth” and “was not made a man before the season”, so that “preserved” is plain and “season” picks up “bloom”. “Was made a man” keeps the Greek passive in place of “prove my manhood”, and the note says the sense is sexual.

check.note: The Greek words mean “of this sort, such-like”, pointing at familiar things, not “of a certain kind”, which sounds like a particular type left unnamed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “nor torches and statues of this sort”. The Greek words describe the torches and statues and do not add a third item, so “and things of that sort” is not used.

check.note: “The like display” is archaic.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and similar show”.

check.note: “Draw oneself in very close to a private person” reads as moving physically near someone. The sense is to reduce oneself very nearly to the level of a private citizen.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “draw oneself in until one is very nearly a private person”, which no longer sounds like moving near someone. The Greek picture of drawing in is kept, and “way of living” is not added.

check.note: The Greek word, said of bearing, is “mean, abject, undignified”; “be lower toward what has to be done” is not clear English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done”. “Lowly” is used in place of “meaner”, which today is heard as “more unkind”.

check.note: The diminutive, “their little bodies”, is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “nor deformed in their little bodies”, which keeps the diminutive.

check.note: The Greek has no “them”: “did not defer it in the expectation that it would be done later”. The expectation may be his own reasoning, not a hope held out to them.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “them” is removed and the English now reads “did not put it off with the hope that, since they were still young”, the thing would be done later. “With the hope” is kept so that the hope can be his own or one held out to them, as in the Greek; a note gives both.

check.greek: ταῖς ἐκεῖθεν διαδόσεσι καὶ συλλήψεσι καὶ ἐπιπνοίαις
check.note: Three parallel nouns, all “from there”: gifts, helps and inspirations. The English made the first a clause and the other two look like an explanation of it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “with the gifts, help and inspirations that come from there”, three parallel nouns.

check.note: “Did come into the passions of love” is stiff, the emphatic “did” is not in the Greek, and the last verb is “was cured, got well”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “but that later too” and then “fell into the passions of love”, without the emphatic “did”. “Recovered” stays, since the Greek verb is “got well” and names no one who did the curing; “was cured” is in the note.

check.note: The infinitive carries no time, “is” or “was”; the English has chosen the present.
check.decided: Accepted: “That my wife is as she is” stays, and the note records that the Greek infinitive would also allow “was”.

check.note: The Greek is “fall into the hands of”; “fall in with” suggests keeping company by choice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “did not fall into the hands of some sophist”.

check.note: Found while settling: “no like need” is an old-fashioned turn, of the same kind as “the like display” above.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and that no similar need befell me myself, so as to take from another”.

part.left_out: Τὰ ἐν Κουάδοις πρὸς τῷ Γρανούᾳ.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 1.14 at 'could not have been' and opens its 1.15 with the chapter's closing note, 'In the country of the Quadi at Granua'.

passages.casaubon: From the gods I received that I had good grandfathers, and parents, a good sister, good masters, good domestics, loving kinsmen, almost all that I have; and that I never through haste and rashness transgressed against any of them, notwithstanding that my disposition was such, as that such a thing (if occasion had been) might very well have been committed by me, but that It was the mercy of the gods, to prevent such a concurring of matters and occasions, as might make me to incur this blame. That I was not long brought up by the concubine of my father; that I preserved the flower of my youth. That I took not upon me to be a man before my time, but rather put it off longer than I needed. That I lived under the government of my lord and father, who would take away from me all pride and vainglory, and reduce me to that conceit and opinion that it was not impossible for a prince to live in the court without a troop of guards and followers, extraordinary apparel, such and such torches and statues, and other like particulars of state and magnificence; but that a man may reduce and contract himself almost to the state of a private man, and yet for all that not to become the more base and remiss in those public matters and affairs, wherein power and authority is requisite. That I have had such a brother, who by his own example might stir me up to think of myself; and by his respect and love, delight and please me. That I have got ingenuous children, and that they were not born distorted, nor with any other natural deformity. That I was no great proficient in the study of rhetoric and poetry, and of other faculties, which perchance I might have dwelt upon, if I had found myself to go on in them with success. That I did by times prefer those, by whom I was brought up, to such places and dignities, which they seemed unto me most to desire; and that I did not put them off with hope and expectation, that (since that they were yet but young) I would do the same hereafter. That I ever knew Apollonius and Rusticus, and Maximus. That I have had occasion often and effectually to consider and meditate with myself, concerning that life which is according to nature, what the nature and manner of it is: so that as for the gods and such suggestions, helps and inspirations, as might be expected from them, nothing did hinder, but that I might have begun long before to live according to nature; or that even now that I was not yet partaker and in present possession of that life, that I myself (in that I did not observe those inward motions, and suggestions, yea and almost plain and apparent instructions and admonitions of the gods,) was the only cause of it. That my body in such a life, hath been able to hold out so long. That I never had to do with Benedicta and Theodotus, yea and afterwards when I fell into some fits of love, I was soon cured. That having been often displeased with Rusticus, I never did him anything for which afterwards I had occasion to repent. That it being so that my mother was to die young, yet she lived with me all her latter years. That as often as I had a purpose to help and succour any that either were poor, or fallen into some present necessity, I never was answered by my officers that there was not ready money enough to do it; and that I myself never had occasion to require the like succour from any other. That I have such a wife, so obedient, so loving, so ingenuous. That I had choice of fit and able men, to whom I might commit the bringing up of my children. That by dreams I have received help, as for other things, so in particular, how I might stay my casting of blood, and cure my dizziness, as that also that happened to thee in Cajeta, as unto Chryses when he prayed by the seashore. And when I did first apply myself to philosophy, that I did not fall into the hands of some sophists, or spent my time either in reading the manifold volumes of ordinary philosophers, nor in practising myself in the solution of arguments and fallacies, nor dwelt upon the studies of the meteors, and other natural curiosities. All these things without the assistance of the gods, and fortune, could not have been.

nearest.title: What I learned, and from whom

passages.greek: Πάντα ἐκεῖνα, ἐφ’ ἃ διὰ περιόδου εὔχῃ ἐλθεῖν, ἤδη ἔχειν δύνασαι, ἐὰν μὴ σαυτῷ φθονῇς. τοῦτο δέ ἐστιν, ἐὰν πᾶν τὸ παρελθὸν καταλίπῃς καὶ τὸ μέλλον ἐπιτρέψῃς τῇ προνοίᾳ καὶ τὸ παρὸν μόνον ἀπευθύνῃς πρὸς ὁσιότητα καὶ δικαιοσύνην. ὁσιότητα μέν, ἵνα φιλῇς τὸ ἀπονεμόμενον· σοὶ γὰρ αὐτὸ ἡ φύσις ἔφερε καὶ σὲ τούτῳ· δικαιοσύνην δέ, ἵνα ἐλευθέρως καὶ χωρὶς περιπλοκῆς λέγῃς τε τἀληθῆ καὶ πράσσῃς τὰ κατὰ νόμον καὶ κατ’ ἀξίαν· μὴ ἐμποδίζῃ δέ σε μήτε κακία ἀλλοτρία μήτε ὑπόληψις μήτε φωνὴ μηδὲ μὴν αἴσθησις τοῦ περιτεθραμμένου σοι σαρκιδίου· ὄψεται γὰρ τὸ πάσχον. ἐὰν οὖν, ὅτε δήποτε πρὸς ἐξόδῳ γένῃ, πάντα τὰ ἄλλα καταλιπὼν μόνον τὸ ἡγεμονικόν σου καὶ τὸ ἐν σοὶ θεῖον τιμήσῃς καὶ μὴ τὸ παύσεσθαί ποτε τοῦ ζῆν φοβηθῇς, ἀλλὰ τό γε μηδέποτε ἄρξασθαι κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν, ἔσῃ ἄνθρωπος ἄξιος τοῦ γεννήσαντος κόσμου καὶ παύσῃ ξένος ὢν τῆς πατρίδος καὶ θαυμάζων ὡς ἀπροσδόκητα τὰ καθ’ ἡμέραν γινόμενα καὶ κρεμάμενος ἐκ τοῦδε καὶ τοῦδε.
passages.english: All those things you pray to reach by a roundabout road you can have already, if you do not begrudge yourself. That is: if you leave all the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present toward piety and justice. Piety, so that you love what is allotted, for nature brought it to you and you to it. Justice, so that, freely and without winding about, you speak the truth and do what accords with law and with what each deserves. And do not be hindered by another person’s badness, or judgment, or voice, or even by the sensation of the bit of flesh that has grown up around you, for the part that suffers will see to that. So if, whenever it is that you come close to your exit, you leave everything else behind and honor only your ruling part and what is divine in you, and if what you fear is not that you will some day stop living but rather never beginning to live according to nature, then you will be a human being worthy of the universe that gave you birth. You will stop being a stranger in your own country, stop wondering at what happens every day as if it were unexpected, and stop hanging on this and that.

notes.note: Literally “by way of a circuit”. The English takes it of a roundabout route; it can also be taken of time, a cycle or period that has to pass first.
notes.other_reading: that you pray to reach in the course of time

notes.note: ὁσιότης is right dealing toward the divine, as justice is toward people. “Piety” is the nearest plain word; the next sentence defines it as loving what is allotted.
notes.other_reading: holiness and justice

notes.note: Literally “without entwining”: without twisting or winding, said of speech that goes round about and of dealings that are not straight. “Without winding about” keeps the image and covers both the speaking and the doing.
notes.other_reading: without evasion

notes.note: “According to worth”: in proportion to what is deserved. The Greek does not say whose worth, a person’s or a thing’s, and “each” leaves that open.
notes.other_reading: and do what accords with law and with the worth of each thing

notes.note: A subjunctive as given. The English reads it as standing on its own, as a command; it may still depend on the “so that” before it. The Greek is active, “let neither … hinder you”; the English is passive to carry the list.
notes.other_reading: and so that nothing may hinder you, neither …

notes.greek: μήτε κακία ἀλλοτρία μήτε ὑπόληψις μήτε φωνὴ
notes.note: “Another person’s” stands with “badness” and can carry over to the two nouns after it, so that these are what others think and say; or the judgment may be one’s own. The English is built so that the words can carry over in the same way. “Judgment” is this translation’s word for ὑπόληψις.
notes.other_reading: by another person’s badness, or by your own judgment, or by anything said

notes.note: An idiom: “it will see”, meaning “that is its own business”. The part that suffers is the flesh, as against the ruling part.
notes.other_reading: for that is the business of the part that is affected

notes.note: “At whatever time you come to be near the exit.” It may be general (whenever that turns out to be) or pointed (now that you are at last near it). The English keeps it general.
notes.other_reading: now that you are at last close to your exit

notes.greek: ἀλλὰ τό γε μηδέποτε ἄρξασθαι κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν
notes.note: The Greek verb form here carries no time: “never beginning” covers both never having begun so far and never coming to begin. The fear of stopping, by contrast, is put in the future.
notes.other_reading: but that you never began to live according to nature

notes.note: Literally “hanging from this and this”. The image is of depending on one thing after another, or one person after another: the Greek form can be either, and “this and that” leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: depending on this person and that

check.greek: μήτε κακία ἀλλοτρία μήτε ὑπόληψις μήτε φωνὴ
check.note: The one Greek word for “another person’s” may cover all three nouns: other people’s badness, opinion and talk. Bare “judgment” and “voice” do not tell a reader whose they are.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “by another person’s badness, or judgment, or voice”, with the repeated “by” removed, so that “another person’s” can cover all three nouns as the one Greek adjective can. “Judgment” is kept as this translation’s fixed word for ὑπόληψις and “voice” as what φωνή says, and a note gives both readings.

check.note: The Greek word means twisting or roundabout speech and dealing, and “entanglement” does not tell a reader of today that plain, straight speaking is meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “without winding about”. The Greek word is an image of twisting, which “evasion” would drop, and it goes with the doing as well as the speaking; “winding about” shows that straight speech and dealing are meant.

check.note: “Do what accords with worth” is unclear. The Greek means in proportion to what each thing or person deserves.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “with what each deserves”. The Greek says only “according to worth” and has no word for “thing”, so “each” is left without a noun and can be a person or a thing.

check.greek: ἀλλὰ τό γε μηδέποτε ἄρξασθαι κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν
check.note: The Greek verb form carries no time, “never beginning to live according to nature”, where the English fixes it as a finished past fact. The small word for “rather” is also dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “but rather never beginning to live according to nature”. The Greek form carries no time and has a word for “rather”; a note gives the past reading.

check.note: The Greek “this and this” can be a person as well as a thing, which “thing” closes off, and “hanging on” is less clear than “depending on”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “stop hanging on this and that”. “Thing” is dropped so that a person can be meant as well; “hanging” is kept because it is the Greek image, and a note gives “depending on”.

check.note: “To you” is supplied; the Greek has only “what is allotted”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “what is allotted”. The Greek has no “to you” here, and the next clause supplies it.

check.note: “Them” is supplied; the Greek says only “if you do not begrudge yourself”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “if you do not begrudge yourself”. The Greek names only the person begrudged and no object.

passages.casaubon: Whatsoever thou doest hereafter aspire unto, thou mayest even now enjoy and possess, if thou doest not envy thyself thine own happiness. And that will be, if thou shalt forget all that is past, and for the future, refer thyself wholly to the Divine Providence, and shalt bend and apply all thy present thoughts and intentions to holiness and righteousness. To holiness, in accepting willingly whatsoever is sent by the Divine Providence, as being that which the nature of the universe hath appointed unto thee, which also hath appointed thee for that, whatsoever it be. To righteousness, in speaking the truth freely, and without ambiguity; and in doing all things justly and discreetly. Now in this good course, let not other men's either wickedness, or opinion, or voice hinder thee: no, nor the sense of this thy pampered mass of flesh: for let that which suffers, look to itself. If therefore whensoever the time of thy departing shall come, thou shalt readily leave all things, and shalt respect thy mind only, and that divine part of thine, and this shall be thine only fear, not that some time or other thou shalt cease to live, but thou shalt never begin to live according to nature: then shalt thou be a man indeed, worthy of that world, from which thou hadst thy beginning; then shalt thou cease to be a stranger in thy country, and to wonder at those things that happen daily, as things strange and unexpected, and anxiously to depend of divers things that are not in thy power.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek:
Ἄνωθεν ἐπιθεωρεῖν ἀγέλας μυρίας καὶ τελετὰς μυρίας καὶ πλοῦν παντοῖον ἐν χειμῶσι καὶ γαλήναις καὶ διαφορὰς γινομένων, συγγινομένων, ἀπογινομένων. ἐπινόει δὲ καὶ τὸν ὑπ’ ἄλλων πάλαι βεβιωμένον βίον καὶ τὸν μετὰ σὲ βιωθησόμενον καὶ τὸν νῦν ἐν τοῖς βαρβάροις ἔθνεσι βιούμενον· καὶ ὅσοι μὲν οὐδὲ ὄνομά σου γινώσκουσιν, ὅσοι δὲ τάχιστα ἐπιλήσονται, ὅσοι δ’ ἐπαινοῦντες ἴσως νῦν σε τάχιστα ψέξουσι· καὶ ὡς οὔτε ἡ μνήμη ἀξιόλογόν γε οὔτε ἡ δόξα οὔτε ἄλλο τι τὸ σύμπαν.

Ἀταραξία μὲν περὶ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκτὸς αἰτίας συμβαίνοντα, δικαιότης δὲ ἐν τοῖς παρὰ τὴν ἐκ σοῦ αἰτίαν ἐνεργουμένοις· τουτέστιν, ὁρμὴ καὶ πρᾶξις καταλήγουσα ἐπ’ αὐτὸ τὸ κοινωνικῶς πρᾶξαι ὡς τοῦτό σοι κατὰ φύσιν ὄν.
passages.english:
To look down from above on countless herds and countless rites, on every kind of voyage in storms and in calms, and on the differences among those coming to be, coming together, and passing away. Think too of the life lived long ago by others, the life that will be lived after you, and the life being lived now among the barbarian peoples; and how many do not even know your name, how many will very quickly forget it, how many who perhaps praise you now will very quickly blame you; and that neither being remembered is of any account, nor reputation, nor anything else at all.

Freedom from disturbance about the things that happen from the cause outside; justice in the things done through the cause that comes from you. That is, impulse and action ending in just this, acting socially, as being what is according to nature for you.

notes.note: An infinitive used as an instruction, with no person. It is kept as “To look”; the next sentence turns to a direct command, “Think”.
notes.other_reading: Look down from above on

notes.note: ἀγέλη is a herd of animals, and also any crowd or band of people. “Herds” is kept.
notes.other_reading: countless crowds

notes.note: τελετή is a religious rite, especially a rite of initiation.
notes.other_reading: countless ceremonies of initiation

notes.note: One verb with three prefixes: coming to be, being or coming together, being away. The forms can be people or things, and the middle word can mean keeping company (also of sexual union) or combining. The English takes all three of people, since the herds, rites and voyages before them are human scenes.
notes.other_reading: the variety of what comes to be, comes together and passes away

notes.greek: ἐπαινοῦντες ἴσως νῦν σε τάχιστα ψέξουσι
notes.note: “Perhaps” stands inside the phrase about praise, between “praising” and “now”, and the English takes it there. It could be taken with the verb that follows.
notes.other_reading: how many who praise you now will perhaps very quickly blame you

notes.note: Literally “worth speaking of”, with a small word of emphasis. “Of any account” carries both.
notes.other_reading: is worth mentioning

notes.note: Used as an adverb, “altogether”, “at all”.
notes.other_reading: nor, in short, anything else

notes.note: The sentence has no verb: two nouns set down like headings. ἀταραξία is the state of not being disturbed.
notes.other_reading: Calm about the things that happen

notes.note: παρά with this case here means “owing to”. The pair is the cause outside you and the cause that is you.
notes.other_reading: in the things whose cause lies in you

notes.note: “Socially” follows this translation’s fixed word for κοινωνικός. It does not mean being sociable: it means acting as a member of the human community, for the common good.
notes.other_reading: ending in just this, acting for the common good

notes.greek: ὡς τοῦτό σοι κατὰ φύσιν ὄν
notes.note: The Greek gives this as the ground on which the person acts, “as being”, and not as the writer’s own statement of a cause.
notes.other_reading: because this is according to nature for you

check.note: The three Greek forms can be things as well as people, and the English restricts them to people. The middle word is “being or coming together”, which “living together” narrows.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “the differences among those coming to be, coming together, and passing away”. “Coming together” replaces “living together”, which narrowed the middle word; “those” still takes the three of people, since everything else in the list is a human scene, and a note gives the reading of things.

check.greek: ἐπαινοῦντες ἴσως νῦν σε τάχιστα ψέξουσι
check.note: The Greek “perhaps” stands between the two verbs and may go with the future: those who praise you now will perhaps very quickly blame you.
check.decided: Declined: “Perhaps” stands in the Greek inside the phrase “praising … you now”, before the words for “will very quickly blame”, and the clause before it, “will very quickly forget”, has no “perhaps”. The English keeps “who perhaps praise you now”, and a note gives the other reading.

check.note: The Greek word is “of any account”, stronger than “worth mentioning”, and its word of emphasis is not carried.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “is of any account”. “At all” is not added here because it already closes the sentence for another Greek word; “any” carries the emphasis.

check.greek: ὡς τοῦτό σοι κατὰ φύσιν ὄν
check.note: The Greek gives the ground as the person acting holds it, “as being”. “Because” turns it into the writer’s flat statement of a cause.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “as being what is according to nature for you”. “For you” is kept because the Greek says “for you” and not “your nature”.

check.note: “Acting socially” today suggests being sociable. The Greek means acting as a member of the community, for the common good.
check.decided: Declined: “Social” is the settled word of this translation for κοινωνικός, and “acting socially” keeps it so that the word can be followed from passage to passage. A note says that acting for the common good, and not being sociable, is meant.

passages.casaubon: From some high place as it were to look down, and to behold here flocks, and there sacrifices, without number; and all kind of navigation; some in a rough and stormy sea, and some in a calm: the general differences, or different estates of things, some, that are now first upon being; the several and mutual relations of those things that are together; and some other things that are at their last. Their lives also, who were long ago, and theirs who shall be hereafter, and the present estate and life of those many nations of barbarians that are now in the world, thou must likewise consider in thy mind. And how many there be, who never so much as heard of thy name, how many that will soon forget it; how many who but even now did commend thee, within a very little while perchance will speak ill of thee. So that neither fame, nor honour, nor anything else that this world doth afford, is worth the while. The sum then of all; whatsoever doth happen unto thee, whereof God is the cause, to accept it contentedly: whatsoever thou doest, whereof thou thyself art the cause, to do it justly: which will be, if both in thy resolution and in thy action thou have no further end, than to do good unto others, as being that, which by thy natural constitution, as a man, thou art bound unto.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek:
Ὡς ἀποτεθνηκότα δεῖ καὶ μέχρι νῦν βεβιωκότα τὸ λοιπὸν ἐκ τοῦ περιόντος ζῆσαι κατὰ τὴν φύσιν.

Μόνως φιλεῖν τὸ ἑαυτῷ συμβαῖνον καὶ συγκλωθόμενον· τί γὰρ ἁρμοδιώτερον;

Ἐφ’ ἑκάστου συμβάματος ἐκείνους πρὸ ὀμμάτων ἔχειν, οἷς τὰ αὐτὰ συνέβαινεν, ἔπειτα ἤχθοντο, ἐξενίζοντο, ἐμέμφοντο· νῦν οὗν ἐκεῖνοι ποῦ; οὐδαμοῦ. τί οὖν; καὶ σὺ θέλεις ὁμοίως; οὐχὶ δὲ τὰς μὲν ἀλλοτρίας τροπὰς καταλιπεῖν τοῖς τρέπουσι καὶ τρεπομένοις, αὐτὸς δὲ περὶ τὸ πῶς χρῆσθαι αὐτοῖς ὅλος γίνεσθαι; χρήσῃ γὰρ καλῶς καὶ ὕλη σοι ἔσται, μόνον πρόσεχε καὶ θέλε σεαυτῷ καλὸς εἶναι ἐπὶ παντός, οὖ πράσσεις, καὶ μέμνησο ἀμφοτέρων, ὅτι καὶ διάφορον ἐφ’ οὗ ἡ πρᾶξις.

Ἔνδον σκάπτε, ἔνδον ἡ πηγὴ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ ἀεὶ ἀναβλύειν δυναμένη, ἐὰν ἀεὶ σκάπτῃς.
passages.english:
As someone who has died and whose life has been lived up to now, one must live what is left, as a surplus, according to nature.

To love only what happens to oneself and is spun into one’s own thread. For what fits better?

At each thing that happens, to keep before one’s eyes the people to whom the same things happened, and who then were vexed, found it strange, complained. So where are they now? Nowhere. Well then, do you too want to be like them? Do you not rather want to leave the turns that belong to others to those who turn and are turned, and yourself be wholly taken up with how to use the things that happen? For you will use them well, and they will be material for you. Only pay attention, and want to be honorable in your own eyes in everything you do; and remember both things, for what the action is done on also makes a difference.

Dig within. Within is the spring of the good, and it can always well up, if you always dig.

notes.note: The Greek tense marks the living as finished: the life is counted as over at this moment. “Whose life has been lived up to now” is meant in that sense.
notes.other_reading: and has lived up to now

notes.note: Literally “out of what is left over”: the rest of life treated as an extra, beyond a life already counted as finished.
notes.other_reading: live the rest as a bonus

notes.note: An adverb, “solely”. The English takes it with the object: love that and nothing else. It could also limit the verb: do nothing but love it.
notes.other_reading: To do nothing but love what happens to oneself

notes.note: “Spun together with” one: the image of the Fates spinning a person’s thread. “Thread” is supplied to make the image readable.
notes.other_reading: what happens to oneself and is spun together with one

notes.note: From the word for a stranger: they treated what happened as something foreign.
notes.other_reading: were astonished

notes.greek: τὰς μὲν ἀλλοτρίας τροπὰς καταλιπεῖν τοῖς τρέπουσι καὶ τρεπομένοις
notes.note: Three forms of one word, “turn”, all kept. What turns are meant is not said: other people’s changes of mood or direction, or changes that are not one’s own affair.
notes.other_reading: leave other people’s changes to those who cause them and those who undergo them

notes.note: The Greek says only “them”. It cannot be the turns (the Greek gender is wrong for that). It is most likely the things that happen, named at the start of the chapter and called “material” in the next sentence, and the English says so. It could be the people who turn and are turned.
notes.other_reading: with how to deal with those people

notes.note: καλός (fine, honorable) echoes καλῶς (“well”) just before. English could keep the echo only with “good”, which this passage needs for another Greek word in “the spring of the good”. “To yourself” is taken as “in your own eyes”.
notes.other_reading: want to be fine toward yourself

notes.greek: καὶ μέμνησο ἀμφοτέρων, ὅτι καὶ διάφορον ἐφ’ οὗ ἡ πρᾶξις
notes.note: Obscure as it stands, and the English is left as obscure. “Both” has no clear pair: it may be the two commands just given, or the use and the material. The last clause may give a reason (“for”) or the content (“that”), and its main word can mean “makes a difference” or “different”; from memory, unchecked, some editors change it to the Stoic term “indifferent”.
notes.other_reading: and remember both things, and that what the action is done on is indifferent

notes.note: The Greek as given says “dig”. From memory, unchecked, the manuscripts have “look” here and “dig” is an editor’s correction.
notes.other_reading: Look within

check.note: The Greek “them” cannot be the turns, which are feminine. It is either the things that happen or the people who turn and are turned, but in the English “them” reads as the turns.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “how to use the things that happen”. The Greek “them” cannot be the turns, and the next sentence calls it material, so the things that happen are named; a note gives the reading of the people.

check.note: The Greek opens a new question that expects yes, “Will you not rather leave …?”. The English fragment reads as a continuation of “do you want to be like them” and can be taken the wrong way round.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Do you not rather want to leave … and yourself be wholly taken up with …?”, a full question that expects yes. “Want” is repeated because the Greek verbs still depend on it.

check.note: “It” has no referent in the English. The subject is the things that happen: they will be your material.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “and they will be material for you”. The subject is the things that happen.

check.note: The point is that the life is over as of now. “Has lived up to now” is true of anyone alive and loses the point.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “whose life has been lived up to now”. The Greek tense marks the living as complete, which “has been lived” says; “ended at this moment” would add a verb the Greek does not have.

check.note: “Both” has no clear pair in the Greek as given, and the linking word can be “that” as well as “for”; editors have doubted the place. The English should be marked uncertain and not smoothed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English is left as obscure as the Greek, “remember both things, for what the action is done on also makes a difference”, and the note now says that the place is doubtful and gives “that” and the reading “indifferent”. A mark of doubt is not put into the English itself.

check.note: The Greek “well” is picked up at once by the word for “fine” or “honorable”, which is so translated in 2.11, while “good” is this translation’s word for another Greek word.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “want to be honorable in your own eyes”. “Good” is needed in this passage for another Greek word, in “the spring of the good”; the lost echo of “well” is recorded in a note.

check.note: The Greek word for “so” is dropped. It carries the step of the argument.
