check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “So where are they now?”.

check.note: The Greek is “spun together with” the person; “thread” is supplied to finish the image.
check.decided: Declined: The Greek verb says “spun together with” and names nothing spun, so English has to supply a noun either way. “Thread” is what the Fates spin and stays inside the Greek image, where “lot” would bring in a second idea; the note says that “thread” is supplied.

passages.casaubon: As one who had lived, and were now to die by right, whatsoever is yet remaining, bestow that wholly as a gracious overplus upon a virtuous life. Love and affect that only, whatsoever it be that happeneth, and is by the fates appointed unto thee. For what can be more reasonable? And as anything doth happen unto thee by way of cross, or calamity, call to mind presently and set before thine eyes, the examples of some other men, to whom the self-same thing did once happen likewise. Well, what did they? They grieved; they wondered; they complained. And where are they now? All dead and gone. Wilt thou also be like one of them? Or rather leaving to men of the world (whose life both in regard of themselves, and them that they converse with, is nothing but mere mutability; or men of as fickle minds, as fickle bodies; ever changing and soon changed themselves) let it be thine only care and study, how to make a right use of all such accidents. For there is good use to be made of them, and they will prove fit matter for thee to work upon, if it shall be both thy care and thy desire, that whatsoever thou doest, thou thyself mayst like and approve thyself for it. And both these, see, that thou remember well, according as the diversity of the matter of the action that thou art about shall require. Look within; within is the fountain of all good. Such a fountain, where springing waters can never fail, so thou dig still deeper and deeper.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek: Ὅσον οὐδέπω σποδὸς ἢ σκελετὸς καὶ ἤτοι ὄνομα ἢ οὐδὲ ὄνομα, τὸ δὲ ὄνομα ψόφος καὶ ἀπήχημα. τὰ δὲ ἐν τῷ βίῳ πολυτίμητα κενὰ καὶ σαπρὰ καὶ μικρὰ καὶ κυνίδια διαδακνόμενα καὶ παιδία φιλόνεικα, γελῶντα, εἶτα εὐθὺς κλαίοντα· πίστις δὲ καὶ αἰδὼς καὶ δίκη καὶ ἀλήθεια πρὸς Ὄλυμπον ἀπὸ χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης. τί οὖν ἔτι τὸ ἐνταῦθα κατέχον, εἴ γε τὰ μὲν αἰσθητὰ εὐμετάβλητα καὶ οὐχ ἑστῶτα, τὰ δὲ αἰσθητήρια ἀμυδρὰ καὶ εὐπαρατύπωτα, αὐτὸ δὲ τὸ ψυχάριον ἀναθυμίασις ἀφ’ αἵματος, τὸ δὲ εὐδοκιμεῖν παρὰ τοιούτοις κενόν; τί οὖν; περιμένεις ἵλεως τὴν εἴτε σβέσιν εἴτε μετάστασιν· ἕως δὲ ἐκείνης ὁ καιρὸς ἐφίσταται, τί ἀρκεῖ; τί δὲ ἄλλο ἢ θεοὺς μὲν σέβειν καὶ εὐφημεῖν, ἀνθρώπους δὲ εὖ ποιεῖν καὶ ἀνέχεσθαι αὐτῶν καὶ ἀπέχεσθαι· ὅσα δὲ ἐντὸς ὅρων τοῦ κρεᾳδίου καὶ τοῦ πνευματίου, ταῦτα μεμνῆσθαι μήτε σὰ ὄντα μήτε ἐπὶ σοί.
passages.english: Any moment now, ash or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; and the name is a noise and an echo. The things highly prized in life are empty and rotten and small, little dogs biting one another, quarrelsome children laughing and then at once crying. But good faith, a sense of shame, justice and truth: “to Olympus from the earth of the wide ways.” What is there, then, that still holds one here, seeing that the things the senses perceive change easily and do not stand still, the organs of sense are dim and easily take false imprints, the little soul itself is a vapor rising from blood, and a good name among such people is empty? What then? You wait cheerfully for what is either an extinguishing or a move elsewhere. And until the right time for that is at hand, what is enough? What else but to revere the gods and speak well of them, to do good to human beings, to bear with them and to hold back; and, as for everything inside the limits of the bit of flesh and the little breath, to remember that it is neither yours nor up to you.

notes.note: An idiom, “all but now”, “in next to no time”. The sentence has no verb and no subject; “you” is understood but not said, and it is not added.
notes.other_reading: Very soon you will be ash or a skeleton

notes.note: Literally “a dried-up thing”: a skeleton or a dried corpse.
notes.other_reading: ash or a dried-up corpse

notes.note: Part of a line of epic verse, with no verb in Marcus’s sentence. From memory, unchecked, it is from Hesiod’s Works and Days, where Shame and Nemesis leave the earth for the gods. Olympus is the mountain home of the gods; the last word is an epic compound, “with wide ways”.
notes.other_reading: have gone “to Olympus from the wide-wayed earth”

notes.note: “What holds here”: the Greek names no person. The English has “one” and not “you”.
notes.other_reading: What is there, then, that still keeps you here

notes.note: “If, that is”, or “seeing that”: the conditions that follow are taken as fact.
notes.other_reading: if the things the senses perceive change easily

notes.note: A plain present as given, “you wait”. With a different accent it would be a future, and it could also be punctuated as a question. ἵλεως is “well disposed”, “kindly”, also “cheerful”; “cheerfully” stands for it here and “cheerful” in 2.17.
notes.other_reading: Will you not wait serenely

notes.note: σβέσις is the putting out of a flame; μετάστασις is a removal to another place. Marcus leaves open which of the two death is.
notes.other_reading: for the end, whether it is extinction or a change of place

notes.note: Two verbs that differ by one letter, a rhyming pair (from memory, unchecked, a watchword of Epictetus). The second, “hold oneself off”, may stand alone, “to refrain”, or take “them” as its object, “to keep away from them”. The English leaves it without an object.
notes.other_reading: to bear with them and to keep away from them

notes.note: “Inside the limits” as given: the body and breath themselves and what belongs to them are not yours. From memory, unchecked, some editors read “outside” here.
notes.other_reading: everything outside the limits of the bit of flesh and the little breath

check.note: “Them” belongs to the first verb, and the second may stand alone, “to refrain”. “Hold back from them” makes people its object and sounds like keeping away from people.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “to bear with them and to hold back”. “From them” is dropped, since “them” stands in the Greek with the first verb and the second may stand alone; “hold back” is kept as the plain sense of the verb, and a note gives both readings.

check.note: The Greek word means serenely, in good cheer. “Graciously” today means courteously and misleads slightly.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “You wait cheerfully”. “Graciously” is heard today as “courteously”; the Greek word means well disposed and cheerful, which “calmly” would lose, and the same choice is made in 2.17.

check.note: The Greek is “if indeed”, “seeing that”: the conditions are taken as fact. Plain “if” leaves them open.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “seeing that the things the senses perceive …”. The Greek takes the conditions as fact.

check.note: “Wide-wayed” is an archaic compound. It is verse, so some lift is fair, but a reader of today may stumble.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “from the earth of the wide ways”, which says in plain words what the epic compound says.

passages.casaubon: Within a very little while, thou wilt be either ashes, or a sceletum; and a name perchance; and perchance, not so much as a name. And what is that but an empty sound, and a rebounding echo? Those things which in this life are dearest unto us, and of most account, they are in themselves but vain, putrid, contemptible. The most weighty and serious, if rightly esteemed, but as puppies, biting one another: or untoward children, now laughing and then crying. As for faith, and modesty, and justice, and truth, they long since, as one of the poets hath it, have abandoned this spacious earth, and retired themselves unto heaven. What is it then that doth keep thee here, if things sensible be so mutable and unsettled? and the senses so obscure, and so fallible? and our souls nothing but an exhalation of blood? and to be in credit among such, be but vanity? What is it that thou dost stay for? an extinction, or a translation; either of them with a propitious and contented mind. But still that time come, what will content thee? what else, but to worship and praise the Gods; and to do good unto men. To bear with them, and to forbear to do them any wrong. And for all external things belonging either to this thy wretched body, or life, to remember that they are neither thine, nor in thy power.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek: Ὡς ἤδη δυνατοῦ ὄντος ἐξιέναι τοῦ βίου, οὕτως ἕκαστα ποιεῖν καὶ λέγειν καὶ διανοεῖσθαι. τὸ δὲ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀπελθεῖν, εἰ μὲν θεοὶ εἰσίν, οὐδὲν δεινόν· κακῷ γάρ σε οὐκ ἂν περιβάλοιεν· εἰ δὲ ἤτοι οὐκ εἰσὶν ἢ οὐ μέλει αὐτοῖς τῶν ἀνθρωπείων, τί μοι ζῆν ἐν κόσμῳ κενῷ θεῶν ἢ προνοίας κενῷ; ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰσὶ καὶ μέλει αὐτοῖς τῶν ἀνθρωπείων καὶ τοῖς μὲν κατ’ ἀλήθειαν κακοῖς ἵνα μὴ περιπίπτῃ ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ τὸ πᾶν ἔθεντο· τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν εἴ τι κακὸν ἦν, καὶ τοῦτο ἂν προείδοντο, ἵνα ἐπὶ παντὶ ᾖ τὸ μὴ περιπίπτειν αὐτῷ. ὃ δὲ χείρω μὴ ποιεῖ ἄνθρωπον, πῶς ἂν τοῦτο βίον ἀνθρώπου χείρω ποιήσειεν; οὔτε δὲ κατ’ ἄγνοιαν οὔτε εἰδυῖα μέν, μὴ δυναμένη δὲ προφυλάξασθαι ἢ διορθώσασθαι ταῦτα ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις παρεῖδεν ἄν, οὔτ’ ἂν τηλικοῦτον ἥμαρτεν ἤτοι παρ’ ἀδυναμίαν ἢ παρ’ ἀτεχνίαν, ἵνα τὰ ἀγαθὰ καὶ τὰ κακὰ ἐπίσης τοῖς τε ἀγαθοῖς ἀνθρώποις καὶ τοῖς κακοῖς πεφυρμένως συμβαίνῃ. θάνατος δέ γε καὶ ζωή, δόξα καὶ ἀδοξία, πόνος καὶ ἡδονή, πλοῦτος καὶ πενία, πάντα ταῦτα ἐπίσης συμβαίνει ἀνθρώπων τοῖς τε ἀγαθοῖς καὶ τοῖς κακοῖς, οὔτε καλὰ ὄντα οὔτε αἰσχρά. οὔτ’ ἄρ’ ἀγαθὰ οὔτε κακά ἐστι.
passages.english: To do and say and think each thing in the knowledge that it is possible to leave life at this very moment. As for going away from among human beings: if gods exist, it is nothing to fear, for they would not throw you into anything bad. And if either they do not exist or they do not care about human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe empty of gods or empty of providence? But they do exist, and they do care about human affairs; and they have put it wholly in a person’s own power not to fall into the things that are truly bad. And if any of the rest were bad, they would have provided for that too, so that it would be in everyone’s power not to fall into it. But what does not make a human being worse, how could that make a human being’s life worse? The nature of the whole would not have overlooked these things, either through ignorance or because, though it knew, it could not guard against them beforehand or set them right; nor would it have made so great a mistake, through lack of power or lack of skill, that good things and bad things happen alike and in a jumble to good people and to bad. Now death and life, good repute and ill repute, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty, all these happen alike to the good and to the bad among human beings, and they are neither fine nor shameful. So they are neither good nor bad.

notes.greek: Ὡς ἤδη δυνατοῦ ὄντος ἐξιέναι τοῦ βίου
notes.note: Literally “on the footing that it is possible to leave life right now”. The Greek is impersonal, with infinitives for the instruction; the English keeps “To do” and names no person.
notes.other_reading: To do and say and think each thing as someone who can leave life at this very moment

notes.greek: κακῷ γάρ σε οὐκ ἂν περιβάλοιεν
notes.note: The argument of the whole chapter turns on one word, κακόν, used of things and of people. “Bad” stands for it every time, and “good” for its opposite. The verb is literally “throw around”, to involve someone in something.
notes.other_reading: for they would not involve you in any evil

notes.note: Literally “what to this speaker is living”: what good is living. The Greek changes here from the second person to the first.
notes.other_reading: why should I go on living

notes.note: “Saw beforehand”, and so “made provision”. It answers in sense to “providence” earlier in the chapter, though it is not the same Greek root.
notes.other_reading: they would have foreseen that too

notes.note: Taken as “in every person’s power”, matching “in a person’s own power” just before. It could also mean “in every case”.
notes.other_reading: so that in every case it would be possible not to fall into it

notes.note: From a verb for kneading or mixing up: without sorting, all in a mess.
notes.other_reading: indiscriminately

notes.note: The small words bring in the next step of the argument, as “Now” does in English. They do not object to what was just said.
notes.other_reading: But death and life

notes.note: πόνος is both hard toil and pain. Set against pleasure, it is taken as “pain”.
notes.other_reading: toil and pleasure

notes.note: καλόν and αἰσχρόν are the morally fine and the morally ugly, a different pair from good and bad; the last sentence draws the conclusion from them. The participle may give a reason (“since they are”); the English has a plain “and”.
notes.other_reading: since they are neither honorable nor shameful

check.greek: Ὡς ἤδη δυνατοῦ ὄντος ἐξιέναι τοῦ βίου
check.note: The Greek is impersonal: “since it is possible to leave life right now”. “Someone who can leave” sounds like an option the person holds and not something that may come.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “in the knowledge that it is possible to leave life at this very moment”. The Greek is impersonal, so “someone who can” is gone; “you” is not added, since the Greek has no person here.

check.note: The Greek words bring in the second premise of the argument, “Now …”. “Yet” can read as an objection to what was just said.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Now death and life …”. The Greek words bring in the next step of the argument and do not object to what was said.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek uses one verb three times of the gods, and the English had “there are” the first time and “exist” after that.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “if gods exist”, so that the three steps, “if gods exist”, “if they do not exist” and “they do exist”, are heard as one word.

passages.casaubon: Whatsoever thou dost affect, whatsoever thou dost project, so do, and so project all, as one who, for aught thou knowest, may at this very present depart out of this life. And as for death, if there be any gods, it is no grievous thing to leave the society of men. The gods will do thee no hurt, thou mayest be sure. But if it be so that there be no gods, or that they take no care of the world, why should I desire to live in a world void of gods, and of all divine providence? But gods there be certainly, and they take care for the world; and as for those things which be truly evil, as vice and wickedness, such things they have put in a man's own power, that he might avoid them if he would: and had there been anything besides that had been truly bad and evil, they would have had a care of that also, that a man might have avoided it. But why should that be thought to hurt and prejudice a man's life in this world, which cannot any ways make man himself the better, or the worse in his own person? Neither must we think that the nature of the universe did either through ignorance pass these things, or if not as ignorant of them, yet as unable either to prevent, or better to order and dispose them. It cannot be that she through want either of power or skill, should have committed such a thing, so as to suffer all things both good and bad, equally and promiscuously, to happen unto all both good and bad. As for life therefore, and death, honour and dishonour, labour and pleasure, riches and poverty, all these things happen unto men indeed, both good and bad, equally; but as things which of themselves are neither good nor bad; because of themselves, neither shameful nor praiseworthy.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek:
Διὰ τῆς τῶν ὅλων οὐσίας ὡς διὰ χειμάρρου διεκπορεύεται πάντα τὰ σώματα, τῷ ὅλῳ συμφυῆ καὶ συνεργὰ ὡς τὰ ἡμέτερα μέλη ἀλλήλοις. πόσους ἤδη ὁ αἰὼν Χρυσίππους, πόσους Σωκράτεις, πόσους Ἐπικτήτους καταπέπωκε. τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐπὶ παντὸς οὑτινοσοῦν σοι ἀνθρώπου τε καὶ πράγματος προσπιπτέτω.

Ἐμὲ ἓν μόνον περισπᾷ, μή τι αὐτὸς ποιήσω, ὃ ἡ κατασκευὴ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐ θέλει ἢ ὡς οὐ θέλει ἢ ὃ νῦν οὐ θέλει.

Ἐγγὺς μὲν ἡ σὴ περὶ πάντων λήθη, ἐγγὺς δὲ ἡ πάντων περὶ σοῦ λήθη.

Ἴδιον ἀνθρώπου φιλεῖν καὶ τοὺς πταίοντας. τοῦτο δὲ γίνεται, ἐὰν συμπροσπίπτῃ σοι, ὅτι καὶ συγγενεῖς καὶ δι’ ἄγνοιαν καὶ ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνουσι καὶ ὡς μετ’ ὀλίγον ἀμφότεροι τεθνήξεσθε, καὶ πρὸ πάντων, ὅτι οὐκ ἔβλαψέ σε· οὐ γὰρ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν σου χεῖρον ἐποίησεν ἢ πρόσθεν ἦν.
passages.english:
All bodies pass through and out of the substance of the whole, as through a winter torrent, grown together with the whole and working with it, as our limbs do with one another. How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has eternity already swallowed down. Let the same thought strike you about any human being whatever and any thing.

Only one thing troubles me: that I myself might do something that the constitution of a human being does not want, or in a way it does not want, or that it does not want now.

Your forgetting of all is near, and near is the forgetting of you by all.

It is proper to a human being to love even those who stumble. This happens if it strikes you at the same moment that they are your kin, that they go wrong through ignorance and against their will, that in a little while both of you will be dead, and above all that the person has not harmed you, for that person has not made your ruling part worse than it was before.

notes.note: οὐσία here is the stuff of which everything is made. “Substance” keeps it apart from “nature”, which this translation uses for φύσις.
notes.other_reading: through the matter of the whole

notes.note: A verb with two prefixes, “through” and “out”: bodies pass through the stream and out of it again.
notes.other_reading: all bodies make their way

notes.note: αἰών is a long age, or the whole of time; “eternity” keeps it apart from the ordinary word for time. Chrysippus was a head of the Stoic school; Epictetus a Stoic teacher of the generation before Marcus.
notes.other_reading: has time already swallowed down

notes.note: Literally “pulls away”, “distracts”, the sense it has in 6.22. With the clause of fear that follows, it comes to “troubles”.
notes.other_reading: Only one thing distracts me

notes.note: κατασκευή is how a thing is built or equipped. “Constitution” in the sense of makeup.
notes.other_reading: the way a human being is made

notes.note: “All” in both halves can be all things or all people. In the first half it is what you forget; in the second it is most naturally everyone who forgets you. “All” is kept bare in both.
notes.other_reading: Your forgetting of all things is near, and near is everyone’s forgetting of you

notes.note: The same verb as “strike you” in 7.19 with a prefix added, “together with”: the thought must come at the very moment of the offense.
notes.other_reading: if it also occurs to you

notes.note: “Unwilling”: they do not mean to go wrong. The Stoic view is that nobody errs on purpose.
notes.other_reading: and without meaning to

notes.note: The Greek moves from the plural (“they go wrong”) to a singular with no subject named: the one person in front of you. The English has “the person” and “that person”, since the Greek does not say “he”.
notes.other_reading: that he has not harmed you, for he has not made your ruling part worse

check.note: The Greek word is eternity, the whole span of the ages. “Time” is this section’s word for another Greek word, and the larger word is the point of the sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “has eternity already swallowed down”. “Time” is this section’s word for another Greek word, and the larger word is the point.

check.note: The verb is “pass through and out”. “Make their way” loses the passing out the other side.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “All bodies pass through and out of the substance of the whole”. The verb has both “through” and “out”.

check.note: With the clause of fear after it the sense is “troubles” or “worries”. “Distracts me: that I might do” does not read naturally.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Only one thing troubles me: that I myself might do …”. With a clause of fear after it the verb means “troubles”; a note gives the literal “pulls away” and its use in 6.22.

check.greek: οὐ γὰρ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν σου χεῖρον ἐποίησεν
check.note: The Greek has moved to the singular. After the plural “they” for the wrongdoers and then “the person”, a singular “they” is confusing.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “for that person has not made your ruling part worse”, so that the singular is clear. “He” is not used, because the Greek verb does not single out a man.

check.note: The Greek “all” in the first half can be “everyone”, as in the second half. The English makes the first “things” and the second people.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “Your forgetting of all is near, and near is the forgetting of you by all”. “Things” is dropped from the first half so that both halves have the same bare “all”, which can be things or people as in the Greek.

passages.casaubon: Through the substance of the universe, as through a torrent pass all particular bodies, being all of the same nature, and all joint workers with the universe itself as in one of our bodies so many members among themselves. How many such as Chrysippus, how many such as Socrates, how many such as Epictetus, hath the age of the world long since swallowed up and devoured? Let this, be it either men or businesses, that thou hast occasion to think of, to the end that thy thoughts be not distracted and thy mind too earnestly set upon anything, upon every such occasion presently come to thy mind. Of all my thoughts and cares, one only thing shall be the object, that I myself do nothing which to the proper constitution of man, (either in regard of the thing itself, or in regard of the manner, or of the time of doing,) is contrary. The time when thou shalt have forgotten all things, is at hand. And that time also is at hand, when thou thyself shalt be forgotten by all. Whilst thou art, apply thyself to that especially which unto man as he is a mart, is most proper and agreeable, and that is, for a man even to love them that transgress against him. This shall be, if at the same time that any such thing doth happen, thou call to mind, that they are thy kinsmen; that it is through ignorance and against their wills that they sin; and that within a very short while after, both thou and he shall be no more. But above all things, that he hath not done thee any hurt; for that by him thy mind and understanding is not made worse or more vile than it was before.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.english:
Notice at last that you have in yourself something stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions and that, in a word, pull you about on strings. What is my thought at this moment? Can it be fear? Suspicion? Desire? Anything else of that kind?

First, not at random and not without a point of reference. Second, to take as the point of reference nothing other than the social end.

That before long you will be no one and nowhere, nor will any of the things you now see be, nor any of the people now living. For it is the nature of all things to change, to turn and to perish, so that other things may come to be after them.

notes.note: ποτέ with a command is “at some point”, with a note of impatience: “at last”, “for once”.
notes.other_reading: Notice, some time,

notes.note: κρεῖττον is both “stronger” and “better”. The second word is formed from δαίμων, the divine being within a person, so “more divine”.
notes.other_reading: something better and more godlike

notes.note: The verb for working a puppet by its strings. The Greek word carries the image by itself; “on strings” is the English for it here, as in 2.2 and 7.3.
notes.other_reading: the things that pull your strings

notes.note: “Thought” is this translation’s word for διάνοια: here the thinking part as a whole and the state it is in at this moment, not one thought. The Greek changes here from the second person to the first.
notes.other_reading: What is my mind at this moment?

notes.note: A question with μή: it expects or hopes for the answer no, or asks with some unease. “Can it be” stands for the first and the rest are left bare.
notes.other_reading: It is not fear, is it?

notes.note: Literally “without a reference”: without something the action is referred back to. The next sentence uses a near twin, “to make the referring”. “Point of reference” stands for both. Neither sentence has a main verb.
notes.other_reading: First, not at random and not without an aim. Second, to aim at nothing other than the social end.

notes.note: “Social” is this translation’s word for κοινωνικός: the end that concerns the community, the common good.
notes.other_reading: the good of the community as its end

notes.note: The chapter opens with a bare “That”, as a thought to keep in mind. It is kept.
notes.other_reading: Remember that before long

check.note: The two Greek nouns both mean referring an act back to an end. “Aim” and “to aim” keep the link but lose the idea of reference, and the second sentence then only repeats the first.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “not without a point of reference” and “to take as the point of reference nothing other than the social end”. Both Greek nouns speak of referring an act to something, and the second sentence now says what the reference must be.

check.note: “The social end” is unclear to a reader of today. The Greek is the end that concerns the community.
check.decided: Declined: “Social” is the settled word of this translation for κοινωνικός and is kept so that the word can be followed from passage to passage. A note now says that the end that concerns the community is meant.

check.greek: τί μου νῦν ἐστιν ἡ διάνοια
check.note: The Greek word is the mind or the understanding, not a single thought: the question is what the mind now is, what it is taken up with.
check.decided: Declined: “Thought” is the settled word for διάνοια, and “my thought” in English can mean the whole of a person’s thinking, which is what the question asks about. The note gives “mind”.

check.note: One Greek verb; “on strings” and “like a puppet” both unpack it. Either would do.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “pull you about on strings”. “Like a puppet” is dropped, since one unpacking of the one Greek verb is enough; “on strings” is kept over “pull your strings”, which today is a worn phrase for influence, and it matches the same verb in 2.2 and 7.3.

passages.casaubon: It is high time for thee, to understand that there is somewhat in thee, better and more divine than either thy passions, or thy sensual appetites and affections. What is now the object of my mind, is it fear, or suspicion, or lust, or any such thing? To do nothing rashly without some certain end; let that be thy first care. The next, to have no other end than the common good. For, alas! yet a little while, and thou art no more: no more will any, either of those things that now thou seest, or of those men that now are living, be any more. For all things are by nature appointed soon to be changed, turned, and corrupted, that other things might succeed in their room.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek: Τρία ταῦτα δεῖ πρόχειρα ἔχειν· ἐπὶ μὲν ὧν ποιεῖς, εἰ μήτε εἰκῇ μήτε ἄλλως ἢ ὡς ἂν ἡ Δίκη αὐτὴ ἐνήργησεν· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἔξωθεν συμβαινόντων, ὅτι ἤτοι κατ’ ἐπιτυχίαν ἢ κατὰ πρόνοιαν· οὔτε δὲ τῇ ἐπιτυχίᾳ μεμπτέον οὔτε τῇ προνοίᾳ ἐγκλητέον. δεύτερον τό· ὁποῖον ἕκαστον ἀπὸ σπέρματος μέχρι ψυχώσεως καὶ ἀπὸ ψυχώσεως μέχρι τοῦ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀποδοῦναι καὶ ἐξ οἵων ἡ σύγκρισις καὶ εἰς οἷα ἡ λύσις. τρίτον, εἰ ἄφνω μετέωρος ἐξαρθεὶς κατασκέψαιο τὰ ἀνθρώπεια καὶ τὴν πολυτροπίαν, ὅτι καταφρονήσεις συνιδὼν ἅμα καὶ ὅσον τὸ περιοικοῦν ἐναερίων καὶ ἐναιθερίων· καὶ ὅτι, ὁσάκις ἂν ἐξαρθῇς, ταὐτὰ ὄψῃ, τὸ ὁμοειδές, τὸ ὀλιγοχρόνιον. ἐπὶ τούτοις ὁ τῦφος.
passages.english: These three things must be kept ready to hand. About what you do: whether it is neither at random nor otherwise than Justice herself would have acted. About what happens from outside: that it comes either by chance or by providence, and that one must neither blame chance nor bring a charge against providence. Second: what each thing is like from seed to the receiving of a soul, and from the receiving of a soul to the giving back of the soul; and out of what kind of things it is put together and into what kind of things it is dissolved. Third: that if you were suddenly lifted high into the air and looked down on human affairs and their many turns, you will despise them, seeing at the same time how much there is that dwells all around, in the air and in the ether; and that however often you are lifted up, you will see the same things: how alike in kind, how short-lived. And over these things, the puffed-up pride.

notes.note: The clause has no verb. εἰ is taken as “whether”, a question to put to oneself about each action. It could be “if”, with the thought left hanging.
notes.other_reading: About what you do: that it be neither at random nor otherwise than

notes.note: ἐπιτυχία is how things happen to fall out. The pair is chance against providence.
notes.other_reading: either by accident or by providence

notes.note: The Greek says “second” here although no “first” was named: the first of the three is the double point about what you do and what happens from outside.
notes.other_reading: The second is this:

notes.note: The moment a living thing gets its soul, set against the later moment of “giving back the soul”, that is, dying.
notes.other_reading: from seed to quickening, and from quickening to the giving up of life

notes.note: Literally “many-turning-ness”: the variety of human affairs, or their shiftiness. “Many turns” keeps the image and both senses.
notes.other_reading: human affairs and their variety

notes.note: The grammar is loose: “if you were to look” (a supposed case) is followed by “that you will despise” (a plain future). The mismatch is kept.
notes.other_reading: that you would despise them

notes.greek: ὅσον τὸ περιοικοῦν ἐναερίων καὶ ἐναιθερίων
notes.note: Literally “how great is what dwells around, of those in the air and those in the ether”. The ether is the bright upper air above the air that is breathed. It can be the number of those living there or the extent of the region so lived in, and whether these are living beings or simply everything up there is not said; the word “dwells” points to beings.
notes.other_reading: how great is the company that dwells all around, of beings in the air and in the ether

notes.note: Two adjectives used as nouns, said of the things seen: that they are of one kind and that they last a short time.
notes.other_reading: the sameness, the shortness of their time

notes.note: No verb: “over these, the τῦφος”. The word is literally smoke (so translated in 2.17), and so empty pride or delusion. Here it is taken as people’s pride in such things, and “puffed-up” keeps something of the smoke.
notes.other_reading: And these are what people are puffed up about.

check.note: The Greek word describes the things seen: their short-livedness. “The shortness of time” says something about time instead.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “how alike in kind, how short-lived”. The Greek word describes the things seen, not time.

check.note: The Greek is a curt exclamation, “and over these things, the pride!”. The English is flat and “the conceit” is unclear; the same word is “smoke” in 2.17.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “And over these things, the puffed-up pride.” The Greek is a curt phrase with no verb and names no people, so none are added; “pride” replaces “conceit”, and a note links the word to “smoke” in 2.17.

check.note: The Greek word is variety, manifoldness. “How many turns they take” is harder than the Greek.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “human affairs and their many turns”. This is plainer than before and keeps the image of turning that the Greek word has, which “variety” would drop; a note gives “variety”.

check.note: The Greek can be the population dwelling around or the extent of the region so lived in; “company” chooses the first.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “how much there is that dwells all around, in the air and in the ether”. It says only how much, as the Greek does, and a note gives both readings.

passages.casaubon: These three things thou must have always in a readiness: first concerning thine own actions, whether thou doest nothing either idly, or otherwise, than justice and equity do require: and concerning those things that happen unto thee externally, that either they happen unto thee by chance, or by providence; of which two to accuse either, is equally against reason. Secondly, what like unto our bodies are whilest yet rude and imperfect, until they be animated: and from their animation, until their expiration: of what things they are compounded, and into what things they shall be dissolved. Thirdly, how vain all things will appear unto thee when, from on high as it were, looking down thou shalt contemplate all things upon earth, and the wonderful mutability, that they are subject unto: considering withal, the infinite both greatness and variety of things aerial and things celestial that are round about it. And that as often as thou shalt behold them, thou shalt still see the same: as the same things, so the same shortness of continuance of all those things. And, behold, these be the things that we are so proud and puffed up for.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek:
Πείρασον πῶς σοι χωρεῖ καὶ ὁ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἀνθρώπου βίος τοῦ ἀρεσκομένου μὲν τοῖς ἐκ τῶν ὅλων ἀπονεμομένοις, ἀρκουμένου δὲ τῇ ἰδίᾳ πράξει δικαίᾳ καὶ διαθέσει εὐμενεῖ.

Ἑώρακας ἐκεῖνα, ἴδε καὶ ταῦτα. σεαυτὸν μὴ τάρασσε· ἅπλωσον σεαυτόν. ἁμαρτάνει τις; ἑαυτῷ ἁμαρτάνει. συμβέβηκέ σοί τι ; καλῶς· ἐκ τῶν ὅλων ἀπʼ ἀρχῆς σοι συγκαθείμαρτο καὶ συνεκλώθετο πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον. τὸ δ’ ὅλον, βραχὺς ὁ βίος· κερδαντέον τὸ παρὸν σὺν εὐλογιστίᾳ καὶ δίκῃ. νῆφε ἀνειμένως.
passages.english:
Try how the life of the good person, too, goes for you: the person who is pleased with what is allotted from the whole and content with their own action being just and their disposition kind.

You have seen those things; look at these too. Do not disturb yourself: make yourself simple. Someone does wrong? They do wrong to themselves. Something has happened to you? That is well: everything that happens was, from the beginning, fated along with you out of the whole and spun into your thread. In sum, life is short. The present must be turned to profit, with good reasoning and justice. Be sober, without strain.

notes.note: χωρεῖ is “goes”, “turns out”, “succeeds”: see how this life works out when you try it.
notes.other_reading: Try how the life of the good person suits you

notes.greek: καὶ ὁ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἀνθρώπου βίος
notes.note: The small word καί, “also”, goes with the life and implies that other lives have been tried already. It is kept as “too”, set next to “the life of the good person”.
notes.other_reading: Try how even the life of the good person goes for you

notes.note: The Greek does not say what “those” and “these” are. They are left bare.
notes.other_reading: You have seen that side; now look at this one too

notes.note: “Make yourself single”: simple, of one piece. The verb can also mean to unfold or spread out.
notes.other_reading: be simple

notes.note: The dative marks who is affected: the wrong lands on the one who does it.
notes.other_reading: It is their own loss

notes.note: “Well”, as an answer to the question. “Good” is avoided because this passage uses it for another Greek word, in “the good person”.
notes.other_reading: Good

notes.note: Two verbs with the prefix “together with”: fated along with you and spun along with you. The second is the image of the Fates’ thread; “thread” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: was fated together with you and spun together with you

notes.note: A word from trade: the present is to be made a gain of.
notes.other_reading: One must profit from the present

notes.note: “Be sober” (not drunk, and so clear-headed) with an adverb meaning “loosely”, “without strain”. The two pull against each other on purpose.
notes.other_reading: Keep a clear head, but be at ease

check.greek: καὶ ὁ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἀνθρώπου βίος
check.note: The Greek “also” goes with the life: “the good person’s life too”. At the end of the clause “as well” reads as “for you too”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Try how the life of the good person, too, goes for you”. The Greek “also” goes with the life, not with “you”.

check.note: Both verbs have the prefix “together with”. The first loses the prefix in English; the second gains “your thread”, which is not in the Greek.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “fated along with you out of the whole and spun into your thread”. The first verb now has its “together with”; “thread” is kept in the second, as in 7.57, because the verb is the spinning of the Fates and English needs the thing spun, and the note says it is supplied.

check.note: “Be sober, in a relaxed way” is clumsy. The Greek is two words: be sober, without strain.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “Be sober, without strain.” The Greek is two words with no “but”, so none is added.

check.note: Found while settling: “Good” answered the question with this translation’s word for another Greek word, which the passage uses just before in “the good person”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “That is well”, which is what the Greek adverb says, and a note records it.

passages.casaubon: Try also how a good man's life; (of one, who is well pleased with those things whatsoever, which among the common changes and chances of this world fall to his own lot and share; and can live well contented and fully satisfied in the justice of his own proper present action, and in the goodness of his disposition for the future:) will agree with thee. Thou hast had experience of that other kind of life: make now trial of this also. Trouble not thyself any more henceforth, reduce thyself unto perfect simplicity. Doth any man offend? It is against himself that he doth offend: why should it trouble thee? Hath anything happened unto thee? It is well, whatsoever it be, it is that which of all the common chances of the world from the very beginning in the series of all other things that have, or shall happen, was destinated and appointed unto thee. To comprehend all in a few words, our life is short; we must endeavour to gain the present time with best discretion and justice. Use recreation with sobriety.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek:
Τὴν ὑποληπτικὴν δύναμιν σέβε. ἐν ταύτῃ τὸ πᾶν, ἵνα ὑπόληψις τῷ ἡγεμονικῷ σου μηκέτι ἐγγένηται ἀνακόλουθος τῇ φύσει καὶ τῇ τοῦ λογικοῦ ζῴου κατασκευῇ, αὕτη δὲ ἐπαγγέλλεται ἀπροπτωσίαν καὶ τὴν πρὸς ἀνθρώπους οἰκείωσιν καὶ τὴν τοῖς θεοῖς ἀκολουθίαν.

Πάντα οὖν ῥίψας ταῦτα μόνα τὰ ὀλίγα σύνεχε καὶ ἔτι συμμνημόνευε, ὅτι μόνον ζῇ ἕκαστος τὸ παρὸν τοῦτο, τὸ ἀκαριαῖον· τὰ δὲ ἄλλα ἢ βεβίωται ἢ ἐν ἀδήλῳ, μικρὸν μὲν οὖν ὃ ζῇ ἕκαστος· μικρὸν δὲ τὸ τῆς γῆς γωνίδιον ὅπου ζῇ· μικρὸν δὲ καὶ ἡ μηκίστη ὑστεροφημία καὶ αὕτη δὲ κατὰ διαδοχὴν ἀνθρωπαρίων τάχιστα τεθνηξομένων καὶ οὐκ εἰδότων οὐδὲ ἑαυτοὺς οὐδέ γε τὸν πρόπαλαι τεθνηκότα.
passages.english:
Revere the power of forming judgments. Everything lies in this, that there should no longer arise in your ruling part a judgment that does not follow nature and the constitution of the rational animal. And this promises freedom from haste, affinity with human beings, and following the gods.

So throw everything away and hold on to only these few things; and remember as well that each person lives only this present, an instant. The rest has either been lived or is uncertain. Small, then, is what each person lives, and small the little corner of the earth where they live; small too is even the longest fame after death, and even that is handed down a line of little human beings who will die very soon and who do not know even themselves, let alone someone who died long ago.

notes.note: The power that forms a ὑπόληψις, “judgment” in this translation: the faculty of taking a view of things.
notes.other_reading: Revere the faculty of opinion

notes.note: “In this is everything”, then a clause with the word that usually means “so that”. The English takes the clause as spelling out what the “everything” is. It may instead give a purpose.
notes.other_reading: Everything lies in this, so that there may no longer arise in your ruling part a judgment

notes.note: “Not following”, “out of line with”. The same root returns at the end of the sentence in “following the gods”, so “follow” stands in both places.
notes.other_reading: a judgment inconsistent with nature

notes.note: “This” can point back to the constitution of the rational animal, the nearest noun, to nature, or to the power of forming judgments at the start. The English leaves “this” bare, as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: And this power promises

notes.note: A Stoic term, literally “not falling forward”: not giving assent to an impression too quickly.
notes.other_reading: freedom from rash assent

notes.note: A Stoic term for treating something as one’s own, as belonging to one’s household. “Affinity” stands for it, and “kinship” is left for another Greek word in this section.
notes.other_reading: a sense of belonging with human beings

notes.greek: Πάντα οὖν ῥίψας ταῦτα μόνα τὰ ὀλίγα σύνεχε
notes.note: The Greek says “everything”, not “everything else”. As given there is no comma, so “these” could just be taken with “everything” (throw all these away); the sense requires it with “only the few”.
notes.other_reading: So let everything else go and keep hold of these few things alone

notes.note: “The momentary”: the present that lasts an instant.
notes.other_reading: this present, which is only a moment

notes.note: Literally “in the unclear”: not visible, not known.
notes.other_reading: or lies hidden

notes.note: “By a succession”, as in a relay; “is handed down” stands for a verb the Greek leaves out. The word for human beings is a belittling diminutive.
notes.other_reading: and it depends on a relay of poor little people

check.note: The Greek “this” may be the constitution (the nearest noun), nature, or the power of judging with which the passage began. The English names one without warning.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “And this promises”. The Greek has only “this”, which can be the constitution, nature or the power of judging; a note lists the three.

check.note: The Greek clause explains the “everything”: it all depends on this, that no judgment should arise. It is not the purpose of some earlier act, and “Everything lies in this, so that” does not connect in English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “Everything lies in this, that there should no longer arise in your ruling part a judgment …”. The clause is taken as saying what the “everything” is, which connects in English; “lies in this” is kept for the Greek “in this”, and a note gives the reading of purpose.

check.note: The Greek word is affinity, a sense of belonging with. “Kinship” is this section’s word for another Greek word in 12.26, a different idea.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “affinity with human beings”. “Kinship” is this section’s word for another Greek word; “affinity” is closer than “fellow-feeling” to a term that means treating something as one’s own.

check.note: “Mere” is added; the Greek is “the momentary”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “only this present, an instant”. “Mere” is not in the Greek.

passages.casaubon: Use thine opinative faculty with all honour and respect, for in her indeed is all: that thy opinion do not beget in thy understanding anything contrary to either nature, or the proper constitution of a rational creature. The end and object of a rational constitution is, to do nothing rashly, to be kindly affected towards men, and in all things willingly to submit unto the gods. Casting therefore all other things aside, keep thyself to these few, and remember withal that no man properly can be said to live more than that which is now present, which is but a moment of time. Whatsoever is besides either is already past, or uncertain. The time therefore that any man doth live, is but a little, and the place where he liveth, is but a very little corner of the earth, and the greatest fame that can remain of a man after his death, even that is but little, and that too, such as it is whilst it is, is by the succession of silly mortal men preserved, who likewise shall shortly die, and even whiles they live know not what in very deed they themselves are: and much less can know one, who long before is dead and gone.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek:
Ὅτι οὐδὲν ἧττον τὰ αὐτὰ ποιήσουσι, κἂν σὺ διαρραγῇς.

Τὸ πρῶτον μὴ ταράσσου· πάντα γὰρ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ ὅλου φύσιν καὶ ὀλίγου χρόνου οὐδεὶς οὐδαμοῦ ἔσῃ, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ Ἁδριανὸς οὐδὲ Αὔγουστος. ἔπειτα ἀτενίσας εἰς τὸ πρᾶγμα ἴδε αὐτὸ καὶ συμμνημονεύσας ὅτι ἀγαθόν σε ἄνθρωπον εἶναι δεῖ καὶ τί τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἡ φύσις ἀπαιτεῖ, πρᾶξον τοῦτο ἀμεταστρεπτὶ καὶ εἰπέ, ὡς δικαιότατον φαίνεταί σοι· μόνον εὐμενῶς καὶ αἰδημόνως καὶ ἀνυποκρίτως.
passages.english:
That they will do the same things none the less, even if you burst.

First, do not be disturbed: for all things are according to the nature of the whole, and in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, just as Hadrian is not, nor Augustus. Next, fix your eyes on the matter and see it; and, remembering as well that you must be a good human being and what the nature of a human being demands, do that without turning aside, and speak as seems to you most just: only kindly, modestly and without pretense.

notes.note: The chapter opens with a bare “That”, as a thought to keep in mind. It is kept.
notes.other_reading: Remember that they will do the same things none the less

notes.note: Literally “burst apart”, said of bursting with anger or effort.
notes.other_reading: even if you burst with rage

notes.note: πρᾶγμα is the thing in hand: the matter, the business, the task.
notes.other_reading: fix your eyes on the task

notes.note: “Without turning round”: without looking back or swerving.
notes.other_reading: without looking back

notes.note: “Speak, as seems most just to you”: the Greek is about the way of speaking. The clause may go with “speak” alone, as the English has it, or with both “do” and “speak”.
notes.other_reading: do that without turning aside, and say what seems to you most just

notes.note: From αἰδώς, a sense of shame and of respect for others.
notes.other_reading: with respect

check.note: The Greek word is “as”, “in the way that”: it is the manner of speaking that is to be most just, not a statement picked out as most just.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “and speak as seems to you most just”. The Greek word is “as”: it is the manner of speaking that is to be most just, not one statement picked out.

passages.casaubon: What they have done, they will still do, although thou shouldst hang thyself. First; let it not trouble thee. For all things both good and evil: come to pass according to the nature and general condition of the universe, and within a very little while, all things will be at an end; no man will be remembered: as now of Africanus (for example) and Augustus it is already come to pass. Then secondly; fix thy mind upon the thing itself; look into it, and remembering thyself, that thou art bound nevertheless to be a good man, and what it is that thy nature requireth of thee as thou art a man, be not diverted from what thou art about, and speak that which seemeth unto thee most just: only speak it kindly, modestly, and without hypocrisy.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek: Τοῦ ἀνθρωπίνου βίου ὁ μὲν χρόνος στιγμή, ἡ δὲ οὐσία ῥέουσα, ἡ δὲ αἴσθησις ἀμυδρά, ἡ δὲ ὅλου τοῦ σώματος σύγκρισις εὔσηπτος, ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ ῥόμβος, ἡ δὲ τύχη δυστέκμαρτον, ἡ δὲ φήμη ἄκριτον· συνελόντι δὲ εἰπεῖν, πάντα τὰ μὲν τοῦ σώματος ποταμός, τὰ δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς ὄνειρος καὶ τῦφος, ὁ δὲ βίος πόλεμος καὶ ξένου ἐπιδημία, ἡ δὲ ὑστεροφημία λήθη. τί οὖν τὸ παραπέμψαι δυνάμενον; ἓν καὶ μόνον φιλοσοφία· τοῦτο δὲ ἐν τῷ τηρεῖν τὸν ἔνδον δαίμονα ἀνύβριστον καὶ ἀσινῆ, ἡδονῶν καὶ πόνων κρείσσονα, μηδὲν εἰκῇ ποιοῦντα μηδὲ διεψευσμένως καὶ μεθ̓ ὑποκρίσεως, ἀνενδεῆ τοῦ ἄλλον ποιῆσαί τι ἢ μὴ ποιῆσαι· ἔτι δὲ τὰ συμβαίνοντα καὶ ἀπονεμόμενα δεχόμενον ὡς ἐκεῖθέν ποθεν ἐρχόμενα, ὅθεν αὐτὸς ἦλθεν· ἐπὶ πᾶσι δὲ τὸν θάνατον ἵλεῳ τῇ γνώμῃ περιμένοντα ὡς οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ λύσιν τῶν στοιχείων, ἐξ ὧν ἕκαστον ζῷον συγκρίνεται. εἰ δὲ αὐτοῖς τοῖς στοιχείοις μηδὲν δεινὸν ἐν τῷ ἕκαστον διηνεκῶς εἰς ἕτερον μεταβάλλειν, διὰ τί ὑπίδηταί τις τὴν πάντων μεταβολὴν καὶ διάλυσιν; κατὰ φύσιν γάρ· οὐδὲν δὲ κακὸν κατὰ φύσιν. Τὰ ἐν Καρνούντῳ.
passages.english: In human life, the time is a point, the substance is in flux, perception is dim, the compound of the whole body is ready to rot, the soul is a whirl, fortune is hard to make out, fame is undiscerning. To put it briefly: everything of the body is a river, everything of the soul is a dream and smoke, life is a war and a stranger’s stay abroad, and fame after death is forgetting. What, then, can escort a person through? One thing and only one: philosophy. And this lies in keeping the spirit within free from abuse and unharmed, stronger than pleasures and pains, doing nothing at random, nothing falsely or with pretense, not needing another person to do something or not do it; and further, accepting what happens and what is allotted as coming from that same place, wherever it is, from which it came itself; and, on top of all this, waiting for death with a cheerful mind, as nothing other than a dissolving of the elements of which every living thing is put together. And if for the elements themselves there is nothing terrible in each one continually changing into another, why should anyone look with suspicion on the change and dissolution of all? For it is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad. At Carnuntum.

notes.note: οὐσία is the stuff a human being is made of. “In flux” prepares the river in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: its matter is flowing

notes.note: A thing that is whirled round (a top, or a bull-roarer spun on a cord) or the whirling motion itself. “A whirl” covers both.
notes.other_reading: the soul is a spinning top

notes.note: ἄκριτος can be active, “not judging”, “undiscerning”, or passive, “not decided”, “not to be judged”. The English takes the first: what people say is said without discernment.
notes.other_reading: fame is an uncertain thing

notes.note: τῦφος is literally smoke or vapor, and by extension delusion and empty pride. The image is kept beside “dream”; the same word is “puffed-up pride” in 12.24.
notes.other_reading: a dream and a delusion

notes.note: A foreigner’s stay in a town that is not his own.
notes.other_reading: a visit to a strange land

notes.note: The verb is used of escorting or convoying a traveler. The Greek names no object; “a person” and “through” are supplied.
notes.other_reading: What, then, can guide one on the way?

notes.note: δαίμων is a divine being of lower rank than a god; here the divine part allotted to each person. “Spirit” stands for it, as in 5.10b.
notes.other_reading: the divinity within

notes.note: Not subjected to ὕβρις, which is insult and wanton violence together. “Abuse” covers both.
notes.other_reading: unviolated

notes.note: “It itself” is masculine and is taken of the spirit, which all the words around it describe. It could be the person.
notes.other_reading: from which he himself came

notes.note: “On top of all”: the last item of the list. It can also be heard as “above all”, which would rank this item highest.
notes.other_reading: and above all

notes.note: The same word as “cheerfully” in 5.33: well disposed, kindly, also cheerful.
notes.other_reading: with a serene mind

notes.note: “Of all” can be of all the elements, set against “each one” just before, or of all things. The English leaves “all” bare.
notes.other_reading: the change and dissolution of all things

notes.note: Literally “The things at Carnuntum”, a label and not part of the argument. Carnuntum was a Roman army base on the Danube. From memory, unchecked, editors differ on whether it closes this book or heads the next.
notes.other_reading: Written at Carnuntum.

check.note: The Greek word is a whirling motion or a thing whirled round. “A spinning top” picks one object; “a whirl” keeps both.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the soul is a whirl”. The Greek word is the whirling or a thing whirled, and “a whirl” does not pick one object; the note names the top.

check.note: The Greek word can be “undiscerning” or “not to be judged, uncertain”. “Fame is without judgment” is unclear either way.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “fame is undiscerning”. This says clearly which of the two senses is taken, and the note gives the other.

check.note: “Gracious” today means courteous. The Greek is a serene, cheerful mind, the same word as in 5.33.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “with a cheerful mind”. “Gracious” is heard today as “courteous”; “cheerful” is within the Greek word’s range and keeps its good will, which “calm” would lose, and it matches 5.33.

check.note: The Greek phrase is “on top of everything”, “finally”. “Above all” ranks this item highest, which the Greek need not say.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “and, on top of all this,”. The Greek phrase closes the list and need not rank this item highest; a note gives “above all”.

check.note: The Greek “of all” can be “all things” as well as “all the elements”. “Of them all” ties it to the elements.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “the change and dissolution of all”. The Greek “of all” may be all the elements, set against “each one”, or all things, so the English leaves it bare and a note gives both.

check.note: “Free from outrage” is unclear today; the sense is unviolated, not abused.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “free from abuse”. The Greek word covers insult and violence together, for which “abuse” is the plain word of today, where “unviolated” is rare.

check.note: “Written” is supplied; the Greek is only “the things at Carnuntum”. It is also unsettled whether this label closes this book or heads the next.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “At Carnuntum.” “Written” is not in the Greek; the note says what the label is and that its place is disputed.

check.note: The Greek word is “smoke” here and “conceit” in 12.24. Each fits its place, but the reader cannot see it is one word.
check.decided: Declined: “Smoke” is the literal sense of the word and stands here as an image beside “dream”, and images are kept. The notes on this passage and on 12.24 now say that it is one Greek word.

passages.casaubon: The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending to corruption. His soul is restless, fortune uncertain, and fame doubtful; to be brief, as a stream so are all things belonging to the body; as a dream, or as a smoke, so are all that belong unto the soul. Our life is a warfare, and a mere pilgrimage. Fame after life is no better than oblivion. What is it then that will adhere and follow? Only one thing, philosophy. And philosophy doth consist in this, for a man to preserve that spirit which is within him, from all manner of contumelies and injuries, and above all pains or pleasures; never to do anything either rashly, or feignedly, or hypocritically: wholly to depend from himself and his own proper actions: all things that happen unto him to embrace contentedly, as coming from Him from whom he himself also came; and above all things, with all meekness and a calm cheerfulness, to expect death, as being nothing else but the resolution of those elements, of which every creature is composed. And if the elements themselves suffer nothing by this their perpetual conversion of one into another, that dissolution, and alteration, which is so common unto all, why should it be feared by any? Is not this according to nature? But nothing that is according to nature can be evil. _Whilst I was at Carnuntum._

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek:
Ἀναβιῶναί σοι ἔξεστιν· ἴδε πάλιν τὰ πράγματα, ὡς ἑώρας· ἐν τούτῳ γὰρ τὸ ἀναβιῶναι.

Πομπῆς κενοσπουδία, ἐπὶ σκηνῆς δράματα, ποίμνια, ἀγέλαι, διαδορατισμοί, κυνιδίοις ὀστάριον ἐρριμμένον, ψωμίον εἰς τὰς τῶν ἰχθύων δεξαμενάς, μυρμήκων ταλαιπωρίαι καὶ ἀχθοφορίαι, μυιδίων ἐπτοημένων διαδρομαί, σιγιλλάρια νευροσπαστούμενα. χρὴ οὖν ἐν τούτοις εὐμενῶς μὲν καὶ μὴ καταφρυαττόμενον ἑστάναι, παρακολουθεῖν μέντοι, ὅτι τοσούτου ἄξιος ἕκαστός ἐστιν, ὅσου ἄξιά ἐστι ταῦτα περὶ ἃ ἐσπούδακεν.
passages.english:
You can come back to life. See things again as you used to see them: for in this lies the coming back to life.

The empty seriousness of a procession, plays on a stage, flocks, herds, spear fights, a little bone thrown to little dogs, a scrap of bread into the fish tanks, the toils and load-carrying of ants, the scurrying of frightened little mice, puppets pulled on strings. Among these things, then, one must stand kindly and without snorting at them, and yet keep in view that each person is worth just as much as the things they have taken seriously are worth.

notes.note: A past tense of repeated action: as you used to see them, at some earlier and better time.
notes.other_reading: as you once saw them

notes.note: “Empty earnestness”. The same root comes back in the last words of the chapter, so “seriousness” stands here and “taken seriously” there.
notes.other_reading: The hollow pomp of a procession

notes.note: A rare word, “fighting it out with spears”. It may be battle or a show of combat.
notes.other_reading: bouts with the spear

notes.greek: ψωμίον εἰς τὰς τῶν ἰχθύων δεξαμενάς
notes.note: No verb of its own: “thrown” is understood from the bone before it and is not repeated. The last word is a tank or pond.
notes.other_reading: a crumb tossed into the fish ponds

notes.note: A diminutive. It is taken from the word for mouse; the form is close to the word for a fly.
notes.other_reading: the darting about of startled little flies

notes.note: The first word is Latin (sigillaria, small figures or dolls) in Greek letters; the second is the verb for working puppets by strings.
notes.other_reading: little dolls jerked about on strings

notes.note: From the snorting of a proud horse: to behave with insolent contempt toward something. The snort is kept.
notes.other_reading: without looking down one’s nose at them

check.note: “All” is added; the Greek is “among these things”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Among these things”. The Greek has no “all”.

part.left_out: Τὰ δόγματα πῶς ἄλλως δύναται νεκρωθῆναι, ἐὰν μὴ αἱ κατάλληλοι αὐτοῖς φαντασίαι σβεσθῶσιν, ἃς διηνεκῶς ἀναζωπυρεῖν ἐπὶ σοί ἐστι. δύναμαι περὶ τούτου ὃ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν· εἰ δύναμαι, τί ταράσσομαι; τὰ ἔξω τῆς ἐμῆς διανοίας οὐδὲν ὅλως πρὸς τὴν ἐμὴν διάνοιαν. τοῦτο μάθε καὶ ὀρθὸς εἶ.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the first part of chapter 7.2, down to 'thou wilt be right', in its section 7.2 and begins its 7.3 here, with the lines on living again.

passages.casaubon: That which most men would think themselves most happy for, and would prefer before all things, if the Gods would grant it unto them after their deaths, thou mayst whilst thou livest grant unto thyself; to live again. See the things of the world again, as thou hast already seen them. For what is it else to live again? Public shows and solemnities with much pomp and vanity, stage plays, flocks and herds; conflicts and contentions: a bone thrown to a company of hungry curs; a bait for greedy fishes; the painfulness, and continual burden-bearing of wretched ants, the running to and fro of terrified mice: little puppets drawn up and down with wires and nerves: these be the objects of the world among all these thou must stand steadfast, meekly affected, and free from all manner of indignation; with this right ratiocination and apprehension; that as the worth is of those things which a man doth affect, so is in very deed every man's worth more or less.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek:
Ἐγὼ τὸ ἐμαυτοῦ καθῆκον ποιῶ, τὰ ἄλλα με οὐ περισπᾷ· ἤτοι γὰρ ἄψυχα ἢ ἄλογα ἢ πεπλανημένα καὶ τὴν ὁδὸν ἀγνοοῦντα.

Τοῖς μὲν ἀλόγοις ζῴοις καὶ καθόλου πράγμασι καὶ ὑποκειμένοις, ὡς λόγον ἔχων λόγον μὴ ἔχουσι, χρῶ μεγαλοφρόνως καὶ ἐλευθέρως· τοῖς δὲ ἀνθρώποις, ὡς λόγον ἔχουσι, χρῶ κοινωνικῶς· ἐφ’ ἅπασι δὲ θεοὺς ἐπικαλοῦ. καὶ μὴ διαφέρου πρὸς τὸ πόσῳ χρόνῳ ταῦτα πράξεις· ἀρκοῦσι γὰρ καὶ τρεῖς ὧραι τοιαῦται.
passages.english:
I do my own duty; the other things do not distract me. For they are either without life, or without reason, or have gone astray and do not know the road.

Animals without reason, and in general things and objects, treat with a large mind and freely, as one who has reason treats what has none. Human beings, since they have reason, treat socially. And in everything call on the gods. And do not trouble yourself about how long you will be doing this: for even three hours of this kind are enough.

notes.note: A Stoic term: the act that is fitting for one, what falls to one to do.
notes.other_reading: I do what is fitting for me

notes.note: “Without λόγος”, without reason. The next chapter turns on having and not having reason, so “without reason” and “has reason” stand throughout.
notes.other_reading: or irrational

notes.note: Two near synonyms: things, and what lies to hand as material.
notes.other_reading: things and materials

notes.note: The verb is “use” or “deal with”; the same verb is used of people in the next clause, so “treat” stands for both. The first adverb is literally “with a great mind”, the second “as a free person does”.
notes.other_reading: use them generously and like a free person

notes.note: “Socially” follows this translation’s fixed word for κοινωνικός. It does not mean sociably: it means dealing with them as fellow members of a community.
notes.other_reading: treat as fellows in a community

notes.note: “In all things” or “on every occasion”; it could also be “over all of them”.
notes.other_reading: And on every occasion call on the gods

notes.note: Literally “do not make a difference to yourself about”: do not be anxious, do not let it matter.
notes.other_reading: And let it make no difference to you how long

notes.note: “Three hours of this kind”: hours spent so. The number is as the Greek has it.
notes.other_reading: even three such hours

check.note: “Treat socially” is not clear English and suggests sociability. The Greek is to deal with them as fellow members of a community.
check.decided: Declined: “Social” is the settled word of this translation for κοινωνικός, and “treat socially” keeps it so that the word can be followed from passage to passage. A note now says that dealing with them as fellow members of a community is meant, not sociability.

check.note: The Greek word is high-mindedly, with a large spirit. “Generously” suggests giving.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “treat with a large mind and freely”. The Greek word is “with a great mind”; “generously” suggests giving.

passages.casaubon: I for my part will do what belongs unto me; as for other things, whether things unsensible or things irrational; or if rational, yet deceived and ignorant of the true way, they shall not trouble or distract me. For as for those creatures which are not endued with reason and all other things and-matters of the world whatsoever I freely, and generously, as one endued with reason, of things that have none, make use of them. And as for men, towards them as naturally partakers of the same reason, my care is to carry myself sociably. But whatsoever it is that thou art about, remember to call upon the Gods. And as for the time how long thou shalt live to do these things, let it be altogether indifferent unto thee, for even three such hours are sufficient.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek: Ὅ τί ποτε τοῦτό εἰμι, σαρκία ἐστὶ καὶ πνευμάτιον καὶ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν. ἄφες τὰ βιβλία· μηκέτι σπῶ. οὐ δέδοται, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἤδη ἀποθνῄσκων τῶν μὲν σαρκίων καταφρόνησον· λύθρος καὶ ὀστάρια καὶ κροκύφαντος, ἐκ νεύρων, φλεβίων, ἀρτηριῶν πλεγμάτιον. θέασαι δὲ καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα ὁποῖόν τί ἐστιν· ἄνεμος, οὐδὲ ἀεὶ τὸ αὐτό, ἀλλὰ πάσης ὥρας ἐξεμούμενον καὶ πάλιν ῥοφούμενον. τρίτον οὖν ἐστι τὸ ἡγεμονικόν. ὧδε ἐπινοήθητι· γέρων εἶ· μηκέτι τοῦτο ἐάσῃς δουλεῦσαι, μηκέτι καθ’ ὁρμὴν ἀκοινώνητον νευροσπαστηθῆναι, μηκέτι τὸ εἱμαρμένον ἢ παρὸν δυσχερᾶναι ἢ μέλλον ὑπιδέσθαι.
passages.english: Whatever this is that I am, it is bits of flesh, a little breath, and the ruling part. Let the books go. Be pulled no longer. It is not allowed. Instead, as one already dying, despise the bits of flesh: gore, little bones, a web, a small plaiting of sinews, little veins and arteries. Look too at what kind of thing the breath is: wind, and not even always the same, but at every moment vomited out and gulped in again. Third, then, is the ruling part. Think of it this way: you are old. No longer let this be a slave, no longer let it be pulled about on strings by unsocial impulse, no longer let it be discontented with what is fated now or look with suspicion on what is fated to come.

notes.note: A diminutive of πνεῦμα, breath: for the Stoics the warm breath that keeps a body alive. The flesh is a diminutive too.
notes.other_reading: a puff of breath

notes.note: The verb is “pull”, “drag”; in this form “be pulled”, that is, distracted, or “pull yourself”. After the books it could also be “do not grasp at them”.
notes.other_reading: stop grasping at them

notes.note: “It has not been granted.” What is not granted is not said: the time for books, most likely.
notes.other_reading: That has not been given to you

notes.note: A woven net, such as a hairnet. The next phrase explains it as a small plaited thing made of sinews, veins and arteries.
notes.other_reading: a mesh

notes.note: νεῦρα are sinews or tendons, and also nerves; the two were not sharply told apart.
notes.other_reading: of nerves, veins and arteries

notes.note: Literally “every hour”, in the loose sense of at all times.
notes.other_reading: every hour

notes.note: “Unsocial” is the negative of this translation’s “social”: impulse that takes no account of the community. The verb after it is the one for working a puppet by its strings, as in 12.19 and 7.3.
notes.other_reading: by selfish impulse

notes.greek: τὸ εἱμαρμένον ἢ παρὸν δυσχερᾶναι ἢ μέλλον ὑπιδέσθαι
notes.note: “What is fated” is said once and goes with both halves, the present and the coming. The last verb is to look at something from under the brows, with mistrust or dread, the same verb as in 2.17.
notes.other_reading: no longer let it complain of its present lot or dread the one to come

check.note: Breath goes out and in at every moment. The Greek word here is not the clock hour.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “at every moment”. Breath goes out and in all the time, and the Greek phrase has that loose sense; the note gives the literal “every hour”.

check.note: The diminutive, “little veins”, is dropped, though the other belittling diminutives in the passage are kept.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “little veins”. The Greek word is a diminutive like the others in the passage.

check.note: The Greek form may mean “do not distract yourself” or, following the books, “stop grasping at them”. The English chooses the passive of distraction and adds “this way and that”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “Be pulled no longer.” “This way and that” is dropped as an addition; the passive of being pulled is kept as the plainest reading of the form, with nothing more supplied, and the note gives the others.

check.note: Found while settling: “on strings” and “like a puppet” both unpacked the one Greek verb, as in 12.19.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “pulled about on strings by unsocial impulse”, with “like a puppet” dropped, so that the verb reads the same here and in 12.19.

passages.casaubon: Whatsoever I am, is either flesh, or life, or that which we commonly call the mistress and overruling part of man; reason. Away with thy books, suffer not thy mind any more to be distracted, and carried to and fro; for it will not be; but as even now ready to die, think little of thy flesh: blood, bones, and a skin; a pretty piece of knit and twisted work, consisting of nerves, veins and arteries; think no more of it, than so. And as for thy life, consider what it is; a wind; not one constant wind neither, but every moment of an hour let out, and sucked in again. The third, is thy ruling part; and here consider; Thou art an old man; suffer not that excellent part to be brought in subjection, and to become slavish: suffer it not to be drawn up and down with unreasonable and unsociable lusts and motions, as it were with wires and nerves; suffer it not any more, either to repine at anything now present, or to fear and fly anything to come, which the destiny hath appointed thee.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek: δεῖ παραμυθούμενον ἑαυτὸν περιμένειν τὴν φυσικὴν λύσιν καὶ μὴ ἀσχάλλειν τῇ διατριβῇ, ἀλλὰ τούτοις μόνοις προσαναπαύεσθαι· ἑνὶ μὲν τῷ, ὅτι οὐδὲν συμβήσεταί μοι ὃ οὐχὶ κατὰ τὴν τῶν ὅλων φύσιν ἐστίν· ἑτέρῳ δέ, ὅτι ἔξεστί μοι μηδὲν πράσσειν παρὰ τὸν ἐμὸν θεὸν καὶ δαίμονα· οὐδεὶς γὰρ ὁ ἀναγκάσων τοῦτον παραβῆναι.
passages.english: One must comfort oneself and wait for the natural dissolution, and not chafe at the delay, but rest in these things alone. One: that nothing will happen to me that is not according to the nature of the whole. The other: that it is in my power to do nothing against my god and spirit, for there is no one who will force me to go against him.

notes.note: The Greek begins in mid-sentence and in the impersonal (“one must”), and moves to the first person further on. The words just before the cut, “for, on the contrary”, belong to this sentence and are not translated; the English starts a new sentence with a capital and adds nothing else.
notes.other_reading: one has to wait, encouraging oneself, for

notes.note: λύσις is a loosening or undoing: death as the coming apart of what a person is made of.
notes.other_reading: the release that nature brings

notes.note: διατριβή is the spending of time, and so a delay; it can also be simply one’s stay or way of passing the time.
notes.other_reading: and not be vexed at the time spent here

notes.note: δαίμων is the divine being allotted to each person, here set beside “god” as one and the same. “Spirit” stands for it, as in 2.17.
notes.other_reading: against the god and divinity that is within

notes.note: “To transgress against this one.” The Greek does not say who is forced; the first person is supplied from the sentence before.
notes.other_reading: there is no one who can compel anyone to disobey him

part.left_out: Τὰ μὲν πράγματα ἐν τοιαύτῃ τρόπον τινὰ ἐγκαλύψει ἐστίν, ὥστε φιλοσόφοις οὐκ ὀλίγοις οὐδὲ τοῖς τυχοῦσιν ἔδοξε παντάπασιν ἀκατάληπτα εἶναι, πλὴν αὐτοῖς γε τοῖς Στωικοῖς δυσκατάληπτα δοκεῖ· καὶ πᾶσα ἡ ἡμετέρα συγκατάθεσις μεταπτώτη· ποῦ γὰρ ὁ ἀμετάπτωτος; μέτιθι τοίνυν ἐπ’ αὐτὰ τὰ ὑποκείμενα ὡς ὀλιγοχρόνια καὶ εὐτελῆ καὶ δυνάμενα ἐν κτήσει κιναίδου ἢ πόρνης ἢ λῃστοῦ εἶναι. μετὰ τοῦτο ἔπιθι ἐπὶ τὰ τῶν συμβιούντων ἤθη, ὧν μόλις ἐστὶ καὶ τοῦ χαριεστάτου ἀνασχέσθαι, ἵνα μὴ λέγω, ὅτι καὶ ἑαυτόν τις μόγις ὑπομένει. ἐν τοιούτῳ οὖν ζόφῳ καὶ ῥύπῳ καὶ τοσαύτῃ ῥύσει τῆς τε οὐσίας καὶ τοῦ χρόνου καὶ τῆς κινήσεως καὶ τῶν κινουμένων τί ποτέ ἐστι τὸ ἐκτιμηθῆναι ἢ τὸ ὅλως σπουδασθῆναι δυνάμενον, οὐδ’ ἐπινοῶ. τοὐναντίον γὰρ
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the first part of the chapter, down to 'For indeed they are things contrary', at the end of its section 5.9 and begins its 5.10 here, at 'Thou must comfort thyself'.

passages.casaubon: Thou must comfort thyself in the expectation of thy natural dissolution, and in the meantime not grieve at the delay; but rest contented in those two things. First, that nothing shall happen unto thee, which is not according to the nature of the universe. Secondly, that it is in thy power, to do nothing against thine own proper God, and inward spirit. For it is not in any man's power to constrain thee to transgress against him.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek:
Βάλε ἔξω τὴν ὑπόληψιν· σέσωσαι. τίς οὖν ὁ κωλύων ἐκβάλλειν;

Ὅταν δυσφορῇς ἐπί τινι, ἐπελάθου τοῦ, ὅτι πάντα κατὰ τὴν τῶν ὅλων φύσιν γίνεται, καὶ τοῦ, ὅτι τὸ ἁμαρτανόμενον ἀλλότριον, καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις τοῦ, ὅτι πᾶν τὸ γινόμενον οὕτως ἀεὶ ἐγίνετο καὶ γενήσεται καὶ νῦν πανταχοῦ γίνεται· τοῦ, ὅση ἡ συγγένεια ἀνθρώπου πρὸς πᾶν τὸ ἀνθρώπειον γένος· οὐ γὰρ αἱματίου ἢ σπερματίου, ἀλλὰ νοῦ κοινωνία. ἐπελάθου δὲ καὶ τοῦ, ὅτι ὁ ἑκάστου νοῦς θεὸς καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἐρρύηκεν· τοῦ, ὅτι οὐδὲν ἴδιον οὐδενός, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ τεκνίον καὶ τὸ σωμάτιον καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ψυχάριον ἐκεῖθεν ἐλήλυθεν· τοῦ, ὅτι πάνθ’ ὑπόληψις· τοῦ, ὅτι τὸ παρὸν μόνον ἕκαστος ζῇ καὶ τοῦτο ἀποβάλλει.
passages.english:
Throw out the judgment: you are saved. Who then is stopping you from throwing it out?

Whenever you take something hard, you have forgotten that all things come about according to the nature of the whole; and that the wrong done is another’s; and, on top of these, that everything that comes about has always come about in this way, and will come about, and is coming about now everywhere; and how great is the kinship of a human being with the whole human race, for it is a sharing not of a little blood or a little seed but of mind. And you have forgotten too that each person’s mind is a god and has flowed from there; that nothing is anyone’s own, but even one’s little child and little body and the little soul itself have come from there; that everything is judgment; that each person lives only the present, and this is what they lose.

notes.note: A perfect: the saving is already done the moment the judgment is thrown out.
notes.other_reading: and you are safe

notes.note: A simple past, “you forgot”. English needs “you have forgotten”. The list that follows hangs on this verb, repeated once.
notes.other_reading: you forgot this: that

notes.note: ἀλλότριον is “belonging to another”, and so also “not your concern”. The English keeps the first, the literal sense, as in 12.1.
notes.other_reading: that the wrong done is not your affair

notes.note: Both words are belittling diminutives, like the child, body and soul further on. Each is kept as “little”.
notes.other_reading: not of a drop of blood or a bit of seed

notes.note: κοινωνία is having something in common, a partnership. It is the noun behind this translation’s “social”.
notes.other_reading: a community of mind

notes.note: θεός has no article, so “a god” or “god”. “From there” is left as vague as the Greek: from the divine source.
notes.other_reading: each person’s mind is god and has flowed from that source

notes.note: “Everything is judgment”: everything is as you judge it to be. The same word as in the first line of the passage.
notes.other_reading: that all is as you take it

notes.note: “And loses this.” “Only” stands with “lives” in the Greek and is not repeated with “loses”.
notes.other_reading: and it is only this that they lose

check.note: The Greek word is “another’s” and also “not your affair”. The English keeps only the first.
check.decided: Declined: “Another’s” is what the Greek word says first, and it is the same word as “another person’s” in 12.1. The further sense, “not your affair”, follows from it and is given in the note.

passages.casaubon: Cast away from thee opinion, and thou art safe. And what is it that hinders thee from casting of it away? When thou art grieved at anything, hast thou forgotten that all things happen according to the nature of the universe; and that him only it concerns, who is in fault; and moreover, that what is now done, is that which from ever hath been done in the world, and will ever be done, and is now done everywhere: how nearly all men are allied one to another by a kindred not of blood, nor of seed, but of the same mind. Thou hast also forgotten that every man's mind partakes of the Deity, and issueth from thence; and that no man can properly call anything his own, no not his son, nor his body, nor his life; for that they all proceed from that One who is the giver of all things: that all things are but opinion; that no man lives properly, but that very instant of time which is now present. And therefore that no man whensoever he dieth can properly be said to lose any more, than an instant of time.

nearest.title: Nothing happens that a human being cannot bear

passages.greek: Τί ἐπιζητεῖς; τὸ διαπνεῖσθαι; ἀλλὰ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι; τὸ ὁρμᾶν; τὸ αὔξεσθαι; τὸ λήγειν αὖθις; τὸ φωνῇ χρῆσθαι; τὸ διανοεῖσθαι; τί τούτων πόθου σοι ἄξιον δοκεῖ; εἰ δὲ ἕκαστα εὐκαταφρόνητα, πρόιθι ἐπὶ τελευταῖον τὸ ἕπεσθαι τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τῷ θεῷ. ἀλλὰ μάχεται τὸ τιμᾶν ταῦτα, τὸ ἄχθεσθαι εἰ διὰ τοῦ τεθνηκέναι στερήσεταί τις αὐτῶν.
passages.english: What are you looking for? To breathe? Or to have sensation? To have impulse? To grow? And then to stop? To use your voice? To think? Which of these seems to you worth longing for? But if each of them is easy to despise, go on to the last thing, following reason and god. But to value these things, to be vexed that by being dead a person will be deprived of them, conflicts with that.

notes.note: Literally “to be blown through”: breathing, or the passing of air through a body, the lowest function of life. From memory, unchecked, Marcus uses the word elsewhere of plants, and some editions print a different verb here, “to go on living”.
notes.other_reading: To go on breathing?

notes.note: “But” in a string of questions: “or, if not that, then”.
notes.other_reading: Well then, to have sensation?

notes.note: “To cease in turn”, set against “to grow”: to stop growing, or to decline. The Greek does not say what stops.
notes.other_reading: And then to stop growing?

notes.note: “To the last”: the one thing left when the others have been set aside.
notes.other_reading: go on to what remains at the end

notes.greek: ἀλλὰ μάχεται τὸ τιμᾶν ταῦτα, τὸ ἄχθεσθαι
notes.note: “But it fights”: the Greek does not say with what, and “with that”, meaning following reason and god, is supplied. “These things” are taken as the functions listed, and being vexed as what valuing them comes to. The words can also be read as two things set against each other, with “these” as reason and god, though for that the Greek would regularly put “being vexed” in another case.
notes.other_reading: But honoring these conflicts with being vexed that by being dead a person will be deprived of the others
