notes.note: “Through having died”, the state of being dead and not the act of dying.
notes.other_reading: to be vexed that death will take them from one

check.greek: ἀλλὰ μάχεται τὸ τιμᾶν ταῦτα, τὸ ἄχθεσθαι
check.note: The Greek gives no object for “conflicts”, and “with this” is supplied. It can also be read with two terms set against each other: honoring these, reason and god, conflicts with being vexed at losing the others.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “But to value these things, to be vexed that by being dead a person will be deprived of them, conflicts with that.” “These things” now stands for the Greek “these”, and the note says that “with that” is supplied. The other reading is given in the note and not taken, because “being vexed” is not in the case the Greek uses for the thing fought against.

check.note: The Greek word is “in turn”, “afterwards”: to grow, and then to stop growing. “To stop again” suggests stopping a second time.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “And then to stop?”. The Greek word means “in turn”, not “a second time”; “growing” is not supplied, since the Greek does not say what stops, and the note gives it.

check.note: The verb as given is “to breathe”; “go on” is added. Some editions print a different verb here, one meaning “to go on living”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “To breathe?”. “Go on” is not in the Greek as given.

passages.casaubon: What doest thou desire? To live long. What? To enjoy the operations of a sensitive soul; or of the appetitive faculty? or wouldst thou grow, and then decrease again? Wouldst thou long be able to talk, to think and reason with thyself? Which of all these seems unto thee a worthy object of thy desire? Now if of all these thou doest find that they be but little worth in themselves, proceed on unto the last, which is, in all things to follow God and reason. But for a man to grieve that by death he shall be deprived of any of these things, is both against God and reason.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek:
Μὴ σικχαίνειν μηδὲ ἀπαυδᾶν μηδὲ ἀποδυσπετεῖν, εἰ μὴ καταπυκνοῦταί σοι τὸ ἀπὸ δογμάτων ὀρθῶν ἕκαστα πράσσειν, ἀλλὰ ἐκκρουσθέντα πάλιν ἐπανιέναι καὶ ἀσμενίζειν, εἰ τὰ πλείω ἀνθρωπικώτερα, καὶ φιλεῖν τοῦτο, ἐφ̓ ὃ ἐπανέρχῃ, καὶ μὴ ὡς πρὸς παιδαγωγὸν τὴν φιλοσοφίαν ἐπανιέναι, ἀλλ’ ὡς οἱ ὀφθαλμιῶντες πρὸς τὸ σπογγάριον καὶ τὸ ᾠόν, ὡς ἄλλος πρὸς κατάπλασμα, ὡς πρὸς καταιόνησιν. οὕτως γὰρ οὐδὲν ἐπιδείξῃ τὸ πειθαρχεῖν τῷ λόγῳ, ἀλλὰ προσαναπαύσῃ αὐτῷ. μέμνησο δὲ ὅτι φιλοσοφία μόνα θέλει ἃ ἡ φύσις σου θέλει· σὺ δὲ ἄλλο ἤθελες οὐ κατὰ φύσιν. τί γὰρ τούτων προσηνέστερον; ἡ γὰρ ἡδονὴ οὐχὶ διὰ τοῦτο σφάλλει; ἀλλὰ θέασαι, εἰ προσηνέστερον μεγαλοψυχία, ἐλευθερία, ἁπλότης, εὐγνωμοσύνη, ὁσιότης, αὐτῆς γὰρ φρονήσεως τί προσηνέστερον, ὅταν τὸ ἄπταιστον καὶ εὔρουν ἐν πᾶσι τῆς παρακολουθητικῆς καὶ ἐπιστημονικῆς δυνάμεως ἐνθυμηθῇς;

Τὰ μὲν πράγματα ἐν τοιαύτῃ τρόπον τινὰ ἐγκαλύψει ἐστίν, ὥστε φιλοσόφοις οὐκ ὀλίγοις οὐδὲ τοῖς τυχοῦσιν ἔδοξε παντάπασιν ἀκατάληπτα εἶναι, πλὴν αὐτοῖς γε τοῖς Στωικοῖς δυσκατάληπτα δοκεῖ· καὶ πᾶσα ἡ ἡμετέρα συγκατάθεσις μεταπτώτη· ποῦ γὰρ ὁ ἀμετάπτωτος; μέτιθι τοίνυν ἐπ’ αὐτὰ τὰ ὑποκείμενα ὡς ὀλιγοχρόνια καὶ εὐτελῆ καὶ δυνάμενα ἐν κτήσει κιναίδου ἢ πόρνης ἢ λῃστοῦ εἶναι. μετὰ τοῦτο ἔπιθι ἐπὶ τὰ τῶν συμβιούντων ἤθη, ὧν μόλις ἐστὶ καὶ τοῦ χαριεστάτου ἀνασχέσθαι, ἵνα μὴ λέγω, ὅτι καὶ ἑαυτόν τις μόγις ὑπομένει. ἐν τοιούτῳ οὖν ζόφῳ καὶ ῥύπῳ καὶ τοσαύτῃ ῥύσει τῆς τε οὐσίας καὶ τοῦ χρόνου καὶ τῆς κινήσεως καὶ τῶν κινουμένων τί ποτέ ἐστι τὸ ἐκτιμηθῆναι ἢ τὸ ὅλως σπουδασθῆναι δυνάμενον, οὐδ’ ἐπινοῶ. τοὐναντίον γὰρ
passages.english:
Do not be disgusted, do not give up, do not lose patience, if doing each thing from right principles does not come to you time after time; but when you have been knocked aside, come back again, and be glad if most of what you do is more in keeping with a human being, and love what you are coming back to. And do not come back to philosophy as to a schoolboy’s minder, but as people with sore eyes go to the little sponge and the egg, as another goes to a poultice, as to a medicinal wash. For in this way you will make no show of obeying reason, but will find rest in it. Remember that philosophy wants only what your nature wants; but you were wanting something else, not in accord with nature. For what is more agreeable than these things? For is it not through this that pleasure trips us up? But look whether greatness of soul, freedom, simplicity, fairness of mind, reverence are more agreeable. For what is more agreeable than wisdom itself, when you think of how the power of understanding and knowledge never stumbles and flows smoothly in everything?

Things are, in a way, so veiled that to not a few philosophers, and not ordinary ones, they have seemed altogether impossible to grasp; except that to the Stoics themselves, at least, they seem hard to grasp. And every assent of ours can shift: for where is the person who does not shift? Pass on, then, to the objects themselves: how short-lived they are, how cheap, how they can be in the possession of a catamite, a prostitute or a robber. After that go on to the characters of the people you live with: one can hardly put up with even the most charming of them, not to say that a person can hardly bear even themselves. In such gloom and filth, then, and in so great a flow of substance and of time, of movement and of the things moved, what there is that can be highly valued, or pursued in earnest at all, I cannot even imagine. For on the contrary …

notes.note: Literally “is packed thick”; the verb is rare. The English takes it of right action coming close together, “time after time”. It can also be read as “is fully achieved”.
notes.other_reading: if you do not fully succeed in doing each thing from right principles

notes.note: The Greek has no verb and no noun here: “if the greater part more human”. “Of what you do” is supplied. The comparative has nothing to be compared with, and can mean “more as a human being should be” or, modestly, “human enough”.
notes.other_reading: if most of it is human enough

notes.note: The paidagogos was the slave who walked a boy to school and kept him in order, not a teacher. The English reads “a schoolboy’s minder”.
notes.other_reading: as to a schoolmaster

notes.note: Remedies for sore eyes: a small sponge for bathing them, and egg, probably the white, laid on them. The second detail is from memory, unchecked.
notes.other_reading: the eye-sponge and the egg-white

notes.note: A medical word for pouring liquid over a sore part. The English reads “a medicinal wash”; the Greek does not say whether the liquid is warm.
notes.other_reading: a fomentation

notes.greek: οὐδὲν ἐπιδείξῃ τὸ πειθαρχεῖν τῷ λόγῳ, ἀλλὰ προσαναπαύσῃ αὐτῷ
notes.note: Both verbs are read as second-person futures: “you will make no show, you will rest”. “It” can be reason or the obeying; in the English it follows “reason”.
notes.other_reading: you will not be showing off your obedience to reason; you will be resting on that obedience

notes.note: “These” is open: the things that nature and philosophy want, or the thing wanted against nature, which makes the question an objection that the remark about pleasure answers. The English keeps “these things” and marks no change of voice. The word for “agreeable” also means gentle or soothing, which suits the remedies just named.
notes.other_reading: “But what is more pleasant than those things?”, said by the self that wanted them

notes.note: The verb (trip, make fall, mislead) has no object in the Greek; “us” is supplied. The image comes back below in “never stumbles”, which is a different Greek word.
notes.other_reading: Is it not through this that pleasure deceives?

notes.note: The word covers good sense, fairness, kindness and readiness to make allowances. The English reads “fairness of mind”.
notes.other_reading: kindness

notes.note: Phronesis, one of the four chief virtues: practical wisdom, good sense in action. The English reads “wisdom”, the word also used for it in 5.12.
notes.other_reading: good sense

notes.note: Literally “the power that follows along and knows”: the faculty of following things with understanding and of sure knowledge. Whether one power or two is meant is not marked.
notes.other_reading: the faculty of attention and of knowledge

notes.note: The first word can be “except that” (the Stoics, unlike those others, say “hard to grasp” and not “impossible”) or “and yet even”. The English takes the first. Marcus names the Stoics in the third person.
notes.other_reading: and even to the Stoics themselves they seem hard to grasp

notes.note: Assent (συγκατάθεσις) is the Stoic term for the mind’s agreeing to an impression. μεταπτώτη and ἀμετάπτωτος are one word and its negative, “liable to shift” and “not shifting”; “shift” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: all human assent is fallible; for where is the infallible man?

notes.note: Literally “the underlying things”: the objects one deals with, the things themselves as against a grasp of them. The word after it can be “how” or “as being”; the English reads “how”.
notes.other_reading: Turn then to the things themselves, as short-lived and cheap

notes.note: A term of contempt for a man who lets himself be used sexually by other men; it is also thrown loosely at any lewd man. “Catamite” is the nearest single English word.
notes.other_reading: a lewd man

notes.greek: ὧν μόλις ἐστὶ καὶ τοῦ χαριεστάτου ἀνασχέσθαι
notes.note: “Of them” can be the people or their characters: the Greek relative fits either, and “the most charming” can be masculine or neuter. The English leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: even the most agreeable of these characters can hardly be put up with

notes.note: The section cut falls in the middle of a sentence, so the Greek breaks off here. The two words are translated and the break is marked with three dots, which are not in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: For the opposite

check.note: The Greek has one verb, “is packed thick”. The English gives it twice, as “time after time” and “without a gap”, and “without a gap” sets a stricter standard than the Greek states.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “does not come to you time after time”. “Without a gap” is dropped, since the verb speaks of things packed close and not of an unbroken run; “time after time” is kept as the plain way to say that.

check.note: The “but” that sets coming back against the three “do nots” is lost in a sentence break, and “off course” is an image the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the sentence now runs on with “but when you have been knocked aside, come back again”. The “but” is restored and “off course” is gone; “aside” stands for the prefix of the verb, which means knocked out or away.

check.note: The Greek says only “if the greater part is more human”. “Worthy of” adds praise, the comparative can be read modestly as “human enough”, and “of what you do” is supplied.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “if most of what you do is more in keeping with a human being”, which drops the praise in “worthy”. “More human” alone was not used because in today’s English it suggests weakness, and “of what you do” stays because the sentence is about acting; the note gives the modest reading.

check.note: “A schoolboy’s minder” is an odd phrase; the point is the slave who walks a boy to school and keeps him in line, someone gone back to unwillingly.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek has the one noun, the slave who minded a boy, and “a schoolboy’s minder” says that. The suggestions add a rod, or a boy going back, which the Greek does not have; the note explains the figure.

check.note: The word means a pouring-on or bathing of a sore part. “Warm” is not in the Greek.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “warm” is dropped and the English now reads “a medicinal wash”. The word is a doctor’s term, so “medicinal” says what kind of wash it is without adding heat or soothing.

check.note: The Greek gives no sign of who is speaking. The question can be an objection, answered by the next question about pleasure, and the turn could be marked.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek has no mark of a change of voice, and its plural “these” fits the things nature wants as well as the single “something else” that was wanted against nature. The English stays as open as the Greek, and the note sets out both readings.

check.note: “Wrapped up” can be read as “finished” or “absorbed”. The Greek is “in such a veiling”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Things are, in a way, so veiled”.

check.greek: πλὴν αὐτοῖς γε τοῖς Στωικοῖς δυσκατάληπτα δοκεῖ
check.note: The words can be a climax, “and even to the Stoics themselves they seem hard to grasp”, where the English makes the Stoics a partial exception.
check.decided: Declined: the first word means “except” or “only”, and the small word after “themselves” most often limits, “at least”, so “except that to the Stoics themselves, at least” follows the words as they stand. Either way the Stoics say “hard” where the others say “impossible”; the note gives the climax reading.

check.note: The word is specific and contemptuous: a man who lets himself be used sexually. “A lewd man” is vaguer and milder.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a catamite”, and the note says what the word means.

check.note: “Scarcely possible” is weakened to “hard”, and the twin word in the next clause is “can hardly”, so the pair no longer matches.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “one can hardly put up with even the most charming of them”, so that “hardly” answers “hardly” as the two Greek words answer each other.

check.greek: ὧν μόλις ἐστὶ καὶ τοῦ χαριεστάτου ἀνασχέσθαι
check.note: The relative most naturally picks up “characters”, so it is the most agreeable character that can barely be endured; “of them” will be read as “of the people”.
check.decided: Declined: “the most charming” can be masculine or neuter in the Greek, and the clause that follows speaks of a person bearing themselves, which suits people at least as well as characters. “Of them” can be heard either way, as the Greek can; a note now records the point.

check.greek: τί ποτέ ἐστι τὸ ἐκτιμηθῆναι ἢ τὸ ὅλως σπουδασθῆναι δυνάμενον
check.note: The “can” belongs with the two verbs: “what there is that can be highly valued or seriously pursued at all”. “Is to be” turns ability into obligation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what there is that can be highly valued, or pursued in earnest at all”.

check.note: “I cannot even think” reads as unfinished English. The verb is “conceive, imagine”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “I cannot even imagine”.

check.note: Found while settling: the word is “flowing well”, an image of a stream, and “runs smoothly” blurred it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “flows smoothly”.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek is “the one who does not shift”, with no “never”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “where is the person who does not shift?”.

check.note: Found while settling: the “and” that joins this instruction to the ones before it was lost in a sentence break.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now begins “And do not come back to philosophy”.

part.left_out: δεῖ παραμυθούμενον ἑαυτὸν περιμένειν τὴν φυσικὴν λύσιν καὶ μὴ ἀσχάλλειν τῇ διατριβῇ, ἀλλὰ τούτοις μόνοις προσαναπαύεσθαι· ἑνὶ μὲν τῷ, ὅτι οὐδὲν συμβήσεταί μοι ὃ οὐχὶ κατὰ τὴν τῶν ὅλων φύσιν ἐστίν· ἑτέρῳ δέ, ὅτι ἔξεστί μοι μηδὲν πράσσειν παρὰ τὸν ἐμὸν θεὸν καὶ δαίμονα· οὐδεὶς γὰρ ὁ ἀναγκάσων τοῦτον παραβῆναι.
part.why: The 1634 translation runs its section 5.9 on through most of chapter 5.10, down to 'For indeed they are things contrary', and begins its 5.10 here, at 'Thou must comfort thyself'.

passages.casaubon: Be not discontented, be not disheartened, be not out of hope, if often it succeed not so well with thee punctually and precisely to do all things according to the right dogmata, but being once cast off, return unto them again: and as for those many and more frequent occurrences, either of worldly distractions, or human infirmities, which as a man thou canst not but in some measure be subject unto, be not thou discontented with them; but however, love and affect that only which thou dust return unto: a philosopher's life, and proper occupation after the most exact manner. And when thou dust return to thy philosophy, return not unto it as the manner of some is, after play and liberty as it were, to their schoolmasters and pedagogues; but as they that have sore eyes to their sponge and egg: or as another to his cataplasm; or as others to their fomentations: so shalt not thou make it a matter of ostentation at all to obey reason but of ease and comfort. And remember that philosophy requireth nothing of thee, but what thy nature requireth, and wouldest thou thyself desire anything that is not according to nature? for which of these sayest thou; that which is according to nature or against it, is of itself more kind and pleasing? Is it not for that respect especially, that pleasure itself is to so many men's hurt and overthrow, most prevalent, because esteemed commonly most kind, and natural? But consider well whether magnanimity rather, and true liberty, and true simplicity, and equanimity, and holiness; whether these be not most kind and natural? And prudency itself, what more kind and amiable than it, when thou shalt truly consider with thyself, what it is through all the proper objects of thy rational intellectual faculty currently to go on without any fall or stumble? As for the things of the world, their true nature is in a manner so involved with obscurity, that unto many philosophers, and those no mean ones, they seemed altogether incomprehensible, and the Stoics themselves, though they judge them not altogether incomprehensible, yet scarce and not without much difficulty, comprehensible, so that all assent of ours is fallible, for who is he that is infallible in his conclusions? From the nature of things, pass now unto their subjects and matter: how temporary, how vile are they I such as may be in the power and possession of some abominable loose liver, of some common strumpet, of some notorious oppressor and extortioner. Pass from thence to the dispositions of them that thou doest ordinarily converse with, how hardly do we bear, even with the most loving and amiable! that I may not say, how hard it is for us to bear even with our own selves, in such obscurity, and impurity of things: in such and so continual a flux both of the substances and time; both of the motions themselves, and things moved; what it is that we can fasten upon; either to honour, and respect especially; or seriously, and studiously to seek after; I cannot so much as conceive For indeed they are things contrary.

passages.greek: Καὶ τοῦτο πρὸς τὸ ἀκενόδοξον φέρει, ὅτι οὐκέτι δύνασαι τὸν βίον ὅλον ἢ τόν γε ἀπὸ νεότητος φιλόσοφον βεβιωκέναι, ἀλλὰ πολλοῖς τε ἄλλοις καὶ αὐτὸς σεαυτῷ δῆλος γέγονας πόρρω φιλοσοφίας ὤν. πέφυρσαι οὖν, ὥστε τὴν μὲν δόξαν τὴν τοῦ φιλοσόφου κτήσασθαι οὐκέτι σοι ῥᾴδιον· ἀνταγωνίζεται δὲ καὶ ἡ ὑπόθεσις. εἴπερ οὖν ἀληθῶς ἑώρακας ποῦ κεῖται τὸ πρᾶγμα, τὸ μὲν τί δόξεις ἄφες, ἀρκέσθητι δέ, εἰ κἂν τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ βίου ὅσον δήποτε, ὡς ἡ σὴ φύσις θέλει, βιώσῃ. κατανόησον οὖν τί θέλει, καὶ ἄλλο μηδέν σε περισπάτω· πεπείρασαι γὰρ περὶ πόσα πλανηθεὶς οὐδαμοῦ εὗρες τὸ εὖ ζῆν, οὐκ ἐν συλλογισμοῖς, οὐκ ἐν πλούτῳ, οὐκ ἐν δόξῃ, οὐκ ἐν ἀπολαύσει, οὐδαμοῦ. ποῦ οὖν ἐστιν; ἐν τῷ ποιεῖν ἃ ἐπιζητεῖ ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσις. πῶς οὖν ταῦτα ποιήσεις; ἐὰν δόγματα ἔχῃς ἀφ’ ὧν αἱ ὁρμαὶ καὶ αἱ πράξεις. τίνα δόγματα; περὶ ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν, ὡς οὐδενὸς μὲν ἀγαθοῦ ὄντος ἀνθρώπῳ ὃ οὐχὶ ποιεῖ δίκαιον, σώφρονα, ἀνδρεῖον, ἐλεύθερον, οὐδενὸς δὲ κακοῦ ὃ οὐχὶ ποιεῖ τἀναντία τοῖς εἰρημένοις.
passages.english: This too helps you not to care for empty reputation: that you can no longer have lived your whole life, or at least your life since youth, as a philosopher, but to many others, and to you yourself, it has become plain that you are far from philosophy. So you are muddied, so that winning the reputation of a philosopher is no longer easy for you; and your situation fights against it too. If, then, you have truly seen where the matter lies, let go of what reputation you will have, and be content if you live at least the rest of your life, however much it may be, as your nature wants. So understand what it wants, and let nothing else pull you away. For you have learned by trial how many things you wandered among and nowhere found the good life: not in syllogisms, not in wealth, not in reputation, not in enjoyment, nowhere. Where is it, then? In doing what human nature asks for. How, then, will you do these things? If you have principles from which your impulses and actions come. What principles? Those about good things and bad: that nothing is a good thing for a human being which does not make them just, self-controlled, brave, free, and nothing is a bad thing which does not make them the opposite of these.

notes.note: The word is built on δόξα, which runs through the passage as “reputation” (δόξαν, ἐν δόξῃ, and the verb in τί δόξεις). Literally “leads towards being without empty reputation”. The English reads “helps you not to care for empty reputation”; “you” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: This too tends to free you from vanity

notes.note: φιλόσοφον goes with “life” (a philosophic life), not with “you”. The English reads “as a philosopher”.
notes.other_reading: to have lived your whole life as a philosophic one

notes.note: Perfect passive of a verb meaning to mix, knead, soil or jumble. It can mean “you are stained” or “you are in confusion”; “muddied” is meant to keep both.
notes.other_reading: So you are in a muddle

notes.note: ὑπόθεσις is what a life is founded on: one’s position, role or plan of life. Presumably that of emperor is meant, which the Greek does not say. The English reads “your situation”, the word used in 11.7; the verb is that of an opponent in a contest.
notes.other_reading: and the basis of your life works against it too

notes.note: Literally “let go the ‘what will you seem’”. The verb is from the same root as “reputation”, so the English reads “what reputation you will have”.
notes.other_reading: give up the question of how you will seem

notes.greek: εἰ κἂν τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ βίου ὅσον δήποτε
notes.note: κἄν here is “at least, if only”. ὅσον δήποτε is “however much it turns out to be”.
notes.other_reading: if you live even what is left of your life, be it long or short

notes.note: Formal logical arguments. “Syllogisms” is kept because it names the thing.
notes.other_reading: in logical arguments

notes.greek: ὃ οὐχὶ ποιεῖ δίκαιον, σώφρονα, ἀνδρεῖον, ἐλεύθερον
notes.note: The adjectives are singular, “makes [a person] just”; the English has “them” for the person. “A good thing” stands for the Greek noun, “a good” (ἀγαθοῦ ὄντος ἀνθρώπῳ); it is not the glossary’s “is good for” (συμφέρει).
notes.other_reading: that there is no good for man except what makes him just, temperate, brave and free

check.greek: ἀλλὰ πολλοῖς τε ἄλλοις καὶ αὐτὸς σεαυτῷ δῆλος γέγονας
check.note: The “but” is dropped by starting a new sentence: you can no longer have lived as a philosopher, but on the contrary it is plain that you are far from it.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now runs on, “as a philosopher, but to many others, and to you yourself, it has become plain that you are far from philosophy”.

check.note: The verb means “mixed up, jumbled” and also “soiled”. “Muddied” picks the stain; the other reading is “you are in a muddle”.
check.decided: Declined: “muddied” is kept because it can be heard both ways, as dirtied and as stirred up and unclear, and the Greek verb has both senses. The note gives “in a muddle”.

check.note: “In life” is added; the word alone is what is laid down as a basis, one’s station or role. The suggestion is “your position”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “in life” is dropped and the English now reads “your situation fights against it too”. “Situation” is kept so that the word matches 11.7, and “fights” keeps the Greek verb’s picture of an opponent in a contest.

check.note: This verb belongs with the noun for “reputation” used just before and again in the list. “How you will seem” loosens the link.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “let go of what reputation you will have”, so that the word “reputation” runs through the passage as its Greek root does.

check.greek: εἰ κἂν τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ βίου
check.note: The particle means “at least, if only”. “Even the rest” suggests that the rest is the surprising or large part.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “be content if you live at least the rest of your life”.

check.note: The Greek repeats “then” in its questions (where then, how then) and has “these things”; the English varies to “And how will you do that?”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “How, then, will you do these things?”.

check.note: Found while settling: “nothing is good for a human being” uses the phrase the glossary keeps for another Greek verb, “is good for”, where the Greek here has the noun, “a good”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “nothing is a good thing for a human being” and “nothing is a bad thing”.

passages.casaubon: This also, among other things, may serve to keep thee from vainglory; if thou shalt consider, that thou art now altogether incapable of the commendation of one, who all his life long, or from his youth at least, hath lived a philosopher's life. For both unto others, and to thyself especially, it is well known, that thou hast done many things contrary to that perfection of life. Thou hast therefore been confounded in thy course, and henceforth it will be hard for thee to recover the title and credit of a philosopher. And to it also is thy calling and profession repugnant. If therefore thou dost truly understand, what it is that is of moment indeed; as for thy fame and credit, take no thought or care for that: let it suffice thee if all the rest of thy life, be it more or less, thou shalt live as thy nature requireth, or according to the true and natural end of thy making. Take pains therefore to know what it is that thy nature requireth, and let nothing else distract thee. Thou hast already had sufficient experience, that of those many things that hitherto thou hast erred and wandered about, thou couldst not find happiness in any of them. Not in syllogisms, and logical subtilties, not in wealth, not in honour and reputation, not in pleasure. In none of all these. Wherein then is it to be found? In the practice of those things, which the nature of man, as he is a man, doth require. How then shall he do those things? if his dogmata, or moral tenets and opinions (from which all motions and actions do proceed), be right and true. Which be those dogmata? Those that concern that which is good or evil, as that there is nothing truly good and beneficial unto man, but that which makes him just, temperate, courageous, liberal; and that there is nothing truly evil and hurtful unto man, but that which causeth the contrary effects.

passages.greek: Μῖμος, πόλεμος, πτοία, νάρκα, δουλεία· καθ’ ἡμέραν ἀπαλείψεταί σου τὰ ἱερὰ ἐκεῖνα δόγματα, ὁπόσα ἀφυσιολογήτως φαντάζῃ καὶ παραπέμπεις. δεῖ δὲ πᾶν οὕτω βλέπειν καὶ πράσσειν ὥστε καὶ τὸ πρακτικὸν ἅμα συντελεῖσθαι καὶ ἅμα τὸ θεωρητικὸν ἐνεργεῖσθαι καὶ τὸ ἐκ τῆς περὶ ἑκάστων ἐπιστήμης αὔθαδες σῴζεσθαι λανθάνον, οὐχὶ κρυπτόμενον. πότε γὰρ ἁπλότητος ἀπολαύσεις; πότε δὲ σεμνότητος; πότε δὲ τῆς ἐφ’ ἑκάστου γνωρίσεως, τί τε ἐστὶ κατ’ οὐσίαν καὶ τίνα χώραν ἔχει ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ καὶ ἐπὶ πόσον πέφυκεν ὑφίστασθαι καὶ ἐκ τίνων συγκέκριται καὶ τίσι δύναται ὑπάρχειν καὶ τίνες δύνανται αὐτὸ διδόναι τε καὶ ἀφαιρεῖσθαι;
passages.english: Farce, war, panic, numbness, slavery: day by day those sacred principles of yours will be wiped out, all those that you picture without study of nature and let go by. But everything must be looked at and done in such a way that at one and the same time the practical side is carried out and the contemplative side is at work, and that the self-assurance which comes from knowledge of each thing is kept, unnoticed but not hidden. For when will you enjoy simplicity? When dignity? When the recognition, in each case, of what the thing is in its substance, what place it has in the universe, how long it is in its nature to last, what it is put together from, who can have it, and who can give it and take it away?

notes.note: Five bare nouns with no verb. μῖμος is the mime, a low stage farce; πτοία is fright or flutter; νάρκα is numbness. How the list connects with what follows is left to the reader, as in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: A stage farce, a war, a fright, a stupor, a slavery

notes.note: Future middle, read here as passive, “will be wiped out”, with the principles as subject.
notes.other_reading: day by day it will wipe out those sacred principles of yours

notes.note: The text here is doubted, and ἀφυσιολογήτως may be an editor’s correction (from memory, unchecked). As given: “all those you picture without study of nature and send on their way”, with the relative attached to “principles”. It can also be taken loosely, of everything pictured in that way, and παραπέμπεις can mean let pass, dismiss or neglect.
notes.other_reading: wiped out, whenever you form impressions without study of nature and let them pass

notes.greek: τὸ πρακτικὸν ἅμα συντελεῖσθαι καὶ ἅμα τὸ θεωρητικὸν ἐνεργεῖσθαι
notes.note: Literally “the practical” and “the contemplative”: either the two sides of a task or the two powers of the person. The English reads “side”. The Greek says “at once” twice, which “at one and the same time” carries.
notes.other_reading: that the power to act is brought to completion and the power to contemplate is exercised at the same time

notes.note: Usually a bad word, “self-willed, stubborn”. Here it is good: the self-assurance that knowledge gives.
notes.other_reading: the confidence

notes.note: “Escaping notice, not being hidden”: not put on show, but not concealed either.
notes.other_reading: unobtrusive, yet not concealed

notes.note: γνώρισις is getting to know a thing, recognising it in the single case. It is a different word from ἐπιστήμη, “knowledge”, just above.
notes.other_reading: the knowledge of each thing

notes.note: οὐσία is both “being, essence” and the Stoic “substance”, the stuff of things. The English reads “in its substance”, as in 3.11.
notes.other_reading: in its essence

notes.note: The dative can be “to whom it can belong” or “to what things it can belong”. It is taken of persons, because “who can give it” comes next.
notes.other_reading: what it can belong to

check.note: From memory: this clause is a known difficulty and editors have altered it in different ways. As given it construes and the English follows it word for word, but the sense is strained.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, as suggested, since the Greek as given construes, and the note says that the wording rests on a doubted text (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: The relative can pick up “principles”, or stand loosely for all the things one forms impressions of, so that the principles are wiped out by them. The last verb can also be “dismiss”.
check.decided: Declined: the relative is a neuter plural with nothing to attach to in the Greek as given except “principles”, so the English keeps “all those that you picture”. The note now gives the looser reading and “dismiss”.

check.note: The “but” that turns from the danger to the remedy is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But everything must be looked at and done”. The new wording also keeps the Greek impersonal, “it is necessary”, where the draft had “you must”.

check.note: The Greek says “at once” twice; one is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “at one and the same time the practical side is carried out and the contemplative side is at work”.

check.note: The word is usually a fault, self-will or stubborn self-assurance. It is meant well here, but “confidence” is milder than the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the self-assurance which comes from knowledge of each thing”.

check.note: Two different Greek words, systematic “knowledge” above and “recognition” here, are both “the knowledge of each thing”, so the English seems to repeat itself where the Greek moves on.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the recognition, in each case, of what the thing is”, and “knowledge” is left to the earlier word alone.

check.note: “How long it is by nature to last” is awkward English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “how long it is in its nature to last”. “Made to last” would bring in a maker and lose the Greek verb, which speaks of a thing’s nature.

passages.casaubon: Toys and fooleries at home, wars abroad: sometimes terror, sometimes torpor, or stupid sloth: this is thy daily slavery. By little and little, if thou doest not better look to it, those sacred dogmata will be blotted out of thy mind. How many things be there, which when as a mere naturalist, thou hast barely considered of according to their nature, thou doest let pass without any further use? Whereas thou shouldst in all things so join action and contemplation, that thou mightest both at the same time attend all present occasions, to perform everything duly and carefully and yet so intend the contemplative part too, that no part of that delight and pleasure, which the contemplative knowledge of everything according to its true nature doth of itself afford, might be lost. Or, that the true and contemnplative knowledge of everything according to its own nature, might of itself, (action being subject to many lets and impediments) afford unto thee sufficient pleasure and happiness. Not apparent indeed, but not concealed. And when shalt thou attain to the happiness of true simplicity, and unaffected gravity? When shalt thou rejoice in the certain knowledge of every particular object according to its true nature: as what the matter and substance of it is; what use it is for in the world: how long it can subsist: what things it doth consist of: who they be that are capable of it, and who they that can give it, and take it away?

passages.greek:
Ὁποῖον δεῖ καταληφθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ θανάτου καὶ σώματι καὶ ψυχῇ· τὴν βραχύτητα τοῦ βίου· τὴν ἀχάνειαν τοῦ ὀπίσω καὶ πρόσω αἰῶνος· τὴν ἀσθένειαν πάσης ὕλης.

Γυμνὰ τῶν φλοιῶν θεάσασθαι τὰ αἰτιώδη· τὰς ἀναφορὰς τῶν πράξεων· τί πόνος· τί ἡδονή· τί θάνατος· τί δόξα· τίς ὁ ἑαυτῷ ἀσχολίας αἴτιος· πῶς οὐδεὶς ὑπ’ ἄλλου ἐμποδίζεται· ὅτι πάντα ὑπόληψις.

Ὅμοιον δ’ εἶναι δεῖ ἐν τῇ τῶν δογμάτων χρήσει παγκρατιαστῇ, οὐχὶ μονομάχῳ· ὁ μὲν γὰρ τὸ ξίφος ᾧ χρῆται ἀποτίθεται καὶ ἀναιρεῖται· ὁ δὲ τὴν χεῖρα ἀεὶ ἔχει καὶ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ συστρέψαι αὐτὴν δεῖ.
passages.english:
What a person ought to be like, in body and in soul, when death catches them. The shortness of life. The gaping expanse of time behind and ahead. The weakness of all matter.

To look at what is causal, bare of its husks. The aims of actions. What pain is. What pleasure is. What death is. What reputation is. Who is the cause of a person’s own busyness. How no one is hindered by another. That everything is judgment.

And in the use of principles one must be like the all-in fighter, not the gladiator. For the gladiator puts down the sword he uses and picks it up; but the other always has his hand, and needs only to clench it.

notes.greek: Ὁποῖον δεῖ καταληφθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ θανάτου
notes.note: The chapter is a list of headings with no main verb; the accusatives that follow depend on an unstated “think of”, and they are left as bare headings. Ὁποῖον is masculine, “what kind of man”, with no man singled out, so the English has “a person” and “them”.
notes.other_reading: In what state of body and soul death ought to find one

notes.note: A yawning gulf, an immensity. αἰών, which follows, is unbounded time.
notes.other_reading: the abyss of eternity behind and before

notes.note: φλοιός is bark, rind or husk.
notes.other_reading: stripped of their bark

notes.note: “The causal things”: the cause or active principle in each thing, as against its matter, which closes the paragraph before. The infinitive θεάσασθαι has no verb governing it.
notes.other_reading: the causes of things, seen bare of their coverings

notes.note: ἀναφορά is the “carrying back” of an act to its end: what the act is done with reference to. The English reads “aims”. The same root is in 3.13 (συναναφορᾶς), where it is “referring”.
notes.other_reading: what actions are referred to

notes.note: πόνος is toil, hardship or pain; set beside pleasure, it is taken as pain.
notes.other_reading: what toil is

notes.note: Literally “who [is] the one who is to himself the cause of want of leisure”. ἀσχολία is busyness, being taken up with things, and so trouble. The implied answer is each person themselves.
notes.other_reading: who it is that makes trouble for himself

notes.note: The pankration (“all powers”) was a Greek contest of boxing and wrestling combined, fought with bare hands; the English reads “all-in fighter”. μονομάχος is a gladiator.
notes.other_reading: like a pancratiast, not a gladiator

notes.note: ἀναιρεῖται can be middle, “takes up”, or passive, “is killed”. It is taken as middle, with the sword as object of both verbs: he has his weapon only when he picks it up.
notes.other_reading: the one lays aside the sword he uses, and is killed

notes.note: To twist together: here, to ball the hand into a fist.
notes.other_reading: has only to close it

check.note: The Greek is “the causal [parts]”, the active or forming element in a thing as against its matter. “The causes of things” reads as what brought things about, and “of things” is added.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To look at what is causal, bare of its husks”.

check.note: “What actions are referred to” will be read as “which actions are mentioned”. The Greek is a noun phrase, “the references of actions”: what each action is directed to, its aim.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The aims of actions”, and the note gives the literal sense.

check.note: The word is both “pain” and “toil”. Paired with pleasure, “pain” is the likelier, but the other is possible.
check.decided: Accepted: “What pain is” stands, as suggested, and the note records “toil”.

check.note: The word is “lack of leisure”, which covers both being busy and being troubled. “Busyness” picks one.
check.decided: Declined: “busyness” is kept because being without leisure, taken up with things, is the first sense of the Greek word. The note gives “trouble” as the other.

check.note: The connecting “and” or “but” is dropped; a small thing across a chapter join.
check.decided: Accepted: the paragraph now begins “And in the use of principles”.

check.note: “All-in fighter” is a dated expression and does not tell a reader of today that he fights with bare hands; that comes out only in the next sentence.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek word names the contest, “all powers”, and does not itself say “bare-handed”. Like the Greek, the English leaves that to the next sentence, where he “always has his hand”; “all-in” renders the first half of the Greek name, and the note explains the contest.

check.note: The second verb can be “takes up” or “is killed”. The English has chosen the first; the contrast with the hand works with either.
check.decided: Accepted: “picks it up” stands, as suggested, because “the sword” reads most easily as the object of both verbs, and the note records “is killed”.

passages.casaubon: Let these be the objects of thy ordinary meditation: to consider, what manner of men both for soul and body we ought to be, whensoever death shall surprise us: the shortness of this our mortal life: the immense vastness of the time that hath been before, and will he after us: the frailty of every worldly material object: all these things to consider, and behold clearly in themselves, all disguisement of external outside being removed and taken away. Again, to consider the efficient causes of all things: the proper ends and references of all actions: what pain is in itself; what pleasure, what death: what fame or honour, how every man is the true and proper ground of his own rest and tranquillity, and that no man can truly be hindered by any other: that all is but conceit and opinion. As for the use of thy dogmata, thou must carry thyself in the practice of them, rather like unto a pancratiastes, or one that at the same time both fights and wrestles with hands and feet, than a gladiator. For this, if he lose his sword that he fights with, he is gone: whereas the other hath still his hand free, which he may easily turn and manage at his will.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek: Τοῖς δὲ εἰρημένοις παραστήμασιν ἓν ἔτι προσέστω, τὸ ὅρον ἢ ὑπογραφὴν ἀεὶ ποιεῖσθαι τοῦ ὑποπίπτοντος φανταστοῦ, ὥστε αὐτὸ ὁποῖόν ἐστι κατ’ οὐσίαν, γυμνόν, ὅλον δι’ ὅλων διῃρημένως βλέπειν καὶ τὸ ἴδιον ὄνομα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα ἐκείνων, ἐξ ὧν συνεκρίθη καὶ εἰς ἃ ἀναλυθήσεται, λέγειν παρ’ ἑαυτῷ. οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως μεγαλοφροσύνης ποιητικόν, ὡς τὸ ἐλέγχειν ὁδῷ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ ἕκαστον τῶν τῷ βίῳ ὑποπιπτόντων δύνασθαι καὶ τὸ ἀεὶ οὕτως εἰς αὐτὰ ὁρᾶν, ὥστε συνεπιβάλλειν ὁποίῳ τινὶ τῷ κόσμῳ ὁποίαν τινὰ τοῦτο χρείαν παρεχόμενον τίνα μὲν ἔχει ἀξίαν ὡς πρὸς τὸ ὅλον, τίνα δὲ ὡς πρὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, πολίτην ὄντα πόλεως τῆς ἀνωτάτης, ἧς αἱ λοιπαὶ πόλεις ὥσπερ οἰκίαι εἰσίν·
passages.english: To the precepts already named let one more be added: always to make a definition or outline of the thing that comes up in an impression, so as to see it as it is in its substance, bare, whole and entire, and taken apart, and to say to oneself its own name and the names of the things it was put together from and into which it will be broken up. For nothing so produces greatness of mind as being able to test methodically and truly each of the things that come up in life, and always to look into them in such a way as to take in at the same time what kind of use this thing supplies to what kind of universe, what worth it has in relation to the whole, and what in relation to the human being, who is a citizen of the highest city, of which the other cities are like houses.

notes.note: A rare word: “things that stand by one”, rules or aids kept at one’s side. It refers back to what came before in the book, outside this passage.
notes.other_reading: To the aids already named

notes.note: Terms of logic: ὅρος is a strict definition, ὑπογραφή a looser outline or sketch of a thing.
notes.other_reading: a definition or description

notes.note: φανταστόν is the thing that gives rise to an impression (φαντασία). ὑποπίπτω, “fall under, present itself”, comes again below (ὑποπιπτόντων); “come up” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: of the object that presents itself to the mind

notes.note: Literally “whole, through wholes, dividedly”. The grouping is open: “whole and entire, and taken apart”, or “taken apart through and through”.
notes.other_reading: bare, entire, analysed through and through

notes.note: The whole instruction is impersonal, infinitives after “let there be added”. The English keeps “oneself” and does not have “you”.
notes.other_reading: to say to yourself

notes.note: “Greatness of mind”, a different word from μεγαλοψυχία, “greatness of soul”, in 5.9. The same sentence comes again at 10.11.
notes.other_reading: high-mindedness

notes.note: ὁδῷ is “by a road”, that is, in an orderly way, by method; ἀληθείᾳ is “by truth”.
notes.other_reading: by method and in truth

notes.greek: ὁποίῳ τινὶ τῷ κόσμῳ ὁποίαν τινὰ τοῦτο χρείαν παρεχόμενον
notes.note: One packed clause: “this thing, supplying what kind of use to what kind of universe, has what worth”. The English keeps the two “what kind of” questions together and lets the questions of worth follow.
notes.other_reading: what worth it has for the whole, given the kind of universe this is and the kind of service the thing does it

notes.note: οἰκία is a house or household. The section cut falls at the colon after these words and the Greek sentence goes on; the English ends with a full stop.
notes.other_reading: are like households

check.note: The word is “things set beside one”, used for standing rules or precepts. “Aids” is one side of it; “precepts” is the other.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To the precepts already named”, since what follows is itself a rule of practice; the note gives “aids”.

check.note: Three Greek words become eleven. “Whole through wholes” is an idiom for “entire, through and through”; “parts” is not in the Greek, and “each taken separately” expands one adverb.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “bare, whole and entire, and taken apart”. “Parts” and “each taken separately” are gone; “taken apart” stands for the adverb, which is made from the verb “to divide”, where “distinctly” would be heard as “clearly”.

check.greek: ὁποίῳ τινὶ τῷ κόσμῳ ὁποίαν τινὰ τοῦτο χρείαν παρεχόμενον
check.note: The Greek is one clause hanging on “this thing”: for what kind of universe it performs what kind of service, and so what worth it has. The English makes “what kind of universe this is” a separate question, with a “this” the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what kind of use this thing supplies to what kind of universe, what worth it has in relation to the whole”.

check.note: “By method and in truth” is faithful, but “in truth” reads as a filler; the pair means “methodically and truly”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to test methodically and truly”. “Truthfully” was not used because in English it is said of honest speech, not of sound testing.

part.left_out: τί ἐστὶ καὶ ἐκ τίνων συγκέκριται καὶ πόσον χρόνον πέφυκε παραμένειν τοῦτο τὸ τὴν φαντασίαν μοι νῦν ποιοῦν καὶ τίνος ἀρετῆς πρὸς αὐτὸ χρεία, οἷον ἡμερότητος, ἀνδρείας, πίστεως, ἀφελείας, αὐταρκείας, τῶν λοιπῶν. διὸ δεῖ ἐφ̓ ἑκάστου λέγειν· τοῦτο μὲν παρὰ θεοῦ ἥκει, τοῦτο δὲ κατὰ τὴν σύλληξιν καὶ τὴν συμμηρυομένην σύγκλωσιν καὶ τὴν τοιαύτην σύντευξίν τε καὶ τύχην, τοῦτο δὲ παρὰ τοῦ συμφύλου καὶ συγγενοῦς καὶ κοινωνοῦ, ἀγνοοῦντος μέντοι ὅ τι αὐτῷ κατὰ φύσιν ἐστίν. ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐκ ἀγνοῶ· διὰ τοῦτο χρῶμαι αὐτῷ κατὰ τὸν τῆς κοινωνίας φυσικὸν νόμον εὔνως καὶ δικαίως, ἅμα μέντοι τοῦ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἐν τοῖς μέσοις συστοχάζομαι.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 3.11 here, at the city of which other cities are houses, and begins its 3.12 with the rest of the chapter.

passages.casaubon: To these ever-present helps and mementoes, let one more be added, ever to make a particular description and delineation as it were of every object that presents itself to thy mind, that thou mayest wholly and throughly contemplate it, in its own proper nature, bare and naked; wholly, and severally; divided into its several parts and quarters: and then by thyself in thy mind, to call both it, and those things of which it doth consist, and in which it shall be resolved, by their own proper true names, and appellations. For there is nothing so effectual to beget true magnanimity, as to be able truly and methodically to examine and consider all things that happen in this life, and so to penetrate into their natures, that at the same time, this also may concur in our apprehensions: what is the true use of it? and what is the true nature of this universe, to which it is useful? how much in regard of the universe may it be esteemed? how much in regard of man, a citizen of the supreme city, of which all other cities in the world are as it were but houses and families?

passages.greek: Πῶς εἰς ἄλληλα πάντα μεταβάλλει, θεωρητικὴν μέθοδον κτῆσαι καὶ διηνεκῶς πρόσεχε καὶ συγγυμνάσθητι περὶ τοῦτο τὸ μέρος· οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως μεγαλοφροσύνης ποιητικόν.
passages.english: How all things change into one another: get yourself a method for contemplating it, attend to it constantly, and train yourself in this field. For nothing so produces greatness of mind.

notes.note: “A method of contemplation”; the “how” clause that opens the sentence is its object. θεωρητικός is the word rendered “contemplative” in 10.9.
notes.other_reading: Acquire a systematic way of observing how all things change into one another

notes.note: Literally “about this part”: this department of philosophy or of study. The English reads “field”.
notes.other_reading: in this part

notes.note: The same words as in 3.11. The section cut falls here; the chapter goes on in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: for nothing is so apt to make a mind great

check.note: “This part” is literal but has nothing to be a part of in the English. The Greek means this department or branch of study.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “train yourself in this field”, and the note gives the literal “part”.

part.left_out: ἐξεδύσατο τὸ σῶμα καὶ ἐννοήσας ὅτι ὅσον οὐδέπω πάντα ταῦτα καταλιπεῖν ἀπιόντα ἐξ ἀνθρώπων δεήσει, ἀνῆκεν ὅλον ἑαυτὸν δικαιοσύνῃ μὲν εἰς τὰ ὑφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐνεργούμενα, ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις συμβαίνουσι τῇ τῶν ὅλων φύσει. τί δ’ ἐρεῖ τις ἢ ὑπολήψεται περὶ αὐτοῦ ἢ πράξει κατ’ αὐτοῦ, οὐδ’ εἰς νοῦν βάλλεται, δύο τούτοις ἀρκούμενος, εἰ αὐτὸς δικαιοπραγεῖ τὸ νῦν πρασσόμενον καὶ φιλεῖ τὸ νῦν ἀπονεμόμενον ἑαυτῷ· ἀσχολίας δὲ πάσας καὶ σπουδὰς ἀφῆκε καὶ οὐδὲν ἄλλο βούλεται ἢ εὐθεῖαν περαίνειν διὰ τοῦ νόμου καὶ εὐθεῖαν περαίνοντι ἕπεσθαι τῷ θεῷ.
part.why: The 1634 translation makes the chapter's first sentence its section 10.11 and begins its 10.12 with the rest of the chapter.

passages.casaubon: To find out, and set to thyself some certain way and method of contemplation, whereby thou mayest clearly discern and represent unto thyself, the mutual change of all things, the one into the other. Bear it in thy mind evermore, and see that thou be throughly well exercised in this particular. For there is not anything more effectual to beget true magnanimity.

passages.greek: Οἷον δὴ τὸ φαντασίαν λαμβάνειν ἐπὶ τῶν ὄψων καὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἐδωδίμων, ὅτι νεκρὸς οὗτος ἰχθύος, οὗτος δὲ νεκρὸς ὄρνιθος ἢ χοίρου· καὶ πάλιν, ὅτι ὁ Φάλερνος χυλάριόν ἐστι σταφυλίου καὶ ἡ περιπόρφυρος τριχία προβατίου αἱματίῳ κόγχης δεδευμένα· καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ τὴν συνουσίαν ἐντερίου παράτριψις καὶ μετά τινος σπασμοῦ μυξαρίου ἔκκρισις· οἷαι δὴ αὗταί εἰσιν αἱ φαντασίαι καθικνούμεναι αὐτῶν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ διεξιοῦσαι δι’ αὐτῶν, ὥστε ὁρᾶν οἷά τινά ποτέ ἐστιν· οὕτως δεῖ παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον ποιεῖν καὶ ὅπου λίαν ἀξιόπιστα τὰ πράγματα φαντάζεται, ἀπογυμνοῦν αὐτὰ καὶ τὴν εὐτέλειαν αὐτῶν καθορᾶν καὶ τὴν ἱστορίαν ἐφ’ ᾗ σεμνύνεται περιαιρεῖν. δεινὸς γὰρ ὁ τῦφος παραλογιστὴς καὶ ὅτε δοκεῖς μάλιστα περὶ τὰ σπουδαῖα καταγίνεσθαι, τότε μάλιστα καταγοητεύῃ.
passages.english: Just as, over cooked dishes and other such things to eat, one takes the impression that this is the dead body of a fish, and this the dead body of a bird or a pig; and again, that Falernian wine is a little juice from a little bunch of grapes, and the purple-bordered robe is little hairs of a little sheep soaked in a little blood from a shellfish; and, over what belongs to sex, that it is the rubbing of a bit of gut and, with a kind of spasm, the discharge of a little slime: just as these impressions reach the things themselves and go right through them, so that one sees what they really are, so one must do through the whole of life, and where things give the impression of being very trustworthy, strip them bare, see their cheapness plainly, and strip off the story on which they pride themselves. For conceit is a formidable cheat, and it is when you think you are most occupied with serious things that you are most bewitched.

notes.note: The sentence runs “As it is to take the impression …, as these impressions are …, so one must do”. The infinitive has no stated subject; the English has “one”. οἷον δή could also be an exclamation.
notes.other_reading: How good it is to take the impression

notes.note: ὄψον is cooked food eaten with bread, above all fish and meat.
notes.other_reading: over meats

notes.note: Falernian was a famous Italian wine; “wine” is supplied from the masculine article, which implies it. The nouns here and below (juice, grape-bunch, hairs, sheep, blood, gut, slime) are diminutives, used to belittle; they are marked with “a little”, “little” and “a bit of”.
notes.other_reading: Falernian is the juice of a bunch of grapes

notes.note: “The purple-bordered”: the robe with a purple border worn by Roman magistrates; “robe” is supplied. Purple dye came from a sea-snail.
notes.other_reading: the purple-edged toga

notes.greek: ἐντερίου παράτριψις καὶ μετά τινος σπασμοῦ μυξαρίου ἔκκρισις
notes.note: ἐντέριον is a diminutive of “gut, intestine”, here used of the inner flesh; μυξάριον is a diminutive of “mucus, slime”. There is no verb: the words stand as the content of the impression, and “that it is” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: friction of a membrane and, with a kind of convulsion, the ejection of a little mucus

notes.note: φαντάζεται is the verb of “impression” (φαντασία): things “present themselves”. λίαν is “very much”, shading into “too much”.
notes.other_reading: where things seem all too plausible

notes.note: ἱστορία is an account or story; the word may have been doubted here (from memory, unchecked). σεμνύνεται can be middle, “pride themselves”, or passive, “are made grand”.
notes.other_reading: the talk by which they are made to look solemn

notes.note: τῦφος is literally smoke: conceit, a puffed-up illusion of importance. It is part of σεμνοτυφία in 9.29. παραλογιστής is one who cheats by false reasoning, and δεινός is both “fearsome” and “clever”.
notes.other_reading: For pride is a clever sophist

notes.note: “You are bewitched”, as by a sorcerer: passive, second person, where the instruction before was impersonal.
notes.other_reading: you are most taken in

check.note: The opening can be an exclamation, “What a thing it is to take the impression”, and not the first half of a comparison.
check.decided: Accepted: the comparison stands, as the first suggestion has it, because “so one must do” later in the sentence answers the opening “as”. The note records the exclamation.

check.note: “Wine” is added to explain. Harmless, but an addition.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek has the masculine article with “Falernian”, which is the Greek way of saying “the Falernian wine” with the noun left out, so “wine” is in the grammar. The note says that the word is supplied.

check.note: The Greek is a diminutive, “little hairs”, not a small number. “A few” changes belittling into counting.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “little hairs of a little sheep”.

check.greek: καὶ ὅπου λίαν ἀξιόπιστα τὰ πράγματα φαντάζεται
check.note: The “and” that ties this to “so one must do through the whole of life” is lost in the sentence break, and “very much worth trusting” is clumsy; the sense is “all too convincing”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the sentence now runs on, “and where things give the impression of being very trustworthy, strip them bare”. “Give the impression” is kept because the Greek verb is the verb of “impression”, the word the passage turns on, and “very” is kept because the Greek adverb does not by itself say “too”.

check.note: The verb is “strip off from around”, continuing the image of undressing in “strip them bare”. “Take away” drops the image.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “strip off the story on which they pride themselves”.

check.note: “A terrible cheat” can be read as “bad at cheating”. The Greek is a formidable, clever misleader of reasoning.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a formidable cheat”. “Formidable” covers both sides of the Greek adjective, fearsome and clever; “cheat” is kept as the plain word for one who tricks by false reasoning.

part.left_out: ὅρα γοῦν ὁ Κράτης τί περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ξενοκράτους λέγει.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 6.11 here and makes the chapter's last sentence, on Crates and Xenocrates, its section 6.12.

passages.casaubon: How marvellous useful it is for a man to represent unto himself meats, and all such things that are for the mouth, under a right apprehension and imagination! as for example: This is the carcass of a fish; this of a bird; and this of a hog. And again more generally; This phalernum, this excellent highly commended wine, is but the bare juice of an ordinary grape. This purple robe, but sheep's hairs, dyed with the blood of a shellfish. So for coitus, it is but the attrition of an ordinary base entrail, and the excretion of a little vile snivel, with a certain kind of convulsion: according to Hippocrates his opinion. How excellent useful are these lively fancies and representations of things, thus penetrating and passing through the objects, to make their true nature known and apparent! This must thou use all thy life long, and upon all occasions: and then especially, when matters are apprehended as of great worth and respect, thy art and care must be to uncover them, and to behold their vileness, and to take away from them all those serious circumstances and expressions, under which they made so grave a show. For outward pomp and appearance is a great juggler; and then especially art thou most in danger to be beguiled by it, when (to a man's thinking) thou most seemest to be employed about matters of moment.

passages.greek: ὡς εὐτελῆ δὲ καὶ τὰ πολιτικὰ ταῦτα καί, ὡς οἴεται, φιλοσόφως πρακτικὰ ἀνθρώπια· μυξῶν μεστά.—ἄνθρωπε, τί ποτε; ποίησον ὃ νῦν ἡ φύσις ἀπαιτεῖ, ὅρμησον, ἐὰν διδῶται, καὶ μὴ περιβλέπου εἴ τις εἴσεται. μὴ τὴν Πλάτωνος πολιτείαν ἔλπιζε, ἀλλὰ ἀρκοῦ, εἰ τὸ βραχύτατον πρόεισι, καὶ τούτου αὐτοῦ τὴν ἔκβασιν ὡς μικρόν τί ἐστι διανοοῦ. δόγμα γὰρ αὐτῶν τίς μεταβαλεῖ; χωρὶς δὲ δογμάτων μεταβολῆς τί ἄλλο ἢ δουλεία στενόντων καὶ πείθεσθαι προσποιουμένων; ὕπαγε νῦν καὶ Ἀλέξανδρον καὶ Φίλιππον καὶ Δημήτριον τὸν Φαληρέα μοι λέγε. ὄψονται, εἰ εἶδον, τί ἡ κοινὴ φύσις ἤθελε, καὶ ἑαυτοὺς ἐπαιδαγώγησαν· εἰ δὲ ἐτραγῴδησαν, οὐδείς με κατακέκρικε μιμεῖσθαι. ἁπλοῦν ἐστι καὶ αἰδῆμον τὸ φιλοσοφίας ἔργον· μή με ἄπαγε ἐπὶ σεμνοτυφίαν.
passages.english: And how cheap, too, are these little people who are busy with public affairs and, as they suppose, practical in a philosophic way: full of snot. Man, what then? Do what nature now demands. Set out, if it is given to you, and do not look around to see whether anyone will know. Do not hope for Plato’s republic, but be content if the smallest thing goes forward, and think of the outcome of even this as a small thing. For who will change a principle of theirs? And without a change of principles, what is there but the slavery of people who groan and pretend to be persuaded? Go on now and tell me of Alexander and Philip and Demetrius of Phalerum. It is for them to see whether they saw what the common nature wanted and schooled themselves; but if they played the tragic hero, no one has condemned me to imitate them. The work of philosophy is simple and modest: do not lead me off into solemn conceit.

notes.note: The passage begins in the middle of chapter 9.29, so “and … too” looks back to something outside it.
notes.other_reading: And how cheap as well

notes.note: The verb is singular. With the neuter plural subject it can mean “as they think”; it could also be “as he thinks” or “as people think”.
notes.other_reading: as one supposes

notes.note: ἀνθρώπια is a belittling diminutive, “little people”. Literally “these little people of public affairs and, as they think, practical in a philosophic way”.
notes.other_reading: these little men of politics who think they are putting philosophy into practice

notes.note: “Full of mucus”: snotty-nosed, like small children.
notes.other_reading: drivelling

notes.note: A bare “man, what ever?” with the verb left out. The edition marks a break before it with a dash; the English begins a new sentence instead.
notes.other_reading: Man, what are you to do?

notes.note: The verb of ὁρμή, “impulse”: start, set yourself moving. “If it is given” has no stated giver; “to you” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: act on the impulse, if you are allowed

notes.note: πολιτεία is “constitution, state” and also the title of Plato’s book describing a perfect city. The English reads “Plato’s republic”, the state itself, which is what one could hope for.
notes.other_reading: Plato’s Republic, the book

notes.note: The words can be the subject, “the smallest thing”, or a measure of how far things go forward. The English takes the first, since “this very thing” in the next clause picks it up.
notes.other_reading: if things go forward by the smallest step

notes.note: As the Greek stands: “think of the outcome of this very thing as something small”. Some editors may read the opposite, “as no small thing” (from memory, unchecked). The English translates what is given.
notes.other_reading: and count even that result as no small thing

notes.note: “Theirs” has no stated reference inside this passage: the people one would be trying to reform. The noun is singular and has no article.
notes.other_reading: For who can change what people believe?

notes.note: πείθεσθαι is both “to be persuaded” and “to obey”.
notes.other_reading: who pretend to obey

notes.greek: Ἀλέξανδρον καὶ Φίλιππον καὶ Δημήτριον τὸν Φαληρέα
notes.note: Alexander the Great, his father Philip of Macedon, and Demetrius of Phalerum, a philosopher and statesman who governed Athens in the late fourth century BC (the last detail from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: Alexander, Philip and Demetrius the Phalerean

notes.note: An idiom: “they will see to it”, that is, it is their own business. Literally “they will see whether they saw”.
notes.other_reading: They will see whether they saw what the common nature wanted

notes.note: “The common nature”: nature as shared by all things, the same as the nature of the whole.
notes.other_reading: universal nature

notes.note: “Played tragedy”: acted a grand part, struck heroic poses.
notes.other_reading: if they merely put on a tragic show

notes.note: A compound of “solemn” and τῦφος, the “conceit” of 6.13: pompous self-importance.
notes.other_reading: pomposity

check.note: The Greek is “men of action in a philosophical way”. “Acting as philosophers” loses “practical” and can be read as play-acting.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “practical in a philosophic way”, which gives the adjective and the adverb as they stand in the Greek.

check.note: “Well” is added, and “now” is not in the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Man, what then?”.

check.note: With a capital this is the book. The Greek is equally Plato’s state, the ideal commonwealth itself, which is what one could hope for.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Plato’s republic”, without the capital, and the note says that the word is also the title of the book.

check.note: The words can be the subject, “the smallest thing”, or a measure, “if it goes forward by the least step”. The English picks the first.
check.decided: Declined: “the smallest thing” is kept because the next words, “the outcome of this very thing”, pick it up as a thing. A note now records “by the smallest step”.

check.note: The English follows the Greek as given. From memory: editors have suspected that a “not” has fallen out, which would give “no small thing”, the opposite sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, as suggested, because the Greek as given construes and the “for” that follows explains small hopes well enough. The note records the doubt (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: The verb is both “be persuaded” and “obey”. “Be persuaded” fits the point about unchanged convictions better.
check.decided: Accepted: “pretend to be persuaded” stands, as suggested, and the note records “obey”.

check.note: The noun is singular and probably collective, “their conviction”. “A principle of theirs” sounds like one out of many.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek noun is singular and has no article, which is what “a principle of theirs” says. “Principle” is the settled word for it, and it lets “a change of principles” in the next sentence be heard as the same word.

part.left_out: Χειμάρρους ἡ τῶν ὅλων οὐσία· πάντα φέρει.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the chapter's first sentence, the torrent, at the end of its section 9.27 and begins its 9.28 here.

passages.casaubon: And these your professed politicians, the only true practical philosophers of the world, (as they think of themselves) so full of affected gravity, or such professed lovers of virtue and honesty, what wretches be they in very deed; how vile and contemptible in themselves? O man! what ado doest thou keep? Do what thy nature doth now require. Resolve upon it, if thou mayest: and take no thought, whether anybody shall know it or no. Yea, but sayest thou, I must not expect a Plato's commonwealth. If they profit though never so little, I must be content; and think much even of that little progress. Doth then any of them forsake their former false opinions that I should think they profit? For without a change of opinions, alas! what is all that ostentation, but mere wretchedness of slavish minds, that groan privately, and yet would make a show of obedience to reason, and truth? Go too now and tell me of Alexander and Philippus, and Demetrius Phalereus. Whether they understood what the common nature requireth, and could rule themselves or no, they know best themselves. But if they kept a life, and swaggered; I (God be thanked) am not bound to imitate them. The effect of true philosophy is, unaffected simplicity and modesty. Persuade me not to ostentation and vainglory.

passages.greek: Οἵαν ὕλην καὶ ὑπόθεσιν φεύγεις· τί γάρ ἐστι πάντα ταῦτα ἄλλο πλὴν γυμνάσματα λόγου ἑωρακότος ἀκριβῶς καὶ φυσιολόγως τὰ ἐν τῷ βίῳ; μένε οὖν, μέχρι ἐξοικειώσῃς σεαυτῷ καὶ ταῦτα, ὡς ὁ ἐρρωμένος στόμαχος πάντα ἐξοικειοῖ, ὡς τὸ λαμπρὸν πῦρ, ὅ τι ἂν ἐμβάλῃς, φλόγα ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐγὴν ποιεῖ.
passages.english: What material, what a subject, you are running away from! For what are all these things but exercises for a reason that has looked exactly, and as a student of nature, at the things in life? Stay, then, until you have made these things too your own, as a strong stomach makes everything its own, as a bright fire makes flame and light out of whatever you throw into it.

notes.note: Can be an exclamation or a question. The passage begins mid-chapter, so “all these things” points to what came before it. ὑπόθεσις here is the subject set before one to work on; in 8.1 and 11.7, where it is the footing of a life, the English has “situation”.
notes.other_reading: What kind of material and what subject are you running away from?

notes.note: The genitive can be “exercises for reason” or “exercises of reason”.
notes.other_reading: the exercises of a reason that has seen

notes.note: “In the manner of one who studies nature”; the same root as ἀφυσιολογήτως in 10.9.
notes.other_reading: scientifically

notes.note: To make a thing οἰκεῖον, one’s own, at home with oneself; of the stomach, to assimilate. “Make your own” and “makes its own” are kept for both.
notes.other_reading: until you have assimilated these things too

notes.greek: φλόγα ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐγὴν ποιεῖ
notes.note: αὐγή is brightness, the light a fire gives.
notes.other_reading: makes flame and a blaze out of it

check.note: “To work on” is added to make the word clear. Reasonable, but an addition.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “What material, what a subject, you are running away from!”.

part.left_out: Σατυρίωνα ἰδὼν Σωκρατικὸν φαντάζου ἢ Εὐτύχην ἢ Ὑμένα, καὶ Εὐφράτην ἰδὼν Εὐτυχίωνα ἢ Σιλουανὸν φαντάζου, καὶ Ἀλκίφρονα Τροπαιοφόρον φαντάζου, καὶ Σευῆρον ἰδὼν Κρίτωνα ἢ Ξενοφῶντα φαντάζου, καὶ εἰς σεαυτὸν ἀπιδὼν τῶν Καισάρων τινὰ φαντάζου, καὶ ἐφ’ ἑκάστου τὸ ἀνάλογον. εἶτα συμπροσπιπτέτω σοι· ποῦ οὖν ἐκεῖνοι; οὐδαμοῦ ἢ ὁπουδή. οὕτως γὰρ συνεχῶς θεάσῃ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα καπνὸν καὶ τὸ μηδέν, μάλιστα ἐὰν συμμνημονεύσῃς ὅτι τὸ ἅπαξ μεταβαλὸν οὐκέτι ἔσται ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ χρόνῳ. τί οὖν ἐντείνῃ; τί δ’ οὐκ ἀρκεῖ σοι τὸ βραχὺ τοῦτο κοσμίως διαπερᾶσαι;
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the first part of the chapter in its section 10.31 and begins its 10.32 here; its 10.33 begins at chapter 10.32.

passages.casaubon: What a subject, and what a course of life is it, that thou doest so much desire to be rid of. For all these things, what are they, but fit objects for an understanding, that beholdeth everything according to its true nature, to exercise itself upon? Be patient, therefore, until that (as a strong stomach that turns all things into his own nature; and as a great fire that turneth in flame and light, whatsoever thou doest cast into it) thou have made these things also familiar, and as it were natural unto thee.

passages.greek: λίαν γὰρ ἐνδέχεται θεῖον ἄνδρα γενέσθαι καὶ ὑπὸ μηδενὸς γνωρισθῆναι. τούτου μέμνησο ἀεὶ καὶ ἔτι ἐκείνου, ὅτι ἐν ὀλιγίστοις κεῖται τὸ εὐδαιμόνως βιῶσαι καὶ μή, ὅτι ἀπήλπισας διαλεκτικὸς καὶ φυσικὸς ἔσεσθαι, διὰ τοῦτο ἀπογνῷς καὶ ἐλεύθερος καὶ αἰδήμων καὶ κοινωνικὸς καὶ εὐπειθὴς θεῷ.
passages.english: For it is very possible to become a godlike man and to be recognised by no one. Remember this always, and this as well: that living happily lies in very few things. And do not, because you have given up hope of being a logician and a student of nature, for that reason give up on being free, modest, social and obedient to god.

notes.note: The passage begins mid-chapter with “for”. λίαν is “very much”: it is entirely possible.
notes.other_reading: For it is quite possible

notes.note: θεῖος is “divine, godlike”; ἄνδρα is the word for a man, not for a person in general.
notes.other_reading: a divine man

notes.note: “Lies in very few things”: the superlative of “few”.
notes.other_reading: depends on the fewest things

notes.note: The dialectician is the expert in logic and argument, the φυσικός the expert in the study of nature: the two parts of Stoic philosophy besides ethics.
notes.other_reading: a dialectician and a natural philosopher

notes.note: ἀπήλπισας and ἀπογνῷς both mean to give up hope; the English has “given up hope” and “give up on”. The adjectives that follow are nominative, with “being” left out.
notes.other_reading: do not for that reason despair of being free

notes.note: Having αἰδώς, a sense of shame and respect before others and oneself. The English reads “modest”, as for αἰδῆμον in 9.29.
notes.other_reading: self-respecting

notes.note: “Social” in the sense of living and acting as a member of the community, for the common good; not “sociable”. It is the word kept for κοινωνικός throughout this translation.
notes.other_reading: a good member of the community

notes.note: “Readily obedient to god”; there is no article, so “god” and not “the god”.
notes.other_reading: ready to obey god

check.note: “Social” in today’s English suggests “sociable”. The word is “acting for the community, for the common good”.
check.decided: Declined: “social” is the word settled for κοινωνικός across this translation, and a phrase such as “a good member of the community” would break the Greek run of four single adjectives. A note now says what the word means.

part.left_out: Ἡ φύσις οὐχ οὕτως συνεκέρασε τῷ συγκρίματι, ὡς μὴ ἐφεῖσθαι περιορίζειν ἑαυτὸν καὶ τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ὑφ’ ἑαυτῷ ποιεῖσθαι·
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the chapter's first sentence at the end of its section 7.37 and begins its 7.38 here.

passages.casaubon: For it is a thing very possible, that a man should be a very divine man, and yet be altogether unknown. This thou must ever be mindful of, as of this also, that a man's true happiness doth consist in very few things. And that although thou dost despair, that thou shalt ever be a good either logician, or naturalist, yet thou art never the further off by it from being either liberal, or modest, or charitable, or obedient unto God.

passages.greek:
Πεποίηκά τι κοινωνικῶς· οὐκοῦν ὠφέλημαι. τοῦτο ἵνα ἀεὶ πρόχειρον ἀπαντᾷ, καὶ μηδαμοῦ παύου.

Τίς σου ἡ τέχνη; ἀγαθὸν εἶναι. τοῦτο δὲ πῶς καλῶς γίνεται ὴ ἐκ θεωρημάτων, τῶν μὲν περὶ τῆς τοῦ ὅλου φύσεως, τῶν δὲ περὶ τῆς ἰδίας τοῦ ἀνθρώπου κατασκευῆς.
passages.english:
I have done something as a social being: then I have been benefited. See that this always comes to hand, and never stop.

What is your craft? To be good. And how does that come about well, except from points of theory, some about the nature of the whole, others about the make-up proper to the human being?

notes.note: The adverb of κοινωνικός, “social”: as a member of the community, for the common good. The glossary word is kept, in the phrase “as a social being”.
notes.other_reading: I have done something for the common good

notes.note: Perfect: “I have been benefited”, the benefit being in the act itself.
notes.other_reading: then I have my reward

notes.note: ἵνα with the subjunctive standing alone as a command: “see that this always meets you ready to hand”. The English joins the verb and the adjective in “comes to hand”.
notes.other_reading: Let this thought always be ready when you need it

notes.note: Literally “stop nowhere”. What is not to stop is not said: the doing of such acts, or the keeping of the thought at hand.
notes.other_reading: and do not leave off at any point

notes.note: A craft, skill or profession.
notes.other_reading: What is your profession?

notes.note: ὴ is a slip in the copy for ἢ, “than”: “how … other than from”, though the Greek has no “other” for it to lean on. θεωρήματα are the propositions a science or craft rests on, literally “things contemplated”; the English reads “points of theory”. The Greek ends with a full stop; the English has a question mark.
notes.other_reading: except from theorems

notes.note: κατασκευή is how a thing is built, its constitution.
notes.other_reading: the particular constitution of man

check.note: “In a social way” is unclear in English. The sense is “for the common good, as a member of the community”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “I have done something as a social being”. “Social” is the settled word for this family of Greek words and is kept; the new phrase says more plainly that the act is that of a member of the community.

check.note: Both Greek words are rendered in full, “comes to meet you ready at hand”, and the result is heavy.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “See that this always comes to hand”, in which “comes” is the Greek verb and “to hand” the Greek adjective. “When you need it” is not added, since the Greek does not have it.

check.greek: πῶς καλῶς γίνεται ὴ ἐκ θεωρημάτων
check.note: The letter printed ὴ must be the word for “than”. Even so the Greek is harsh, since “than” has nothing to lean on; the English supplies “except”, the only sense available.
check.decided: Accepted: “except” stands, as suggested, and the note records the slip in the copy and the roughness of the Greek.

check.note: One word, “theorems” or “things contemplated”, becomes four, and “truths” asserts more than the Greek.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “points of theory”, which drops “truths” and keeps the Greek root. “Principles” was not used because it is this translation’s word for δόγμα.

passages.casaubon: Have I done anything charitably? then am I benefited by it. See that this upon all occasions may present itself unto thy mind, and never cease to think of it. What is thy profession? to be good. And how should this be well brought to pass, but by certain theorems and doctrines; some Concerning the nature of the universe, and some Concerning the proper and particular constitution of man?

passages.greek: Ὁποῖά τινά ἐστι τὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς δοκοῦντα ἀγαθά, κἂν ἐντεῦθεν λάβοις. εἰ γάρ τις ἐπινοήσειεν ὑπάρχοντά τινα ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθά, οἷον φρόνησιν, σωφροσύνην, δικαιοσύνην, ἀνδρείαν, οὐκ ἂν ταῦτα προεπινοήσας ἐπακοῦσαι δυνηθείη τό· ʽὑπὸ τῶν ἀγαθῶνʼ, οὐ γὰρ ἐφαρμόσει. τὰ δέ γε τοῖς πολλοῖς φαινόμενα ἀγαθὰ προεπινοήσας τις ἐπακούσεται καὶ ῥᾳδίως δέξεται ὡς οἰκείως ἐπιλεγόμενον τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ κωμικοῦ εἰρημένον. οὕτως καὶ οἱ πολλοὶ φαντάζονται τὴν διαφοράν· οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο μὲν οὐ προσέκοπτε καὶ ἀπηξιοῦτο, τὸ δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ πλούτου καὶ τῶν πρὸς τρυφὴν ἢ δόξαν εὐκληρημάτων παρεδεχόμεθα ὡς ἱκνουμένως καὶ ἀστείως εἰρημένον. πρόιθι οὖν καὶ ἐρώτα, εἰ τιμητέον καὶ ἀγαθὰ ὑποληπτέον τὰ τοιαῦτα, ὧν προεπινοηθέντων οἰκείως ἂν ἐπιφέροιτο τὸ τὸν κεκτημένον αὐτὰ ὑπὸ τῆς εὐπορίας ʽοὐκ ἔχειν ὅποι χέσῃʼ.
passages.english: What kind of things they are that seem good to most people, you can gather from this as well. For if a person had in mind certain things that truly are good, such as wisdom, self-control, justice, courage, then with these in mind first they could not listen to the words “because of the good things”, for it will not fit. But a person who has first in mind the things that appear good to most people will listen, and will readily accept what the comic poet said as a fitting thing to add. So even most people have an impression of the difference. For otherwise this line would not jar and be refused in the one case, while when it is said of wealth and of the pieces of good luck that make for luxury or reputation we accept it as aptly and wittily said. Go on, then, and ask whether one should honour and judge to be good the kind of things which, when they have first been brought to mind, can fittingly be followed by the line that their owner, because of the plenty, “has nowhere to shit”.

notes.note: “You could grasp even from this”: from the test that follows.
notes.other_reading: you may learn from the following too

notes.note: ὡς ἀληθῶς is “truly”. The phrase can be “certain things that truly are good” or “certain existing things as truly good”.
notes.other_reading: if someone thought of certain real things as truly good

notes.note: “Having thought of beforehand”. The verb comes three times with this prefix and once without (ἐπινοήσειεν); “in mind” and “first” are kept for it, and “brought to mind” for the passive at the end.
notes.other_reading: having first conceived of these

notes.note: The opening words of a comic line whose end is given at the close of the passage: a man has so many good things that he “has nowhere to shit”. The Greek here is only “because of the good things”.
notes.other_reading: “for all his goods”

notes.note: To give ear to. It can also be taken as “to hear in addition”, that is, to hear the line tacked on.
notes.other_reading: could not bear to hear added

notes.note: “The comic poet”, not named. The line may be Menander’s (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: the writer of comedy

notes.greek: οὕτως καὶ οἱ πολλοὶ φαντάζονται τὴν διαφοράν
notes.note: καί is “even”: even ordinary people have an impression of the difference between the two kinds of good. φαντάζονται is the verb of “impression”.
notes.other_reading: So the many too perceive the difference

notes.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο μὲν οὐ προσέκοπτε
notes.note: The second οὐ is hard: taken strictly, the two negatives cancel and give the wrong sense. It is read as the first negative repeated, “for otherwise this would not jar”; editors may remove or bracket it (from memory, unchecked). “Otherwise”, “line” and “in the one case” are supplied.
notes.other_reading: for otherwise this would not fail to jar

notes.note: The verb is in the first person plural, where the rest of the passage speaks of “a person” and “most people”. Its tense is past, inside the “otherwise”, which is how Greek states what would be so now; the English has the present.
notes.other_reading: while we would be accepting it
