notes.note: Pieces of good luck, lucky gains.
notes.other_reading: the advantages that bring luxury or fame

notes.note: From the verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment”.
notes.other_reading: to be supposed good

notes.note: The coarse word is in the Greek. τὸν κεκτημένον is masculine, “the man who owns them”, with no man singled out; the English has “their owner”.
notes.other_reading: that he who has them is so well off that he “has no place left to relieve himself”

check.greek: ἐπινοήσειεν ὑπάρχοντά τινα ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθά
check.note: The Greek can be “conceived of certain things as being truly good”, the person’s own conception and not the writer’s statement that they are good.
check.decided: Declined: the participle “being” can equally stand with “truly good” as a description of the things, and the next sentence sets against them “the things that appear good to most people”, which is the writer’s own division. The note gives the other construction.

check.note: “Go on to” is added here, but the same verb two lines later is plain “will listen”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they could not listen to the words”, so the verb is “listen” both times. The note records the sense “hear in addition”.

check.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο μὲν οὐ προσέκοπτε καὶ ἀπηξιοῦτο
check.note: The Greek as given has two negatives and, taken strictly, says “would not fail to jar”. The English translates one, which the argument needs; from memory, editors remove or bracket the second. “Line” and “in the one case” are supplied.
check.decided: Accepted: the sense stands, as suggested, and the note says that the second negative is passed over as a repetition of the first and names the words supplied.

check.note: The tense is past in Greek, inside the unreal condition. The present makes it a plain fact.
check.decided: Declined: in Greek a past tense with this particle is the ordinary way to state what would be so now, and one negative governs both halves of the sentence, so “would not jar” followed by “while we accept it” gives the same sense in English. The note records the tense.

check.greek: τῶν πρὸς τρυφὴν ἢ δόξαν εὐκληρημάτων
check.note: “That go to” is unclear. The sense is the strokes of good fortune that make for luxury or fame.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the pieces of good luck that make for luxury or reputation”. “Reputation” is kept for the Greek word, as in the other passages of this section.

check.note: “This” is not in the Greek, which has “because of his abundance”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “because of the plenty”, with the Greek article and no “this”.

check.note: Found while settling: “picture the difference” is not plain English, and the verb is the verb of “impression”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “have an impression of the difference”.

passages.casaubon: What those things are in themselves, which by the greatest part are esteemed good, thou mayest gather even from this. For if a man shall hear things mentioned as good, which are really good indeed, such as are prudence, temperance, justice, fortitude, after so much heard and conceived, he cannot endure to hear of any more, for the word good is properly spoken of them. But as for those which by the vulgar are esteemed good, if he shall hear them mentioned as good, he doth hearken for more. He is well contented to hear, that what is spoken by the comedian, is but familiarly and popularly spoken, so that even the vulgar apprehend the difference. For why is it else, that this offends not and needs not to be excused, when virtues are styled good: but that which is spoken in commendation of wealth, pleasure, or honour, we entertain it only as merrily and pleasantly spoken? Proceed therefore, and inquire further, whether it may not be that those things also which being mentioned upon the stage were merrily, and with great applause of the multitude, scoffed at with this jest, that they that possessed them had not in all the world of their own, (such was their affluence and plenty) so much as a place where to avoid their excrements. Whether, I say, those ought not also in very deed to be much respected, and esteemed of, as the only things that are truly good.

passages.greek: Πῶς ἐναργὲς προσπίπτει τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἄλλην βίου ὑπόθεσιν εἰς τὸ φιλοσοφεῖν οὕτως ἐπιτήδειον ὡς ταύτην, ἐν ᾗ νῦν ὢν τυγχάνεις.
passages.english: How plainly it comes home that there is no other situation in life so suited to philosophy as this one in which you now happen to be.

notes.note: An exclamation. προσπίπτει, “strikes, falls upon”, is the word used of impressions; it has no object, so the English reads “comes home”.
notes.other_reading: How clearly it strikes you

notes.note: ὑπόθεσις as in 8.1: the footing or position of a life. The English reads “situation in life”.
notes.other_reading: no other calling in life

notes.note: “For philosophising”: the practice, not the subject.
notes.other_reading: for the practice of philosophy

passages.casaubon: How clearly doth it appear unto thee, that no other course of thy life could fit a true philosopher's practice better, than this very course, that thou art now already in?

passages.greek: Ὥσπερ οἱ ἰατροὶ ἀεὶ τὰ ὄργανα καὶ σιδήρια πρόχειρα ἔχουσι πρὸς τὰ αἰφνίδια τῶν θεραπευμάτων, οὕτω τὰ δόγματα σὺ ἕτοιμα ἔχε πρὸς τὸ τὰ θεῖα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα εἰδέναι, καὶ πᾶν καὶ τὸ μικρότατον οὕτω ποιεῖν ὡς τῆς ἀμφοτέρων πρὸς ἄλληλα συνδέσεως μεμνημένον. οὔτε γὰρ ἀνθρώπινόν τι ἄνευ τῆς ἐπὶ τὰ θεῖα συναναφορᾶς εὖ πράξεις οὔτ’ ἔμπαλιν.
passages.english: As doctors always have their instruments and blades at hand for emergency treatments, so have your principles ready for knowing things divine and human, and for doing everything, even the smallest thing, as one who remembers the bond that ties the two to each other. For you will not do any human thing well without referring it at the same time to the divine, nor the other way round.

notes.note: σιδήρια is “irons”: the surgeon’s iron tools, knives and lancets.
notes.other_reading: their instruments and irons

notes.note: Literally “for the sudden ones among treatments”.
notes.other_reading: for treatments needed suddenly

notes.greek: πρὸς τὸ τὰ θεῖα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα εἰδέναι
notes.note: “For knowing” governs “things divine and human”; the same “for” is taken to run on to “doing everything”. “Knowledge of things divine and human” was a standing definition of wisdom (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: for understanding divine and human things

notes.note: “A referring together”: carrying the human act back to the divine along with it. The root is that of ἀναφοράς in 12.8, where the English has “aims”.
notes.other_reading: without relating it to the divine as well

notes.note: “Nor the reverse”: nor anything divine without reference to the human.
notes.other_reading: nor the opposite

check.note: The Greek is “for the sudden ones among their treatments”, that is, emergencies. The English is right but stiff.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “for emergency treatments”, which is plainer and still keeps the Greek noun “treatments”.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek is a plain command, “have ready”, with the same verb as the doctors’ “have”; “you should have” softened it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “so have your principles ready”.

passages.casaubon: As physicians and chirurgeons have always their instruments ready at hand for all sudden cures; so have thou always thy dogmata in a readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human: and whatsoever thou dost, even in the smallest things that thou dost, thou must ever remember that mutual relation, and connection that is between these two things divine, and things human. For without relation unto God, thou shalt never speed in any worldly actions; nor on the other side in any divine, without some respect had to things human.

passages.greek: Μέμνησο ὅτι τὸ νευροσπαστοῦν ἐστιν ἐκεῖνο τὸ ἔνδον ἐγκεκρυμμένον· ἐκεῖνο ῥητορεία, ἐκεῖνο ζωή, ἐκεῖνο, εἰ δεῖ εἰπεῖν, ἄνθρωπος. μηδέποτε συμπεριφαντάζου τὸ περικείμενον ἀγγειῶδες καὶ τὰ ὀργάνια ταῦτα τὰ περιπεπλασμένα· ὅμοια γάρ ἐστι σκεπάρνῳ, μόνον διαφέροντα, καθότι προσφυῆ ἐστιν. ἐπεί τοι οὐ μᾶλλόν τι τούτων ὄφελός ἐστι τῶν μορίων χωρὶς τῆς κινούσης καὶ ἰσχούσης αὐτὰ αἰτίας, ἢ τῆς κερκίδος τῇ ὑφαντρίᾳ καὶ τοῦ καλάμου τῷ γράφοντι καὶ τοῦ μαστιγίου τῷ ἡνιόχῳ.
passages.english: Remember that what pulls the strings is that thing hidden inside. That is oratory, that is life, that, if one must say it, is the human being. Never picture along with it the vessel-like thing that surrounds it and these little tools moulded around it. For they are like a carpenter’s axe, differing only in being grown on. For without the cause that moves them and holds them in check these parts are in fact of no more use than the weaver’s shuttle, the writer’s pen and the charioteer’s little whip.

notes.note: “What pulls the strings”, as of a puppet worked by cords.
notes.other_reading: the puppet-master

notes.note: ῥητορεία is oratory, public speaking. It sits oddly beside “life” and “the human being”, and the word may have been doubted (from memory, unchecked). It is translated as it stands.
notes.other_reading: that is the power of speech

notes.note: “If one must say it”: an apology for the bold wording.
notes.other_reading: if the word may be allowed

notes.note: A compound of the verb of “impression”: do not take in, in the same picture, what lies around it.
notes.other_reading: never include in your thought of it

notes.note: “The vessel-like thing lying round it”: the body as a container.
notes.other_reading: the vessel that encloses it

notes.note: ὀργάνια is a diminutive of ὄργανον, which is both “tool” and bodily “organ”. The comparison with the carpenter’s axe turns on the first sense, so the English reads “little tools”.
notes.other_reading: these organs moulded round it

notes.note: A carpenter’s axe or adze, a tool for shaping wood.
notes.other_reading: an adze

notes.note: “In that they are grown on”: attached by growth.
notes.other_reading: in that they are part of the body’s growth

notes.note: ἴσχω is to hold, hold back or check: the cause that sets the parts moving and stops them.
notes.other_reading: the cause that moves and sustains them

notes.note: Literally “than [there is use] of the shuttle to the weaver, of the pen to the writer, of the little whip to the charioteer”. The comparison is compressed: “without the cause that moves them” has to be carried over to the three tools, and the English puts those words first so that they are heard over both halves. ὑφαντρίᾳ is a woman weaver.
notes.other_reading: than the shuttle is without the weaver, the pen without the writer, or the whip without the charioteer

check.note: “Oratory” is literal and puzzling in English. The word can be taken more widely as speech, the power of persuading.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek word is the art of the public speaker, not the general word for speech, so “oratory” is what it says, odd as it is. The note records the wider sense and that the word may have been doubted (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: “Adze” is correct but rare; the tool is a carpenter’s axe.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “like a carpenter’s axe”.

check.note: Read by itself the English says a shuttle is of little use to a weaver. The Greek is compressed in the same way, and “without the cause that moves it” has to be carried over to the shuttle, the pen and the whip.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “without the cause that moves them and holds them in check these parts are in fact of no more use than the weaver’s shuttle, the writer’s pen and the charioteer’s little whip”. With “without” placed first it is heard over both halves of the comparison; “without the weaver” was not written because the Greek has “to the weaver”, and the note marks what is left unsaid.

check.note: The Greek word is feminine, “the weaving woman”.
check.decided: Declined: English “weaver” serves for a woman as for a man, and “weaving woman” would put a weight on the word that the Greek does not. The note says that the Greek word is feminine.

check.note: The verb is “holds”: either “restrains” or “holds together, sustains”. The English picks the first.
check.decided: Accepted: “holds them in check” stands, as suggested, and the note records “sustains”.

passages.casaubon: Remember, that that which sets a man at work, and hath power over the affections to draw them either one way, or the other way, is not any external thing properly, but that which is hidden within every man's dogmata, and opinions: That, that is rhetoric; that is life; that (to speak true) is man himself. As for thy body, which as a vessel, or a case, compasseth thee about, and the many and curious instruments that it hath annexed unto it, let them not trouble thy thoughts. For of themselves they are but as a carpenter's axe, but that they are born with us, and naturally sticking unto us. But otherwise, without the inward cause that hath power to move them, and to restrain them, those parts are of themselves of no more use unto us, than the shuttle is of itself to the weaver, or the pen to the writer, or the whip to the coachman.

nearest.title: The reasonable soul and its powers

passages.greek: Μή, εἴ τι αὐτῷ σοὶ δυσκαταπόνητον, τοῦτο ἀνθρώπῳ ἀδύνατον ὑπολαμβάνειν, ἀλλ’ εἴ τι ἀνθρώπῳ δυνατὸν καὶ οἰκεῖον, τοῦτο καὶ σεαυτῷ ἐφικτὸν νόμιζε.
passages.english: Do not, if something is hard for you yourself to carry out, judge it impossible for a human being; but if something is possible for a human being and proper to them, consider it within your own reach too.

notes.note: “Hard to work through to the end”, hard to master by effort.
notes.other_reading: hard for you to master

notes.note: An infinitive used as a command, the verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment”. The second half has a plain imperative, νόμιζε, “consider”.
notes.other_reading: do not suppose

notes.note: οἰκεῖον is what belongs to a being by its nature. The English reads “proper to them” for the human being.
notes.other_reading: possible and natural to man

passages.casaubon: Do not ever conceive anything impossible to man, which by thee cannot, or not without much difficulty be effected; but whatsoever in general thou canst Conceive possible and proper unto any man, think that very possible unto thee also.

nearest.title: The morning, and the question before each action

passages.greek: Εἰ μὲν κρεῖττον εὑρίσκεις ἐν τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ βίῳ δικαιοσύνης, ἀληθείας, σωφροσύνης, ἀνδρείας καὶ καθάπαξ τοῦ ἀρκεῖσθαι ἑαυτῇ τὴν διάνοιάν σου, ἐν οἷς κατὰ τὸν λόγον τὸν ὀρθὸν πράσσοντά σε παρέχεται, καὶ ἐν τῇ εἱμαρμένῃ ἐν τοῖς ἀπροαιρέτως ἀπονεμομένοις· εἰ τούτου, φημί, κρεῖττόν τι ὁρᾷς, ἐπʼ ἐκεῖνο ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τραπόμενος τοῦ ἀρίστου εὑρισκομένου ἀπόλαυε. εἰ δὲ μηδὲν κρεῖττον φαίνεται αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἐνιδρυμένου ἐν σοὶ δαίμονος, τάς τε ἰδίας ὁρμὰς ὑποτεταχότος ἑαυτῷ καὶ τὰς φαντασίας ἐξετάζοντος καὶ τῶν αἰσθητικῶν πείσεων, ὡς ὁ Σωκράτης ἔλεγεν, ἑαυτὸν ἀφειλκυκότος καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς ὑποτεταχότος ἑαυτὸν καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων προκηδομένου· εἰ τούτου πάντα τὰ ἄλλα μικρότερα καὶ εὐτελέστερα εὑρίσκεις, μηδενὶ χώραν δίδου ἑτέρῳ, πρὸς ὃ ῥέψας ἅπαξ καὶ ἀποκλίνας οὐκέτι ἀπερισπάστως τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐκεῖνο, τὸ ἴδιον καὶ τὸ σόν, προτιμᾶν δυνήσῃ. ἀντικαθῆσθαι γὰρ τῷ λογικῷ καὶ πολιτικῷ ἀγαθῷ οὐ θέμις οὐδʼ ὁτιοῦν ἑτερογενές, οἷον τὸν παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν ἔπαινον ἢ ἀρχὰς ἢ πλοῦτον ἢ ἀπολαύσεις ἡδονῶν· πάντα ταῦτα, κἂν πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐναρμόζειν δόξῃ, κατεκράτησεν ἄφνω καὶ παρήνεγκεν. σὺ δέ, φημί, ἁπλῶς καὶ ἐλευθέρως ἑλοῦ τὸ κρεῖττον καὶ τούτου ἀντέχου· “κρεῖττον δὲ τὸ συμφέρον.” εἰ μὲν τὸ ὡς λογικῷ, τοῦτο τήρει· εἰ δὲ τὸ ὡς ζῴῳ, ἀπόφηναι, καὶ ἀτύφως φύλασσε τὴν κρίσιν· μόνον ὅπως ἀσφαλῶς τὴν ἐξέτασιν ποιήσῃ.
passages.english: If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage, and, in a word, than your thought being content with itself in the things where it has you acting according to right reason, and in fate, in the things that are allotted without your choosing; if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best. But if nothing appears better than the spirit itself that is seated in you, which has put its own impulses under itself, which examines the impressions, which has pulled itself away, as Socrates used to say, from the feelings of the senses, and has put itself under the gods, and cares for human beings; if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else. Once you have tipped and turned aside toward anything else, you will no longer be able, without being pulled about, to honor above all else that good which is proper to you and is yours. For it is not permitted that anything whatever of a different kind, such as praise from the many, or offices, or wealth, or the enjoyment of pleasures, should take up a position against the rational and civic good. All these, even if for a little while they seem to fit, suddenly take control and carry you off course. But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it. “But the better is what benefits.” If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so, and guard your verdict without conceit. Only see that you make the examination without slipping.

notes.note: διάνοια is the thinking faculty here. The glossary’s “thought” is kept so that the word matches 3.7, where it stands beside νοῦς (“mind”).
notes.other_reading: your mind being content with itself

notes.greek: καὶ ἐν τῇ εἱμαρμένῃ ἐν τοῖς ἀπροαιρέτως ἀπονεμομένοις
notes.note: The Greek as given has ἐν, “in”, before “fate”, and the English follows it: the thought is content with itself in two fields, where it acts by right reason and, in fate, where things are allotted without choice. Without that ἐν the words mean “content with fate”, with fate as the partner of “itself”. From memory, unchecked: editors print the text without it.
notes.other_reading: and content with fate in the things that are allotted without your choosing

notes.note: εὑρισκομένου is a present participle, “being found”, and answers “if you find” at the start, so the English keeps the finding open. It can also be heard as a finished event.
notes.other_reading: enjoy the best thing, now that it is found

notes.greek: αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἐνιδρυμένου ἐν σοὶ δαίμονος
notes.note: δαίμων is a divine being; here it is the divine part housed in each person, which Marcus elsewhere equates with mind and reason. “Spirit” is used for it throughout this section. ἐνιδρυμένου is the word for a god’s statue or shrine set up in a place, so “seated” is weaker than the Greek.
notes.other_reading: the god itself that has its shrine in you

notes.note: πεῖσις here is from πάσχω, “what is undergone”, not from πείθω, “persuasion”: what the senses are made to feel. From memory, unchecked: the saying of Socrates is a loose recollection of Plato’s Phaedo, where the soul is told to withdraw from the senses, and not an exact quotation.
notes.other_reading: from the affections of the senses; or, on the other derivation, from the persuasions of the senses

notes.greek: πρὸς ὃ ῥέψας ἅπαξ καὶ ἀποκλίνας
notes.note: ῥέπω is the tipping of a scale pan and ἀποκλίνω a leaning off to one side; the image is a balance, and both verbs go with “toward which”. The Greek is a relative clause on “nothing else”; the English begins a new sentence and writes “anything else” for the relative.
notes.other_reading: toward which, once you have inclined and turned aside, you will no longer be able

notes.note: Literally “without being dragged around”, that is, without distraction. It can go with “be able” or with “honor above all”; the sense is the same.
notes.other_reading: to honor undistracted

notes.note: Two words for one thought: ἴδιον is what belongs to a being as its own and no other’s, σόν is simply “yours”. The English reads “proper to you” for the first so that the pair does not say the same thing twice.
notes.other_reading: that good which is your own and yours

notes.greek: ἀντικαθῆσθαι γὰρ τῷ λογικῷ καὶ πολιτικῷ ἀγαθῷ οὐ θέμις
notes.note: ἀντικαθῆσθαι is to sit over against, used of an army encamped opposite another. θέμις is what divine law allows, so “not permitted” is still weaker than the Greek.
notes.other_reading: For it is not lawful that anything of another kind should sit encamped against the good of a rational being and a citizen

notes.note: πολιτικός means “of a citizen, made for life in a city”. “Civic” is used for it throughout this section to keep it apart from κοινωνικός, “social”.
notes.other_reading: the good of a rational being and a citizen

notes.note: In the Greek the examples follow “of a different kind” at the end of the clause. The English moves the whole phrase before the verb so that the examples are not read as examples of the good.
notes.other_reading: For it is not permitted that there should take up a position against the rational and civic good anything whatever of a different kind, such as praise from the many

notes.note: Two aorists of what regularly happens, with no object in the Greek. The English puts them in the present and supplies “you” with the second verb.
notes.other_reading: have suddenly prevailed and carried away

notes.note: An objection from an imagined speaker, as the edition’s quotation marks show. The Greek names no one who is benefited and the English leaves that open too; “you” in the reply is supplied from the commands that follow. “Benefits” is used and not the glossary’s “is good for”, because this passage also speaks of “the good” (ἀγαθόν) and the two would run together.
notes.other_reading: “But the better is what is good for a person.”

notes.greek: εἰ μὲν τὸ ὡς λογικῷ, τοῦτο τήρει· εἰ δὲ τὸ ὡς ζῴῳ, ἀπόφηναι
notes.note: Very compressed: “if the [benefit] as to a rational [being], keep this; if the one as to an animal, declare”. What is to be declared is not said; the English takes it as an admission that this is the kind of benefit meant. ζῷον is “animal” here because the contrast is with the rational being; in other passages of this section, where no such contrast is drawn, the word is “living being”.
notes.other_reading: If it is your benefit as a rational being, watch over it; but if as a living being, declare it

notes.note: τῦφος is smoke, and so puffed-up delusion or conceit. κρίσις is the deciding or its result; “verdict” keeps it apart from ὑπόληψις, “judgment”, as in 11.16. The clause can also be heard as “keep your judgment free of delusion”.
notes.other_reading: and keep your decision without self-deception

notes.note: ἀσφαλῶς is literally “without tripping”: securely, on firm footing. ἐξέτασις, “examination”, is the noun of the verb used above of the spirit that “examines the impressions”.
notes.other_reading: Only see that you make the examination securely.

check.greek: καὶ ἐν τῇ εἱμαρμένῃ ἐν τοῖς ἀπροαιρέτως ἀπονεμομένοις
check.note: The Greek as given has ἐν before “fate”, so fate is not the thing the thought is content with. The English translated a bare dative, “content with fate”, and the departure should be a decision and not silent.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now follows the Greek as given and reads “and in fate, in the things that are allotted without your choosing”, so that the thought is content with itself in both fields. “Content with fate”, the sense without the ἐν, is recorded in the note.

check.note: The participle is present. “Now that it is found” makes the finding a finished event, where the Greek can as well mean “what is found to be best”, matching “if you find” at the start.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “enjoy what is found to be best”. The participle is present and passive, so the finding stays open and no “you” is added; the finished-event reading is kept in the note.

check.note: The Greek says “the impressions”; “its own” is said only of the impulses in the clause before.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “which examines the impressions”. “Its own” belongs only to the impulses.

check.greek: πρὸς ὃ ῥέψας ἅπαξ καὶ ἀποκλίνας
check.note: Both participles hang on “toward which”. “Leaned away” with nothing after it reads as leaning away from something unnamed, which the Greek does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “Once you have tipped and turned aside toward anything else”, with both verbs governing “toward”. “Anything else” stands for the Greek relative and picks up “nothing else” from the sentence before.

check.note: “Your own and yours” reads as saying the same thing twice. The first word is “proper, peculiar to you”, the second “yours”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “that good which is proper to you and is yours”. The second “is” is added so that “you and yours” is not heard as one phrase.

check.note: θέμις is what sacred law or the established order allows; “not right” is the weaker, everyday word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “it is not permitted”. The Greek word is about what divine law allows, which “not right” did not reach.

check.greek: οἷον τὸν παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν ἔπαινον ἢ ἀρχὰς ἢ πλοῦτον ἢ ἀπολαύσεις ἡδονῶν
check.note: The examples belong to “anything of a different kind”. In the English they stood directly after “the rational and civic good” and read as examples of that good, the opposite of what is meant.
check.decided: Accepted: the list now stands directly after “anything whatever of a different kind”, and “the rational and civic good” closes the sentence. In the Greek the examples follow “of a different kind”, so this is their place.

check.note: There is no “me” in the Greek. Adding it settles in advance the question the next sentence asks: benefits you as rational, or as an animal.
check.decided: Accepted: the objection reads “But the better is what benefits.” The Greek names no one, and it is the reply that asks whose benefit is meant.

check.note: The contrast is rational being against mere animal. A rational being is also a living being, so “living being” does not make the contrast.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “But if as an animal”. The contrast is with the rational being, which “living being” would include; the note says that the word is “living being” in other passages of the section.

check.note: “Safely” is unclear here; the Greek word is “securely, without slipping”, that is, a test that cannot go wrong.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “Only see that you make the examination without slipping.” That is the literal sense of the Greek word and is clearer than “safely”; “soundly” is left for the word “soundest” in 4.51.

check.note: Found while settling: “hold your verdict” can be heard as “hold it back”, which the Greek does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “guard your verdict without conceit”. φύλασσε is the word for keeping watch over something.

passages.casaubon: If thou shalt find anything in this mortal life better than righteousness, than truth, temperance, fortitude, and in general better than a mind contented both with those things which according to right and reason she doth, and in those, which without her will and knowledge happen unto thee by the providence; if I say, thou canst find out anything better than this, apply thyself unto it with thy whole heart, and that which is best wheresoever thou dost find it, enjoy freely. But if nothing thou shalt find worthy to be preferred to that spirit which is within thee; if nothing better than to subject unto thee thine own lusts and desires, and not to give way to any fancies or imaginations before thou hast duly considered of them, nothing better than to withdraw thyself (to use Socrates his words) from all sensuality, and submit thyself unto the gods, and to have care of all men in general: if thou shalt find that all other things in comparison of this, are but vile, and of little moment; then give not way to any other thing, which being once though but affected and inclined unto, it will no more be in thy power without all distraction as thou oughtest to prefer and to pursue after that good, which is thine own and thy proper good. For it is not lawful, that anything that is of another and inferior kind and nature, be it what it will, as either popular applause, or honour, or riches, or pleasures; should be suffered to confront and contest as it were, with that which is rational, and operatively good. For all these things, if once though but for a while, they begin to please, they presently prevail, and pervert a man's mind, or turn a man from the right way. Do thou therefore I say absolutely and freely make choice of that which is best, and stick unto it. Now, that they say is best, which is most profitable. If they mean profitable to man as he is a rational man, stand thou to it, and maintain it; but if they mean profitable, as he is a creature, only reject it; and from this thy tenet and conclusion keep off carefully all plausible shows and colours of external appearance, that thou mayest be able to discern things rightly.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Ἐὰν τὸ παρὸν ἐνεργῇς ἑπόμενος τῷ ὀρθῷ λόγῳ, ἐσπουδασμένως, ἐρρωμένως, εὐμενῶς, καὶ μηδὲν παρεμπόρευμα, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονα καθαρὸν ἑστῶτα τηρῇς, ὡσεὶ καὶ ἤδη ἀποδοῦναι δέοι· ἐὰν τοῦτο συνάπτῃς μηδὲν περιμένων μηδὲ Φεύγων, ἀλλὰ τῇ παρούσῃ κατὰ Φύσιν ἐνεργείᾳ καὶ τῇ ὧν λέγεις καὶ Φθέγγῃ ἡρωικῇ ἀληθείᾳ ἀρκούμενος, εὐζωήσεις. ἔστι δὲ οὐδεὶς ὁ τοῦτο κωλῦσαι δυνάμενος.
passages.english: If you do the work that is present, following right reason, earnestly, vigorously, with good will, and with nothing as a side business, but keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment; if you join this together, waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing, but content with the present work that is according to nature and with heroic truth in what you say and utter, you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.

notes.note: ἐνεργῇς here and ἐνεργείᾳ below are the same word, verb and noun, and “present” is repeated with them. The English reads “do the work that is present” and “the present work” so that the close is heard picking up the opening. The word is strictly “be active” and “activity”.
notes.other_reading: If you are active in what is present

notes.note: There is no verb in the Greek: literally “and nothing a side-trade”. παρεμπόρευμα is goods dealt in on the side of one’s main trade. The English supplies “with” and “as” and takes the phrase with the doing of the present work; it can also be heard as a first object of “keep”.
notes.other_reading: and admit nothing as a sideline

notes.greek: τὸν ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονα καθαρὸν ἑστῶτα τηρῇς
notes.note: ἑαυτοῦ stands for “your own”, a common late use. δαίμων is “spirit” as in 3.6. ἑστῶτα is “standing”, with no “and” between it and “pure”; it may also be a quality of its own, standing firm or steady.
notes.other_reading: keep your own spirit pure and standing firm

notes.note: “To give back” what was lent or entrusted. The Greek does not say to whom.
notes.other_reading: as if you had to return it at once

notes.note: συνάπτω is to fasten or join together, the verb of “joining one good to another” in 12.29. The Greek does not say what is joined to what: it may be the present work and the pure spirit joined to each other, or the practice kept unbroken from one moment to the next.
notes.other_reading: if you keep this joined up without a break

notes.note: “Heroic truth” is a strange phrase and is translated as it stands: truthfulness of the kind the heroes of old had. From memory, unchecked: editors have doubted the adjective.
notes.other_reading: the truthfulness of a hero

notes.note: One word, “you will live well”, in the sense of a good and happy life.
notes.other_reading: you will have a happy life

check.note: “Carry out what is present” is not clear English; the Greek means the thing in hand.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “do the work that is present”. “In front of you” is not used, because the Greek word is “present” and it returns at the close, where the English has to be able to repeat it.

check.note: The Greek has no verb here: “and nothing a by-work”. The English supplies “with” and “as” smoothly, which is a fair repair but a repair.
check.decided: Accepted: “and with nothing as a side business” stays, and the note now says outright that the Greek has no verb and that “with” and “as” are supplied.

check.note: ἑστῶτα can be a second quality of its own, “standing firm, steady”, and not only the posture of the pure spirit.
check.decided: Declined: “standing pure” stays. The Greek has no “and” between the two words, so the closest English keeps them as one phrase; “pure and standing firm” is recorded in the note.

check.note: The verb in the active with an object is “join, fasten together”, as in 12.29, not “hold fast to”, which would need another form and case. The participles say how the joining is done: waiting for nothing, fleeing nothing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “if you join this together”. The verb is active with an object and means to join or fasten, as in 12.29; the note says that the Greek leaves open what is joined to what.

check.note: The close picks up the opening word for word, but the English had “carry out what is present” and then “present activity”. The article was also dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “content with the present work that is according to nature”, with the article, and the opening reads “do the work that is present”, so the same two words open and close the passage.

passages.casaubon: If thou shalt intend that which is present, following the rule of right and reason carefully, solidly, meekly, and shalt not intermix any other businesses, but shall study this only to preserve thy spirit unpolluted, and pure, and shall cleave unto him without either hope or fear of anything, in all things that thou shalt either do or speak, contenting thyself with heroical truth, thou shalt live happily; and from this, there is no man that can hinder thee.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Κάλλιστα διαζῆν, δύναμις αὕτη ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ, ἐὰν πρὸς τὰ ἀδιάφορά τις ἀδιαφορῇ. ἀδιαφορήσει δέ, ἐὰν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν θεωρῇ διῃρημένως καὶ ὁλικῶς καὶ μεμνημένος ὅτι οὐδὲν αὐτῶν ὑπόληψιν περὶ αὐτοῦ ἡμῖν ἐμποιεῖ οὐδὲ ἔρχεται ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἀτρεμεῖ, ἡμεῖς δέ ἐσμεν οἱ τὰς περὶ αὐτῶν κρίσεις γεννῶντες καὶ οἷον γράφοντες ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ἐξὸν μὲν μὴ γράφειν, ἐξὸν δέ, κἄν που λάθῃ, εὐθὺς ἐξαλεῖψαι· ὅτι ὀλίγου χρόνου ἔσται ἡ τοιαύτη προσοχὴ καὶ λοιπὸν πεπαύσεται ὁ βίος. τί μέντοι δύσκολον ἄλλως ἔχειν ταῦτα; εἰ μὲν γὰρ κατὰ φύσιν ἐστί, χαῖρε αὐτοῖς καὶ ῥᾴδια ἔστω σοι· εἰ δὲ παρὰ φύσιν, ζήτει τί ἐστί σοι κατὰ τὴν σὴν φύσιν καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦτο σπεῦδε, κἂν ἄδοξον ᾖ· παντὶ γὰρ συγγνώμη τὸ ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν ζητοῦντι.
passages.english: To live life through in the finest way: this power is in the soul, if a person is indifferent toward the things that are indifferent. And a person will be indifferent if they look at each of these things taken apart and as a whole, and remember that none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one somehow escapes notice, to wipe it out at once; and remember that this kind of attention will be for a short time, and after that life will be over. But what is hard in it, if these things are otherwise? For if they are according to nature, rejoice in them and let them be easy for you. And if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry toward that, even if it brings no reputation. For there is pardon for everyone who looks for their own good.

notes.greek: Κάλλιστα διαζῆν, δύναμις αὕτη ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ
notes.note: The opening is loose: an infinitive phrase, then “this power [is] in the soul”. The English keeps the looseness with a colon. κάλλιστα is “most finely, most nobly”.
notes.other_reading: The power to live life through in the noblest way is in the soul

notes.note: A play on one word. τὰ ἀδιάφορα is the Stoic term for things neither good nor bad in themselves, such as health, wealth, reputation and death; the verb says to be toward them as they are.
notes.other_reading: if one makes no difference of the things that make no difference

notes.note: Two adverbs: “dividedly and wholly”, that is, looking at the thing split into its parts and also as one whole.
notes.other_reading: by analysis and as a whole

notes.note: ὑπόληψις is “judgment” by the glossary; κρίσεις in the next clause is “verdicts” to keep the two words apart, though Marcus seems to mean much the same by both.
notes.other_reading: none of them produces in us an opinion about itself

notes.note: No subject is given: “even if perhaps it escapes notice”. The English takes the subject to be a verdict that got written without being noticed. που is “somehow, perhaps” and need not mean a place.
notes.other_reading: and, even if one has been written unawares

notes.greek: ὅτι ὀλίγου χρόνου ἔσται ἡ τοιαύτη προσοχὴ
notes.note: A bare “that” in the Greek, with no “and remember”; the English supplies the two words, taking the clause as a second thing to remember. The same Greek word can mean “because”, giving a reason for what goes before.
notes.other_reading: because this kind of attention will be for a short time

notes.greek: τί μέντοι δύσκολον ἄλλως ἔχειν ταῦτα;
notes.note: Word for word: “What, however, [is] hard [in] these things being otherwise?” The English keeps “hard”, which “easy” in the next sentence answers, and leaves “otherwise” as bare as the Greek, where the likeliest sense is “other than you would wish”. From memory, unchecked: some editors change ἄλλως to καλῶς, giving “what is hard about getting these things right?”
notes.other_reading: Yet what is so hard to bear if these things are other than you would wish?

notes.note: ἄδοξον is “without reputation”: either bringing no fame or held in low regard.
notes.other_reading: even if it is looked down on

notes.note: συγγνώμη is pardon or allowance that is available, not a forgiveness already given. The Greek has no verb: “for to everyone [there is] pardon who seeks their own good”.
notes.other_reading: for anyone may be excused for seeking their own good

check.greek: ἀδιαφορήσει δέ, ἐὰν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν θεωρῇ
check.note: Coming straight after “the things that are indifferent”, “they will be indifferent” reads first as said of the things. The subject is the person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “And a person will be indifferent if they look at each of these things”, so that the sentence cannot be heard as said of the things.

check.note: The Greek is “even if”, and the small word after it is more likely “somehow, at some point” than a place. “Slipped in” brings an image of its own; the Greek only says that it escaped notice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “even if one somehow escapes notice”. “Even” is restored and “slipped in somewhere” goes, since the Greek speaks only of escaping notice.

check.note: The Greek resumes with a bare “that”, with no “and remember”. The supplement is reasonable but it is added.
check.decided: Declined: “and remember” stays. The Greek “that” hangs on “remember” many lines above and the English sentence cannot be followed without the repeat; the note records that the two words are supplied.

check.greek: τί μέντοι δύσκολον ἄλλως ἔχειν ταῦτα;
check.note: The English is word for word and leaves the reader asking “otherwise than what?”; it can even be heard as “what is hard about changing these things”. The likelier sense is “what is there to resent if these things are not as you would have them”, which the next sentence answers.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “But what is hard in it, if these things are otherwise?”, which can no longer be heard as a question about changing them. “Hard” is kept because “easy” answers it in the next sentence, and “than you would wish” stays in the note because the Greek does not say it.

check.greek: τί ἐστί σοι κατὰ τὴν σὴν φύσιν
check.note: The Greek “for you” is dropped: “what there is for you that is according to your own nature”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature”, restoring “for you”. “According to nature” is kept as the one phrase for κατὰ φύσιν in this passage.

check.note: The Greek word is allowance or pardon available, not a forgiveness already granted. “Is forgiven” implies a fault committed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “For there is pardon for everyone who looks for their own good.” This no longer implies a fault already committed, and it keeps “everyone”, which “anyone” would weaken.

passages.casaubon: To live happily is an inward power of the soul, when she is affected with indifferency, towards those things that are by their nature indifferent. To be thus affected she must consider all worldly objects both divided and whole: remembering withal that no object can of itself beget any opinion in us, neither can come to us, but stands without still and quiet; but that we ourselves beget, and as it were print in ourselves opinions concerning them. Now it is in our power, not to print them; and if they creep in and lurk in some corner, it is in our power to wipe them off. Remembering moreover, that this care and circumspection of thine, is to continue but for a while, and then thy life will be at an end. And what should hinder, but that thou mayest do well with all these things? For if they be according to nature, rejoice in them, and let them be pleasing and acceptable unto thee. But if they be against nature, seek thou that which is according to thine own nature, and whether it be for thy credit or no, use all possible speed for the attainment of it: for no man ought to be blamed, for seeking his own good and happiness.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.greek: Μὴ τιμήσῃς ποτὲ ὡς συμφέρον σεαυτοῦ, ὃ ἀναγκάσει σέ ποτε τὴν πίστιν παραβῆναι, τὴν αἰδῶ ἐγκαταλιπεῖν, μισῆσαί τινα, ὑποπτεῦσαι, καταράσασθαι, ὑποκρίνασθαι, ἐπιθυμῆσαί τινος τοίχων καὶ παραπετασμάτων δεομένου. ὁ γὰρ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ νοῦν καὶ δαίμονα καὶ τὰ ὄργια τῆς τούτου ἀρετῆς προελόμενος τραγῳδίαν οὐ ποιεῖ, οὐ στενάζει, οὐκ ἐρημίας, οὐ πολυπληθείας δεήσεται· τὸ μέγιστον, ζήσει μήτε διώκων μήτε φεύγων, πότερον δὲ ἐπὶ πλέον διάστημα χρόνου τῷ σώματι περιεχομένῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ἢ ἐπ’ ἔλασσον χρήσεται, οὐδ᾽ ὁτιοῦν αὐτῷ μέλει· κἂν γὰρ ἤδη ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι δέῃ, οὕτως εὐλύτως ἄπεισιν, ὡς ἄλλο τι τῶν αἰδημόνως καὶ κοσμίως ἐνεργεῖσθαι δυναμένων ἐνεργήσων, τοῦτο μόνον παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον εὐλαβούμενος, τὸ τὴν διάνοιαν ἔν τινι ἀνοικείῳ νοεροῦ καὶ πολιτικοῦ ζῴου τροπῇ γενέσθαι.
passages.english: Never value as a benefit to yourself anything that will one day force you to break faith, to abandon your self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, to desire something that needs walls and curtains. For whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue, does not make a tragedy of things, does not groan, will need neither solitude nor a crowd. Greatest of all, they will live neither pursuing nor fleeing. Whether they will have the use of the soul, enclosed in the body, for a longer stretch of time or a shorter one matters to them not at all. For even if they have to depart this moment, they will go as free of ties as if they were about to do any other of the things that can be done with self-respect and in good order, on their guard through their whole life against this one thing only: that their thought should take any turn foreign to a living being that has mind and is civic.

notes.note: τὸ συμφέρον with a genitive, “an advantage of your own”. The English reads “a benefit to yourself” and not the glossary’s “good for”, so that the word answers the objection that closes 3.6, the chapter before this one in the book: “the better is what benefits”.
notes.other_reading: as good for yourself

notes.note: πίστις is trust, good faith, a pledge given. “Break faith” covers both breaking a promise and betraying a trust.
notes.other_reading: to break your word

notes.note: αἰδώς is the sense of shame that holds a person back from what is unworthy of them. The English reads “self-respect” and keeps the same word for the adverb αἰδημόνως later in the passage.
notes.other_reading: to abandon your sense of shame

notes.note: The word for acting on a stage, and so for pretending.
notes.other_reading: to be a hypocrite

notes.note: προαιρέομαι is to choose one thing in preference to others. The Greek does not say “before everything”.
notes.other_reading: has chosen first

notes.note: ὄργια are the secret rites of a mystery cult; the person is pictured as the worshipper of the spirit within. τούτου, “of this one”, is taken as the spirit. ἀρετή is “virtue” or “excellence”.
notes.other_reading: the worship of its excellence

notes.note: Literally “does not compose a tragedy”: does not turn their life into a stage lament. The English keeps the word “tragedy” and supplies “of things”.
notes.other_reading: does not play the tragic actor

notes.note: The Greek moves from the present (“does not make a tragedy, does not groan”) to the future here and in what follows; the English keeps the shift.
notes.other_reading: needs neither solitude nor a crowd

notes.note: εὐλύτως is “in a way easily loosed”, like something untied without trouble; “free of ties” keeps that picture.
notes.other_reading: they will go as easily

notes.note: τροπή is a turning or change of direction; literally the thought “comes to be in a turn” that is foreign to such a being. The verb εὐλαβούμενος already means “guarding against”, so the Greek has no “not”.
notes.other_reading: that their thought should fall into any condition foreign to

notes.note: νοερός is “of mind” by the glossary, matching νοῦς, “mind”, earlier in the passage, so the English reads “that has mind”. πολιτικός is “civic”, as in 3.6: made for life among fellow citizens.
notes.other_reading: a thinking creature and a citizen

check.note: 3.6 ends on the same word, there “what benefits”, and 3.7 opens by picking it up, but here it became “good for”, and “good” is also the word for ἀγαθόν in 3.6. The link between the two chapters is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “Never value as a benefit to yourself”. The word now matches “what benefits” at the end of 3.6, which this chapter takes up, and the note says why the glossary’s “good for” is not used here.

check.note: The verb is “choose, prefer”; “before everything” presses the prefix harder than the Greek does.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit”. The verb is to choose one thing over others, and “before everything” said more than that.

check.note: “Makes no tragedy” is not an English idiom; the sense is striking no tragic pose, making no drama.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “does not make a tragedy of things”, which is an English idiom and keeps the Greek’s own word. “Drama” would lose the stage tragedy that the Greek names.

check.note: The adverb is “easily loosed, unencumbered”, the image of something that comes untied without trouble; “easily” keeps only half of it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “they will go as free of ties”. That gives the untying in the Greek word in one phrase; “as lightly” beside it would make two words out of one.

check.note: The same verb twice in the Greek, two verbs in the English (“carry out”, “done”).
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “do any other of the things that can be done”, one verb for the one Greek verb.

check.greek: ἔν τινι ἀνοικείῳ νοεροῦ καὶ πολιτικοῦ ζῴου τροπῇ γενέσθαι
check.note: “Come into any turn” is not English, and the double “that … that” is hard to follow.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “that their thought should take any turn foreign to a living being that has mind and is civic”. “Take any turn” and “foreign to” are adopted; “a living being that has mind” is kept, because “mind” has to answer the same word earlier in the passage.

passages.casaubon: Never esteem of anything as profitable, which shall ever constrain thee either to break thy faith, or to lose thy modesty; to hate any man, to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything, that requireth the secret of walls or veils. But he that preferreth before all things his rational part and spirit, and the sacred mysteries of virtue which issueth from it, he shall never lament and exclaim, never sigh; he shall never want either solitude or company: and which is chiefest of all, he shall live without either desire or fear. And as for life, whether for a long or short time he shall enjoy his soul thus compassed about with a body, he is altogether indifferent. For if even now he were to depart, he is as ready for it, as for any other action, which may be performed with modesty and decency. For all his life long, this is his only care, that his mind may always be occupied in such intentions and objects, as are proper to a rational sociable creature.

passages.greek: Σωτηρία βίου ἕκαστον δι’ ὅλου αὐτὸ τί ἐστιν ὁρᾶν, τί μὲν αὐτοῦ τὸ ὑλικόν, τί δὲ τὸ αἰτιῶδες· ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ δίκαια ποιεῖν καὶ τἀληθῆ λέγειν. τί λοιπὸν ἢ ἀπολαύειν τοῦ ζῆν συνάπτοντα ἄλλο ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ ἀγαθόν, ὥστε μηδὲ τὸ βραχύτατον διάστημα ἀπολείπειν;
passages.english: What keeps a life safe: to see each thing through and through, what it is in itself, what in it is the material and what the cause; with the whole soul to do what is just and to say what is true. What is left but to enjoy living, joining one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap?

notes.note: Two words with no verb: “safety of life” or “the saving of a life”. The English turns them into a clause.
notes.other_reading: The salvation of life is this

notes.note: With the preposition before it the phrase is “through the whole”: either seeing the whole of each thing or seeing it thoroughly. αὐτὸ τί ἐστιν is “what it is itself”.
notes.other_reading: to see what each thing is in itself, as a whole

notes.greek: τί μὲν αὐτοῦ τὸ ὑλικόν, τί δὲ τὸ αἰτιῶδες
notes.note: The two Stoic principles: the matter a thing is made of and the cause that shapes and moves it. Marcus uses the pair often.
notes.other_reading: what its matter is and what its causal part

notes.note: The same words as in 3.6, where the English has “with your whole soul” because a command is addressed to “you”. Here the Greek is impersonal throughout and the article is kept.
notes.other_reading: with your whole soul

notes.note: “Fastening one good onto another”, like links in a chain. ἀγαθόν is neuter, “a good thing”; in context it is probably a good act.
notes.other_reading: linking one good deed to the next

notes.note: An interval, here of time left empty between one good and the next.
notes.other_reading: the briefest interval

check.note: The same phrase is “with your whole soul” in 3.6. Nothing is wrong in the passage itself; only the two should match.
check.decided: Declined: “with the whole soul” stays. The Greek has “the whole soul” in both places and no “your”; in 3.6 “your” comes from the command addressed to “you”, while this passage is impersonal from start to finish. A note now records the match.

passages.casaubon: Herein doth consist happiness of life, for a man to know thoroughly the true nature of everything; what is the matter, and what is the form of it: with all his heart and soul, ever to do that which is just, and to speak the truth. What then remaineth but to enjoy thy life in a course and coherence of good actions, one upon another immediately succeeding, and never interrupted, though for never so little a while?

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Παρατήρει τί σου ἡ φύσις ἐπιζητεῖ ὡς ὑπὸ φύσεως μόνον διοικουμένου· εἶτα ποίει αὐτὸ καὶ προσίεσο, εἰ μὴ χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαί σου ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις. ἑξῆς δὲ παρατηρητέον τί ἐπιζητεῖ σου ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις, καὶ πᾶν τοῦτο παραληπτέον, εἰ μὴ χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαι ἡ ὡς ζῴου λογικοῦ φύσις· ἔστι δὲ τὸ λογικὸν εὐθὺς καὶ πολιτικόν. τούτοις δὴ κανόσι χρώμενος μηδὲν περιεργάζου.
passages.english: Watch what your nature asks for, taking yourself as something governed by nature only. Then do it and accept it, unless your nature as an animal is going to be put in a worse state. Next you must watch what your nature as an animal asks for, and all of this is to be taken up, unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state. And what is rational is by that very fact also civic. Using these rules, then, do not busy yourself with anything further.

notes.note: φύσις here has its narrow Stoic sense: the power of growth and nourishment that governs plants, below the soul that governs animals. So the first step is what you need simply as a growing body. ὡς with the participle means “regarded as”, not a statement that this is all you are.
notes.other_reading: as one governed only by the nature of a growing thing

notes.note: προσίεσο is “let it come to you, admit it”.
notes.other_reading: do it and allow it

notes.note: ζῷον is a being with soul and sensation, one step above a thing that only grows. The English reads “animal” here so that the three steps stay apart: a growing thing, an animal, a rational animal. In other passages of this section, where no such ladder is in play, the word is “living being”.
notes.other_reading: your nature as a living being

notes.note: Literally “is going to be disposed worse”.
notes.other_reading: is going to be the worse for it

notes.greek: ἔστι δὲ τὸ λογικὸν εὐθὺς καὶ πολιτικόν
notes.note: εὐθύς is “straight away, immediately”: being rational brings being civic with it at once. πολιτικός is “civic” as in 3.6.
notes.other_reading: and the rational is at once also made for a city

notes.note: περιεργάζομαι is to do more than is needed, to fuss, or to meddle in what is not one’s business. The English takes the prefix as “beyond what these rules ask”.
notes.other_reading: do not fuss over anything

check.note: The Greek is “as (the nature) of something governed only by nature”, that is, taking yourself for the moment as a thing that merely grows. “Insofar as you are” states it as a fact, and the reader has no sign that “nature” here is the narrow sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “taking yourself as something governed by nature only”. The Greek asks for this way of regarding yourself at the first step and does not state it as a fact; the note explains the narrow sense of “nature”.

check.note: The passage climbs three steps: a growing thing, an animal, a rational animal. A growing thing is a living being too, so “living being” does not mark the second step off from the first.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “your nature as an animal” and “your nature as a rational animal”. A growing thing is alive too, so “living being” did not mark the second step off from the first.

check.greek: εἰ μὴ χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαί σου ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις
check.note: “By it” is supplied, here and in the next sentence. Harmless.
check.decided: Accepted: “by it” is removed in both sentences. The Greek does not have it and the condition is clear without it.

check.note: The verb is to fuss, meddle, be over-curious. “Anything further” is one way to take the prefix; the other is simply “do not fuss over anything”.
check.decided: Declined: “do not busy yourself with anything further” stays. The verb is to be busy beyond what is needed, and “further” gives that prefix; “do not fuss over anything” is recorded in the note.

passages.casaubon: As one who is altogether governed by nature, let it be thy care to observe what it is that thy nature in general doth require. That done, if thou find not that thy nature, as thou art a living sensible creature, will be the worse for it, thou mayest proceed. Next then thou must examine, what thy nature as thou art a living sensible creature, doth require. And that, whatsoever it be, thou mayest admit of and do it, if thy nature as thou art a reasonable living creature, will not be the worse for it. Now whatsoever is reasonable, is also sociable, Keep thyself to these rules, and trouble not thyself about idle things.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Τούτων ἀεὶ δεῖ μεμνῆσθαι, τίς ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις καὶ τίς ἡ ἐμὴ καὶ πῶς αὕτη πρὸς ἐκείνην ἔχουσα καὶ ὁποῖόν τι μέρος ὁποίου τοῦ ὅλου οὖσα καὶ ὅτι οὐδεὶς ὁ κωλύων τὰ ἀκόλουθα τῇ φύσει, ἧς μέρος εἶ, πράσσειν τε ἀεὶ καὶ λέγειν.
passages.english: These things must always be remembered: what the nature of the whole is, and what mine is, and how this one stands to that one, and what kind of part it is of what kind of whole; and that there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part.

notes.note: Glossary rendering. The Greek is plural, “of all things together”.
notes.other_reading: the nature of all things

notes.greek: ὁποῖόν τι μέρος ὁποίου τοῦ ὅλου οὖσα
notes.note: Literally “being what sort of part of what sort of whole”.
notes.other_reading: what sort of part it is, and of what sort of whole

notes.note: The Greek moves from “mine” to “you are”, and the English keeps the shift. “You” after “prevents” is supplied from this clause.
notes.other_reading: of which I am a part

notes.note: Literally “the things that follow nature”, as a companion follows: what is consistent with it, not what is deduced from it.
notes.other_reading: what follows from the nature

check.note: The Greek word with this case is “in keeping with, consistent with”; “follows from” suggests a logical deduction.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part”. The Greek word means following as a companion does, not following as a conclusion does.

passages.casaubon: These things thou must always have in mind: What is the nature of the universe, and what is mine--in particular: This unto that what relation it hath: what kind of part, of what kind of universe it is: And that there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature, whereof thou art a part.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Συντιθέναι δεῖ τὸν βίον κατὰ μίαν πρᾶξιν καὶ εἰ ἑκάστη τὸ ἑαυτῆς παρέχει ὡς οἷόν τε, ἀρκεῖσθαι· ἵνα δὲ τὸ ἑαυτῆς παρέχῃ, οὐδὲ εἷς σε κωλῦσαι δύναται.—ἀλλʼ ἐνστήσεταί τι ἔξωθεν.—οὐδὲν εἴς γε τὸ δικαίως καὶ σωφρόνως καὶ εὐλογίστως, ἄλλο δέ τι ἴσως ἐνεργητικὸν κωλυθήσεται, ἀλλὰ τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ κώλυμα εὐαρεστήσει καὶ τῇ ἐπὶ τὸ διδόμενον εὐγνώμονι μεταβάσει εὐθὺς ἄλλη πρᾶξις ἀντικαθίσταται ἐναρμόσουσα εἰς τὴν σύνθεσιν, περὶ ἧς ὁ λόγος.
passages.english: You must put your life together one action at a time, and if each action does its own part as far as it can, be content. And no one at all can prevent you from having it do its own part. “But something from outside will stand in the way.” Nothing will, at least not in the way of acting justly, with self-control and with good sense. Some other kind of activity will perhaps be prevented; but through being well pleased with the very thing that prevents it, and through moving over with good grace to what is given, another action at once takes its place, one that will fit into the putting together of which we are speaking.

notes.note: The verb and the noun σύνθεσιν at the end are one word; the English reads “put together” and “the putting together” so the link shows.
notes.other_reading: You must compose your life

notes.note: “By one action”, that is, action by single action.
notes.other_reading: action by action

notes.note: Literally “supplies what is its own”, with the noun left unsaid. The English reads “does its own part”; the words can also mean that the action reaches its own end.
notes.other_reading: achieves its own end

notes.note: The edition marks a change of speaker with dashes. The English uses quotation marks for the objection and none for the reply.
notes.other_reading: “But some outside thing will block it.”

notes.greek: οὐδὲν εἴς γε τὸ δικαίως καὶ σωφρόνως καὶ εὐλογίστως
notes.note: There is no verb: “nothing, at least for the justly and self-controlledly and reasonably”. The English supplies “acting”. εὐλογίστως is “with sound reckoning”.
notes.other_reading: Nothing, at least, that stops you being just, self-controlled and reasonable

notes.note: “Something else of an active kind”: some outward doing, as against the manner of acting just named.
notes.other_reading: but perhaps some other exercise of your activity

notes.note: κώλυμα is the noun of the verb “prevent” used twice before it in the passage: the thing that prevents. The English writes it out as “the very thing that prevents it” so that the three can be heard together.
notes.other_reading: the obstacle itself

notes.note: A noun in the dative, “by a being well pleased”, not a verb. “Well pleased” is used for this word family here and in 10.6, to keep it apart from ἀρκεῖσθαι, “be content”.
notes.other_reading: by accepting the obstacle itself gladly

notes.note: εὐγνώμων is fair-minded, sensible, good-tempered; μετάβασις is a stepping across.
notes.other_reading: by a sensible change over to what is given

check.note: “Delivers what is its own” is literal and unclear to a reader; the sense is that each action yields what belongs to it, does its own part.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “does its own part”, here and in the next sentence. The literal “supplies what is its own” is kept in the note.

check.greek: ἄλλο δέ τι ἴσως ἐνεργητικὸν κωλυθήσεται
check.note: One hedge in the Greek with a plain future, two in the English (“may perhaps”).
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “Some other kind of activity will perhaps be prevented”, one hedge and a plain future as in the Greek.

check.greek: τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ κώλυμα εὐαρεστήσει
check.note: Three words of one family in the Greek became “prevent”, “prevented” and then “obstacle”, so the point that the very thing that hinders becomes the material is less visible.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the three words are now one family in English, “prevent”, “prevented” and “the very thing that prevents it”. “Prevent” is kept and not “hinder”, because it is the word for this verb in 3.12, 2.9 and 6.58.

passages.casaubon: Contract thy whole life to the measure and proportion of one single action. And if in every particular action thou dost perform what is fitting to the utmost of thy power, let it suffice thee. And who can hinder thee, but that thou mayest perform what is fitting? But there may be some outward let and impediment. Not any, that can hinder thee, but that whatsoever thou dost, thou may do it, justly, temperately, and with the praise of God. Yea, but there may be somewhat, whereby some operation or other of thine may be hindered. And then, with that very thing that doth hinder, thou mayest he well pleased, and so by this gentle and equanimious conversion of thy mind unto that which may be, instead of that which at first thou didst intend, in the room of that former action there succeedeth another, which agrees as well with this contraction of thy life, that we now speak of.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: ʽὈλίγα πρῆσσε, φησίν, εἰ μέλλεις εὐθυμήσειν.ʼ μήποτε ἄμεινον τἀναγκαῖα πράσσειν καὶ ὅσα ὁ τοῦ φύσει πολιτικοῦ ζῴου λόγος αἱρεῖ καὶ ὡς αἱρεῖ; τοῦτο γὰρ οὐ μόνον τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ καλῶς πράσσειν εὐθυμίαν φέρει, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀλίγα πράσσειν. τὰ πλεῖστα γὰρ ὧν λέγομεν καὶ πράσσομεν οὐκ ἀναγκαῖα ὄντα ἐάν τις περιέλῃ, εὐσχολώτερος καὶ ἀταρακτότερος ἔσται. ὅθεν δεῖ καὶ παῤ ἕκαστα ἑαυτὸν ὑπομιμνῄσκειν· μήτι τοῦτο τῶν οὐκ ἀναγκαίων; δεῖ δὲ μὴ μόνον πράξεις τὰς μὴ ἀναγκαίας περιαιρεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ φαντασίας· οὕτως γὰρ οὐδὲ πράξεις παρέλκουσαι ἐπακολουθήσουσιν.
passages.english: “Do few things,” he says, “if you mean to be cheerful.” Might it not be better to do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a living being that is civic by nature requires, and in the way it requires? For this brings not only the cheerfulness that comes from doing things well, but also the cheerfulness that comes from doing few things. For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a person strips it away they will have more leisure and be less troubled. So on each occasion one must also remind oneself: “Is this perhaps one of the things that are not necessary?” And one must strip away not only the actions that are not necessary but impressions too, for then superfluous actions will not follow after them either.

notes.note: The quotation is in Ionic dialect (πρῆσσε for πρᾶσσε), and “he says” names no one. From memory, unchecked: it is a saying of Democritus.
notes.other_reading: “Do little,” it is said

notes.note: εὐθυμία is good spirits, a settled and contented mind and not a passing mood. “Cheerful” and “cheerfulness” are kept for the verb and the noun.
notes.other_reading: if you mean to be of good heart

notes.note: In later Greek this opens a cautious suggestion, “perhaps”. The edition prints the sentence as a question.
notes.other_reading: Perhaps it is better

notes.note: ὁ λόγος αἱρεῖ is a set phrase, “reason proves, reason dictates”; literally reason “takes” or “chooses”.
notes.other_reading: chooses, and as it chooses

notes.note: πράσσειν is “do” throughout the passage, so “doing things well” is kept; the sense is acting rightly, not prospering.
notes.other_reading: from acting rightly

notes.note: Two comparatives: “more at leisure and more undisturbed”.
notes.other_reading: will have more free time and more calm

notes.note: The Greek does not repeat “not necessary” with the impressions and has no article. The words are most naturally carried over from the actions, and the English leaves them to be carried over in the same way.
notes.other_reading: but unnecessary impressions too

notes.note: Literally “dragging alongside”: trailing after to no purpose, superfluous.
notes.other_reading: idle actions

check.note: The Greek word is settled good spirits, contentment of mind; “cheerful” and “cheerfulness” are lighter and more a matter of mood.
check.decided: Declined: “cheerful” and “cheerfulness” stay. The Greek word is literally good spirits, “cheerful” is the plain word of today for that, and the note records the fuller sense of a settled mind.

check.note: “At each thing” is not natural English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “on each occasion”, which is what the Greek phrase means. “At every step” would bring in a picture the Greek does not have.

check.note: There is no article in the Greek, and “not necessary” carries over from the actions: unnecessary impressions. “The impressions” reads as all impressions.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the article is dropped and the English reads “but impressions too”. “Unnecessary” is not written in, because the Greek leaves it to be carried over from the actions and the English sentence does the same; a note says so.

check.note: The participle is “superfluous, redundant”. “Idle actions” suggests doing nothing, and there is no article.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “superfluous actions”, without the article. “Idle” could be heard as doing nothing.

passages.casaubon: They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt live cheerfully. Certainly there is nothing better, than for a man to confine himself to necessary actions; to such and so many only, as reason in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command and enjoin. This will not only procure that cheerfulness, which from the goodness, but that also, which from the paucity of actions doth usually proceed. For since it is so, that most of those things, which we either speak or do, are unnecessary; if a man shall cut them off, it must needs follow that he shall thereby gain much leisure, and save much trouble, and therefore at every action a man must privately by way of admonition suggest unto himself, What? may not this that now I go about, be of the number of unnecessary actions? Neither must he use himself to cut off actions only, but thoughts and imaginations also, that are unnecessary for so will unnecessary consequent actions the better be prevented and cut off.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Εἴτε ἄτομοι εἴτε φύσις, πρῶτον κείσθω ὅτι μέρος εἰμὶ τοῦ ὅλου ὑπὸ φύσεως διοικουμένου· ἔπειτα, ὅτι ἔχω πως οἰκείως πρὸς τὰ ὁμογενῆ μέρη. τούτων γὰρ μεμνημένος, καθότι μὲν μέρος εἰμί, οὐδενὶ δυσαρεστήσω τῶν ἐκ τοῦ ὅλου ἀπονεμομένων· οὐδὲν γὰρ βλαβερὸν τῷ μέρει ὃ τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρει. οὐ γὰρ ἔχει τι τὸ ὅλον ὃ μὴ συμφέρει ἑαυτῷ, πασῶν μὲν φύσεων κοινὸν ἐχουσῶν τοῦτο, τῆς δὲ τοῦ κόσμου προσειληφυίας τὸ μηδὲ ὑπό τινος ἔξωθεν αἰτίας ἀναγκάζεσθαι βλαβερόν τι ἑαυτῇ γεννᾶν. κατὰ μὲν δὴ τὸ μεμνῆσθαι ὅτι μέρος εἰμὶ ὅλου τοῦ τοιούτου, εὐαρεστήσω παντὶ τῷ ἀποβαίνοντι, καθόσον δὲ ἔχω πως οἰκείως πρὸς τὰ ὁμογενῆ μέρη, οὐδὲν πράξω ἀκοινώνητον, μᾶλλον δὲ στοχάσομαι τῶν ὁμογενῶν καὶ πρὸς τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον πᾶσαν ὁρμὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ἄξω καὶ ἀπὸ τοὐναντίου ἀπάξω. τούτων δὲ οὕτως περαινομένων ἀνάγκη τὸν βίον εὐροεῖν, ὡς ἂν καὶ πολίτου βίον εὔρουν ἐπινοήσειας προιόντος διὰ πράξεων τοῖς πολίταις λυσιτελῶν καὶ ὅπερ ἂν ἡ πόλις ἀπονέμῃ, τοῦτο ἀσπαζομένου.
passages.english: Whether it is atoms or nature, let this first be laid down: that I am a part of the whole, which is governed by nature. Next, that I stand in a kind of kinship to the parts that are of the same kind as I am. For if I remember these things, then insofar as I am a part, I will not be displeased with anything that is allotted from the whole. For nothing that is good for the whole is harmful to the part. For the whole has nothing that is not good for itself. All natures have this in common, but the nature of the universe has this in addition, that it is not even forced by any cause from outside to produce anything harmful to itself. So by remembering that I am a part of a whole of this kind, I will be well pleased with everything that comes about. And insofar as I stand in a kind of kinship to the parts of the same kind, I will do nothing unsocial. Rather I will make those of my own kind my aim, and I will lead my every impulse toward what is good for all in common and lead it away from the opposite. When these things are carried through in this way, life must flow well, just as you would think that a citizen’s life flows well when that citizen goes forward through actions that profit the citizens, and welcomes whatever the city allots.

notes.note: The Epicurean account (atoms moving at random) against the Stoic one (an ordering nature). The Greek has no verb. The next clause already says the whole is “governed by nature”, which sits oddly with leaving the question open; it is translated as it stands.
notes.other_reading: Whether there are atoms or a nature

notes.note: οἰκείως ἔχειν is to be related to something as to what belongs to one’s own household. πως, “in some way”, softens it.
notes.other_reading: to be in some way closely bound to

notes.note: “The parts of the same kind”, or of the same birth. The words “as I am” are supplied.
notes.other_reading: the kindred parts

notes.note: δυσαρεστεῖν and εὐαρεστεῖν later in the passage are a matched pair; the English reads “displeased” and “well pleased”.
notes.other_reading: to resent nothing

notes.greek: οὐδὲν γὰρ βλαβερὸν τῷ μέρει ὃ τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρει
notes.note: Word order in the Greek: “for nothing is harmful to the part which is good for the whole”. The English turns it round so the relative clause is not misread as describing the part. συμφέρει is “is good for” by the glossary; in τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον below, “what is good for all in common”, the words “for all” are supplied.
notes.other_reading: for nothing harms the part that benefits the whole

notes.note: The negative of κοινωνικός, “social”: an act that takes no share in the common life. The Greek answers it at once with κοινῇ, “in common”, an echo the English does not keep.
notes.other_reading: nothing that breaks the common bond

notes.note: στοχάζομαι is to aim at a target, and so to have something in view; the English keeps the picture of aiming without the sound of an attack. The genitive may be masculine (those of the same kind) or neuter (the parts of the same kind), and the possessive is supplied.
notes.other_reading: to have regard for the parts of the same kind

notes.note: Glossary rendering, “carried through”.
notes.other_reading: When this is accomplished in this way

notes.note: “To flow well”. From memory, unchecked: “a good flow of life” is an early Stoic description of happiness. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: life must go smoothly

notes.note: The passage is in the first person, but this verb is second person, “you would think”, and is kept so. The citizen is masculine in the Greek but stands for any citizen, so the English avoids “he”.
notes.other_reading: just as one would think

check.note: The word is “good for” throughout this passage but “what benefits” in 3.6, and “good” is the word for ἀγαθόν elsewhere in the section.
check.decided: Declined: “is good for” stays. It is the rendering this translation has settled for συμφέρει, and this passage does not use the word “good” for anything else, so nothing runs together here; 3.6 and 3.7 have “benefits” for a reason given in their notes.

check.greek: τὸ μηδὲ ὑπό τινος ἔξωθεν αἰτίας ἀναγκάζεσθαι
check.note: The Greek has “not even”: other natures can at least be forced from outside, this one not even that. The “even” is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “that it is not even forced by any cause from outside”. The Greek has “not even”, and the point is that other natures can at least be forced.

check.note: The Greek word is answered at once by “in common”; the echo is lost in “unsocial … in common”.
check.decided: Declined: “nothing unsocial” stays. “Social” is the settled word for κοινωνικός and this is its negative, while “the common bond” would bring in a picture the Greek does not have. The note now points out the echo with “in common”.

check.note: “Aim at” people sounds hostile in English; the sense is to keep them in view as the target of what one does.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now makes “those of my own kind” the aim, in the words “make those of my own kind my aim”. This removes the hostile sound of “aim at” and keeps the Greek picture of aiming at a target, which “keep in view” would lose.

check.note: “Other” is added.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “actions that profit the citizens”. “Other” is not in the Greek.

passages.casaubon: Either with Epicurus, we must fondly imagine the atoms to be the cause of all things, or we must needs grant a nature. Let this then be thy first ground, that thou art part of that universe, which is governed by nature. Then secondly, that to those parts that are of the same kind and nature as thou art, thou hast relation of kindred. For of these, if I shall always be mindful, first as I am a part, I shall never be displeased with anything, that falls to my particular share of the common chances of the world. For nothing that is behoveful unto the whole, can be truly hurtful to that which is part of it. For this being the common privilege of all natures, that they contain nothing in themselves that is hurtful unto them; it cannot be that the nature of the universe (whose privilege beyond other particular natures, is, that she cannot against her will by any higher external cause be constrained,) should beget anything and cherish it in her bosom that should tend to her own hurt and prejudice. As then I bear in mind that I am a part of such an universe, I shall not be displeased with anything that happens. And as I have relation of kindred to those parts that are of the same kind and nature that I am, so I shall be careful to do nothing that is prejudicial to the community, but in all my deliberations shall they that are of my kind ever be; and the common good, that, which all my intentions and resolutions shall drive unto, as that which is contrary unto it, I shall by all means endeavour to prevent and avoid. These things once so fixed and concluded, as thou wouldst think him a happy citizen, whose constant study and practice were for the good and benefit of his fellow citizens, and the carriage of the city such towards him, that he were well pleased with it; so must it needs be with thee, that thou shalt live a happy life.

passages.greek: Δύνασαι ἀεὶ εὐροεῖν, εἴ γε καὶ εὐοδεῖν, εἴ γε καὶ ὁδῷ ὑπολαμβάνειν καὶ πράσσειν. δύο ταῦτα κοινὰ τῇ τε τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τῇ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ παντὸς λογικοῦ ζῴου ψυχῇ· τὸ μὴ ἐμποδίζεσθαι ὑπ’ ἄλλου καὶ τὸ ἐν τῇ δικαικῇ διαθέσει καὶ πράξει ἔχειν τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἐνταῦθα τὴν ὄρεξιν ἀπολήγειν.
passages.english: You can always have your life flow well, if indeed you can also travel a good road, if indeed you can also judge and act step by step, as along a road. These two things are common to the soul of god, and of a human being, and of every rational living being: not to be hindered by anything else; and to have its good in a just disposition and just action, and to have its desire stop there.

notes.note: The Greek says simply “you can always flow well”. “Have your life” is supplied because 10.6 uses the same verb of a life and English does not say that a person flows.
notes.other_reading: You can always flow well

notes.note: A chain of sound and sense: εὐροεῖν (flow well), εὐοδεῖν (have a good road), ὁδῷ (by a road). ὁδῷ is an idiom for “methodically, in due order”; the English gives the sense as “step by step”, as in 6.26, and adds “as along a road” so that the play can be followed.
notes.other_reading: if you can also go on your way well, if you can also judge and act methodically

notes.note: The verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment” in the glossary: to form a judgment about things.
notes.other_reading: to think

notes.note: “The god” with the article, which in Marcus is god in general or the god of the universe. Lower case by the glossary.
notes.other_reading: the soul of the god

notes.note: ἄλλου can be masculine, “by another person”, or neuter, “by anything else”. The English takes the wider sense, which includes the other.
notes.other_reading: not to be hindered by another

notes.greek: ἐν τῇ δικαικῇ διαθέσει καὶ πράξει
notes.note: δικαικῇ is a rare adjective, “of justice”, read here as the edition’s δικαϊκῇ. It governs both nouns, so “just” is repeated.
notes.other_reading: in the disposition and action that belong to justice

notes.note: ὄρεξιν is taken as the subject of the infinitive, “desire coming to a stop there”. It can also be the object, “to bring desire to a stop there”.
notes.other_reading: and to end its desire there

check.note: “Your life” is supplied; the Greek is the bare verb, “you can always flow well”. Reasonable beside 10.6, but added.
check.decided: Declined: “have your life flow well” stays. English does not say of a person that they flow, the same verb is said of a life in 10.6, and the note records that “your life” is supplied.

check.note: ὁδῷ is the set phrase “by a road”, that is, in order, methodically; in 6.26 the same word is “step by step”. “As one who keeps to a road” saves the play but is obscure and does not match.
