check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “judge and act step by step, as along a road”. “Step by step” now matches the same word in 6.26, and the road is kept beside it so that the play with “a good road” can still be heard.

check.note: The Greek word can be neuter, “by anything else”. “By another” limits it to a person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “not to be hindered by anything else”. The Greek word can be a person or a thing, and the wider wording covers both; the note records “by another”.

check.note: Found while settling: “keep to a good road” suggests staying on course by effort, but εὐοδεῖν is to have a good road, an easy passage.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “travel a good road”, which says that the going is good and not that the traveler holds the line.

passages.casaubon: Thou mayest always speed, if thou wilt but make choice of the right way; if in the course both of thine opinions and actions, thou wilt observe a true method. These two things be common to the souls, as of God, so of men, and of every reasonable creature, first that in their own proper work they cannot be hindered by anything: and secondly, that their happiness doth consist in a disposition to, and in the practice of righteousness; and that in these their desire is terminated.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Ἐπὶ τὴν σύντομον ἀεὶ τρέχε· σύντομος δὲ ἡ κατὰ φύσιν, ὥστε κατὰ τὸ ὑγιέστατον πᾶν λέγειν καὶ πράσσειν. ἀπαλλάσσει γὰρ ἡ τοιαύτη πρόθεσις κόπων καὶ στραγγείας καὶ πάσης οἰκονομίας καὶ κομψείας.
passages.english: Always run to the short road. And the short road is the one according to nature, so that you say and do everything in the soundest way. For a purpose of this kind frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.

notes.note: The noun is left out, as Greek does with “road”: “the short [road]”. ἐπί with the accusative is “to” or “for”: make for the short road and take it.
notes.other_reading: Always run by the short road.

notes.greek: ὥστε κατὰ τὸ ὑγιέστατον πᾶν λέγειν καὶ πράσσειν
notes.note: ὥστε with the infinitive gives the result. ὑγιέστατον is “healthiest”, and so soundest. No subject is expressed; “you” comes from the command before.
notes.other_reading: so as to say and do everything in the healthiest way

notes.note: πρόθεσις is a purpose set before oneself. The verb has no object; “you” is supplied from the command that opens the passage.
notes.other_reading: For such a resolve sets a person free

notes.note: A rare word, “loitering, hanging back, delay”, translated as given. From memory, unchecked: the word is an editor’s correction, and the manuscripts have στρατείας, “campaigning, warfare”.
notes.other_reading: from toils and campaigning

notes.note: οἰκονομία is managing a household and so, in speech and conduct, arranging things for effect; κομψεία is smartness, refinement put on for show. Both are meant in a bad sense.
notes.other_reading: from all management and cleverness

check.note: The preposition with this case is “to, onto”: make for the short road. “By” is close but not the same picture.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “Always run to the short road.” The preposition is “to” or “onto”, not “by”.

check.note: There is no object in the Greek; the passage is addressed to “you”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “frees you”. The Greek has no object, and the passage opens with a command to “you”.

check.note: The English fits the word as given. From memory, this word is an editor’s correction of the transmitted word for “campaigning”, so the point may want a note.
check.decided: Accepted: “hanging back” stays as the sense of the word given, and the note now says, from memory and unchecked, that the word is an editor’s correction of “campaigning”.

check.note: The word here is calculated arrangement, contriving how to present things. “Managing” does not convey that and is unclear.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “all contriving”. The word here is arranging things for effect, which “managing” did not convey.

check.note: The word is affected refinement, showy elegance; “cleverness” misses the affectation.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “affectation”, which says that the refinement is put on. “Showing off” would narrow it to display in front of others.

passages.casaubon: Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect. For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife, dissembling, and ostentation.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Κατὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς σῆς φύσεως βιοῦν σε οὐδεὶς κωλύσει· παρὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως οὐδέν σοι συμβήσεται.
passages.english: No one will prevent you from living according to the reason of your own nature. Nothing will happen to you contrary to the reason of the common nature.

notes.greek: Κατὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς σῆς φύσεως
notes.note: λόγος is “reason” by the glossary; it could also be heard as the principle or law of your nature. The Greek puts the two prepositional phrases first, in sharp parallel: “according to … contrary to …”.
notes.other_reading: according to the principle of your own nature

notes.note: “The common nature” is the nature shared by all things, the nature of the whole.
notes.other_reading: of universal nature

passages.casaubon: No man can hinder thee to live as thy nature doth require. Nothing can happen unto thee, but what the common good of nature doth require.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Ἐάν τίς σοι προβάλῃ πῶς γράφεται τὸ Ἀντωνίνου ὄνομα, μήτι κατεντεινόμενος προοίσῃ ἕκαστον τῶν στοιχείων; τί οὖν ἐὰν ὀργίζωνται, μήτι ἀντοργιῇ; μήτι οὐκ ἐξαριθμήσῃ πρᾴως προιὼν ἕκαστον τῶν γραμμάτων; οὕτως οὖν καὶ ἐνθάδε μέμνησο ὅτι πᾶν καθῆκον ἐξ ἀριθμῶν τινῶν συμπληροῦται. τούτους δεῖ τηροῦντα καὶ μὴ θορυβούμενον μηδὲ τοῖς δυσχεραίνουσιν ἀντιδυσχεραίνοντα περαίνειν ὁδῷ τὸ προκείμενον.
passages.english: If someone sets you the question how the name Antoninus is written, surely you will not strain as you bring out each of its letters? What then if they get angry: surely you will not get angry back? Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters? So here too, remember that every duty is made complete out of certain counted parts. These you must keep to, and, without being thrown into confusion and without answering those who are annoyed with annoyance of your own, carry through step by step what lies before you.

notes.note: Antoninus is Marcus’s own name as emperor, so the example is spelling his own name.
notes.other_reading: the name of Antoninus

notes.note: μήτι expects the answer no, so the English reads “surely you will not”. κατεντεινόμενος is “straining hard”, whether of the voice or of effort in general; προφέρω is to utter aloud.
notes.other_reading: surely you will not shout out each letter at full stretch?

notes.note: στοιχεῖα here and γραμμάτων below both mean the letters of the name; the first is strictly the elements or sounds, the second the written characters. The English has “letters” for both.
notes.other_reading: each of its elements

notes.note: The Greek moves from “someone” to an unnamed plural “they”.
notes.other_reading: if people get angry

notes.note: πρᾴως, “gently”, stands between “count off” and “going on” and can go with either. The English puts it before both.
notes.other_reading: Will you not go on gently and count off each of the letters?

notes.note: καθῆκον is the Stoic term for an act that it falls to one to do, a fitting or appropriate act. “Duty” is the plain word nearest to it.
notes.other_reading: every fitting act

notes.note: ἀριθμοί, “numbers”, are the counted items that make a thing complete, picking up ἐξαριθμήσῃ, “count off”, just before. The English reads “counted parts” so the link shows; “parts” is supplied. From memory, unchecked: Stoics spoke of a right act as having all its “numbers”.
notes.other_reading: is made complete out of certain numbers

notes.note: περαίνειν is “carry through” by the glossary. ὁδῷ, literally “by a road”, is the idiom for “methodically, in order”; it is “step by step” here and in 5.34, where the road itself is also kept.
notes.other_reading: carry through, keeping to the road, what lies before you

check.note: μήτι expects the answer no: “surely you will not …?”. The plain “will you” loses that, and the same holds for “will you get angry back?”.
check.decided: Accepted: both questions now read “surely you will not”, since the Greek word that opens them expects the answer no.

check.note: “Voice” is not in the Greek: the word is straining, exerting oneself hard. Shouting is one way to picture it, not the only one.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “strain as you bring out each of its letters”. “Voice” is not in the Greek.

check.note: Two Greek words, στοιχεῖα and γράμματα, are both “letters”. Little is lost, but the point should be known.
check.decided: Declined: both Greek words stay “letters”. In the spelling of a name they are the same things, and “elements” for the first would puzzle a reader; the note records the two words.

check.note: The adverb more naturally goes with the main verb: “count off calmly, going through each letter”. The English ties “gently” to the going on.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters?”, so that “gently” covers the counting as well as the going on. “Gently” is kept and not “calmly”, because the Greek word is the opposite of the anger just mentioned.

check.note: “Certain numbers” is obscure. The Greek “numbers” are the counted items that make a thing up, and the word answers “count off” just before.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “is made complete out of certain counted parts”. “Counted” keeps the link with “count off”; “steps” is not used because “step by step” is needed for another word at the end of the passage.

passages.casaubon: if any should put this question unto thee, how this word Antoninus is written, wouldst thou not presently fix thine intention upon it, and utter out in order every letter of it? And if any shall begin to gainsay thee, and quarrel with thee about it; wilt thou quarrel with him again, or rather go on meekly as thou hast begun, until thou hast numbered out every letter? Here then likewise remember, that every duty that belongs unto a man doth consist of some certain letters or numbers as it were, to which without any noise or tumult keeping thyself thou must orderly proceed to thy proposed end, forbearing to quarrel with him that would quarrel and fall out with thee.

nearest.title: Gravity, and keeping the names I have taken

passages.greek: Πρὸς τοὺς ἐπιζητοῦντας· ποῦ γὰρ ἰδὼν τοὺς θεοὺς ἢ πόθεν κατειληφὼς ὅτι εἰσὶν οὕτως σέβεις; πρῶτον μὲν καὶ ὄψει ὁρατοί εἰσιν· ἔπειτα μέντοι οὐδὲ τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ἑώρακα καὶ ὅμως τιμῶ· οὕτως οὖν καὶ τοὺς θεούς, ἐξ ὧν τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶν ἑκάστοτε πειρῶμαι, ἐκ τούτων ὅτι τε εἰσὶ καταλαμβάνω καὶ αἰδοῦμαι.
passages.english: To those who ask: “Well, where have you seen the gods, or from what have you grasped that they exist, that you revere them as you do?” First, they are visible even to the eye. Second, though, I have not seen my own soul either, and yet I honour it. So with the gods too: from what I experience of their power on every occasion, from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them.

notes.note: A heading with no verb. The prefix of the verb can mean asking further or asking insistently, or it may add nothing; the English reads the plain “ask”, since no earlier question stands in the passage for “further” to follow.
notes.other_reading: To those who go on to ask; To those who press the question

notes.note: The particle γὰρ in a question marks it as a challenge and is not “for” here; “Well,” stands for it. The question is the questioners’ own words, so it is set in quotation marks, which the Greek does not have.
notes.other_reading: Why, where have you seen

notes.note: The Stoic school’s word for a sure grasp of a fact (katalepsis). The same verb comes back at the end (καταλαμβάνω), so the English reads “grasp” both times.
notes.other_reading: from what have you made sure that they exist

notes.note: Literally “you revere in this way”, with “them” supplied; “so” can point to the manner or to the degree, and “as you do” keeps both. The verb also covers acts of worship. “Revere” is used so that the noun of the same root in 4.16 (σεβασμὸν) can be “reverence”.
notes.other_reading: that you worship them so devoutly

notes.note: Literally “they are visible even to sight”. The small word καὶ can be “even” or “also” (visible to sight as well as known in other ways); the English reads “even”. The Greek does not say which gods: the sun, moon and stars, which were counted as gods, are probably meant, but nothing is added.
notes.other_reading: they are visible to the eye as well

notes.greek: ἐξ ὧν τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶν ἑκάστοτε πειρῶμαι
notes.note: The verb means to make trial of or to have experience of something. The adverb ἑκάστοτε is “each time” or “on every occasion”, and so can also be “constantly”.
notes.other_reading: from the proofs of their power that are met with again and again

notes.note: A third verb, after “revere” (σέβεις) and “honour” (τιμῶ): it means respect mixed with shame or awe before someone. Three English verbs are kept for the three Greek ones.
notes.other_reading: and respect them

check.note: The Greek word answers “first” and gives the second of two numbered replies. “But then” is heard as “but then again”, so the count of two answers is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Second, though, I have not seen my own soul either”. The Greek word picks up “first” and brings in the second of two replies, which “But then” hid.

check.greek: ὅτι τε εἰσὶ καταλαμβάνω καὶ αἰδοῦμαι
check.note: The Greek ties the two verbs together with “both … and” under “from that”: the same experience is the ground of knowing that the gods exist and of revering them. The comma and the fresh “I” cut the second verb loose.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them”. The Greek joins the two verbs under “from that”, so the one experience is the ground of both.

check.note: “Each time” has nothing to refer to in the English. The Greek word is “on every occasion”, “again and again”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “on every occasion”, the plain sense of the Greek word. “At every turn” is not taken because it brings in a figure of speech that the Greek does not have.

check.note: The verb is to ask further, to go on to inquire. “Press the question” adds a note of insistence that the verb does not have to carry.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “press the question” is dropped, since the verb need not carry insistence, and the English now reads “To those who ask”. “Go on to ask” is not taken because no earlier question stands in the passage for it to follow; the note records both.

check.note: The particle γὰρ in the question is dropped. It gives the question its challenging tone.
check.decided: Accepted: the question now begins “Well, where have you seen the gods”, so that the challenge the particle carries is heard.

check.note: The small word καὶ can be “even” or “also”, and the Greek states a fact (“they are visible”) where the English states a possibility (“can be seen”).
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now states a fact, “they are visible even to the eye”, as the Greek does. “Even” is kept, since the questioners asked where the gods had been seen and the reply meets that word; “also” is recorded in the note.

check.note: Found while settling: “worship” here and “reverence” in 4.16 stood for one Greek root (σέβεις, σεβασμὸν), while “revere” at the end of this passage stood for a different verb (αἰδοῦμαι).
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “revere” for σέβεις and “stand in awe of” for αἰδοῦμαι. “Revere” and “reverence” now answer to the one root in the two passages, and the three verbs of this passage stay distinct.

passages.casaubon: To them that ask thee, Where hast thou seen the Gods, or how knowest thou certainly that there be Gods, that thou art so devout in their worship? I answer first of all, that even to the very eye, they are in some manner visible and apparent. Secondly, neither have I ever seen mine own soul, and yet I respect and honour it. So then for the Gods, by the daily experience that I have of their power and providence towards myself and others, I know certainly that they are, and therefore worship them.

passages.greek: ʽΣυζῆν θεοῖς.ʼ συζῇ δὲ θεοῖς ὁ συνεχῶς δεικνὺς αὐτοῖς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν ἀρεσκομένην μὲν τοῖς ἀπονεμομένοις, ποιοῦσαν δὲ ὅσα βούλεται ὁ δαίμων, ὃν ἑκάστῳ προστάτην καὶ ἡγεμόνα ὁ Ζεὺς ἔδωκεν, ἀπόσπασμα ἑαυτοῦ. οὗτος δέ ἐστιν ὁ ἑκάστου νοῦς καὶ λόγος.
passages.english: “To live with the gods.” And the one who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them their own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that the spirit wants, the spirit that Zeus has given to each person as protector and leader, a fragment of himself. And this spirit is each person’s mind and reason.

notes.note: A bare infinitive, which the edition sets in quotation marks as a saying. It can be a heading or a command; the English keeps the infinitive, and the next sentence then says who does live so.
notes.other_reading: “Live with the gods.”

notes.greek: συζῇ δὲ θεοῖς ὁ συνεχῶς δεικνὺς
notes.note: Literally “and he lives with the gods who constantly shows them”. The English turns this into “the one who … is the one who …” so that the long description does not trail far from its subject.
notes.other_reading: And a person lives with the gods who constantly shows them

notes.note: The Greek is “his own soul”: the soul of the person, not of the gods. “Their own” is written to avoid “he” for a subject not singled out as a man, so “them” is the gods and “their” is the person’s.
notes.other_reading: shows them his own soul

notes.note: Two participles say what the soul is shown to be: content, and doing. The Greek can equally be put as a clause with “that”.
notes.other_reading: constantly shows them that their own soul is content with what is allotted and does all that the spirit wants

notes.note: Literally “the things being dealt out”. The Greek does not say by whom or to whom, and the English adds neither.
notes.other_reading: pleased with what is assigned to it

notes.note: The daimon: a divine being that attends each person. The English reads “the spirit”, since the passage itself goes on to call it a protector and to say what it is. The word is repeated twice (“the spirit that Zeus”, “this spirit”) where the Greek has a relative pronoun and a “this”.
notes.other_reading: the guardian spirit; the divinity

notes.note: The first word is one who stands in front: a protector, guardian, patron or chief. The second is a leader, one who gives the lead and is followed; it is the root of the Stoic term “the ruling part” (τὸ ἡγεμονικόν), so “ruler” is also possible, and “guide” is its milder sense.
notes.other_reading: as guardian and guide; as chief and ruler

notes.note: The noun is from a verb meaning to tear or pull away, and names a detached portion of something. “Fragment” is the plain word for it; the more literal rendering spells out the root.
notes.other_reading: a piece torn off from himself

notes.note: Two nouns for one thing; both are kept, with this translation’s usual words for them. They may be meant as a single idea.
notes.other_reading: each person’s reasoning mind

check.note: The Greek is definite: “his own soul”. “A soul of their own” sounds like one soul among several, and is awkward after the singular “a person”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “their own soul”, definite as in the Greek. “Their” is the person’s, as the note says.

check.note: The Greek is an infinitive, which can be a heading or quoted phrase as well as a command. The English had made it a command, and the next sentence suits the heading at least as well.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To live with the gods.”, keeping the Greek infinitive, which can be a heading or a command. The command is recorded in the note.

check.greek: συζῇ δὲ θεοῖς ὁ συνεχῶς δεικνὺς
check.note: The relative clause is stranded far from “a person”, which makes the sentence hard to follow. The Greek is a plain definition of the one who lives with the gods.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now reads “the one who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them …”, so the description is no longer stranded from its subject. The Greek is a plain statement of who lives with the gods.

check.note: “To it” is added and fixes the receiver as the soul. The Greek says only “the things that are allotted”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what is allotted”. The Greek names no receiver.

check.note: The second Greek word is a leader or commander, one who gives the lead and is obeyed. “Guide” is milder and loses the note of authority.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “protector and leader”. “Leader” keeps the authority of the second Greek word; “protector” stays for the first, which means one who stands in front of another, and “guardian” is recorded in the note.

check.note: The noun is by origin something pulled off, but in use it is simply a detached portion. “Torn off” spells out the root and adds a violence the plain noun need not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a fragment of himself”. The Greek noun names a detached portion, and its root, to pull away, is kept in the note.

check.note: “Spirit” alone is vague in today’s English and stands here beside “soul”. The Greek word names a personal divinity given to each person, and the English repeats “spirit” twice more, so the word carries the whole passage; “the guardian spirit” is proposed for the first mention.
check.decided: Declined: “the spirit” stays, because “guardian” is not in the Greek word itself: the next words call the spirit a protector, and the last sentence says what it is, so “guardian spirit” would say one thing twice. The note records “the guardian spirit” as the other reading.

passages.casaubon: To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.

passages.greek: Ἐντὸς δέκα ἡμερῶν θεὸς αὐτοῖς τούτοις δόξεις οἷς νῦν θηρίον καὶ πίθηκος, ἐὰν ἀνακάμψῃς ἐπὶ τὰ δόγματα καὶ τὸν σεβασμὸν τοῦ λόγου.
passages.english: Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you turn back to the principles and to reverence for reason.

notes.note: Literally “within ten days”. It may be a round figure for “very soon”; the number is kept.
notes.other_reading: In a few days

notes.note: There is no verb in this clause; “you seem” is carried over from the main verb. The first noun is a wild animal.
notes.other_reading: to whom you are now a wild animal and a monkey

notes.note: The verb is to bend back or turn back on one’s course, so it implies a return to something left behind.
notes.other_reading: if you return

notes.note: The Greek has only the article, “the principles”, and the English keeps it. Since the verb speaks of turning back, the article may stand for “your”: the principles once held and since left.
notes.other_reading: to your principles

notes.note: The genitive is taken as the thing revered: reverence for reason. The Greek does not say whether this is a person’s own reason or the reason that runs through everything, and “reason” without an article keeps both. The noun is from the same root as “revere” (σέβεις) in 12.28.
notes.other_reading: the worship of reason

check.note: “Your” is supplied; the Greek has only the article, “the principles”. The article can stand for a possessive, so this is a choice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the principles”, since the Greek has only the article. “Your principles” is recorded in the note.

check.note: The genitive is taken as the thing revered, which is the natural reading. Whether a person’s own reason or the reason that runs through everything is meant is left open, and “reason” without an article keeps both, so nothing needs changing.
check.decided: Accepted: “reverence for reason” stays, as the point itself proposes. The note now says that the Greek leaves open whose reason is meant.

passages.casaubon: Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring of reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an ape.

passages.greek: Οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι· ἕωθεν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀφορᾶν, ἵν’ ὑπομιμνῃσκώμεθα τῶν ἀεὶ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως τὸ ἑαυτῶν ἔργον διανυόντων καὶ τῆς τάξεως καὶ τῆς καθαρότητος καὶ τῆς γυμνότητος· οὐδὲν γὰρ προκάλυμμα ἄστρου.
passages.english: The Pythagoreans: to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn, so that we are reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way, and of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.

notes.note: A nominative with no verb, like a heading, followed by an infinitive that gives their instruction. The English keeps it as a jotting and does not supply “say” or “tell us”.
notes.other_reading: The Pythagoreans tell us to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn

notes.note: Literally “from dawn”. It is used both for “at dawn” and more loosely for “early in the morning”.
notes.other_reading: early in the morning

notes.note: The verb is to look away from other things and fix the eyes on one; the Greek names no direction. “Our” is supplied from the “we” of the next verb.
notes.other_reading: to look up at the sky

notes.greek: τῶν ἀεὶ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως τὸ ἑαυτῶν ἔργον διανυόντων
notes.note: The participle can be masculine (“those who”) or neuter (“the things that”); the last clause shows the stars are meant, so the English reads “those that”.
notes.other_reading: the beings who for ever complete their own task

notes.note: A set pair for what never varies (a phrase of Plato’s, from memory, unchecked). The first half is literally “according to the same things”; “along the same lines” is the English for it.
notes.other_reading: in the same respects and in like manner

notes.note: The verb is to bring to completion, and is also used of finishing a journey, which suits the stars’ courses. The English reads “complete”.
notes.other_reading: carry out; accomplish

notes.greek: καὶ τῆς τάξεως καὶ τῆς καθαρότητος καὶ τῆς γυμνότητος
notes.note: Three more things to be reminded of. The Greek has only the article, “the order, the purity, the nakedness”; “their” is supplied, since the last clause gives a star as the reason. The three can also be read as things named in themselves.
notes.other_reading: and of order, purity and nakedness

notes.note: Literally “for there is no covering of a star”, with no verb. The noun is anything hung in front to hide: a curtain, a veil.
notes.other_reading: for nothing covers a star

check.note: “On the same terms” suggests the conditions of an agreement. The Greek is “in the same respects”, “along the same lines”: the point is unchanging regularity.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “along the same lines and in the same way”. The Greek phrase is about what never varies, and “terms” suggested the conditions of an agreement.

check.note: The verb is to bring to an end, to complete, often of a course or journey. “Carry out” keeps the doing but loses the completing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “complete their own work”. The Greek verb is to bring to completion, as of a course or a journey.

check.greek: τῆς τάξεως καὶ τῆς καθαρότητος καὶ τῆς γυμνότητος
check.note: “Their” is supplied three times; the Greek has only the article. The three qualities can belong to the heavenly bodies, which the last clause supports, or can be named as things in themselves.
check.decided: Declined: “their order, their purity and their nakedness” stays. The Greek has the article with each noun, which points to a particular order, purity and nakedness, and the last clause gives a star as the reason; the note records the reading without “their”.

check.note: “Up” is supplied. The verb is to look away from other things and fix the eyes on one; the English gives a direction and loses the turning away.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn”, without “up”. “Our” is written and not “one’s” because the next verb is “we”.

passages.casaubon: The Pythagoreans were wont betimes in the morning the first thing they did, to look up unto the heavens, to put themselves in mind of them who constantly and invariably did perform their task: as also to put themselves in mind of orderliness, or good order, and of purity, and of naked simplicity. For no star or planet hath any cover before it.

passages.greek: Ἐν τοῖς τῶν Ἐπικουρείων γράμμασι παράγγελμα ἔκειτο συνεχῶς ὑπομιμνῄσκεσθαι τῶν παλαιῶν τινος τῶν ἀρετῇ χρησαμένων.
passages.english: In the writings of the Epicureans a rule was laid down: to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue.

notes.note: The English follows the text as given. From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts read “of the Ephesians” here and “Epicureans” is an editor’s correction, made because Seneca reports a similar precept from Epicurus.
notes.other_reading: In the writings of the Ephesians

notes.note: The word covers anything written: writings, books, or letters.
notes.other_reading: In the letters of the Epicureans

notes.note: Literally “an instruction lay”, that is, stood written or was laid down as a rule. The tense is past and continuing.
notes.other_reading: there stood a precept

notes.note: The verb is the same as “are reminded” in 11.27; here the form can be “to remind oneself” or “to be reminded”. “Constantly” is the same word as in 5.27.
notes.other_reading: to be continually reminded of

notes.greek: τῶν παλαιῶν τινος τῶν ἀρετῇ χρησαμένων
notes.note: Literally “some one of the ancients, of those who made use of virtue”. The Greek has the singular: one such person, not the ancients in general.
notes.other_reading: some one of the ancients who lived by virtue

check.note: From memory, the manuscripts here read “of the Ephesians” and “Epicureans” is an editor’s correction. The English follows the Greek as given, so this is a question about the text and not a fault in the translation.
check.decided: Accepted: “Epicureans” stays, as the text given reads, and the note says that the name is believed to be an editor’s correction (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: “Precept” is bookish, and “there was … laid down” says the one Greek verb twice over. The Greek is simply “a rule stood”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a rule was laid down”, with “rule” for “precept” and a single verb. “Laid down” is kept because the Greek verb says that the rule stood written, which “there was” alone would lose.

passages.casaubon: In the ancient mystical letters of the Ephesians, there was an item, that a man should always have in his mind some one or other of the ancient worthies.

nearest.title: Gravity, and keeping the names I have taken

passages.greek: Ὅ τι ἂν τῶν ἀπροαιρέτων ὑποστήσῃ σαυτῷ ἀγαθὸν ἢ κακόν, ἀνάγκη κατὰ τὴν περίπτωσιν τοῦ τοιούτου κακοῦ ἢ τὴν ἀπότευξιν τοῦ τοιούτου ἀγαθοῦ μέμψασθαί σε θεοῖς καὶ ἀνθρώπους δὲ μισῆσαι τοὺς αἰτίους ὄντας ἢ ὑποπτευομένους ἔσεσθαι τῆς ἀποτεύξεως ἢ τῆς περιπτώσεως· καὶ ἀδικοῦμεν δὴ πολλὰ διὰ τὴν πρὸς ταῦτα διαφοράν. ἐὰν δὲ μόνα τὰ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν ἀγαθὰ καὶ κακὰ κρίνωμεν, οὐδεμία αἰτία καταλείπεται οὔτε θεῷ ἐγκαλέσαι οὔτε πρὸς ἄνθρωπον στῆναι στάσιν πολεμίου.
passages.english: Whatever you set up for yourself as good or bad among the things that are not yours to choose, it must follow that when you meet with such a bad thing or miss such a good one, you blame the gods, and hate people too: those who are the cause, or are suspected of being about to be the cause, of your missing the one or meeting with the other. And indeed we do many wrongs because of the difference these things make to us. But if we judge only the things that are up to us to be good and bad, no cause is left either for accusing a god or for taking an enemy’s stand against a person.

notes.note: The word means the things that do not fall under choice (προαίρεσις), what a person cannot decide. It is the opposite of “the things that are up to us” (τὰ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν) later in the passage; the English keeps two different phrases because the Greek has two.
notes.other_reading: the things that lie outside your will

notes.note: The verb is to lay something down as a basis, to posit. “For yourself” can go with the verb, as the English takes it, or with “good or bad”.
notes.other_reading: Whatever you suppose to be good or bad for you

notes.greek: κατὰ τὴν περίπτωσιν τοῦ τοιούτου κακοῦ ἢ τὴν ἀπότευξιν τοῦ τοιούτου ἀγαθοῦ
notes.note: Two nouns of the Stoic school: περίπτωσις is falling into what one wanted to avoid, ἀπότευξις is failing to get what one wanted. The Greek has nouns; the English turns them into verbs with “you” as subject.
notes.other_reading: upon the falling into such a bad thing or the failure to obtain such a good thing

notes.note: A passive with a future infinitive: “suspected that they will be (the cause)”. The Greek does not say who suspects, and the English keeps the passive.
notes.other_reading: or whom you suspect will be the cause

notes.note: Literally “because of the difference toward these things”. The English takes it as the opposite of Stoic indifference: these things are allowed to make a difference. The noun can also mean a quarrel or disagreement; the verb of the same idiom is at 9.40.
notes.other_reading: because of our quarrels over these things

notes.note: αἰτία is a cause and also a ground for a charge. It answers “those who are the cause” (τοὺς αἰτίους) above, so the English says “cause” in both places.
notes.other_reading: no ground is left

notes.note: Verb and noun are from one root: “to stand the stand of an enemy”. The noun στάσις is also the ordinary word for faction and civil strife, which may be heard here.
notes.other_reading: to take up an enemy’s position against a person

check.note: The noun belongs with the verb used at 9.40 and means either making a difference over these things or being at odds over them. “How much these things matter” adds a degree the Greek does not have, and the link with 9.40 is lost.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “because of the difference these things make to us”, which keeps the Greek noun “difference” and drops the added “how much”. At 9.40 the verb is now “to let what is not up to you make a difference to you”, so the two chapters share one wording; the reading “quarrels” stays in the note.

check.note: The participle is passive and names no one who suspects; the English made “you” the one who suspects.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “those who are the cause, or are suspected of being about to be the cause”, with no suspecting person supplied, as in the Greek.

check.note: The particle δή, which marks the statement as the plain outcome, is dropped.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “And indeed we do many wrongs”. “Indeed” gives the particle its weight; “so” is not used because the Greek has no word of consequence here.

check.note: αἰτία answers τοὺς αἰτίους above, and “cause” there with “reason” here hides the echo.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “no cause is left either for accusing a god or for taking an enemy’s stand against a person”, so that “cause” stands in both places, and a note records the sense “ground for a charge”.

passages.casaubon: What things soever are not within the proper power and jurisdiction of thine own will either to compass or avoid, if thou shalt propose unto thyself any of those things as either good, or evil; it must needs be that according as thou shalt either fall into that which thou dost think evil, or miss of that which thou dost think good, so wilt thou be ready both to complain of the Gods, and to hate those men, who either shall be so indeed, or shall by thee be suspected as the cause either of thy missing of the one, or falling into the other. And indeed we must needs commit many evils, if we incline to any of these things, more or less, with an opinion of any difference. But if we mind and fancy those things only, as good and bad, which wholly depend of our own wills, there is no more occasion why we should either murmur against the Gods, or be at enmity with any man.

nearest.title: What is not in my power

passages.greek: Πῶς ποτε πάντα καλῶς καὶ φιλανθρώπως διατάξαντες οἱ θεοὶ τοῦτο μόνον παρεῖδον, τὸ ἐνίους τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ πάνυ χρηστοὺς καὶ πλεῖστα πρὸς τὸ θεῖον ὥσπερ συμβόλαια θεμένους καὶ ἐπὶ πλεῖστον δι’ ἔργων ὁσίων καὶ ἱερουργιῶν συνήθεις τῷ θείῳ γενομένους, ἐπειδὰν ἅπαξ ἀποθάνωσι, μηκέτι αὖθις γίνεσθαι, ἀλλ’ εἰς τὸ παντελὲς ἀπεσβηκέναι; τοῦτο δὲ εἴπερ ἄρα καὶ οὕτως ἔχει, εὖ ἴσθι ὅτι, εἰ ὡς ἑτέρως ἔχειν ἔδει, ἐποίησαν ἄν· εἰ γὰρ δίκαιον ἦν, ἦν ἃν καὶ δυνατόν, καὶ εἰ κατὰ φύσιν, ἤνεγκεν ἂν αὐτὸ ἡ φύσις. ἐκ δὴ τοῦ μὴ οὕτως ἔχειν, εἴπερ οὐχ οὕτως ἔχει, πιστούσθω σοι τὸ μὴ δεῆσαι οὕτως γίνεσθαι· ὁρᾷς γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸς ὅτι τοῦτο παραζητῶν δικαιολογῇ πρὸς τὸν θεόν· οὐκ ἂν δ’ οὕτως διελεγόμεθα τοῖς θεοῖς, εἰ μὴ ἄριστοι καὶ δικαιότατοί εἰσιν. εἰ δὲ τοῦτο, οὐκ ἄν τι περιεῖδον ἀδίκως καὶ ἀλόγως ἠμελημένον τῶν ἐν τῇ διακοσμήσει.
passages.english: How can it be that the gods, who arranged all things well and with love for humankind, overlooked this one thing only: that some people, and very good ones, who had made a great many contracts, so to speak, with the divine, and who through holy deeds and sacred rites had come to be on the closest terms with the divine, once they have died, do not come to be again any more, but are completely extinguished? But if this really is so, be sure that if it ought to have been otherwise, they would have made it otherwise. For if it were just, it would also be possible, and if it were in accord with nature, nature would have brought it about. So from its not being so, if indeed it is not so, be assured that it ought not to have come about so. For you see for yourself that in prying into this you are arguing a case of justice with god. And we would not be reasoning with the gods like this unless they are best and most just. And if that is so, they would not have let anything in the order of things be neglected unjustly and against reason.

notes.note: συμβόλαια are contracts or business dealings between parties; “so to speak” (ὥσπερ) marks it as a figure. The English keeps the commercial image.
notes.other_reading: who had had, as it were, the most dealings with the divine

notes.note: Literally “no longer come to be again”. The verb is the general one for coming into being, so it does not decide between being born again and existing again in some other way.
notes.other_reading: are never born again

notes.note: The verb is used of a flame or lamp that has gone out. “Extinguished” keeps the image.
notes.other_reading: have gone out completely

notes.greek: ἐκ δὴ τοῦ μὴ οὕτως ἔχειν, εἴπερ οὐχ οὕτως ἔχει
notes.note: The same word “so” (οὕτως) changes what it points to: earlier, “if this really is so” meant that the good are completely extinguished, and here “its not being so” means its not being the other way, that they come to be again. The English keeps “so” each time, as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: So from the fact that it is not that other way, if indeed it is not

notes.greek: πιστούσθω σοι τὸ μὴ δεῆσαι οὕτως γίνεσθαι
notes.note: A third-person command: “let it be made sure for you”. The infinitive δεῆσαι is a past form and answers “ought” (ἔδει) above, so the English says “ought not to have”. The sense is that the other arrangement was not called for; the word can also mean bare need.
notes.other_reading: let it be your assurance that there was no need for it to come about so

notes.note: A rare compound of “to seek”. The prefix marks the search as beside the point or as going beyond what is proper; “prying” takes the second.
notes.other_reading: in raising this needless question

notes.note: The verb is to plead one’s case, to argue what is just, as before a court. The Greek has the singular with the article here, between plurals before and after: god in general, not one god already named.
notes.other_reading: you are pleading your rights against the god

notes.note: The verb is to talk a thing through with someone, to reason it out. “Reasoning” is used so that it is not confused with “arguing a case of justice” (δικαιολογῇ) just before.
notes.other_reading: we would not be talking with the gods like this

notes.greek: εἰ μὴ ἄριστοι καὶ δικαιότατοί εἰσιν
notes.note: The Greek has a plain present, “if they are not”, where an unreal condition would lead one to expect “if they were not”. The English keeps the present, which states their goodness as a fact.
notes.other_reading: if they were not best and most just

notes.note: This answers “overlooked” (παρεῖδον) in the first sentence with a near twin: there the verb is to look past, here to look on and let happen. English cannot keep the echo.
notes.other_reading: they would not have overlooked anything

notes.note: Literally “of the things in the setting-in-order”, a noun from the same root as κόσμος and the regular Stoic word for the ordering of the universe. The English uses the common phrase “the order of things”.
notes.other_reading: anything in the ordering of the universe

check.note: The prefix of παραζητῶν makes the inquiry one that is beside the mark or out of place; “pressing” says only that the question is pushed hard.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in prying into this”, which says that the inquiry goes where it should not. The note gives the other force of the prefix, “needless”.

check.note: δεῆσαι is a past form and picks up ἔδει, “ought to have been”; the present “ought not to come about” reads like a rule for the future.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that it ought not to have come about so”, a past form that pairs with “ought to have been otherwise”. “Come about” is kept, not “been”, because the Greek verb here is γίνεσθαι, the same as “come to be again” above.

check.note: The verb is of a flame put out, and “have gone out” with a human subject is first heard as leaving the house.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but are completely extinguished”, which keeps the flame and cannot be misheard.

check.note: After δικαιολογῇ the verb means reasoning a point out with someone, not simply talking.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “we would not be reasoning with the gods like this”. “Arguing” is not used because it already stands for another Greek verb, δικαιολογῇ, in the sentence before, and one English word for two Greek ones would make a false echo.

check.note: “The god” sounds like one particular god already named, while the Greek singular with the article is generic.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “with god”, lower case and without the article, as the settled renderings have it. “The divine” is not used because in this passage it already stands for another Greek word, τὸ θεῖον.

check.note: Found while settling: ἐποίησαν ἄν was rendered “they would have made it so”, where “so” stands for no οὕτως and points the other way from the “so” that the passage repeats.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they would have made it otherwise”, so that “so” stands only where the Greek has οὕτως.

passages.casaubon: how come it to pass that the Gods having ordered all other things so well and so lovingly, should be overseen in this one only thing, that whereas then hath been some very good men that have made many covenants as it were with God and by many holy actions and outward services contracted a kind of familiarity with Him; that these men when once they are dead, should never be restored to life, but be extinct for ever. But this thou mayest be sure of, that this (if it be so indeed) would never have been so ordered by the Gods, had it been fit otherwise. For certainly it was possible, had it been more just so and had it been according to nature, the nature of the universe would easily have borne it. But now because it is not so, (if so be that it be not so indeed) be therefore confident that it was not fit it should be so for thou seest thyself, that now seeking after this matter, how freely thou doest argue and contest with God. But were not the Gods both just and good in the highest degree, thou durst not thus reason with them. Now if just and good, it could not be that in the creation of the world, they should either unjustly or unreasonably oversee anything.

nearest.title: What is not in my power

passages.greek: Εἰ μὲν ἐπὶ ·σοί, τί αὐτὸ ποιεῖς; εἰ δὲ ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ, τίνι μέμφῃ; ταῖς ἀτόμοις ἢ τοῖς θεοῖς; ἀμφότερα μανιώδη. Οὐδενὶ μεμπτέον. εἰ μὲν γὰρ δύνασαι, διόρθωσον· εἰ δὲ τοῦτο μὴ δύνασαι, τό γε πρᾶγμα αὐτό· εἰ δὲ μηδὲ τοῦτο, πρὸς τί ἔτι σοι φέρει τὸ μέμψασθαι; εἰκῇ γὰρ οὐδὲν ποιητέον.
passages.english: If it is up to you, why do you do it? If it is up to another, whom or what do you blame? The atoms or the gods? Both are madness. No one is to be blamed. For if you can, set the other right. If you cannot do that, set right at least the thing itself. And if not even that, what end does blaming still serve for you? For nothing is to be done without an aim.

notes.greek: Εἰ μὲν ἐπὶ ·σοί, τί αὐτὸ ποιεῖς
notes.note: The raised dot before σοί is a slip of the digitised text; the words are ἐπὶ σοί, “up to you”. The Greek never says what “it” is: whatever is going wrong.
notes.other_reading: If it is in your power, why do you do this?

notes.note: The form τίνι is “whom” and “what” alike, and the first answer offered, the atoms, is a thing, so the English gives both. In the same way “no one” (Οὐδενί) in “No one is to be blamed” is equally “nothing”.
notes.other_reading: whom do you blame?

notes.note: The two rival accounts of how things happen: the atoms of Epicurus, moving by chance, or the gods. The pair is often set side by side in this book.
notes.other_reading: Chance or providence?

notes.note: Neuter plural: both things, that is, both kinds of blaming, are like madness.
notes.other_reading: Either would be insane.

notes.note: The command “set right” has no object in the Greek. The contrast with “the thing itself” in the next clause shows that the first object is whoever is responsible; “the other” is supplied, taken from “another” two sentences before.
notes.other_reading: For if you can, set the person right

notes.note: Literally “toward what does it still carry for you”: what does it lead to, what does it serve.
notes.other_reading: what good does blaming still do you?

notes.note: The adverb means at random, with no purpose in view.
notes.other_reading: For nothing should be done at random.

check.note: The command has no object in the Greek; “the person” is supplied, a likely reading, but the alternatives just named were the atoms or the gods.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “set the other right”, so that the supplied object is only the “another” the Greek has already named and is not narrowed to a person. “Him” is not used because the Greek singles out no man, and the note says plainly that the object is supplied.

check.greek: πρὸς τί ἔτι σοι φέρει τὸ μέμψασθαι
check.note: ἔτι goes with the verb, “what does blaming still lead to”; “what further end” suggests that blaming has already served some end.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “what end does blaming still serve for you?”, with “still” on the verb. “End” is kept for πρὸς τί, “toward what”, because the Greek has no word for “good” here and the next sentence speaks of doing nothing without an aim.

check.note: τίνι is masculine or neuter alike and the first answer offered is a thing, the atoms; “whom” settles it as a person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whom or what do you blame?”, and a note says the same openness holds for “no one” below.

passages.casaubon: If it were thine act and in thine own power, wouldest thou do it? If it were not, whom dost tin accuse? the atoms, or the Gods? For to do either, the part of a mad man. Thou must therefore blame nobody, but if it be in thy power, redress what is amiss; if it be not, to what end is it to complain? For nothing should be done but to some certain end.

nearest.title: What is not in my power

passages.greek:
Τοῖς πράγμασιν γὰρ οὐχὶ θυμοῦσθαι χρεών· μέλει γὰρ αὐτοῖς οὐδέν.

Ἀθανάτοις τε θεοῖς καὶ ἡμῖν χάρματα δοίης.

Βίον θερίζειν ὥστε κάρπιμον στάχυν καὶ τὸν μὲν εἶναι, τὸν δὲ μή.

Εἰ δ’ ἠμελήθην ἐκ θεῶν καὶ παῖδ’ ἐμώ, ἔχει λόγον καὶ τοῦτο.

Τὸ γὰρ εὖ μετ’ ἐμοῦ καὶ τὸ δίκαιον.

Μὴ συνεπιθρηνεῖν, μὴ σφύζειν.
passages.english:
“For one must not be angry with things, for they do not care at all.”

“May you give joys to the immortal gods and to us.”

“To reap life like a ripe ear of grain, and for one to be and another not.”

“But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.”

“For what is right is with me, and what is just.”

No joining in the wailing, no racing pulse.

notes.greek: Τοῖς πράγμασιν γὰρ οὐχὶ θυμοῦσθαι χρεών
notes.note: A line of verse quoted with no name: from memory, unchecked, it is from a lost play of Euripides. The quotation marks here and in the next four chapters are added; the Greek has none. πράγματα can be things, affairs or circumstances.
notes.other_reading: For one must not be angry with circumstances

notes.note: A wish, “may you give”, in a line of epic metre whose source is not identified here. χάρματα are joys or causes of joy.
notes.other_reading: May you bring delight to the immortal gods and to us.

notes.note: The Greek is a bare infinitive with no governing verb, so it does not construe alone: the quotation is cut out of a sentence (from memory, unchecked, a line of Euripides in which a word for “it is necessary” governs it). The English leaves it a fragment and does not supply the verb.
notes.other_reading: Life must be reaped like a ripe ear of grain

notes.note: Literally “fruit-bearing”: an ear carrying its grain, and so ready for the reaper. “Ripe” gives that sense in the word English uses of grain.
notes.other_reading: like a fruitful ear of grain

notes.greek: τὸν μὲν εἶναι, τὸν δὲ μή
notes.note: “One to be, and another not”: “be” in the sense of exist, live. The masculine “one … another” can be an ear of grain or a person; the English leaves it open as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: and that one man lives while another does not

notes.note: The form is a dual: exactly two children. The word can mean sons or children; from memory, unchecked, this too is a verse from a lost tragedy.
notes.other_reading: my two sons

notes.note: Literally “this too has reason”, λόγος: there is a reason for it, it can be accounted for.
notes.other_reading: there is an account to be given of this too

notes.greek: Τὸ γὰρ εὖ μετ’ ἐμοῦ καὶ τὸ δίκαιον
notes.note: τὸ εὖ is the adverb “well” made into a noun: what is well, what is right. It is not the word for “the good” (τὸ ἀγαθόν), so the English does not say “the good”. The Greek has no verb; “is” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: For right is on my side, and justice.

notes.note: Two infinitives used as instructions, and not, as far as can be told, a quotation. The first is to join others in lamenting over something; the second is used of the pulse beating hard, hence of feverish agitation. The English keeps the pulse.
notes.other_reading: Do not lament along with them; do not throb with agitation.

check.greek: καὶ τὸν μὲν εἶναι, τὸν δὲ μή
check.note: The sense is that one should be alive and another not, but “and that one is, another is not” is hard to parse: “that one” is first read as a pointing word.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and for one to be and another not”, which runs on from “to reap” and cannot be misread. “Man” is not added, because the Greek “one … another” can be an ear of grain as well as a person.

check.note: κάρπιμος is bearing its crop, ready for reaping; “in fruit” is not said of grain in English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “like a ripe ear of grain”, and a note gives the literal “fruit-bearing”.

check.note: The particle δέ is dropped; the Greek has “But if”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods”.

check.note: τὸ εὖ is the adverb made a noun, “what is well”; “the good” is the standing word for τὸ ἀγαθόν and a reader will take the two as one term.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “For what is right is with me, and what is just”, which keeps τὸ εὖ apart from “the good”. “What is right” is used in place of “the right”, which could be heard as a right or a side.

passages.casaubon: Out of several poets and comics. 'It will but little avail thee, to turn thine anger and indignation upon the things themselves that have fallen across unto thee. For as for them, they are not sensible of it, &c. Thou shalt but make thyself a laughing-stock; both unto the Gods and men, &c. Our life is reaped like a ripe ear of corn; one is yet standing and another is down, &c. But if so be that I and my children be neglected by the gods, there is some reason even for that, &c. As long as right and equity is of my side, &c. Not to lament with them, not to tremble, &c.'

nearest.title: What is not in my power

passages.greek:
Οἱ θεοί, ἀθάνατοι ὄντες, οὐ δυσχεραίνουσιν ὅτι ἐν τοσούτῳ αἰῶνι δεήσει αὐτοὺς πάντως ἀεὶ τοιούτων ὄντων καὶ τοσούτων φαύλων ἀνέχεσθαι· προσέτι δὲ καὶ κήδονται αὐτῶν παντοίως. σὺ δέ, ὅσον οὐδέπω λήγειν μέλλων, ἀπαυδᾷς, καὶ ταῦτα εἶς ὢν τῶν φαύλων;

Γελοῖόν ἐστι τὴν μὲν ἰδίαν κακίαν μὴ φεύγειν, ὃ καὶ δυνατόν ἐστι, τὴν δὲ τῶν ἄλλων φεύγειν, ὅπερ ἀδύνατον.
passages.english:
The gods, who are immortal, are not vexed that through so long a time they will certainly always have to put up with bad people, such as they are and so many. More than that, they care for them in every kind of way. But you, who are about to come to an end any moment now, do you give up, and that when you are one of the bad ones?

It is ridiculous not to flee one’s own vice, which is in fact possible, but to flee that of others, which is impossible.

notes.note: αἰών is an age, a very long or endless stretch of time; it can also mean a lifetime, which for the immortal gods comes to the same.
notes.other_reading: in so long a life

notes.greek: πάντως ἀεὶ τοιούτων ὄντων καὶ τοσούτων φαύλων
notes.note: φαῦλοι is the Stoic word for everyone who is not wise: bad, worthless people. πάντως, “certainly”, “without fail”, goes with “will have to”.
notes.other_reading: they will without fail have to put up always with worthless people, who are what they are and so many

notes.note: The verb is to care for, to look after, as for one’s own family. “Them” is the bad people.
notes.other_reading: they look after them in all sorts of ways

notes.note: Literally “about to cease all but now”. The Greek says only “cease”, meaning to stop living; “come to an end” keeps it as plain as that.
notes.other_reading: you, who are on the very point of dying

notes.note: The verb is to say no more, to give up from exhaustion. The sentence is punctuated as a question in the Greek and the English keeps it.
notes.other_reading: do you refuse to go on

notes.note: The verb is both to run from a thing and to get clear of it. The English uses “flee” in both halves, which like the Greek verb covers the attempt and the success. κακία is rendered “vice” to keep it apart from φαῦλοι, “bad people”, in the chapter before.
notes.other_reading: not to escape one’s own wickedness, which is possible, but to try to escape other people’s

check.note: πάντως goes with “will have to” and means “without fail”, not “in each case”; the English also joins the two adverbs with an “and” the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “they will certainly always have to put up with bad people”, with πάντως on the verb and no added “and”. “Certainly” is used in place of the suggested “no way round it”, and the same word now stands for πάντως at 9.40.

check.note: δέ sets “you” against the gods, which is the point of the chapter; “And” flattens it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But you”.

check.note: λήγειν is to come to an end, to cease to be, and ὅσον οὐδέπω is “any moment now”; “all but about to stop” is heavy and leaves the reader asking what stops.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “who are about to come to an end any moment now”.

check.note: The verb is to give up from weariness; “give out” is said of a machine or a supply more than of a person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “do you give up”.

check.note: With “which is possible” and “which is impossible” the verb has to mean getting clear of something, not the act of running, since anyone can run.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not to flee one’s own vice … but to flee that of others”. “Flee”, like the Greek verb, covers getting clear as well as running, and it serves in both halves, where “escape” would need an added “try to” in the second and so give one Greek word two English forms.

check.note: The particle καί in “which is in fact possible” is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “which is in fact possible”.

check.note: “An age” in this sense is bookish; the Greek is simply “in so great a stretch of time”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “through so long a time”. “Vast” is left out as more colour than the Greek word “so great” has, and a note gives the other sense of αἰών, “lifetime”.

passages.casaubon: Can the Gods, who are immortal, for the continuance of so many ages bear without indignation with such and so many sinners, as have ever been, yea not only so, but also take such care for them, that they want nothing; and dust thou so grievously take on, as one that could bear with them no longer; thou that art but for a moment of time? yea thou that art one of those sinners thyself? A very ridiculous thing it is, that any man should dispense with vice and wickedness in himself, which is in his power to restrain; and should go about to suppress it in others, which is altogether impossible.

nearest.title: What is not in my power

passages.greek: Ἤτοι οὐδὲν δύνανται οἱ θεοὶ ἢ δύνανται. εἰ μὲν οὖν μὴ δύνανται, τί εὔχῃ; εἰ δὲ δύνανται, διὰ τί οὐχὶ μᾶλλον εὔχῃ. διδόναι αὐτοὺς τὸ μήτε φοβεῖσθαί τι τούτων μήτε ἐπιθυμεῖν τινος τούτων μήτε λυπεῖσθαι ἐπί τινι τούτων, μᾶλλον ἤπερ τὸ μὴ παρεῖναί τι τούτων ἢ τὸ παρεῖναι; πάντως γάρ, εἰ δύνανται συνεργεῖν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ εἰς ταῦτα δύνανται συνεργεῖν. ἀλλὰ ἴσως ἐρεῖς ὅτι· ἐπ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτὰ οἱ θεοὶ ἐποίησαν. εἶτα οὐ κρεῖσσον χρῆσθαι τοῖς ἐπὶ σοὶ μετ’ ἐλευθερίας ἣ διαφέρεσθαι πρὸς τὰ μὴ ἐπὶ σοὶ μετὰ δουλείας καὶ ταπεινότητος; τίς δέ σοι εἶπεν ὅτι οὐχὶ καὶ εἰς τὰ ἐφ̓ ἡμῖν οἱ θεοὶ συλλαμβάνουσιν; ἄρξαι γοῦν περὶ τούτων εὔχεσθαι καὶ ὄψει. οὗτος εὔχεται· πῶς κοιμηθῶ μετ’ ἐκείνης· σύ· πῶς μὴ ἐπιθυμήσω τοῦ κοιμηθῆναι μετ’ ἐκείνης. ἄλλος· πῶς στερηθῶ ἐκείνου· σύ· πῶς μὴ χρῄζω τοῦ στερηθῆναι. ἄλλος· πῶς μὴ ἀποβάλω τὸ τεκνίον· σύ· πῶς μὴ φοβηθῶ ἀποβαλεῖν. ὅλως ὧδε ἐπίστρεψον τὰς εὐχὰς καὶ θεώρει τί γίνεται.
passages.english: Either the gods can do nothing or they can. Now if they cannot, why do you pray? But if they can, why do you not rather pray that they grant you not to fear any of these things, not to desire any of them, not to be pained at any of them, rather than that any of them be absent or be present? For certainly, if they can work with people, they can work with them toward these things too. But perhaps you will say: “The gods have left these things up to me.” Then is it not better to use what is up to you in freedom than to let what is not up to you make a difference to you, in slavery and degradation? And who told you that the gods do not also lend a hand with the things that are up to us? Begin, at any rate, to pray about these, and you will see. This man prays: “How may I sleep with that woman?” You: “How may I not desire to sleep with that woman?” Another: “How may I be rid of that one?” You: “How may I not want to be rid of that one?” Another: “How may I not lose my little child?” You: “How may I not be afraid of losing it?” In short, turn your prayers round like this and watch what happens.

notes.note: The verb is “can”, “have power”. The argument repeats it six times, so the English keeps “can” throughout.
notes.other_reading: Either the gods have no power or they have power.

notes.note: The full stop after εὔχῃ in the text as given breaks one sentence in two, a slip of the digitised copy; the English reads a single question ending at the question mark after παρεῖναι. “You” after “grant” is added: the Greek says only “that they give the not fearing”.
notes.other_reading: why not rather pray for them to give freedom from fear of any of these things

notes.note: “These things” has nothing before it to point to. It means the things people pray to get or to be spared, as the examples at the end show.
notes.other_reading: any of the things in question

notes.greek: ἐπ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτὰ οἱ θεοὶ ἐποίησαν
notes.note: Literally “the gods made them upon me”, that is, placed them in the speaker’s power: the objection is that there is then no need to pray for them. The English says “left” for “made” so that “up to” can stand as in the rest of the passage. The quotation marks are added.
notes.other_reading: The gods have put these things in my own power.

notes.greek: ἣ διαφέρεσθαι πρὸς τὰ μὴ ἐπὶ σοὶ
notes.note: ἣ is a slip for ἢ, “than”. The verb διαφέρεσθαι πρός can mean to treat a thing as making a difference, to be concerned about it, or to be at odds with it. The English takes the first, as for the noun of the same idiom at 6.41.
notes.other_reading: than to be at odds with what is not up to you

notes.note: Literally “with slavery and lowness”, set against “with freedom”. ταπεινότης is the state of one brought low, abject.
notes.other_reading: like a slave and a beggar

notes.note: The verb is to take hold together with someone, to help with a task. It is a different word from “work with” (συνεργεῖν) above, so the English gives it a different phrase.
notes.other_reading: that the gods do not help us even with the things that are up to us

notes.note: Each prayer is put as a question beginning “how”, which is a request, not a real question. The quotation marks are added. The verb is literally “to go to bed”.
notes.other_reading: Let me sleep with that woman.

notes.note: The verb is literally “be deprived of”. ἐκείνου can be a man or a thing, and “that one” leaves it open. In the answer the Greek has no object, and “of that one” is repeated to complete the English.
notes.other_reading: How may I be rid of that man?

notes.note: χρῄζω is to need and also to want, to crave. “Want” is taken because the answer runs parallel to “not desire” in the answer before.
notes.other_reading: How may I not need to be rid of that one?

notes.note: A diminutive of “child”, tender in tone. The Greek word is neuter, which is why the English has “it”.
notes.other_reading: my little one

check.greek: διαφέρεσθαι πρὸς τὰ μὴ ἐπὶ σοὶ
check.note: διαφέρεσθαι πρός is to make a difference over a thing, to set store by it, or to be at odds over it, as in the noun at 6.41. “Anxious” adds a feeling the verb does not name.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “than to let what is not up to you make a difference to you”, which names no feeling and matches “the difference these things make to us” at 6.41. The suggested “set your heart on” is not used because it brings in an image the Greek does not have.

check.note: “Made these things up to me” is first read as “invented these things”; the Greek is that the gods put them in the speaker’s power.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The gods have left these things up to me.”, which keeps “up to” as in the rest of the passage. The note says the Greek verb is “made”.

check.note: ἐκείνου is masculine or neuter, “that man” or “that thing”, and “be deprived of” suits a thing at least as well.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “How may I be rid of that one?”, which leaves man or thing open as the Greek does. The note records the choice and gives “that man” as the other reading.

check.note: χρῄζω is as much “want” as “need”, and the parallel with “desire” just before points to wanting; “of him” is supplied, since the Greek has no object.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “How may I not want to be rid of that one?”. “Want” is taken; the object English needs after “rid” repeats “that one” in place of “it”, so that man or thing stays open, and the note says it is supplied.

check.note: ταῦτα is plural: the three things just listed, not fearing, not desiring, not being pained.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “toward these things too”.

check.note: The full stop after εὔχῃ cuts the infinitive off from its verb; it is a slip of the digitised text, and the English rightly reads one question.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged and reads one question, and the note on these words now names the stop as a slip of the digitised copy.

check.note: Found while settling: πάντως was “surely” here and is “certainly” at 7.70 as settled; “surely” can also be heard as asking for agreement.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For certainly”, the same word as for πάντως at 7.70.

passages.casaubon: Either the Gods can do nothing for us at all, or they can still and allay all the distractions and distempers of thy mind. If they can do nothing, why doest thou pray? If they can, why wouldst not thou rather pray, that they will grant unto thee, that thou mayst neither fear, nor lust after any of those worldly things which cause these distractions and distempers of it? Why not rather, that thou mayst not at either their absence or presence, be grieved and discontented: than either that thou mayst obtain them, or that thou mayst avoid them? For certainly it must needs be, that if the Gods can help us in anything, they may in this kind also. But thou wilt say perchance, 'In those things the Gods have given me my liberty: and it is in mine own power to do what I will.' But if thou mayst use this liberty, rather to set thy mind at true liberty, than wilfully with baseness and servility of mind to affect those things, which either to compass or to avoid is not in thy power, wert not thou better? And as for the Gods, who hath told thee, that they may not help us up even in those things that they have put in our own power? whether it be so or no, thou shalt soon perceive, if thou wilt but try thyself and pray. One prayeth that he may compass his desire, to lie with such or such a one, pray thou that thou mayst not lust to lie with her. Another how he may be rid of such a one; pray thou that thou mayst so patiently bear with him, as that thou have no such need to be rid of him. Another, that he may not lose his child. Pray thou that thou mayst not fear to lose him. To this end and purpose, let all thy prayer be, and see what will be the event.

nearest.title: What is not in my power

passages.greek: Ἅλις τοῦ ἀθλίου βίου καὶ γογγυσμοῦ καὶ πιθηκισμοῦ.—τί ταράσσῃ; τί τούτων καινόν; τί σε ἐξίστησι; τὸ αἴτιον; ἴδε αὐτό. ἀλλ’ ἡ ὕλη; ἴδε αὐτήν. ἔξω δὲ τούτων οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς θεοὺς ἤδη ποτὲ ἁπλούστερος καὶ χρηστότερος γενοῦ.
passages.english: Enough of the wretched life, the grumbling, the aping. Why are you troubled? What in this is new? What puts you beside yourself? The cause? Look at it. Or the material? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing. But toward the gods too, now at last, become simpler and better.

notes.greek: Ἅλις τοῦ ἀθλίου βίου καὶ γογγυσμοῦ καὶ πιθηκισμοῦ
notes.note: Three nouns joined by “and”; “wretched” stands only with “life” but may colour all three. πιθηκισμός is playing the ape: mimicry, putting on an act. The dash that follows in the Greek is replaced with a new sentence.
notes.other_reading: Enough of this wretched life of grumbling and monkey tricks.

notes.note: The verb is to put someone out of their place, and so out of their wits. “Beside yourself” is the English idiom with the same picture.
notes.other_reading: What is upsetting you?

notes.note: “The cause” and “the material” (ἡ ὕλη) are the usual two-part analysis of any thing in this book: the active principle that makes it what it is, and the stuff it is made of. The questions ask which of the two is the trouble.
notes.other_reading: Is it the form of the thing?

notes.note: ἀλλά here brings in the second of two alternatives, so the English says “or”. ὕλη is the stuff a thing is made of, often rendered “matter”; “material” avoids the other sense of “the matter”.
notes.other_reading: But the matter?

notes.greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς θεοὺς ἤδη ποτὲ
notes.note: “But also toward the gods”: the turn is abrupt in the Greek, and no link is added. ἤδη ποτέ is “now at last”, with a note of impatience.
notes.other_reading: And in your dealings with the gods as well, it is high time

notes.note: ἁπλοῦς is single, without doubleness: simple, straightforward. χρηστός is good in the sense of decent, honest, kind; “better” matches “very good” for the same word at 12.5.
notes.other_reading: more straightforward and kinder

check.note: Right in sense, but the English idiom is “beside yourself”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “What puts you beside yourself?”, the English idiom for being put out of one’s place.

check.note: ἀλλά here brings in the second alternative, “or is it”; “But the matter?” is abrupt, and “the matter” can be heard as “what is the matter”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Or the material? Look at it.”, with “or” for the second alternative and “material” so that “the matter” is not misheard. The bare noun as a question and the repeated “Look at it” are kept, because the Greek has no “is it” and uses the same pronoun both times.

part.left_out: Ἴσον τὸ ἑκατὸν ἔτεσι καὶ τὸ τρισὶ ταῦτα ἱστορῆσαι.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 9.35 before the chapter's last sentence and makes that sentence its section 9.36.

passages.casaubon: Will this querulousness, this murmuring, this complaining and dissembling never be at an end? What then is it, that troubleth thee? Doth any new thing happen unto thee? What doest thou so wonder at? At the cause, or the matter? Behold either by itself, is either of that weight and moment indeed? And besides these, there is not anything. But thy duty towards the Gods also, it is time thou shouldst acquit thyself of it with more goodness and simplicity.

nearest.title: What is not in my power

passages.greek: τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ φύσει. Μήτε θεοῖς μεμπτέον· οὐδὲν γὰρ ἑκόντες ἢ ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνουσι· μήτε ἀνθρώποις· οὐδὲν γὰρ οὐχὶ ἄκοντες. ὥστε οὐδενὶ μεμπτέον.
passages.english:
What follows in order on nature.

The gods are not to be blamed, for they go wrong in nothing, willingly or unwillingly. Nor are people, for they go wrong in nothing except unwillingly. So no one is to be blamed.

notes.note: A phrase without a verb, cut from its sentence: “the next-in-order to nature”, what comes in sequence with nature. It does not construe alone and is left a fragment, in a paragraph of its own because the passage gives it as the end of chapter 11. It can also be taken with the sentence that follows; from memory, unchecked, editors differ on whether these words end chapter 11 or begin chapter 12.
notes.other_reading: As to what comes next in the order of nature: the gods are not to be blamed

notes.greek: οὐδὲν γὰρ ἑκόντες ἢ ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνουσι
notes.note: The verb is to miss the mark, to go wrong; it covers error as well as wrongdoing. “Willingly or unwillingly” denies both ways of going wrong.
notes.other_reading: for they do no wrong, either on purpose or against their will

notes.note: The verb is carried over from the clause before, and the English repeats it. Literally “for nothing not unwillingly”: whatever they go wrong in, they do against their will, the Socratic teaching that no one goes wrong willingly.
notes.other_reading: for they do no wrong that is not against their will

check.note: The words stand alone with a full stop and are translated as a detached phrase, but they can also be construed with the next sentence; ἑξῆς is “next in sequence”, so “what comes next in the course of nature” is closer than “follows on”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “What follows in order on nature.”, with “in order” added for ἑξῆς, “next in sequence”. “In the course of nature” is not used because “nature” is in the case that goes with “next to”, and the phrase stays a paragraph alone because the passage gives it as the end of chapter 11; the note records the other construction.

part.left_out: Ἡλίκην ἐξουσίαν ἔχει ἄνθρωπος μὴ ποιεῖν ἄλλο ἢ ὅπερ μέλλει ὁ θεὸς ἐπαινεῖν, καὶ δέχεσθαι πᾶν ὃν νέμῃ αὐτῷ ὁ θεός.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 12.8 before the last three words of chapter 12.11 and opens its section 12.9 with them, joined to chapter 12.12.

passages.casaubon: Whatsoever doth happen in the ordinary course and consequence of natural events, neither the Gods, (for it is not possible, that they either wittingly or unwittingly should do anything amiss) nor men, (for it is through ignorance, and therefore against their wills that they do anything amiss) must be accused. None then must be accused.

nearest.title: What is not in my power

passages.greek: φυγὰς ὁ φεύγων τὸν πολιτικὸν λόγον· τυφλὸς ὁ καταμύων τῷ νοερῷ ὄμματι· πτωχὸς ὁ ἐνδεὴς ἑτέρου καὶ μὴ πάντα ἔχων παρ’ ἑαυτοῦ τὰ εἰς τὸν βίον χρήσιμα· ἀπόστημα κόσμου ὁ ἀφιστάμενος καὶ χωρίζων ἑαυτὸν τοῦ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως λόγου διὰ τοῦ δυσαρεστεῖν τοῖς συμβαίνουσιν· ἐκείνη γὰρ φέρει τοῦτο, ἣ καὶ σὲ ἤνεγκεν· ἀπόσχισμα πόλεως ὁ τὴν ἰδίαν ψυχὴν τῆς τῶν λογικῶν ἀποσχίζων, μιᾶς οὔσης.
passages.english: An exile is whoever exiles themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens. Blind is whoever shuts the eye of the mind. A beggar is whoever is in need of another and does not have from themselves everything that is useful for life. An abscess standing apart from the universe is whoever stands apart and separates themselves from the reason of the common nature by being displeased with what happens: for that nature brings this forth, the same one that brought you forth too. A piece split off from the city is whoever splits their own soul off from the soul of rational beings, which is one.

notes.note: A play on one root: φυγάς is a banished person, an exile (it can also mean a fugitive), and φεύγειν is both “to flee” and the ordinary verb for being in exile. The English reads “exile” and “exiles themselves” so that the echo is heard and the list stays about a person’s standing in the city; the sense of running away is given up. The passage begins partway through chapter 4.29; nothing was added apart from the “is” that each of these verbless Greek sentences needs in English.
notes.other_reading: A fugitive is whoever flees from the reason that belongs to citizens.

notes.note: πολιτικός means “of citizens, of their life together in a city”; the city meant is the one that all rational beings share, named at the end of the passage. λόγος is “reason” as in the glossary, here and in “the reason of the common nature” below. “The reason that belongs to citizens” is read in place of the closer “the reason of the city”, which is hard to take in.
notes.other_reading: the reason of the city, or: the principle of life as a citizen

notes.note: καταμύω is “to shut the eyes”, and the dative says with which eye: literally “who shuts their eyes with the eye of the mind”. The English makes the eye the object. νοερός is “of the mind” as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: whoever keeps their eyes shut where the eye of the mind is concerned

notes.note: The form can be masculine (another person) or neuter (something else). “Another” is kept because the Greek sets this one word against “from themselves” in the next clause; an English reader will hear a person first.
notes.other_reading: whoever is in need of something else

notes.note: Literally “from beside oneself”, that is, supplied by oneself. The English keeps the literal “from themselves”.
notes.other_reading: from their own resources

notes.note: A play on one root: ἀπόστημα is the medical word for an abscess, literally “a standing away” (matter that has drawn apart in the body), and ἀφιστάμενος is “standing away, withdrawing”, a word also used of revolt. The English keeps the abscess and spells out the literal sense of the noun as “standing apart from the universe”, so that “stands apart” can echo it as “split off” does in the next sentence. The Greek has only “an abscess of the universe”.
notes.other_reading: An abscess on the universe is whoever withdraws, or revolts

notes.greek: ἐκείνη γὰρ φέρει τοῦτο, ἣ καὶ σὲ ἤνεγκεν
notes.note: The Greek has only “that one”, feminine, which picks up the common nature just named, and the English supplies “nature”; the same verb (φέρω: bring, bear, produce) comes twice, so “bring forth” is used twice. “This” is as bare and singular in the Greek: the particular thing that happens and displeases. The Greek turns to “you” here with no warning, and the English keeps that.
notes.other_reading: for the nature that produces this is the same one that produced you

notes.greek: ἀπόσχισμα πόλεως ὁ τὴν ἰδίαν ψυχὴν τῆς τῶν λογικῶν ἀποσχίζων, μιᾶς οὔσης
notes.note: The Greek repeats one root (ἀπόσχισμα, ἀποσχίζων), which “split off” keeps. “Soul” has to be supplied with “of rational beings”: literally “from that of the rational ones, it being one”. The last two words can be a plain statement (“which is one”) or a concession (“though it is one”); the English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: A fragment torn from the city is whoever tears their own soul away from the soul of rational beings, although that soul is one.

check.note: The Greek noun and verb are one word (“a standing off” and “standing off”), so the name is explained by the act, as with “split off” in the next sentence. “Abscess” and “stands apart” lose the link.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “An abscess standing apart from the universe is whoever stands apart”, so that the literal sense of the noun is spelled out and the verb echoes it. “Abscess” is kept, because ἀπόστημα is the medical name of the thing and the image has to stay; “growth” would name a different thing.

check.note: Noun and verb share a root in the Greek. “Exile” and “flees” drop the echo.
