check.note: εὐποιία is the act of doing good, not the good received. “The benefit of human beings” shifts from what one does to what they get.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “referring it to the doing of good to human beings”, which keeps the stress on the doing, as the Greek word does.

check.note: πηγή is a spring of water. “Source” is right but loses the picture.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the spring of all things”. The Greek word is the ordinary one for a spring of water, and the image is kept as an image.

check.note: μηρύομαι is to draw out or wind thread, and with “from which” the picture is of events drawn out together from one source. “Wound from” does not quite work in English; “spun out together” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: “is wound together” stands. The Greek verb is of winding yarn, not of spinning, for which Greek has another word, so “spun” would change the picture. The note explains the image.

passages.casaubon: Shall I do it? I will; so the end of my action be to do good unto men. Doth anything by way of cross or adversity happen unto me? I accept it, with reference unto the Gods, and their providence; the fountain of all things, from which whatsoever comes to pass, doth hang and depend.

passages.greek: ὁπουδήποτε καταληφθείς, εὔμοιρος ἄνθρωπος· τὸ δὲ εὔμοιρος, ἀγαθὴν μοῖραν σεαυτῷ ἀπονείμας· ἀγαθαὶ δὲ μοῖραι ἀγαθαὶ τροπαὶ ψυχῆς, ἀγαθαὶ ὁρμαί, ἀγαθαὶ πράξεις.
passages.english: … wherever caught, a person whose lot is good. And “whose lot is good” means having assigned yourself a good lot; and good lots are good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions.

notes.note: The passage begins in the middle of a sentence and has no finite verb: the 1634 division puts the opening words of the sentence, “Once I was”, at the end of the section before. Nothing is supplied here, and the three dots mark the cut. καταληφθείς is “caught”, “overtaken” or “found”, and the Greek does not say by what.
notes.other_reading: wherever overtaken; in whatever place found

notes.note: εὔμοιρος ordinarily means “fortunate”, but it is built on μοῖρα, a share or lot, and the next two clauses argue from that. The English reads “whose lot is good” so that “lot” can be repeated.
notes.other_reading: a fortunate person

notes.note: The article quotes the word just used and there is no verb; “means” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: And “fortunate” is: having assigned a good fortune to yourself

notes.note: Second person: “to yourself”, with the participle in the nominative. ἀπονέμω is “assign” or “deal out” and is not formed from μοῖρα, so the English does not echo “lot” in it.
notes.other_reading: having dealt yourself a good portion

notes.note: τροπαί are turns or changes of direction, and ψυχῆς has no article. “Turnings” is written because “good turns” in English means favours.
notes.other_reading: good dispositions of the soul; good changes of the soul

notes.note: ὁρμή, “impulse”: the movement of the soul toward an action, the Stoic term.
notes.other_reading: good strivings

check.note: The Greek as given has no verb because the cut falls in mid-sentence, and the English is a verbless fragment too. A reader cannot tell who is spoken of or in what tense; the fragment should be marked as the end of a sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now begins with three dots and a small letter, “… wherever caught, a person whose lot is good.” Nothing is supplied, and the note says where the opening words of the sentence stand.

check.note: καταλαμβάνω in the passive is “caught, come upon, overtaken” by events. “Wherever overtaken” with no agent is unclear and might be read as “left behind”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “wherever caught”, the plainest sense of the verb, with the agent left unsaid as in the Greek.

check.note: “Allotted yourself a good lot” makes a word-echo that is not in the Greek: the echo there is εὔμοιρος, μοῖραν, μοῖραι only, and ἀπονέμω is a different word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “having assigned yourself a good lot”, so that only the three Greek words that share a root share “lot”. It also matches “assigns” for the simple verb in 12.11a.

check.note: τροπαί are turns: changes of direction, hence inclinations or movements of the soul. “Turnings” is literal and odd; “good turns of the soul” is suggested, and the Greek has no article.
check.decided: Declined: “good turnings of the soul” stands. τροπαί are changes of direction, which “turnings” says, while “good turns” is heard in English as favours done. The missing article is recorded in the note.

part.left_out: Μὴ ὁλοσχερῶς τῇ φαντασίᾳ συναρπάζεσθαι, ἀλλὰ βοηθεῖν μὲν κατὰ δύναμιν καὶ κατ’ ἀξίαν, κἂν εἰς τὰ μέσα ἐλαττῶνται, μὴ μέντοι βλάβην αὐτὸ φαντάζεσθαι· κακὸν γὰρ ἔθος. ἀλλ’ ὡς ὁ γέρων ἀπελθὼν τὸν τοῦ θρεπτοῦ ῥόμβον ἀπῄτει, μεμνημένος ὅτι ῥόμβος, οὕτως οὖν καὶ ὧδε. ἐπεί τοι γίνῃ καλῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐμβόλων. ἄνθρωπε, ἐπελάθου τί ταῦτα ἦν;—ναί· ἀλλὰ τούτοις περισπούδαστα.—διὰ τοῦτ’ οὖν καὶ σὺ μωρὸς γένῃ; Ἐγενόμην ποτέ,
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 5.29 with the words 'Once I was' (Ἐγενόμην ποτέ) and begins its section 5.30 with the words that follow them.

passages.casaubon: Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will, I may be εὔμοιρος, or a happy man, nevertheless. For he is a happy man, who in his lifetime dealeth unto himself a happy lot and portion. A happy lot and portion is, good inclinations of the soul, good desires, good actions.

passages.greek: Ὡς εὔκολον ἀπώσασθαι καὶ ἀπαλεῖψαι πᾶσαν φαντασίαν τὴν ὀχληρὰν ἢ ἀνοίκειον καὶ εὐθὺς ἐν πάσῃ γαλήνῃ εἶναι.
passages.english: How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troublesome or out of place, and at once to be in a complete calm.

notes.note: To wipe out or rub out, as writing from a tablet or a mark from a surface. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: to erase

notes.note: φαντασία, “impression”: what presents itself to the mind, the Stoic term.
notes.other_reading: every thought; every appearance

notes.note: ὀχληρός is troublesome, pressing in on one. ἀνοίκειος is not one’s own, foreign, and also unfitting. “Out of place” is taken as the English that says “does not belong here”.
notes.other_reading: every impression that is disturbing or alien

notes.note: γαλήνη is the stillness of the sea, and “a calm” is meant to keep that. πάσῃ is “all”, here “complete”; it answers πᾶσαν, “every”, earlier in the sentence, an echo the English does not keep.
notes.other_reading: in all calm; in perfect stillness

check.note: ἀνοίκειος is “not one’s own, alien” as well as “unfitting”. “Out of place” takes the second sense.
check.decided: Declined: “out of place” stands. It says of an impression that it does not belong where it is, which covers both sides of the Greek word. “Alien” is given in the note.

check.note: ἀπαλείφω is to wipe out, erase, as writing from a tablet. “Wipe off” suggests cleaning a surface of dirt.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “wipe out”, which is said of a mark or of writing and so suits an impression.

check.note: πᾶσαν and πάσῃ answer each other in the Greek (every impression, all calm), and “every” and “complete” lose the echo. γαλήνη is the stillness of the sea, which “a complete calm” only half keeps.
check.decided: Declined: “in a complete calm” stands. “Complete” gives the full force of πάσῃ, “in all calm” is not English as it is written today, and “a calm” is the English word for stillness at sea. The echo is recorded in the note.

passages.casaubon: How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and tranquillity!

passages.greek: Ἀτύφως μὲν λαβεῖν, εὐλύτως δὲ ἀφεῖναι.
passages.english: To take without conceit, and to let go readily.

notes.note: Without τῦφος: literally smoke, and so conceit, a head puffed up. The English reads “without conceit”.
notes.other_reading: without vanity; without arrogance

notes.note: The two infinitives stand alone. They can be a maxim (“to take”) or commands to oneself. No object is expressed: what is taken and let go is left open, and λαβεῖν covers both “take” and “receive”, as “take” does in English.
notes.other_reading: Receive without conceit; let go readily.

notes.note: From a word for what is easily untied or loosened: with no knot to work at, and so without clinging. The English reads “readily”.
notes.other_reading: with ease; with a loose hand

check.note: εὔλυτος is “easily loosed”: the point is letting go readily, without clinging. “With ease” can be read as “without effort”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to let go readily”. The Greek word is about how easily the hold comes loose, not about the effort of the one who lets go.

check.note: λαβεῖν is “receive” as much as “take”. Paired with ἀφεῖναι and ἀτύφως, “receive” is the likelier sense; “take” suggests reaching for a thing.
check.decided: Declined: “take” stands. λαβεῖν covers taking and receiving alike, and English “take” does the same (one takes what is given), so the wider word matches the Greek. “Receive” is given in the note.

passages.casaubon: Receive temporal blessings without ostentation, when they are sent and thou shalt be able to part with them with all readiness and facility when they are taken from thee again.

passages.greek: Οὐχὶ τοῦτο μόνον δεῖ λογίζεσθαι, ὅτι καθ’ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἀπαναλίσκεται ὁ βίος καὶ μέρος ἔλαττον αὐτοῦ καταλείπεται, ἀλλὰ κἀκεῖνο λογιστέον, ὅτι, εἰ ἐπὶ πλέον βιῴη τις, ἐκεῖνό γε ἄδηλον, εἰ ἐξαρκέσει ὁμοία αὖθις ἡ διάνοια πρὸς τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ τῆς θεωρίας τῆς συντεινούσης εἰς τὴν ἐμπειρίαν τῶν τε θείων καὶ τῶν ἀνθρωπείων. ἐὰν γὰρ παραληρεῖν ἄρξηται, τὸ μὲν διαπνεῖσθαι καὶ τρέφεσθαι καὶ φαντάζεσθαι καὶ ὁρμᾶν καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα τοιαῦτα, οὐκ ἐνδεήσει· τὸ δὲ ἑαυτῷ χρῆσθαι καὶ τοὺς τοῦ καθήκοντος ἀριθμοὺς ἀκριβοῦν καὶ τὰ προφαινόμενα διαρθροῦν καὶ περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ εἰ ἤδη ἐξακτέον αὑτὸν ἐφιστάνειν καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα λογισμοῦ συγγεγυμνασμένου πάνυ χρῄζει, προαποσβέννυται. χρὴ οὖν ἐπείγεσθαι οὐ μόνον τῷ ἐγγυτέρω τοῦ θανάτου ἑκάστοτε γίνεσθαι, ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τὸ τὴν ἐννόησιν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ τὴν παρακολούθησιν προαπολήγειν.
passages.english: It is not only this that has to be reckoned with, that life is being used up day by day and a smaller part of it is left. This too has to be reckoned with: if a person were to live longer, this at least is unclear, whether their mind will later on be equal, unchanged, to the understanding of things and of the study that is directed toward close acquaintance with divine and human things. For if a person begins to lose their wits, there will be no lack of breathing, of taking nourishment, of having impressions and impulses, and of everything else of that kind. But making use of oneself, getting every point of duty exact, setting out clearly what appears before one, stopping to consider this very question, whether it is now time to lead oneself out of life, and everything of that kind that needs thoroughly trained reasoning: this is extinguished first. So one must hurry, not only because one comes nearer to death at every moment, but also because the grasp of things and the power to follow them give out first.

notes.note: λογίζεσθαι, then λογιστέον, and further on the noun λογισμοῦ are one family of words (to reckon, to reason). The English reads “reckoned with” for the two verbs and “reasoning” for the noun, so the link is only half kept.
notes.other_reading: It is not only this that one must reason about

notes.note: αὖθις is “later on” or “again”, and ὁμοία is “the same, alike”, said of the mind. The English reads “later on” and “unchanged”.
notes.other_reading: whether their mind will again be equal to it in the same way

notes.note: The glossary gives “thought” for διάνοια and allows “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty that may fail with age, so the English reads “mind”.
notes.other_reading: whether their thought will later on be equal

notes.greek: πρὸς τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ τῆς θεωρίας
notes.note: τῆς θεωρίας is in the genitive, so as the Greek stands it depends on σύνεσιν together with τῶν πραγμάτων: understanding of things and of the study. An accusative would make the study a second thing the mind must be equal to, and editors have doubted the case (from memory, unchecked). The English keeps the genitive as given.
notes.other_reading: equal to understanding things and to the study that is directed toward close acquaintance with divine and human things

notes.note: ἐμπειρία is familiarity won by experience and practice, not knowledge in the abstract. The English reads “close acquaintance”.
notes.other_reading: toward experience of divine and human things

notes.note: παραληρεῖν is to talk beside the point, as in delirium or senility; the English gives the sense, “lose their wits”. The subject is not stated: it can be the person, as the English has it, or the mind, the nearest noun.
notes.other_reading: For if it begins to wander

notes.note: Literally “to be breathed through”. It can mean plain breathing or the wider passing of air and vapour through the body and its skin. The English keeps the plain word.
notes.other_reading: transpiring

notes.note: Literally “to make exact the numbers of duty”. In Stoic speech a duty (τὸ καθῆκον, what is fitting to do) has “numbers”, the separate points that must all be met for the act to be complete. The English reads “every point” for “the numbers”.
notes.other_reading: getting the numbers of duty exact

notes.note: διαρθροῦν is to divide by joints, to set out part by part. τὰ προφαινόμενα is “the things that show themselves”, which can be what comes into view in general or first appearances in particular.
notes.other_reading: analysing first appearances part by part

notes.note: Literally “one must lead oneself out”, the Stoic expression for leaving life by one’s own act. “Of life” is added so that the English says what is meant, and “must now” is turned into “it is now time to”.
notes.other_reading: whether one must now lead oneself out

notes.note: πάνυ, “very”, stands between the participle and the verb and can go with either. The English takes it with the participle: “thoroughly trained”.
notes.other_reading: that very much needs trained reasoning

notes.note: The image is of a flame going out beforehand. “First” stands for the prefix προ-, before the other functions or before death; the Greek does not say which. προαπολήγειν in the last sentence has the same prefix and reads “first” there too.
notes.other_reading: is extinguished beforehand

check.note: αὖθις is “later on, afterwards”, not “still”, and “as before” is not in the Greek: ὁμοία is simply “the same, unchanged”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “whether their mind will later on be equal, unchanged, to the understanding of things”. “Later on” stands for αὖθις and “unchanged” for ὁμοία, with nothing added; the suggested “in the same way” is not used because ὁμοία describes the mind itself.

check.note: The genitive τῆς θεωρίας hangs on σύνεσιν, giving “the understanding of things and of the study”, which is odd, since the study looks like a second thing the mind must be equal to. Editors have doubted the case (from memory).
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “the understanding of things and of the study”, as the point itself advises, because that is what the Greek as given says. The note now records that the phrase is awkward, that an accusative would give “and to the study”, and that the case has been doubted (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: ἐμπειρία is acquaintance won by experience, practised familiarity, not knowledge in general.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “close acquaintance with” in place of “knowledge of”, since the Greek word means familiarity got by practice. “Experience of” is given in the note.

check.greek: τῶν τε θείων καὶ τῶν ἀνθρωπείων
check.note: “Things divine and human”, with the adjectives after the noun, is an old-fashioned English turn.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “divine and human things”.

check.note: The subject of ἄρξηται is not stated: it can be the person as well as the mind, and παραληρεῖν is more naturally said of a person. “Ramble” is also weaker than the Greek, which means losing one’s wits.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For if a person begins to lose their wits”. The verb is used of people who talk nonsense in delirium or old age, and the list that follows (breathing, taking nourishment) is of the person’s functions; the note gives the reading with the mind as subject.

check.note: διαπνεῖσθαι is “to be breathed through, to transpire”, a wider bodily process than respiration, and “breathing” narrows it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the point holds that the Greek word is wider than breathing with the lungs, but “breathing” is kept as the plain word, which the point allows. The note now says what the wider sense is and gives “transpiring” as the other reading.

check.note: “The numbers of duty” is word for word but means nothing to a reader of today; the ἀριθμοί are the items or points that make up a duty in full.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “getting every point of duty exact”. “Numbers” here is a set Stoic expression for the points that make an act complete, not a picture the argument uses, so the sense is given and the note keeps the literal “numbers”; “what duty requires” is not used because the Greek has only “of duty”.

check.note: “Of life” is not in the Greek, which says only “lead oneself out”; it is a needed gloss but an addition.
check.decided: Accepted: “to lead oneself out of life” stands, as the point advises, since “lead oneself out” alone would not be understood. The note says that “of life” is added.

check.note: πάνυ stands between the participle and the verb and can go with either, but the English renders it twice, as “badly” and as “well”, and adds “power of”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “that needs thoroughly trained reasoning”, with πάνυ rendered once and “power of” removed. A new note gives the other reading, “very much needs”.

check.note: “Put out” is ambiguous in English (annoyed, set outside); the image is of a flame going out before the rest does.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “this is extinguished first”, which can only be heard of a flame.

passages.casaubon: A man must not only consider how daily his life wasteth and decreaseth, but this also, that if he live long, he cannot be certain, whether his understanding shall continue so able and sufficient, for either discreet consideration, in matter of businesses; or for contemplation: it being the thing, whereon true knowledge of things both divine and human, doth depend. For if once he shall begin to dote, his respiration, nutrition, his imaginative, and appetitive, and other natural faculties, may still continue the same: he shall find no want of them. But how to make that right use of himself that he should, how to observe exactly in all things that which is right and just, how to redress and rectify all wrong, or sudden apprehensions and imaginations, and even of this particular, whether he should live any longer or no, to consider duly; for all such things, wherein the best strength and vigour of the mind is most requisite; his power and ability will be past and gone. Thou must hasten therefore; not only because thou art every day nearer unto death than other, but also because that intellective faculty in thee, whereby thou art enabled to know the true nature of things, and to order all thy actions by that knowledge, doth daily waste and decay: or, may fail thee before thou die.

passages.greek: Κἂν τρὶς χίλια ἔτη βιώσεσθαι μέλλῃς, κἂν τοσαυτάκις μύρια, ὅμως μέμνησο ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἄλλον ἀποβάλλει βίον ἢ τοῦτον ὃν ζῇ, οὐδὲ ἄλλον ζῇ ἢ ὃν ἀποβάλλει. εἰς ταὐτὸν οὖν καθίσταται τὸ μήκιστον τῷ βραχυτάτῳ. τὸ γὰρ παρὸν πᾶσιν ἴσον καὶ τὸ ἀπολλύμενον οὖν ἴσον καὶ τὸ ἀποβαλλόμενον οὕτως ἀκαριαῖον ἀναφαίνεται. οὔτε γὰρ τὸ παρῳχηκὸς οὔτε τὸ μέλλον ἀποβάλοι ἄν τις· ὃ γὰρ οὐκ ἔχει, πῶς ἄν τις τοῦτο αὐτοῦ ἀφέλοιτο; τούτων οὖν τῶν δύο δεῖ μεμνῆσθαι· ἑνὸς μέν, ὅτι πάντα ἐξ ἀιδίου ὁμοειδῆ καὶ ἀνακυκλούμενα καὶ οὐδὲν διαφέρει, πότερον ἐν ἑκατὸν ἔτεσιν ἢ ἐν διακοσίοις ἢ ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ τὰ αὐτά τις ὄψεται· ἑτέρου δέ, ὅτι καὶ ὁ πολυχρονιώτατος καὶ ὁ τάχιστα τεθνηξόμενος τὸ ἴσον ἀποβάλλει. τὸ γὰρ παρόν ἐστι μόνον, οὗ στερίσκεσθαι μέλλει, εἴπερ γε ἔχει καὶ τοῦτο μόνον καὶ ὃ μὴ ἔχει τις οὐκ ἀποβάλλει.
passages.english: Even if you are going to live three thousand years, or even three times ten thousand, still remember that no one loses any life other than this one they are living, and no one lives any life other than the one they are losing. So the longest comes to the same thing as the shortest. For the present is equal for everyone, so what perishes is equal too, and in this way what is lost shows itself to be an instant. For no one could lose either the past or the future, for how could anyone take from a person what that person does not have? So these two things must be remembered. One is that all things from eternity are of the same kind and come round in a circle, and that it makes no difference whether a person will see the same things for a hundred years, or for two hundred, or for time without limit. The other is that the one who lives longest and the one who will die soonest lose an equal amount. For the present is the only thing a person is going to be deprived of, if indeed this is the only thing they have, and a person does not lose what they do not have.

notes.note: Literally “so many times ten thousand”, where “so many times” picks up the “three times” of three thousand. The English says “three times ten thousand” outright.
notes.other_reading: or even that many times ten thousand

notes.note: ἀποβάλλειν, literally to throw off or let drop, is the word the argument turns on and comes six times. The English reads “lose” every time.
notes.other_reading: no one throws away any life other than

notes.note: This is a different verb from ἀποβάλλειν: ἀπόλλυσθαι, to perish or be lost. The English reads “perishes” to keep it apart from “lose”, though it could be heard as one more word for the same loss. ἴσον is “equal” throughout the passage.
notes.other_reading: so what is being lost is equal too

notes.note: The word means of the shortest possible length, of a hair’s breadth of time. The English gives the noun “an instant” for the adjective.
notes.other_reading: shows itself to be momentary

notes.note: Literally “being wheeled round again”. The English keeps the circle.
notes.other_reading: and recur in cycles

notes.note: Literally “in the unlimited”, with “time” understood after the hundred and two hundred years. ἐν with a number of years means over that span, so the English reads “for”; “in a hundred years” would be heard as “a hundred years from now”.
notes.other_reading: or for ever

notes.greek: εἴπερ γε ἔχει καὶ τοῦτο μόνον
notes.note: εἴπερ γε can state a condition (“if indeed”) or a ground taken as agreed (“since”). The English keeps “if indeed”. The subject is unstated and is taken to be the same impersonal “a person” as in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: since this is in fact the only thing they have

check.note: The second “even if” (κἂν) is flattened to “or”, and “that many times ten thousand” is hard to follow; it means three times ten thousand.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “or even three times ten thousand”. “Even” restores the second κἂν, and the number is said outright; the note gives the literal “so many times”.

check.note: The γάρ that makes this question the reason for the sentence before is replaced by a colon.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for how could anyone take from a person what that person does not have?”, with the “for” of the Greek restored.

check.greek: ἐν ἑκατὸν ἔτεσιν ἢ ἐν διακοσίοις ἢ ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ
check.note: “Will see the same things in a hundred years” reads in English as “a hundred years from now”; the Greek means over a span of a hundred years, two hundred, or without end.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for a hundred years, or for two hundred, or for time without limit”, since ἐν with a number of years means during that span.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek says “this one that they are living”, and the draft’s “the one they are living” left “this” out.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “any life other than this one they are living”.

passages.casaubon: If thou shouldst live three thousand, or as many as ten thousands of years, yet remember this, that man can part with no life properly, save with that little part of life, which he now lives: and that which he lives, is no other, than that which at every instant he parts with. That then which is longest of duration, and that which is shortest, come both to one effect. For although in regard of that which is already past there may be some inequality, yet that time which is now present and in being, is equal unto all men. And that being it which we part with whensoever we die, it doth manifestly appear, that it can be but a moment of time, that we then part with. For as for that which is either past or to come, a man cannot be said properly to part with it. For how should a man part with that which he hath not? These two things therefore thou must remember. First, that all things in the world from all eternity, by a perpetual revolution of the same times and things ever continued and renewed, are of one kind and nature; so that whether for a hundred or two hundred years only, or for an infinite space of time, a man see those things which are still the same, it can be no matter of great moment. And secondly, that that life which any the longest liver, or the shortest liver parts with, is for length and duration the very same, for that only which is present, is that, which either of them can lose, as being that only which they have; for that which he hath not, no man can truly be said to lose.

passages.greek: Ἰδιωτικὸν μέν, ὅμως δὲ ἀνυστικὸν βοήθημα πρὸς θανάτου καταφρόνησιν ἡ ἀναπόλησις τῶν γλίσχρως ἐνδιατριψάντων τῷ ζῆν. τί οὖν αὐτοῖς πλέον ἢ τοῖς ἀώροις; πάντως πού ποτε κεῖνται, Καδικιανός, Φάβιος, Ἰουλιανός, Λέπιδος ἢ εἴ τις τοιοῦτος, οἳ πολλοὺς ἐξήνεγκαν, εἶτα ἐξηνέχθησαν· ὅλον, μικρόν ἐστι τὸ διάστημα καὶ τοῦτο δι’ ὅσων καὶ μεθ’ οἵων ἐξαντλούμενον καὶ ἐν οἵῳ σωματίῳ; μὴ οὖν ὡς πρᾶγμα. βλέπε γὰρ ὀπίσω τὸ ἀχανὲς τοῦ αἰῶνος καὶ τὸ πρόσω ἄλλο ἄπειρον. ἐν δὴ τούτῳ τί διαφέρει ὁ τριήμερος τοῦ τριγερηνίου;
passages.english: A layman’s help toward contempt of death, but an effective one all the same, is to call back to mind those who clung on and lingered in life. What more do they have, then, than those who died before their time? In any case they lie somewhere or other, Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus or anyone else of that kind, who carried many out to burial and then were carried out themselves. Altogether, the interval is small, and even this, through how many things, in what company and in what a little body it is drained out! So do not treat it as something that matters. For look behind at the yawning expanse of eternity, and ahead at another that has no limit. In this, then, what difference is there between a child three days old and a Nestor of three generations?

notes.note: ἰδιωτικός is what belongs to a private person or a non-expert, here as against a philosopher’s argument. It can carry a slight of “crude” or “vulgar”.
notes.other_reading: An unphilosophical help

notes.note: γλίσχρως is “stickily”, used of clinging and of stinginess. Literally “those who spent their time stickily in living”; the English gives the adverb as “clung on”. ἀναπόλησις before it is a going over again in the mind, here “call back to mind”.
notes.other_reading: those who hung on greedily to being alive

notes.note: πού ποτε can be “somewhere or other” or “somewhere, at some time”, and πάντως can be “in any case” or “surely”. κεῖνται, “they lie”, is the ordinary word for the dead lying in their graves.
notes.other_reading: Surely they lie somewhere at last

notes.note: The name is transliterated as it is given. From memory, unchecked: other editions print Καιδικιανός, Caedicianus. The four men are not explained in the text; the context makes them people known for living long.
notes.other_reading: Caedicianus

notes.note: ἐκφέρειν, “to carry out”, is the set word for carrying a body out to its funeral. “To burial” is added once so that the sense is clear.
notes.other_reading: who carried out many, then were carried out

notes.note: With the comma as given, ὅλον is an adverb, “on the whole, in sum”. Without it the words would say “the whole interval is small”.
notes.other_reading: The whole interval is small

notes.greek: καὶ τοῦτο δι’ ὅσων καὶ μεθ’ οἵων ἐξαντλούμενον καὶ ἐν οἵῳ σωματίῳ;
notes.note: The Greek as given ends this sentence with a question mark, but its words (“through how many”, “with what sort”, “in what a”) are those of an exclamation, not of a question. There is also no finite verb after “and even this”, only a participle. The English makes it an exclamation and supplies “it is”.
notes.other_reading: Altogether, is the interval not small, and even this drained out through how many things, in what company and in what a little body?

notes.note: The image is of baling or draining water out to the last, used for toiling through something. “Through how many” and “with what sort” do not say whether things or people are meant: the English reads the first as things, most likely troubles, and the second as people, “in what company”. σωματίῳ is a diminutive that belittles the body.
notes.other_reading: and even this is toiled through amid how many troubles, with what sort of things and in what a poor little body

notes.note: There is no verb: literally “not, then, as a matter”, with πρᾶγμα in the sense of something that counts. The English supplies “treat it” and gives πρᾶγμα as “something that matters”.
notes.other_reading: So, not as though it were something

notes.note: τὸ ἀχανές is “the yawning”, an adjective used as a noun, so English must supply a noun: “expanse”. αἰών is the whole of time, given as “eternity”.
notes.other_reading: the gaping gulf of time

notes.note: ἄπειρον can be taken with an understood “expanse” (another, without limit, ahead) or as a noun (what lies ahead is another infinity). The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: and what lies ahead, another infinity

notes.note: A made-up word that plays on “Gerenian”, Homer’s standing name for Nestor, the old king who outlived three generations, and on γέρων, “old man”: one who is three times a Nestor. The English names Nestor and gives the three as generations. τριήμερος before it is “of three days”, taken as a child three days old.
notes.other_reading: between the one who lives three days and the one who lives three generations

check.note: ἀναπόλησις is going over something again in the mind; “to go back over those” is not clear English when the object is people.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is to call back to mind those who clung on and lingered in life”. “Back” keeps the “again” of the Greek word.

check.note: ποτε (“at some point, at last”) is not rendered, and πάντως is more “assuredly, one way or another” than “in any case”.
check.decided: Declined: “somewhere or other” already renders πού ποτε, where ποτε is taken as the word that makes “somewhere” indefinite, and “in any case” is an ordinary sense of πάντως. The other way of taking the words, “surely” and “at last”, is recorded in the note.

check.note: ἢ is “or”, not “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “or anyone else of that kind”.

check.greek: καὶ τοῦτο δι’ ὅσων καὶ μεθ’ οἵων ἐξαντλούμενον καὶ ἐν οἵῳ σωματίῳ;
check.note: The Greek is an exclamation built on “how many, what sort”, and as an English question it is unclear. δι’ ὅσων is plural, “through how many things”, that is troubles, and “poor” is added to the diminutive σωματίῳ.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and even this, through how many things, in what company and in what a little body it is drained out!”, an exclamation, with “poor” removed. “Things” is kept and not “troubles”, because the Greek does not name them, and “drained out” is kept; a note records that the Greek as given ends in a question mark.

check.note: “Great” is not in the Greek, which says only “not, then, as a thing (that matters)”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “So do not treat it as something that matters”. The verb still has to be supplied, as the note says.

check.note: αἰών is the whole of time, eternity, not time in general, and “gaping gulf” gives two words for the one word ἀχανές.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the yawning expanse of eternity”. “Yawning” is the Greek adjective and “expanse” the plain noun English needs to carry it.

check.note: “Another without limit” is awkward English; the Greek is “another infinity ahead”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and ahead at another that has no limit”, with “expanse” understood. “Another infinity” is given in the note.

check.note: τριγερηνίου is a play on Nestor “the Gerenian”, who outlived three generations, and the allusion is dropped. τριήμερος is a child three days old.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “between a child three days old and a Nestor of three generations”, so the name the Greek points to is in the text. The note explains the made-up word.

passages.casaubon: It is but an ordinary coarse one, yet it is a good effectual remedy against the fear of death, for a man to consider in his mind the examples of such, who greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a long time enjoy their lives. What have they got more, than they whose deaths have been untimely? Are not they themselves dead at the last? as Cadiciant's, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus, or any other who in their lifetime having buried many, were at the last buried themselves. The whole space of any man's life, is but little; and as little as it is, with what troubles, with what manner of dispositions, and in the society of how wretched a body must it be passed! Let it be therefore unto thee altogether as a matter of indifferency. For if thou shalt look backward; behold, what an infinite chaos of time doth present itself unto thee; and as infinite a chaos, if thou shalt look forward. In that which is so infinite, what difference can there be between that which liveth but three days, and that which liveth three ages?

passages.greek: Μέμνησο ἐκ πόσου ταῦτα ἀναβάλλῃ καὶ ὁποσάκις προθεσμίας λαβὼν παρὰ τῶν θεῶν οὐ χρᾷ αὐταῖς. δεῖ δὲ ἤδη ποτὲ αἰσθέσθαι τίνος κόσμου μέρος εἶ καὶ τίνος διοικοῦντος τὸν κόσμον ἀπόρροια ὑπέστης καὶ ὅτι ὅρος ἐστί σοι περιγεγραμμένος τοῦ χρόνου, ᾧ ἐὰν εἰς τὸ ἀπαιθριάσαι μὴ χρήσῃ, οἰχήσεται οἰχήσῃ καὶ αὖθις οὐκ ἐξέσται.
passages.english: Remember how long you have been putting these things off, and how many times you have been given a set time by the gods and make no use of it. Now at last you must perceive what universe you are a part of, and from what governor of the universe you came into being as an outflow, and that a limit of time has been marked out for you. If you do not use it to clear away the clouds, it will be gone, you will be gone, and it will not be possible again.

notes.note: A legal word: the day fixed in advance by which something must be done, or the period allowed. The Greek is plural, one term after another being granted; the English reads “a set time” in the singular after “how many times”.
notes.other_reading: how many times you have been given deadlines by the gods and make no use of them

notes.note: τίνος asks “which” or “what”, and in such a phrase can lean toward “what kind of”.
notes.other_reading: what kind of universe you are a part of

notes.note: ἀπόρροια is a flowing off, a stream that runs out from a source. ὑπέστης is “you came to exist”. Literally “of what governor of the universe you came to exist as an outflow”.
notes.other_reading: and from what governor of the universe you exist as an emanation

notes.note: The verb is made from the word for a cloudless sky: to bring fair weather, to drive off the clouds. No object is given, and the weather stands for clearing one’s own mind; the English keeps the image and does not add “your mind”. The verb can also be taken as “to become clear”.
notes.other_reading: if you do not use it to become clear, as the sky does

notes.note: The two verbs stand side by side with no connecting word in the Greek as given: “it will be gone” (the time) and “you will be gone”. From memory, unchecked: editions print a καὶ between them, and its absence may be a slip of the digitised copy. The English keeps the two without “and”.
notes.other_reading: it will be gone and you will be gone

notes.note: Literally “it will not be allowed (or possible) again”, with nothing said about what: the chance to use the time.
notes.other_reading: and there will be no second chance

check.note: προθεσμία is an appointed day, a deadline or period of grace; “fixed terms” is unclear to a reader of today.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a set time”, not “a deadline” or “a set date”. The Greek goes on to say that the times are not used, and a time can be used where a date cannot.

check.note: After “you have received”, “and do not use them” jars; the Greek is a participle and a present, “having received them, you make no use of them”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how many times you have been given a set time by the gods and make no use of it”.

check.greek: τίνος διοικοῦντος τὸν κόσμον ἀπόρροια ὑπέστης
check.note: The content is right but the trailing “from as an outflow” is clumsy.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and from what governor of the universe you came into being as an outflow”.

check.note: The image of clearing the sky is kept, but nothing tells the reader it is the sky of his own mind, so the phrase puzzles. The verb can also be taken as “to become clear”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to clear away the clouds”. The verb is made from the word for a cloudless sky and means to bring fair weather, so the image is the same, and English speaks of clouds in this way when it means the mind; “to become clear” is in the note.

check.note: The two verbs stand side by side with no connective in the Greek as given; from memory the editions print καὶ between them, so this looks like a slip in the digitised text. The English is right either way.
check.decided: Accepted: “it will be gone, you will be gone” stands, as the point advises, following the Greek as given. The note says that a καὶ may have dropped out (from memory, unchecked).

passages.casaubon: Remember how long thou hast already put off these things, and how often a certain day and hour as it were, having been set unto thee by the gods, thou hast neglected it. It is high time for thee to understand the true nature both of the world, whereof thou art a part; and of that Lord and Governor of the world, from whom, as a channel from the spring, thou thyself didst flow: and that there is but a certain limit of time appointed unto thee, which if thou shalt not make use of to calm and allay the many distempers of thy soul, it will pass away and thou with it, and never after return.

passages.greek: Μὴ ὡς μύρια μέλλων ἔτη ζῆν. τὸ χρεὼν ἐπήρτηται· ἕως ζῇς, ἕως ἔξεστιν, ἀγαθὸς γενοῦ.
passages.english: Not as though you were going to live ten thousand years. What must come hangs over you. While you live, while it is possible, become good.

notes.greek: Μὴ ὡς μύρια μέλλων ἔτη ζῆν
notes.note: The sentence has no main verb: “Not as one who is going to live ten thousand years”. A verb such as “live” or “act” is left to be understood, and the English leaves it out as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: Do not live as though you were going to live ten thousand years

notes.note: τὸ χρεών is “what must be”, fate, with a sense of a debt that falls due: here death. ἐπήρτηται is “has been hung over”. The Greek does not say over whom; “you” is added.
notes.other_reading: Fate hangs overhead

notes.note: γενοῦ is “become”, which can also stand for a plain “be” in a command.
notes.other_reading: be good

passages.casaubon: Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live. Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.

passages.greek: Μηκέτι πλανῶ· οὔτε γὰρ τὰ ὑπομνημάτιά σου μέλλεις ἀναγινώσκειν οὔτε τὰς τῶν ἀρχαίων Ῥωμαίων καὶ Ἑλλήνων πράξεις καὶ τὰς ἐκ τῶν συγγραμμάτων ἐκλογάς, ἃς εἰς τὸ γῆρας σαυτῷ ἀπετίθεσο. σπεῦδε οὖν εἰς τέλος καὶ τὰς κενὰς ἐλπίδας ἀφεὶς σαυτῷ βοήθει, εἴ τί σοι μέλει σαυτοῦ, ἕως ἔξεστιν.
passages.english: Stop wandering. For you are not going to read either your little notebooks or the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks and the extracts from the writings, which you were putting away for yourself for old age. So hurry to the end, and letting go of empty hopes, come to your own rescue, if you care at all about yourself, while it is possible.

notes.note: πλανᾶσθαι is to wander, to stray, and so to be led off the point or be mistaken. Literally “wander no more”.
notes.other_reading: Stop going astray

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for notes or memoranda. It may mean notebooks like this one or other notes he kept; the Greek does not say.
notes.other_reading: your own little notes

notes.note: “Deeds”, as something to be read, so written accounts of them. It may be a collection he had made himself; the English keeps the plain word.
notes.other_reading: the histories of the ancient Romans and Greeks

notes.note: συγγράμματα are written works, treatises. The Greek says only “the writings” and does not say whose; the authors he read are the likely sense.
notes.other_reading: the selections from their books

notes.greek: ἃς εἰς τὸ γῆρας σαυτῷ ἀπετίθεσο
notes.note: The relative ἃς is feminine plural: what was being put away is the extracts, or the deeds and the extracts together, not the writings, which are neuter. The English “which” after the comma is to be heard the same way.
notes.other_reading: all of which you were putting away for your old age

notes.note: τέλος is both “end” and “goal, the aim of life”, and εἰς τέλος can also mean “to completion”. The English reads “the end”, which can be heard as the finish or as the aim.
notes.other_reading: So hurry on to your goal

notes.note: Literally “help yourself”, the verb for running to someone’s aid. “Help yourself” is avoided because in English it is heard as “take what you like”.
notes.other_reading: rescue yourself

check.note: The inverted order of “Wander no longer” is old-fashioned English, and πλανῶ is also “go astray”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Stop wandering”. “Going astray” is given in the note.

check.greek: καὶ τὰς ἐκ τῶν συγγραμμάτων ἐκλογάς, ἃς εἰς τὸ γῆρας σαυτῷ ἀπετίθεσο
check.note: ἃς is feminine plural, so what was being put away is the extracts (and possibly the deeds too), not the writings, which are neuter; in the English “that” attaches to “the writings”. The Greek also joins deeds and extracts with “and” under one “nor”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “either your little notebooks or the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks and the extracts from the writings, which you were putting away for yourself for old age”. The comma and “which” take the clause back to the extracts, or to the deeds and extracts together, as the Greek allows, and “and” joins the two as in the Greek.

check.note: τέλος can be the end or the goal, and εἰς τέλος can also mean “to completion”; “the end” in English is heard as death, which settles the question silently.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “the end” is kept, as the point allows, because like τέλος it can mean both the finish and the aim, where “goal” would shut out the first. The note now gives all three senses, and “hasten” becomes the plainer “hurry”.

check.note: “Come to your own help” is not an English phrase.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “come to your own rescue”.

passages.casaubon: Be not deceived; for thou shalt never live to read thy moral commentaries, nor the acts of the famous Romans and Grecians; nor those excerpta from several books; all which thou hadst provided and laid up for thyself against thine old age. Hasten therefore to an end, and giving over all vain hopes, help thyself in time if thou carest for thyself, as thou oughtest to do.

passages.greek: Ὥσπερ εἴ τίς σοι θεῶν εἶπεν, ὅτι αὔριον τεθνήξῃ ἢ πάντως γε εἰς τρίτην, οὐκέτ’ ἂν παρὰ μέγα ἐποιοῦ τὸ εἰς τρίτην μᾶλλον ἢ αὔριον, εἴ γε μὴ ἐσχάτως ἀγεννὴς εἶ· πόσον γάρ ἐστι τὸ μεταξύ; οὕτως καὶ τὸ εἰς πολλοστὸν ἔτος μᾶλλον ἢ αὔριον μηδὲν μέγα εἶναι νόμιζε.
passages.english: Just as, if one of the gods told you that you will die tomorrow or at any rate the day after, you would no longer count it a great thing that it should be the day after rather than tomorrow, unless you are utterly abject (for how much is the gap between?), so too think it nothing great that it should be many years from now rather than tomorrow.

notes.note: Literally “on the third (day)”. Greek counts today as the first, so this is the day after tomorrow.
notes.other_reading: or at any rate on the third day

notes.note: An idiom: to reckon something as making a great difference.
notes.other_reading: you would no longer make much of the day after as against tomorrow

notes.note: ἀγεννής is “low-born” and so “ignoble, without spirit, cowardly”. English must pick one; “abject” keeps both the lowness and the want of spirit.
notes.other_reading: unless you are a coward to the last degree

notes.note: “How much” is asked expecting the answer “very little”. The question is kept as it stands and set in brackets, so that the sentence can run on to “so too” as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: for how small is the difference!

notes.note: Literally “in the many-eth year”, an ordinal made from “many”: in a year a long way down the count.
notes.other_reading: that it should be in some far-off year rather than tomorrow

check.note: ἀγεννής is ignoble, abject, cowardly. “Mean-spirited” today means unkind or petty, which misleads, and “in the last degree” is dated.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “unless you are utterly abject”.

check.note: The English runs the “Just as” clause, the condition and this question into one sentence that ends in a question mark though its main clause is a statement, and “So too” then starts a new sentence. It is hard to follow.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the question now stands in brackets and the sentence runs on to “so too”, as in the Greek. It is kept as a question, “for how much is the gap between?”, and not turned into the exclamation “how small”, because the Greek asks “how much”.

passages.casaubon: Even as if any of the gods should tell thee, Thou shalt certainly die to-morrow, or next day, thou wouldst not, except thou wert extremely base and pusillanimous, take it for a great benefit, rather to die the next day after, than to-morrow; (for alas, what is the difference!) so, for the same reason, think it no great matter to die rather many years after, than the very next day.

passages.greek: Μήτι δυσχεραίνεις ὅτι τοσῶνδέ τινων λιτρῶν εἶ καὶ οὐ τριακοσίων; οὕτω δὴ καὶ ὅτι μέχρι τοσῶνδε ἐτῶν βιωτέον σοι καὶ οὐ μέχρι πλείονος· ὥσπερ γὰρ τῆς οὐσίας ὅσον ἀφώρισταί σοι στέργεις, οὕτως καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ χρόνου.
passages.english: You are not upset, are you, that you weigh so many pounds and not three hundred? So too, then, with having to live to so many years and no more. For just as you are content with the amount of matter that has been marked off for you, so too with time.

notes.note: μήτι opens a question that expects the answer no. δυσχεραίνειν is to take something hard, to be annoyed or put out.
notes.other_reading: Surely you do not resent

notes.note: Literally “you are of so many pounds”; the English reads “weigh”. The λίτρα is the Roman pound. From memory, unchecked: about 327 grams, so three hundred of them is a little under a hundred kilograms.
notes.other_reading: that you are of such and such a number of pounds

notes.note: The second sentence has no verb of its own: “so too, then, that you must live to so many years”. The verb “be upset” is carried over from the question, and the English leaves it unstated too.
notes.other_reading: Then do not be upset either that you must live to so many years and no more

notes.note: οὐσία is “substance”, the stuff a thing is made of, here the matter of the body, which fits the pounds just mentioned. The same word is also the ordinary Greek for a person’s property.
notes.other_reading: the amount of property that has been marked off for you

notes.note: στέργειν is to be content with, to put up with gladly, and also to feel affection for. The English takes the cooler sense.
notes.other_reading: you accept with affection

check.greek: μέχρι τοσῶνδε ἐτῶν βιωτέον σοι καὶ οὐ μέχρι πλείονος
check.note: “Live up to” is an English idiom with another meaning (to match expectations), and “no further” is spatial where the Greek is “not up to more”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “with having to live to so many years and no more”.

check.note: “Substance” for οὐσία is a technical term; here it is simply the bodily matter allotted to you, which is what the weight comparison is about.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the amount of matter that has been marked off for you”. The note keeps “substance” as the literal sense of the word.

passages.casaubon: Dost thou grieve that thou dost weigh but so many pounds, and not three hundred rather? Just as much reason hast thou to grieve that thou must live but so many years, and not longer. For as for bulk and substance thou dost content thyself with that proportion of it that is allotted unto thee, so shouldst thou for time.

passages.greek:
Εἰς μὲν τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα μία ψυχὴ διῄρηται, εἰς δὲ τὰ λογικὰ μία νοερὰ ψυχὴ μεμέρισται, ὥσπερ καὶ μία γῆ ἐστιν ἁπάντων τῶν γεωδῶν καὶ ἑνὶ φωτὶ ὁρῶμεν καὶ ἕνα ἀέρα ἀναπνέομεν, ὅσα ὁρατικὰ καὶ ἔμψυχα.

Πάντα ὅσα κοινοῦ τινος μετέχει πρὸς τὸ ὁμογενὲς σπεύδει. τὸ γεῶδες πᾶν ῥέπει ἐπὶ γῆν· τὸ ὑγρὸν πᾶν σύρρουν· τὸ ἀερῶδες ὁμοίως, ὥστε χρῄζειν τῶν διειργόντων καὶ βίας· τὸ πῦρ ἀνωφερὲς μὲν διὰ τὸ στοιχειῶδες πῦρ, παντὶ δὲ πυρὶ ἐνταῦθα πρὸς τὸ συνεξάπτεσθαι ἕτοιμον οὕτως, ὥστε καὶ πᾶν τὸ ὑλικὸν τὸ ὀλίγῳ ξηρότερον εὐέξαπτον εἶναι διὰ τὸ ἔλαττον ἐγκεκρᾶσθαι αὐτῷ τὸ κωλυτικὸν πρὸς ἔξαψιν. καὶ τοίνυν πᾶν τὸ κοινῆς νοερᾶς φύσεως μέτοχον πρὸς τὸ συγγενὲς ὁμοίως σπεύδει ἢ καὶ μᾶλλον· ὅσῳ γάρ ἐστι κρεῖττον παρὰ τὰ ἄλλα, τοσούτῳ καὶ πρὸς τὸ συγκιρνᾶσθαι τῷ οἰκείῳ καὶ συγχεῖσθαι ἑτοιμότερον. εὐθὺς γοῦν ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν ἀλόγων εὑρέθη σμήνη καὶ ἀγέλαι καὶ νεοσσοτροφίαι καὶ οἷον ἔρωτες· ψυχαὶ γὰρ ἤδη ἦσαν ἐνταῦθα καὶ τὸ συναγωγὸν ἐν τῷ κρείττονι ἐπιτεινόμενον εὑρίσκετο, οἷον οὔτε ἐπὶ φυτῶν ἦν οὔτε ἐπὶ λίθων ἢ ξύλων. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν λογικῶν ζῴων πολιτεῖαι καὶ φιλίαι καὶ οἶκοι καὶ σύλλογοι καὶ ἐν πολέμοις συνθῆκαι καὶ ἀνοχαί. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἔτι κρειττόνων καὶ ἐκ διεστηκότων τρόπον τινὰ ἕνωσις ὑπέστη οἵα ἐπὶ τῶν ἄστρων· οὕτως ἡ ἐπὶ τὸ κρεῖττον ἐπανάβασις συμπάθειαν καὶ ἐν διεστῶσιν ἐργάσασθαι ἐδύνατο. ὅρα οὖν τὸ νῦν γινόμενον· μόνα γὰρ τὰ νοερὰ νῦν ἐπιλέλησται τῆς πρὸς ἄλληλα σπουδῆς καὶ συννεύσεως καὶ τὸ σύρρουν ὧδε μόνον οὐ βλέπεται. ἀλλ’ ὅμως καίτοι φεύγοντες περικαταλαμβάνονται· κρατεῖ γὰρ ἡ φύσις. ὄψει δὲ ὃ λέγω παραφυλάσσων· θᾶσσον γοῦν εὕροι τις ἂν γεῶδές τι μηδενὸς γεώδους προσαπτόμενον ἤπερ ἄνθρωπον ἀνθρώπου ἀπεσχισμένον.
passages.english:
One soul has been divided among the animals without reason, and one soul that has mind has been portioned out among the rational ones, just as there is one earth for all earthy things, and we see by one light and breathe one air, all of us that have sight and a soul.

All things that share in something common hurry toward what is of their own kind. Everything earthy tends toward earth. Everything wet flows together. What is airy does the same, so that it takes things to hold them apart, and force. Fire is carried upward because of the elemental fire, yet it is so ready to be kindled together with every fire here that even everything material that is a little drier is easy to kindle, because less of what hinders kindling is mixed into it. So too, then, everything that shares in a common nature of mind hurries toward its kin in the same way, or even more. For the better it is compared with the rest, the readier it is to mix with what is its own and to be poured together with it. At any rate, right from the start, among the animals without reason there were found swarms and herds and the rearing of nestlings and what one might call loves; for here there were already souls, and the thing that draws together was found growing stronger in what is better, of a kind that did not exist in plants, or in stones or timber. Among the rational animals there were states and friendships and households and gatherings, and in wars treaties and truces. Among those better still, even out of things that stand apart there came to be, in a way, a union, such as there is among the stars. In this way the climb toward the better was able to produce a shared feeling even in things that stand apart. See, then, what is happening now. For only the beings that have mind have now forgotten their hurrying toward one another and their leaning together, and only here is the flowing together not to be seen. And yet, though they run away, they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same; for nature prevails. You will see what I mean if you watch closely. At any rate, one would sooner find something earthy touching nothing earthy than a human being split off from a human being.

notes.note: νοερός is “of mind, able to think”. “Mind” is kept as the one word for it through the passage (“one soul that has mind”, “a common nature of mind”, “the beings that have mind”) so the chain can be followed. The verb differs from “divided” in the first clause and has a different English verb.
notes.other_reading: one thinking soul has been shared out

notes.note: A neuter plural (“whatever things can see and have soul in them”) attached to verbs in “we”. ἔμψυχα is literally “ensouled”, in ordinary Greek simply “alive”; “soul” is kept because the sentence is about soul.
notes.other_reading: all of us creatures that can see and are alive

notes.note: σπεύδω is “hurry, press eagerly toward”, and also “strive”. “Hurry” is used for the verb both times and “hurrying” for the noun σπουδή near the end, since the argument turns on the repetition.
notes.other_reading: strive toward what is of their own kind

notes.note: The word for a scale pan going down: to incline, to tend. “Tends” is used so that “leaning” can be kept for a different word near the end.
notes.other_reading: Everything earthy sinks toward earth

notes.greek: ὥστε χρῄζειν τῶν διειργόντων καὶ βίας
notes.note: The Greek has no subject: “so that there is need of things that keep apart, and of force”. The clause may cover the wet as well as the airy.
notes.other_reading: so that barriers and force are needed

notes.note: Literally “because of the elemental fire”. It is taken as the pure fire of the upper region, toward which fire down here rises; the words could also name the fiery element within the flame itself.
notes.other_reading: because of the element of fire in it

notes.note: Three words in this sentence are made from one verb for setting alight. “Kindle” is used for all three.
notes.other_reading: to catch light together

notes.note: ὑλικός is “material, made of matter”, but ὕλη is also the ordinary word for wood and fuel, and that sense is close to the surface here. “Even” is taken with the whole phrase: not only fire itself but anything material.
notes.other_reading: even all fuel that is a little drier

notes.greek: ὅσῳ γάρ ἐστι κρεῖττον παρὰ τὰ ἄλλα
notes.note: κρείττων is “better”, also “stronger” or “superior”. The word returns four times as the rungs of a ladder; “better” is kept each time and not “higher”, since the Greek has no image of height until the “climb” later on.
notes.other_reading: For the higher it stands above the rest

notes.note: εὐθύς is “straight away” and can mark the first moment in time or the first case in a list; the past tenses that follow tell the ladder of beings as if it were a history. “Right from the start” leaves both senses possible. γοῦν, “at any rate”, brings in the evidence, as it does again in the last sentence.
notes.other_reading: To begin with, at any rate,

notes.note: A school term: wholes made of members that stand physically apart, as opposed to one continuous body. The same word comes back as διεστῶσιν in the next sentence; “things that stand apart” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: even out of separated things

notes.note: “In a way” stands between “things that stand apart” and “union” and could soften either. It is taken with the union.
notes.other_reading: even out of things that in a way stand apart there came to be a union

notes.note: A Stoic term for parts of the universe being affected together, as if by one feeling. The English word “sympathy” now means pity, so the English reads “a shared feeling”.
notes.other_reading: sympathy

notes.greek: τὸ σύρρουν ὧδε μόνον οὐ βλέπεται
notes.note: μόνον is taken with ὧδε: “here alone it is not seen”. μόνον οὐ can also be an idiom for “all but”, but “is all but seen” gives no sense here. “The flowing together” repeats the word used of water above.
notes.other_reading: and in this one case the running together is not seen

notes.note: The participle turns masculine: the neuter “beings that have mind” have become people. The verb is one word, “overtake and surround”; the English needs two.
notes.other_reading: though they flee, they are caught all the same

check.greek: ὥστε χρῄζειν τῶν διειργόντων καὶ βίας
check.note: The Greek has no subject (“there is need of things that keep apart, and of force”). “They need” has no clear referent and can be read as if the elements wanted to be held apart.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “so that it takes things to hold them apart, and force”. The Greek clause has no subject, and the point is that it takes something outside them, and force, to stop them joining.

check.note: The word is the tilt of a scale: inclines, tends. “Sinks” adds a downward fall and loses the idea of a tendency, which the argument goes on to generalise.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “tends toward earth”. The word names a tendency, not a fall; “leans” is not used because “leaning together” is kept for a different Greek word later in the passage.

check.greek: ὥστε καὶ πᾶν τὸ ὑλικὸν τὸ ὀλίγῳ ξηρότερον
check.note: “Even” goes with “any material thing” (not only fire itself), not with “a little”. “Every material” is also unclear English.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “that even everything material that is a little drier is easy to kindle”. “Even” belongs with the whole phrase, and “everything” keeps the Greek “all”.

check.note: “At any rate” (γοῦν) is dropped here though it is given in the last sentence. εὐθύς may mean “straight away, at the very first step” and not merely open a list.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “At any rate, right from the start”. “At any rate” is restored, as in the last sentence; “right from the start” is used and not “already”, because “already” comes as a separate Greek word in the next clause.

check.note: The word is made from “nestling, chick”. The three examples are bees, herd animals and birds, and “young” in general loses the third picture.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the rearing of nestlings”. The Greek word names nestlings, so the picture of birds is kept.

check.note: “For” is dropped. The sentence gives the reason for “See what is happening now”.
check.decided: Accepted: The sentence now begins “For only the beings that have mind”. The Greek marks it as the ground for the sentence before.

check.note: The verb is “prevails, has the mastery”. There is no comparison in the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “for nature prevails”. The Greek verb makes no comparison, so “stronger” said more than it does.

check.note: The compound is “overtaken and hemmed in on every side”. “Caught” keeps the result but drops the picture of being surrounded.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same”. The one Greek verb says both that they are caught up with and that they are surrounded.

check.note: “In a way” stands between “things that stand apart” and “union” and could soften either. The English chose the union without any sign.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “even out of things that stand apart there came to be, in a way, a union”, which follows the Greek order. “In a way” is still taken with the union, since the stars stand apart without qualification; a note gives the other reading.

check.note: The verb is to hurry, to press eagerly toward; “strive” suggests effort against resistance. The chain of three is rightly kept in one word; only the word chosen is a shade off.

check.greek: οἷον οὔτε ἐπὶ φυτῶν ἦν οὔτε ἐπὶ λίθων ἢ ξύλων
check.note: “Such as it was not in plants or in stones or in timber” is accurate but stiff, and a reader has to stop to parse it.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “of a kind that did not exist in plants, or in stones or timber”. “Did not exist” is used and not “not found”, because the Greek has a plain “was” here and “found” in the clause before.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave λογικός as “reasoning” and ἄλογος as “unreasoning”, where the renderings settled for this translation have “rational” for λογικός and “reason” for λόγος.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the rational ones”, “the rational animals” and “the animals without reason”. “Without reason” keeps the pair audible beside “rational”.

check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “one soul that has mind”, “a common nature of mind” and “the beings that have mind”. “Mind” is the constant word, so the chain can still be followed.

check.note: Found while settling: three words in one sentence are made from the same Greek verb for setting alight, and the draft gave them as “catch light”, “set alight” and “kindling”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “to be kindled together”, “easy to kindle” and “what hinders kindling”, one English word for the one Greek root.

passages.casaubon: Of all unreasonable creatures, there is but one unreasonable soul; and of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt them all. As of all earthly things there is but one earth, and but one light that we see by; and but one air that we breathe in, as many as either breathe or see. Now whatsoever partakes of some common thing, naturally affects and inclines unto that whereof it is part, being of one kind and nature with it. Whatsoever is earthly, presseth downwards to the common earth. Whatsoever is liquid, would flow together. And whatsoever is airy, would be together likewise. So that without some obstacle, and some kind of violence, they cannot well be kept asunder. Whatsoever is fiery, doth not only by reason of the elementary fire tend upwards; but here also is so ready to join, and to burn together, that whatsoever doth want sufficient moisture to make resistance, is easily set on fire. Whatsoever therefore is partaker of that reasonable common nature, naturally doth as much and more long after his own kind. For by how much in its own nature it excels all other things, by so much more is it desirous to be joined and united unto that, which is of its own nature. As for unreasonable creatures then, they had not long been, but presently begun among them swarms, and flocks, and broods of young ones, and a kind of mutual love and affection. For though but unreasonable, yet a kind of soul these had, and therefore was that natural desire of union more strong and intense in them, as in creatures of a more excellent nature, than either in plants, or stones, or trees. But among reasonable creatures, begun commonwealths, friendships, families, public meetings, and even in their wars, conventions, and truces. Now among them that were yet of a more excellent nature, as the stars and planets, though by their nature far distant one from another, yet even among them began some mutual correspondency and unity. So proper is it to excellency in a high degree to affect unity, as that even in things so far distant, it could operate unto a mutual sympathy. But now behold, what is now come to pass. Those creatures that are reasonable, are now the only creatures that have forgotten their natural affection and inclination of one towards another. Among them alone of all other things that are of one kind, there is not to be found a general disposition to flow together. But though they fly from nature, yet are they stopt in their course, and apprehended. Do they what they can, nature doth prevail. And so shalt thou confess, if thou dost observe it. For sooner mayst thou find a thing earthly, where no earthly thing is, than find a man that naturally can live by himself alone.

passages.greek: Οἷα ἂν πολλάκις φαντασθῇς, τοιαύτη σοι ἔσται ἡ διάνοια· βάπτεται γὰρ ὑπὸ τῶν φαντασιῶν ἡ ψυχή. βάπτε οὐν αὐτὴν τῇ συνεχείᾳ τῶν τοιούτων φαντασιῶν· οἷον, ὅτι ὅπου ζῆν ἐστιν, ἐκεῖ καὶ εὖ ζῆν· ἐν αὐλῇ δὲ ζῆν ἐστιν· ἔστιν ἄρα καὶ εὖ ζῆν ἐν αὐλῇ. καὶ πάλιν, ὅτι οὗπερ ἕνεκεν ἕκαστον κατεσκεύασται, πρὸς τοῦτο φέρεται· πρὸς ὃ φέρεται δέ, ἐν τούτῳ τὸ τέλος αὐτοῦ· ὅπου δὲ τὸ τέλος, ἐκεῖ καὶ τὸ συμφέρον καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἑκάστου· τὸ ἄρα ἀγαθὸν τοῦ λογικοῦ ζῴου κοινωνία. ὅτι γὰρ πρὸς κοινωνίαν γεγόναμεν, πάλαι δέδεικται· ἢ οὐκ ἦν ἐναργὲς ὅτι τὰ χείρω τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν, τὰ δὲ κρείττω ἀλλήλων; κρείττω δὲ τῶν μὲν ἀψύχων τὰ ἔμψυχα, τῶν δὲ ἐμψύχων τὰ λογικά.
passages.english: Whatever kind of impressions you often form, your thought will be of that kind; for the soul is dyed by its impressions. So dye it with an unbroken run of impressions such as these. For example: where it is possible to live, there it is also possible to live well; but it is possible to live at court; therefore it is also possible to live well at court. And again: each thing is carried toward that for the sake of which it was built; and what it is carried toward, in that lies its goal; and where its goal is, there also is the benefit and the good of each thing; therefore the good of a rational animal is community. For that we were born for community has long since been shown. Or was it not plain that the worse things are for the sake of the better, and the better for the sake of one another? And things with a soul are better than things without one, and rational things better than things with a soul.

notes.note: The verb is the one from which φαντασία (“impression”) is made: “whatever sort of things you often have appear to you”. The English reads “impressions you often form” so that verb and noun stay one word.
notes.other_reading: Whatever kind of things you often picture to yourself

notes.note: διάνοια is “thought, understanding”, and also the mind as the thing that thinks. “Thought” is used, as elsewhere in this translation.
notes.other_reading: your mind will be of that kind

notes.note: Literally “is dipped”, the dyer’s word; the same verb is the command in the next sentence, and “dye” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: is steeped

notes.note: Literally “by the continuity of such impressions”, made concrete as “an unbroken run”.
notes.other_reading: by having such impressions continually

notes.note: αὐλή is a courtyard and then a ruler’s court: his household and the life lived around him. Marcus means his own. The building is not the point.
notes.other_reading: in a palace

notes.note: The form can be passive (“is carried”) or middle (“moves, tends”). “Is carried” is kept both times; it need not imply an outside force.
notes.other_reading: each thing tends toward that for the sake of which it was built

notes.note: “What is good for a thing”, built on the same verb as “is carried” just before; the echo cannot be kept in English. “Benefit” is used here because “the good” follows at once as a separate word.
notes.other_reading: what is good for each thing

notes.note: The word covers “sharing, partnership, fellowship, community”. “Community” is used here and in the next sentence. It is the noun behind the adjective given as “social” elsewhere in this translation.
notes.other_reading: fellowship

notes.note: “Has been shown long ago”: the Greek does not say whether earlier in his own notes or in the teaching of his school is meant. The English leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: was proved long ago

notes.note: Plain comparatives, “worse” and “better”; they can also be heard as “lower” and “higher” in a scale of beings.
notes.other_reading: the lower exist for the sake of the higher

notes.note: Taken as a comparison, in parallel with the clause before: rational things are better than things that have a soul and no more. The words can also be read as picking the rational ones out from among things with a soul.
notes.other_reading: and among things with a soul the rational ones are better

check.note: The word is the court, the ruler’s household and its way of life, not the building. Marcus is speaking of his own life at court; “in a palace” makes it any grand house.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “at court” both times. The word names the ruler’s court and the life lived there, which is Marcus’s own, and not a building.

check.note: The parallel clause before is a comparison (“better than things without a soul”), so this one is most naturally “and rational things better than those with a soul”. The English made it “among things with a soul”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “and rational things better than things with a soul”. The Greek sets the two clauses in exact parallel, so the same comparison is read in both; a note gives the other reading.

check.note: The form can be passive (“is carried”) or middle (“moves, tends”). “Is carried” suggests an outside force; “tends toward” is equally possible.
check.decided: Declined: “Is carried toward” stands in both places. The Greek form allows either sense and “carry” is the plain meaning of the verb, on which the passage plays again in its word for “benefit”; a note now records “tends toward”.

check.greek: Οἷα ἂν πολλάκις φαντασθῇς, τοιαύτη σοι ἔσται ἡ διάνοια
check.note: Found while settling: the draft began “Your mind will be of the same kind as the impressions you often form”, which reversed the Greek order (first the impressions, then what follows from them) and gave διάνοια as “mind”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Whatever kind of impressions you often form, your thought will be of that kind”. The order of thought follows the Greek, and “thought” is the word used for διάνοια elsewhere in this translation.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave λογικός as “reasoning”, where this translation uses “rational”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a rational animal” and, in the last sentence, “rational things”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave τὸ συμφέρον as “the advantage”, where this translation uses “is good for” or “benefits” for the verb.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “the benefit and the good of each thing”. “What is good for” is not used here because “the good” follows at once as a separate Greek word and the two would run together.

passages.casaubon: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it with the assiduity of these cogitations. As for example. Wheresoever thou mayest live, there it is in thy power to live well and happy. But thou mayest live at the Court, there then also mayest thou live well and happy. Again, that which everything is made for, he is also made unto that, and cannot but naturally incline unto it. That which anything doth naturally incline unto, therein is his end. Wherein the end of everything doth consist, therein also doth his good and benefit consist. Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature. For that we are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated. Or can any man make any question of this, that whatsoever is naturally worse and inferior, is ordinarily subordinated to that which is better? and that those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that have, those best that have rational souls?

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Εἴ ποτε εἶδες χεῖρα ἀποκεκομμένην ἢ πόδα ἢ κεφαλὴν ἀποτετμημένην, χωρίς πού ποτε ἀπὸ τοῦ λοιποῦ σώματος κειμένην· τοιοῦτον ἑαυτὸν ποιεῖ, ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ, ὁ μὴ θέλων τὸ συμβαῖνον καὶ ἀποσχίζων ἑαυτὸν ἢ ὁ ἀκοινώνητόν τι πράσσων. ἀπέρριψαί πού ποτε ἀπὸ τῆς κατὰ φύσιν ἑνώσεως· ἐπεφύκεις γὰρ μέρος· νῦν δὲ σεαυτὸν ἀπέκοψας. ἀλλ’ ὧδε κομψὸν ἐκεῖνο, ὅτι ἔξεστί σοι πάλιν ἑνῶσαι σεαυτόν. τοῦτο ἄλλῳ μέρει οὐδενὶ θεὸς ἐπέτρεψεν, χωρισθέντι καὶ διακοπέντι πάλιν συνελθεῖν, ἀλλὰ σκέψαι τὴν χρηστότητα ᾗ τετίμηκε τὸν ἄνθρωπον· καὶ γὰρ ἵνα τὴν ἀρχὴν μὴ ἀπορραγῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ ὅλου ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ἐποίησε, καὶ ἀπορραγέντι πάλιν ἐπανελθεῖν καὶ συμφῦναι καὶ τὴν τοῦ μέρους τάξιν ἀπολαβεῖν ἐποίησεν.
passages.english: If you have ever seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a severed head, lying somewhere or other apart from the rest of the body: that is what a person makes of themselves, as far as it is in their power, when they do not want what happens and split themselves off, or when they do something unsocial. You lie somewhere or other, thrown away from the union that accords with nature; for you were by nature a part, but now you have cut yourself off. But here is the neat thing: you are allowed to unite yourself again. To no other part has god granted this, to come together again once it has been separated and cut through. But consider the kindness with which he has honoured the human being: for he put it in the human being’s power not to be broken off from the whole in the first place, and, for one who has been broken off, he made it possible to come back again and grow together and take up again the place of a part.

notes.note: The “if” clause never gets a main clause; the sentence breaks off and starts again with “that is what”. The break is kept with a colon.
notes.other_reading: Have you ever seen a hand cut off? That is what

notes.note: The head has a different verb from the hand: “cut away”. “Severed” keeps the two apart.
notes.other_reading: a head cut away

notes.note: πού ποτε (“somewhere, at some time”) is repeated in the next sentence of you yourself, so the thrown-away self lies where the hand lay. “Somewhere or other” is used both times; the “at some time” is only faintly there.
notes.other_reading: lying at some time, in some place, apart

notes.note: “As far as rests with oneself.” The same phrase comes back at the end, of what god has made to rest with the human being; “power” is used in both places.
notes.other_reading: as far as it lies with them

notes.note: “What happens”, with the sense “what happens to them”. The Greek has no “to them”.
notes.other_reading: what befalls them

notes.note: The adjective negates the word for community: “something that has no share in community”. “Unsocial” is used as the negative of “social”, the word for κοινωνικός throughout this translation; it does not here mean keeping to oneself.
notes.other_reading: something that goes against community

notes.note: The form is either passive (“you have been thrown away, you lie thrown away”) or reflexive (“you have thrown yourself away”). The passive is taken, because the next clause adds an express “yourself” and this one does not, and because it matches the severed limb “lying” somewhere.
notes.other_reading: You have thrown yourself somewhere or other away from the union

notes.note: A past form of the verb “grow”, the verb behind φύσις (“nature”) just before and “grow together” at the end: “you had grown as, you were by nature, a part”.
notes.other_reading: for you grew as a part

notes.note: κομψός is “neat, elegant, clever”, said of a nice touch or a pretty arrangement.
notes.other_reading: But here is the fine thing

notes.note: No article: “god”, “a god”, or the one god of the next sentence, who honoured the human being. Lower-case “god” is used, as throughout this translation.
notes.other_reading: no god has granted this to any other part

notes.note: τὴν ἀρχήν is the adverbial idiom “at all, in the first place”, not “the beginning”. The verb is “be broken or torn off”, stronger than the “cut” words above.
notes.other_reading: so as not to be torn away at all

notes.note: τάξις is a post or rank in a formation: “the station of the part”.
notes.other_reading: its post as a part

check.note: The form can be “you have been cast away”, “you lie cast off” or “you have cast yourself away”. The next clause marks self-action with an express “yourself” and this one does not, so the passive is at least as likely and matches the limb “lying” somewhere.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “You lie somewhere or other, thrown away from the union that accords with nature”. The form allows both, but only the next clause has an express “yourself”, and the passive answers the limb “lying” somewhere; a note gives the reflexive reading.

check.note: The form means “you were by nature a part”. “Grew as a part” describes a process, not what he was by nature.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “for you were by nature a part”. The form states what he was by nature, and “by nature” keeps the link with “the union that accords with nature” just before.

check.note: Keeping the two Greek verbs apart is right, but “a head cut away” is not natural English.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a severed head”. The two Greek verbs are still kept apart, “cut off” for the hand and “severed” for the head.

check.note: The word negates the word for community. “Unsocial” today suggests keeping to oneself and hides the link.
check.decided: Declined: “Something unsocial” stands. κοινωνικός is “social” throughout this translation and this word is its negative, so “unsocial” keeps one English word for the family; a note now says that it does not mean keeping to oneself and gives the suggested wording.

check.note: The word is neat, clever, elegant: the neat twist in the arrangement. “Fine” is vaguer.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “But here is the neat thing”. The word is said of a clever touch in an arrangement.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “himself”, “him” and “he” for the person who splits off and for the human being at the end, where the Greek does not single out a man.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a person makes of themselves … when they do not want what happens” and, at the end, “the human being’s power” and “for one who has been broken off”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “God” with a capital, where this translation uses lower-case “god”.
