check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “To no other part has god granted this”. The word order keeps “god” away from the start of the sentence, so that the lower case can be seen.

check.note: Found while settling: the same Greek phrase, “resting with oneself”, stands near the start and near the end. The draft gave it as “as far as it lies with him” and “in the person’s own power”, and added “own”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “as far as it is in their power” and “he put it in the human being’s power”, so that the echo can be heard.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft left out the “for” that makes the last sentence the ground for “consider the kindness”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “for he put it in the human being’s power”.

passages.casaubon: If ever thou sawest either a hand, or a foot, or a head lying by itself, in some place or other, as cut off from the rest of the body, such must thou conceive him to make himself, as much as in him lieth, that either is offended with anything that is happened, (whatsoever it be) and as it were divides himself from it: or that commits anything against the natural law of mutual correspondence, and society among men: or, he that, commits any act of uncharitableness. Whosoever thou art, thou art such, thou art cast forth I know not whither out of the general unity, which is according to nature. Thou went born indeed a part, but now thou hast cut thyself off. However, herein is matter of joy and exultation, that thou mayst be united again. God hath not granted it unto any other part, that once separated and cut off, it might be reunited, and come together again. But, behold, that GOODNESS how great and immense it is! which hath so much esteemed MAN. As at first he was so made, that he needed not, except he would himself, have divided himself from the whole; so once divided and cut off, IT hath so provided and ordered it, that if he would himself, he might return, and grow together again, and be admitted into its former rank and place of a part, as he was before.

passages.greek: Οἷόν ἐστιν ἐν ἡνωμένοις τὰ μέλη τοῦ σώματος, τοῦτον ἔχει τὸν λόγον ἐν διεστῶσι τὰ λογικά, πρὸς μίαν τινὰ συνεργίαν κατεσκευασμένα. μᾶλλον δέ σοι ἡ τούτου νόησις προσπεσεῖται, ἐὰν πρὸς ἑαυτὸν πολλάκις λέγῃς, ὅτι μέλος εἰμὶ τοῦ ἐκ τῶν λογικῶν συστήματος. ἐὰν δὲ διὰ τοῦ ῥῶ στοιχείου μέρος εἶναι ἑαυτὸν λέγῃς, οὔπω ἀπὸ καρδίας φιλεῖς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους· οὔπω σε καταληκτικῶς εὐφραίνει τὸ εὐεργετεῖν· ἔτι ὡς πρέπον αὐτὸ ψιλὸν ποιεῖς, οὔπω ὡς ἑαυτὸν εὖ ποιῶν.
passages.english: The relation that the limbs of the body have in things that are united is the relation that rational beings have in things that stand apart, being built to do some one work together. The thought of this will strike you more if you often say to yourself: “I am a limb [melos] of the whole made up of rational beings.” But if, by using the letter rho, you say that you are a part [meros], you do not yet love people from the heart; doing good does not yet delight you fully; you still do it as no more than the proper thing, not yet as doing good to yourself.

notes.note: A school distinction (from memory, unchecked): bodies that are one continuous whole, such as an animal, against wholes made of members that stand apart, such as an army or a chorus. The second term is ἐν διεστῶσι in the next clause. “United” is used because the Greek word is made from “one”, like “union” in the neighbouring passages.
notes.other_reading: in bodies that are all of one piece

notes.note: λόγος here is “relation, proportion”, not “reason”, though it is the word from which λογικά (“rational beings”) is made, and the echo may be intended.
notes.other_reading: the same account holds for

notes.note: μέλος is a limb or bodily member. “Limb” is used because the passage goes on to set it against “part”.
notes.other_reading: the members of the body

notes.note: Literally “for some one working-together”: the activity of working together, not a thing produced.
notes.other_reading: for a certain single cooperation

notes.note: Literally “will fall upon you”: the thought will hit you, come home to you.
notes.other_reading: will come home to you more

notes.note: σύστημα is a whole put together out of members: a body of people, an organised group. It is a different word from the one given as “the whole” elsewhere (τὸ ὅλον). Its English descendant, “system”, sounds mechanical today.
notes.other_reading: the system made up of rational beings

notes.note: The point is a play on two Greek words one letter apart: μέλος (limb) and μέρος (part), with rho (r) in place of lambda (l). Since the passage is talking about the words themselves, both are added in square brackets; the brackets and what is in them are not in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: by changing the l to an r

notes.note: A rare adverb and a doubted reading (from memory, unchecked). As it stands it comes from the verb “to come to an end, to stop”, and is taken as “to the end, fully”; it could also mean “as the point at which one stops”. Editors have proposed καταληπτικῶς, a Stoic term for a firm grasp (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: doing good does not yet delight you as an end in itself; or, with the proposed reading, with full conviction

notes.note: Literally “as a bare fitting thing”: what is proper and nothing more. “Duty” is avoided, since that is a different Stoic word.
notes.other_reading: simply as a bare duty

check.note: A rare adverb from the verb “to come to an end”: roughly “finally, conclusively, completely”. “As an end in itself” is a confident philosophical phrase that says more than the word does, and some editors print a different word here (from memory).
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “doing good does not yet delight you fully”. The adverb is rare and comes from a verb meaning “to come to an end”, and “as an end in itself” made a settled philosophical claim out of it. The note marks the reading as doubted and gives the other senses.

check.note: The transliterations “(melos)” and “(meros)” are not in the Greek. They are needed for the play on one letter, but as printed they sit inside Marcus’s sentence as if his.
check.decided: Accepted: The two Greek words now stand in square brackets, “[melos]” and “[meros]”, and a note says that the brackets and their contents are not in the Greek. They are kept because the play on one letter cannot be followed without them.

check.note: The word for “a certain” is dropped, and the noun is the activity of working together, not a work produced.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “being built to do some one work together”. “Some” restores the dropped word and “to do … together” makes it an activity; “as one” is not used because the Greek says one work, not one worker.

check.note: “System” sounds technical or mechanical in today’s English. The word is a whole composed of members, which is what makes “limb” fit.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the whole made up of rational beings”. The Greek word is a whole composed of members; a note says that it is a different word from the one given elsewhere as “the whole”.

check.note: “In things that are unified … in things that stand apart” is literal and accurate but hard to picture. The contrast is between a body that is one continuous thing and one made of separate individuals.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “in things that are united”, a plainer word than “unified” and one that links with “union” in the neighbouring passages. “Things that stand apart” is kept, because the same Greek word is so given in 9.8–9 and the Greek says “things”, not “bodies” or “members”; the note explains the contrast.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave λογικός as “reasoning beings”, where this translation uses “rational”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “rational beings” both times.

passages.casaubon: As several members in one body united, so are reasonable creatures in a body divided and dispersed, all made and prepared for one common operation. And this thou shalt apprehend the better, if thou shalt use thyself often to say to thyself, I am μέλος, or a member of the mass and body of reasonable substances. But if thou shalt say I am μέρος, or a part, thou dost not yet love men from thy heart. The joy that thou takest in the exercise of bounty, is not yet grounded upon a due ratiocination and right apprehension of the nature of things. Thou dost exercise it as yet upon this ground barely, as a thing convenient and fitting; not, as doing good to thyself, when thou dost good unto others.

passages.greek: Εἰ τὸ νοερὸν ἡμῖν κοινόν, καὶ ὁ λόγος, καθʼ ὃν λογικοί ἐσμεν, κοινός· εἰ τοῦτο, καὶ ὁ προστακτικὸς τῶν ποιητέων ἢ μὴ λόγος κοινός· εἰ τοῦτο, καὶ ὁ νόμος κοινός· εἰ τοῦτο, πολῖταί ἐσμεν· εἰ τοῦτο, πολιτεύματός τινος μετέχομεν· εἰ τοῦτο, ὁ κόσμος ὡσανεὶ πόλις ἐστί· τίνος γὰρ ἄλλου φήσει τις τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων πᾶν γένος κοινοῦ πολιτεύματος μετέχειν; ἐκεῖθεν δέ, ἐκ τῆς κοινῆς ταύτης πόλεως, καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ νοερὸν καὶ λογικὸν καὶ νομικὸν ἡμῖν ἢ πόθεν; ὥσπερ γὰρ τὸ γεῶδές μοι ἀπό τινος γῆς ἀπομεμέρισται καὶ τὸ ὑγρὸν ἀφʼ ἑτέρου στοιχείου καὶ τὸ πνευματικὸν ἀπὸ πηγῆς τινος καὶ τὸ θερμὸν καὶ πυρῶδες ἔκ τινος ἰδίας πηγῆς (οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ μηδενὸς ἔρχεται, ὥσπερ μηδʼ εἰς τὸ οὐκ ὂν ἀπέρχεται), οὕτω δὴ καὶ τὸ νοερὸν ἥκει ποθέν.
passages.english: If mind is common to us, then reason too, by which we are rational, is common. If that is so, then the reason that commands what is to be done or not done is also common. If that is so, law too is common. If that is so, we are citizens. If that is so, we share in some civic body. If that is so, the universe is, as it were, a city. For in what other common civic body will anyone say that the whole race of human beings shares? And it is from there, from this common city, that our very mind and reason and sense of law come; or from where else? For just as what is earthy in me has been portioned off from some earth, and what is wet from another element, and what is breath from some source, and what is warm and fiery from some source of its own (for nothing comes from nothing, just as nothing goes away into what is not), so too mind has come from somewhere.

notes.note: Literally “the thing of mind”, the part of us that thinks. “Mind” is used for it throughout this passage.
notes.other_reading: If the power to think is common to us

notes.note: The adjective made from λόγος, “reason”: “having reason”. “Rational” is used, as throughout this translation; the Greek link with “reason” is closer than the English shows.
notes.other_reading: by which we are reasoning beings

notes.greek: ὁ προστακτικὸς τῶν ποιητέων ἢ μὴ λόγος
notes.note: “The reason that gives orders about things to be done or not”: this reads as a school definition of law, which is why “law” follows at once. The Greek leaves “to be done” to be supplied after “or not”.
notes.other_reading: the reason that prescribes what we must do and what we must not

notes.note: πολίτευμα is made from the word for citizen and can mean a constitution, a government, a state, or the body of citizens. “Civic body” is used and kept in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: we share in some kind of state

notes.note: κόσμος is the ordered whole of things, “the universe” throughout this translation. ὡσανεί softens the claim: “as if, so to speak”.
notes.other_reading: the world is like a city

notes.note: Three adjectives under one article, answering to mind, reason and law in the chain above: “the thing in us that is of mind, of reason and of law”. νομικόν is literally “having to do with law”; “sense of law” marks that it is the capacity in us, not law itself, which was an earlier step.
notes.other_reading: the very thing in us that thinks, reasons and keeps law

notes.note: πνευματικόν is “what is of breath or wind”. “From some source” is oddly vague beside “from some source of its own” in the following phrase, and the words have been doubted (from memory, unchecked). The English translates what stands.
notes.other_reading: the airy part from some spring

notes.note: ἥκω is a present with perfect sense: “has come, is here”.
notes.other_reading: comes from somewhere

check.greek: καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ νοερὸν καὶ λογικὸν καὶ νομικὸν ἡμῖν
check.note: The Greek has “to us” once, and the English gave it twice (“in us” and “to us”).
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “that our very mind and reason and sense of law come”. “Our” gives the one Greek “to us” once.

check.note: The three words are adjectives used as nouns: the thinking, the reasoning and the law-observing element in us. Law itself was an earlier step of the chain; here it is the capacity for law.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “sense of law”. The word names what in us has to do with law, not law itself.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave κόσμος as “the world”, where this translation uses “the universe” unless the inhabited earth is meant.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the universe is, as it were, a city”. The whole ordered sum of things is meant, since mind, earth, water, breath and fire are all drawn from it.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave λογικοί as “reasoning beings”, where this translation uses “rational”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “by which we are rational”. A note says that the Greek word is made from the word for “reason”.

passages.casaubon: If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all. If reason is general, then is that reason also, which prescribeth what is to be done and what not, common unto all. If that, then law. If law, then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city. For which other commonweal is it, that all men can be said to be members of? From this common city it is, that understanding, reason, and law is derived unto us, for from whence else? For as that which in me is earthly I have from some common earth; and that which is moist from some other element is imparted; as my breath and life hath its proper fountain; and that likewise which is dry and fiery in me: (for there is nothing which doth not proceed from something; as also there is nothing that can be reduced unto mere nothing:) so also is there some common beginning from whence my understanding hath proceeded.

passages.greek: Ὥσπερ αὐτὸς σὺ πολιτικοῦ συστήματος συμπληρωτικὸς εἶ, οὕτως καὶ πᾶσα πρᾶξίς σου συμπληρωτικὴ ἔστω ζωῆς πολιτικῆς. ἥτις ἐὰν οὖν πρᾶξίς σου μὴ ἔχῃ τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἴτε προσεχῶς εἴτε πόρρωθεν, ἐπὶ τὸ κοινωνικὸν τέλος, αὕτη διασπᾷ τὸν βίον καὶ οὐκ ἐᾷ ἕνα εἶναι καὶ στασιώδης ἐστίν, ὥσπερ ἐν δήμῳ ὁ τὸ καθ’ αὑτὸν μέρος διιστάμενος ἀπὸ τῆς τοιαύτης συμφωνίας.
passages.english: Just as you yourself help to complete a civic whole, so too let every action of yours help to complete a civic life. So any action of yours that does not refer, whether directly or at a distance, to the social goal tears your life apart and does not let it be one, and it is seditious, like the person in a citizen body who, for their own part, stands apart from such harmony.

notes.note: πολιτικός is “of citizens, of the city”; “civic” is used for both occurrences. σύστημα is an organised whole made of members, a different word from the one given as “the whole” elsewhere (τὸ ὅλον).
notes.other_reading: a civic system

notes.note: An adjective: “such as to fill up together”, said of a member without which the whole is not complete. “Help to complete” gives the “together” of the Greek prefix; the Greek has no noun such as “part” here.
notes.other_reading: you yourself go to make up a civic whole

notes.note: Two words for life in this passage: ζωή here (being alive, life as lived) and βίος in the next sentence (a life as a course or career). English has one word for both.
notes.other_reading: a life lived as a citizen

notes.note: “Reference”, a carrying-back of the act to what it is for.
notes.other_reading: that is not directed

notes.note: Literally “whether next in line or from afar”: directly or through other steps.
notes.other_reading: whether closely or from far off

notes.note: κοινωνικός, “social”, is the adjective of κοινωνία, community. τέλος is “end” in the sense of what a thing is for; “goal” avoids the other sense of “end”.
notes.other_reading: to the end that is community

notes.note: The Greek has “the life” with no possessive. “Your” is supplied because the action is yours; it could be read more generally.
notes.other_reading: tears life apart

notes.note: The adjective of στάσις, faction or civil strife inside a city: “of the nature of civil strife”.
notes.other_reading: and it is a kind of civil strife

notes.note: δῆμος is the people as a political body; it can also mean the popular assembly or a democracy.
notes.other_reading: in a popular assembly

notes.note: “Their own part” is taken as adverbial (“as far as they are concerned”) and the verb as “stands apart”. It could also be taken as “withdrawing their own share (or party)”. The verb is the one used elsewhere for things that “stand apart”.
notes.other_reading: who pulls their own party away from such harmony

notes.note: Literally “sounding together”, a musical word also used for agreement.
notes.other_reading: agreement

check.note: The Greek is one adjective, “completing, going to make up”. “A part” is not in the Greek, and “part” is a marked word in these passages that occurs in this very sentence in another sense; “helps to” also softens it. The same holds for the second occurrence.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “you yourself help to complete a civic whole” and “help to complete a civic life”. “A part” is removed, since the Greek has no such noun; “help to” is kept because the Greek prefix says that the completing is done together with others. The same wording is used in 11.8a.

check.note: “In a people” is not clear English. The word here is the citizen body, the people as a political community or assembly.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “in a citizen body”. The word is the people as a political community.

check.note: “Factious” is rare today and easily misread. The Greek is the adjective of the word for civil strife.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “and it is seditious”. An adjective is kept, and not “a kind of civil strife”, because the Greek goes on to compare the action with a person; the note gives the root sense.

check.note: The word is a sounding together: harmony, concord. “Agreement” flattens the image and can sound like a contract.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “from such harmony”. The Greek word is a musical one, and “agreement” lost the image.

check.note: Taken adverbially (“as far as he is concerned”), which is the likelier reading. It can also be heard as closer to an object (“who sets his own share apart”), and the choice was made without sign.
check.decided: Declined: “For their own part” stands. It is the likelier reading, as the point itself says, and it keeps the word “part” in view; the other reading is recorded in a note.

check.note: The first word is “immediately, directly” (next in line), set against “at a distance”. “Closely” is not the natural opposite and suggests a degree of attention.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “whether directly or at a distance”. The Greek sets what is next in line against what is far off.

check.note: As in 7.13, “system” sounds technical; the word is a whole made up of members.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a civic whole”, in line with 7.13.

check.note: The Greek has one word for life here and another in the next sentence, and both become “life”. The reader may take them as the same thing.
check.decided: Declined: “A civic life” stands. The Greek repeats one adjective for the whole and for the life, so “civic” is repeated; the suggested wording would still give both Greek words as “life”, and the note records the two words.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave κοινωνικός as “communal”, where this translation uses “social”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “to the social goal”. The note says that the word is the adjective of the word for community.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “the man … his own part”, where the Greek does not single out a man. It also left out the “too” in “so too”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “like the person in a citizen body who, for their own part, stands apart” and, in the first sentence, “so too let every action of yours”.

passages.casaubon: As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and consummation, being a member of it, of a common society; so must every action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that is truly sociable. What action soever of thine therefore that either immediately or afar off, hath not reference to the common good, that is an exorbitant and disorderly action; yea it is seditious; as one among the people who from such and such a consent and unity, should factiously divide and separate himself.

passages.greek: Ἓν φῶς ἡλίου, κἂν διείργηται τοίχοις, ὄρεσιν, ἄλλοις μυρίοις. μία οὐσία κοινή, κἂν διείργηται ἰδίως ποιοῖς σώμασι μυρίοις. μία ψυχή, κἂν φύσεσι διείργηται μυρίαις καὶ ἰδίαις περιγραφαῖς. μία νοερὰ ψυχή, κἂν διακεκρίσθαι δοκῇ. τὰ μὲν οὖν ἄλλα μέρη τῶν εἰρημένων, οἷον πνεύματα καὶ ὑποκείμενα, ἀναίσθητα καὶ ἀνοικείωτα ἀλλήλοις· καίτοι κἀκεῖνα τὸ ἑνοῦν συνέχει καὶ τὸ ἐπὶ τὰ αὐτὰ βρῖθον. διάνοια δὲ ἰδίως ἐπὶ τὸ ὁμόφυλον τείνεται καὶ συνίσταται καὶ οὐ διείργεται τὸ κοινωνικὸν πάθος.
passages.english: One light of the sun, even if it is divided by walls, by mountains, by countless other things. One common substance, even if it is divided by countless bodies, each with its own quality. One soul, even if it is divided by countless natures and individual outlines. One soul that has mind, even if it seems to be separated. Now the other parts of the things just named, such as breaths and the matter that underlies things, are without sensation and have no attachment to one another; and yet even those are held together by what makes them one and by the weight that bears toward the same place. But thought, in a way of its own, stretches toward what is of the same kind and joins with it, and the social feeling is not divided.

notes.note: The first four sentences have no verb “is”, and are left so. The verb διείργω (“keep apart, bar off”) comes four times in the passage; “divided” is used every time, including the last sentence, where the repetition makes the point.
notes.other_reading: There is one light of the sun, even if it is shut off by walls

notes.note: ἰδίως ποιόν is a Stoic term for an individual thing marked off by a quality that is its own. The dative is read as in the first sentence, “by”: the one thing is divided by the many. It could also be heard as “among”.
notes.other_reading: even if it is shared out among countless individually qualified bodies

notes.note: περιγραφή is a line drawn around something: an outline or limit. ἰδίαις is “own, individual”; “countless” may cover the outlines as well as the natures.
notes.other_reading: by countless natures and their own boundaries

notes.note: νοερά is “of mind, able to think”; “that has mind” keeps “mind” for this word, as in the other passages. διάνοια in the last sentence is a different word and is given as “thought”.
notes.other_reading: One thinking soul

notes.note: A different verb from “divided”: “to be separated out, distinguished”. The change is marked with “separated”.
notes.other_reading: even if it seems to have been split up

notes.greek: τὰ μὲν οὖν ἄλλα μέρη τῶν εἰρημένων
notes.note: “The other parts of the things said” is loose in the Greek too. It is taken as the portions of the things just listed other than the soul that has mind. It could also mean the remaining constituents of the bodies and natures just mentioned.
notes.other_reading: the remaining parts of the wholes just mentioned

notes.note: πνεῦμα is breath or wind, and in Stoic physics the breath that holds a body together; ὑποκείμενα are “things that underlie”, the material a thing is made of. Both are kept literal, and the plural “breaths” is kept because separate portions are meant.
notes.other_reading: such as currents of air and material things

notes.note: “Without perception or feeling.” “Sensation” is used so that “feeling” can be kept for a different word in the last sentence.
notes.other_reading: without feeling

notes.note: A negative made from the Stoic word for treating something as one’s own (οἰκείωσις): “not made one another’s own, with no sense of belonging to one another”.
notes.other_reading: and have no kinship with one another

notes.note: “That which makes one”, from the word “one” that opens each of the first four sentences. This is a correction, and the manuscripts have τὸ νοοῦν, “that which thinks” (from memory, unchecked). The English translates the text given.
notes.other_reading: by what thinks

notes.note: Literally “that which weighs down toward the same things”: a pull like weight toward a common point.
notes.other_reading: and by what presses toward the same things

notes.note: διάνοια is “thought, understanding, mind”. ἰδίως, “in a way peculiar to itself”, picks up the words given above as “its own quality” and “individual outlines”, used there of what divides.
notes.other_reading: But mind, in a special way,

notes.note: “Combines, joins, holds together” with its own kind; the parts of the word are “stand” and “together”.
notes.other_reading: and stands together with it

notes.note: “The social feeling” is taken as the subject. It could instead be an accusative of respect, with thought still the subject. πάθος is something undergone, a feeling; κοινωνικόν, “social”, is the adjective of the word for community.
notes.other_reading: and is not divided in its social feeling

check.greek: κἂν διείργηται ἰδίως ποιοῖς σώμασι μυρίοις
check.note: The datives in the second and third sentences are the same construction as “by walls, by mountains” in the first, yet the English switches from “by” to “among”. The Greek picture is the same each time: the one thing is shut off by the many.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “divided by countless bodies” and “divided by countless natures”. The construction is the same as with the walls and mountains, so the same “by” is used; “among” made the one thing something shared out.

check.note: “Their” ties the outlines to the natures. The Greek sets two things side by side, and “countless” may cover both.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “by countless natures and individual outlines”. The Greek does not tie the outlines to the natures; “individual” is used because the Greek word is “own, individual”.

check.note: “Without sense” can be read as “senseless, meaningless”. The word means without perception or feeling.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “without sensation”. “Feeling” is not used because it is kept for a different Greek word in the last sentence.

check.note: “Breaths and underlying materials” is literal but will be opaque to a reader of today, and no plain equivalent is obvious.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “such as breaths and the matter that underlies things”. The plural “breaths” is kept, since the Greek plural marks separate portions; the note explains both terms.

check.note: The word is from the verb “to make one’s own”: they have no attachment or affinity to one another. “No kinship” suggests that they are unrelated in kind, which the Greek does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “have no attachment to one another”. The word says that they do not treat one another as their own, not that they differ in kind.

check.note: The verb is to combine, to cohere, to join with. “Stands together” copies the parts of the Greek word and not its meaning.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “joins with it”.

check.note: Keeping one word for the repeated verb is right, but “a feeling is not parted” is odd English and the reader may miss that it answers the walls and mountains. “Shut off” throughout would read plainly.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The chain word is changed throughout, but to “divided”, so that the last clause reads “and the social feeling is not divided” and plainly answers the walls and mountains. “Shut off” is not used because the Greek verb is “keep apart”, and a substance “shut off by countless bodies” gives the wrong picture.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave νοερά as “thinking” and διάνοια as “mind”, where this translation uses “mind” for the first word and “thought” for the second.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “One soul that has mind” and “But thought, in a way of its own”. The two Greek words stay two English words.

check.note: Found while settling: with “divided” now used for the repeated verb, this different verb needs a different English word.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “even if it seems to be separated”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave κοινωνικόν as “of community”, where this translation uses “social”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the social feeling”.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek word is “that which makes one”, built on the “one” that opens each of the first four sentences. “What unites them” lost that echo.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “held together by what makes them one”.

check.note: Found while settling: “in a way of its own … of its own kind” gave two “own” words in a row where the Greek has two different words.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “stretches toward what is of the same kind”. The Greek word is “of the same stock”.

passages.casaubon: There is but one light of the sun, though it be intercepted by walls and mountains, and other thousand objects. There is but one common substance of the whole world, though it be concluded and restrained into several different bodies, in number infinite. There is but one common soul, though divided into innumerable particular essences and natures. So is there but one common intellectual soul, though it seem to be divided. And as for all other parts of those generals which we have mentioned, as either sensitive souls or subjects, these of themselves (as naturally irrational) have no common mutual reference one unto another, though many of them contain a mind, or reasonable faculty in them, whereby they are ruled and governed. But of every reasonable mind, this the particular nature, that it hath reference to whatsoever is of her own kind, and desireth to be united: neither can this common affection, or mutual unity and correspondency, be here intercepted or divided, or confined to particulars as those other common things are.

passages.greek: ʽὯι μὴ εἶς καὶ ὁ αὐτός ἐστιν ἀεὶ τοῦ βίου σκοπός, οὗτος εἷς καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς δι’ ὅλου τοῦ βίου εἶναι οὐ δύναται.ʼ οὐκ ἀρκεῖ τὸ εἰρημένον, ἐὰν μὴ κἀκεῖνο προσθῇς, ὁποῖον εἶναι δεῖ τοῦτον τὸν σκοπόν. ὥσπερ γὰρ οὐχ ἡ πάντων τῶν ὁπωσοῦν τοῖς πλείοσι δοκούντων ἀγαθῶν ὑπόληψις ὁμοία ἐστίν, ἀλλ’ ἡ τῶν τοιῶνδέ τινων, τουτέστι τῶν κοινῶν, οὕτω καὶ τὸν σκοπὸν δεῖ τὸν κοινωνικὸν καὶ πολιτικὸν ὑποστήσασθαι. ὁ γὰρ εἰς τοῦτον πάσας τὰς ἰδίας ὁρμὰς ἀπευθύνων πάσας τὰς πράξεις ὁμοίας ἀποδώσει καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ἀεὶ ὁ αὐτὸς ἔσται.
passages.english: “A person who does not always have one and the same aim in life cannot be one and the same through the whole of life.” The saying is not enough unless you also add what kind of aim this must be. For just as judgment is not alike about all the things that in one way or another seem good to the majority, but is alike about those of a certain kind, that is, the common goods, so too the aim to be set up must be the social and civic one. For whoever directs all their private impulses toward this aim will make all their actions alike, and in this way will always be the same.

notes.note: The edition marks the first sentence as a quotation; the source is not named. The Greek has simply “he for whom” and “this one”, and “a person” is supplied. “One and the same” is said first of the aim and then of the person, and the same English is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: that man cannot be one and the same through his whole life

notes.note: σκοπός is the mark an archer aims at. “Aim” is used for it throughout.
notes.other_reading: target in life

notes.note: Literally “what has been said”.
notes.other_reading: What has been said is not enough

notes.greek: τῶν ὁπωσοῦν τοῖς πλείοσι δοκούντων ἀγαθῶν
notes.note: ὁπωσοῦν (“in whatever way”) is taken with “seem good”. οἱ πλείονες is “the majority, most people”.
notes.other_reading: all the things most people somehow or other think good

notes.note: ὑπόληψις is a judgment taken up about something. “Alike” is understood as the same from one person to the next, and is kept for the same adjective in the last sentence. The Greek does not repeat “is alike” after “but”; it is repeated for clarity.
notes.other_reading: people do not judge alike about all the things

notes.note: “The common ones”: goods that are shared, or that concern everyone; the Greek does not say which more exactly. “Goods” is supplied from the clause before, so that “common” is not heard as “ordinary”.
notes.other_reading: that is, the shared ones

notes.note: Two adjectives, “social” and “of citizens (of the city)”. In Greek the first is made from the word “common” just used, a link that “social” does not show; “social” is kept because it is the word for κοινωνικός throughout this translation.
notes.other_reading: the communal and civic one

notes.note: “To set under oneself”: to lay down as a basis.
notes.other_reading: must be laid down as one’s foundation

notes.note: ἴδιος is “one’s own”, and also “private” as against “common” above; “private” is used so that the contrast can be heard. ὁρμή is the Stoic “impulse”, the movement toward an action.
notes.other_reading: all their own impulses

notes.note: “In accordance with this”: either “in this way, by this means” or “in this respect”. The first is taken, as the result of aiming everything at one mark.
notes.other_reading: and in this respect will always be the same

check.note: The phrase can be “in this respect” or “by this, in this way”. “In this respect” reads as a limit, whereas the argument wants a result, and the choice was made without sign.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “and in this way will always be the same”. The phrase allows either, and the sentence states what follows from aiming everything at one mark; the note gives “in this respect”.

check.note: “The opinion held is not alike about” is accurate in its parts but hard to follow. The Greek says that people’s judgment is not the same about all such things, only about some.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “For just as judgment is not alike about all the things that in one way or another seem good to the majority, but is alike about those of a certain kind”. The noun “judgment” is kept, since it is the set word for ὑπόληψις in this translation, and “people” and “only” are not added because the Greek does not have them.

check.note: “Common” alone can be read as “ordinary”. The word is the root of the word for “communal” just after and means the goods that are shared.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “that is, the common goods”. The noun is supplied from the clause before so that “common” cannot be heard as “ordinary”; “common” itself is kept because it is the word used for κοινός in the other passages.

check.note: The word is set against “common” and “communal”: private, individual impulses directed at the common aim. “His own” reads as a mere possessive and the contrast is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “all their private impulses”. The Greek word is the opposite of “common” just before.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave κοινωνικός as “communal”, where this translation uses “social”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the social and civic one”. A note says that the Greek word is made from “common”, a link the draft’s “communal” had shown, and gives that wording.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “his own impulses … his actions”, where the Greek does not single out a man.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “whoever directs all their private impulses toward this aim will make all their actions alike”.

passages.casaubon: He that hath not one and the self-same general end always as long as he liveth, cannot possibly be one and the self-same man always. But this will not suffice except thou add also what ought to be this general end. For as the general conceit and apprehension of all those things which upon no certain ground are by the greater part of men deemed good, cannot be uniform and agreeable, but that only which is limited and restrained by some certain proprieties and conditions, as of community: that nothing be conceived good, which is not commonly and publicly good: so must the end also that we propose unto ourselves, be common and sociable. For he that doth direct all his own private motions and purposes to that end, all his actions will be agreeable and uniform; and by that means will be still the same man.

passages.greek: Μηκέτι μόνον συμπνεῖν τῷ περιέχοντι ἀέρι, ἀλλ’ ἤδη καὶ συμφρονεῖν τῷ περιέχοντι πάντα νοερῷ. οὐ γὰρ ἧττον ἡ νοερὰ δύναμις πάντῃ κέχυται καὶ διαπεφοίτηκε τῷ σπάσαι δυναμένῳ ἤπερ ἡ ἀερώδης τῷ ἀναπνεῦσαι δυναμένῳ.
passages.english: No longer only to breathe together with the surrounding air, but from now on also to think together with the mind that surrounds all things. For the power of mind is poured out everywhere and has spread all through, for the one able to draw it in, no less than the power of air for the one able to breathe it.

notes.note: The Greek uses bare infinitives as a rule set down for himself, with no “you”. The infinitive is kept and not turned into a command.
notes.other_reading: Do not any longer only breathe together

notes.note: Literally “breathe with”; in ordinary Greek the word also means “be in accord with”, which prepares the second half.
notes.other_reading: to be of one breath with

notes.note: Built to match “breathe with”: “think with”. Its usual sense is “be of one mind with, agree with”; “think together with” keeps the pairing.
notes.other_reading: to be of one mind with

notes.note: Literally “the thing of mind that surrounds all things”. περιέχω is “surround” and also “contain, hold”; “surround” is kept to match the air. “Mind” is used for νοερόν here and “power of mind” for the adjective in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: the intelligence that contains all things

notes.note: “Has gone through and through”: pervaded. The one “everywhere” in the Greek serves both verbs.
notes.other_reading: has passed through all things

notes.note: σπάω is “draw, pull in”, as one draws breath or a drink. The dative is “for” the one who can.
notes.other_reading: for anyone able to take it in

notes.note: “The airy (power)”: the word “power” is carried over from the first half.
notes.other_reading: than the air is

check.note: “Everything” is supplied. The Greek has one “everywhere” for both verbs.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “is poured out everywhere and has spread all through”. The Greek has one “everywhere” for both verbs and no “everything”.

check.note: The bare infinitive is Marcus’s note form for an instruction to himself. Kept literally it may read as a fragment to a reader of today; flagged for a decision, not as an error.
check.decided: Declined: The infinitive stands. The Greek is impersonal note form with no “you”, and the rules of this translation keep an impersonal form where the Greek has one; the note gives the command form.

check.note: The verb is normally “to be of one mind with, to agree with”. “Think together with” keeps the pairing with “breathe together with” at a small cost to the usual sense.
check.decided: Declined: “Think together with” stands, as the point itself allows. It keeps the pairing with “breathe together with” that the Greek builds, and the note gives the usual sense, “be of one mind with”.

passages.casaubon: Not only now henceforth to have a common breath, or to hold correspondency of breath, with that air, that compasseth us about; but to have a common mind, or to hold correspondency of mind also with that rational substance, which compasseth all things. For, that also is of itself, and of its own nature (if a man can but draw it in as he should) everywhere diffused; and passeth through all things, no less than the air doth, if a man can but suck it in.

passages.greek: Κλάδος τοῦ προσεχοῦς κλάδου ἀποκοπεὶς οὐ δύναται μὴ καὶ τοῦ ὅλου φυτοῦ ἀποκεκόφθαι. οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἄνθρωπος ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἀποσχισθεὶς ὅλης τῆς κοινωνίας ἀποπέπτωκε. κλάδον μὲν οὖν ἄλλος ἀποκόπτει· ἄνθρωπος δὲ αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν τοῦ πλησίον χωρίζει μισήσας καὶ ἀποστραφείς, ἀγνοεῖ δὲ ὅτι καὶ τοῦ ὅλου πολιτεύματος ἅμα ἀποτέτμηκεν ἑαυτόν. πλὴν ἐκεῖνό γε δῶρον τοῦ συστησαμένου τὴν κοινωνίαν Διός· ἔξεστι γὰρ ἡμῖν πάλιν συμφῦναι τῷ προσεχεῖ καὶ πάλιν τοῦ ὅλου συμπληρωτικοῖς γενέσθαι. πλεονάκις μέντοι γινόμενον τὸ κατὰ τὴν τοιαύτην διαίρεσιν δυσένωτον καὶ δυσαποκατάστατον τὸ ἀποχωροῦν ποιεῖ. ὅλως τε οὐχ ὅμοιος ὁ κλάδος ὁ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς συμβλαστήσας καὶ σύμπνους συμμείνας τῷ μετὰ τὴν ἀποκοπὴν αὖθις ἐγκεντρισθέντι, ὅ τι ποτὲ λέγουσιν οἱ φυτουργοί.
passages.english: A branch cut off from the branch next to it cannot help being cut off from the whole plant as well. So too a human being split off from one human being has fallen away from the whole community. Now a branch is cut off by someone else; but it is the human being who separates themselves from their neighbour, by coming to hate and turning away, and they do not know that they have at the same time cut themselves away from the whole civic body as well. Yet there is this gift from Zeus, who put the community together: we are allowed to grow together again with the one next to us and again to help to complete the whole. But when this kind of division happens many times, it makes what withdraws hard to unite and hard to restore. And in general, the branch that sprouted together from the beginning and has stayed together, sharing one breath, is not like the one grafted in again after being cut off, whatever it is that the gardeners say.

notes.note: προσεχής is “adjoining, next in line”. The same word is used later of the person “next to us”, and “next to” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: from the neighbouring branch

notes.note: The general word for anything planted; a tree is meant, but the Greek says “plant”.
notes.other_reading: the whole tree

notes.note: A different verb from the “cut off” used of the branch: “split, torn off”. A third verb, “cut away”, comes later; the three are kept apart.
notes.other_reading: severed from one human being

notes.note: Two past participles, “having come to hate and having turned away”; they give the acts by which the separation is made. The Greek names no object for the hatred.
notes.other_reading: when they hate their neighbour and turn their back

notes.note: πολίτευμα: a state, a constitution, or the body of citizens. “Civic body” is used, as in 4.4.
notes.other_reading: the whole commonwealth

notes.note: Zeus is the chief god of the Greeks, for the Stoics a name for the reason that governs the universe. The verb is “set up, put together”, from which the word for a whole made of members (σύστημα) comes.
notes.other_reading: of Zeus, who founded the community

notes.note: An adjective: “such as to fill up the whole together”. “Help to complete” is used as in 9.23; the Greek has no noun such as “parts”.
notes.other_reading: and once more to go to make up the whole

notes.note: A roundabout phrase, “the matter of such a division”, given simply as “this kind of division”.
notes.other_reading: what happens in such a separation

notes.note: Three words in a row begin with the prefix “together”: sprouted together, breathing together, stayed together. The Greek does not say with what; the rest of the plant is understood.
notes.other_reading: the branch that sprouted with the plant from the beginning and has stayed with it

notes.note: “Breathing together”, of one breath. The verb of the same make is given as “breathe together with” in 8.54.
notes.other_reading: and has stayed of one breath

notes.greek: ὅ τι ποτὲ λέγουσιν οἱ φυτουργοί
notes.note: Open: literally “whatever it is that the plant-workers say”, which can be a concession (“whatever the gardeners may say”), a shrug at their trade word for grafting, or a pointer to a saying of theirs. The English keeps the literal wording so that all three stay possible. The chapter’s closing sentence, which belongs to the next passage, follows at once and runs roughly: to grow on the same stock, but not to hold the same principles.
notes.other_reading: or whatever the gardeners call it

check.greek: ὅ τι ποτὲ λέγουσιν οἱ φυτουργοί
check.note: The English reads as a brush-off: no matter what the gardeners claim. The clause can equally point to a saying of theirs, which the chapter’s closing sentence may be, and the dismissive reading was chosen without sign.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The wording “whatever it is that the gardeners say” is kept, because the Greek is indefinite (“whatever it is that”) and does not say “which is just what”. The note now sets out the three ways the clause can be taken and gives the sentence that follows, to which it may point.

check.note: As in 9.23: one adjective, “completing, going to make up”. “Parts” is not in the Greek and “help to” softens it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “and again to help to complete the whole”. “Parts” is removed, since the Greek has no such noun; “help to” is kept for the prefix “together”, as in 9.23.

check.note: The word for “also, as well” is dropped and only “at the same time” is given. It answers “from the whole plant as well” in the first sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “at the same time cut themselves away from the whole civic body as well”. “As well” gives the dropped word and answers the first sentence.

check.note: Both are past participles: “having come to hate and turned away”, the acts by which he separates himself. The English present and the supplied “him” are small shifts.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “by coming to hate and turning away”. The participles give the acts by which the separation is made; no “him” is supplied, since the Greek has none.

check.note: “The plant” is supplied to carry the prefix “together”. Fair, but it is the translator’s word.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the branch that sprouted together from the beginning and has stayed together, sharing one breath”. “The plant” and “with it” are removed; the Greek has only the prefix “together”, three times.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “himself”, “his” and “he” of the human being, where the Greek does not single out a man.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “it is the human being who separates themselves from their neighbour … and they do not know that they have at the same time cut themselves away”.

part.left_out: Ὁμοθαμνεῖν μέν, μὴ ὁμοδογματεῖν δέ.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 11.7 before the chapter’s last sentence and opens its 11.8 with it.

passages.casaubon: A branch cut off from the continuity of that which was next unto it, must needs be cut off from the whole tree: so a man that is divided from another man, is divided from the whole society. A branch is cut off by another, but he that hates and is averse, cuts himself off from his neighbour, and knows not that at the same time he divides himself from the whole body, or corporation. But herein is the gift and mercy of God, the Author of this society, in that, once cut off we may grow together and become part of the whole again. But if this happen often the misery is that the further a man is run in this division, the harder he is to be reunited and restored again: and however the branch which, once cut of afterwards was graffed in, gardeners can tell you is not like that which sprouted together at first, and still continued in the unity of the body.

passages.greek:
Ὁ λόγος καὶ ἡ λογικὴ τέχνη δυνάμεις εἰσὶν ἑαυταῖς ἀρκούμεναι καὶ τοῖς καθ’ ἑαυτὰς ἔργοις. ὁρμῶνται μὲν οὖν ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκείας ἀρχῆς, ὁδεύουσι δὲ εἰς τὸ προκείμενον τέλος, καθὸ κατορθώσεις αἱ τοιαῦται πράξεις ὀνομάζονται τὴν ὀρθότητα τῆς ὁδοῦ σημαίνουσαι.

Οὐδὲν τούτων ῥητέον ἀνθρώπου, ἃ ἀνθρώπῳ, καθὸ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν, οὐκ ἐπιβάλλει. οὐκ ἔστιν ἀπαιτήματα ἀνθρώπου οὐδὲ ἐπαγγέλλεται αὐτὰ ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσις οὐδὲ τελειότητές εἰσι τῆς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσεως. οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ τὸ τέλος ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐστι τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ κείμενον οὐδέ γε τὸ συμπληρωτικὸν τοῦ τέλους, τὸ ἀγαθόν. ἐπεὶ εἴ τι τούτων ἦν ἐπιβάλλον τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, οὐκ ἂν τὸ ὑπερφρονεῖν αὐτῶν καὶ κατεξανίστασθαι ἐπιβάλλον ἦν οὐδὲ ἐπαινετὸς ἦν ὁ ἀπροσδεῆ τούτων ἑαυτὸν παρεχόμενος, οὐδ’ ἂν ὁ ἐλαττωτικὸς ἑαυτοῦ ἔν τινι τούτων ἀγαθὸς ἦν, εἴπερ ταῦτα ἀγαθὰ ἦν. νῦν δ᾽, ὅσῳπερ πλείω τις ἀφαιρῶν ἑαυτοῦ τούτων ἢ τοιούτων ἑτέρων ἢ καὶ ἀφαιρούμενός τι τούτων ἀνέχηται, τοσῷδε μᾶλλον ἀγαθός ἐστιν.
passages.english:
Reason and the art of reasoning are powers that are content with themselves and with the works that are their own. So they set out from their own starting point and travel towards the end set before them, which is why actions of this kind are called katorthōseis, “acts that go straight”, as signifying the straightness of the road.

None of the things that do not fall to a human being, as a human being, should be called a human being’s. They are not requirements of a human being, human nature does not promise them, and they are not perfections of human nature. So the end for a human being does not lie in them either, nor does that which makes the end complete, the good. For if any of these things did fall to a human being, it would not fall to a human being to look down on them and rise up against them, nor would a person who proves to be in no need of them be praiseworthy, nor would a person who stints themselves in any of them be good, if these things really were goods. But as it is, the more of these things, or of others like them, a person bears to take away from themselves, or even bears having one of them taken away, the better that person is.

notes.note: The verb with a dative usually means “to be content with”, but it can also be heard as “to be enough for”. The English takes “content with”, as in the opening of 8.7.
notes.other_reading: powers that are sufficient for themselves and for the works that are their own

notes.note: This can mean logic as a discipline, or more loosely the skill of using reason. “The art of reasoning” allows both.
notes.other_reading: the art of logic

notes.note: A Stoic term for fully right actions. The word contains the Greek for “straight”, and the sentence explains the term by that, so the Greek word is kept in the English. The gloss “acts that go straight” is added for the reader and is not in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: which is why such actions are called “right acts”, as signifying the rightness of the road

notes.note: Chapter 15 begins here. The Greek says “none of those things … which do not fall to a human being” and never names the things; from what follows they seem to be outward things one can have or lose. No noun is supplied.
notes.other_reading: None of these things, which do not fall to a human being as a human being, should be called a human being’s

notes.note: The verb means “falls to one’s share, is one’s proper business”, and it comes three times in the argument. “Fall to” is used each time.
notes.other_reading: that are not a human being’s proper concern as a human being

notes.note: The Greek can mean things demanded of a human being, or things a human being requires or has a claim to. “Requirements of a human being” leaves it as open as the Greek.
notes.other_reading: They are not demanded of a human being

notes.note: The word is built on the Greek for “end”, which follows in the next sentence: a perfection is a thing’s having reached its end. English cannot show the link. “Complete” is kept for a different Greek word in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: and they are not ways in which human nature reaches its end

notes.note: Literally “the one inclined to make himself less”, that is, to go short. The word is rare, and it can also be heard as taking less than one’s due.
notes.other_reading: a person who takes less than their share of any of them

notes.greek: ἢ καὶ ἀφαιρούμενός τι τούτων ἀνέχηται
notes.note: “Bears” is the only finite verb here and is taken with both participles: bearing to take things from oneself, and bearing to have one taken. It could be attached to the second only.
notes.other_reading: the more of these things, or of others like them, a person takes away from themselves, or even bears having one of them taken away, the better that person is

check.note: The Greek particles tie this sentence to the first as its unfolding (“so”, “then”); the English began it with no link.
check.decided: Accepted: The sentence now begins “So they set out from their own starting point”, which gives the Greek connecting word its place.

check.greek: κατορθώσεις αἱ τοιαῦται πράξεις ὀνομάζονται τὴν ὀρθότητα τῆς ὁδοῦ σημαίνουσαι
check.note: The English adds a transliterated Greek term with a gloss folded into the text, and makes “the name” the subject where the Greek participle “signifying” agrees with the actions.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The Greek word and its gloss stay, because the sentence explains a Greek word by the “straight” inside it and cannot be followed without them; a note says the gloss is added. “The name marks” is replaced by “as signifying the straightness of the road”, so that it is again the actions so named that signify, as in the Greek.

check.greek: Οὐδὲν τούτων ῥητέον ἀνθρώπου, ἃ ἀνθρώπῳ, καθὸ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν, οὐκ ἐπιβάλλει
check.note: Faithful, but hard to parse: the relative clause stands far from “None of these things” and the sentence has to be read twice.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “None of the things that do not fall to a human being, as a human being, should be called a human being’s”, with the relative clause beside its noun. The plural “things” is kept, and not the suggested “Nothing”, so that “They” in the next sentence has something to refer to.

check.note: The genitive can mean things demanded of a human being or things a human being requires or has a claim to; the English silently took the first.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “They are not requirements of a human being”, which can be heard both ways, as the Greek can. The note gives the narrower reading.

check.note: This word is cognate with the word for “end” that follows, while the word rendered “makes the end complete” is a different one; “completions” and “complete” made two Greek words share one English root and hid the real link.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “perfections of human nature”, and “complete” is left to the different Greek word in the next sentence. A note says that “perfections” is built on the Greek for “end”, a link English cannot show.

check.greek: ὁ ἐλαττωτικὸς ἑαυτοῦ ἔν τινι τούτων
check.note: The Greek says “the one inclined to make himself go short in any of these”; “less than his share” brings in a due portion that the Greek does not state.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a person who stints themselves in any of them”, where the person is the thing lessened and no due share is mentioned. The note keeps “takes less than their share” as the other reading.

check.greek: ὅσῳπερ πλείω τις ἀφαιρῶν ἑαυτοῦ τούτων ἢ τοιούτων ἑτέρων ἢ καὶ ἀφαιρούμενός τι τούτων ἀνέχηται
check.note: “Bears” is the only finite verb and most naturally governs both participles. The English attached it to the second only, added a second “the more”, and dropped “or even”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the more of these things, or of others like them, a person bears to take away from themselves, or even bears having one of them taken away”. “Bears” governs both halves, “the more” stands once and counts the things given up, and “or even” is restored.

check.note: “The more he is good” is unidiomatic English for a simple Greek comparative.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the better that person is”. “Better” is still heard as the comparative of “good”, the word the argument has just used twice.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek words for “human being” and “a person” do not single out a man, but the draft had “he”, “him” and “himself” throughout chapter 15.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now uses “a human being”, “a person” and “they” throughout, as in the passages settled earlier.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek has a strengthened “if” (“if indeed”), which the draft gave as a bare “if”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “if these things really were goods”.

passages.casaubon: Reason, and rational power, are faculties which content themselves with themselves, and their own proper operations. And as for their first inclination and motion, that they take from themselves. But their progress is right to the end and object, which is in their way, as it were, and lieth just before them: that is, which is feasible and possible, whether it be that which at the first they proposed to themselves, or no. For which reason also such actions are termed κατορθώσεις, to intimate the directness of the way, by which they are achieved. Nothing must be thought to belong to a man, which doth not belong unto him as he is a man. These, the event of purposes, are not things required in a man. The nature of man doth not profess any such things. The final ends and consummations of actions are nothing at all to a man's nature. The end therefore of a man, or the _summum bonum_ whereby that end is fulfilled, cannot consist in the consummation of actions purposed and intended. Again, concerning these outward worldly things, were it so that any of them did properly belong unto man, then would it not belong unto man, to condemn them and to stand in opposition with them. Neither would he be praiseworthy that can live without them; or he good, (if these were good indeed) who of his own accord doth deprive himself of any of them. But we see contrariwise, that the more a man doth withdraw himself from these wherein external pomp and greatness doth consist, or any other like these; or the better he doth bear with the loss of these, the better he is accounted.

nearest.title: The work that belongs to me

passages.greek: Ἀρκεῖται πᾶσα φύσις ἑαυτῇ εὐοδούσῃ, φύσις δὲ λογικὴ εὐοδεῖ ἐν μὲν φαντασίαις μήτε ψευδεῖ μήτε ἀδήλῳ συγκατατιθεμένη, τὰς ὁρμὰς δὲ ἐπὶ τὰ κοινωνικὰ ἔργα μόνα ἀπευθύνουσα, τὰς ὀρέξεις δὲ καὶ τὰς ἐκκλίσεις τῶν ἐφ’ ἡμῖν μόνων πεποιημένη, τὸ δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως ἀπονεμόμενον πᾶν ἀσπαζομένη· μέρος γὰρ αὐτῆς ἐστιν ὡς ἡ τοῦ φύλλου φύσις τῆς τοῦ φυτοῦ φύσεως· πλὴν ὅτι ἐκεῖ μὲν ἡ τοῦ φύλλου φύσις μέρος ἐστὶ φύσεως καὶ ἀναισθήτου καὶ ἀλόγου καὶ ἐμποδίζεσθαι δυναμένης, ἡ δὲ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσις μέρος ἐστὶν ἀνεμποδίστου φύσεως καὶ νοερᾶς καὶ δικαίας, εἴγε ἴσους καὶ κατ’ ἀξίαν τοὺς μερισμοὺς χρόνων, οὐσίας, αἰτίου, ἐνεργείας, συμβάσεως ἑκάστοις ποιεῖται. σκόπει δέ, μὴ εἰ τὸ ἓν πρὸς τὸ ἓν ἴσον εὑρήσεις ἐπὶ παντός, ἀλλὰ εἰ συλλήβδην τὰ πάντα τοῦδε πρὸς ἀθρόα τὰ τοῦ ἑτέρου.
passages.english: Every nature is content with itself when its road goes well. And a rational nature’s road goes well when, among its impressions, it assents to nothing false and nothing unclear; when it directs its impulses only to social acts; when it has confined its desires and aversions to the things that are up to us alone; and when it welcomes everything allotted by the common nature. For it is a part of that nature, as the nature of the leaf is a part of the nature of the plant; except that there the nature of the leaf is part of a nature that is without sensation, without reason, and able to be hindered, while the nature of the human being is part of a nature that is unhindered, has mind and is just, seeing that it makes the apportionments of time, substance, cause, activity and circumstance equal for each thing and according to what each deserves. But look, not at whether you will find one thing equal to one thing in every case, but at whether all that belongs to this one, taken together, is equal to the whole of what belongs to the other.

notes.note: The verb literally means “to have a good road” and commonly just “to prosper”. The road is kept, since road language runs through the neighbouring passages.
notes.other_reading: Every nature is content with itself when it prospers

notes.note: “Assent” is the Stoic term for accepting an impression as true. The second adjective means “not evident”, what has not been made clear.
notes.other_reading: assenting neither to what is false nor to what is not evident

notes.note: The adjective means “belonging to fellowship or community”. “Social” is the word used for it throughout this translation; it does not mean sociable. The noun is literally “works”.
notes.other_reading: works that serve the community

notes.greek: τὰς ὀρέξεις δὲ καὶ τὰς ἐκκλίσεις
notes.note: Two Stoic terms, literally “reachings-for and turnings-away”. The Greek says the rational nature “has made them of the things up to us only”; “confined … to” is the English for that.
notes.other_reading: when it has made its desires and avoidances to be only of the things in our power

notes.note: The nature common to all things, that is, the nature of the whole. “The common nature” is kept wherever this phrase occurs.
notes.other_reading: by universal nature

notes.note: An adjective from the Greek noun for mind: “having mind”. “Mind” is kept for this root throughout the translation.
notes.other_reading: a nature that is unhindered, intelligent and just

notes.note: Either “seeing that” (giving the ground for calling it just) or “if, that is” (a condition, which the closing “But look” would then help to test). The English takes it as the ground.
notes.other_reading: if, that is, it makes the apportionments equal for each thing

notes.note: A bare list. The first word is a plural, “times”, that is, spans of time. “Substance” is the stuff a thing is made of and “cause” the forming principle in it, a pair Marcus uses often; the last word means what befalls a thing.
notes.other_reading: of spans of time, matter, form, activity and what happens

notes.greek: συλλήβδην τὰ πάντα τοῦδε πρὸς ἀθρόα τὰ τοῦ ἑτέρου
notes.note: The Greek is compressed and has no adjective here; “is equal” is carried over from the clause before.
notes.other_reading: but whether, taken all together, the whole of this one against the total of the other

check.note: The Greek is “has made”: it has made its desires and aversions be of the things up to us alone. “Kept … for” suggests saving something up, where the Greek is about confining.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “when it has confined its desires and aversions to the things that are up to us alone”. “Alone” keeps the Greek “only”.

check.note: The Greek has two coordinate qualities joined by “and”: the apportionments are equal and according to worth. The English dropped “and” and made the second a trailing qualifier.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “it makes the apportionments of time, substance, cause, activity and circumstance equal for each thing and according to what each deserves”. Both qualities are joined by “and”, and both are what the common nature makes the apportionments be, as the Greek word order has it.

check.note: The word can give a ground (“seeing that”) or a real condition (“if, that is”); the English takes it as settled fact, though the following “But look” would also suit the condition.
check.decided: Declined: “Seeing that” stays. With a plain statement of fact after it this word commonly gives a ground that is taken as granted, and the sentence has just called that nature just without qualification. The note sets out the conditional reading and what speaks for it.

check.note: “Social works” is not natural English and may suggest social work or charity.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “social acts”, which removes the echo of “social work”. “Social” stays because it is the one word used for this Greek adjective across the translation, and the note says what it means.

check.note: The literal plural “of times” reads oddly in an English list of abstract nouns.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “of time”. The note records that the Greek is a plural, spans of time.

check.greek: τὸ δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως ἀπονεμόμενον πᾶν ἀσπαζομένη
check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “everything allotted to it”, but the Greek has no “to it”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “everything allotted by the common nature”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “intelligent” for an adjective built on the Greek noun for mind, where the passages settled earlier keep “mind” for this root.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a nature that is unhindered, has mind and is just”, and a note gives “intelligent” as the other wording.

passages.casaubon: Every particular nature hath content, when in its own proper course it speeds. A reasonable nature doth then speed, when first in matter of fancies and imaginations, it gives no consent to that which is either false uncertain. Secondly, when in all its motions and resolutions it takes its level at the common good only, and that it desireth nothing, and flieth from nothing, bet what is in its own power to compass or avoid. And lastly, when it willingly and gladly embraceth, whatsoever is dealt and appointed unto it by the common nature. For it is part of it; even as the nature of any one leaf, is part of the common nature of all plants and trees. But that the nature of a leaf, is part of a nature both unreasonable and unsensible, and which in its proper end may be hindered; or, which is servile and slavish: whereas the nature of man is part of a common nature which cannot be hindered, and which is both reasonable and just. From whence also it is, that according to the worth of everything, she doth make such equal distribution of all things, as of duration, substance form, operation, and of events and accidents. But herein consider not whether thou shalt find this equality in everything absolutely and by itself; but whether in all the particulars of some one thing taken together, and compared with all the particulars of some other thing, and them together likewise.

nearest.title: The work that belongs to me

passages.greek: Μὴ περιβλέπου ἀλλότρια ἡγεμονικά, ἀλλ’ ἐκεῖ βλέπε κατ’ εὐθὺ ἐπὶ τί σε ἡ φύσις ὁδηγεῖ, ἥ τε τοῦ ὅλου διὰ τῶν συμβαινόντων σοι καὶ ἡ σὴ διὰ τῶν πρακτέων ὑπὸ σοῦ· πρακτέον δὲ ἑκάστῳ τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ κατασκευῇ· κατεσκεύασται δὲ τὰ μὲν λοιπὰ τῶν λογικῶν ἕνεκεν, ὥσπερ καὶ ἐπὶ παντὸς ἄλλου τὰ χείρω τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν, τὰ δὲ λογικὰ ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν. τὸ μὲν οὖν προηγούμενον ἐν τῇ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου κατασκευῇ τὸ κοινωνικόν ἐστι, δεύτερον δὲ τὸ ἀνένδοτον πρὸς τὰς σωματικὰς πείσεις· λογικῆς γὰρ καὶ νοερᾶς κινήσεως ἴδιον περιορίζειν ἑαυτὴν καὶ μήποτε ἡττᾶσθαι μήτε αἰσθητικῆς μήτε ὁρμητικῆς κινήσεως· ζῳώδεις γὰρ ἑκάτεραι, ἡ δὲ νοερὰ ἐθέλει πρωτιστεύειν καὶ μὴ κατακρατεῖσθαι ὑπ’ ἐκείνων. δικαίως γε· πέφυκε γὰρ χρηστικὴ πᾶσιν ἐκείνοις. τρίτον ἐν τῇ λογικῇ κατασκευῇ τὸ ἀπρόπτωτον καὶ ἀνεξαπάτητον. τούτων οὖν ἐχόμενον τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν εὐθεῖαν περαινέτω καὶ ἔχει τὰ ἑαυτοῦ.
passages.english: Do not look around at other people’s ruling parts, but look straight ahead to where nature is leading you, both the nature of the whole, through the things that happen to you, and your own nature, through the things you have to do. What each being has to do is what follows from its make-up. Now everything else has been made for the sake of the rational beings, just as in every other case the inferior things are for the sake of the superior, and the rational beings have been made for the sake of one another. So what comes first in the human make-up is being social. Second is not giving way to what the body undergoes; for it is proper to movement that is rational and of mind to draw a boundary around itself and never to be beaten by the movement of the senses or the movement of impulse. For both of those are of the animal kind, while the movement of mind wants to hold first place and not to be overpowered by them. And rightly so, for it is by nature fitted to make use of all of those. Third in the rational make-up is not being hasty and not being deceived. So let the ruling part hold to these and carry its straight road through, and it has what is its own.

notes.note: The Stoic term for the commanding part of the soul, rendered “the ruling part”. The plural is unusual in English.
notes.other_reading: Do not look around at what rules in other people

notes.note: Literally “guides along a road”, which prepares the “straight road” at the end of the passage.
notes.other_reading: to where nature is guiding you on your road

notes.note: The noun means how a thing is constructed, and the verb from the same root follows at once. “Make-up” and “made” are used so the link shows.
notes.other_reading: what is in line with its constitution

notes.note: Literally “what goes in front”: first in rank among the features of the human make-up, with “second” and “third” following. “What comes first” is used for this word here and in 5.20 and 4.1.
notes.other_reading: So the principal thing in the constitution of a human being

notes.note: A neuter adjective used as a noun: “the social”, the fact of being made for fellowship. The English turns it as “being social”.
notes.other_reading: is fellowship with others

notes.note: The noun means being acted on, as opposed to acting: here whatever the body is made to feel. “Undergo” is used for this word here and in 9.16.
notes.other_reading: not yielding to the feelings of the body

notes.note: The second adjective is built on the Greek noun for mind. “Of mind” is the wording kept for it throughout the translation.
notes.other_reading: for it is proper to rational and intelligent movement

notes.note: Literally “to mark a boundary round itself”. It can be heard as keeping itself apart or as keeping within its own limits.
notes.other_reading: to keep itself within its own limits

notes.note: The first is a Stoic term, literally “not falling forward”, meaning not assenting before one should. “Hasty” is used for this root here and in 11.10.
notes.other_reading: freedom from rash assent and from being deceived

notes.greek: εὐθεῖαν περαινέτω καὶ ἔχει τὰ ἑαυτοῦ
notes.note: “Straight” is a feminine adjective with “road” understood, and the verb means to carry a thing through to completion. The last verb is a plain present, “it has”, not a future or a command.
notes.other_reading: let it finish a straight course, and it is in possession of what belongs to it

check.greek: ἐκεῖ βλέπε κατ’ εὐθὺ ἐπὶ τί
check.note: The Greek is directional: “look straight there, to where nature is guiding you”. “At this: what” turns a direction into a topic.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “look straight ahead to where nature is leading you”, which keeps the direction and fits the road image of the verb.

check.note: Found while settling: the same Greek word was “the leading thing” here and “leading aim” in 5.20 and 4.1, where “aim” was questioned.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “what comes first in the human make-up”, which counts on naturally to “Second” and “Third”, and the same words are used in 5.20 and 4.1.

check.greek: λογικῆς γὰρ καὶ νοερᾶς κινήσεως ἴδιον
check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “intelligent” for the adjective built on the Greek noun for mind, and “it belongs to” for the word rendered “proper to” in 8.26.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “it is proper to movement that is rational and of mind” and, further on, “the movement of mind”, so that “mind” is kept for this root as in the passages settled earlier.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “go straight on to the end of its road”, which can be heard as going on until death; the Greek verb means to carry a thing through.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “carry its straight road through”, in line with “is carried through” for the same verb in the passages settled earlier.

passages.casaubon: Look not about upon other men's minds and understandings; but look right on forwards whither nature, both that of the universe, in those things that happen unto thee; and thine in particular, in those things that are done by thee: doth lead, and direct thee. Now every one is bound to do that, which is consequent and agreeable to that end which by his true natural constitution he was ordained unto. As for all other things, they are ordained for the use of reasonable creatures: as in all things we see that that which is worse and inferior, is made for that which is better. Reasonable creatures, they are ordained one for another. That therefore which is chief in every man's constitution, is, that he intend the common good. The second is, that he yield not to any lusts and motions of the flesh. For it is the part and privilege of the reasonable and intellective faculty, that she can so bound herself, as that neither the sensitive, nor the appetitive faculties, may not anyways prevail upon her. For both these are brutish. And therefore over both she challengeth mastery, and cannot anyways endure, if in her right temper, to be subject unto either. And this indeed most justly. For by nature she was ordained to command all in the body. The third thing proper to man by his constitution, is, to avoid all rashness and precipitancy; and not to be subject to error. To these things then, let the mind apply herself and go straight on, without any distraction about other things, and she hath her end, and by consequent her happiness.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.greek: Τὸ μὲν πνευμάτιόν σου καὶ τὸ πυρῶδες πᾶν, ὅσον ἐγκέκραται, καίτοι φύσει ἀνωφερῆ ὄντα, ὅμως πειθόμενα τῇ τῶν ὅλων διατάξει παρακρατεῖται ἐνταῦθα ἐπὶ τοῦ συγκρίματος. καὶ τὸ γεῶδες δὲ τὸ ἐν σοὶ πᾶν καὶ τὸ ὑγρόν, καίτοι κατωφερῆ ὄντα, ὅμως ἐγήγερται καὶ ἕστηκε τὴν οὐχ ἑαυτῶν φυσικὴν στάσιν. οὕτως ἄρα καὶ τὰ στοιχεῖα ὑπακούει τοῖς ὅλοις, ἐπειδάν που καταταχθῇ σὺν βίᾳ, μένοντα μέχρις ἂν ἐκεῖθεν πάλιν τὸ ἐνδόσιμον τῆς διαλύσεως σημήνῃ. οὐ δεινὸν οὖν μόνον τὸ νοερόν σου μέρος ἀπειθὲς εἶναι καὶ ἀγανακτεῖν τῇ ἑαυτοῦ χώρᾳ; καίτοι οὐδέν γε βίαιον τούτῳ ἐπιτάσσεται, ἀλλὰ μόνα ὅσα κατὰ φύσιν ἐστὶν αὐτῷ· οὐ μέντοι ἀνέχεται, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐναντίαν φέρεται. ἡ γὰρ ἐπὶ τὰ ἀδικήματα καὶ τὰ ἀκολαστήματα καὶ τὰς ὀργὰς καὶ τὰς λύπας καὶ τοὺς φόβους κίνησις οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ ἀφισταμένου τῆς φύσεως. καὶ ὅταν δέ τινι τῶν συμβαινόντων δυσχεραίνῃ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, καταλείπει καὶ τότε τὴν ἑαυτοῦ χώραν· πρὸς ὁσιότητα γὰρ καὶ θεοσέβειαν κατεσκεύασται οὐχ ἧττον ἢ πρὸς δικαιοσύνην. καὶ γὰρ ταῦτα ἐν εἴδει ἐστὶ τῆς εὐκοινωνησίας, μᾶλλον δὲ πρεσβύτερα τῶν δικαιοπραγημάτων.
passages.english: Your bit of breath and all the fiery part that is mixed into you, though by nature they tend upwards, all the same obey the ordering of the whole and are held here in the compound. And all the earthy part in you, and the wet, though they tend downwards, have all the same been raised up and stand in a position that is not naturally theirs. So even the elements heed the whole: once they have been posted somewhere by force, they stay until, from there in turn, the signal for dissolution is given. Is it not terrible, then, that only the part of you that is of mind is disobedient and resents its own post? And yet nothing forced is ordered of it, only the things that are in accordance with its nature. Still it does not bear them, but is carried the opposite way. For the movement towards acts of injustice and acts of self-indulgence, towards angers and griefs and fears, is nothing other than the movement of one who is deserting nature. And whenever the ruling part is discontented with any of the things that happen, then too it leaves its own post. For it has been made for holiness and reverence for the gods no less than for justice. For these too come under good fellowship, or rather they come before acts of justice.

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for breath or air, one of the four elements in the body here. The diminutive is slightly belittling.
notes.other_reading: Your little portion of air

notes.note: The Greek has a plural, “the wholes”, Marcus’s usual phrase for the universe, rendered “the whole” throughout. The noun means an arrangement and is used of troops drawn up; “ordering” is meant to carry both arranging and commanding, since “posted” and “ordered” further on are from the same root.
notes.other_reading: the arrangement of the universe

notes.note: “The compound” is the body seen as a mixture of the elements.
notes.other_reading: here in the mixture that is you

notes.note: A different verb from “obey” in the first sentence: literally “listen to”, “answer a call”. “Heed” keeps it apart from “obey” and “disobedient”, the pair the argument runs on.
notes.other_reading: So even the elements obey the whole

notes.note: The verb is a military one, “to be posted”. “By force” can go with being posted, as the edition punctuates, or with staying.
notes.other_reading: once they have been posted somewhere, they stay there under force until

notes.greek: ἐκεῖθεν πάλιν τὸ ἐνδόσιμον τῆς διαλύσεως σημήνῃ
notes.note: The noun is the note given to start a song or a movement, a cue. “From there” is from the whole that posted them, and the adverb is taken as “in turn” (the order that posted them is answered by one that breaks them up), not as “a second time”. The verb has no stated subject.
notes.other_reading: until from there the cue is given for them to be dissolved back again

notes.note: The adjective is built on the Greek noun for mind. “Of mind” is the wording kept for it throughout the translation.
notes.other_reading: only the intelligent part of you

notes.note: The word means “place”, and also a soldier’s station. “Post” is taken because of the military verbs around it, and kept for the second occurrence.
notes.other_reading: resents its own place

notes.note: Literally “of one standing away from nature”. The verb is used of rebels and deserters, and that sense is taken.
notes.other_reading: of one who is withdrawing from nature

notes.note: A compound, “god-reverence”, that does not say whether one god or many is meant. The plural is taken, as in “the eldest of the gods” in 9.1.
notes.other_reading: reverence for god

notes.note: Literally “are in the form of good fellowship”, that is, are a kind of it. The noun is very rare; it is built on the root of the word rendered “social” elsewhere.
notes.other_reading: For these too are a kind of good fellowship

notes.note: Literally “older than”, which in Greek also means higher in rank or more to be honoured. “Come before” is meant to allow both.
notes.other_reading: or rather they are older than acts of justice
