Nature is named as the one acting, which the run of the sentence requires, while “this craft” is kept because the Greek says “this”, not “nature’s”. “Its own” before “boundary” is dropped, since the Greek has only “itself”.

check.note: The comparative is dropped: “what is more decayed”, “the rather rotten parts”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “what is too rotten”, which gives the comparative. “Rotten” is kept instead of “decayed” so that this word stays apart from “decaying”, which renders a different Greek verb earlier in the sentence.

passages.casaubon: Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way? avoid them. Let this suffice. Add not presently speaking unto thyself, What serve these things for in the world? For, this, one that is acquainted with the mysteries of nature, will laugh at thee for it; as a carpenter would or a shoemaker, if meeting in either of their shops with some shavings, or small remnants of their work, thou shouldest blame them for it. And yet those men, it is not for want of a place where to throw them that they keep them in their shops for a while: but the nature of the universe hath no such out-place; but herein doth consist the wonder of her art and skill, that she having once circumscribed herself within some certain bounds and limits, whatsoever is within her that seems either corrupted, or old, or unprofitable, she can change it into herself, and of these very things can make new things; so that she needeth not to seek elsewhere out of herself either for a new supply of matter and substance, or for a place where to throw out whatsoever is irrecoverably putrid and corrupt. Thus she, as for place, so for matter and art, is herself sufficient unto herself.

passages.greek: Φέρει καρπὸν καὶ ἄνθρωπος καὶ θεὸς καὶ ὁ κόσμος· ἐν ταῖς οἰκείαις ὥραις ἕκαστα φέρει. εἰ δὲ ἡ συνήθεια κυρίως τέτριφεν ἐπὶ ἀμπέλου καὶ τῶν ὁμοίων, οὐδὲν τοῦτο. ὁ λόγος δὲ καὶ κοινὸν καὶ ἴδιον καρπὸν ἔχει καὶ γίνεται ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοιαῦθ’ ἕτερα, ὁποῖόν τι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ λόγος.
passages.english: A human being bears fruit, and so does god, and so does the universe; each bears it in its own seasons. But if usage has made the phrase well worn, in its strict sense, for the vine and things like it, that makes no difference. And reason has fruit, both shared and its own, and from it come other things of much the same kind as reason itself.

notes.note: No article: “god” or “a god”. The English reads “god” with a small letter and no article.
notes.other_reading: and so does a god

notes.note: The verb is the one for rubbing a thing smooth by use, and of words it means making them well worn, current. The Greek gives it no object; the English supplies “the phrase”, that is, “bear fruit”. κυρίως is taken as “in the proper, strict sense”; it can also mean “chiefly”.
notes.other_reading: But if usage has chiefly worn the phrase in on the vine and things like it

notes.note: Literally “this is nothing”.
notes.other_reading: that is nothing

notes.note: λόγος is “reason” but also “speech, word, account”. The English takes “reason”, as the thing that bears fruit in a human being; the sentence may also glance at “speech” after the remark on usage.
notes.other_reading: And speech has fruit

notes.note: “Fruit both common and private”: fruit shared with everyone and fruit that belongs to reason itself. The Greek does not say more.
notes.other_reading: fruit both for all in common and for itself

notes.greek: τοιαῦθ’ ἕτερα, ὁποῖόν τι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ λόγος
notes.note: “Other things of some such kind as reason itself is”: what reason produces is like reason, as fruit is like the plant. The small word τι loosens the likeness a little, which “much the same” gives.
notes.other_reading: and what grows from it is more of the same sort of thing as reason itself

check.greek: εἰ δὲ ἡ συνήθεια κυρίως τέτριφεν ἐπὶ ἀμπέλου καὶ τῶν ὁμοίων
check.note: τέτριφεν is “has made habitual by use”, applied to the vine, and κυρίως says this is where the word has its proper sense. “Worn the phrase down to its strict sense” turns this into erosion and makes the strict sense a result; δέ (“but”) is also dropped.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “But if usage has made the phrase well worn, in its strict sense, for the vine and things like it”. “But” is restored and the strict sense is no longer a result of the wearing. “Well worn” is used instead of “kept”, because the verb is about a word made familiar by rubbing, not about a word reserved.

check.greek: ὁ λόγος δὲ καὶ κοινὸν καὶ ἴδιον καρπὸν ἔχει
check.note: The first καί is the partner of the second (“both shared and its own”), which the English also translates as “both”. So καί is used twice and “too” has nothing to stand on.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And reason has fruit, both shared and its own”. “Too” is gone, and “And” gives δέ.

check.note: “Common” beside “fruit” reads today as “ordinary”. The pair is shared with all against private to itself.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “both shared and its own”.

check.note: One Greek word (οἰκείαις) is given twice, as “own” and “proper”, and “proper” in this sense is dated.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in its own seasons”.

check.greek: ὁποῖόν τι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ λόγος
check.note: τι softens the likeness: “of much the same kind”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “of much the same kind as reason itself”.

passages.casaubon: Man, God, the world, every one in their kind, bear some fruits. All things have their proper time to bear. Though by custom, the word itself is in a manner become proper unto the vine, and the like, yet is it so nevertheless, as we have said. As for reason, that beareth both common fruit for the use of others; and peculiar, which itself doth enjoy. Reason is of a diffusive nature, what itself is in itself, it begets in others, and so doth multiply.

passages.greek: Δεῖ κατὰ λέξιν παρακολουθεῖν τοῖς λεγομένοις καὶ καθ’ ἑκάστην ὁρμὴν τοῖς γινομένοις, καὶ ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ ἑτέρου εὐθὺς ὁρᾶν ἐπὶ τίνα σκοπὸν ἡ ἀναφορά, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ ἑτέρου παραφυλάσσειν τί τὸ σημαινόμενον.
passages.english: One must follow what is said word by word, and what is done impulse by impulse; and in the latter case see at once what aim it is directed at, and in the former watch closely for what is meant.

notes.note: “Word by word” or “phrase by phrase”: λέξις is a single expression. It is matched by “at each impulse” for actions; ὁρμή, “impulse”, is the Stoic term for the movement of the mind toward doing something.
notes.other_reading: follow what is said expression by expression

notes.note: Literally “the things that happen” or “come about”. Paired with “impulse” and set against “what is said”, it is taken as “what is done”.
notes.other_reading: and what happens, at each impulse

notes.note: The Greek says only “in the one case, in the other”, without saying which is which. The sense shows that the order is crossed: the aim belongs to what is done, and what is meant belongs to what is said. The English says “latter” and “former” so that a reader does not pair them the wrong way.
notes.other_reading: and in the one case see at once what aim it is directed at, and in the other watch closely for what is meant

notes.note: “The reference”: what the action is referred to as its goal. There is no verb; the English supplies “is directed”.
notes.other_reading: to what target the reference is

check.greek: ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ ἑτέρου εὐθὺς ὁρᾶν ἐπὶ τίνα σκοπὸν ἡ ἀναφορά, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ ἑτέρου παραφυλάσσειν τί τὸ σημαινόμενον
check.note: The Greek says “in the one, in the other” without saying which is which, and the sense shows the order is crossed: the aim belongs to actions, what is signified to words. In English “the one, the other” is normally read as former and latter, which gives the reverse of the sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in the latter case see at once what aim it is directed at, and in the former watch closely for what is meant”. The order of the Greek is kept and nothing is named that the Greek does not name; the note records that the Greek has only “the one” and “the other”.

check.note: γινόμενα is “what happens, what is going on”; “what is done” narrows it to actions. With “at each impulse” the narrowing is probably right, but it is a choice.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “what is done”. The word is tied to “at each impulse”, and an impulse in the Stoic sense is a movement toward acting, so what comes about impulse by impulse is action. The note gives “what happens”.

passages.casaubon: Word after word, every one by itself, must the things that are spoken be conceived and understood; and so the things that are done, purpose after purpose, every one by itself likewise. And as in matter of purposes and actions, we must presently see what is the proper use and relation of every one; so of words must we be as ready, to consider of every one what is the true meaning, and signification of it according to truth and nature, however it be taken in common use.

nearest.title: Being good for its own sake

passages.greek: Πρῶτον αἱ τραγῳδίαι παρήχθησαν ὑπομνηστικαὶ τῶν συμβαινόντων καὶ ὅτι ταῦτα οὕτως πέφυκε γίνεσθαι καὶ ὅτι, οἷς ἐπὶ τῆς σκηνῆς ψυχαγωγεῖσθε, τούτοις μὴ ἄχθεσθε ἐπὶ τῆς μείζονος σκηνῆς· ὁρᾶτε γὰρ ὅτι οὕτως δεῖ ταῦτα περαίνεσθαι καὶ ὅτι φέρουσιν αὐτὰ καὶ οἱ κεκραγότες· ʽἰὼ Κιθαιρών.ʼ καὶ λέγεται δέ τινα ὑπὸ τῶν τὰ δράματα ποιούντων χρησίμως· οἷόν ἐστιν ἐκεῖνο μάλιστα· εἰ δ’ ἠμελήθην ἐκ θεῶν καὶ παῖδ’ ἐμώ, ἔχει λόγον καὶ τοῦτο· καὶ πάλιν· τοῖς πράγμασιν γὰρ οὐχὶ θυμοῦσθαι· καί· βίον θερίζειν ὥστε κάρπιμον στάχυν· καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα. μετὰ δὲ τὴν τραγῳδίαν ἡ ἀρχαία κωμῳδία παρήχθη, παιδαγωγικὴν παρρησίαν ἔχουσα καὶ τῆς ἀτυφίας οὐκ ἀχρήστως δι’ αὐτῆς τῆς εὐθυρρημοσύνης ὑπομιμνῄσκουσα· πρὸς οἷόν τι καὶ Διογένης ταυτὶ παρελάμβανε. μετὰ ταύτην ἡ μέση κωμῳδία καὶ λοιπὸν ἡ νέα πρὸς τί ποτε παρείληπται, ἣ κατ’ ὀλίγον ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκ μιμήσεως φιλοτεχνίαν ὑπερρύη, ἐπίστησον. ὅτι μὲν γὰρ λέγεται καὶ ὑπὸ τούτων τινὰ χρήσιμα οὐκ ἀγνοεῖται, ἀλλὰ ἡ ὅλη ἐπιβολὴ τῆς τοιαύτης ποιήσεως καὶ δραματουργίας πρὸς τίνα ποτὲ σκοπὸν ἀπέβλεψεν;
passages.english: First, tragedies were brought on as reminders of the things that happen, and that it is in the nature of these things to happen this way, and that what charms you on the stage should not weigh on you on the larger stage. For you see that these things have to be carried through this way, and that even those who cry out “O Cithaeron!” bear them. And some things are said usefully by those who write the plays. This above all, for example: “But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.” And again: “For one should not be angry with events.” And: “To reap life like a fruitful ear of grain.” And everything of that kind. After tragedy, the Old Comedy was brought on. It had a tutor’s frankness and, by its very plainness of speech, reminded people, not uselessly, of freedom from conceit. It was for some such purpose that Diogenes too took these things up. As for the Middle Comedy after it, and lastly the New, which little by little slipped down into cleverness at imitation, consider just what it has been taken up for. For it is not unknown that some useful things are said by these writers too; but the whole undertaking of this kind of poetry and play-making, just what aim did it look to?

notes.note: “Were brought forward, introduced”; the verb is also the ordinary one for bringing something on stage. “Brought on” is used here and for the Old Comedy, where the verb is repeated. “First” could also be read as “at first, originally”.
notes.other_reading: Tragedies were first introduced as reminders

notes.note: The Greek slips into a direct command to an audience in the plural: “do not be weighed down by these things”. The English turns it into “should not weigh on you” so that the sentence runs on. ψυχαγωγεῖσθε before it is literally “you have your souls led”, said of being entertained.
notes.other_reading: and that: “what entertains you on the stage, do not be vexed by on the larger stage”

notes.note: The form can be “you see” or the command “see”. With “for” it is taken as a statement.
notes.other_reading: For see that these things have to be carried through this way

notes.note: “To be carried through, completed”; the word suits both a plot and events in life. “To their end” is not added, since in English it would be heard as dying.
notes.other_reading: that this is how these things must be accomplished

notes.note: The cry of Oedipus in Sophocles’ Oedipus the King, addressed to Mount Cithaeron, where he was left to die as a baby (from memory, unchecked). ἰώ is a cry of grief.
notes.other_reading: “Alas, Cithaeron!”

notes.note: “This too has a reason”, or “this too makes sense”. The line and the two that follow are verse quotations, all three thought to be from lost plays of Euripides (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: this too is reasonable

notes.note: A dual: “my two children”. The form does not say whether they are sons.
notes.other_reading: I and my two sons

notes.note: As quoted, the line is a bare infinitive, “for not to be angry with things”, and stops before the word that governs it. The full verse is thought to end with a word for “one must” (from memory, unchecked), so “one should” in the English is supplied. πράγματα is “things, affairs, circumstances”.
notes.other_reading: “For to be angry with things is not ...”

notes.note: Again an infinitive cut loose from its sentence; in the original it probably said that life must be reaped. ὥστε is the poetic “like”. κάρπιμον is “bearing fruit”.
notes.other_reading: “that life is harvested like a ripe ear of grain”

notes.note: παρρησία is saying everything openly: frankness, outspokenness. The adjective is from παιδαγωγός, the attendant who minded a boy and corrected his behaviour, so the sense is frankness that disciplines and teaches.
notes.other_reading: an educating outspokenness

notes.note: “Absence of τῦφος”, the smoke of vanity and self-importance: so modesty, freedom from conceit. The comedy is said to remind people of this quality.
notes.other_reading: reminding people of modesty

notes.greek: πρὸς οἷόν τι καὶ Διογένης ταυτὶ παρελάμβανε
notes.note: Diogenes is the Cynic philosopher, known for blunt speech. “These things” is vague: probably this manner of plain speaking, possibly actual lines or devices of comedy. The verb is the same one used just after of comedy being “taken up”, so “took up” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: With some such end in view Diogenes too adopted this sort of thing

notes.greek: μετὰ ταύτην ἡ μέση κωμῳδία καὶ λοιπὸν ἡ νέα πρὸς τί ποτε παρείληπται
notes.note: “After it” belongs to the Middle Comedy, which came after the Old, as “after tragedy” does above. The verb is singular and treats the Middle and the New as one thing. ποτε sharpens the question, here and in the last sentence; “just what” gives it in both places.
notes.other_reading: After this, consider whatever the Middle Comedy, and lastly the New, has been taken up for

notes.greek: ἣ κατ’ ὀλίγον ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκ μιμήσεως φιλοτεχνίαν ὑπερρύη
notes.note: The verb is “slid, sank gradually”. φιλοτεχνία is love of craft, and so ingenuity or clever workmanship; “from imitation” says that the cleverness lies in lifelike representation. “Which” most naturally refers to the New Comedy, the nearest noun, but can be read of this later comedy as a whole.
notes.other_reading: comedy which by degrees sank into a love of craft in mimicry

notes.note: ἐπιβολή is a setting oneself to something: design, attempt, undertaking. σκοπός at the end is a mark aimed at; the English reads “aim”.
notes.other_reading: the whole design of this kind of poetry and play-making

check.note: As given, the quotation is a bare infinitive with no governing word, and “one should” supplies it. From memory the verse ends with a word for “one must”, but that word is not in the text supplied.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “For one should not be angry with events”, since a bare “for not to be angry” cannot be read as English, and the note now says outright that “one should” is supplied and that the fuller verse is recalled from memory, unchecked.

check.note: μετὰ ταύτην is “after it”, after the Old Comedy, and belongs to the Middle Comedy’s coming, parallel to “after tragedy” above. Placed before “consider” it reads as an instruction about the order of thinking.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “As for the Middle Comedy after it, and lastly the New, ... consider just what it has been taken up for”, so that “after it” belongs to the Middle Comedy.

check.greek: καὶ λοιπὸν ἡ νέα πρὸς τί ποτε παρείληπται, ἣ
check.note: The relative ἥ has no noun repeated in the Greek. It is nearest to the New Comedy but can be read of this later comedy as a whole; the English repeated “the New” and so settled the question in the text.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “the New” is no longer repeated, and the English reads “and lastly the New, which little by little slipped down”. The clause stands next to “the New” because that is the nearest noun in the Greek too, and the note gives the wider reading.

check.note: “A love of craft in imitation” is hard to follow as English. φιλοτεχνία is ingenuity or showy workmanship, and ἐκ μιμήσεως says it comes from, or consists in, imitation.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “slipped down into cleverness at imitation”. “Mere” is not added, because the Greek has no word for it; the fall is already in the verb. The note gives the literal “love of craft”.

check.note: ποτε is dropped here, though the same particle is kept as “ever” in the last sentence. The perfect is “has been taken up”, against the past tenses used of tragedy and the Old Comedy.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “consider just what it has been taken up for”, with the perfect tense. The last sentence now reads “just what aim did it look to?”, so one English phrase answers the one Greek particle in both places.

check.note: The dual is “my two children”; sons or not is not said in the words given.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “my two children”. A note gives “my two sons”.

check.note: παρρησία here is outspokenness, saying things straight, as the next clause shows. “Freedom of speech” today means a civil right; “a tutor’s” is acceptable for the adjective.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a tutor’s frankness”. “Tutor” is kept instead of “schoolmaster”, because the Greek word names the attendant who minded and corrected one boy, not the teacher of a class.

check.note: Found while settling: the quoted verse begins with δέ (“but”), which the draft left out, though it kept the “for” at the head of the next quotation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.”

passages.casaubon: Tragedies were at first brought in and instituted, to put men in mind of worldly chances and casualties: that these things in the ordinary course of nature did so happen: that men that were much pleased and delighted by such accidents upon this stage, would not by the same things in a greater stage be grieved and afflicted: for here you see what is the end of all such things; and that even they that cry out so mournfully to Cithaeron, must bear them for all their cries and exclamations, as well as others. And in very truth many good things are spoken by these poets; as that (for example) is an excellent passage: 'But if so be that I and my two children be neglected by the Gods, they have some reason even for that,' &c. And again, 'It will but little avail thee to storm and rage against the things themselves,' &c. Again, 'To reap one's life, as a ripe ear of corn;' and whatsoever else is to be found in them, that is of the same kind. After the tragedy, the ancient comedy was brought in, which had the liberty to inveigh against personal vices; being therefore through this her freedom and liberty of speech of very good use and effect, to restrain men from pride and arrogancy. To which end it was, that Diogenes took also the same liberty. After these, what were either the Middle, or New Comedy admitted for, but merely, (Or for the most part at least) for the delight and pleasure of curious and excellent imitation? 'It will steal away; look to it,' &c. Why, no man denies, but that these also have some good things whereof that may be one: but the whole drift and foundation of that kind of dramatical poetry, what is it else, but as we have said?

passages.greek: ʽἘρᾷ μὲν ὄμβρου γαῖα, ἐρᾷ δὲ ὁ σεμνὸς αἰθήρ,ʼ ἐρᾷ δὲ ὁ κόσμος ποιῆσαι ὃ ἂν μέλλῃ γίνεσθαι. λέγω οὖν τῷ κόσμῳ ὅτι σοὶ συνερῶ. μήτι δὲ οὕτω κἀκεῖνο λέγεται, ὅτι· φιλεῖ τοῦτο γίνεσθαι;
passages.english: “The earth loves the rain, and the holy sky loves,” and the universe loves to bring about whatever is to come. So I say to the universe: “I love along with you.” And is that, too, perhaps said in this sense: “this loves to happen”?

notes.note: The quoted line of verse stops here without saying what the sky loves. The English leaves it just as bare.
notes.other_reading: and the holy sky loves it too

notes.note: αἰθήρ is the bright upper air or heaven; σεμνός is “revered”, “holy”, “majestic”.
notes.other_reading: the majestic heaven

notes.note: The poet’s words end before this; from here Marcus speaks, reusing the poet’s verb. It is the verb of being in love and of strong desire. “Loves” is used for it throughout so that the last sentence can be heard.
notes.other_reading: and the universe longs to bring about

notes.note: The word means both the universe and its order. 'Universe' is used here and in 4.23.
notes.other_reading: the world

notes.note: The verb can mean simply “is about to” or “is destined to”. The plain future sense is translated.
notes.other_reading: whatever is destined to happen

notes.note: One compound verb, “I love together with you”; no object is given, so what is loved is left to the context.
notes.other_reading: I long along with you

notes.note: The particle μήτι usually opens a question expecting “no” (as in 6.43), but it can also float a tentative suggestion. It is taken as a suggestion here, since the sentence completes the thought.
notes.other_reading: Surely that, too, is not said in this sense: “this loves to happen”?

notes.note: An everyday Greek idiom: “loves to happen” means “tends to happen, usually happens”. The literal “loves” is kept because Marcus’s point depends on hearing the love in it. It is a different Greek verb from the “loves” of the lines above.
notes.other_reading: This tends to happen

check.note: φιλεῖ with an infinitive is the everyday Greek idiom for 'this tends to happen, this usually happens'. Marcus's point is that the ordinary idiom literally says 'loves'; the English gives only the literal half, and since 'this loves to happen' is not an English saying, the reader cannot see that a common phrase is being reread.
check.decided: Kept the literal “loves” and explained the idiom in a note; the English cannot carry both senses in the words alone.

check.note: ἐρᾷ is the verb of being in love and desiring passionately, and the whole passage is a chain of love words ending in φιλεῖ ('loves'). English switches from 'longs' (four times) to 'loves' at the last step, so the link that makes the final question follow is cut exactly at the punchline.
check.decided: Accepted. “Loves” throughout, so the last question follows from the first line.

check.note: μήτι normally marks a question expecting 'no' (as it does twice in 6.43); here the English reads it as a tentative 'perhaps', leaning toward yes. The sense of the passage supports that, but it is a choice, and the same particle is rendered two different ways in this set without any signal.
check.decided: Kept as a tentative question (“perhaps”); the reading that expects “no” is in the notes. In 6.43 the same particle is translated as expecting “no”.

check.note: 'other' and 'saying' have no Greek behind them (κἀκεῖνο is just 'that too'), and λέγεται is 'is said', not 'is meant'. 'That other saying' also implies that what came before was a saying of the same kind.
check.decided: Accepted: “And is that, too, perhaps said in this sense”.

check.note: σεμνός is 'revered, august, holy'; 'solemn' in current English leans toward 'grave, unsmiling'. αἰθήρ is specifically the bright upper air or heaven; 'sky' is acceptable but flatter. Note also that the quotation is cut off with no object for the second 'loves', which the English rightly keeps.
check.decided: Changed to “holy”; “majestic” is in the notes.

check.note: ποιῆσαι is 'do / make / bring about'; 'to make whatever is going to happen' is odd English ('make' wants an object that is a thing, not an event). μέλλῃ can be plain future ('is going to') or 'is destined to'; the English picks the plain future.
check.decided: Accepted: “to bring about whatever is to come”.

check.note: 'long along' is an accidental jingle. Formally συνερῶ could also be a future 'I will speak with you / on your side', which would pick up λέγω; the run of ἐρᾷ before it settles the sense as 'love with', so this is only a possible undertone.
check.decided: Accepted: “I love along with you”.

passages.casaubon: The earth, saith the poet, doth often long after the rain. So is the glorious sky often as desirous to fall upon the earth, which argues a mutual kind of love between them. And so (say I) doth the world bear a certain affection of love to whatsoever shall come to pass With thine affections shall mine concur, O world. The same (and no other) shall the object of my longing be which is of thine. Now that the world doth love it is true indeed so is it as commonly said, and acknowledged ledged, when, according to the Greek phrase, imitated by the Latins, of things that used to be, we say commonly, that they love to be.

nearest.title: What the whole sends in its season

passages.greek: Πᾶν μοι συναρμόζει ὃ σοὶ εὐάρμοστόν ἐστιν, ὦ κόσμε· οὐδέν μοι πρόωρον οὐδὲ ὄψιμον ὃ σοὶ εὔκαιρον. πᾶν μοι καρπὸς ὃ φέρουσιν αἱ σαὶ ὧραι, ὦ φύσις· ἐκ σοῦ πάντα, ἐν σοὶ πάντα, εἰς σὲ πάντα. ἐκεῖνος μέν φησιν· ʽὦ πόλι φίλη Κέκροπος·ʼ σὺ δὲ οὐκ ἐρεῖς· ʽὦ πόλι φίλη Διός;ʼ
passages.english: Universe, everything that fits well with you fits well with me. Nothing that is timely for you is too early or too late for me. Nature, everything your seasons bear is fruit to me. All things from you, all things in you, all things into you. One man says, “Dear city of Cecrops.” But you, will you not say, “Dear city of Zeus”?

notes.greek: Πᾶν μοι συναρμόζει ὃ σοὶ εὐάρμοστόν ἐστιν
notes.note: Both words come from the root for fitting together, which covers a carpenter's joint and a musical tuning. I chose 'fits'.
notes.other_reading: Everything that is in tune with you is in tune with me

notes.note: Universe, or world, or the ordered whole; the same choice as in 10.21.
notes.other_reading: world

notes.greek: οὐδέν μοι πρόωρον οὐδὲ ὄψιμον ὃ σοὶ εὔκαιρον
notes.note: The words for “too early” and “too late” are also used of crops that come before or after their season, which leads into the fruit of the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: Nothing that is timely for you is unripe or overdue for me

notes.note: The word means seasons and also hours or times in general. 'Seasons' goes with the fruit.
notes.other_reading: your hours

notes.greek: ἐκ σοῦ πάντα, ἐν σοὶ πάντα, εἰς σὲ πάντα
notes.note: The Greek has no verbs, only “out of you”, “in you”, “into you”. None is supplied.
notes.other_reading: All things come from you, exist in you and go back into you

notes.note: The speaker is not named, only pointed to as 'that one'; the words quoted look like a line of verse. Cecrops was the legendary first king of Athens, so his city is Athens.
notes.other_reading: The poet says

notes.note: 'Dear' can go with 'city' (dear city, belonging to Cecrops) or with the name (city dear to Cecrops). The same holds for the phrase about Zeus that copies it.
notes.other_reading: O city dear to Cecrops ... O city dear to Zeus

notes.note: Up to here 'you' was the universe and then nature. This 'you' is set against 'that man' and is most naturally Marcus speaking to himself; the Greek does not say so, and does not say what the city of Zeus is. The question expects the answer yes.

check.greek: ἐκ σοῦ πάντα, ἐν σοὶ πάντα, εἰς σὲ πάντα
check.note: The Greek has no verb at all: three bare prepositional phrases, 'out of you, in you, into you'. English supplies 'come', 'are' and 'go', and 'to you' is weaker than εἰς, which is 'into'.
check.decided: Accepted: no verbs supplied, and “into you”.

check.greek: πρόωρον οὐδὲ ὄψιμον ὃ σοὶ εὔκαιρον
check.note: πρόωρον ('before its season', same root as ὧραι, 'seasons', in the next sentence) and ὄψιμον ('late in the season', used of crops and rain) are farming words that prepare the fruit image; 'too early or too late' is clock language and the link is lost. 'In good time' in English can also mean 'eventually' or 'with time to spare'; εὔκαιρον is 'timely, at the right moment'.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “timely” for εὔκαιρον. “Too early or too late” is kept as the plain sense; the crop sense is in the notes.

check.note: With καρπός the verb φέρειν is the regular word for 'bear' (fruit). 'Bring' is the other live sense and is not wrong, but it drops the idiom the image rests on.
check.decided: Accepted: “bear”.

check.note: The ἁρμ- words mean both 'fitted together' (joinery) and 'in tune, harmonious' (music). English keeps the repeated root, which is good, but picks the joinery sense only.
check.decided: No change. The word also means “in tune”; a reader should know both senses are there.

check.note: Up to this point 'you' has been the universe and nature; here σύ is the writer turning on himself (or the reader), set against ἐκεῖνος. The Greek makes the same unannounced switch, but δέ is contrastive ('but you'), and 'And you' lets an English reader think nature is still being addressed. οὐκ expecting 'yes' and the future tense are rendered correctly.
check.decided: Accepted: “But you”.

check.note: ἐκεῖνος is 'that one', often 'the well-known one'; it introduces a quoted line of verse. 'That man' sounds dismissive in English and gives the reader no hint that a poet's line is being quoted. The Greek does not say 'poet', so that word could only go in a note.
check.decided: Changed to “One man says”. That the words are a line of verse is in the notes; the Greek does not say “poet”.

check.note: The contrast is Athens (city of its legendary king Cecrops) against the world as the city of Zeus. A modern reader with no Greek will not know Cecrops, so the point of the last two sentences is invisible without a note.
check.decided: The name is kept without a gloss inside the translation; the note says the city is Athens.

check.note: Both addresses are marked in Greek with ὦ. A bare lower-case 'universe' and 'nature' tacked on after a comma reads awkwardly and is easy to misread as part of the sentence rather than as the one spoken to.
check.decided: Accepted: “Universe,” and “Nature,” now open their sentences.

check.greek: ἐκ σοῦ πάντα, ἐν σοὶ πάντα, εἰς σὲ πάντα
check.note: A question for the article: do these words say that all things work or tend toward one end?
check.decided: No. Three phrases without a verb: out of you, in you, into you. That is origin, containment and destination. Working together toward the same thing is said in 6.43, not here. The “you” is nature.

passages.casaubon: Whatsoever is expedient unto thee, O World, is expedient unto me; nothing can either be 'unseasonable unto me, or out of date, which unto thee is seasonable. Whatsoever thy seasons bear, shall ever by me be esteemed as happy fruit, and increase. O Nature! from thee are all things, in thee all things subsist, and to thee all tend. Could he say of Athens, Thou lovely city of Cecrops; and shalt not thou say of the world, Thou lovely city of God?

nearest.title: What the whole sends in its season

passages.greek: Μήτι ὁ ἥλιος τὰ τοῦ ὑετοῦ ἀξιοῖ ποιεῖν; μήτι ὁ Ἀσκληπιὸς τὰ τῆς Καρποφόρου; τί δὲ τῶν ἄστρων ἕκαστον; οὐχὶ διάφορα μέν, συνεργὰ δὲ πρὸς ταὐτόν;
passages.english: Surely the sun does not think it should do the rain’s part? Or Asclepius the part of the fruit-bearing goddess? And what of each of the stars? Are they not different, yet working together toward the same thing?

notes.note: This particle marks a question expecting the answer no, here and in the next question; “Surely … not” carries that.
notes.other_reading: Does the sun think it should do the rain’s part?

notes.note: The verb ranges from “thinks it right” and “sees fit” to “claims” and “demands”.
notes.other_reading: Surely the sun does not claim the rain’s part?

notes.note: Literally “the things of the rain”: what belongs to the rain to do.
notes.other_reading: the rain’s work

notes.note: “The Fruit-Bearer” (feminine) is a title of a goddess of crops, usually Demeter, sometimes Earth. Asclepius is the god of healing.
notes.other_reading: the part of Demeter, bringer of crops

notes.note: The question has no verb: literally 'and what each of the stars?'
notes.other_reading: And what does each of the stars do?

notes.greek: οὐχὶ διάφορα μέν, συνεργὰ δὲ πρὸς ταὐτόν;
notes.note: The adjectives are neuter plural and may describe the stars alone or everything just named (sun, rain, the two gods, the stars). The Greek also does not say what 'the same thing' is.
notes.other_reading: Are all these not different, yet working together toward the same end?

check.note: μήτι marks a question that expects the answer 'no'. The English questions are neutral, so the expected 'of course not' is left for the reader to guess; the next question (οὐχί, expecting 'yes') is rendered with its expectation, which makes the unevenness visible.
check.decided: Accepted: “Surely … not”.

check.note: ἀξιοῖ is 'think it right, think oneself entitled, expect, demand'. 'Claim' picks the 'demand as one's due' sense, but in English 'claim to do' also means 'assert that one does', which is not in the Greek.
check.decided: Changed to “think it should do”.

check.greek: μήτι ὁ Ἀσκληπιὸς τὰ τῆς Καρποφόρου
check.note: The Greek does not repeat the verb; it is carried over whole from the first question ('claim to do'). English repeats 'claim' but drops 'to do', so the second question becomes 'lay claim to the work', a slightly different construction from the first.
check.decided: Accepted: “Or Asclepius the part of …”, with the verb carried over as in the Greek.

check.note: The article is feminine: this is a goddess's title (the giver of crops, Demeter or the Earth), set beside the god Asclepius. English loses the gender, and a reader with no Greek cannot tell that a goddess is meant or which one.
check.decided: Accepted: “the fruit-bearing goddess”.

check.note: Greek says only 'the things of the rain' (its business, its part). 'Work' is supplied, twice, which builds a work / work / working-together echo that in the Greek exists only in συνεργά.
check.decided: Accepted: “the rain’s part”. “Working together” now translates only συνεργά.

check.greek: οὐχὶ διάφορα μέν, συνεργὰ δὲ πρὸς ταὐτόν
check.note: 'They' and 'thing' are supplied. The neuter plurals can describe the stars just mentioned or everything named in the passage, and the English 'they' is equally open, which is fair; πρὸς ταὐτόν is 'toward the same', where 'the same end' is the other natural filling.
check.decided: No change; the English “they” and “thing” are as open as the Greek.

passages.casaubon: Doth either the sun take upon him to do that which belongs to the rain? or his son Aesculapius that, which unto the earth doth properly belong? How is it with every one of the stars in particular? Though they all differ one from another, and have their several charges and functions by themselves, do they not all nevertheless concur and co-operate to one end?

nearest.title: What the whole sends in its season

passages.greek: Συμφέρει ἑκάστῳ ὃ φέρει ἑκάστῳ ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις, καὶ τότε συμφέρει ὅτε ἐκείνη φέρει.
passages.english: What the nature of the whole brings to each is good for each, and it is good at the time when nature brings it.

notes.note: A play on words: “brings” (φέρει) and “is good for”, literally “brings together” (συμφέρει), which means to benefit or be to the advantage of. English cannot keep the echo, so the sense is kept.
notes.other_reading: What the nature of the whole brings to each benefits each

notes.note: The form can be masculine or neuter: each person or each thing. “Each” leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: to each thing

notes.note: Literally “the nature of the wholes”, a set phrase for the nature of the universe taken as a whole.
notes.other_reading: the nature of all things

notes.greek: καὶ τότε συμφέρει ὅτε ἐκείνη φέρει
notes.note: 'Then ... when': the benefit is tied to the moment of the bringing. The Greek does not add 'only' or 'exactly'; a stronger wording would be an interpretation.
notes.other_reading: and it is good for them exactly when nature brings it

check.note: The sentence is built on a pun: συμφέρει ('is of benefit', literally 'brings together') against φέρει ('brings'), each twice. 'Brings' and 'is good for' share nothing, so what is close to a proof-by-wordplay in Greek reads in English as a flat assertion.
check.decided: Not carried into English: a forced echo would be less clear than the sense. The play on words is in the notes.

check.note: συμφέρει is 'is advantageous, benefits, is in the interest of'. 'Is good for' is close in everyday English, but 'good' is the word normally kept for ἀγαθόν, so it makes the claim sound more like a statement about the good than the Greek does.
check.decided: Kept “is good for” as the plain reading; “benefits, is to the advantage of” is in the notes.

check.note: ἐκείνη is just 'that one / she', pointing back to nature. 'That nature' is stilted and suggests there is some other nature it is being distinguished from.
check.decided: Accepted: “when nature brings it”.

check.note: Greek repeats the same word, 'to each ... to each', which may be 'each person' or 'each thing'. 'Each one' keeps that open, but 'that one' breaks the repetition and is awkward.
check.decided: Accepted: “to each … for each”.

check.note: The Greek is plural, 'of all things / of the totality'. 'The nature of the whole' is defensible but opaque to a modern reader ('the whole' of what?), and it is a different word from κόσμος, which the same translator renders 'universe' elsewhere.
check.decided: Kept “the nature of the whole”; “of all things” is in the notes.

passages.casaubon: That is best for every one, that the common nature of all doth send unto every one, and then is it best, when she doth send it.

nearest.title: What the whole sends in its season

passages.greek: Ὁ ἥλιος κατακεχύσθαι δοκεῖ καὶ πάντῃ γε κέχυται, οὐ μὴν ἐκκέχυται. ἡ γὰρ χύσις αὕτη τάσις ἐστίν· ἀκτῖνες γοῦν αἱ αὐγαὶ αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐκτείνεσθαι λέγονται. ὁποῖον δέ τι ἐστὶν ἀκτίς, ἴδοις ἄν, εἰ διά τινος στενοῦ εἰς ἐσκιασμένον οἶκον τὸ ἀφ’ ἡλίου φῶς εἰσδυόμενον θεάσαιο· τείνεται γὰρ κατ’ εὐθὺ καὶ ὥσπερ διερείδεται πρὸς τὸ στερέμνιον ὅ τι ἂν ἀπαντήσῃ διεῖργον τὸν ἐπέκεινα ἀέρα, ἐνταῦθα δὲ ἔστη καὶ οὐ κατώλισθεν οὐδὲ ἔπεσε. τοιαύτην οὖν τὴν χύσιν καὶ διάχυσιν τῆς διανοίας εἶναι χρή, μηδαμῶς ἔκχυσιν, ἀλλὰ τάσιν, καὶ πρὸς τὰ ἀπαντῶντα κωλύματα μὴ βίαιον μηδὲ ῥαγδαίαν τὴν ἐπέρεισιν ποιεῖσθαι μηδὲ μὴν καταπίπτειν, ἀλλὰ ἵστασθαι καὶ ἐπιλάμπειν τὸ δεχόμενον· αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑαυτὸ στερήσει τῆς αὐγῆς τὸ μὴ παραπέμπον αὐτήν.
passages.english: The sun seems to be poured down, and indeed it is poured in every direction, yet it is not poured out. For this pouring is an extension; its beams, at any rate, are called aktines (“rays”) from ekteinesthai (“to be extended”). You could see what a ray is if you watched the sun’s light coming through something narrow into a shaded room. For it extends in a straight line and leans, so to speak, against whatever solid thing it meets that shuts off the air beyond; there it stands, and it does not slip down or fall. So the pouring and spreading of thought should be like that: in no way a pouring out, but an extension. It should not lean on the obstacles it meets with force or like a torrent, nor fall down, but stand and light up whatever receives it. For whatever does not give the beam passage will deprive itself of the beam.

notes.note: 'The sun' stands for its light. The verb form can be passive ('be poured down') or reflexive ('pour itself down'), and δοκεῖ can be 'seems' or 'is thought'.
notes.other_reading: The sun is thought to pour itself down

notes.note: 'Poured out' in the sense of spilled away and used up. I kept the same verb 'pour' so the three forms (down, everywhere, out) stay visible.
notes.other_reading: yet it does not run out

notes.greek: ἡ γὰρ χύσις αὕτη τάσις ἐστίν
notes.note: τάσις is stretching, extension or tension, a term of Stoic physics. “Extension” is used because the next clause derives “ray” from the verb “to be extended”.
notes.other_reading: For this pouring is a stretching

notes.greek: ἀκτῖνες γοῦν αἱ αὐγαὶ αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐκτείνεσθαι λέγονται
notes.note: Marcus derives the word for rays (aktines) from the verb “to be extended” (ekteinesthai) because they sound alike. The Greek words are given in Latin letters so the claim still makes sense in English.
Literally a “shaded” house or room.
notes.other_reading: a darkened house

notes.note: The verb means to lean on or brace oneself against something; ὥσπερ (“so to speak”) marks it as a figure. The text of this word has been doubted, and another reading gives “is divided”; that doubt was not checked against a critical edition’s notes.
notes.other_reading: and presses, so to speak, against

notes.note: The participle goes with the solid thing: it bars the way to the air on the far side. It could also be taken as the solid thing marking off the air beyond.
notes.other_reading: that separates off the air beyond

notes.greek: ἐνταῦθα δὲ ἔστη καὶ οὐ κατώλισθεν οὐδὲ ἔπεσε
notes.note: The Greek verbs are past tense, either a general truth or the moment of watching. I used the English present.
notes.other_reading: there it has stopped, and it did not slip down or fall

notes.note: The word covers thought, thinking and the mind.
notes.other_reading: of the mind

notes.greek: μὴ βίαιον μηδὲ ῥαγδαίαν τὴν ἐπέρεισιν ποιεῖσθαι
notes.note: The noun for leaning picks up the verb used of the sunbeam; the second adjective is the one used of a driving storm. No subject is stated: it may be thought or a general “one”.
notes.other_reading: one should not make the contact forced or violent

notes.greek: αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑαυτὸ στερήσει τῆς αὐγῆς τὸ μὴ παραπέμπον αὐτήν
notes.note: The last verb means to escort, convey or let pass. The sense is open: the thing that does not let the beam through, or the thing that does not take it in, as against “whatever receives it” just before.
notes.other_reading: For whatever does not take the beam in will deprive itself of it

notes.note: Both nouns, and the “pouring out” after them, are built on one root. English cannot keep that without strain.
notes.other_reading: the pouring and wide pouring

check.note: The comparison is carried by repeated verbs: the ray 'stood' (ἔστη) and did not 'fall' (ἔπεσε), so the mind must not 'fall down' (καταπίπτειν) but 'stand' (ἵστασθαι). English gives stops / fall for the ray and collapse / stand for the mind, so the ray and the mind no longer do the same things in the same words.
check.decided: Accepted: the ray “stands” and does not “fall”; thought must not “fall down” but “stand”.

check.note: παραπέμπειν is 'escort, conduct, convey along, let pass'. English picks 'transmit onward', which gives a puzzling thought (a wall that does not pass light on is still lit); the other live sense is 'does not give it passage / does not take it along', the opposite of τὸ δεχόμενον, 'what receives it'. The English is unclear to a modern reader as it stands.
check.decided: Changed to “does not give the beam passage”; the other reading is in the notes.

check.note: αὐγή was 'beams' earlier (αἱ αὐγαὶ αὐτοῦ) and φῶς was 'light'; at the end αὐγή becomes 'light' too, so two Greek words share one English word and the closing echo of the opening 'beams' is lost. The pronoun αὐτήν ('it') is expanded to 'the light', and 'that' has no Greek behind it.
check.decided: Accepted: “beam” at the end as at the start.

check.note: γε stresses πάντῃ: 'and in every direction, at that'. The contrast is between down (κατα-), everywhere (πάντῃ) and out (ἐκ-); 'really is' moves the stress onto a seeming-versus-reality contrast that the Greek does not draw so sharply.
check.decided: Accepted: “and indeed it is poured in every direction”.

check.note: μηδαμῶς is 'in no way, by no means', not a word of time. 'Never' is idiomatic but makes the statement temporal.
check.decided: Accepted: “in no way”.

check.note: διάχυσις has the same root as χύσις and ἔκχυσις ('pouring abroad'); the passage runs on one root seven times. 'Spreading' steps out of the pouring vocabulary at the point where the image is applied to the mind. The connecting οὖν ('so, then') is also dropped.
check.decided: “Spreading” is kept and “So” is restored. The shared root is in the notes.

check.note: The ἐρειδ- words mean 'lean on, prop oneself against, rest firmly on' as much as 'press'. English keeps the echo between the two places, which is right, but 'press' sounds more forceful than the Greek, in a passage whose point is that the contact must not be forced.
check.decided: Accepted: “leans”.

check.note: ῥαγδαῖος is 'violent, tempestuous', typically used of driving rain and storms, so it continues the water imagery. 'Fury' turns it into an emotion.
check.decided: Accepted: “like a torrent”.

check.greek: τάσις ἐστίν· ἀκτῖνες γοῦν αἱ αὐγαὶ αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐκτείνεσθαι λέγονται
check.note: The Greek derives the word for 'rays' from the verb 'to be extended' by sound; that cannot be done in English, and the bracketed Greek is an editorial addition inside the sentence. As written, 'called rays from being stretched out' still makes no sense until the reader works out from the brackets that aktines is meant to sound like ekteinesthai. τάσις is also 'tension, extension', a term of Stoic physics; 'stretching' picks the plainest sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the Greek words are given in Latin letters with their meanings beside them.

check.note: διάνοια is 'thought, thinking, understanding' as well as 'mind'. What is poured and extended is more naturally the activity (thought) than the faculty; the English picks the faculty.
check.decided: Accepted: “thought”.

check.note: οἶκος is 'house' or 'room', and ἐσκιασμένον is 'shaded, in shadow' rather than 'made dark'. 'Darkened room' is a reasonable choice but slightly more definite than the Greek; 'gap' in 'narrow gap' is also supplied, since the Greek says only 'something narrow'.
check.decided: Accepted: “a shaded room”, “something narrow”.

check.note: γάρ ('for') is dropped: in Greek this sentence gives the reason why watching the light shows what a ray is. τείνεται is also middle or passive ('is stretched, extends'), which the active-sounding 'stretches' blurs a little.
check.decided: Accepted: “For it extends”.

passages.casaubon: The sun seemeth to be shed abroad. And indeed it is diffused but not effused. For that diffusion of it is a τάσις or an extension. For therefore are the beams of it called ἀκτῖνες from the word ἐκτείνεσθαι to be stretched out and extended. Now what a sunbeam is, thou mayest know if thou observe the light of the sun, when through some narrow hole it pierceth into some room that is dark. For it is always in a direct line. And as by any solid body, that it meets with in the way that is not penetrable by air, it is divided and abrupted, and yet neither slides off, or falls down, but stayeth there nevertheless: such must the diffusion in the mind be; not an effusion, but an extension. What obstacles and impediments soever she meeteth within her way, she must not violently, and by way of an impetuous onset light upon them; neither must she fall down; but she must stand, and give light unto that which doth admit of it. For as for that which doth not, it is its own fault and loss, if it bereave itself of her light.

nearest.title: What the whole sends in its season

passages.greek: Εὐχὴ Ἀθηναίων· ὗσον, ὗσον, ὦ φίλε Ζεῦ, κατὰ τῆς ἀρούρας τῆς Ἀθηναίων καὶ τῶν πεδίων. ἤτοι οὐ δεῖ εὔχεσθαι ἢ οὕτως ἁπλῶς καὶ ἐλευθέρως.
passages.english: A prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, down on the ploughland of the Athenians and the plains.” Either one should not pray, or one should pray like this: simply and like a free person.

notes.note: The Greek has no quotation marks; I take the prayer to run from 'Rain, rain' to 'the plains', with Marcus's comment after it. There is no article, so it could also be 'An Athenian prayer'.
notes.other_reading: An Athenian prayer

notes.note: A command to Zeus himself, “rain!”, said twice.
notes.other_reading: Send rain, send rain

notes.greek: κατὰ τῆς ἀρούρας τῆς Ἀθηναίων καὶ τῶν πεδίων
notes.note: ἄρουρα is ploughed or sown land. One preposition governs both nouns, so the plains may be the Athenians’ own or simply “the plains”; the English leaves that open.
notes.other_reading: on the ploughland and plains of the Athenians

notes.greek: ἤτοι οὐ δεῖ εὔχεσθαι ἢ οὕτως
notes.note: The second half has no verb; “one should pray” is supplied from the first. δεῖ can be “should” or “must”.
notes.other_reading: Either one must not pray, or only like this

notes.note: The first word is “simply, plainly, sincerely”; the second is “in the manner of a free person”: frankly, without servility, perhaps open-handedly. Marcus does not say what this is set against. οὕτως may also measure the two words: “as simply and freely as this”.
notes.other_reading: plainly and frankly

check.note: ἐλευθέρως is 'in the manner of a free person': frankly, without servility, possibly open-handedly. Bare 'freely' in English suggests 'without restraint, as much as you like', which is not a sense of the Greek, and hides the two senses that are live (unservile / generous).
check.decided: Accepted: “like a free person”.

check.note: ἁπλῶς covers 'plainly, without elaboration', 'straightforwardly, sincerely, single-mindedly' and 'without qualification'. 'Simply' is the natural choice but in English it leans toward 'in few words' and loses 'sincerely / with nothing held back'.
check.decided: Kept “simply”; “plainly, sincerely” is in the notes.

check.note: The second 'one should pray' is supplied (the Greek has only 'or thus simply and freely'), which is unavoidable. The comma then decides that 'simply and freely' explains 'in this way'; the Greek equally allows 'as simply and freely as this', with οὕτως measuring the adverbs.
check.decided: The second “one should pray” is supplied because English needs it. The other construction, “as simply and freely as this”, is in the notes.

check.greek: ὗσον, ὗσον, ὦ φίλε Ζεῦ, κατὰ
check.note: ὗσον is an imperative addressed to Zeus as the one who rains, and κατά with the genitive is 'down upon'. In English 'Rain, rain' reads at first as a noun (as in the nursery rhyme), and 'on' drops 'down'.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, down on”.

check.greek: τῆς ἀρούρας τῆς Ἀθηναίων καὶ τῶν πεδίων
check.note: Repeating 'on' makes the plains a second, separate target and leaves open whose plains they are. The Greek has one preposition and can equally be 'the Athenians' ploughland and plains' (their own); how far the prayer reaches depends on this, so the English should not settle it.
check.decided: Accepted: one “on”, so the English does not decide whose plains they are.

check.note: δεῖ is 'it is necessary, one must'. 'Should' is a little weaker, and the first half means 'one must not pray at all', which the English leaves to be inferred.
check.decided: Kept “should”; “must” is in the notes. “At all” was not added because the Greek does not say it.

check.note: A question for the article: does the Greek say that the point of the prayer is to pray for the whole community rather than for oneself?
check.decided: No. The Greek has no word for community, for others or for oneself. Marcus says only how to pray: simply and like a free person. That his example is a public prayer for shared land is the reader’s inference. Casaubon’s “and not every one for himself in particular alone” has nothing behind it in this Greek text.

passages.casaubon: The form of the Athenians' prayer did run thus: 'O rain, rain, good Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.' Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not every one for himself in particular alone.

nearest.title: What the whole sends in its season

passages.greek: Τίνα τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ τούτων καὶ περὶ οἷα ἐσπουδάκασι καὶ δι’ οἷα φιλοῦσι καὶ τιμῶσι· γυμνὰ νόμιζε βλέπειν τὰ ψυχάρια αὐτῶν. ὅτε δοκοῦσι βλάπτειν ψέγοντες ἢ ὠφελεῖν ἐξυμνοῦντες, ὅση οἴησις.
passages.english: What the ruling parts of these people are, what sort of things they are in earnest about, and for what sort of things they love and honour. Think of yourself as looking at their little souls naked. When they suppose that they do harm by blaming or do good by singing praises, how much conceit.

notes.note: There is no verb. It can be a direct question or the heading of something to consider; the English keeps it as a thing to consider, running on into the two clauses that follow. τὸ ἡγεμονικόν is the Stoic term for the part of the soul that directs the rest, “the ruling part”.
notes.other_reading: What are the ruling parts of these people?

notes.note: A perfect with present force: what they are busy about and take seriously now. English has to choose between effort and seriousness.
notes.other_reading: what sort of things they have put their effort into

notes.note: The two verbs have no object in the Greek and the English gives them none. The sense is the kind of reasons for which these people give their love and honour.
notes.other_reading: and what sort of things make them love and honour a person

notes.note: The imperative can mean “consider that you see” or “make it your practice to see”. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: Make it your habit to look at their little souls naked.

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for soul, belittling in tone.
notes.other_reading: their souls

notes.note: The verb can mean “they think” or “they seem”. The English takes it as what they themselves think, which fits the word for conceit that follows.
notes.other_reading: When they seem to do harm by blaming or good by singing praises

notes.note: Literally “how great the conceit”, with a word of measure. The noun covers self-importance and also mere supposing, so it answers the verb “suppose” just before.
notes.other_reading: how great the delusion

check.note: “Ruling parts” is a term of the school that a reader of today cannot place without help. “The minds that govern these people” is suggested, here and in 4.38 and 9.18.
check.decided: Declined: τὸ ἡγεμονικόν is a fixed term of the school that returns through the whole book, and the glossary settles it as “the ruling part” so that it stays one English phrase from passage to passage. The note on the first words says what the term means.

check.note: The Greek perfect has present force: what they are in earnest about now. “Have put their effort into” reads as effort already spent.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what sort of things they are in earnest about”. The perfect of this verb describes a present state, not effort spent in the past.

check.note: The verb can also mean “they seem” to do harm by blaming. The English has chosen “they suppose” without a sign.
check.decided: Accepted: “they suppose” is kept, since the closing word for conceit is also a word for supposing, and the note on the verb records “when they seem to do harm”.

check.note: The Greek has a word of quantity, “how great” or “how much”. “What conceit” drops the measure.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how much conceit”, which keeps the Greek word of measure.

passages.casaubon: What are their minds and understandings; and what the things that they apply themselves unto: what do they love, and what do they hate for? Fancy to thyself the estate of their souls openly to be seen. When they think they hurt them shrewdly, whom they speak ill of; and when they think they do them a very good turn, whom they commend and extol: O how full are they then of conceit, and opinion!

passages.greek: Τοῦτον ἰδοὺ τὸν χρόνον σεαυτῷ χάρισαι. οἱ τὴν ὑστεροφημίαν μᾶλλον διώκοντες οὐ λογίζονται ὅτι ἄλλοι τοιοῦτοι μέλλουσιν ἐκεῖνοι εἶναι, οἷοί εἰσιν οὗτοι οὓς βαροῦνται· κἀκεῖνοι δὲ θνητοί. τί δὲ ὅλως πρὸς σέ, ἂν ἐκεῖνοι φωναῖς τοιαύταις ἀπηχῶσιν ἢ ὑπόληψιν τοιαύτην περὶ σοῦ ἔχωσιν;
passages.english: Look: make a gift of this present time to yourself. People who chase fame after death instead do not take into account that those people will be others of the same kind as these whom they find hard to bear; and those people too are mortal. And what is it to you at all, if those people echo with sounds of such a kind, or hold a judgment of such a kind about you?

notes.greek: Τοῦτον ἰδοὺ τὸν χρόνον σεαυτῷ χάρισαι
notes.note: The Greek has only “this time”: the time that is here now, set against the time of later fame. “Present” is added so that the words are not heard as “on this occasion”. The verb is to give freely, as a favour or present.
notes.other_reading: Look: grant this time to yourself.

notes.note: A compound, literally “after-fame”: what is said of a person later. “After death” is the sense but “death” is not in the word.
notes.other_reading: what will be said of them afterwards

notes.note: “Rather”: they chase later fame in preference to the present time just mentioned. The English reads “instead”.
notes.other_reading: People who prefer to chase fame after death

notes.greek: ἄλλοι τοιοῦτοι μέλλουσιν ἐκεῖνοι εἶναι, οἷοί εἰσιν οὗτοι οὓς βαροῦνται
notes.note: The Greek has only “those” and “these”: “those” are the people among whom the later fame would live, “these” the people of the present. “Those people” is kept for the one Greek word all three times. The last verb is literally to be weighed down by someone.
notes.other_reading: that those will be others such as these who weigh on them

notes.note: The verb means to sound back, echo or ring out; the noun covers voices, sounds and words. The phrase makes their talk about you into mere noise.
notes.other_reading: if those people ring out with voices of such a kind

notes.note: The word “such”, here and with “sounds”, can point back to “of the same kind” above, the sounds and the judgment that people of that kind produce. It can also be indefinite, “this or that”. “Of such a kind” leaves both possible.
notes.other_reading: if those people echo with this or that sound, or hold this or that judgment about you

notes.note: The Stoic word for a judgment or opinion taken up about something; “judgment” follows the glossary.
notes.other_reading: an opinion of such a kind about you

check.note: In English “this time” is first heard as “on this occasion”. The Greek means the stretch of time that is present now, set against the time after death.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “make a gift of this present time to yourself”. The Greek means the time that is here now, and the note says that “present” is added to the bare “this time”.

check.note: “Reckon” today mostly means “suppose”. The Greek is “do not take into account”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “do not take into account that”, which is the sense of the Greek verb of reckoning and is not heard as “suppose”.

check.note: The Greek has only “those” set against “these”; “of that time”, “just” and “now” are added. The same Greek word is then “those people” twice, so it has two English forms.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the added words are removed and the English reads “those people will be others of the same kind as these whom they find hard to bear”. “Those people” is kept, not the bare “those”, so that the one Greek word has one English form in all three places; the sentence now opens “People who chase” so that “those people” is not taken for the chasers.

check.note: “Sound back with voices” is not clear English. The verb is of an echo or a noise given back, and the noun can be sounds or cries as well as voices.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “echo with sounds of such a kind”. “Echo” and “sounds” are taken as suggested; “of such a kind” stands in place of “of this kind or that” so that the Greek word for “such” is not narrowed, as the next point explains.

check.note: The two words for “such” are taken as indefinite, “this or that”. They can also point back to “others of the same kind”: sounds and an opinion of the kind such people produce.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “sounds of such a kind” and “a judgment of such a kind”, which can point back to “of the same kind” or be heard loosely, as the Greek can. A new note gives the indefinite reading, “this or that”.

check.note: ὑπόληψις is an opinion or assumption. “Judgment” here and in 12.4 runs into “judges” in 9.18, a different Greek word; “opinion” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: ὑπόληψις is the school’s word for the view a mind takes up of a thing, and the glossary settles it as “judgment” so that it stays one English word across the book. The “judges” of 9.18 stand in another passage, and the note here gives “opinion”.

passages.casaubon: This time that is now present, bestow thou upon thyself. They that rather hunt for fame after death, do not consider, that those men that shall be hereafter, will be even such, as these whom now they can so hardly bear with. And besides they also will be mortal men. But to consider the thing in itself, if so many with so many voices, shall make such and such a sound, or shall have such and such an opinion concerning thee, what is it to thee?

passages.greek: Οἷοί εἰσιν οἷς θέλουσιν ἀρέσκειν, καὶ δι’ οἷα περιγινόμενα καὶ δι’ οἵων ἐνεργειῶν. ὡς ταχέως ὁ αἰὼν πάντα καλύψει καὶ ὅσα ἐκάλυψεν ἤδη.
passages.english: What sort of people those are whom they want to please, and for what sort of gains, and through what sort of activities. How quickly eternity will cover everything, and how much it has covered already.

notes.note: An exclamation or a thing to consider, with no main verb beyond “are”. The “they” who want to please are not named: people in general.
notes.other_reading: What are they like, the people they want to please?

notes.note: The participle means things that result or are left over as profit. The preposition with this case gives the reason or aim: for the sake of what results.
notes.other_reading: and for what sort of results

notes.note: The same preposition with a different case, now the means. The noun is “activity”, as in 6.51.
notes.other_reading: and by what sort of actions

notes.note: The word covers an age, a lifetime and the whole of unending time. It is a larger word than the ordinary one for time, so the English reads “eternity”.
notes.other_reading: How quickly time will cover everything

notes.note: Literally “and how many things it has covered already”. It can be a second exclamation, as the English takes it, or a second object of “will cover”.
notes.other_reading: and all that it has covered already

check.note: Two “they” with different people behind them stand in one clause, and the reader has to work out which is which.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “What sort of people those are whom they want to please”, so that the two groups in the clause can be told apart.

check.note: αἰών is the whole of time, eternity, not the ordinary word for time that is “time” in 8.44. “Time” for both loses the larger word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “How quickly eternity will cover everything”. αἰών is the whole of unending time, a larger word than the ordinary word for time, and the note gives “time”.

passages.casaubon: What manner of men they be whom they seek to please, and what to get, and by what actions: how soon time will cover and bury all things, and how many it hath already buried!

passages.greek:
Ὁ περὶ τὴν ὑστεροφημίαν ἐπτοημένος οὐ φαντάζεται ὅτι ἕκαστος τῶν μεμνημένων αὐτοῦ τάχιστα καὶ αὐτὸς ἀποθανεῖται· εἶτα πάλιν ὁ ἐκεῖνον διαδεξάμενος, μέχρι καὶ πᾶσα ἡ μνήμη ἀποσβῇ διὰ ἁπτομένων καὶ σβεννυμένων προιοῦσα. ὑπόθου δ᾽, ὅτι καὶ ἀθάνατοι μὲν οἱ μεμνησόμενοι, ἀθάνατος δὲ ἡ μνήμη· τί οὖν τοῦτο πρὸς σέ; καὶ οὐ λέγω, ὅτι οὐδὲν πρὸς τὸν τεθνηκότα, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸν ζῶντα τί ὁ ἔπαινος, πλὴν ἄρα δι’ οἰκονομίαν τινά; πάρες γὰρ νῦν ἀκαίρως τὴν φυσικὴν δόσιν ἄλλου τινὸς ἐχομένην λόγου λοιπόν.

Πᾶν τὸ καὶ ὁπωσοῦν καλὸν ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ καλόν ἐστι καὶ ἐφ’ ἑαυτὸ καταλήγει, οὐκ ἔχον μέρος ἑαυτοῦ τὸν ἔπαινον· οὔτε γοῦν χεῖρον ἣ κρεῖττον γίνεται τὸ ἐπαινούμενον. τοῦτό φημι καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κοινότερον καλῶν λεγομένων, οἷον ἐπὶ τῶν ὑλικῶν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν τεχνικῶν κατασκευασμάτων (τὸ γὰρ δὴ ὄντως καλὸν τίνος χρείαν ἔχει; οὐ μᾶλλον ἣ νόμος, οὐ μᾶλλον ἣ ἀλήθεια, οὐ μᾶλλον ἢ εὔνοια ἢ αἰδώς)· τί τούτων διὰ τὸ ἐπαινεῖσθαι καλόν ἐστιν ἢ ψεγόμενον φθείρεται; σμαράγδιον γὰρ ἑαυτοῦ χεῖρον γίνεται, ἐὰν μὴ ἐπαινῆται; τί δὲ χρυσός, ἐλέφας, πορφύρα, λύρα, μαχαίριον, ἀνθύλλιον, δενδρύφιον;
passages.english:
Whoever is worked up about fame after death does not picture that each of those who remember them will very soon die too; then in turn the one who takes over from that one, until the whole memory also goes out, as it passes on through those that are lit and go out. But suppose even that those who will remember are immortal, and the memory immortal: what then is that to you? And I do not speak of its being nothing to the dead; but to the living, what is praise, except perhaps for the sake of managing some matter? For leave aside now, out of season, the gift of nature, which from here on belongs to some other discussion.

Everything that is beautiful in any way at all is beautiful of itself and ends in itself, and does not have praise as a part of itself. At any rate, what is praised becomes neither worse nor better. I say this also of the things called beautiful in the more ordinary way, such as material things and things made by craft (for what does the truly beautiful need? No more than law does, no more than truth, no more than goodwill or a sense of shame). Which of these is beautiful because it is praised, or is ruined when it is blamed? For does a little emerald become worse than itself if it is not praised? And what of gold, ivory, purple, a lyre, a small knife, a little flower, a little tree?

notes.note: A participle meaning fluttered, startled or excited, used of people carried away by a passion. “Worked up” gives the agitation in plain English.
notes.other_reading: Whoever is in a flutter about fame after death

notes.note: The verb belongs with φαντασία, the Stoic “impression”: the fact does not appear to this person.
notes.other_reading: does not form the impression that

notes.note: The verb is to receive something in succession from another, as an heir or the next runner does. “Takes over from” keeps that; the plainer sense is only that this one comes next.
notes.other_reading: then in turn the one who comes after that one

notes.note: The image is of a flame handed on. The two participles can be neuter, things such as lamps or torches, or masculine, the people who remember; “those that” leaves the image whole, and “go out” repeats the verb of “goes out” just before, as the Greek does. From memory, unchecked: the first participle is an editor’s correction of the manuscripts here.
notes.other_reading: as it passes on through people who are lit and put out

notes.greek: καὶ οὐ λέγω, ὅτι οὐδὲν πρὸς τὸν τεθνηκότα, ἀλλὰ
notes.note: Literally “and I do not say that it is nothing to the dead, but”. This is the idiom of passing over a smaller point to make a larger one, not a denial that praise is nothing to the dead. “It” has no word of its own in the Greek and picks up “that” in the question before.
notes.other_reading: And I do not say merely that it is nothing to the dead, but what is praise even to the living

notes.note: The noun is the managing of a household or of affairs, and so expediency: praise may be useful as a means of getting something done. It can also mean a larger ordering of things.
notes.other_reading: unless, it may be, on account of some arrangement of things

notes.greek: πάρες γὰρ νῦν ἀκαίρως τὴν φυσικὴν δόσιν ἄλλου τινὸς ἐχομένην λόγου λοιπόν
notes.note: The Greek as given does not construe cleanly: the adverb “out of season” belongs to the command “leave aside”, which makes no sensible order, and the last word, “for the rest” or “from here on”, hangs loose. The English sets the words down in order without mending them, and what “the gift of nature” refers to is not clear. From memory, unchecked: the text is doubted, and editors have read an indicative, “you are neglecting”, and a participle agreeing with “you”.
notes.other_reading: For now you are neglecting, at the wrong moment, the gift of nature, and holding on to some other account.

notes.note: The words are read as “belonging to some other discussion”. They can also mean “hanging on someone else’s word”, with “someone else” a person: the gift of nature made to depend on what another says, which would tie the sentence to praise.
notes.other_reading: the gift of nature, which then hangs on someone else’s word

notes.note: The adjective means beautiful, fine and morally noble at once. The examples run from emeralds to law and truth, so no one English word fits all; “beautiful” is kept throughout the chapter so the argument can be followed.
notes.other_reading: Everything that is fine in any way at all

notes.note: Literally “comes to a stop at itself”: its beauty is complete in itself and points to nothing further.
notes.other_reading: and comes to rest in itself

notes.note: A comparative adverb: “in a more common way”, that is, in the looser everyday sense of the word, as against the truly beautiful named next.
notes.other_reading: the things more commonly called beautiful

notes.greek: ἐπὶ τῶν ὑλικῶν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν τεχνικῶν κατασκευασμάτων
notes.note: The last noun, “things constructed”, may go with both adjectives or only with the second. The English takes it with the second only, since the list that follows has raw materials and living things as well as made objects.
notes.other_reading: such as products of matter and products of craft

notes.greek: τὸ γὰρ δὴ ὄντως καλὸν τίνος χρείαν ἔχει; οὐ μᾶλλον ἣ νόμος
notes.note: The question is left without a stated answer: the truly beautiful needs nothing, any more than law does. The ἣ here, the one after it and the one in “neither worse nor better” above are slips in the copy for ἢ, “than” or “or”.
notes.other_reading: for what is truly beautiful needs nothing more, any more than law does

notes.note: The word covers a sense of shame, modesty and respect for others.
notes.other_reading: modesty

notes.note: A diminutive, as are the knife, the flower and the tree at the end of the list. “Little” or “small” is kept for each.
notes.other_reading: an emerald

notes.note: The purple dye from shellfish, or cloth dyed with it.
notes.other_reading: purple cloth

check.note: The Greek is a word of strong agitation or passionate excitement. “In a flutter” is light and a little quaint for it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Whoever is worked up about fame after death”. The Greek word is one of strong agitation, and the note keeps the literal “in a flutter”.

check.note: The English past tense sits oddly in a sentence about the future, and “took over from” suggests an office. The Greek only says that this one came next.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the past tense is gone and the English reads “the one who takes over from that one”. “Takes over from” is kept because the Greek verb is of receiving in succession from another, which the handed-on flame of the next clause picks up; a new note gives “comes after”.

check.note: The Greek does not say “people”: the participles can as well be neuter, things kindled and quenched, which keeps the image whole. They can also be read as “catch fire and go out”.
check.decided: Accepted: “people” is removed and the English reads “through those that are lit and go out”. The Greek does not say whether people or things are meant, and “go out” now answers “goes out” just before, as the one Greek verb does.

check.note: The Greek “even” is dropped. It marks the supposition as the extreme case.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But suppose even that those who will remember are immortal”, which restores the Greek “even”.

check.greek: καὶ οὐ λέγω, ὅτι οὐδὲν πρὸς τὸν τεθνηκότα, ἀλλὰ
check.note: The Greek “but” is replaced by a colon, so the turn from one point to the other is lost and the English is clumsy. “Its” also supplies a subject that the Greek leaves unsaid.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “but” is restored and the English reads “And I do not speak of its being nothing to the dead; but to the living, what is praise”. “I do not speak of” stands in place of the suggested “I do not mean”, which would be heard as denying that praise is nothing to the dead. “It” is kept because English needs a subject, and it picks up “that” in the question before.

check.note: “Practical” is added, and “practical arrangement” tells the reader little. The Greek word is the managing of affairs, expediency, and can also be a larger ordering of things.
check.decided: Accepted: “practical” is removed and the English reads “except perhaps for the sake of managing some matter”. The note records that the word can also mean a larger ordering of things.

check.greek: πάρες γὰρ νῦν ἀκαίρως τὴν φυσικὴν δόσιν ἄλλου τινὸς ἐχομένην λόγου λοιπόν
check.note: The Greek as given does not construe cleanly: the adverb is attached to the command and the last word hangs loose. The English smooths this, and the sentence should carry a mark of doubt.
check.decided: Accepted: the adverb is no longer turned into a description of the topic, and the English reads “For leave aside now, out of season, the gift of nature, which from here on belongs to some other discussion”, close to the words as they stand. The note says that the Greek does not construe cleanly and that the text is doubted.

check.note: The words can also mean “hanging on someone else’s word”, which would tie the sentence to praise. The English has chosen “another discussion” without a sign.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “belongs to some other discussion”, the ordinary sense of the Greek phrase, and a new note records the second reading, “hangs on someone else’s word”.

check.note: The Greek adjective is also “fine” or “noble”. “Beautiful” suits the emerald and the flower but narrows the word where the examples are law, truth, goodwill and shame.
check.decided: Accepted: “beautiful” is kept throughout so that one English word serves the one Greek word, and the note on the first words of the chapter says that it is a choice and gives “fine”.

check.note: The Greek “for” is dropped: the question about the emerald is offered as the ground for the one before it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For does a little emerald become worse than itself”, which restores the Greek “for”.

passages.casaubon: He who is greedy of credit and reputation after his death, doth not consider, that they themselves by whom he is remembered, shall soon after every one of them be dead; and they likewise that succeed those; until at last all memory, which hitherto by the succession of men admiring and soon after dying hath had its course, be quite extinct. But suppose that both they that shall remember thee, and thy memory with them should be immortal, what is that to thee? I will not say to thee after thou art dead; but even to thee living, what is thy praise? But only for a secret and politic consideration, which we call οἰκονομίαν, or dispensation. For as for that, that it is the gift of nature, whatsoever is commended in thee, what might be objected from thence, let that now that we are upon another consideration be omitted as unseasonable. That which is fair and goodly, whatsoever it be, and in what respect soever it be, that it is fair and goodly, it is so of itself, and terminates in itself, not admitting praise as a part or member: that therefore which is praised, is not thereby made either better or worse. This I understand even of those things, that are commonly called fair and good, as those which are commended either for the matter itself, or for curious workmanship. As for that which is truly good, what can it stand in need of more than either justice or truth; or more than either kindness and modesty? Which of all those, either becomes good or fair, because commended; or dispraised suffers any damage? Doth the emerald become worse in itself, or more vile if it be not commended? Doth gold, or ivory, or purple? Is there anything that doth though never so common, as a knife, a flower, or a tree?

passages.greek: Οἷόν ἐστιν ὃ ποιοῦσι. τοὺς μὲν ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ χρόνου καὶ μεθ’ ἑαυτῶν ζῶντας ἀνθρώπους εὐφημεῖν οὐ θέλουσιν, αὐτοὶ δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν μεταγενεστέρων εὐφημηθῆναι, οὓς οὔτε εἶδόν ποτε οὔτε ὄψονται, περὶ πολλοῦ ποιοῦνται. τοῦτο δὲ ἐγγύς ἐστι τῷ λυπηθῆναι ἄν, ὅτι οὐχὶ καὶ οἱ προγενέστεροι περὶ σοῦ λόγους εὐφήμους ἐποιοῦντο.
passages.english: What a thing it is that they do. The people who live at the same time as them and alongside them they are unwilling to speak well of, yet they set great store by being spoken well of themselves by those who come after, whom they have never seen and never will see. This is close to what it would be to be pained that those who came before did not also speak well of you.

notes.note: Literally “what sort of thing it is that they do”, an exclamation of surprise. “They” are not named.
notes.other_reading: How strange is what they do.

notes.note: The same word comes three times, as a verb active and passive and then in the phrase “well-speaking words”. “Speak well of” is kept each time.
notes.other_reading: to praise

notes.note: Literally “with themselves”: in their own company.
notes.other_reading: and in their own company

notes.note: The particle makes the infinitive hypothetical: it is close to how it would be if one were pained.
notes.other_reading: This is close to being pained

notes.greek: οὐχὶ καὶ οἱ προγενέστεροι περὶ σοῦ
notes.note: The passage turns to “you” here, after “they” throughout. The Greek “also” goes with those who came before: they as well as those who come after.
notes.other_reading: that the earlier generations as well did not speak well of you

check.note: The English idiom is “set great store by”, not “on”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “set great store by”, which is the English idiom.

check.note: The Greek particle makes the case a supposed one: it is like what it would be to grieve. The English states it flatly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “This is close to what it would be to be pained that”. The Greek particle makes the case a supposed one.

check.note: The Greek “also” belongs with “those who came before”: they as well as those who come after. “Of you too” reads as “you as well as someone else”.
