check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “did not also speak well of you”, with “also” moved so that it goes with those who came before. The suggested “either” is not taken, because it would say that those who come after do not speak well of you, which the Greek does not say.

passages.casaubon: Who can choose but wonder at them? They will not speak well of them that are at the same time with them, and live with them; yet they themselves are very ambitious, that they that shall follow, whom they have never seen, nor shall ever see, should speak well of them. As if a man should grieve that he hath not been commended by them, that lived before him.

passages.greek:
Ὁ μὲν μὴ εἰδὼς ὅ τι ἐστὶ κόσμος, οὐκ οἶδεν ὅπου ἐστίν. ὁ δὲ μὴ εἰδὼς πρὸς ὅ τι πέφυκεν, οὐκ οἶδεν ὅστις ἐστὶν οὐδὲ τί ἐστι κόσμος. ὁ δὲ ἕν τι τούτων ἀπολιπὼν οὐδὲ πρὸς ὅ τι αὐτὸς πέφυκεν εἴποι. τίς οὖν φαίνεταί σοι ὁ τὸν τῶν κροτούντων ἔπαινον φεύγων ἢ διώκων, οἳ οὔθ’ ὅπου εἰσὶν οὔτε οἵτινές εἰσι γινώσκουσιν;

Ἐπαινεῖσθαι θέλεις ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπου τρὶς τῆς ὥρας ἑαυτῷ καταρωμένου; ἀρέσκειν θέλεις ἀνθρώπῳ ὃς οὐκ ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ; ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ ὁ μετανοῶν ἐφ’ ἅπασι σχεδὸν οἷς πράσσει;
passages.english:
Whoever does not know what the universe is does not know where they are. Whoever does not know what it is by nature for does not know who they are, nor what the universe is. And whoever is missing any one of these could not even say what they themselves are by nature for. What, then, does a person seem to you to be who runs from the praise of those who clap, or chases it, people who know neither where they are nor who they are?

Do you want to be praised by a person who curses themselves three times an hour? Do you want to please a person who is not pleased with themselves? Is a person pleased with themselves who regrets nearly everything they do?

notes.note: The noun has no article here or below: “what a universe is”. The word also means order. The English keeps the glossary’s “the universe”.
notes.other_reading: what a universe is

notes.greek: ὁ δὲ μὴ εἰδὼς πρὸς ὅ τι πέφυκεν
notes.note: The subject of the last verb is not stated. It can be the universe just named or the person. The English takes the universe, because the next sentence adds an emphatic “they themselves” to the same verb, which reads as a contrast with a different subject here.
notes.other_reading: Whoever does not know what they are by nature for

notes.note: Literally “has grown” or “is by nature”, with a preposition of aim: what a thing’s nature fits it for. No maker is named.
notes.other_reading: what it has come to be for

notes.note: The participle can mean having left out, or falling short in. “These” are the points of knowledge just listed.
notes.other_reading: whoever has left out any one of these

notes.note: An optative with no particle, where “could say” would normally have one. The English reads it as “could say”.
notes.other_reading: may they not even say what they themselves are by nature for

notes.greek: ὁ τὸν τῶν κροτούντων ἔπαινον φεύγων ἢ διώκων
notes.note: Literally “the one fleeing or pursuing the praise of the clappers”. The verb for clapping is used of applause and of any rattling noise. Running from praise is odd beside chasing it, but that is what the Greek as given says; from memory, unchecked: the words have been suspected, with blame as the thing fled.
notes.other_reading: who runs from the blame of those who clap, or chases their praise

notes.note: Literally “three times in the hour”. The noun can also mean a season or a moment.
notes.other_reading: three times every hour

notes.greek: ἀρέσκειν θέλεις ἀνθρώπῳ ὃς οὐκ ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ; ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ
notes.note: One verb, “please”, three times: please a person who does not please themselves. English “please oneself” means to do as one likes, so the English reads “is pleased with themselves” and keeps the root.
notes.other_reading: Do you want to please a person who does not satisfy themselves?

notes.note: To change one’s mind afterwards, to regret.
notes.other_reading: who repents of nearly everything they do

check.greek: ὁ δὲ μὴ εἰδὼς πρὸς ὅ τι πέφυκεν
check.note: The verb has no stated subject and can be the universe just named; the emphatic “they themselves” in the next sentence supports that. The English takes the person without a sign, and “made” brings in a maker the Greek does not name.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Whoever does not know what it is by nature for”, with the universe as subject, and “made” is gone from both sentences. The emphatic “they themselves” in the next sentence reads as a contrast with a different subject here; the note gives the reading with the person.

check.note: “Left out” sounds like an item omitted from a list. The sense is of someone who falls short in, or lacks, one of these pieces of knowledge.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whoever is missing any one of these”, since what is meant is a piece of knowledge the person lacks, not an item dropped from a list.

check.note: The Greek as given has the optative without the particle that “could” needs. The English reads “could”, which the sense requires; no change is asked for.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged, “could not even say”, and the note on the verb records that the Greek as given lacks the particle that “could” would normally have.

check.note: The English follows the Greek as given. Running from praise is odd beside chasing it, and from memory the words have been suspected; the doubt should be noted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged and follows the Greek as given. The note now records the doubt about the words, marked as from memory and unchecked.

passages.casaubon: He that knoweth not what the world is, knoweth not where he himself is. And he that knoweth not what the world was made for, cannot possibly know either what are the qualities, or what is the nature of the world. Now he that in either of these is to seek, for what he himself was made is ignorant also. What then dost thou think of that man, who proposeth unto himself, as a matter of great moment, the noise and applause of men, who both where they are, and what they are themselves, are altogether ignorant? Dost thou desire to be commended of that man, who thrice in one hour perchance, doth himself curse himself? Dost thou desire to please him, who pleaseth not himself? or dost thou think that he pleaseth himself, who doth use to repent himself almost of everything that he doth?

passages.greek: Οἷοί εἰσιν ἐσθίοντες, καθεύδοντες, ὀχεύοντες, ἀποπατοῦντες, τὰ ἄλλα· εἶτα οἷοι ἀνδρονομούμενοι καὶ γαυρούμενοι ἢ χαλεπαίνοντες καὶ ἐξ ὑπεροχῆς ἐπιπλήττοντες, πρὸ ὀλίγου δὲ ἐδούλευον πόσοις καὶ δι’ οἷα· καὶ μετ’ ὀλίγον ἐν τοιούτοις ἔσονται.
passages.english: What they are like when eating, sleeping, mating, emptying their bowels, and the rest. Then what they are like when lording it and giving themselves airs, or getting angry and scolding from a position of superiority. Yet a little while ago they were slaves, to how many, and for what sort of things. And in a little while they will be in the same sort of case.

notes.note: A word used of male animals covering females. Applied to people it is blunt.
notes.other_reading: coupling

notes.note: Literally “stepping aside”, the ordinary word for relieving the bowels.
notes.other_reading: relieving themselves

notes.note: A very rare word of uncertain sense, built from “man” and a root for managing or ruling, and middle or passive in form. “Lording it” is a guess from its parts and from the context of pride, and should not be read as certain. From memory, unchecked: editors doubt the word and have proposed others.
notes.other_reading: when playing the man

notes.note: To prance or plume oneself, used of a proud horse.
notes.other_reading: and strutting

notes.note: Literally “rebuking from superiority”: from a higher position.
notes.other_reading: and scolding from above

notes.note: The verb is to be a slave. It is probably meant of serving and courting others, not of legal slavery, but the image is kept. “To how many, and for what” is an exclamation inside the sentence.
notes.other_reading: they were dancing attendance on how many, and for what ends

notes.note: Literally “they will be in such things”. The English takes it as pointing back to the slavery just mentioned; it can also point to the bodily state of the opening, or forward to death.
notes.other_reading: they will be in such a state

check.note: The word is known from nowhere else and the Greek is suspect. “Lording it over people” is a guess from its parts that does not explain the middle or passive form, and should not read as certain.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “lording it”, without “over people”, since the form is middle or passive and an object is not supported. The rendering stays a guess from the word’s parts, and the note marks the word as doubtful.

check.note: The Greek is plural, “in such things”, and can point back to the slavery or forward to death. “Such a state” gives the reader nothing to attach it to.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “they will be in the same sort of case”, pointing back to the slavery just mentioned. The suggested “again” is not added, because the Greek does not have it; the note keeps the other readings.

check.note: “From on high” suggests heaven. The Greek is from a position of superiority.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “scolding from a position of superiority”, which is what the Greek says and does not suggest heaven.

passages.casaubon: Consider them through all actions and occupations, of their lives: as when they eat, and when they sleep: when they are in the act of necessary exoneration, and when in the act of lust. Again, when they either are in their greatest exultation; and in the middle of all their pomp and glory; or being angry and displeased, in great state and majesty, as from an higher place, they chide and rebuke. How base and slavish, but a little while ago, they were fain to be, that they might come to this; and within a very little while what will be their estate, when death hath once seized upon them.

passages.greek: Πολλάκις ἐθαύμασα πῶς ἑαυτὸν μὲν ἕκαστος μᾶλλον πάντων φιλεῖ, τὴν δὲ ἑαυτοῦ περὶ αὑτοῦ ὑπόληψιν ἐν ἐλάττονι λόγῳ τίθεται ἢ τὴν τῶν ἄλλων. ἐὰν γοῦν τινα θεὸς ἐπιστὰς ἢ διδάσκαλος ἔμφρων κελεύσῃ μηδὲν καθ’ ἑαυτὸν ἐνθυμεῖσθαι καὶ διανοεῖσθαι ὃ μὴ ἄμα καὶ γεγωνίσκων ἐξοίσει, οὐδὲ πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν τοῦτο ὑπομενεῖ. οὕτως τοὺς πέλας μᾶλλον αἰδούμεθα, τί ποτε περὶ ἡμῶν φρονήσουσιν, ἢ ἑαυτούς.
passages.english: I have often wondered how it is that each person loves themselves more than everyone else, yet sets less value on their own judgment about themselves than on that of others. At any rate, if a god appears beside someone, or a sensible teacher, and tells them to turn over nothing in their mind and think nothing to themselves that they will not at the same moment bring out, crying it aloud, they will not put up with this for even one day. So it is that we feel more shame before those near us, at what they will think of us, than before ourselves.

notes.note: Literally “more than all”, which can be all people or all things. The English takes people, since the sentence goes on to set each person against “the others”.
notes.other_reading: more than everything

notes.note: The judgment or opinion one holds; “judgment” follows the glossary.
notes.other_reading: their own opinion of themselves

notes.note: An idiom: to put in a lesser account. λόγος here is “account” or “reckoning”, not reason.
notes.other_reading: holds in less account

notes.note: The participle is used of a god or a dream figure appearing and standing by a person.
notes.other_reading: if a god stood over someone

notes.note: Two verbs for inward thinking, the second from the word the glossary gives as “thought”. “By oneself” means privately, inside.
notes.other_reading: to have no idea and no thought in private

notes.note: Literally “will bring out, shouting it”: the verb is to cry out so as to be heard.
notes.other_reading: that they will not at once shout out loud

notes.note: To feel shame before someone, to stand in awe of them or respect them.
notes.other_reading: So much more do we respect our neighbours

notes.note: Literally “those nearby”, the usual phrase for other people.
notes.other_reading: our neighbours

check.note: The Greek “all” can be “all people” or “all things”. The English has chosen people.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “more than everyone else”, since the sentence goes on to set each person against “the others”, and the note records “more than everything”.

check.note: The participle is of someone appearing at one’s side; “stood over” adds menace. The English tenses also clash, where the Greek is a plain condition about the future.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if a god appears beside someone, or a sensible teacher, and tells them”. The participle is of one who comes and stands by, without menace, and the present tenses now fit the Greek condition about the future.

check.note: The verb is to cry out so as to be heard, to proclaim. “Saying it aloud” is weaker.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “crying it aloud”. The Greek verb is to cry out so as to be heard, which “saying” was too weak for.

check.note: As in 8.44, ὑπόληψις is an opinion, and “judgment” runs into “judges” in 9.18. “Their own opinion about themselves” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: ὑπόληψις is the school’s word for the view a mind takes up of a thing, and the glossary settles it as “judgment” so that it stays one English word across the book. The “judges” of 9.18 stand in another passage, and the note here gives “opinion”.

passages.casaubon: I have often wondered how it should come to pass, that every man loving himself best, should more regard other men's opinions concerning himself than his own. For if any God or grave master standing by, should command any of us to think nothing by himself but what he should presently speak out; no man were able to endure it, though but for one day. Thus do we fear more what our neighbours will think of us, than what we ourselves.

passages.greek: Τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ αὐτῶν διάβλεπε καὶ τοὺς φρονίμους, οἷα μὲν φεύγουσιν, οἷα δὲ διώκουσιν.
passages.english: Look closely into their ruling parts, and at the wise as well: what sort of things they run from, and what sort of things they chase.

notes.note: “Their”: the people are not named, and the line has no context. It is presumably people in general.
notes.other_reading: Look closely into people’s ruling parts

notes.note: To look straight at or see through. τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, its object, is “the ruling part”.
notes.other_reading: See right through

notes.note: “The wise” stands in the same case as “ruling parts”, a second thing to look at, and its point is open. It can mean “even the wise”, with contempt, or “and look at the wise” as the contrast and model; “as well” leaves both possible. From memory, unchecked: the words have been doubted.
notes.other_reading: and even at the wise

notes.greek: οἷα μὲν φεύγουσιν, οἷα δὲ διώκουσιν
notes.note: The subject can be the wise alone or everyone whose ruling part is being looked at. The verbs are “flee” and “pursue”, the same pair as in 8.52.
notes.other_reading: what sort of things they avoid and what sort they pursue

check.note: The small word can be “even”: look into their ruling minds, even those of the sensible among them, one group and not two. The English makes the wise a second group and leaves “they” unclear; from memory the words have been doubted.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek sets “the wise” in the same case as “ruling parts”, as a second thing to look at, where “those of the wise” would need another case. “And at the wise as well” keeps that and leaves open, as the Greek does, whether they are a further target or a model; the note gives “even the wise” and records the doubt about the words.

passages.casaubon: Behold and observe, what is the state of their rational part; and those that the world doth account wise, see what things they fly and are afraid of; and what things they hunt after.

passages.greek: Δίελθε ἔσω ἔσω εἰς τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ αὐτῶν καὶ ὄψει τίνας κριτὰς φοβῇ, οἵους καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν ὄντας κριτάς.
passages.english: Pass inside, right inside, into their ruling parts, and you will see what judges you are afraid of, and what sort of judges they are of themselves as well.

notes.note: “Inside” is written twice. The English takes the doubling as emphasis; it could also be a copying slip for a single word.
notes.other_reading: Pass inside

notes.note: “What judges”, with the sense of what kind. The verb is present: you fear them now.
notes.other_reading: what kind of judges you fear

notes.greek: οἵους καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν ὄντας κριτάς
notes.note: Literally “being what sort of judges about themselves too”. The pronoun as printed is reflexive. The small word given as “as well” can also be “even”.
notes.other_reading: and what poor judges they are even of themselves

check.note: The meaning is right and the doubled word is kept, but “go through” followed by “to” is clumsy and hides the plain sense of passing inside.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Pass inside, right inside, into their ruling parts”. The clumsy “go through” is gone, but “pass” keeps the verb’s sense of going through, and “inside” is still said twice, as in the Greek, which the suggested “deep inside” would not do.

passages.casaubon: Sift their minds and understandings, and behold what men they be, whom thou dost stand in fear of what they shall judge of thee, what they themselves judge of themselves.

passages.greek: Ἀλλήλων καταφρονοῦντες ἀλλήλοις ἀρεσκεύονται καὶ ἀλλήλων ὑπερέχειν θέλοντες ἀλλήλοις ὑποκατακλίνονται.
passages.english: Despising one another, they fawn on one another; and wanting to be above one another, they take the lower place beneath one another.

notes.note: From the word for an over-eager pleaser: to play up to someone, to fawn. It has the same root as “please” in 6.59 and 8.53 but is a harsher verb.
notes.other_reading: they try to please one another

notes.note: Literally “to hold oneself over”, to be superior. The spatial sense is kept because the next verb answers it with “under”.
notes.other_reading: wanting to outdo one another

notes.note: Literally “to lie down beneath”, used of taking the lower place on a dining couch and so of giving way to someone.
notes.other_reading: they give way to one another

check.note: This is the verb of the fawner, harsher than the plain “please” of 6.59 and 8.53. “Try” is added and the contempt is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they fawn on one another”. It is the verb of the over-eager pleaser, a different and harsher word than “please”, and “try” was not in the Greek.

check.note: The Greek has a picture: lying down in the lower place, giving way. The English keeps the above and beneath but not the gesture.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “they take the lower place beneath one another”, which gives the picture of the lower place at table. The suggested “bow down” is not taken: it is a different gesture, and it loses the “above” and “beneath” that the two Greek verbs set against each other.

passages.casaubon: They contemn one another, and yet they seek to please one another: and whilest they seek to surpass one another in worldly pomp and greatness, they most debase and prostitute themselves in their better part one to another.

passages.greek: Ὁ μὲν φιλόδοξος ἀλλοτρίαν ἐνέργειαν ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν ὑπολαμβάνει, ὁ δὲ φιλήδονος ἰδίαν πεῖσιν, ὁ δὲ νοῦν ἔχων ἰδίαν πρᾶξιν.
passages.english: The lover of fame takes their own good to be another person’s activity; the lover of pleasure, their own feeling; the person who has sense, their own action.

notes.note: Literally a lover of δόξα, which is reputation and also other people’s opinion.
notes.other_reading: The lover of reputation

notes.note: The line turns on “another’s” against “one’s own”, the second word coming three times. Another’s activity is the praising that other people do. The Greek names the activity first; the English puts “their own good” first so that “their” is clearly the lover of fame.
notes.other_reading: takes another person’s activity to be their own good

notes.note: The verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment” in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: judges

notes.note: Literally “their own being acted on”: what is passively felt, set against activity and action.
notes.other_reading: what they themselves undergo

notes.note: The everyday idiom for being sensible, literally “having mind”. The glossary gives “mind” for the noun; the English reads “sense” because the idiom is the point.
notes.other_reading: the person who has mind

notes.note: A different noun from the “activity” of the first clause: a deed, something one does.
notes.other_reading: what they themselves do

check.note: After “another person’s”, “their own good” can be read as that other person’s good. The Greek is the fame-lover’s own good.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “takes their own good to be another person’s activity”, with “their own good” set next to the lover of fame so that it cannot be read as the other person’s good.

check.note: The sentence turns on “own” three times against “another’s”. The English breaks the middle one into a clause; “their own experience” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “own” now comes three times, as in the Greek, and the English reads “their own feeling”. “Feeling” stands in place of the suggested “experience” because the Greek noun is what is passively felt, and “experience” in English also covers what a person does.

passages.casaubon: The ambitious supposeth another man's act, praise and applause, to be his own happiness; the voluptuous his own sense and feeling; but he that is wise, his own action.

passages.greek: Ἀράχνιον μυῖαν θηρᾶσαν μέγα φρονεῖ, ἄλλος δὲ λαγίδιον, ἄλλος δὲ ὑποχῇ ἀφύην, ἄλλος δὲ συίδια, ἄλλος δὲ ἄρκτους, ἄλλος Σαρμάτας. οὗτοι γὰρ οὐ λῃσταί, ἐὰν τὰ δόγματα ἐξετάζῃς;
passages.english: A little spider thinks a great deal of itself for having hunted down a fly; someone else for a little hare, another for a sprat in a hand net, another for little boars, another for bears, another for Sarmatians. For are these not robbers, if you examine their principles?

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for spider; the same form can also mean a spider’s web.
notes.other_reading: A spider

notes.note: Literally “thinks big”: is proud.
notes.other_reading: is proud

notes.note: “Another” is masculine, so a person and not another spider, which is why the English reads “someone else” the first time. The participle “having hunted” is carried over from the first clause. The hare is a diminutive.
notes.other_reading: another man when he has caught a leveret

notes.note: The first word is a kind of fishing net held under the catch; the second is small fry, a named tiny fish such as a sprat or an anchovy.
notes.other_reading: an anchovy in a scoop net

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for pig or boar. Among things hunted it is presumably wild boar.
notes.other_reading: piglets

notes.note: A people beyond the Danube against whom Marcus himself fought as emperor, so the last hunter is himself.
There is no verb, and the particle “for” opens the question. The noun covers robbers, bandits and pirates.
notes.other_reading: Why, are these not bandits

notes.note: “The principles”, the Stoic word for the settled beliefs a person acts on. The Greek has “the”; the English reads “their”.
notes.other_reading: if you examine the beliefs behind it

check.note: The Greek names a particular tiny fish, small fry such as a sprat or anchovy, as every other item in the list is a named creature. “A small fish” is less.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a sprat in a hand net”. The Greek names a particular tiny fish, as every other item in the list is a named creature.

passages.casaubon: As the spider, when it hath caught the fly that it hunted after, is not little proud, nor meanly conceited of herself: as he likewise that hath caught an hare, or hath taken a fish with his net: as another for the taking of a boar, and another of a bear: so may they be proud, and applaud themselves for their valiant acts against the Sarmatai, or northern nations lately defeated. For these also, these famous soldiers and warlike men, if thou dost look into their minds and opinions, what do they for the most part but hunt after prey?

passages.greek: Τῷ ἀναρριφέντι λίθῳ οὐδὲν κακὸν τὸ κατενεχθῆναι οὐδὲ ἀγαθὸν τὸ ἀνενεχθῆναι.
passages.english: For a stone that has been thrown upward, it is nothing bad to be carried down, and nothing good to be carried up.

notes.note: The two infinitives are passive forms of one verb (φέρω, “carry”) with opposite prefixes, down and up. The passive is also the ordinary Greek for a thing moving down or up, with no carrier in view. “Be carried” is kept for both so that the pairing shows and the stone, which was thrown, stays passive in both directions.
notes.other_reading: to come down … to go up; or: to fall … to rise

notes.note: Literally “nothing bad”, with “nor good” following and no second “nothing”; “nothing” is repeated in the second half for the English. κακόν and ἀγαθόν are the ordinary words for bad and good, and can also be heard as nouns, “an evil” and “a good”.
notes.other_reading: it is no evil to be carried down, nor a good to be carried up

notes.note: A dative of the one concerned, with the article used generically, and a participle of completed action: the stone has already been thrown when its coming down is judged. The English reads “a stone” and “upward”, since “thrown up” has another sense in English.
notes.other_reading: For the stone that has been thrown up

notes.note: The Greek names the coming down first and the going up second, though the stone goes up first; the Greek order is kept. The aorist infinitive marks the event, not a past time, so the English does not read “to have been carried up”.
notes.other_reading: nor good to have been carried up

check.note: The passive of this verb, said of a thing in the air, simply means to come down or fall, and “carried down” makes a reader look for someone carrying. The second reader calls this a matter of taste, not of sense, and suggests “to come down … to go up” or “to fall … to rise”.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “to be carried down” and “to be carried up”. Both are passive forms of one Greek verb, “carry”, that differ only in the prefix, and the stone has been thrown, so it is moved in both directions and does not move itself. The note gives “to come down … to go up” and “to fall … to rise”.

check.note: The participle is aorist, a stone that has been thrown up, so the rise is already behind it when the fall is called no harm. “That has been thrown up” would keep the sequence better than “thrown upward”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “For a stone that has been thrown upward”, so that the throw is already over when the coming down is judged. “Upward” stays in place of “up”, because “thrown up” has another sense in English.

passages.casaubon: To the stone that is cast up, when it comes down it is no hurt unto it; as neither benefit, when it doth ascend.

passages.greek: Ὀρθός, μὴ ὀρθούμενος.
passages.english: Upright, not held upright.

notes.note: The Greek has no verb: a bare masculine nominative, “upright” (also “straight”, “right”), and the English is left without a verb too. It is probably meant as a rule, with “be” or “one must be” understood. The negative μή would show that in older Greek, but in the Greek of Marcus’s time it is also the usual negative with a participle, so it does not settle the question alone.
notes.other_reading: Be upright, not held upright.

notes.note: A present participle of ὀρθόω, “set upright, straighten, put right”, from the same root as ὀρθός, taken as passive: kept upright by someone or something else. The present tense marks a state that goes on, so the English reads “held upright”, and “upright” is repeated so that the play on the one root shows.
notes.other_reading: Upright, not set upright. Or: Straight, not straightened.

notes.note: From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts are said to read ἢ (“or”) here, and μή (“not”) is an editor’s correction supported by the similar sentence in 3.5. The English follows the text as given, so the “not” is uncertain.
notes.other_reading: Upright, or held upright.

check.note: The negative is μή, not οὐ, so the two words are a precept with “be” or “one must be” understood, not a description. The English, with no verb, can be read as a description of someone.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English stays without a verb, as the Greek has none, and the note now says that the two words are probably a rule and gives “Be upright” as the other reading. In the Greek of Marcus’s time μή is also the usual negative with a participle, so the negative alone does not prove a command.

check.note: The participle is present passive or middle: being kept or held upright as a continuing state, while “set upright” reads as a single finished act. The verb also means to set straight, so “straight, not straightened” is the other reading.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Upright, not held upright”, since the present participle describes a state that goes on and not one finished act. “Straight, not straightened” is recorded in the note.

check.note: From the second reader’s memory, the manuscripts read ἢ here (“upright, or set upright”) and μή is a correction made on the strength of the parallel in 3.5. The English rightly follows the Greek as given, but the word should be marked as doubtful.
check.decided: Accepted: “not” is kept, following the Greek as given, and the note marks the word as uncertain, from memory and unchecked.

passages.casaubon: Straight of itself, not made straight.

passages.greek: Τὸ τῷ σμήνει μὴ συμφέρον οὐδὲ τῇ μελίσσῃ συμφέρει.
passages.english: What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee either.

notes.note: σμῆνος means both the beehive and the swarm of bees that lives in it. The contrast is between the community of bees and the single bee. The English reads “hive”, which also names the colony and not only its box, while “swarm” in English suggests bees on the move.
notes.other_reading: What is not good for the swarm

notes.greek: μὴ συμφέρον οὐδὲ τῇ μελίσσῃ συμφέρει
notes.note: The same verb, συμφέρω, “be to the advantage of, benefit”, stands on both sides, first as a participle and then as a finite verb, and “is good for” renders it both times, as elsewhere in this translation. It is not ἀγαθόν, the word for “good” in 9.17.
notes.other_reading: What does not benefit the hive does not benefit the bee either.

notes.note: οὐδέ can be “not … either” or the stronger “not even”. The weaker sense is taken, since the sentence moves from the group to its member.
notes.other_reading: is not good even for the bee

check.note: The Greek word is “what benefits, what is to the advantage of”, not ἀγαθόν. Since 9.17 in the same section uses “good” for ἀγαθόν, one English word covers two Greek words that Marcus keeps apart; “benefit” would separate them.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “is good for”, the rendering of συμφέρει settled for this whole translation, and 9.17 is a separate chapter from another book with no argument running between the two. The note now says that the Greek word here is “be to the advantage of” and not the “good” of 9.17, and gives “benefit” as the other reading.

check.note: The word means both the hive and the swarm, the colony of bees itself. “Hive” is defensible and reads naturally, but the point is about the community, which “swarm” says more directly.
check.decided: Declined: “hive” stays. The Greek word names the hive and the bees in it at once, and English “hive” does the same, while “swarm” in English suggests bees in flight away from their home; the note gives “swarm”.

passages.casaubon: That which is not good for the bee-hive, cannot be good for the bee.

passages.greek: Ἄριστος τρόπος τοῦ ἀμύνεσθαι τὸ μὴ ἐξομοιοῦσθαι.
passages.english: The best way to fight back is to not become like them.

notes.note: The middle of ἀμύνω covers both “defend oneself, ward off” and “pay back, take revenge on”. “Fight back” is chosen because it can be heard either way. The Greek is impersonal and names no “you”.
notes.other_reading: The best way to defend oneself. Or: The best way to retaliate.

notes.note: The verb means “to be made like” or “to make oneself like” and has no object here: the Greek does not say like whom. “Them” is supplied as the smallest word English allows, and stands for whoever is being fought, one person or many. The negative belongs to the infinitive, “the not becoming like”, which “is to not become” makes plain.
notes.other_reading: is to not become like the one who did the wrong. Or, as a passive: is to not be made like them.

notes.note: τρόπος is “way, manner”, and also “character”. The plain sense “way” is what the genitive that follows needs.
notes.other_reading: The best manner of fighting back

check.note: The middle verb means both to defend oneself, to ward off, and to pay someone back. “Retaliate” picks the second and narrows it to hitting back; a word that holds both would be safer.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “The best way to fight back”, which can be heard both as warding off and as paying back, as the Greek verb can. “Defend yourself” was not used because it keeps only one of the two senses and adds a “you” that the Greek does not have.

check.note: The Greek has no object: “not to become like”. English needs one, but “them” is supplied and the plural is a choice, since nothing says whether one wrongdoer or many is meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “them” stays as the smallest object English can supply, and in today’s English it stands for one person or many, so it does not decide the number. The note says the word is supplied and gives a singular reading.

check.note: “Is not to become” can be read for a moment as “is not, to become like them”. Putting the negative with the infinitive removes the stumble.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is to not become like them”, which puts the negative with the infinitive, where the Greek has it, and removes the reading “is not the best way”.

passages.casaubon: The best kind of revenge is, not to become like unto them.

passages.greek: ὅταν γένηται ʽσφαῖρος κυκλοτερὴς μονίῃʼ.
passages.english: once it has become a “rounded sphere, in stillness”.

notes.note: This is a subordinate clause only, and the English begins in lower case to show it. Its main clause stands in the part of 8.41 that is not given, which says that nothing at all touches the mind; “it” is the mind. ὅταν with the aorist subjunctive is “once” or “whenever”.
notes.other_reading: whenever it becomes

notes.note: A quotation of verse, from memory, unchecked, a line of Empedocles that goes on with a word meaning “rejoicing”, which governs the dative μονίῃ. Marcus stops before that word, so the dative is left hanging. The English gives it as “in stillness” and adds nothing from the rest of the line.
notes.other_reading: a “rounded sphere”, in stillness (with the dative outside the quotation); or, with the rest of the line supplied, “a rounded sphere rejoicing in its stillness”

notes.note: A rare poetic noun that can be derived from μένω, “stay”, giving “rest, stillness, steadfastness”, or from μόνος, “alone”, giving “solitude”. The English takes the first. From memory, unchecked, scholars are divided on which the poet meant.
notes.other_reading: in solitude

notes.note: From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts are said to end here with μένει, “it stays”, which gives the clause a verb of its own, and μονίῃ is an editor’s restoration from the same verse quoted at greater length in 12.3. The English follows the text as given.
notes.other_reading: once it has become a rounded sphere, it stays so

notes.note: A masculine form of the usual feminine σφαῖρα, “ball, sphere”, the poet’s name for his perfectly round whole. Marcus applies it to the mind as an image, so the English has no capital. κυκλοτερής, “rounded, circular”, repeats the idea of roundness, and both words are kept.
notes.other_reading: a well-rounded Sphere; or: a round ball

check.note: The noun is disputed: from μένω it is rest, stillness, staying put; from μόνος it is solitude, being alone. The English chooses stillness; the other reading is “in its solitude”, and the other sense should at least be noted.
check.decided: Accepted: “stillness” is kept and the note sets out both derivations and gives “in solitude” as the other reading.

check.note: As given the Greek does not fully construe: the dative has nothing to depend on, because the line of verse is cut off before the word that governs it. The English turns the bare dative into a phrase with “in” and adds “its”, and the reader is not told that the quotation breaks off.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “its” is removed and the English now reads “in stillness”, the barest English for a dative. No mark of a break is put into the English, since the Greek has none, and the note says that the quotation stops before the word that governs the dative.

check.note: From the second reader’s memory, the manuscripts end here with μένει (“once it has become a rounded sphere, it stays so”), which gives the clause its main verb, and μονίῃ is an editor’s restoration from the verse quoted in full at 12.3. The English rightly follows the Greek as given, but the last word should be marked.
check.decided: Accepted: the English follows the Greek as given, and a new note says, from memory and unchecked, that the last word is an editor’s restoration and that the manuscripts are said to read “it stays”.

check.note: The clause is subordinate and hangs on the sentence before it, which is not given, so with a capital and a full stop it reads as a broken sentence. The supplied “it” is correct, and “once” would give ὅταν with the aorist more exactly than “when”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now begins in lower case and reads “once it has become”, so that it shows as the end of a sentence whose beginning is not given. “It” stays: the words just before, which are not part of the passage, show that the subject is the mind.

check.note: The adjective is “round, circular”, an epic word, and the noun is the masculine σφαῖρος, the poet’s name for the cosmic Sphere, not the ordinary σφαῖρα. “Rounded sphere” is acceptable, but a capital would show that it is a proper name in the verse.
check.decided: Declined: “rounded sphere” stays without a capital. The Greek as given has no capital, and Marcus uses the poet’s words as an image for the mind, not as a name; the note on σφαῖρος says that it is the poet’s name for his round whole.

part.left_out: Ἐμποδισμὸς αἰσθήσεως κακὸν ζωτικῆς φύσεως. ἐμποδισμὸς ὁρμῆς ὁμοίως κακὸν ζωτικῆς φύσεως. ἔστι δέ τι ἄλλο ὁμοίως ἐμποδιστικὸν καὶ κακὸν τῆς φυτικῆς κατασκευῆς. οὕτως τοίνυν ἐμποδισμὸς νοῦ κακὸν νοερᾶς φύσεως. πάντα δὴ ταῦτα ἐπὶ σεαυτὸν μετάφερε. πόνος, ἡδονὴ ἅπτεταί σου; ὄψεται ἡ αἴσθησις. ὁρμήσαντι ἔνστημα ἐγένετο; εἰ μὲν ἀνυπεξαιρέτως ὥρμας, ἤδη ὡς λογικοῦ κακόν, εἰ δὲ τὸ κοινὸν λαμβάνεις, οὔπω βέβλαψαι οὐδὲ ἐμπεπόδισαι. τὰ μέντοι τοῦ νοῦ ἴδια οὐδεὶς ἄλλος εἴωθεν ἐμποδίζειν· τούτου γὰρ οὐ πῦρ, οὐ σίδηρος, οὐ τύραννος, οὐ βλασφημία, οὐχ ὁτιοῦν ἅπτεται,
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 8.39 just before the closing image of the rounded sphere and makes that image its whole section 8.40.

passages.casaubon: If once round and solid, there is no fear that ever it will change.
